⚠️ The two tasks that can lose the entire cluster

Notice the two 🔴 rows — etcd backups and certificate renewal. An un-tested backup and a silently-expired cert are the two classic ways admins lose (or lock themselves out of) a cluster, which is exactly why the CKA weights them heavily and this guide gives each a full chapter. Most other mistakes you can recover from; these two you must plan ahead of.

💡 Where you fit in — the easypj journey

This guide follows easypj — our Django jobpost board — from a single-server app to a production-grade cluster. You'll containerize it, deploy it, scale it, secure it, break it, fix it, and ship it. By the end you'll pass the CKA and be able to run real clusters.

1.7 The Object Model & the Kubernetes API

Everything you will ever create is a Kubernetes object — a persisted record of intent the cluster works to make real. Four ideas make the whole API click: the shape of every object, how you name it, how the API is organised & versioned, and the ways you apply it. Master these and manifests stop being magic.

① The four required fields — in every manifest, no exceptions

Every object you write carries the same four top-level fields. Omit one — or mis-case kind — and the apiserver rejects the manifest before it ever reaches etcd.

FieldWhat it iseasypj example
apiVersionWhich API group + version defines this object (so the server knows its schema)apps/v1
kindThe object type — what you're creatingDeployment
metadataIdentity: name (required), namespace, labels, annotations, and the server-set uidname: easypj-web
specYour desired state — the shape varies per kindreplicas: 3

② spec vs status — desired vs actual, inside the object itself

Almost every object has two halves: a spec you write (the goal) and a status the cluster writes (reality). The reconciliation loop from §1.4 is just "keep status matching spec." You never edit status — reading it is how you troubleshoot.

kubectl get deploy easypj-web -o yaml (trimmed)
spec:                 # 👈 YOU declare this — desired state
  replicas: 3
status:               # 👈 KUBERNETES writes this — actual state (read-only)
  replicas: 3
  readyReplicas: 2    # only 2 are Ready right now → a controller is closing the gap
  conditions:
  - type: Available
    status: "False"

③ Naming rules — why easypj_web is rejected

Object names aren't free-form. Most objects — Pods, Deployments, ConfigMaps, and even Nodes — follow the DNS Subdomain rule; only a few — namespaces (and Services, under the related RFC 1035) — must be a stricter DNS Label. Break the rule and you get a validation error, not a running object.

RuleUsed byMaxAllowed✅ valid · ❌ invalid
DNS Subdomainmost objects: Deployments, ConfigMaps, Secrets…253lowercase a–z 0–9 - .; start/end alphanumeric (may start with a digit)✅ easypj-web, app.prod · ❌ easypj_web, EasyPJ
DNS Labelnamespaces (RFC 1123 label)63lowercase a–z 0–9 - (no dots); start with a letter, end alphanumeric✅ easypj-prod · ❌ my.ns, NS-1, 9ns
DNS Label (RFC 1035)Service names63same, but must start with a letter (a feature gate relaxes this)✅ easypj-web · ❌ 9web
UIDevery object (set by the server)—cluster-unique, auto-generated, never user-suppliedtells apart two objects that reused a name over time

④ API groups, versions & stability levels

The API is split into groups, each versioned independently. The apiVersion you write picks the group + version; the stability ladder tells you what's safe to depend on.

how apiVersion resolves to an API path
   apiVersion: v1          → CORE group    → /api/v1           Pod · Service · ConfigMap · Namespace · Node
   apiVersion: apps/v1     → "apps" group  → /apis/apps/v1     Deployment · ReplicaSet · StatefulSet · DaemonSet
   apiVersion: batch/v1    → "batch" group → /apis/batch/v1    Job · CronJob
   apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1                    Role · RoleBinding · ClusterRole
   └─ kubectl api-resources   lists every kind → its group, version & whether it's namespaced
LevelMeansOn by default?In a name
Alphaexperimental — may change or vanish, may have bugsno (needs a feature gate)v1alpha1
Betawell-tested; details may still change before GAvaries (newer betas off)v1beta1
Stable / GAproduction-ready, backward-compatibleyesv1

Deprecation policy: a GA (stable) API version is never removed within a major version — a v1 API lasts for all of Kubernetes 1.x; a deprecated beta version is dropped after 9 months or 3 releases (whichever is longer); alpha can change or vanish in any release. There's no LTS: each minor release is maintained ~14 months (≈12 months support + a ~2-month maintenance window) — read the release notes and upgrade before EOL.

⑤ Three ways to manage objects — and why the exam loves apply

ApproachCommandIdempotent?Use it for
Imperative commandkubectl create deploy easypj-web --image=easypj:v2no — errors if it existsexam speed & quick fixes; keeps no file
Imperative object configkubectl create -f f.yaml / replace -fnorarely — forces delete-then-recreate
Declarativekubectl apply -f f.yamlyes — run 100×, same resultproduction & GitOps; the default to reach for

💡 Server-Side Apply (kubectl apply --server-side) moves the merge into the apiserver and tracks field ownership, so several controllers can co-own one object without clobbering each other. ⚡ Exam speed: kubectl create deploy … --dry-run=client -o yaml > d.yaml scaffolds a manifest you then edit & apply.

⑥ Add-ons — what a fresh cluster still needs

A brand-new cluster can schedule pods but is missing pieces you'll assume are there. These ship as add-ons (themselves pods), not part of the core binaries.

🧭 CoreDNS

In-cluster DNS — every pod resolves name.namespace.svc.cluster.local here. Normally installed; no DNS → no name-based service discovery.

📊 metrics-server

Feeds CPU/memory to the API. Required for kubectl top and the HorizontalPodAutoscaler. Not installed by default.

🌍 Ingress controller

Terminates & routes external HTTP(S) to Services (e.g. ingress-nginx). You must pick & install one — none ships by default.

🖥️ Dashboard

Optional web UI. Handy, never required for admin work — and one more thing to secure if you deploy it.

⑦ Labels, selectors, annotations & ownership — the glue that wires objects together

The four required fields give an object its identity; three more metadata ideas are how objects find and own each other. These aren't cosmetic — they're the wiring behind Services, controllers, and cascading deletes, and confusing them is the single most common cause of "my Service has no endpoints."

ConceptWhat it isKubernetes uses it to…
labelskey/value tags meant for selection (app: easypj, tier: web)let selectors find groups of objects — the basis of all wiring
selectorsa query over labels (app=easypj)connect a Service to its Pods, a Deployment to its Pods, a NetworkPolicy to its targets
annotationskey/value metadata not for selection (URLs, checksums, tool config)carry non-identifying info tools read, e.g. kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration
ownerReferencesa pointer from child → parent (Pod → ReplicaSet → Deployment)drive cascading deletion & adoption of orphans
Labels wire a Service to Pods; ownerReferences chain the delete
   WIRING (by label selector)                      OWNERSHIP (by ownerReferences)
   ┌────────────────────────────┐                   Deployment easypj-web
   │ Service easypj-web           │                        │ owns
   │   selector:  app=easypj      │                        ▼
   └──────────────┬─────────────┘                    ReplicaSet easypj-web-6d8f9
                  │ matches the label                       │ owns
        ┌─────────┼─────────┐                               ▼
        ▼         ▼         ▼                        📦 Pod   📦 Pod   📦 Pod
   📦 app=easypj 📦 app=easypj 📦 app=easypj          delete the Deployment ⇒ the whole
   (Ready pods → EndpointSlice → traffic)            chain is garbage-collected ⬇ (cascade)

   ⚠️ if the pod labels ≠ the Service selector → 0 endpoints → the Service "works" but nothing answers
💡 Finalizers — why a namespace sometimes hangs in "Terminating"

A finalizer is a key in metadata.finalizers that tells the API server "run cleanup before you actually delete me." A delete sets deletionTimestamp and then waits until the responsible controller removes its finalizer. It's the mechanism behind orderly teardown — and the reason a stuck controller can leave a namespace in Terminating indefinitely (you'll diagnose exactly that in Ch 32).

📖 The takeaway that saves you hours later

Labels are load-bearing. Services, Deployments, NetworkPolicies, and DaemonSets all target pods by label selector, so a one-character label typo silently breaks the wiring with no error — the object looks healthy, it just selects nothing. Whenever something is mysteriously unreachable, an early check is kubectl get pods --show-labels against the selector.

💡 Label & selector rules worth knowing (they bite on the exam)
  • A label value is ≤63 chars; the key may carry an optional DNS-subdomain prefix (≤253 chars) before a /.
  • The kubernetes.io/ and k8s.io/ prefixes are reserved for Kubernetes core components — don't invent your own keys under them.
  • Selectors support equality (=, !=) and set-based (in, notin, exists) conditions; multiple conditions are AND-ed by commas. There is no OR operator.

Where objects live — the four built-in namespaces

Every namespaced object lives in exactly one namespace (a virtual cluster for isolation & quotas). A fresh cluster ships with four you must recognize:

NamespaceWhat's in it
defaultwhere your objects land if you don't specify one (easypj should get its own namespace instead)
kube-systemthe control plane & add-ons — CoreDNS, kube-proxy, the static-pod mirrors, Leases
kube-publicworld-readable (even to unauthenticated clients) cluster info; rarely used directly
kube-node-leaseone Lease per node for the fast node heartbeats (see Under the Hood ⑥)

📖 Namespaces can't be nested, and a resource lives in only one. The control plane stamps every namespace with an immutable kubernetes.io/metadata.name label (equal to its own name), so you can select namespaces by name. Set your working namespace once with kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=easypj — full depth in Chapter 4.

Under the Hood — the reconciliation loop that powers everything

Self-healing isn't magic — it's a closed control loop running forever inside the controller-manager. Each controller does three things, over and over:

   ┌──────────── CONTROL LOOP (runs continuously) ────────────┐
   │                                                          │
   │   👁️ OBSERVE  ──▶  🧮 DIFF  ──▶  🛠️ ACT  ──┐             │
   │   read actual     desired vs     make a change           │
   │   state from      actual          (create/delete/        │
   │   the API          (a gap?)        update an object)     │
   │        ▲                                    │            │
   │        └────────────────────────────────────┘            │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   easypj example: desired replicas=3, actual=2  →  create 1 pod  →  repeat
🗺️ The Full Trace — Deploying easypj with 3 Replicas, Step by Step

Here is the loop playing out for real. Notice that no single component drives the whole thing — each controller independently reconciles its own slice, and the result emerges:

 1. USER declares desired state (deploy.yaml):
    ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ apiVersion: apps/v1                        │
    │ kind: Deployment                           │
    │ spec:                                      │
    │   replicas: 3                              │
    │   template:                                │
    │     spec:                                  │
    │       containers:                          │
    │       - name: web                          │
    │         image: easypj:v2                   │
    └───────────────────────────────────────────┘

 2. kubectl apply → API server → persisted in etcd
    /registry/deployments/easypj/easypj-web = {replicas:3, image:v2}

 3. Deployment controller OBSERVES: desired replicas=3, image=v2
                            ACTUAL: no ReplicaSet, no Pods   → DIFF: everything missing
 4. Deployment controller ACTS:  creates ReplicaSet easypj-web-7d8f9

 5. ReplicaSet controller OBSERVES: want 3 pods (app=easypj-web)
                             ACTUAL: 0 pods                  → DIFF: 3 needed
 6. ReplicaSet controller ACTS:  creates 3 Pod objects (nodeName empty → Pending)

 7. Scheduler OBSERVES: 3 Pods with no node
                ACTS:  filters + scores nodes, binds each Pod → a Node

 8. kubelet (on each chosen node) OBSERVES: a Pod is assigned to me
                                     ACTS:  CRI pull image → create → start container
                                            CNI assigns the pod an IP

 9. easypj pods RUNNING :8000  → kubelet reports status up to the API server → etcd

10. Controllers keep watching forever: actual=3 = desired=3 ✅
    ── crash a pod? ReplicaSet makes a new one.  kill a node? Scheduler re-places.
    ── At NO step did anyone say "start these pods on these nodes." It EMERGED.
🔬 Level-Triggered vs Edge-Triggered — Why Controllers Never "Miss" an Event

The deep reason self-healing is reliable: Kubernetes is level-triggered. Controllers don't depend on catching every event — they periodically re-read the whole state. A dropped watch event (network blip) is simply corrected on the next resync.

Edge-triggered (imperative systems)Level-triggered (Kubernetes)
Relies on receiving every eventPeriodically re-reads the full state
Missed event → permanently inconsistentMissed event → caught on next resync
"Start Apache" — if it crashes, nobody restarts it"3 replicas should exist" — a crash is auto-replaced
Needs complex error handlingSelf-healing by design
🔑 CKA Insight. When you kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml you are NOT telling Kubernetes "do these steps" — you're declaring "I want 3 easypj:v2 replicas." The controllers figure out the steps. That's why apply is idempotent: run it 100 times, same result as once. No state machine, no step sequence — just a declared end state and loops that converge on it.

🔬 Deeper (exam + beyond): almost everything in Kubernetes is an API object stored in etcd and reconciled by a controller — Deployments, Services, Nodes, even certificates and namespaces. Master this one pattern and the whole system becomes predictable: to understand any feature, ask "what object, and which controller reconciles it?" This is what makes Kubernetes a universal control plane, not just a container runner.

① How a controller really OBSERVES — list-watch, informers & the work queue

The loop above says "observe actual state," but how? Naively you'd poll — "is it 3 yet? is it 3 yet?" — which would hammer the API server with thousands of controllers asking constantly. Real Kubernetes never polls. It uses the list-watch pattern behind an informer: LIST the full state once, then WATCH a live stream of changes, keeping a local cache in sync.

   🗄️ etcd ──change──▶ 📡 apiserver (watch cache)
                            │  streams events:  ADDED · MODIFIED · DELETED
                            ▼
                 ┌────────────────────────────┐
                 │ 🧠 INFORMER (in the controller)│
                 │  • LIST once → fill a local  │   the cache = a live, in-memory
                 │    cache (the "store")       │   mirror of cluster state, so the
                 │  • WATCH → apply deltas      │   controller reads it WITHOUT
                 │  • fire event handlers       │   touching etcd every time
                 └───────────────┬────────────┘
                                 │ enqueue the changed object's KEY  (namespace/name)
                                 ▼
                 ┌────────────────────────────┐
                 │ 📥 WORK QUEUE                │   dedups duplicates · rate-limits ·
                 │                              │   retries failures with backoff
                 └───────────────┬────────────┘
                                 │ a worker pops one key
                                 ▼
   🔄 Reconcile(key):  read DESIRED + ACTUAL from the cache  →  diff  →  act
                       (this is the OBSERVE → DIFF → ACT loop, in code)
Aspect❌ Naive polling✅ list-watch + informer (real K8s)
API-server loadconstant, heavy (every controller, every second)one LIST + a single long-lived WATCH stream
Latency to reactup to the poll intervalnear-instant — changes are pushed
Reads of "actual state"hit the API/etcd each timeserved from the informer's in-memory cache
Missed eventssilently losta periodic resync re-LISTs and re-reconciles everything (this is level-triggering in practice)
FailuresDIY retry logicwork queue dedups, rate-limits & retries with backoff
🔑 So "observe actual state" is cheap because the controller reads its own informer cache, not etcd — and the cache is kept fresh by one shared WATCH. The periodic resync is the safety net that makes missed events impossible to matter.
② Inside the API server — what kubectl apply passes through before it's saved

"The API server validates and persists" hides a precise 6-stage pipeline. Knowing it tells you exactly which stage rejected a request from the error message alone:

   kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml ─▶ 📡 kube-apiserver
        │
        ├─ 1. 🔐 Authentication      WHO are you?        cert / token / OIDC
        ├─ 2. 🛂 Authorization       MAY you do this?    RBAC (verb + resource)
        ├─ 3. 🧬 Mutating admission   change the object   webhooks: inject sidecars, set defaults
        ├─ 4. 📋 Schema validation    is it well-formed?  OpenAPI schema check
        ├─ 5. ✅ Validating admission policy gate         PodSecurity, ValidatingWebhooks, quota
        └─ 6. 💾 persist to etcd      write + bump resourceVersion  ──▶ controllers WATCH it
StageQuestion it answersTypical rejection you'd see
AuthenticationWho is calling?Unauthorized (401) — bad/expired cert or token
Authorization (RBAC)Are they allowed?Forbidden (403) — "User cannot create deployments…"
Mutating admission—(usually silent — it edits the object, e.g. adds a sidecar)
Schema validationIs the YAML valid?error validating data: unknown field…
Validating admissionDoes it meet policy?admission webhook denied the request / PodSecurity violation
Persist to etcd—Conflict (409) if resourceVersion is stale (see ③)
🔑 Read the error, name the stage. "Forbidden" = stage 2 (fix RBAC). "unknown field" = stage 4 (fix the YAML). "admission webhook denied" = stage 5 (a policy). This single mapping shortcuts a huge share of troubleshooting.
③ etcd under the hood — Raft consensus, MVCC & optimistic concurrency

Stage 6 above ("persist to etcd") is where state actually lives. etcd is a distributed key-value store that stays consistent across replicas via the Raft algorithm and versions every change via MVCC. Every Kubernetes object is just a key:

   Every object is ONE key in etcd (the "/registry" tree):
     /registry/deployments/easypj/easypj-web        = { …spec…, resourceVersion: 4821 }
     /registry/replicasets/easypj/easypj-web-6d8f9  = { …spec…, …status… }
     /registry/pods/easypj/easypj-web-6d8f9-x7k2    = { …spec…, …status… }
     /registry/services/easypj/easypj-web           = { … }

   Writes go through RAFT — a MAJORITY (quorum) must agree before a commit:
     ┌─────────┐   append entry   ┌─────────┐   replicate   ┌─────────┐
     │ etcd-1  │ ───────────────▶ │ etcd-2  │ ────────────▶ │ etcd-3  │
     │(leader) │ ◀─────ack─────── │(follower)│ ◀────ack───── │(follower)│
     └─────────┘                  └─────────┘               └─────────┘
        committed only once a MAJORITY acks  →  3 members tolerate 1 down (quorum = 2)
        ⚠️ lose quorum (2 of 3 down) → etcd goes READ-ONLY → the cluster "freezes"
ConceptWhat it isWhy it matters
MVCC + revisionevery write bumps a global revision; old versions are kept until compactionlets a WATCH replay changes from a point in time → reliable informers
resourceVersionthe per-object version stamped on every read/writethe basis of optimistic concurrency (below)
Optimistic concurrencyan update carries the rv you read; if it changed meanwhile → 409 Conflicttwo controllers can't clobber each other — no locks needed
Raft quoruma majority of members must agree to commituse ODD counts; losing quorum makes the API read-only
Compaction / defragprune old revisions & reclaim diskkeeps etcd healthy — a real Day-2 admin task (Ch 29)

Optimistic concurrency is the quiet hero that lets the level-triggered loop stay correct even when many controllers touch the same object at once — no locks, just retry-on-conflict:

   controller A reads easypj-web   (resourceVersion 4821)
   controller B reads easypj-web   (resourceVersion 4821)
   A writes its change            → accepted → object is now rv 4822
   B writes with rv 4821          → ❌ 409 CONFLICT  (someone moved first)
   B re-reads (gets rv 4822), recomputes the diff, writes again → ✅ accepted
                   └──────────────── this is just the loop running again ────────────────┘
🔑 It's all one machine. The reconcile loop (OBSERVE→DIFF→ACT), the informer/watch that feeds OBSERVE, the API-server pipeline that guards every write, and etcd's revisions + optimistic concurrency are not separate features — they're one coherent design. That's why the right question for any Kubernetes behaviour is always: "which object, which controller, what's the gap?"
🔬 Deeper still — why the loop scales & survives failures

Four production mechanisms keep that loop fast, cheap and reliable across thousands of objects and flaky networks:

MechanismWhat it doesWhy it matters
Shared informerone LIST+WATCH per resource type, cached in memory and shared by every controller that needs itAPI-server load is O(resource types), not O(controllers) — a 50th controller adds no new watch on etcd
Work queue + rate limitera failed reconcile is re-queued with exponential back-off (~5ms, doubling, capped ~1000s), deduped, and reset on successa broken resource is retried calmly, not hammered thousands of times a second
WATCH bookmarksthe apiserver streams periodic BOOKMARK events ("still here, at resourceVersion X") even when nothing changeda client can tell "quiet" from "stalled" and resume from the last rv without a full re-LIST
410 Gonewatching from a resourceVersion older than the apiserver's history window returns HTTP 410 Goneforces a fresh LIST + resync so caches can't silently drift — and is why aggressive etcd compaction (Ch 29) shrinks that window
🔑 The pattern, named: read → compute → write with the resourceVersion you read → on 409 Conflict, re-read & retry. That's lock-free optimistic concurrency: two controllers touching one object never deadlock — the loser just retries and still makes progress.
④ The bootstrap paradox — how the control plane starts itself

Here's a puzzle the diagrams above quietly skip: controllers and the scheduler all run through the API server, and the API server is itself just a program something has to start. On a kubeadm cluster there's no "outer" Kubernetes to launch it — so how does the control plane come up at all? The answer is static pods, and it's a favourite exam trap.

   The kubelet can run pods in TWO ways:
     (a) normal pods  → assigned by the scheduler THROUGH the API server   ← needs the CP up
     (b) STATIC pods  → read straight off local disk, NO API server needed ← breaks the cycle

   On a control-plane node the kubelet watches this folder every few seconds:
     📁 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
         ├── etcd.yaml                      ┐
         ├── kube-apiserver.yaml            │  the kubelet reads these files and runs them
         ├── kube-controller-manager.yaml   │  as pods DIRECTLY — that's how the control
         └── kube-scheduler.yaml            ┘  plane boots when no control plane exists yet

   Boot order:  kubelet starts → sees the manifests → runs etcd + apiserver as static pods
                → the apiserver comes up → NOW scheduler & controllers (also static) can use it
                → the cluster is alive and schedules everything else the normal way.
🔑 Two admin superpowers fall out of this. (1) To change a control-plane component you just edit its file in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — the kubelet notices and recreates the pod automatically, no kubectl apply. (2) When the API server is down and kubectl is dead, you debug these pods on the node with crictl ps, because they don't need the API server to exist. The apiserver also surfaces them as read-only mirror pods so you can see them via kubectl get pods -n kube-system — but you can't manage them that way. This is the backbone of Chapters 12 and 32.
⑤ Leader election — how an HA control plane avoids two brains

A production cluster runs several control-plane nodes for availability, so multiple kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler processes are alive at once. If they all acted, two schedulers could place the same pod twice and two controllers could fight. Kubernetes prevents this with leader election: exactly one instance is active; the rest stand by.

   3 controller-managers alive, but only ONE reconciles at a time:
     ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
     │ ctrl-mgr A   │   │ ctrl-mgr B   │   │ ctrl-mgr C   │
     │ 👑 LEADER    │   │   standby    │   │   standby    │
     └──────┬───────┘   └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘
            │ renews a Lease object every few seconds:
            ▼
     🗄️ Lease  kube-system/kube-controller-manager
        holderIdentity: A   ·   renewTime: 10:00:15   ·   leaseDurationSeconds: 15
            │
            └─ A stops renewing (crash) → the Lease expires → B or C grabs it → new leader
               (failover in ~15s; there is never more than one active leader)
🔑 It's the same primitive, reused. Leader election is just optimistic writes to a Lease object (coordination.k8s.io/v1) — the leader is whoever atomically updates it first; watch it live with kubectl -n kube-system get lease. Contrast the API server: it's active-active (every instance serves traffic behind a load balancer, because it's stateless and etcd is the shared truth). Only the singleton deciders — scheduler and controller-manager — need one leader. HA is drilled in Chapter 35.
⑥ How the control plane knows a node died — heartbeats, conditions & eviction timing

"The node goes NotReady and its pods are rescheduled" hides precise, exam-tested machinery. Every kubelet sends two heartbeats, and specific timers decide when a silent node's pods actually move:

  TWO heartbeats per node:
    ① a lightweight Lease  →  a Lease object in the  kube-node-lease  namespace whose
                              .spec.renewTime the kubelet updates ~every 10s  (cheap, frequent)
    ② the Node .status     →  full status (conditions, capacity) — pushed on change / ~every 5m

  WHEN HEARTBEATS STOP:
    the node-controller checks nodes every ~5s → Ready flips to  Unknown  after
        NodeMonitorGracePeriod (default ~50s)
        │  the control plane then TAINTS the node:
        │     node.kubernetes.io/unreachable  (Ready=Unknown)  or  .../not-ready  (Ready=False)
        ▼
    most pods tolerate that taint for  tolerationSeconds: 300  (5 min)  →  then they're
    evicted and rescheduled onto healthy nodes
Node conditionMeans
Readyhealthy & accepting pods (Unknown = the control plane lost contact)
MemoryPressure · DiskPressure · PIDPressurethe node is low on memory / disk / process-IDs → it begins evicting pods
NetworkUnavailablethe node's network is not correctly configured
🔑 Why the numbers matter. This is why a crashed node's pods take ~40–60s to be flagged and ~5 more minutes to move — never instant. A planned kubectl drain (Ch 30) skips all of it by evicting gracefully up front. The kube-node-lease heartbeat, the node conditions, and these defaults are drilled in Chapters 3 & 32.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Orchestration automates operations — placement, scaling, healing, networking, and rollout, done by software instead of a human at 3 AM.
  • Declarative, not imperative — you declare desired state; control loops drive actual state toward it, forever.
  • The administrator owns everything below the app — install, certs/PKI, etcd, upgrades, nodes, networking, storage, and troubleshooting.
  • The API server is the only path to etcd — every component and every kubectl goes through it, via authN → authZ → admission → validate → persist.
  • The 5 core concepts frame the whole guide — cluster, control plane, worker nodes, pod, and desired-vs-actual state; every later topic is a deeper look at one of these.
  • Every object carries the 4 required fields — apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec; spec is your intent, status is the cluster's observed reality (read-only).
  • Level-triggered reconciliation — controllers react to the current state, not to events, which is why K8s self-heals reliably even after a controller itself restarts.
  • Troubleshooting is 30% of the exam — the biggest single domain; method beats memorization.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "Kubernetes replaces Docker." No — Kubernetes orchestrates containers; a runtime (containerd/CRI-O) still runs them. Only the Docker shim was removed (v1.24), not container images.
  • Thinking imperatively ("start a container on node 2"). Wrong mental model — you declare what (3 replicas) and let K8s decide where/how.
  • Confusing CKA with CKAD. CKAD builds apps; CKA builds and operates the cluster. etcd, kubeadm, certs, and node management are CKA-only.
  • "Control plane" = "master node." Modern Kubernetes dropped the word master — the exam says control plane node. Know its four components: API server, scheduler, controller-manager, etcd.
  • "A Pod is a container." A Pod can hold several containers sharing one network namespace & storage (sidecar / init-container patterns). The Pod, not the container, is the unit K8s schedules.
  • Desired ≠ current state. The exam constantly probes whether you grasp the reconciliation loop — controllers continuously compare the two and self-heal the gap.
  • Editing status in a manifest does nothing. status is read-only, written by the cluster. Only spec is yours — you change reality by changing desired state, then reading status to see what happened.
  • Names must be valid, not pretty. Most objects follow the DNS-Subdomain rule (lowercase a–z 0–9 - .); only a few — namespaces and Services (RFC 1035) — use the stricter DNS-Label rule (no dots, must start with a letter). So easypj_web (underscore) and EasyPJ (uppercase) are rejected everywhere, while 9web is fine as a Deployment but rejected as a namespace/Service name.
⚡ Speed Tips
  • Think in desired state. When something's wrong, ask "what's declared vs what's actually running?" — that's the whole troubleshooting model.
  • kubectl explain is your in-exam manual. kubectl explain pod.spec --recursive beats hunting the docs.
  • Read events first. kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp and describe usually name the cause before you guess.
  • Architecture quick-recall mnemonic: kube-apiserver → front door · etcd → brain · kube-scheduler → which-node · kube-controller-manager → reconciliation. All four run as static pods in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — edit a file there and the kubelet recreates the pod.
  • Prefer kubectl apply -f over create/replace. It's idempotent and re-runnable — the safe default under exam time pressure, and it won't error if the object already exists.

🔑 Commands to Know (Chapter 1)

orient yourself in any cluster 
# Cluster endpoints (API server + CoreDNS URLs)
kubectl cluster-info

# Nodes, roles, versions, internal IPs
kubectl get nodes -o wide

# Control-plane health (older clusters)
kubectl get componentstatuses        # a.k.a. cs

# Every API resource type + its short name + apiVersion
kubectl api-resources

# Client + server (cluster) versions
kubectl version

# All served API group/versions (pairs with api-resources)
kubectl api-versions

# Field-level docs for any kind — your in-exam field manual
kubectl explain deployment.spec        # add --recursive for the full tree

# Declarative, idempotent create/update — the default to reach for
kubectl apply -f easypj.yaml
inspect & explore any object (the day-to-day toolkit) 
# Full object as stored in etcd — spec AND status
kubectl get deploy easypj -o yaml

# Human-readable state + recent Events — your #1 troubleshooting command
kubectl describe pod <name>

# Field-level schema for ANY kind — walk the whole tree
kubectl explain pod.spec.containers --recursive

# Wide output: adds node, pod IP, and more columns
kubectl get pods -o wide

# Cluster-wide events, newest last — what just happened & why
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

# Which kinds are namespaced vs cluster-scoped (matters for RBAC & -n)
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true
kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false

# See the control plane's leaders + node heartbeats (Leases)
kubectl get lease -n kube-system

🧠 Chapter 1 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (15)

Quick recall of the mental model — 15 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Define "container orchestration" in one sentence.
Show Answer
Answer

The automated deployment, scaling, healing, and networking of containerized applications across many machines — performed by software, not humans.

The job❌ By hand✅ Orchestrated
Placementyou pick a server & SSH inthe scheduler decides
Recoveryyou get paged, restart ita controller recreates it
Scalingbuy & configure serverskubectl scale / HPA
Networkinghand-edit nginx upstreamsServices + CoreDNS
Explanation

Containers solved "works on my machine"; orchestration solves "works across a fleet, reliably, unattended." Kubernetes is the industry-standard orchestrator, and the CKA is about running the orchestrator itself.

Q2
easypj's pod crashes at 3 AM. What does Kubernetes do, and why does it work even if a controller missed the crash event?
Show Answer
Answer

A controller observes that actual ≠ desired (2 pods running, 3 wanted) and recreates the missing pod automatically — no human needed.

Level-triggered self-heal — no "event" required
  desired: 3        actual: 2 💥         controller's next pass          actual: 3 ✅
  (in etcd)    →    (a pod died)    →    sees the gap, creates 1    →    healed
Explanation

It's level-triggered: the loop reacts to the current state, not to the crash event. Even if the event was missed or the controller restarted, the next iteration still sees the gap and fixes it — which is why self-healing is reliable.

Q3
Give the one-line definition of Kubernetes.
Show Answer
Answer

"An open-source system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications."

The one idea inside the definition
  📝 you DECLARE intent    ──▶    🔄 control loops    ──▶    ⚙️ K8s makes it real & KEEPS it true
     "3 copies of easypj"          reconcile forever         restart · reschedule · scale
Explanation

The operative word is automating — you declare intent, K8s carries it out and keeps it true. Born from Google's Borg, open-sourced 2014, CNCF-governed, written in Go.

Q4
Explain desired-vs-actual state using a replicas: 3 example.
Show Answer
Answer

Desired = what you declared (replicas: 3, stored in etcd). Actual = what's really running on the nodes. A controller continuously diffs them: if actual is 2, it creates one pod; if actual is 4, it deletes one.

Diff (desired = 3)Controller acts
actual < 3CREATE the missing pod(s)
actual > 3DELETE the extra pod(s)
actual = 3do nothing (idempotent — no churn)
Explanation

This gap-closing loop is the core mental model for the whole exam. Troubleshooting = "find where actual diverged from desired, and why the controller can't close the gap."

Q5
List three tasks that belong to the CKA but NOT the CKAD.
Show Answer
Answer

Any three of: install a cluster with kubeadm; etcd backup & restore; approve/rotate certificates (PKI); cluster upgrades; node management (drain/cordon); configure CNI/CoreDNS.

🔧 CKA owns (below the app)👩‍💻 CKAD owns (the app)
kubeadm install · etcd backup/restorePods · Deployments
certificates / PKI · cluster upgradesServices · ConfigMaps
node drain / cordon · CNI / CoreDNSprobes · resource limits
Explanation

All are below the app. CKAD stays at the workload layer (Pods/Deployments/Services/ConfigMaps); CKA owns the infrastructure those run on.

Q6
Name the four control-plane components and the one that stores all cluster state.
Show Answer
Answer

kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager (plus optional cloud-controller-manager). State lives in etcd.

ComponentRole
kube-apiserverthe only front door — the only component that talks to etcd
etcd🗄️ stores all cluster state (the source of truth)
kube-schedulerassigns unscheduled pods to nodes
kube-controller-managerruns the reconcile loops (self-healing)
Explanation

Only the API server talks to etcd — everything else goes through the API server. That's why an etcd backup is a cluster backup, and why losing etcd without a backup loses the cluster.

Q7
What is a Pod, and what do containers inside one share?
Show Answer
Answer

A Pod is the smallest deployable unit — one or more containers scheduled together. Containers in a pod share the network namespace (one IP, reach each other on localhost) and can share storage volumes.

One pod = one shared sandbox
  📦 POD  (one IP: 10.244.1.5)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  🐍 web :8000         📊 sidecar               │
  │       └──── localhost ────┘   (shared net ns)  │
  │  💾 shared volume ── mounted into both ──       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  co-scheduled on ONE node · they live & die together
Explanation

This is why a sidecar (e.g. a log shipper) can read the app's files and talk to it on localhost. easypj-web runs one container; a sidecar pattern would add a second to the same pod.

Q8
Why is kubectl apply idempotent — running it twice causes no harm?
Show Answer
Answer

Because it's declarative: it sets the desired state, it doesn't issue step-by-step commands. If the cluster already matches, the reconciliation loop finds no gap and does nothing.

idempotent vs not
kubectl apply -f easypj.yaml    # created
kubectl apply -f easypj.yaml    # unchanged ✅  (no gap → no action)
kubectl create -f easypj.yaml   # Error: already exists ❌  (imperative)
Explanation

Contrast with imperative kubectl create, which errors if the object already exists. Declarative + reconciliation is what makes GitOps ("re-apply the repo continuously") safe.

Q9
Match each tool to its job: Calico · Helm · ArgoCD · Prometheus · containerd.
Show Answer
Answer
ToolJob
CalicoCNI — pod networking + NetworkPolicy
HelmPackaging — templated charts
ArgoCDGitOps — sync cluster to Git
PrometheusObservability — metrics
containerdContainer runtime (CRI)
Explanation

Each plugs into a Kubernetes extension point: CNI (networking), runtime (CRI), plus higher-level tooling for packaging, delivery, and monitoring. Knowing the category matters more than the brand.

Q10
Sort "admin-owns vs dev-owns": etcd backup · a Deployment · RBAC · a ConfigMap · a node upgrade.
Show Answer
Answer
🔧 CKA admin owns👩‍💻 CKAD dev owns
etcd backupa Deployment
RBACa ConfigMap
a node upgrade 
Explanation

RBAC is borderline — devs may request roles, but defining and granting cluster access is an admin responsibility. The rule of thumb: if it's below the app, it's CKA.

Q11
Name the four required top-level fields of every manifest, and explain the difference between spec and status.
Show Answer
Answer

apiVersion, kind, metadata, and spec. spec is your desired state (what you declare); status is the cluster's observed reality, written by controllers and read-only to you.

the 4 required fields + spec vs status
apiVersion: apps/v1     # ① group + version
kind: Deployment        # ② object type
metadata:               # ③ identity (name, namespace, labels)
  name: easypj-web
spec:                   # ④ YOUR desired state
  replicas: 3
status:                 # ← the cluster writes this (read-only to you)
  readyReplicas: 3
Explanation

Omit a field (or mis-case kind) and the apiserver rejects the manifest before it reaches etcd. The reconciliation loop is simply "make status match spec" — which is why editing status does nothing, and why reading status is how you troubleshoot.

Q12
Why are easypj_web, EasyPJ, and 9web all rejected as object names? Give the two naming rules.
Show Answer
Answer

Names must be valid DNS. DNS Subdomain (most objects — Pods, Deployments, Nodes… — ≤253 chars): lowercase a–z 0–9 - ., start/end alphanumeric. DNS Label (namespaces; Services use RFC 1035, ≤63 chars): lowercase a–z 0–9 -, no dots, must start with a letter.

So easypj_web ❌ (underscore), EasyPJ ❌ (uppercase), 9web ❌ (starts with a digit, for Label-rule objects).

RuleUsed by✅ valid❌ invalid
DNS Subdomainmost objects (Deployments, ConfigMaps…)easypj-web, app.prodeasypj_web, EasyPJ
DNS Labelnamespaces, Services (RFC 1035)easypj-prodmy.ns, 9ns
Explanation

Names become DNS names — a Service easypj resolves at easypj.<ns>.svc.cluster.local. It's a validation error, not a style choice: the apiserver refuses the object outright.

Q13
What's the difference between the core API group and a named group, and what do v1alpha1, v1beta1, and v1 signal?
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersionGroup → pathExamples
v1core → /api/v1Pod, Service, ConfigMap, Node
apps/v1named → /apis/apps/v1Deployment, ReplicaSet, DaemonSet
batch/v1named → /apis/batch/v1Job, CronJob

Stability ladder: alpha (v1alpha1, off by default, may vanish) → beta (v1beta1, may still change) → GA/stable (v1, backward-compatible).

Explanation

kubectl api-resources maps every kind → its group, version, and namespaced-ness. A GA v1 API is never removed within a major version; a deprecated beta drops after ~9 months / 3 releases. Depend on stable versions.

Q14
Distinguish labels, selectors, and annotations. Why is a label typo the #1 cause of a Service with no endpoints, and what do ownerReferences do?
Show Answer
Answer

Labels = key/value tags for selection. Selectors = a query over labels (how a Service/Deployment/NetworkPolicy finds its pods). Annotations = metadata not used for selection (URLs, checksums, tool config).

A Service matches pods only by label selector, so if the pod labels ≠ the selector, the Service gets zero endpoints — no error, it just selects nothing. ownerReferences point child → parent (Pod → ReplicaSet → Deployment) and drive cascading deletion.

Labels wire the Service — a one-char typo = 0 endpoints
  ✅ selector app=easypj  MATCHES          ❌ selector app=easypj  vs pods app=easypj-web
        │                                        │ matches nothing
        ▼                                        ▼
  📦 app=easypj  📦 app=easypj             📦 app=easypj-web  📦 app=easypj-web
  → EndpointSlice has the pod IPs          → 0 endpoints → the Service answers nobody
Explanation

Labels are load-bearing wiring, not decoration. When something is mysteriously unreachable, compare kubectl get pods --show-labels against the selector. Deleting a Deployment garbage-collects its ReplicaSet and Pods because of the ownerReference chain.

Q15
Why does Kubernetes need a single source of truth (etcd) plus consensus, and how does the control plane vs data plane split speed up troubleshooting?
Show Answer
Answer

Because it's a distributed system: separate machines share no clock or memory and fail independently, so state must live in one authoritative store (etcd), and consensus (Raft — a majority must agree) prevents split-brain. It's also level-triggered, so a dropped message is corrected on the next pass.

The control plane (apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controllers) decides; the data plane (your pods + kube-proxy/CNI) does the work.

🟥 Control plane (decides)🟦 Data plane (does the work)
apiserver · etcd · scheduler · controllersyour pods · kube-proxy · CNI
symptom: "can't create / nothing self-heals"symptom: "app errors / pods unreachable"
if it's down, running apps keep servingthis is the app — user-visible
Explanation

Triage by plane first: "the app errors / pods can't reach each other" = data plane; "I can't create anything / nothing self-heals" = control plane. Running pods survive a control-plane outage (they run on reflex), which is why an etcd/apiserver failure is invisible to users but paralyzing to admins.

⚙️ Chapter 1 — Scenario & Command Drills (16)

Exam-style and hands-on — 16 drills that mirror how the CKA actually asks: a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
A freshly built cluster has its control plane up, but worker nodes show NotReady. You SSH to a worker and find the node agent isn't running. Which component is it, and how do you recover?
Show Answer
Answer

The kubelet — the per-node agent that (1) registers the node with the API server and (2) starts/monitors the pods assigned to it. No kubelet ⇒ the node can't report in ⇒ NotReady.

on the worker node
# Why is it down? Read the logs first.
sudo systemctl status kubelet
sudo journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -30

# Start it and make it survive reboots
sudo systemctl enable --now kubelet

# Verify from the control plane
kubectl get nodes
Explanation

On the CKA, NotReady → always check the kubelet first: systemctl status kubelet and journalctl -u kubelet. Common root causes are a stopped service, a bad /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml, swap enabled, a missing CNI, or a down container runtime (Chapter 32 drills all of these).

Q2
Name the four control-plane components and each one's primary job. Where do they run on a kubeadm cluster?
Show Answer
Answer
ComponentRole
kube-apiserverFront door — REST API, authn/authz/admission; the only component that talks to etcd
etcdDistributed key-value store — the single source of truth for all cluster state
kube-schedulerAssigns unscheduled pods to nodes (resources, affinity, taints/tolerations)
kube-controller-managerRuns reconciliation loops (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node… controllers)
Explanation

On a kubeadm cluster all four run as static pods defined in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ on the control-plane node — edit a manifest there and the kubelet recreates the pod. The topology is a star: every other component (scheduler, controller-manager, kubelet) talks only through the API server, never directly to etcd.

There's an optional fifth component — the cloud-controller-manager — on managed/cloud clusters; it runs the cloud-specific loops (provision LoadBalancers, manage node lifecycle & routes) so the core four stay cloud-agnostic.

Q3
A Deployment specifies replicas: 3. You manually delete one of its pods. What happens, and which component is responsible?
Show Answer
Answer

The ReplicaSet controller (inside kube-controller-manager) sees current=2 ≠ desired=3 and immediately creates a replacement — count returns to 3.

watch self-healing happen
kubectl create deployment easypj --image=easypj:v2 --replicas=3
kubectl get pods                 # 3 running
kubectl delete pod easypj-xxxxx-yyyyy
kubectl get pods                 # still 3 — a new one was created!
Explanation

The declarative model in action: you declared "3," and the control loop (Observe → Diff → Act) continuously enforces it. Controllers never stop watching — this self-healing is heavily tested. (To remove the pod permanently you must change the desired state — scale down or delete the Deployment.)

Q4
What's the difference between a control-plane node and a worker node? Which components run on each — and why does the kubelet run on both?
Show Answer
Answer

Control-plane node: the management components — kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager (as static pods).

Worker node: runs your workloads — needs kubelet, kube-proxy, and a container runtime (containerd/CRI-O).

Both: kubelet and kube-proxy run on control-plane nodes too — because the control-plane components are static pods, and only the kubelet can run static pods.

Component🧠 control-plane node💪 worker node
apiserver · etcd · scheduler · controller-manager✅ (as static pods)—
kubelet✅ (it runs those static pods)✅ (runs your workloads)
kube-proxy · container runtime✅✅
your app pods (easypj)❌ blocked by the NoSchedule taint✅
Explanation

Say "control-plane node," not "master." By default control-plane nodes carry the taint node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule so ordinary workloads (like easypj) don't land there. That taint — and how to tolerate/remove it — is exactly the kind of thing the scheduling chapter (14) covers.

Q5
You run kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml. Trace the request through the architecture — which components act, and in what order?
Show Answer
Answer
  1. kubectl → HTTPS request to the API server
  2. kube-apiserver → authenticate → authorize (RBAC) → admission → validate
  3. etcd → API server persists the Deployment object
  4. Deployment controller → creates a ReplicaSet
  5. ReplicaSet controller → creates Pod objects (nodeName empty)
  6. kube-scheduler → binds each pod to a node
  7. kubelet (on the node) → pulls image via the runtime, starts the container; CNI assigns an IP
Explanation

It's asynchronous and event-driven — no single orchestrator. Each component watches the API server for changes relevant to it and acts independently. That loose coupling is what makes Kubernetes resilient: if the scheduler is briefly down, pods just queue as Pending and get placed when it returns. This flow is the backbone of every troubleshooting scenario (Part 9).

Q6
What is etcd, why is backing it up critical, and what command takes a snapshot?
Show Answer
Answer

etcd is a distributed, consistent key-value store holding all cluster state — every Pod, Service, Secret, ConfigMap, RBAC rule, and CRD. Lose it without a backup and the whole cluster is gone (an etcd snapshot effectively is a cluster backup).

guaranteed exam task
# Snapshot (flags come from the etcd static-pod manifest)
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/etcd-backup.db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

# Verify it's readable
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/etcd-backup.db --write-table
Explanation

Three things the exam checks: (1) use ETCDCTL_API=3; (2) supply the three TLS flags — read the exact paths from /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml; (3) the endpoint is usually https://127.0.0.1:2379. Full backup and restore is drilled end-to-end in Chapter 29.

Q7
What does kube-proxy do? If it stops on a node, what breaks — and what still works?
Show Answer
Answer

kube-proxy programs each node's dataplane (iptables / IPVS) so traffic to a Service VIP is load-balanced to the backing pods. It watches the API server for Service & EndpointSlice objects.

If it's down on a node:

  • ❌ Service (ClusterIP / NodePort) traffic stops reaching pods
  • ❌ DNS via CoreDNS may fail (CoreDNS is reached through a Service)
  • ✅ Pod-to-pod by pod IP still works (that's the CNI, not kube-proxy)
  • ✅ kubectl exec / logs still work (API server → kubelet directly)
two separate dataplanes — which one broke?
  📦 pod ──by pod IP──▶ 📦 pod          🌐 CNI's job        ✅ still works
  📦 pod ──▶ 🔌 Service VIP ──▶ 📦 pod   🔀 kube-proxy's job  ❌ broken (rules not programmed)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  triage: pods ping each other but Services time out  ⇒  suspect kube-proxy
          pods can't even reach other pods by IP      ⇒  suspect the CNI
Explanation

Key distinction for troubleshooting: kube-proxy = Service networking; the CNI plugin = pod-to-pod networking. So if pods can ping each other by IP but Services are unreachable, suspect kube-proxy (Chapter 34 makes this a 4-layer method).

Q8
What is the Container Runtime Interface (CRI)? Name two CRI runtimes. Why was Docker's direct support removed in v1.24 — and do my images still work?
Show Answer
Answer

The CRI is the standard interface the kubelet uses to talk to any container runtime without runtime-specific code. Two runtimes: containerd (most common, extracted from Docker) and CRI-O (purpose-built, common on OpenShift).

Docker didn't implement CRI directly, so K8s shipped a dockershim translation layer — extra complexity for no gain (Docker uses containerd internally anyway). v1.24 removed the shim. Your images still work — they're OCI images, a universal format; only the runtime plumbing changed.

node-level: use crictl, not docker
crictl ps                 # list running containers
crictl logs <container-id>
crictl inspect <container-id>
Explanation

After v1.24 you debug containers on a node with crictl (talks to containerd via CRI), not docker. This matters in Chapter 32 when the API server is down and you must diagnose from the node itself.

Q9
Imperative vs declarative management — what's the difference, and what's the recommended CKA workflow?
Show Answer
Answer

Imperative = tell K8s the steps (kubectl create/run/expose) — fast, one-off, no YAML. Declarative = describe the end state in YAML + kubectl apply -f — idempotent, version-controllable, repeatable.

CKA gold standard: generate YAML imperatively, then apply it declaratively:

imperative generation → declarative apply
# Scaffold YAML instantly — don't write it from scratch
kubectl create deployment easypj --image=easypj:v2 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > easypj.yaml

# Edit in vim (add probes, resources…), then apply
kubectl apply -f easypj.yaml
Explanation

Speed wins the exam. --dry-run=client -o yaml scaffolds correct YAML in seconds; you tweak the bits a one-liner can't express (multi-container, volumes, probes). Pure kubectl create is fine for trivial objects, but the hybrid is the habit to build.

Q10
You're asked to verify overall cluster health under exam time pressure. Write the command sequence and say what each reveals.
Show Answer
Answer
top-down health check
kubectl get nodes                       # 1. all nodes Ready?
kubectl get pods -n kube-system         # 2. control-plane + CNI + CoreDNS Running?
kubectl cluster-info                    # 3. API + CoreDNS endpoints reachable
kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20   # 4. recent failures
kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running   # 5. anything CrashLoop/Error/Pending?
kubectl run dns-test --image=busybox:1.28 --rm -it --restart=Never \
  -- nslookup kubernetes               # 6. DNS resolving?
# 7. if a node is NotReady: ssh in → systemctl status kubelet → journalctl -u kubelet
Explanation

A systematic top-down diagnosis: nodes → control-plane pods → events → DNS → node logs. Look for all nodes Ready, all kube-system pods Running, no CrashLoopBackOff, and DNS resolving kubernetes. If a static-pod component is down, check its manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and that node's kubelet logs — the exact method Part 9 turns into reflex.

Q11
A teammate claims "the control plane is scheduled by Kubernetes like any other pod." Disprove it on a kubeadm control-plane node — where are the API server, scheduler, controller-manager and etcd actually defined?
Show Answer
Answer

They are static pods, run by the kubelet straight from files on disk — not scheduled through the API server. That's how the control plane can boot before any control plane exists (the bootstrap paradox).

on the control-plane node
# The manifests the kubelet runs directly
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
# etcd.yaml  kube-apiserver.yaml  kube-controller-manager.yaml  kube-scheduler.yaml

# They surface as read-only "mirror pods" (note the -<nodename> suffix)
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep -E 'apiserver|scheduler|controller|etcd'

# Edit a manifest → the kubelet auto-recreates that pod (no apply needed)
sudo vim /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
Explanation

You manage these by editing their files, not with kubectl edit (the mirror pod is read-only). This is why "change an apiserver flag" on the exam means "edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml and wait for the kubelet to restart it" — drilled in Chapter 12.

Q12
kubectl commands hang with a connection timeout — the API server looks down. Since kubectl is useless, how do you diagnose from the control-plane node itself?
Show Answer
Answer

Drop to the node and use the container runtime directly via crictl (it talks to containerd, no API server involved), then read the apiserver pod's logs and its static-pod manifest.

API server down — diagnose on the node
# Is the apiserver container even running?
sudo crictl ps -a | grep kube-apiserver

# Read its logs directly from the runtime
sudo crictl logs $(sudo crictl ps -aq --name kube-apiserver | head -1)

# Classic cause: a typo in the static-pod manifest (bad flag / invalid YAML)
sudo less /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml

# Is the kubelet healthy? It's what runs the static pods
sudo systemctl status kubelet; sudo journalctl -u kubelet | tail -30
Explanation

The reflex for the whole "control plane is down" family: no API server ⇒ no kubectl ⇒ debug at the node with crictl + journalctl. A malformed edit to the apiserver manifest is the classic self-inflicted outage — Chapter 32 makes recovering from it routine.

Q13
Classify each symptom as a control-plane or data-plane problem, and say why the split speeds up your fix: (a) easypj returns HTTP 500s; (b) kubectl apply is refused; (c) a deleted pod isn't recreated; (d) two pods can't reach each other by IP.
Show Answer
Answer
SymptomPlaneWhere to look
(a) easypj returns 500s🟦 Data planethe app/container — logs, DB connectivity, config
(b) kubectl apply refused🟥 Control planeapiserver auth / RBAC / admission (or it's down)
(c) deleted pod not recreated🟥 Control planecontroller-manager (the reconcile loops)
(d) pod-to-pod by IP fails🟦 Data planethe CNI plugin / node networking
Explanation

The split halves your search space instantly: control-plane = "I can't manage or reconcile," data-plane = "the workload itself or its packets." Running pods survive a control-plane outage (they run on reflex), which is why (a) and (d) keep failing even when the API server is healthy — and why (b)/(c) can break while the app keeps serving traffic.

Q14
You run kubectl delete ns easypj-test and it sits in Terminating for minutes. What mechanism is holding it, how do you investigate, and what is the safe fix?
Show Answer
Answer

A finalizer is blocking deletion: the namespace has deletionTimestamp set, but the API server won't remove it until the responsible controller finishes cleanup and drops the finalizer. Usually a leftover resource whose controller is gone or broken.

investigate first, force only as last resort
# 1. What's still inside, and which finalizers are set?
kubectl get all -n easypj-test
kubectl get ns easypj-test -o yaml | grep -A5 -E 'finalizers|conditions'   # names the stuck resource

# 2. SAFE fix: delete/repair the offending resource so its finalizer clears itself.

# 3. LAST RESORT (only if its data is already gone): force-remove the finalizer
kubectl get ns easypj-test -o json | jq 'del(.spec.finalizers)' \
  | kubectl replace --raw /api/v1/namespaces/easypj-test/finalize -f -
Explanation

Finalizers exist so deletion is orderly, not instant — so the right instinct is to fix the blocked cleanup, not to rip the finalizer out (which can orphan real resources). Force-clearing is a genuine last resort. This exact scenario recurs in Chapter 32.

Q15
You expose easypj with a Service, but curl to its ClusterIP hangs and kubectl get endpoints easypj shows <none> — yet the pods are Running. What's the most likely cause, and how do you confirm & fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

A label-selector mismatch: the Service's selector doesn't match the pods' labels, so no pod IPs land in its EndpointSlice. The Service looks healthy but points at nothing — the single most common Service bug.

confirm the mismatch, then fix it
# 1. Confirm: no endpoints even though pods are Running
kubectl get endpoints easypj              # ENDPOINTS: <none>

# 2. Compare what the Service SELECTS vs how the pods are LABELLED
kubectl get svc easypj -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}{"\n"}'   # app=easypj-web
kubectl get pods --show-labels                                # app=easypj  ← mismatch!

# 3a. Fix by correcting the Service selector to match the pods…
kubectl patch svc easypj -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"easypj"}}}'
# 3b. …or relabel the pods to match the selector
kubectl label pod -l app=easypj app=easypj-web --overwrite

# 4. Verify the endpoints now populate
kubectl get endpoints easypj              # now lists the pod IPs:port
Explanation

Services find pods only by label selector (§1.7). A one-character difference silently yields zero endpoints — no error, because nothing is technically broken, the selector just matches nothing. get endpoints (or get endpointslices) is the fastest confirmation, and --show-labels reveals the mismatch instantly. This exact bug recurs in Chapter 18.

Q16
Mid-exam you can't recall whether a Deployment's field is spec.strategy or spec.updateStrategy, nor whether CronJob is namespaced. You may open kubernetes.io/docs — but a faster tool is already on the cluster. What do you run?
Show Answer
Answer

Use kubectl explain (the live schema) and kubectl api-resources — no browser needed, and far quicker than hunting the docs.

discover the API from the terminal
# Field-level docs — Deployment uses spec.strategy (StatefulSet/DaemonSet use updateStrategy)
kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy
kubectl explain deployment.spec --recursive | less   # the whole field tree

# Is CronJob namespaced? What's its short name & apiVersion?
kubectl api-resources | grep -i cronjob
# cronjobs   cj   batch/v1   true   CronJob     ← NAMESPACED = true

# All served group/versions if you're unsure of an apiVersion
kubectl api-versions | grep batch
Explanation

kubectl explain reads the cluster's own OpenAPI schema, so it's always correct for that version — the fastest way to settle a field name or check nesting without leaving the terminal. api-resources answers "namespaced?", "short name?", and "which apiVersion?" in one line. Building this reflex saves minutes per task on the real exam.

🔬 Practice Drill 1.1 — Sketch the Cluster from Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

In 5 minutes, from memory, sketch one cluster and label every box: the control-plane components (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager), the worker-node components (kubelet, kube-proxy, runtime), and 3 easypj pods spread across 2 nodes. Then draw an arrow from "replicas: 3" to "3 pods running" and label it reconciliation.

Hint: Group nodes as control-plane vs worker, then trace the reconciliation arrow from replicas: 3 to the pods actually running.
View Solution 
   🗂️ CLUSTER
   ┌──────────────── 🧠 CONTROL PLANE ────────────────┐
   │ 📡 API server · 🗄️ etcd · 📋 scheduler · 🔄 controller-manager │
   └──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┘
                          │  (API server is the only one that talks to etcd)
   ┌────── 💪 NODE 1 ──────┐        ┌────── 💪 NODE 2 ──────┐
   │ 🤖 kubelet · 🔀 kube-proxy │     │ 🤖 kubelet · 🔀 kube-proxy │
   │ 🐋 runtime (containerd)│       │ 🐋 runtime (containerd)│
   │ 📦 easypj  📦 easypj    │       │ 📦 easypj             │
   └──────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘
       "replicas: 3"  ──reconciliation──▶  3 pods always running ✅

Check yourself: control-plane = API server · etcd · scheduler · controller-manager (the "brain"); each node = kubelet · kube-proxy · container runtime (the "muscle"); the 3 easypj pods are spread across the 2 nodes; and the arrow is the control loop closing desired (3) → actual (3). If you drew all of that, you've got Chapter 1's mental model cold.

🔬 Practice Drill 1.2 — Watch Self-Healing Happen (Reconciliation, Live)

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Prove to yourself that Kubernetes is level-triggered, not event-driven. On any cluster (Minikube is fine): create an easypj Deployment with 3 replicas, delete one pod by hand, and confirm the count returns to 3 without you doing anything. Then show that the only way to reduce the count for real is to change the desired state.

Hint: Deleting a pod changes actual state, not desired state — the ReplicaSet controller sees the gap (2 ≠ 3) and closes it. To remove pods permanently you must lower replicas (desired) with kubectl scale.
View Solution
reconciliation, observed live
# 1. Declare desired state: 3 replicas
kubectl create deployment easypj --image=nginx --replicas=3
kubectl get pods -l app=easypj              # 3 pods Running

# 2. Break ACTUAL state — delete ONE pod by name, then look immediately
POD=$(kubectl get pods -l app=easypj -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl delete pod "$POD"
kubectl get pods -l app=easypj              # still 3 — a fresh pod already replaced it

# 3. The count is enforced. To actually reduce it, change DESIRED state:
kubectl scale deployment easypj --replicas=1
kubectl get pods -l app=easypj              # now 1 (desired changed → actual follows)

kubectl delete deployment easypj            # cleanup

Check yourself: the deleted pod came back because you only touched actual state — the controller's next OBSERVE → DIFF → ACT pass saw 2 ≠ 3 and created one. Scaling worked because it changed desired state, which is what the loop reconciles toward. If you internalized "to change what runs, change what's declared," you have Chapter 1's core model cold.

🔬 Practice Drill 1.3 — Match the Symptom to the Broken Component

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

This is the heart of the 30% Troubleshooting domain. For each symptom, name the single most likely component at fault and one command to confirm it — before you touch anything:

  1. kubectl get pods hangs / times out — but easypj keeps serving /jobs/.
  2. A new easypj pod is stuck Pending forever; existing pods are fine.
  3. You delete an easypj pod and it is never replaced; scaling does nothing either.
  4. One worker shows NotReady and its pods get rescheduled elsewhere.
Hint: "app works but I can't manage it" points at the control plane; Pending = placement; "no self-healing" = the reconciliation loops; a single NotReady node = that node's agent.
View Solution
#Broken componentWhyConfirm with
1kube-apiserver (or etcd behind it)It's the only door to the cluster — a dead API means no reads/writes, yet running pods keep running on reflex.crictl ps | grep apiserver · journalctl -u kubelet · inspect /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
2kube-schedulerNothing is left to bind the pod to a node, so it sits unscheduled.kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep scheduler · kubectl describe pod <pending> (Events)
3kube-controller-managerThe reconciliation loops (ReplicaSet, etc.) live here — no loop, no gap-closing.kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep controller-manager
4kubelet on that nodeNo node agent to run/report pods, so the control plane marks the node NotReady.ssh <node>; systemctl status kubelet; journalctl -u kubelet

Check yourself: you diagnosed all four without running a single fix — you matched the symptom to the component using the mental model from §1.4. That "name the component first" reflex turns a 10-minute troubleshooting task into a 2-minute one on the exam.

🔬 Practice Drill 1.4 — Turn an Imperative Command Into Declarative State

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

You deployed easypj imperatively in a hurry. Now make it reproducible: generate a declarative manifest from an imperative command (don't hand-write YAML), apply it, and prove it is idempotent by applying the same file again with no change. This hybrid is the exam-winning workflow.

Hint: --dry-run=client -o yaml prints the manifest instead of creating anything. Re-running kubectl apply on an unchanged file reports unchanged, not an error — that is idempotency.
View Solution
generate imperatively → apply declaratively
# 1. Scaffold YAML from an imperative command — creates nothing yet
kubectl create deployment easypj --image=easypj:v2 --replicas=3 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > easypj.yaml

# 2. Apply it — the desired state is now a versionable file
kubectl apply -f easypj.yaml        # deployment.apps/easypj created

# 3. Prove idempotency — same file, run again
kubectl apply -f easypj.yaml        # deployment.apps/easypj unchanged  ✅

# 4. Contrast: the imperative equivalent is NOT idempotent
kubectl create -f easypj.yaml       # Error: deployments.apps "easypj" already exists

Check yourself: step 3 said unchanged because apply sends desired state and reconciliation found no gap; step 4 errored because create is imperative ("make this now"). The takeaway the exam rewards: generate with --dry-run=client -o yaml, edit, then apply — imperative speed with declarative safety.

🔬 Practice Drill 1.5 — Read the Error, Name the API-Server Stage

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

From Under the Hood you know every write passes through a 6-stage apiserver pipeline (authN → authZ → mutating → schema → validating → etcd). For each real error message, name the stage that rejected it and the fix:

  1. Error from server (Forbidden): deployments.apps is forbidden: User "dev" cannot create resource "deployments"…
  2. error validating data: ValidationError(Deployment.spec): unknown field "replica"
  3. Error from server: admission webhook "pod-policy" denied the request: runAsNonRoot required
  4. Unable to connect to the server: x509: certificate has expired or is not yet valid
Hint: "Forbidden" is about permission; "unknown field" is about shape; "admission webhook denied" is a policy; and a TLS/x509 error never even reaches authorization — it fails at the door.
View Solution
#Stage that rejected itFix
1② Authorization (RBAC)Grant a Role + RoleBinding allowing create deployments (Chapter 24).
2④ Schema validationTypo — it's replicas, not replica. Fix the YAML (kubectl explain deployment.spec).
3⑤ Validating admissionMeet the policy — add securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true (Chapter 27).
4① Authentication (before the pipeline even runs)Renew the client/apiserver certificate; refresh ~/.kube/config (Chapter 26).

Check yourself: you mapped four raw error strings straight to a pipeline stage and a chapter — no guessing. That "read the error → name the stage" habit is one of the highest-leverage troubleshooting skills on the whole exam.

📌 Chapter 1 Visual Summary — from your YAML to a running easypj pod
  👩‍💻 YOU write          🧠 CONTROL PLANE ("the brain")           💪 WORKER NODES ("muscle")
  ┌──────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────────────┐       ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │ deploy.yaml  │ ①apply│ 📡 apiserver — the ONE door    │       │ 🤖 kubelet · 🔀 kube-proxy   │
  │ replicas: 3  │ ─────▶ │   ② writes DESIRED ─▶ 🗄️ etcd   │ ④bind │ 🐋 containerd               │
  │ image:       │       │   ③ 📋 scheduler picks a node   │ ─────▶│  ┌─────────────────────┐  │
  │  easypj:v2   │       │   ④ 🔄 controllers reconcile    │       │  │📦 easypj-web :8000    │  │
  │ resources:   │       │      desired vs actual,        │       │  │📦 easypj-web :8000    │  │
  │  256Mi       │       │      FOREVER                   │ ⑥stat │  │📦 easypj-web :8000    │  │
  └──────────────┘       └──────────────────────────────┘ ◀───── │  └─────────────────────┘  │
                         ⑤ kubelet pulls image · 🌐 CNI gives each pod an IP · starts it      │
                                                                  └───────────────────────────┘
   ① declare desired   ② persist to etcd   ③ schedule to a node   ④ reconcile (keep actual = desired)
   ⑤ kubelet + CNI run it   ⑥ status reported back ─▶ etcd   ……and the loop never stops.
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   You declared "3 easypj-web on v2." Kubernetes GUARANTEES 3 are always up — it heals, scales &
   rolls out on its own. THAT is Kubernetes ☸️ — and operating this whole machine is the CKA's job.

In words: You write a deploy.yaml that describes the end result you want (3 replicas of easypj-web on image easypj:v2) and apply it. You never tell Kubernetes how — only what.

The control plane is the brain: the apiserver is the single front door, it persists your desired state to etcd, the scheduler picks a node for each pod, and controllers keep comparing desired vs actual and acting on the gap — forever. The worker nodes are the muscle: the kubelet pulls the image and starts the containers, CNI gives each pod an IP, and status flows back to etcd.

The takeaway: this never-ending "make actual match desired" loop is reconciliation — the core idea of the whole platform. Because of it, a crashed pod is replaced, a scale-up just works, and a new version rolls out automatically. Operating this machine is exactly what the CKA tests.

Chapter 2 · Containers & Docker — The Unit Kubernetes Runs

Kubernetes schedules, heals, and scales one thing: containers. Before you can operate a cluster, you have to understand the unit it manages — what a container actually is, how an image is built from cached layers, and which runtime runs it on the node. This is also where troubleshooting begins: when an easypj pod won't start, the answer is almost always in the image or the runtime.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2 hours 📖 Hands-On 🐳 Docker · containerd · CRI 🐍 easypj / jobpost

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Why containers solve the "works on my machine" problem
  • ✅ Containers vs Virtual Machines — how each isolates, and when to use which
  • ✅ Docker basics: Dockerfile → image → container → registry, and how layers cache
  • ✅ Build a production, multi-stage, non-root image for easypj
  • ✅ The essential docker / crictl commands — and which to use on a node
  • ✅ The CRI, containerd vs CRI-O, and why Docker was removed in v1.24
🎓 CKA Relevance
Cluster Architecture 25% Troubleshooting 30%
🐳 Container-runtime knowledge on the CKA

The CKA doesn't ask you to write Dockerfiles, but it assumes you understand container runtimes — because they show up everywhere you'll be graded:

  • Cluster install — you configure containerd (and its cgroup driver) during kubeadm setup.
  • Troubleshooting — when a pod fails, you inspect the runtime with crictl.
  • NotReady nodes — a dead container runtime takes the node down with it.
  • ImagePullBackOff — understanding images & layers is how you diagnose failed pulls.

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 2 Learning Arc

This chapter walks the lifecycle of the unit Kubernetes runs: from why containers exist, to what they are vs VMs, to how you build and run one for easypj, to the runtime the cluster actually uses.

2.1 Why Containers? The "Works on My Machine" Problem

Every developer has lived this nightmare: easypj runs perfectly on your laptop, then explodes the moment it hits a server. A container ends the argument by packaging everything the app needs — code and its entire environment — into one immutable, portable unit.

The "works on my machine" problem — and the fix
   👩‍💻 your laptop                          🖥️ production server
   ┌────────────────────────┐              ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ easypj runs ✅          │   deploy →   │ 💀 ModuleNotFoundError: 'psycopg2'   │
   │ Python 3.13 · Django   │              │    (different Python · no psycopg2 · │
   │ psycopg2 · env vars set │              │     missing env vars · different OS) │
   └────────────────────────┘              └────────────────────────────────────┘

   THE FIX — pack EVERYTHING into one image 📦, ship the box, not the recipe:
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ 📦 easypj:v1                                                   │
   │   • Python 3.13            • Django 5.2.5                      │
   │   • gunicorn · psycopg2    • easypj source + settings          │
   │   • env / config baked in  • a slim Debian userland            │
   │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────   │
   │  runs IDENTICALLY:   laptop ✅   staging ✅   production ✅      │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 Key Term — Container

A container is a lightweight, standalone, executable package that bundles everything needed to run a piece of software: code, runtime, system tools, libraries, and settings. Crucially, containers share the host's OS kernel — which is what makes them far lighter and faster than virtual machines.

🚢 Analogy — the shipping container

Before standardized shipping containers, every cargo was loaded by hand and broke in transit. The steel box changed the world because the same sealed unit rides any ship, truck, or crane without anyone caring what's inside. A software container is the same idea: a standard box the cluster can pick up and run anywhere, without caring whether it holds easypj, nginx, or PostgreSQL.

The Four Properties That Matter

📦
Portable

The same image runs on Linux, Mac, Windows, cloud, or bare metal — identical behavior everywhere.

🔒
Isolated

Each container gets its own filesystem, network, and process space — no dependency conflicts between apps.

⚡
Fast

Starts in seconds (not minutes like a VM) — it shares the host kernel, so there's no full OS to boot.

📐
Lightweight

Megabytes, not gigabytes — run dozens (even hundreds) of containers on a single machine.

What's Inside a Container — and What Is Not

This is the misconception that trips up almost everyone, and clearing it up makes the rest of the chapter click: a container image does not contain an operating system. It bundles the app's userland — your code, language runtime, and shared libraries — but it borrows the host's kernel. That single fact is why containers are MB not GB, and why a Linux container needs a Linux kernel underneath.

✅ IN the image (userland — shipped)❌ NOT in the image (shared from the host)
Your code (easypj) + settingsThe Linux kernel itself
Python 3.13 runtime + pip packagesKernel modules & device drivers
System libs (libc, libpq) from a slim DebianThe CPU / memory scheduler
The default command (gunicorn …)Namespaces & cgroups (these are kernel features)
An image is userland on top of the host's kernel
   📦 easypj image  (everything you ship)        ── all containers share ──▶  one kernel
   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
   │ easypj code · gunicorn         │            ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Python 3.13 · psycopg2         │  ───runs──▶ │ 🐧 HOST LINUX KERNEL                   │
   │ libc · libpq (slim Debian)     │   on top of │   scheduling · namespaces · cgroups ·  │
   │ (NO kernel in here!)           │            │   drivers · filesystems                 │
   └──────────────────────────────┘            └──────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 So how do containers run on a Mac or Windows?

They don't, directly — those OSes have no Linux kernel. Docker Desktop quietly runs a tiny Linux VM and starts your containers inside it. On a real Kubernetes node (which is Linux), there's no such trick — the container runs natively on the node's kernel. This is also why a Linux image can't run on a Windows kernel and vice-versa: the userland must match the kernel it's calling.

💡 Why this is the foundation of everything ahead

Kubernetes never runs your code — it runs your image. Every later topic (pods, deployments, rollouts, probes) is just the cluster choreographing copies of an image like easypj:v1. Get the image right here, and the rest of the guide is choreography.

2.2 Containers vs Virtual Machines
