⑦ xDS Failure Recovery — What Happens When the Control Plane Fails
ScenarioEnvoy BehaviorImpact on TrafficRecovery
istiod restart (graceful)Envoy reconnects automaticallyZERO — no traffic disruption< 5 seconds
istiod crash (ungraceful)Envoy uses LAST KNOWN good configZERO — existing config continuesEnvoy retries with backoff, reconnects when istiod is up
istiod down for 1 hourEnvoy continues with cached configExisting traffic: ZERO impact. New pods: can't get config (SYNC: STALE)New pods work once istiod returns; old pods unaffected
New CRD applied while istiod downEnvoy doesn't see the changeNo new routing rules applied; old rules continueAuto-syncs when istiod reconnects (eventual consistency)
Envoy disconnected from istiodEnvoy retries connection every 2s (double to max 30s)ZERO — uses last known config until reconnectAuto-reconnect when network restored
Envoy restart (pod restart)Envoy reads bootstrap from disk, reconnectsBrief (2-5s) — new connections delayed until config syncsFull sync after bootstrap (1-3s typically)
🔑 ICA Insight: Understanding how istiod translates Istio CRDs into Envoy configuration is critical for the ICA exam. Key xDS facts: (1) LDS = Listeners (ports), RDS = Routes (VirtualService), CDS = Clusters (DestinationRule), EDS = Endpoints (pod IPs), SDS = Secrets (certs). (2) istiod uses Aggregated Discovery Service (ADS) — all xDS types over ONE gRPC stream. (3) Envoy applies config changes HOT — no restart, no dropped connections. (4) If istiod goes down, Envoy continues working with LAST KNOWN config. (5) The bootstrap config tells Envoy where to find istiod — without it, Envoy can't get any configuration.
⑧ Capstone — The Full Injection-to-First-Request Timeline (Synthesizing 2.9-2.13)

The five deep dives above each open one door. This closes the loop: one unified timeline showing where each door sits relative to the others, for a single new Pod, start to finish.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — THE FULL INJECTION-TO-FIRST-REQUEST TIMELINE       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  SCENARIO: you deploy skills-service:v2 into anihpj. The cluster runs   │
│  istio-cni (2.12) and Delta xDS is the default transport (2.13).        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ① kubectl apply -f skills-service-v2.yaml → API server admits the Pod  │
│  ② INJECTION PATH DECIDES ITSELF RIGHT HERE (2.9 vs 2.12):              │
│      default: mutating webhook adds istio-init + istio-proxy now        │
│      istio-cni: istio-cni-node already wrote this node's iptables       │
│      rules earlier → no istio-init container is added at all            │
│  ③ kubelet starts istio-proxy (Envoy) → reads its bootstrap file →      │
│      opens ONE mTLS gRPC stream to istiod:15012 (2.11 Phase 1)          │
│  ④ FIRST SYNC IS ALWAYS FULL (2.13 meets 2.11): even with Delta xDS     │
│      on, there is no prior state yet, so istiod answers this proxy's    │
│      first CDS→EDS→LDS→RDS request with one complete snapshot           │
│  ⑤ Envoy applies it (~1-3s) → proxy flips to SYNCED → kubectl shows     │
│      skills-service-v2 as 2/2 READY                                     │
│  ⑥ FIRST REAL REQUEST: inbound Envoy terminates mTLS with a SPIFFE      │
│      cert from istiod's CA, checks AuthorizationPolicy, forwards to     │
│      Django on localhost — the mesh is now live for this pod            │
│  ⑦ STEADY STATE: any later VirtualService edit reaches this Envoy as    │
│      a DELTA push (2.13) — only the changed route, not the whole mesh   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  THE ROAD NOT TAKEN (2.10): on Cilium/eBPF there is no step ②-④ at      │
│  all — no sidecar, no bootstrap handshake, no xDS stream. That gap      │
│  IS the sidecar-vs-eBPF trade-off the exam's concept questions probe.   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 ICA Insight: The five deep dives resolve into one causal chain: the injection path (2.9 or 2.12) decides whether an istio-init container runs at all, xDS bootstrap (2.11) opens the one gRPC stream every Envoy needs before it can proxy anything, the very first sync is always a full snapshot regardless of Delta xDS being the transport default (2.13), and only steady-state changes afterward ride as deltas. Cilium's eBPF path (2.10) skips this whole timeline entirely — that absence of steps is exactly the sidecar-vs-kernel trade-off the exam's conceptual questions probe.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Istio is an open-source service mesh (CNCF Graduated 2023) that adds a dedicated infrastructure layer on top of Kubernetes for managing service-to-service communication.
  • It provides 9 core capabilities: auto mTLS, traffic routing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, fault injection, metrics, distributed tracing, and access control — all via YAML with zero code changes.
  • Kubernetes + Istio complement each other: K8s manages containers; Istio manages communication between them. Both are needed for production.
  • Envoy is the engine: a high-performance L7 C++ proxy injected as a sidecar. istiod is the brain: it reads CRDs and pushes config to Envoy via xDS.
  • Sidecar injection is admission-time, not continuous — the mutating webhook fires once at Pod CREATE; relabeling a namespace never retrofits already-running Pods.
  • Prometheus scrapes port 15020, not 15090 — istio-agent merges the app's own metrics with Envoy's raw stats (15090) into one response so a single scrape target sees both.
  • The control plane and data plane fail independently — if istiod goes down, every Envoy keeps serving traffic on its last-known-good config; only NEW pods and NEW config changes are affected.
  • xDS is the wire, CRDs are the intent — VirtualService/DestinationRule/Gateway/PeerAuthentication/AuthorizationPolicy all compile down to LDS/RDS/CDS/EDS/SDS pushed to Envoy over one gRPC stream.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "Labeling the namespace injects sidecars into running Pods." No — the mutating webhook only fires at Pod CREATE time. Existing Pods must be deleted and recreated by their controller before they get a sidecar.
  • "Prometheus scrapes Envoy's stats port 15090 directly." No — it scrapes port 15020, where istio-agent has already merged the app's own metrics with Envoy's 15090 stats into one response.
  • "If istiod goes down, my mesh stops routing traffic." No — every Envoy keeps working from its last-known-good cached config. Only NEW Pods (no cert, no bootstrap config) and NEW config changes are affected until istiod recovers.
  • "The namespace label always decides injection." Not if the Pod itself disagrees — a Pod-level sidecar.istio.io/inject: "false" always overrides an istio-injection=enabled namespace label.
  • "Cilium's eBPF approach is strictly better than Istio's sidecar model." They're a trade-off — eBPF is near-zero overhead but Envoy's userspace L7 depth (HTTP/2, gRPC, JWT claims) is exactly what kernel eBPF can't match today.
  • "Delta xDS means I only need to check the changed resource." A proxy's very first sync is ALWAYS a full snapshot, even with Delta xDS as the default — only subsequent updates ride as deltas.
  • "A VirtualService with no matching DestinationRule subset will still route somewhere reasonable." No — if a subset name doesn't resolve to any cluster, Envoy has nowhere to send that traffic; this is the #1 cause of silent canary-routing failures.

💼 Chapter 2 — What This Means For Your Daily Work

  • Know exactly what Istio's 9 capabilities are and which solves which problem — when someone says "we need encryption," you know to reach for PeerAuthentication STRICT
  • Understand the K8s vs Istio split: K8s manages containers, Istio manages communication between them
  • Trace a request through Envoy: inbound → your code → outbound → remote Envoy → remote code
  • Know the Istio CRDs: VirtualService (routing), DestinationRule (policies), Gateway (ingress), PeerAuthentication (mTLS), AuthorizationPolicy (access)
  • Understand that Envoy is the "engine" and istiod is the "brain" — sidecar injection is AUTOMATIC, your Dockerfile never changes
  • Have the vocabulary to discuss service mesh with your team: sidecar, data plane, control plane, xDS, mTLS, SPIFFE, CRD
  • For the ICA exam: "Encrypt service traffic" = PeerAuthentication STRICT. "Route by URL path" = VirtualService. "Define LB policies" = DestinationRule.
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 2

Eight quick-fire phrase-to-CRD mappings pulled straight from anihpj's own troubleshooting history — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Encrypt service-to-service traffic" = PeerAuthentication STRICT
  • "Route traffic based on URL path" = VirtualService with http.match.uri
  • "Define mTLS and load balancing policies" = DestinationRule
  • "Accept external HTTPS traffic" = Gateway
  • "Enable sidecar injection" = kubectl label namespace istio-injection=enabled
  • "Sidecar never appeared" = webhook + namespace label + recreate pods
  • "External API blocked under REGISTRY_ONLY" = ServiceEntry
  • "Did my config reach Envoy?" = istioctl proxy-status + proxy-config

🧠 Chapter 2 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Define Istio in one sentence, and name its three creating companies, its implementation language, and its CNCF status.
Show Answer
Answer

Istio is an open-source service mesh for Kubernetes that automatically injects an Envoy sidecar proxy into every Pod to handle service-to-service traffic.

FactValue
Created byGoogle + IBM + Lyft (2017)
LanguageGo
CNCF statusGraduated (2023)
Explanation

"CNCF Graduated" is the highest maturity tier the foundation grants — it signals broad production adoption and a mature governance process, distinct from "Sandbox" or "Incubating" projects.

Q2
In one sentence each, what does Kubernetes own versus what does Istio own in the stack?
Show Answer
Answer

Kubernetes owns WHERE your containers run. Istio owns HOW they communicate.

☸️ Kubernetes🕸️ Istio
Container schedulingTraffic routing between services
Pod restarts, autoscalingmTLS, retries, timeouts
Service discovery (DNS)Circuit breaking, observability
Explanation

They complement, not compete: Istio's own CRDs (VirtualService, DestinationRule, PeerAuthentication) are themselves Kubernetes Custom Resources, applied with the same kubectl apply you already use.

Q3
What physically changes inside a Pod after sidecar injection — container count, ports, and what's shared?
Show Answer
Answer

Container count goes from 1 to 2 — that shared namespace is exactly what lets iptables silently redirect the app's traffic to Envoy.

AspectBeforeAfter
Containers1 (app only)2 (app + istio-proxy)
kubectl get pods1/1 READY2/2 READY
PortsApp port only+ 15001 outbound, 15006 inbound
SharedN/ANetwork namespace, localhost, volumes
Explanation

An istio-init container (or the node-level CNI plugin, 2.12) also runs once to write those iptables rules — but it isn't a persistent third container in the running Pod.

Q4
Name Istio's 9 capabilities and, for three of them, the exact CRD that delivers it.
Show Answer
Answer

Auto mTLS, traffic routing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, fault injection, metrics, distributed tracing, access control.

CapabilityCRD
Auto mTLSPeerAuthentication
Traffic routing / retries / timeouts / fault injectionVirtualService
Circuit breakingDestinationRule
Explanation

Memory hook from 2.8: encrypt = PeerAuthentication; route/retry/timeout/fault = VirtualService; load-balance/circuit-break = DestinationRule; ingress = Gateway; external = ServiceEntry; allow/deny = AuthorizationPolicy.

Q5
What port does Prometheus actually scrape for a meshed Pod's metrics, and why not port 15090?
Show Answer
Answer

Port 15020. It's the istio-agent process inside istio-proxy, merging the app's own metrics endpoint with Envoy's raw stats into ONE HTTP response — so Prometheus needs only one scrape target per Pod.

Two Metrics Sources, One Scrape Target
  Django app metrics ──┐
                        ├──▶ istio-agent :15020 ──▶ Prometheus scrapes HERE
  Envoy raw stats :15090┘         (merged)
Explanation

This is a genuinely common mix-up — 15090 is real and does hold Envoy's raw stats, but it's not the port Prometheus is configured to scrape by default.

Q6
Explain how istiod uses xDS to program Envoy, and what keeps working if istiod goes down.
Show Answer
Answer

istiod watches CRDs and K8s Services/Endpoints via informers, computes a per-proxy view of the mesh, and streams it to each Envoy over ONE gRPC connection (ADS) on port 15012.

During an istiod outageResult
Existing traffic✅ Keeps flowing — cached last-known-good config
New Pods❌ Stuck — no cert, no xDS bootstrap
New config changes⚠️ Stored in etcd but NOT pushed
Explanation

This control-plane/data-plane failure independence is one of the most exam-relevant facts in the whole chapter — control plane failure never interrupts the data plane.

Q7
Distinguish the istio-init and Istio CNI injection paths — when is the CNI plugin required rather than optional?
Show Answer
Answer

The Istio CNI plugin is required, not just preferred, on hardened clusters — Pod Security Admission "restricted" or locked-down OpenShift SCCs block workload-Pod capabilities outright, so Pods never come up without it.

Dimensionistio-init (default)Istio CNI plugin
Runs asinitContainer, per PodDaemonSet, per Node
Privilege neededNET_ADMIN/NET_RAW on every PodOnce, on the DaemonSet only
Works under PSA restricted❌ Blocked✅ Compatible
Explanation

Both paths write the identical iptables rules on the identical ports (15001/15006) — only WHO writes them and WHEN changes; nothing else in the mesh behaves differently.

Q8
A Pod sits in a namespace labeled istio-injection=enabled but also carries the annotation sidecar.istio.io/inject: "false". Does it get a sidecar?
Show Answer
Answer

No. The Pod-level setting always overrides the namespace label — this specific Pod will NOT get a sidecar even though every other Pod in that namespace will.

Namespace LabelPod SettingSidecar?
istio-injection=enabled(none)✅ Yes
istio-injection=enabledinject: "false"❌ No — pod wins
(no label)inject: "true"✅ Yes — pod wins
Explanation

The reverse also holds: a Pod can opt IN via sidecar.istio.io/inject: "true" even in a namespace with no injection label at all. Most specific setting always wins.

Q9
What is Delta xDS, and what does NOT change about it compared to State-of-the-World?
Show Answer
Answer

Delta xDS is the wire format where istiod pushes only the added/changed/removed resources instead of resending a full snapshot on every change.

AspectChanges?
Push contents (all vs only-diff)✅ Changes — that's the whole point
Resource families (LDS/RDS/CDS/EDS/SDS)❌ Unchanged
Transport (gRPC ADS) & istiod port (15012)❌ Unchanged
Explanation

A proxy's very first sync is still always a full snapshot — there's no prior state to diff against yet. Only steady-state updates afterward ride as deltas.

Q10
Envoy adds roughly 3-5ms of overhead per hop. Why is that "worth it," and what specifically do you get for it?
Show Answer
Answer

3-5ms against typical business-logic time of 50-200ms is roughly 2-5% overhead.

Envoy overhead per hop ~4ms
Business logic (DB query, etc.) ~125ms

For that ~2-5% cost you get mTLS encryption, retry logic, timeout enforcement, circuit breaking, metrics collection, and distributed tracing — all consistent, all language-agnostic, all with zero Django code changes.

Explanation

The mTLS handshake is the single most expensive Envoy operation (~2ms) but is cached for subsequent requests on the same connection, not repeated per-request.

⚙️ Chapter 2 — Scenario & Command Drills (Hands-On Lab Scenarios)

Exam-style and hands-on — real anihpj troubleshooting scenarios with full command sequences.

Q1
You've just installed Istio with the demo profile. You deploy jobpost-api in the anihpj namespace but pods show 1/1 READY instead of 2/2. Task: Diagnose why the sidecar wasn't injected. Write the exact command to fix it, redeploy the pods, and verify injection with TWO different verification methods. Explain why simply labeling the namespace doesn't fix already-running pods.
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Diagnose: Check if namespace has injection label
kubectl get namespace anihpj --show-labels | grep istio-injection
# Output: (no istio-injection label — that's the problem!)

# 2. Fix: Enable injection
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled

# 3. Redeploy: Delete pods so webhook injects sidecar on recreation
kubectl delete pods -l app=jobpost-api -n anihpj

# 4. Verify method 1: Check 2/2 READY
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
# Expected: READY 2/2 (app container + istio-proxy)

# 4. Verify method 2: Check proxy sync
istioctl proxy-status
# Expected: SYNCED for all proxies
Explanation

The mutating admission webhook intercepts Pod CREATE requests only — it cannot modify already-running pods. Labeling the namespace tells the webhook "inject sidecars into future pods," but existing pods must be deleted and recreated by their Deployment controller. The two verification methods confirm: (1) the sidecar container exists (2/2 READY), and (2) the sidecar has successfully connected to istiod and received configuration (SYNCED). On the ICA exam, this is the #1 troubleshooting scenario — always check the namespace label first, then redeploy.

Q2
You run kubectl get pods -n istio-system and see only 2 pods: istiod-xxx and istio-ingressgateway-xxx. You expected to also see Kiali, Jaeger, Grafana, and Prometheus. Task: Explain which installation profile you likely used, what each profile includes, whether reinstalling with a different profile will get you the observability pods, and write the correct command(s) to actually get all 4 tools running.
Show Answer
Answer

Diagnosis: You used the default profile (istiod + ingressgateway only). But switching to demo profile will NOT get you Kiali/Jaeger/Prometheus/Grafana either — no install profile bundles the observability addons. They are separate manifests you apply independently, regardless of profile.

# Current profile check
istioctl profile list

# demo profile adds the egress gateway + higher tracing sampling —
# still NOT the observability stack:
istioctl install --set profile=demo -y
kubectl get pods -n istio-system
# istiod-xxx                    1/1   Running
# istio-ingressgateway-xxx      1/1   Running
# istio-egressgateway-xxx       1/1   Running    ← NEW (demo adds this)
# (still no kiali/jaeger/prometheus/grafana!)

# Fix: apply the addon manifests separately (any profile)
kubectl apply -f samples/addons/prometheus.yaml
kubectl apply -f samples/addons/grafana.yaml
kubectl apply -f samples/addons/jaeger.yaml
kubectl apply -f samples/addons/kiali.yaml

# Verify: now you'll see all 4
kubectl get pods -n istio-system
Explanation

Istio ships 7 built-in install profiles — default, demo, minimal, remote, ambient, empty, preview — none of which include Kiali, Jaeger, Prometheus, or Grafana. The demo profile's real difference from default is enabling the egress gateway and turning up tracing sample rate/access logging for learning — it is NOT an "everything bundle." The observability stack is always a separate kubectl apply -f samples/addons/ step, whichever profile you installed with. This is a common real-world (and exam) mistake: assuming profile=demo alone gives you a dashboard.

Q3
Your manager asks: "How do I know Istio is actually WORKING — that the sidecars are injected, configured, and routing traffic?" Task: Write the 4-command verification sequence you'd run after any Istio installation or configuration change. For each command, explain what SUCCESS looks like and what FAILURE looks like. Include the specific istioctl commands to inspect Envoy's listener, cluster, route, and endpoint configuration for a specific pod.
Show Answer
Answer
# VERIFICATION 1: Pods have sidecars injected
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
# ✅ SUCCESS: READY column shows 2/2 for all pods
# ❌ FAILURE: Any pod shows 1/1 → sidecar NOT injected

# VERIFICATION 2: Proxies synced with istiod
istioctl proxy-status
# ✅ SUCCESS: All proxies show SYNCED
# ❌ FAILURE: STALE or NOT SENT → istiod can't reach proxy

# VERIFICATION 3: Configuration validated
istioctl analyze -n anihpj
# ✅ SUCCESS: "No validation issues found"
# ❌ FAILURE: Shows errors → fix YAML before proceeding

# VERIFICATION 4: Deep inspect Envoy config for a specific pod
istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep 15001
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep user-service
istioctl proxy-config route deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj
istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep user-service

SUCCESS means: (1) 2/2 READY, (2) all SYNCED, (3) 0 analyze errors, (4) Envoy shows user-service in its cluster and endpoint tables. If any check fails, Istio is NOT working — investigate before relying on it.

Explanation

This 4-step verification is your ICA exam "health check" routine. Run it after EVERY configuration change. Step 1 confirms injection happened. Step 2 confirms istiod pushed config successfully. Step 3 validates your YAML has no errors. Step 4 proves Envoy actually KNOWS about the upstream services it's supposed to route to. If proxy-config cluster doesn't show an expected service, that service's pods aren't being discovered (label mismatch, Service selector issue, or service not in mesh). On the ICA exam, always verify after applying changes — don't assume it worked.

Q4
You apply a new VirtualService for canary routing (90% v1, 10% v2). After running kubectl apply, you immediately test and see ALL traffic still going to v1. Task: Explain why (hint: it's NOT a bug). Write the exact command to check if the config reached Envoy, what SYNCED/STALE/NOT SENT mean, and how long config propagation typically takes via xDS. Then write the command to verify the VirtualService rules are actually in Envoy's route table.
Show Answer
Answer

Why it seems broken: Config propagation via xDS takes ~1-3 seconds. Your test was too fast. Also, if subset labels don't match pods, Envoy resolves v2 to zero endpoints — ALL traffic silently falls through to v1.

# Check 1: Are proxies synced?
istioctl proxy-status
# SYNCED = config received and applied
# STALE = proxy hasn't acknowledged config in a while
# NOT SENT = istiod couldn't reach the proxy at all

# Check 2: Is the VS route actually in Envoy?
istioctl proxy-config route deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj
# Look for: "jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:8000"
# Check weight: v1=90, v2=10

# Check 3: Does v2 subset resolve to actual endpoints?
istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep "version=v2"
# If empty → subset labels don't match pod labels → 503s
Explanation

xDS uses gRPC bidirectional streaming — istiod pushes changes the moment a CRD is created/updated. No polling delay. But network latency + Envoy processing = ~1-3 seconds end-to-end. On the ICA exam: (1) always wait 5 seconds after applying before testing, (2) always run proxy-status to confirm SYNCED, (3) always check proxy-config route to see the actual rules Envoy received, and (4) always check proxy-config endpoint to confirm subsets resolve to pod IPs. Missing endpoints = the #1 cause of "my VirtualService isn't working."

Q5
Your anihpj deployment has two versions: v1 (3 replicas, label version: v1) and v2 (2 replicas, label version: v2). Both have app: jobpost-api. You create a VirtualService routing 100% to subset v1, but traffic is still randomly distributed between v1 and v2 pods. Task: Diagnose the issue, explain what CRD is MISSING, write it, and explain the two-label contract (what app does vs what version does). Verify the fix with the correct command.
Show Answer
Answer

Diagnosis: You created a VirtualService referencing subset: v1, but you NEVER created a DestinationRule that defines what subset: v1 means. Without a DestinationRule, Envoy doesn't know which pods are "v1."

# Fix: Create the DestinationRule
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: jobpost-api
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2
EOF

# Verify subsets resolve to pods
istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj
# Should show 3 endpoints for v1, 2 for v2

The two-label contract: app: jobpost-api — used by Kubernetes Service selector to group ALL pods. version: v1 — used by DestinationRule subsets to differentiate pods WITHIN the Service. Service sees all pods; DR separates them.

Explanation

This is the most common VirtualService failure on the ICA exam. VirtualService says "route to subset v1" but cannot resolve "v1" without a DestinationRule. The two resources form a mandatory pair: VS = where to go, DR = what the destinations are. Without DR subsets, Envoy treats ALL pods matching the Service selector as one undifferentiated pool. The app label groups pods under a Service (L4 K8s level); the version label differentiates pods for routing (L7 Istio level). Both labels MUST exist on every pod template.

Q6
You're troubleshooting why jobpost-api can't reach user-service. You SSH into the jobpost-api pod and run curl http://user-service:80/users/ — it works. But when your Django code tries the same request, it gets 503. Task: Explain how iptables redirect works (why curl INSIDE the pod on port 80 bypasses Envoy but your Django code doesn't). List all 3 Envoy ports and their purposes. Write the command to check what upstream clusters Envoy knows about for this pod.
Show Answer
Answer

Why curl works but Django fails: When you SSH into the pod and curl directly, you're running as root (UID 0). iptables rules exempt UID 1337 (Envoy's UID) but your root curl hits port 80 directly. However, Django code runs as the app user — its traffic IS caught by iptables and redirected to Envoy on port 15001. The 503 means Envoy knows about user-service but all its endpoints are unhealthy or the circuit breaker is open.

PortDirectionPurpose
15001Outboundiptables redirects all app outbound traffic here
15006InboundReceives traffic from other services' Envoys
15090N/A (stats)Raw Envoy stats — NOT what Prometheus scrapes directly
15020N/A (stats)istio-agent's merged app+Envoy metrics — Prometheus scrapes THIS port
 
# Check what Envoy knows about user-service
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep user-service
# Check endpoints for user-service
istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep user-service
# If HEALTHY=0 → circuit breaker open or all pods unhealthy
Explanation

The iptables redirect is kernel-level — invisible to applications. Your Django code calls requests.get("http://user-service/users/") which resolves to the ClusterIP. The kernel sees this outbound packet and iptables' OUTPUT chain redirects it to localhost:15001 (Envoy's outbound listener). Envoy then handles routing, mTLS, retries, etc. When you SSH and run curl directly, the behavior depends on your UID — but the key insight is that Envoy is a TRANSPARENT proxy. Your code doesn't know it exists. On the ICA exam, knowing port 15001=outbound and port 15006=inbound is essential for debugging.

Q7
You delete the istiod pod in istio-system to test Istio's resilience. Task: Explain exactly what happens to EXISTING traffic, NEW pods, and CONFIGURATION CHANGES during the istiod outage. Write the command to verify proxies are still working. Explain what istiod HA configuration looks like and write the command to scale istiod to 3 replicas with a PodDisruptionBudget.
Show Answer
Answer

During istiod outage:

WhatResult
Existing traffic✅ CONTINUES flowing — Envoy uses cached config
New pods❌ CANNOT start — can't get cert or config from istiod
Config changes❌ NOT propagated — no istiod to process CRD changes
Proxy status🟡 Eventually shows STALE (no heartbeat from istiod)
 
# Verify existing proxies still work:
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | head
# Still shows clusters — cached config intact

# HA configuration:
kubectl scale deployment istiod -n istio-system --replicas=3

# PodDisruptionBudget (min 2 available during voluntary disruptions):
kubectl create pdb istiod-pdb -n istio-system \
  --selector=app=istiod --min-available=2
Explanation

This separation of control plane (istiod) and data plane (Envoy) is the KEY architectural advantage. Envoy proxies store their last-known-good configuration in memory and continue routing traffic even without istiod. The ICA exam tests this: "control plane failure does NOT cause data plane interruption." However, NEW pods can't get SPIFFE certificates or initial config → they'll stay in Init or CrashLoopBackoff until istiod recovers. That's why 3 replicas + PDB is recommended for production — new pods must always have at least one istiod available.

Q8
A new developer on your team accidentally deletes the istio-sidecar-injector MutatingWebhookConfiguration. All new pod deployments in anihpj now show 1/1. Task: Explain what the webhook does and why pods show 1/1 without it. Write the command to verify the webhook exists. Write the command to recreate it (hint: it's in the Istio install manifests). Then explain how you'd verify the fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. Check if webhook exists
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector
# Error: not found → THIS is the problem!

# 2. Recreate the webhook from Istio install manifests
# The webhook is part of istiod's configuration
istioctl install --set profile=demo -y
# This recreates ALL Istio components including the webhook

# 3. Verify webhook is back
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector
# Expected: NAME                         WEBHOOKS
#          istio-sidecar-injector        1

# 4. Redeploy pods to trigger injection
kubectl delete pods -l app=jobpost-api -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
# Expected: 2/2 READY (sidecar injected!)
Explanation

The MutatingAdmissionWebhook is the MAGIC behind automatic sidecar injection. Every time a Pod CREATE request hits the API server, Kubernetes calls ALL registered mutating webhooks. Istio's webhook checks: "Is this namespace labeled istio-injection=enabled?" If yes, it MODIFIES the Pod spec to add the istio-proxy container and istio-init init container BEFORE the Pod is persisted in etcd. Without this webhook, no Pods get sidecars — regardless of namespace labels. On the ICA exam, if ALL pods suddenly show 1/1, check the webhook first.

Q9
Your anihpj services need to call api.stripe.com for payment processing. You've enabled REGISTRY_ONLY mode for production security. Calls to Stripe return 502. Task: Write the complete ServiceEntry YAML to register Stripe. Then write a VirtualService that adds a 5-second timeout to all Stripe API calls. Explain what REGISTRY_ONLY mode does and why the 502 occurred. Explain what other external services might now be broken.
Show Answer
Answer

Root cause: REGISTRY_ONLY blocks ALL external traffic unless explicitly registered via ServiceEntry. Stripe is not registered → 502.

# ServiceEntry: Register Stripe in Istio's registry
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: stripe-payments
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
---
# VirtualService: Add timeout to Stripe calls
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: stripe-timeout
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  http:
  - timeout: 5s
    route:
    - destination:
        host: api.stripe.com

Other broken services: SendGrid (email), AWS S3 (file uploads), Twilio (SMS), Google Maps API — ANY external API your services call now needs a ServiceEntry. Audit all outbound calls BEFORE switching to REGISTRY_ONLY.

Explanation

REGISTRY_ONLY is the production security standard — it implements zero-trust for egress. Only services explicitly registered (via Kubernetes Service or ServiceEntry) can be called. The demo profile defaults to ALLOW_ANY (all external traffic allowed). Always: (1) audit all external dependencies first, (2) create ServiceEntries for each, (3) test with ALLOW_ANY, (4) switch to REGISTRY_ONLY, (5) verify nothing breaks. On the ICA exam, "502 when calling external API" + "REGISTRY_ONLY mode" = missing ServiceEntry. The ServiceEntry makes external APIs first-class citizens — you can apply ALL Istio policies (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers) to them.

Q10
You're asked to explain Istio's architecture to a new team. Task: Draw the complete 12-step request journey from when a user hits GET /jobs/ to when the response returns, including: Gateway, VirtualService, DestinationRule, Envoy (both sides), iptables, mTLS handshake, AuthorizationPolicy check, metrics recording, and tracing span. For each step, note whether it happens at L4 or L7. Then calculate the total Envoy overhead per hop in milliseconds vs the business logic time, and explain why it's worth it.
Show Answer
Answer
StepLayerActionTime
1L4User → istio-ingressgateway (Gateway CRD: host/port match)~1ms
2L7Gateway → VirtualService (match URI /jobs/*, route to v1:90% v2:10%)~0.5ms
3L7DestinationRule: apply LEAST_CONN LB, check circuit breaker~0.5ms
4L4iptables on jobpost-api node: PREROUTING → redirect to :15006<0.1ms
5L4jobpost-api Envoy receives on :15006. mTLS handshake.~2ms
6L7AuthorizationPolicy: is ingressgateway allowed? ✅~0.3ms
7L7Record metrics (istio_requests_total++), start trace span~0.2ms
8L7Forward to Django on localhost:8000 (plain HTTP!)~0.1ms
9—Django processes: GET /jobs/ → query DB → build response50-200ms
10L4iptables: OUTPUT chain → redirect Django's outbound to :15001<0.1ms
11L7Envoy outbound: VirtualService routing, mTLS to user-service~2ms
12L7Record response metrics, complete trace span, return to caller~0.3ms

Envoy overhead per hop: ~3-5ms. Business logic: 50-200ms. Ratio: Envoy adds 2-5% overhead. What you get for 3-5ms: mTLS encryption, retry logic, timeout enforcement, circuit breaking, metrics collection, distributed tracing, and authorization — all consistent, all language-agnostic, all zero code changes. Verdict: ✅ Worth it.

Explanation

This 12-step journey is the mental model you need for the ICA exam. Notice: Django talks plain HTTP on localhost — Envoy handles ALL encryption, routing, and policy enforcement transparently. The iptables redirect is kernel-level (<0.1ms) — near-zero overhead. The mTLS handshake is the most expensive Envoy operation (~2ms) but cached for subsequent requests. On the ICA exam, you'll need to trace request flows through the mesh to debug routing, auth, or mTLS issues. Knowing which step handles what (and at which layer) is essential.

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 2
  • "2/2 READY" is your one-glance sidecar check — 1/1 means the webhook never fired; debug injection before you ever look at Django.
  • istioctl proxy-status beats grepping logs — SYNCED/STALE/NOT SENT tells you exactly which pipeline stage broke.
  • Memorize just two ports — 15001 outbound, 15006 inbound — most "traffic isn't being intercepted" questions collapse to these two.
  • Pod not injecting? Check the pod-level label/annotation before the namespace label — pod-level always wins (2.9).
  • On a hardened cluster (PSA restricted / OpenShift SCC), assume you need CNI mode, not istio-init — NET_ADMIN per Pod is usually the block (2.12).
  • Don't chase "which CRD do I need" from memory — recite capability → CRD from 2.8's table; it's faster and it's exam-exact.

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 2)

Chapter 2's first real kubectl/istioctl commands appear across the deep dives above — this closing reference pulls all 12 of them into one table: the exact commands you reach for anytime a pod won't show 2/2, a route won't apply, or istiod goes quiet.

CommandWhat It Checks / Does in Chapter 2
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabledturn on auto sidecar injection (2.9)
kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labelsconfirm the injection label landed (2.9)
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injectorconfirm the injector webhook exists (2.9)
kubectl delete pods -l app=jobpost-api -n anihpjforce CREATE-time so injection actually fires (2.9)
kubectl get pods -n anihpj2/2 READY = sidecar present (2.4, 2.9)
istioctl install --set profile=demo -y(re)install istiod + the webhook config (2.9, Scenario Q8)

istioctl proxy-config clusters deploy/<name> -n anihpjconfirm a DestinationRule subset exists (2.11)
istioctl proxy-config endpoints deploy/<name> -n anihpjconfirm real pod IPs resolved, not empty (2.11)

🔬 Practice Drill 2.1 — Prove the Sidecar Is Real (anihpj)

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Prove to yourself — with commands, not memory — that jobpost-api's sidecar is really there, really labeled, really listening on the right ports, and really synced with istiod.

  1. kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=jobpost-api -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[*].name}' — confirm you see BOTH jobpost-django and istio-proxy
  2. kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels | grep istio-injection — confirm istio-injection=enabled is present
  3. istioctl proxy-config listeners deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep -E '15001|15006' — confirm both capture ports are bound
  4. istioctl proxy-status | grep jobpost-api — confirm the row reads SYNCED, not STALE
  5. (stretch) kubectl delete pod -l app=jobpost-api -n anihpj && kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w — watch it come back 2/2 READY without touching a single YAML file
Hint: Each of the 4 checks maps to a different layer — container presence (2.4), namespace config (2.9), Envoy's actual listeners (2.11), and control-plane sync state (2.11) — a failure in any ONE doesn't mean the others are broken too.
View Solution

All 4 checks passing means: (1) the Pod spec really has 2 containers, not just a "2/2" READY count that could theoretically mean something else; (2) the webhook's precondition (namespace label) is actually satisfied, not just assumed; (3) Envoy's listeners are bound on the exact two capture ports 2.4/2.11 named, so iptables has somewhere real to redirect to; (4) istiod and this specific Envoy agree on config — a SYNCED sidecar with the wrong routes is a different bug than a STALE one. The stretch step proves injection is reproducible, not a one-time fluke from your original install.

Check yourself: if any single check had failed, could you say WHICH layer broke without re-running all 4? That's the real skill this drill builds — the ICA exam and real 3 AM pages both reward isolating the failing layer fast, not re-verifying everything from scratch.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.2 — Match the Symptom to the Broken Layer

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

For each observation, decide: is this actually broken, and if so, at which layer? Name the layer (or "not a bug") and one command to confirm — before proposing any fix:

  1. After upgrading to Istio 1.22+, a proxy that used to sync in ~2s now takes noticeably longer following one large VirtualService change — but istioctl proxy-status eventually shows SYNCED.
  2. A Pod scheduled on a hardened node (PSA "restricted") gets stuck in Init:Error — the exact same Deployment works fine on a non-restricted node.
  3. kubectl get pods -n istio-system shows only 3 pods after istioctl install --set profile=demo -y, and a colleague insists Kiali should have appeared automatically.
  4. Two teams both claim to "run the mesh" for their services — one shows Envoy sidecars in every pod, the other shows none at all on their nodes.
Hint: Not everything unusual is broken — "eventually SYNCED" and "no sidecars visible" can both be correct behavior depending on which feature is in play (2.13, 2.10/16).
View Solution
#VerdictWhyConfirm with
1Not a bugEven with Delta xDS as the default, a large enough change still costs proportionally more to push — "slower for a big change" ≠ "broken." Only a proxy stuck permanently at STALE is the real problem.istioctl proxy-status — confirm it DID reach SYNCED, not that it stayed slow
2istio-init's capability requestNET_ADMIN/NET_RAW on a per-Pod init container is exactly what PSA "restricted" blocks — this is the textbook case for switching to the Istio CNI plugin.kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> — check Events for a capability/SecurityContext denial
3Not a bugNo install profile — demo included — has ever bundled Kiali, Jaeger, Prometheus, or Grafana. They are always a separate samples/addons/ apply, regardless of profile.kubectl get pods -n istio-system — 3 pods (istiod + 2 gateways) is the CORRECT demo-profile count
4Not a bug — different data-plane modesOne team runs sidecar mode (Envoy per Pod); the other runs ambient mode (no sidecar, ztunnel per node instead). Both are valid, coexisting ways to be "in the mesh."kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=ztunnel on the "no sidecar" team's cluster

Check yourself: did you correctly call 3 of these 4 "not a bug"? The ICA's troubleshooting domain deliberately includes scenarios that LOOK wrong but are actually correct behavior — proposing a fix for something that isn't broken wastes exam time and, in production, risks breaking something that was working.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.3 — Diagnose the 1/1 Pod, Live

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

On any cluster with Istio installed, deliberately break injection, then fix it using ONLY the diagnostic commands from 2.9 — no guessing, no reinstalling from scratch:

  1. Deploy a Pod into a namespace that has NO istio-injection label. Confirm it's 1/1.
  2. Write down, before running anything, the ONE command that tells you why it's 1/1 without you having to already know the answer.
  3. Fix it and get to 2/2 in the fewest possible steps.
Hint: The fastest diagnosis is checking the namespace label first — before touching the Pod, the webhook, or istiod — because it's the precondition every other injection path depends on.
View Solution
fewest-steps diagnosis
# Diagnose in ONE command — check the precondition first:
kubectl get ns <namespace> --show-labels | grep istio-injection
# (no label) → that's the entire root cause, stop investigating further

# Fix: label + recreate (2 commands, no reinstall needed)
kubectl label namespace <namespace> istio-injection=enabled
kubectl delete pod -l app=<your-app> -n <namespace>
kubectl get pods -n <namespace>              # 2/2 READY

Check yourself: did you check the namespace label BEFORE checking the webhook or istiod's health? Most people over-investigate — jumping straight to "is istiod down?" or "is the webhook broken?" — when the namespace label is the fastest, cheapest check and explains the overwhelming majority of real 1/1 tickets.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.4 — Sketch the 12-Step Request, Timed

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

In 5 minutes, from memory, write the 12-step journey of one GET /jobs/ request from 2.5 as a numbered list — Gateway through both Envoys to Django and back. For each step, note L4 or L7. Do NOT reopen 2.5 until you finish.

Hint: Group the 12 steps into 3 phases first — ingress (steps 1-3), inbound Envoy processing (4-8), outbound Envoy processing (9-12) — the phases are easier to recall than 12 individual steps.
View Solution

Compare your list against 2.5's table. The steps most people drop: (a) the AuthorizationPolicy check on the INBOUND side (step 6) — easy to forget since it happens silently on every request; (b) recording BOTH request-start and response-complete trace spans (steps 7 and 12) as two separate events, not one; (c) the fact that Django itself talks plain HTTP on localhost (step 8) — Envoy does all the encryption, not Django.

Check yourself: did you correctly mark which steps are L4 (iptables, raw TCP redirect) versus L7 (anything Envoy actually reads the HTTP content for)? Mixing these up is the most common conceptual error the ICA exam's troubleshooting domain probes.

🔬 Practice Drill 2.5 — Kill istiod and Watch What Actually Happens

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

On any test cluster (NOT production), prove the control-plane/data-plane split with your own eyes instead of reciting it: confirm existing traffic survives an istiod outage, confirm a NEW pod does NOT come up cleanly during that outage, then restore istiod and confirm recovery — all with command output, not assumption.

Hint: "Existing traffic keeps working" needs a Pod that was ALREADY running and synced before you kill istiod — test the wrong Pod and you'll see a false failure.
View Solution
istiod outage, live
# 1. BEFORE: confirm a real, already-synced baseline
istioctl proxy-status                          # note: jobpost-api = SYNCED
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- curl -s localhost:15000/clusters | grep user-service

# 2. Kill istiod
kubectl scale deployment istiod -n istio-system --replicas=0

# 3. DURING outage: existing traffic still works (cached config)
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- curl -s localhost:15000/clusters | grep user-service
# same output as step 1 — Envoy never needed to ask istiod again

# 4. DURING outage: a NEW pod does NOT come up cleanly
kubectl delete pod -l app=jobpost-api -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w                  # stuck — no cert, no xDS bootstrap possible

# 5. AFTER: restore istiod and confirm recovery
kubectl scale deployment istiod -n istio-system --replicas=1
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w                  # the stuck pod finally reaches 2/2
istioctl proxy-status                          # back to SYNCED mesh-wide

Check yourself: did step 3's output genuinely match step 1's — proving Envoy answered from cache with ZERO dependency on istiod being reachable at that moment? And did step 4 actually hang, not just "seem slow"? For production hardening, this exact fragility (a single istiod replacing itself) is why 2.11 recommends 3 replicas plus a PodDisruptionBudget with min-available: 2 — so a routine node drain never reproduces what you just did on purpose.

Chapter 2 started with a plain question — what does Istio actually give you — and answered it by building outward: a definition, a hands-on demo, Istio's exact boundary with Kubernetes, Envoy as the engine doing the work, one request traced hop by hop, a shared vocabulary, a before/after story from anihpj's own on-call history, and all 9 capabilities named against their CRDs.

The five deep dives then pressure-tested that model against the questions a working engineer actually asks — how does injection really happen, why a sidecar instead of eBPF, how does istiod talk to Envoy, how do node-level and no-restart delivery cut real operational cost. Nothing here changed jobpost-api's Django code; what changed is that you can now open Part 3 and go straight to architecture instead of vocabulary.

Chapter 3: Istio Architecture Deep Dive

Now we go under the hood. You'll learn exactly how the data plane and control plane work together, how istiod configures Envoy proxies, how sidecar injection happens automatically, and how iptables silently redirects all your traffic through Envoy — without your Django code ever knowing.

Chapter 2 sold you Istio as a feature list: flip on mTLS, drop in a VirtualService, watch Kiali light up green — all without touching a line of Django. That list is true, but it is also a black box: it never said WHERE any of those features actually run. Chapter 3 pries the box open. Every jobpost-api call you traced with Kiali in 2.2 crosses real iptables rules (3.5), a real Envoy filter chain (3.9), and a real xDS push from istiod (3.2-3.3) — none of that is optional plumbing, it IS the mesh. Skip this chapter and Part 4's install reads like a magic incantation, Part 5's routing YAML feels unreviewable, and Part 9's "the mesh is broken" tickets stay unsolvable coin flips. Learn it once here and every later Part reuses the same two levers: which plane owns this problem, and which xDS table backs the config that is misbehaving.

  • ✅ Trace a VirtualService edit through the xDS pipeline — LDS, RDS, CDS, EDS, SDS — to the exact Envoy table it lands in

💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 3

The ICA exam tests your understanding of Istio's internal architecture. Key exam items:

  • "Check if all proxies are synced" = istioctl proxy-status
  • "What port does Envoy listen on for inbound?" = Port 15006 (inbound), 15001 (outbound)
  • "How does traffic get to Envoy?" = iptables rules set by the istio-init container (or the istio-cni-node DaemonSet, 3.10)
  • "What runs in istio-system?" = istiod, ingressgateway, optional addons (Kiali, Jaeger, Grafana)
  • "What are the four sub-components of istiod?" = Pilot (traffic), Citadel (certs), Galley (validation), and the sidecar injector (webhook)
  • "Verify a workload certificate" = istioctl proxy-config secret or istioctl x describe pod — istioctl authn tls-check was REMOVED years ago; never pick it
  • "Which port does Prometheus scrape?" = 15020 (istio-agent's merged app+Envoy metrics), NOT 15090 (raw Envoy stats)

3.1 The Two Planes: Data Plane and Control Plane

Istio's architecture is split into two distinct layers — the data plane (which does the actual work of handling traffic) and the control plane (which configures and manages the data plane). This separation is the key to Istio's power and scalability.

🔷
Data Plane

ALL the Envoy sidecar proxies running alongside your Pods. They handle actual traffic — millions of requests per second. Each sidecar: routes, encrypts (mTLS), retries, records metrics, injects tracing headers, and enforces circuit breaking.

🧠
Control Plane

istiod — a single binary that manages everything. It reads Istio CRDs (VirtualService, DestinationRule, etc.), converts them to Envoy configuration via xDS, and pushes config to all sidecars. It also issues mTLS certificates and validates YAML.

│  │  │ Pod: skills-svc      │        │ Pod: auth-service    │           │ │
│  │  │ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐ │        │ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐ │           │ │
│  │  │ │ App   │ │ Envoy │ │        │ │ Envoy │ │ App   │ │           │ │
│  │  │ └───────┘ └───────┘ │        │ └───────┘ └───────┘ │           │ │
│  │  └─────────────────────┘        └─────────────────────┘           │ │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 Why Two Planes?

Separating control from data means: (1) Control plane failure does NOT disrupt running traffic — sidecars use cached config. (2) Data plane scales independently — add more sidecars without touching istiod. (3) Configuration changes propagate in ~1-3 seconds via xDS streaming, no proxy restart needed.

3.2 istiod — The Control Plane Deep Dive

Before Istio 1.5, the control plane was 4 separate pods (Pilot, Citadel, Galley, Sidecar-Injector). Since 1.5, they're all merged into a single binary called istiod — simpler to operate, easier to upgrade, fewer failure modes. All four sub-components still exist conceptually — the ICA exam may reference them by their old names — they just run as one process now.

🛩️
Pilot (Traffic Config)

Traffic Configuration Manager. Watches the Kubernetes API for VirtualService, DestinationRule, and Gateway CRD changes. Converts them to Envoy xDS configuration (LDS, RDS, CDS, EDS). Pushes config to all sidecar proxies via gRPC streaming.

🏰
Citadel (Certificate Authority)

Certificate Authority. Issues SPIFFE X.509 SVID certificates to every workload. Certificate identity: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api. Auto-rotates certs every 24 hours. Stored as Kubernetes Secrets, streamed to Envoy over SDS.

📋
Galley (Config Validation)

Config Validation. Runs as a Kubernetes Validating Admission Webhook — validates Istio YAML BEFORE it reaches Pilot. Rejects malformed config so Pilot only ever sees valid CRDs, preventing misconfiguration from ever reaching the mesh.

🪝
Sidecar Injector

Mutating Admission Webhook. Runs inside istiod. When a Pod is created in a namespace labeled istio-injection=enabled, it intercepts the CREATE request and rewrites the Pod spec — adding istio-init and istio-proxy — before the object is ever persisted to etcd (full flow in 3.4).

istiod INTERNAL ARCHITECTURE — What Lives Inside the Single Binary
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        istiod Pod                                 │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│   │   PILOT sub-component (Traffic Config Manager)           │    │
│   │   • VirtualService → Envoy RDS   • Gateway → Envoy LDS   │    │
│   │   • DestinationRule → Envoy CDS  • Endpoints → Envoy EDS │    │
│   │   • Pushes config via gRPC/xDS stream                    │    │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│   │   CITADEL sub-component (Certificate Authority)          │    │
│   │   • Issues SPIFFE X.509 certs • Rotates every 24h        │    │
│   │   • spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api      │    │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│   │   GALLEY sub-component (Config Validation)               │    │
│   │   • Validating Admission Webhook — rejects bad YAML      │    │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│   │   SIDECAR INJECTOR sub-component (Mutating Webhook)      │    │
│   │   • Rewrites Pod spec at CREATE time (3.4)               │    │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                   │
│   External interfaces:                                            │
│   • Port 15010: xDS gRPC (plaintext, mesh-internal only)         │
│   • Port 15012: xDS gRPC (mTLS, production)                      │
│   • Port 15014: Control plane metrics (Prometheus scrape)         │
│   • Port 443:   Webhook endpoint (sidecar injection requests)     │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔧 Under the Hood — Cert Rotation Never Drops a Live Connection

Citadel signs jobpost-api's next cert well before the current one's ~24h TTL expires, then pushes it to the local istio-agent over SDS as a fresh "default" secret — Envoy just presents the new one on the NEXT TLS handshake. Any connection already running on the old cert keeps going until it closes on its own — no istio-proxy restart, and no request is ever dropped.

OLD (Istio < 1.5)NEW (Istio 1.5+)
Pod: pilot (100m/256Mi)Pod: istiod (single binary)
Pod: citadel (50m/128Mi)All four merged into one
Pod: galley (50m/128Mi)Simpler: 1 deployment to manage
Pod: sidecar-injector (50m/128Mi)Easier upgrades and scaling
Total: 4 pods to manageTotal: 1 pod (or 3 for HA)
Complex gRPC between podsIn-process calls (faster)
💡 ICA Exam Note

If the exam asks about "the component that issues mTLS certificates," the answer is Citadel (a sub-component of istiod). If asked about "traffic configuration," the answer is Pilot. If asked "which webhook injects the sidecar," the answer is the sidecar injector, not Galley (Galley only validates). All four are now part of the single istiod binary.

📡 Pilot Watches Every Namespace By Default — Even Non-Mesh Ones

3.1's diagram shows istiod pushing config to mesh Pods, but it under-states what Pilot actually watches: by default, istiod tracks Services and Endpoints across every namespace in the cluster, whether or not that namespace has a single injected sidecar. On a large or high-churn cluster (hundreds of namespaces, frequent Deployments in non-mesh namespaces too), this inflates istiod's memory, CPU, and xDS push latency for work that produces zero mesh-relevant config.

discoverySelectors in the mesh config lets you scope Pilot down to only the namespaces that matter — typically a label like istio-injection: enabled — so istiod stops paying attention to namespaces it will never push config for. This is a real production-scaling knob, distinct from anything in 3.6's per-component resource table: that table sizes the components you already run; discoverySelectors reduces the WORK istiod does in the first place.

3.3 The Envoy Proxy — Deep Dive

Envoy is not just a proxy — it's a programmable L7 proxy written in C++ that serves as Istio's data plane. It understands HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, gRPC, TCP, and WebSockets. istiod configures it via the xDS API. Envoy's capabilities used by Istio: HTTP request/response manipulation, automatic RED metrics generation, distributed-tracing header injection (x-b3-traceid), mTLS termination and origination, circuit breaking and outlier detection, request retries with backoff, and fault injection (delays, aborts).

HOW istiod CONFIGURES ENVOY — The xDS Flow
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  You apply YAML:                                                │
  │  kubectl apply -f virtual-service.yaml                          │
  │         │                                                       │
  │         ▼                                                       │
  │  Kubernetes API Server stores it in etcd                        │
  │         │                                                       │
  │         ▼                                                       │
  │  istiod watches for CRD changes (via K8s informers)             │
  │         │                                                       │
  │         ▼                                                       │
  │  istiod converts VirtualService → Envoy xDS config              │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  LDS (Listener Discovery)  →  which ports to listen on  │   │
  │  │  RDS (Route Discovery)     →  how to route requests     │   │
  │  │  CDS (Cluster Discovery)   →  which upstream services   │   │
  │  │  EDS (Endpoint Discovery)  →  which pod IPs are behind  │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │         │                                                       │
  │         ▼  gRPC streaming (persistent connection)               │
  │  istiod PUSHES config to every affected Envoy proxy             │
  │         │                                                       │
  │         ▼                                                       │
  │  Envoy proxies update routing tables IN-MEMORY                  │
  │  ← No restart needed. LIVE config update! →                     │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ⏱️  Total time: kubectl apply → traffic routing = ~1-3 seconds │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 The 4 xDS Discovery Services

LDS (Listener) — which ports to listen on. RDS (Route) — how to match and route requests. CDS (Cluster) — which upstream services exist. EDS (Endpoint) — which specific pod IPs are behind each service. Together, they form the complete configuration that makes Envoy a "programmable" proxy.

How xDS Actually Works — The Full Picture

Each xDS service handles a different layer of Envoy's configuration, and they build on each other from the bottom up. Here's the complete flow when you apply a VirtualService:

1
You Apply YAML

kubectl apply -f virtual-service.yaml
API server stores it in etcd

2
istiod Watches

istiod uses K8s informers to watch
for CRD changes. No polling — push-based.

3
Pilot Translates

VirtualService YAML → Envoy route config
DestinationRule → cluster config + endpoints

4
xDS Pushes

RDS: "Route /jobs/* to subset v1"
CDS: "Subset v1 = pods with version:v1"
EDS: "v1 pods at 10.244.1.5, 10.244.2.8"

5
Envoy Updates

In-memory routing table updated.
No restart. Traffic flows per new rules.
Total: ~1-3 seconds.

💡 Why xDS Matters on the ICA Exam

When you run istioctl pc route deploy/X -n Y, you're viewing the RDS configuration that istiod pushed to that specific Envoy. When you run istioctl pc endpoint deploy/X -n Y, you're viewing EDS config. If a VirtualService rule doesn't appear in proxy-config route, it means istiod either didn't process it (validation failed) or couldn't push it (proxy not SYNCED). This is how you debug routing issues on the ICA exam.

A Fifth xDS API You Haven't Met Yet — SDS

Envoy actually speaks a fifth xDS API that the diagram above didn't cover — SDS (Secret Discovery Service), the channel istiod uses to stream mTLS certificates straight into Envoy's memory, with no cert ever touching disk. Here are all five discovery services side by side, one card each:

📡 LDS

Listener Discovery. Configures listeners (ports & protocols). No listener = no traffic.

🧭 RDS

Route Discovery. Configures route tables (host/path). VS edits apply live.

🗄️ CDS

Cluster Discovery. Configures upstream clusters (LB, subsets). No cluster = 503.

📍 EDS

Endpoint Discovery. Configures pod IPs behind each cluster. Most dynamic xDS API.

🔑 SDS

Secret Discovery. Configures mTLS certs & keys. Certs never touch disk.

Envoy's Three Roles — One Process, Three Jobs, Every Packet

Strip away the acronyms and Envoy is really doing three jobs on every single packet: proxying it, policing it, and measuring it. anihpj's jobpost-api sidecar runs all three inside the same istio-proxy container, on the same request, every time — and none of the three is optional: a packet that skips policy enforcement never reaches telemetry, and one that isn't measured still gets proxied.

🚚 Zone 1 — Traffic Proxy

Intercepts ALL in/out traffic via iptables (:15006 in, :15001 out). Picks a healthy endpoint via EDS and load-balances the connection. Retries safe failures, enforces the route's per-try timeout. jobpost-api example: routes GET /jobs/42/ to Django on 127.0.0.1:8000.

🛡️ Zone 2 — Policy Enforcement Point

Originates/terminates mTLS on every hop, checking the SPIFFE cert. Evaluates AuthorizationPolicy: allow, or deny with an RBAC 403. Applies rate limits, circuit breaking, and outlier ejection. jobpost-api example: a caller with no valid SPIFFE identity is denied right here — Django never even sees the request.

📊 Zone 3 — Telemetry Collector

Records RED metrics for every request (rate, errors, duration). Writes access logs and stamps trace headers (x-b3-traceid). Exposes /stats/prometheus on :15020 for scraping. jobpost-api example: the p99 = 234ms figure from section 9.2 came from THIS Envoy, not from Django instrumentation.

A Single Request — Full Journey Through the Mesh

Pulling all of the above together, here is one real anihpj trace, hop by hop, with actual timings:

VISUAL: A SINGLE REQUEST — FULL JOURNEY THROUGH THE ISTIO MESH

📖 Without Istio vs With Istio

Without Istio tracing, you'd only know "the page took 255ms." With Istio, you know EXACTLY that skills-service's database is the bottleneck — 190ms of the 255ms total — without adding a single line of instrumentation to Django. That's the trade you're making for Envoy's ~4% overhead.

3.4 Automatic Sidecar Injection — How It Works

One of Istio's most powerful features is automatic sidecar injection — Envoy is added to your Pods without you changing a single line of your Deployment YAML. This happens via a Kubernetes Mutating Admission Webhook (3.2's sidecar-injector sub-component).

SIDECAR INJECTION FLOW — From kubectl apply to Running Pod
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                  │
  │  ① kubectl apply -f jobpost-deployment.yaml                     │
  │         │                                                        │
  │         ▼                                                        │
  │  ② Kubernetes API Server                                         │
  │     "Before I create this Pod, I must call all registered        │
  │      Admission Webhooks..."                                      │
  │         │                                                        │
  │         ▼                                                        │
  │  ③ Istio Mutating Admission Webhook (runs in istiod)             │
  │     "I see istio-injection=enabled on namespace: anihpj"         │
  │     "Let me MODIFY the Pod spec before it's created..."          │
  │         │                                                        │
  │         ▼                                                        │
  │  ④ Modified Pod spec returned to API Server:                     │
  │     + initContainers: [istio-init]    ← sets up iptables        │
  │     + containers:     [istio-proxy]   ← Envoy sidecar added     │
  │     + volumes:        [istio-envoy, istio-certs, ...]           │
  │         │                                                        │
  │         ▼                                                        │
  │  ⑤ Pod is CREATED with sidecar ALREADY inside it                │
  │     Your original jobpost container: COMPLETELY UNCHANGED ✅     │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ENABLE INJECTION:                                               │
  │    Namespace-wide: kubectl label ns anihpj istio-injection=enabled│
  │    Per-Deployment:  annotation: sidecar.istio.io/inject: "true"  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 Two Ways to Get iptables Written — 3.5 vs 3.10

The Pod spec above only adds the istio-proxy container itself. Something still has to write the actual iptables redirect rules — that's the istio-init container's job, covered next in 3.5. On clusters that block a privileged init container per Pod, 3.10 covers the alternative: the istio-cni plugin, which does the same job once per node instead.

3.5 iptables — How Traffic Is Intercepted

The istio-init container runs before your app starts. It sets iptables rules that silently redirect ALL traffic through the Envoy sidecar. Your Django code thinks it's talking directly to user-service:80 — but in reality, every packet is intercepted and routed through Envoy first.

🧠 Analogy — The Hotel Switchboard

iptables interception is like a hotel's phone switchboard. A guest dials another room's extension normally and never learns an operator exists — but every call is silently patched through the operator first, who logs it, times it, and can reroute it. Django "dials" user-service on port 80 the exact same way every time; iptables is the switchboard quietly connecting that call through Envoy instead.

🔴 Outbound — jobpost-api calling user-service

1
Django

requests.get("user-service/api/users/")

2
DNS

user-service → ClusterIP 10.96.45.23:80

3
Linux Stack

Packet dest: 10.96.45.23:80

4
iptables

OUTPUT chain → REDIRECT to 127.0.0.1:15001

5
Envoy In

Receives on port 15001 (outbound listener)

6
Envoy Route

Who is 10.96.45.23? → user-service

7
Policies

Apply routing, timeout, retry, circuit breaker

8
mTLS

Handshake → present SPIFFE certificate

9
Send

Encrypted packet to user-service Pod IP:15006

🟢 Inbound — user-service receiving

1
Packet Arrives

user-service Pod on port 15006

2
iptables

PREROUTING → REDIRECT to 127.0.0.1:15006

3
Envoy In

Receives on port 15006 (inbound listener)

4
Verify mTLS

Check SPIFFE cert from jobpost-api Envoy

5
Authz Check

AuthorizationPolicy — is jobpost-api allowed?

6
Record

Metrics: latency timer starts

7
Forward

127.0.0.1:8000 → Django on localhost

8
Django

Normal HTTP — NO TLS needed!

💡 KEY INSIGHT

Django NEVER sees TLS. Envoy handles ALL encryption between pods. Django talks plain HTTP on localhost:8000. From Django's perspective, it receives a normal HTTP GET request — no certificates, no encryption, no special headers. Your application code changes: ZERO. This is the magic of transparent sidecar proxying.

bash — iptables rules set by istio-init 
# Redirect ALL outbound TCP traffic to Envoy port 15001
iptables -t nat -A OUTPUT -p tcp \
  ! --dport 15001 \                    # skip Envoy's own traffic
  -m owner ! --uid-owner 1337 \        # skip Envoy process (UID 1337)
  -j REDIRECT --to-ports 15001

# Redirect ALL inbound TCP traffic to Envoy port 15006
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp \
  -j REDIRECT --to-ports 15006

# Exception: Envoy's own traffic is NOT redirected (avoid loop)
iptables -t nat -A OUTPUT -m owner \
  --uid-owner 1337 -j RETURN
📖 Why UID 1337?

The istio-proxy container runs as UID 1337. The iptables rules check --uid-owner 1337 and skip redirection for traffic from this UID. Without this exception, Envoy's own outbound traffic would be redirected back to itself, creating an infinite redirection loop. UID 1337 is the safety valve.

🩺 The Redirect You Don't See: kubelet's Health Probes

Turn on STRICT mTLS and a whole new class of ticket shows up: liveness/readiness probes start failing, even though the app is fine. Why: kubelet speaks plain HTTP/TCP — it has no Istio certificate — so a probe that iptables redirected straight into Envoy's inbound listener would be rejected as an untrusted peer.

Istio's real fix is silent and automatic: the mutating webhook rewrites the Pod's own probe spec so kubelet stops hitting the app directly and instead hits pilot-agent on port 15020, which proxies the check through to the real app port over localhost — a path that never touches the mTLS-protected inbound listener at all. Disable it per-Pod with the annotation sidecar.istio.io/rewriteAppHTTPProbers: "false" (you'll then need to handle mTLS-vs-probes yourself).

🎛️ Traffic-Capture Exclusion Annotations — the Escape Hatches

3.5's rules redirect everything by default — but real clusters often need one port or IP range left alone (a legacy TCP dependency, a non-mesh external database, a health-check port a different tool already owns). Four Pod annotations control this without touching the mesh-wide default:

AnnotationEffect
traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeInboundPortsThese inbound ports skip the PREROUTING redirect entirely — traffic reaches the app directly, unencrypted
traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeOutboundPortsOutbound calls to these ports bypass Envoy — no mTLS, no retries, no tracing for that traffic
traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeOutboundIPRangesOutbound calls to these CIDRs (e.g. a non-mesh RDS instance) go direct, not through Envoy
traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeInterfacesExcludes entire network interfaces from capture, not just ports

Every excluded port or range trades security/observability for compatibility — use the narrowest exclusion that solves the actual problem, never a blanket one.

3.7 Sidecar Debugging Checklist — When Things Go Wrong

When your pod shows 1/1 instead of 2/2, or traffic isn't flowing as expected, use this systematic debug checklist. Most "Istio is broken" tickets on anihpj are one of six repeat symptoms — memorize the symptom-to-first-command mapping below.

📖 The Golden Debugging Order

INJECTION → SYNC → CONFIG → TRAFFIC. Never start by editing YAML blindly — observe first, change second. Every check reads LIVE state, either from the Kubernetes API (labels, webhook, events) or from Envoy itself (istioctl proxy-config reads the proxy's in-memory tables).

⚠️ Trap Command — istioctl authn tls-check

istioctl authn tls-check was REMOVED years ago — never answer with it on the exam. The modern replacements are istioctl x describe pod <pod> (one-pod mesh summary: matching VirtualServices, DestinationRules, mTLS mode) and istioctl proxy-config secret.

🔍 SIDECAR DEBUGGING DECISION TREE
Pod shows 1/1 instead of 2/2?
Namespace labeled?
→ kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels
→ Fix: kubectl label ns anihpj istio-injection=enabled
Pod existed before label?
→ Injection only at CREATION time
→ Fix: kubectl delete pod <name> -n anihpj
Webhook working?
→ kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector
→ Fix: Check istiod logs

🔍 SIX REPEAT OFFENDERS — Symptom → First Command

Symptom (what you see)First command to run
Pod READY 1/1 — sidecar container was never injectedkubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels
Pod 2/2 but follows OLD routes minutes after kubectl applyistioctl proxy-status → any STALE / NOT SENT?
Calls to a service return 503 "no healthy upstream"istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/<name>
Plaintext caller gets TCP connection RESET (not 403!)istioctl x describe pod <pod> → mTLS STRICT?
istio-proxy CrashLoopBackOff or pod never leaves Initkubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy -n anihpj
mTLS errors: unknown identity, certificate expiredistioctl proxy-config secret deploy/<name>

🔧 QUICK DEBUG COMMANDS — Keep These Handy

What to CheckCommandExpected Output

🔥 Real Incident — anihpj, Day 12

skills-service came back 1/1 after a node drain. Checklist step 1 → namespace label was fine. Step 2 → the pod was missing from istioctl proxy-status entirely — it had been recreated WHILE the injection webhook was down during an istiod upgrade. Fix: kubectl delete pod → recreated 2/2, SYNCED in ~3s.

3.8 Inside Envoy — Proxy Configuration Hierarchy

Envoy's configuration follows a strict hierarchy. Understanding this helps you debug routing issues quickly.

📖 Key Term — xDS

xDS is the umbrella name for the FOUR discovery protocols stacked below — LDS, RDS, CDS, and EDS. An exam prompt that says "trace it through the xDS pipeline" means this whole four-table stack, not just one API.

🏗️ ENVOY CONFIGURATION HIERARCHY — Bottom to Top
EDS
Endpoints

Pod IPs behind each service.
istioctl pc endpoint → IP list

CDS
Clusters

Upstream services (logical).
istioctl pc cluster → service list

RDS
Routes

How to route (path, headers, weights).
istioctl pc route → VS rules

LDS
Listeners

Which ports Envoy listens on.
istioctl pc listener → 15001, 15006

Istio CRDFeeds xDS Table"Which port owns this?" answered by
GatewayLDS (Listeners)Gateway CRDs + mesh defaults
VirtualServiceRDS (Routes)Which rule matches Host + path
DestinationRuleCDS (Clusters)Which upstream services + subsets exist

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Symptom: calls to skills-service time out or return 503         │
│                                                                  │
│  STEP 1 — EDS (endpoints): are there healthy pod IPs?            │
│    istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj   │
│    ❌ empty or UNHEALTHY → no ready pods / outlier ejection       │
│       (skills-service at 8.1% errors gets ejected!) — STOP HERE  │
│    ✅ healthy IPs listed → continue to STEP 2                     │
│                                                                  │

│    ❌ no outbound|8090||skills-service... → DestinationRule /     │
│       subset problem                                             │
│                                                                  │

│    istioctl proxy-config route deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj      │
│    ❌ rule missing → VS not applied, or host typo                 │
│                                                                  │
│  STEP 4 — LDS (listeners): is Envoy even listening?              │
│    istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj   │

│                                                                  │

└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📖 Debugging Tip: Check Bottom-Up

When traffic isn't routing: (1) Check EDS first — are there healthy endpoints? (2) Check CDS — does the cluster exist? (3) Check RDS — are the routing rules applied? (4) Check LDS — is Envoy listening on the right ports? This bottom-up approach finds the root cause fastest — an empty endpoint list makes every table above it irrelevant.

3.9 Deep Dive — Envoy Filter Chain & Full Request Lifecycle

A filter chain is Envoy's internal assembly line — every packet passes an ordered list of filters before it may leave. When an Istio feature "does nothing," the usual cause is that the packet never reached the filter implementing it. There are three filter layers, always in this fixed order: Listener filters (connection-level peeking — tls_inspector asks "TLS or plaintext?", original_dst recovers the real destination iptables rewrote), Network filters (L4, run for ALL traffic — http_connection_manager for HTTP, tcp_proxy for raw TCP, rbac for authorization), and HTTP filters (L7, ONLY when http_connection_manager runs — jwt_authn, cors, fault, stats, router — router is ALWAYS last). This is exactly why TCP services get no retries or fault-injection: those features live in HTTP filters that plain TCP traffic never reaches.

📖 The Sidecar's Port Map — Memorize for the Exam

15001 outbound capture · 15006 inbound capture · 15021 health/readiness · 15090 raw Envoy stats · 15020 istio-agent's merged app+Envoy metrics — Prometheus scrapes THIS port, not 15090.

🔥 Real Incident — anihpj, Day 19

A fault-injection rule "did nothing" for search-service traffic. Root cause: the Service port was named tcp-search, so Envoy installed only the tcp_proxy network filter, and the fault HTTP filter never saw a request. Renaming the port to http-search switched the chain to L7 — the fault fired instantly. Always check the Service port name before touching any YAML on an "Istio isn't doing anything" ticket.

3.10 The istio-cni Plugin — An Alternative to istio-init

istio-cni is a chained CNI plugin that writes the SAME iptables redirect rules as the istio-init container (3.5), but from one privileged DaemonSet pod per node instead of a privileged init container inside every application Pod. istio-init needs the NET_ADMIN and NET_RAW capabilities on every injected Pod — many clusters block that under the Kubernetes "restricted" Pod Security Admission level, or under org RBAC policy. istio-cni removes that requirement from application namespaces entirely.

📖 How It Works

Enable at install time with components.cni.enabled: true in the IstioOperator spec (or --set pilot.cni.enabled=true in Helm). istio-cni runs as the istio-cni-node DaemonSet, one Pod per node in istio-system — it chains AFTER the primary CNI (Calico, Flannel, etc.) during kubelet's pod-network setup. When a new Pod is scheduled, the chained plugin writes the outbound→15001 / inbound→15006 rules into that Pod's network namespace BEFORE any of its containers ever start. The Pod still gets the istio-proxy sidecar container from the mutating webhook (3.4) — it simply never gets an istio-init entry in its initContainers list. Verify it's active: kubectl get daemonset -n istio-system istio-cni-node → want DESIRED = CURRENT = READY = node count.

istio-init (default)istio-cni plugin
Runs in every PodRuns once per node
Needs NET_ADMIN+NET_RAWOnly the node needs it
Blocked by strict PSAWorks with restricted PSA
Adds an initContainerNo initContainer added
Default behaviorcni.enabled: true
No extra DaemonSetistio-cni-node DaemonSet
