🔥 Real Incident — anihpj, Day 27

The platform-security team enforced Pod Security "restricted" cluster-wide, which silently blocked every new istio-init container (NET_ADMIN denied) and left new Pods running with NO sidecar and no error visible in kubectl describe. Fix: reinstalled with components.cni.enabled: true and re-rolled the Deployments — injection succeeded with zero changes to any Pod spec.

3.11 Inside the istio-proxy Container — pilot-agent + Envoy

The istio-proxy container that injection adds (3.4) is not one process — it runs TWO: pilot-agent (also called istio-agent in the docs) and Envoy, started in that order. SDS certificates, Envoy's bootstrap config, the merged metrics endpoint (3.9's port 15020), and Pod readiness are ALL produced by pilot-agent, not Envoy — when one of those breaks, kubectl logs -c istio-proxy is showing a pilot-agent error, and 3.7's proxy-config commands go quiet because Envoy itself never finished starting.

INSIDE THE istio-proxy CONTAINER — pilot-agent Starts Envoy
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ① pilot-agent starts first inside the istio-proxy container       │
│     builds Envoy bootstrap config: istiod address, node/cluster    │
│     metadata, trust domain — written to disk before Envoy runs     │
│                                                                    │
│  ② pilot-agent creates a private key + CSR, sends the CSR to       │
│     istiod for signing over gRPC (3.2's Citadel sub-component)     │
│                                                                    │
│  ③ pilot-agent execs Envoy as a child process, pointing it at      │
│     that bootstrap file — Envoy then opens its own xDS stream      │
│                                                                    │
│  ④ Envoy asks pilot-agent locally for the signed cert + root CA    │
│     via the Secret Discovery Service (SDS) API — the "default"     │
│     and "ROOTCA" secrets 3.7's proxy-config secret command shows   │
│                                                                    │
│  ⑤ pilot-agent polls Envoy's health endpoint; only then does the   │
│     kubelet readiness probe on :15021 start succeeding             │
│                                                                    │
│  ⑥ pilot-agent keeps serving the merged metrics endpoint on        │
│     :15020 for as long as the Pod is alive (see 3.9)               │

Builds Envoy bootstrap configReads that config at startup

📖 Who Owns iptables — pilot-agent, Every Time

The istio-init container (3.5) runs pilot-agent's istio-iptables logic directly; istio-cni (3.10) reuses that same rule-writing logic from its node DaemonSet instead. Either way, the rules that redirect 15001/15006 come from pilot-agent's code — Envoy itself never touches iptables.

🔥 Real Incident — anihpj, Day 33

istio-proxy sat in CrashLoopBackOff on a freshly drained node. kubectl logs -c istio-proxy showed a pilot-agent error, not an Envoy one — "failed to get certificate: rpc error: context deadline exceeded" — istiod itself was mid-rollout and unreachable on :15012 for about 40s. No proxy-config command could help, because Envoy had never started; the fix was simply waiting out the istiod rollout, confirmed once istioctl proxy-status listed the pod again.

⏱️ pilot-agent Starting First Isn't the Whole Story — Ordering Still Bites

Knowing pilot-agent starts before Envoy explains startup — it doesn't guarantee the APP container waits for either of them. By default, Kubernetes gives NO ordering guarantee between istio-proxy and your app container: the app can send its very first outbound request before Envoy's listener is even open (dropped or reset), and for a Job, istio-proxy is a problem in the other direction — it never exits on its own, so the Job can hang at "Completed: 0/1" forever waiting for a sidecar that never shuts down.

FixHow it works
holdApplicationUntilProxyStartsA postStart hook on the app container blocks until Envoy's :15021 health endpoint answers — solves the "app starts before Envoy" race
Native sidecars (K8s 1.28+, ENABLE_NATIVE_SIDECARS)istio-proxy becomes a restartPolicy: Always init container — Kubernetes itself now guarantees start-before-app AND exits it automatically when the main container finishes, fixing the Job-hang problem natively

This is exactly the mechanism underneath Scenario & Command Drills Q5's db-migration-job scenario: the sidecar.istio.io/inject: "false" annotation sidesteps the problem by removing the sidecar entirely, but native sidecars are the newer fix that lets a Job keep its mesh sidecar without hanging.

│  OBSERVABILITY AT EVERY STEP:                                                 │
│  • Prometheus: request count, latency, status codes at each hop              │
│  • Jaeger: trace spans: Gateway → VS routing → Sidecar → App                │
│  • Kiali: service graph shows all hops with latency + error rates            │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧮 6 Waypoints, One Trip — and Where the p99 Budget Actually Goes

Pulling the filter-chain detail back out to the full journey, a request crosses exactly six waypoints between the browser and the Django code that finally handles it — and for a HEALTHY request (not the skills-service outlier traced in 3.3), here is where the canonical p99 budget of 234ms (section 9.2) is actually spent:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ REQUEST LIFECYCLE — 6 WAYPOINTS AT A GLANCE  (jobpost-api)                     │
│                                                                                │
│ 1. CLIENT — GET https://api.anihpj.com/jobs/42/  (public TLS on :443)          │
│                              ▼                                                │
│ 2. INGRESS GATEWAY ENVOY — standalone Envoy, terminates TLS, matches VS       │
│                              ▼                                                │
│ 3. NETWORK FILTERS (mTLS/authz) — L4 — tls_inspector, istio_authn, rbac       │
│                              ▼                                                │
│ 4. HTTP FILTER CHAIN (routing/retries) — L7 — jwt_authn, cors, fault, router  │
│                              ▼                                                │
│ 5. UPSTREAM CLUSTER SELECTION — CDS + EDS + load balancing                    │
│                              ▼                                                │
│ 6. APPLICATION CONTAINER — Django on 127.0.0.1:8000 — Envoy never touches      │
│    business logic, it only measured and secured the trip getting here         │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ jobpost-api GET /jobs/ — WHERE THE p99 BUDGET (234ms) GOES           │
│                                                                      │
│ Client → Gateway (network hop)      █░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░    2ms      │
│ Gateway Envoy (TLS + route match)   █░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░    2ms      │
│ mTLS handshake (sidecar ↔ sidecar)  █░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░    2ms      │
│ Inbound filter chain (L4 + L7)      █░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░    2ms      │
│ Django app + downstream calls       ████████████████████  224ms      │
│ Outbound re-encrypt + return trip   █░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░    2ms      │
│                                                                      │
│ Mesh/Envoy overhead: 10ms of 234ms total ≈ 4%                        │
│ (matches the ~4% overhead verdict from 3.3's full-journey trace)     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The mesh's own tax is tiny: ~10ms of 234ms, about 4% — matching the "~4% overhead" verdict from the full-journey trace in 3.3. The other 96% was never Envoy's to save; it is Django, its downstream calls, and the database underneath them.

🎯 Capstone — A Canary Rule's Full Journey, YAML to Packet

SCENARIO: you kubectl apply a VirtualService sending 10% of jobpost-api traffic to the v2 subset. Here is EVERY section in this chapter, doing its one job, exactly once, on that single change:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ① kubectl apply -f canary-vs.yaml -- API server persists it to etcd,    │
│    before any Istio component has even noticed                          │
│                                                                         │
│ ② (3.2) istiod's Pilot sub-component's informer sees the new            │
│    VirtualService -- Galley's webhook already rejected it here if the   │
│    YAML were malformed, so Pilot only ever sees valid config            │
│                                                                         │
│ ③ (3.2-3.3) Pilot converts the CRD into an updated Envoy route table:   │
│    one cluster becomes two, weighted 90/10                              │
│                                                                         │
│ ④ (3.3) istiod streams that new RDS config over the persistent xDS      │
│    gRPC stream to every Envoy that routes to jobpost-api (~1-3s)        │
│                                                                         │
│ ⑤ (3.4-3.5, 3.10) each receiving Envoy exists only because, back at     │
│    Pod creation, the mutating webhook added istio-proxy AND iptables    │
│    (or the istio-cni DaemonSet) already redirected ports 15001/15006   │
│    -- the canary push has nowhere to land without that one-time setup   │
│                                                                         │
│ ⑥ (3.11) none of ②-⑤ would have mattered if pilot-agent had never       │
│    finished its own certificate handshake with istiod -- a sidecar      │
│    still starting up cannot receive OR apply any xDS push, canary       │
│    included                                                             │
│                                                                         │
│ ⑦ (3.9) the next real request to hit an updated sidecar walks the       │
│    filter chain -- network filters check identity first, THEN the       │
│    HTTP router filter (always last) now rolls the dice 90/10 between    │
│    v1 and v2                                                            │
│                                                                         │
│ ⑧ (3.7-3.8) verify the whole chain in exactly two commands:             │
│    istioctl proxy-status                    -- SYNCED, not STALE?       │
│    istioctl proxy-config route deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj             │
│                                              -- route shows the 90/10?  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every one of this chapter's eleven sections is exactly one hop on this same road — a YAML edit goes in, enforced bytes come out — and 3.7/3.8's commands are simply how you inspect any single hop without guessing which one is lying to you.

🔑 ICA Insight: The two-plane architecture is the most fundamental Istio concept. ICA WILL test this. Key facts: (1) Control plane (istiod) = "what to do" — computes rules, pushes config. Data plane (Envoy) = "do it" — enforces rules, handles traffic. (2) If istiod goes down, data plane KEEPS WORKING with last known config. (3) Envoy filter chain order: Listener → Network → HTTP → Cluster — understanding this helps debug "why isn't my HTTP rule working?" (answer: check if http_conn_manager is configured). (4) The Gateway is just a special Envoy — same filter chain, but configured for north-south traffic. (5) None of it works without the one-time setup in 3.4/3.5/3.10 and the pilot-agent handshake in 3.11 — the canary capstone above is that whole chapter, end to end, on one YAML edit.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Two planes, two jobs: the control plane (istiod) computes configuration and never touches a live packet; the data plane (every Envoy sidecar) enforces that configuration on every request, in the hot path.
  • istiod is four sub-components in one binary: Pilot (xDS config), Citadel (certs/mTLS), Galley (config validation), and the sidecar injector (mutating webhook) — the exam may still reference the pre-1.5 names.
  • Envoy speaks five xDS APIs, not four: LDS/RDS/CDS/EDS are the well-known set, but SDS (Secret Discovery Service) streams mTLS certs straight into memory and is just as real.
  • Injection adds two separate things to a Pod spec: a one-shot istio-init container that writes iptables rules, and the persistent istio-proxy sidecar (pilot-agent + Envoy) that stays up for the Pod's life.
  • iptables direction, memorized as a pair: inbound → 15006, outbound → 15001 — UID 1337 (Envoy itself) is exempt from both to avoid an infinite redirect loop.
  • istio-cni replaces istio-init's privilege, not its job — same rules, written once per node by a DaemonSet instead of once per Pod by a privileged init container, which is what makes it compatible with restricted Pod Security Admission.
  • The golden debugging order is INJECTION → SYNC → CONFIG → TRAFFIC, and inside CONFIG, always read the xDS hierarchy bottom-up: EDS → CDS → RDS → LDS.
  • A packet walks three filter layers in Envoy, in fixed order: Listener filters, then Network filters (L4, all traffic), then HTTP filters (L7, only if http_connection_manager ran) — router is always the last HTTP filter.
  • istio-proxy is two processes, not one — pilot-agent starts first and builds Envoy's bootstrap config and certificate before ever exec'ing Envoy as a child process.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "Pilot, Citadel, and Galley are separate pods I need to check individually." Not since Istio 1.5 — all four sub-components run in-process inside the single istiod binary. The exam may use the old names, but there is only one Deployment to check.
  • "There are four xDS discovery services." There are five — LDS, RDS, CDS, EDS are the commonly cited four, but SDS (certificates) is just as real and is exactly what istioctl proxy-config secret reads.
  • "istio-init and istio-proxy are the same thing." No — istio-init is a one-shot init container that writes iptables rules and exits; istio-proxy is the persistent sidecar (pilot-agent + Envoy) behind the "2/2 READY" count.
  • "Outbound traffic redirects to 15006 and inbound to 15001." Backwards. Inbound → 15006 (PREROUTING). Outbound → 15001 (OUTPUT). This pair is one of the most commonly swapped facts on the exam.
  • "istio-cni is a completely different mechanism from istio-init." No — it writes the exact same iptables rules, just from a per-node DaemonSet instead of a per-Pod privileged init container. The output is identical; only the privilege model differs.
  • "A TCP service just has retries disabled by default." Not disabled — unreachable. Retries, fault injection, and CORS all live in the HTTP filter chain, which a Service whose port isn't named http-*/grpc-* never reaches at all.
  • "If Envoy isn't responding to proxy-config, the sidecar itself must be broken." Not always — if pilot-agent can't get a certificate from istiod, Envoy never even starts, so every proxy-config command goes quiet even though the "Envoy" container shows as running.

💼 Chapter 3 — What This Means For Your Daily Work

  • Check proxy sync daily: istioctl proxy-status — all proxies should show SYNCED, never STALE/NOT SENT
  • Know the ports cold: 15001 (outbound), 15006 (inbound), 15090 (raw stats), 15020 (Prometheus scrapes this one)
  • Debug in the golden order: INJECTION → SYNC → CONFIG → TRAFFIC — check the namespace label and webhook before you ever open a YAML file
  • Trust the plane split: data plane keeps serving traffic even when istiod is down; only NEW pods and NEW config changes are affected
  • Know what pods run in istio-system and roughly what each one costs — istiod, gateways, Kiali/Prometheus/Grafana/Jaeger
  • Pick the right injection path: istio-init by default, istio-cni on any cluster enforcing restricted Pod Security
  • For ICA: "Check sync" = proxy-status. "How traffic gets to Envoy" = iptables (or istio-cni). "Who issues certs" = Citadel. "Feature does nothing" = check the Service port name (3.9).
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 3

Seven quick-fire phrase-to-command mappings pulled from anihpj's own architecture-debugging history — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Check if all proxies are synced" = istioctl proxy-status
  • "What port does Envoy listen on for inbound traffic?" = 15006
  • "How does traffic get redirected to Envoy?" = iptables rules written by istio-init (or the istio-cni-node DaemonSet)
  • "What runs in istio-system namespace?" = istiod, ingressgateway, optional addons
  • "Traffic not routing — debug order?" = endpoint → cluster → route → listener (bottom-up through EDS/CDS/RDS/LDS)
  • "Verify a workload certificate" = istioctl proxy-config secret (istioctl authn tls-check was REMOVED — never pick it)
  • "Which port does Prometheus scrape?" = 15020 (istio-agent, merged app + Envoy metrics; 15090 is the raw Envoy stats port)

🧠 Chapter 3 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
In one sentence each, what does the data plane own versus what does the control plane own in Istio's architecture?
Show Answer
Answer
PlaneOwns
Data planeEvery Envoy sidecar proxy running alongside your Pods — carries and enforces real traffic, millions of requests per second, directly in the hot path
Control planeistiod, the single binary that computes configuration from CRDs and pushes it out — never touches a live packet itself
Explanation

This split is why the mesh degrades gracefully: istiod is stateless configuration logic, while Envoy is the stateful thing actually holding connections. "Control plane = WHAT to do, data plane = DO it" is the one-line version worth memorizing for the exam.

Q2
Name istiod's four merged sub-components and, in one phrase each, what each one is responsible for.
Show Answer
Answer
Sub-componentResponsible for
PilotConverting CRDs (VirtualService, DestinationRule, Gateway) into Envoy xDS config and pushing it
CitadelIssuing and auto-rotating SPIFFE/X.509 mTLS certificates
GalleyValidating Istio YAML before Pilot ever sees it
Sidecar InjectorRunning the mutating admission webhook that adds istio-proxy to new Pods
Explanation

Before Istio 1.5 these were 4 separate pods with their own gRPC calls between them. The ICA exam may still reference the old names even though all four now run in-process inside one istiod binary.

Q3
Name all five xDS discovery services and, in a few words each, what each one configures inside Envoy.
Show Answer
Answer
ServiceConfigures
LDSListeners — which ports Envoy binds
RDSRoutes — VirtualService host/path rules
CDSClusters — upstream services and subsets
EDSEndpoints — which pod IPs back a cluster
SDSSecrets — mTLS certs streamed straight into memory, never touching disk
Explanation

xDS is the umbrella name for all five. Most guides only mention the first four (LDS/RDS/CDS/EDS) — SDS is easy to forget but is exactly what istioctl proxy-config secret reads.

Q4
Envoy plays "three roles" on every single packet it handles. Name all three and one thing each one does.
Show Answer
Answer
RoleWhat it does
Traffic ProxyIntercepts via iptables and load-balances to a healthy endpoint
Policy Enforcement PointOriginates/terminates mTLS and evaluates AuthorizationPolicy
Telemetry CollectorRecords RED metrics and stamps trace headers
Explanation

None of the three is optional and all three run on the same request inside the same istio-proxy container — a packet that skips policy enforcement never reaches telemetry, and one that isn't measured still gets proxied.

Q5
Sidecar injection modifies a Pod spec in two separate ways. Name both additions and explain the difference between them.
Show Answer
Answer
AdditionLifecycle
istio-init init containerRuns once, as root, before any other container starts — writes the iptables NAT rules, then exits
istio-proxy sidecar containerLong-running (pilot-agent + Envoy) — stays alive for the Pod's entire lifetime
Explanation

Mixing these two up is a common exam trap: istio-init is one-shot setup plumbing that exits immediately (you'll see it as "0/1, Completed" in kubectl describe); istio-proxy is the persistent second container behind the "2/2 READY" count.

Q6
Which port does INBOUND traffic get redirected to, and which port handles OUTBOUND traffic?
Show Answer
Answer
Directioniptables chainRedirected to port
InboundPREROUTING15006
OutboundOUTPUT15001

Envoy's own traffic (UID 1337) is exempted from both redirects to avoid a loop.

Explanation

These two are frequently swapped by mistake on the exam and in diagrams — memorize them as a pair: PREROUTING (inbound) → 15006, OUTPUT (outbound) → 15001.

Q7
Besides istiod, name the other components that can run in the istio-system namespace, and which ones ship bundled with an install profile.
Show Answer
Answer
ComponentBundled by an install profile?
istio-ingressgatewayYes — north-south inbound traffic, a LoadBalancer Service
istio-egressgatewayYes, but optional — controlled outbound
Kiali / Prometheus / Grafana / JaegerNever — always a separate samples/addons/ apply, regardless of profile
Explanation

"Which pods appear after istioctl install --set profile=demo -y?" is a real exam trap — the answer is istiod + 2 gateways (3 pods), never the dashboards. Confirm with kubectl get pods -n istio-system.

Q8
State the golden debugging order for a broken sidecar, and explain why the order itself matters.
Show Answer
Answer
  1. INJECTION — does the Pod even have a sidecar?
  2. SYNC — is that sidecar SYNCED with istiod?
  3. CONFIG — does Envoy's own xDS table hold the rule you expect?
  4. TRAFFIC — only now, test the actual request behavior.

Never start by editing YAML blindly — observe first, change second.

Explanation

Each stage is a precondition for the next being meaningful: a proxy that was never injected can't be SYNCED; one that's STALE can't be trusted to reflect CONFIG; and CONFIG that never reached Envoy can't explain a TRAFFIC symptom. Skipping ahead wastes time chasing a downstream symptom of an upstream cause.

Q9
Put Envoy's three filter layers in their fixed processing order, and name one filter that lives in each layer.
Show Answer
Answer
  1. Listener filters — connection-level peeking, e.g. tls_inspector
  2. Network filters (L4, run for ALL traffic) — e.g. rbac
  3. HTTP filters (L7, only if http_connection_manager ran) — e.g. router, always last
Explanation

This order is exactly why plain TCP services get no retries or fault injection: those features live in the HTTP filter layer, which a raw TCP connection never reaches — it stops after the network filter layer installs tcp_proxy instead of http_connection_manager.

Q10
Two processes run inside every istio-proxy container. Name both and state which one starts first.
Show Answer
Answer
ProcessStartsRole
pilot-agent (istio-agent)1stBuilds Envoy's bootstrap config, gets its certificate signed by istiod
Envoy2ndExecs as pilot-agent's child process, opens its own xDS stream
Explanation

This ordering explains a common failure signature: if pilot-agent can't reach istiod for a cert, kubectl logs -c istio-proxy shows a pilot-agent error and every istioctl proxy-config command goes quiet — because Envoy itself never finished starting.

⚙️ Chapter 3 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
You apply a new VirtualService but traffic still follows old routing rules. You suspect config didn't propagate. Task: Write the command to check proxy sync status for ALL proxies in the anihpj namespace. Explain what SYNCED, STALE, and NOT SENT mean. Then run the 4 proxy-config commands to verify the VirtualService rules are actually in Envoy's tables. Explain which xDS service each command maps to.
Show Answer
Answer
# Check ALL proxy sync status
istioctl proxy-status -n anihpj
# SYNCED  = proxy has latest config from istiod ✅
# STALE   = proxy hasn't acknowledged in a while ⚠️
# NOT SENT = istiod couldn't reach the proxy ❌

# Verify config is actually in Envoy (bottom-up debug):
istioctl pc endpoint deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj  # EDS: pod IPs
istioctl pc cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj   # CDS: upstream services
istioctl pc route deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj     # RDS: VirtualService rules
istioctl pc listener deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj  # LDS: ports (15001, 15006)

Mapping: EDS=endpoints, CDS=DestinationRule, RDS=VirtualService, LDS=listeners. If your VS rule doesn't appear in pc route, istiod didn't push it.

Explanation

These 4 commands are your window into Envoy's brain. They map directly to the xDS API: EDS (Endpoint Discovery) shows pod IPs, CDS (Cluster Discovery) shows upstream services + subsets, RDS (Route Discovery) shows VirtualService rules, LDS (Listener Discovery) shows ports. On the ICA exam, ALWAYS debug bottom-up: check endpoints exist first, then clusters, then routes, then listeners. If endpoints are empty → no healthy pods. If route is missing → VS not applied. If listener is missing → sidecar not injected properly.

Q2
You SSH into a pod and inspect it. You see 3 containers: jobpost-api, istio-proxy, and an init container istio-init that already exited. Task: Identify which istiod sub-component (Pilot, Citadel, or Galley) is responsible for each of the following: (a) injecting the sidecar, (b) issuing the SPIFFE certificate, (c) pushing VirtualService config via xDS. Then explain why these three were merged into one istiod binary in Istio 1.5 and list what the OLD architecture looked like (4 pods vs 1 pod).
Show Answer
Answer
TaskComponentWhat It Does
(a) Sidecar injectionSidecar InjectorRuns the MutatingWebhook; Galley's Validating webhook already rejected the CRD here if malformed
(b) SPIFFE certsCitadelCertificate Authority; issues X.509 SVIDs; auto-rotates every 24h
(c) xDS config pushPilotWatches CRDs → converts to Envoy config → pushes via gRPC xDS

OLD architecture (Istio < 1.5): 4 separate pods — pilot (100m/256Mi), citadel (50m/128Mi), galley (50m/128Mi), sidecar-injector (50m/128Mi). Complex gRPC between them. NEW (1.5+): 1 istiod pod (4-in-1). Fewer failure modes, in-process calls (faster), simpler upgrades.

Explanation

The ICA exam may reference the OLD names (Pilot, Citadel, Galley, sidecar injector). Know that they still exist as sub-components inside istiod. Pilot = traffic configuration brain (CRDs → xDS). Citadel = security brain (SPIFFE certs, mTLS keys). Galley = quality gate (validates YAML). Sidecar injector = the mutating webhook that actually adds the containers. The merge to istiod eliminated 3 failure domains and 3 gRPC connections between components. On the exam, if asked "which component does X," the answer is the sub-component name, even though they all run in one binary now.

Q3
You're debugging why jobpost-api can't connect to user-service. You exec into the pod and run curl http://user-service:80/users/ — it connects fine. But the Django app (running as UID 1000) can't reach user-service. Task: Explain how iptables redirect works. Why did your curl work but Django fails? Write the command to view the iptables rules inside the Envoy container. Explain what would happen if the UID 1337 exemption didn't exist.
Show Answer
Answer

Why curl works but Django fails: When you exec into the pod, you typically run as root (UID 0). iptables rules redirect traffic based on UID — --uid-owner 1337 is EXEMPTED (Envoy's own traffic). Your root curl may bypass the redirect depending on how iptables is configured. Django runs as non-root (UID 1000) — its traffic IS caught by iptables and redirected to Envoy on port 15001.

# View iptables rules inside istio-proxy container:
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- \
  iptables -t nat -L -n -v

# Key rules:
# OUTPUT chain: redirect ALL TCP (except UID 1337) → port 15001
# PREROUTING chain: redirect ALL inbound TCP → port 15006

# Check UID 1337 exemption (critical!):
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- id
# uid=1337(istio-proxy) gid=1337(istio-proxy)

Without UID 1337 exemption: Envoy's own outbound traffic (to other Envoy proxies) would be caught by iptables and redirected back to ITSELF on port 15001 → infinite loop → Envoy crashes. The exemption is NOT optional.

Explanation

iptables operates at kernel level — transparent to applications. When Django calls requests.get("http://user-service"), the kernel resolves user-service to a ClusterIP, creates an outbound TCP packet, and the OUTPUT chain catches it: "Not from UID 1337? → REDIRECT to 127.0.0.1:15001." Envoy receives it, applies routing/mTLS/retry policies, and sends it to the real user-service pod. The entire redirect is invisible to Django — it thinks it connected directly to user-service on port 80. On the ICA exam, the istio-init container sets up these rules. UID 1337 is the Envoy process — always exempt.

Q4
Your production cluster runs 500 pods with Istio sidecars. istiod crashes at 3 AM. Task: Explain exactly what happens to: (a) the 500 existing pods and their traffic, (b) a new Deployment you try to roll out, (c) a VirtualService change you try to apply. Write the command to scale istiod to 3 replicas with a PodDisruptionBudget of minAvailable=2. Explain why separating control plane from data plane is the key architectural decision behind this resilience.
Show Answer
Answer
ScenarioResult
(a) 500 existing pods✅ Traffic flows NORMALLY. Envoy uses cached config in memory.
(b) New deployment❌ Pods stuck in Init. Can't get SPIFFE cert or config from istiod.
(c) VS change❌ Not propagated. No istiod to process the CRD and push via xDS.
 
# Scale to 3 replicas
kubectl scale deployment istiod -n istio-system --replicas=3

# PodDisruptionBudget: ensure at least 2 istiod pods are always available
kubectl create pdb istiod-pdb -n istio-system \
  --selector=app=istiod --min-available=2
Explanation

This is the architectural genius of Istio: control plane (brain) and data plane (muscles) are SEPARATED. If the brain (istiod) dies, the muscles (Envoy sidecars) keep working with their last-known-good configuration. This is like an airplane's autopilot — if air traffic control goes down, planes already in the air continue flying. With 3 replicas + PDB minAvailable=2, even if one node fails and istiod is rolling-updated, at least 2 copies are always available. On the ICA exam: "Does istiod failure cause traffic interruption?" → NO (for existing traffic). YES (for new pods and config changes).

Q5
You labeled the anihpj namespace with istio-injection=enabled and applied a new Deployment. Pods show 2/2 — sidecar injected. But one pod needs to NOT have a sidecar (it's a database migration job that must connect directly). Task: Write the per-pod annotation to opt OUT of sidecar injection while keeping namespace-level injection enabled for other pods. Then write the annotation to opt IN for a specific pod in an unlabeled namespace. Explain when to use namespace-level vs per-pod injection.
Show Answer
Answer
# OPT OUT: Pod in labeled namespace → no sidecar
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: db-migration-job
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    sidecar.istio.io/inject: "false"    # ← Opt OUT
spec:
  # ... job container ...

# OPT IN: Pod in unlabeled namespace → WITH sidecar
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: special-pod
  namespace: default
  annotations:
    sidecar.istio.io/inject: "true"     # ← Opt IN
spec:
  # ... app container ...

# Verify injection status:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj db-migration-job
# Expected: READY 1/1 (no sidecar!)
kubectl get pods -n default special-pod
# Expected: READY 2/2 (sidecar injected!)

When to use namespace-level: All pods in the namespace should be meshed (production default). When to use per-pod: Gradual migration (inject one by one), exceptions (jobs, init containers), or testing.

Explanation

The annotation sidecar.istio.io/inject OVERRIDES the namespace label. Priority: per-pod annotation > namespace label. "false" in a labeled namespace = no injection. "true" in an unlabeled namespace = injection for only that pod. On the ICA exam, you may need to deploy a pod that must NOT have a sidecar (database migration, network test, init-only job). The annotation is the correct approach — don't remove the namespace label. Also: injection is a ONE-TIME event at pod CREATION. Adding the annotation to a running pod does nothing — you must delete and recreate it.

Q6
You run istioctl proxy-status and see one proxy showing STALE. The pod is Running (2/2) and serving traffic, but the config is from 10 minutes ago. Task: Explain what STALE means vs SYNCED vs NOT SENT. Write the commands to: (a) check if the proxy has the latest config version, (b) verify istiod can reach the proxy on port 15012, (c) force the proxy to reconnect. Explain what could cause STALE status.
Show Answer
Answer
# (a) Check config versions
istioctl proxy-status deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj
# Shows CDS/LDS/EDS/RDS version numbers
# Compare with istiod's current version

# (b) Verify istiod→proxy connectivity
kubectl exec deploy/istiod -n istio-system -- \
  nc -zv <proxy-pod-ip> 15012
# Port 15012 = xDS gRPC (istiod→Envoy control channel)

# (c) Force proxy reconnect by restarting the sidecar
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- \
  curl -X POST localhost:15000/quitquitquit
# Envoy restarts and reconnects to istiod automatically

# Alternative: Delete the pod
kubectl delete pod <pod-name> -n anihpj

STALE causes: Network policy blocking port 15012, istiod overloaded (too many proxies), Envoy process hung, or temporary network blip that prevented the periodic heartbeat acknowledgment.

Explanation

SYNCED = proxy acknowledged latest config from istiod. STALE = proxy hasn't acknowledged in a while (config may still be current, but istiod can't confirm). NOT SENT = istiod couldn't even establish the connection. STALE is the most common — the proxy is still working with its last config but isn't getting updates. On the ICA exam, always check proxy-status after applying config changes. If a proxy is STALE, new VirtualService/DestinationRule changes won't reach it. Fix: restart the sidecar or delete the pod.

Q7
You're writing an AuthorizationPolicy that restricts access based on service identity. Task: Write the complete SPIFFE identity for a pod in the anihpj namespace using the jobpost-api service account. Break down each component: trust domain, namespace, service account. Then write the command to verify a specific pod's SPIFFE certificate is valid and has the correct identity. Explain why SPIFFE identities are more secure than IP-based access control.
Show Answer
Answer

SPIFFE Identity: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api

ComponentValueMeaning
Trust Domaincluster.localThe root of trust for this mesh
Namespacens/anihpjKubernetes namespace
Service Accountsa/jobpost-apiKubernetes ServiceAccount
 
# Verify SPIFFE certificate for a pod:
istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj

# One-pod mesh summary, including effective mTLS mode:
istioctl x describe pod jobpost-api-7d9f8b6c5-x2k4p -n anihpj

SPIFFE vs IP: IP can be spoofed (ARP poisoning, IP hijacking). SPIFFE certificate is cryptographic — tied to the ServiceAccount, signed by istiod's CA, impossible to forge without the private key.

Explanation

SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone) is the identity standard that underpins Istio's zero-trust model. Every workload gets a cryptographically verifiable identity tied to its Kubernetes ServiceAccount — not its IP address. An attacker can spoof an IP; they CANNOT spoof a SPIFFE certificate. The trust domain (cluster.local) is configurable — multi-cluster meshes share the same trust domain for cross-cluster mTLS. On the ICA exam, AuthorizationPolicy can match principals using the full SPIFFE identity or patterns like cluster.local/ns/anihpj/*. Note: istioctl authn tls-check was removed years ago — never answer with it.

Q8
You deploy a new pod in the anihpj namespace. It shows 1/1. The namespace IS labeled istio-injection=enabled. Other pods in the same namespace show 2/2. Task: List ALL possible causes (minimum 4) and the diagnostic command for each. Write a systematic debugging checklist in the CORRECT order. Include the webhook check, namespace label verification, and the command to test injection by simulating a pod creation.
Show Answer
Answer
# DEBUG CHECKLIST (in order):
# 1. Verify namespace label (most common miss)
kubectl get namespace anihpj --show-labels | grep istio-injection
# Expected: istio-injection=enabled

# 2. Verify webhook exists
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector
# Expected: NAME=istio-sidecar-injector, WEBHOOKS=1

# 3. Check per-pod annotation (overrides namespace label)
kubectl get pod <name> -n anihpj -o yaml | grep sidecar.istio.io/inject
# If shows "false" → pod opted OUT

# 4. Check if Deployment has injection disabled at template level
kubectl get deployment jobpost-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep sidecar.istio.io/inject

# 5. Test injection by simulating pod creation:
kubectl apply -f - --dry-run=server -o yaml <<EOF | grep istio-proxy
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-inject
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    app: test
spec:
  containers:
  - name: test
    image: nginx
EOF
# If output includes "istio-proxy" → injection IS working
Explanation

This is THE most-asked ICA troubleshooting scenario. The order matters: start with the simplest check (namespace label), then webhook availability, then per-pod overrides, then Deployment template overrides. The --dry-run=server test is the definitive check — it runs the ACTUAL webhook against your spec and shows the modified output. If the dry-run output doesn't include istio-proxy, injection is broken at the webhook level. If it does include it, the issue is specific to that pod's annotations or labels. On the ICA exam, always follow this order — don't jump to complex diagnoses first.

Q9
You need to verify that Envoy is receiving configuration from istiod for a specific service. Task: Write the 4 istioctl proxy-config commands (listener, cluster, route, endpoint) for the jobpost-api deployment. For each command, explain what SUCCESS looks like. Then show how to use these commands to diagnose why traffic to user-service is getting 503s — what would you check and in what order?
Show Answer
Answer
# 1. LISTENER: Which ports is Envoy listening on?
istioctl pc listener deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj
# ✅ SUCCESS: Shows 0.0.0.0:15001 (outbound) and 0.0.0.0:15006 (inbound)
# ❌ MISSING: Sidecar not injected or iptables not configured

# 2. CLUSTER: Which upstream services does Envoy know about?
istioctl pc cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep user-service
# ✅ SUCCESS: Shows "outbound|8000||user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
# ❌ MISSING: Service not in mesh or ServiceEntry not created

# 3. ROUTE: How does Envoy route to user-service?
istioctl pc route deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep -A10 user-service
# ✅ SUCCESS: Shows VirtualService rules (weights, timeouts, retries)
# ❌ MISSING: VirtualService not applied or host mismatch

# 4. ENDPOINT: Which pod IPs are behind user-service?
istioctl pc endpoint deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep user-service
# ✅ SUCCESS: Shows pod IPs with HEALTHY status
# ❌ EMPTY/UNHEALTHY: Circuit breaker open or all pods down

# 503 DEBUG ORDER (bottom-up):
# ENDPOINT → CLUSTER → ROUTE → LISTENER

503 diagnosis: Always start at ENDPOINT. If healthy endpoints exist but you still get 503s, outlier detection may have ejected the destination pods from the load-balancing pool. Check outlierDetection in DestinationRule — Envoy has no "circuit breaker OPEN" state; unhealthy hosts are simply ejected for a baseEjectionTime and returned automatically afterward.

Explanation

The 4 proxy-config commands form Envoy's configuration hierarchy: ENDPOINT (pod IPs, bottom) → CLUSTER (logical service groups) → ROUTE (how requests are matched and forwarded) → LISTENER (ports, top). Debug BOTTOM-UP: if endpoints are empty, nothing else matters — the service has no healthy pods. If endpoints exist but cluster is missing, the DestinationRule isn't applied. If cluster exists but route is missing, the VirtualService isn't applied. On the ICA exam, this bottom-up approach is the FASTEST way to pinpoint routing issues.

Q10
Your security team asks you to explain how Istio prevents a compromised pod from injecting itself as a fake sidecar or intercepting traffic. Task: Explain the full Kubernetes admission chain that a Pod CREATE request goes through (kubectl → API → auth → webhooks → etcd). Explain exactly where Istio's MutatingWebhook sits in this chain. Then explain what happens if someone DELETES the istio-sidecar-injector webhook — how do you detect this, and how do you recover?
Show Answer
Answer

Kubernetes Admission Chain:

1
kubectl

Sends Pod spec to API server

2
Authentication

Who are you? (cert, token, OIDC)

3
Authorization

Are you allowed to create Pods? (RBAC)

4
Mutating Webhooks

⬅️ ISTIO INJECTS SIDECAR HERE
Pod spec MODIFIED before persistence

5
Validating Webhooks

Is the final spec valid?

6
etcd

Final modified spec persisted

# Detect: Webhook deleted
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector
# Error: not found → WEBHOOK IS GONE!

# Detect: New pods show 1/1 despite labeled namespace
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
# All new pods: READY 1/1 (no sidecar being injected)

# Recover: Reinstall Istio components
istioctl install --set profile=demo -y
# This recreates the webhook as part of istiod's configuration

# Verify:
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector
kubectl delete pod <test-pod> -n anihpj  # Force recreation
kubectl get pods -n anihpj  # Should show 2/2
Explanation

The MutatingAdmissionWebhook is Istio's injection mechanism. It runs INSIDE istiod (as the sidecar-injector sub-component). When ANY pod is created in a labeled namespace, the Kubernetes API server calls this webhook with the Pod spec. The webhook returns a MODIFIED spec (adding istio-proxy container + istio-init container). Kubernetes persists the MODIFIED spec to etcd. Your original YAML is never changed on disk — the modification is in-memory only. If the webhook is deleted, pods are created WITHOUT modification → 1/1. On the ICA exam, always check the webhook if injection suddenly stops working cluster-wide.

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 3
  • Triage in one glance: STALE/NOT SENT in istioctl proxy-status means an istiod (control-plane) problem; SYNCED-but-still-wrong means an Envoy (data-plane) problem — that split decides which half of the toolbox you open next.
  • Debug the xDS hierarchy bottom-up — EDS → CDS → RDS → LDS (3.8) — never top-down; an empty endpoint list makes every table above it irrelevant.
  • Run istioctl analyze -n anihpj BEFORE any proxy-config command — a static lint catches a typo'd host or missing subset in under a second, before you burn ten minutes reading live Envoy tables.
  • "TCP behaves like Istio isn't even there" (no retries, no fault injection) is almost always a Service port not named http-*/grpc-* (3.9) — check the port name before touching any YAML.
  • istioctl authn tls-check is a trap answer on the exam — it was removed years ago; the correct commands are istioctl x describe pod and istioctl proxy-config secret.
  • On a "no sidecar" ticket, check the webhook object before the namespace label: kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector — a broken CA bundle silently no-ops injection even when the label is correct.

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 3)

Sixteen commands, three jobs: get the sidecar landed, confirm the control plane actually delivered its config, and read the runtime when a container refuses to start. This closing reference pulls all of them into one table.

CommandWhat It Checks / Does in Chapter 3
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabledturn on auto sidecar injection (3.4)
kubectl apply --dry-run=server -o yaml -f pod.yaml | grep istio-proxyprove the injection webhook fires end-to-end (3.4)
kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injectorconfirm the injector webhook exists (3.2, 3.4)
kubectl get daemonset -n istio-system istio-cni-nodeconfirm istio-cni is active on every node (3.10)
istioctl proxy-statusper-proxy xDS state: SYNCED/STALE/NOT SENT (3.7, 3.8)
istioctl x describe pod <pod> -n anihpjone-pod mesh summary: matching VS/DR, effective mTLS (3.2, 3.7)
istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/<name> -n anihpjLDS: confirm 15001/15006 listeners are bound (3.3, 3.8)
istioctl proxy-config route deploy/<name> -n anihpjRDS: confirm a VirtualService became a route (3.3, 3.8)
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/<name> -n anihpjCDS: confirm a DestinationRule subset exists (3.3, 3.8)
istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/<name> -n anihpjEDS: confirm real pod IPs resolved, not empty (3.3, 3.8)
istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/<name> -n anihpjSDS: confirm the workload's SPIFFE cert is VALID (3.2, 3.7)
istioctl analyze -n anihpjstatic lint of all Istio config in the namespace (3.7)
kubectl logs deploy/<name> -c istio-proxy -n anihpjEnvoy/pilot-agent runtime errors (3.7, 3.11)
kubectl exec deploy/<name> -c istio-proxy -n anihpj -- idconfirm UID 1337 — the iptables exemption (3.5)
kubectl exec <pod> -c istio-proxy -n anihpj -- curl -X POST localhost:15000/quitquitquitforce Envoy to restart and re-subscribe to xDS (3.7)
kubectl delete pod <pod> -n anihpjforce re-injection or a fresh xDS handshake (3.4, 3.7)

🔬 Practice Drill 3.1 — Prove the Two Planes on Live anihpj

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Prove to yourself — with commands, not memory — that the two-plane model is really running underneath anihpj right now.

  1. (2 min) kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide — every jobpost-api/user-service/skills-service/etc pod should show 2/2 READY (data plane: sidecar present)
  2. (2 min) istioctl proxy-status — every proxy should show SYNCED, never STALE/NOT SENT (control plane: config actually delivered)
  3. (2 min) istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj — confirm both capture listeners, 15001 and 15006, exist
  4. (1 min) kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -c istio-proxy -n anihpj -- id — confirm uid=1337(istio-proxy), the UID iptables exempts (3.5)
  5. (1 min) istioctl analyze -n anihpj — confirm "No validation issues found"
Hint: Each of the five checks independently verifies a different layer — sidecar presence, xDS sync, listener binding, the iptables exemption, and static config validity — a failure in any ONE doesn't mean the others are broken.
View Solution

If all five pass, you have independently verified injection, xDS sync, the iptables exemption, and config validity — the same checks 3.7's golden debugging order walks through on a real incident. If any single one fails, that failure tells you exactly which layer to investigate next without re-running the other four.

Check yourself: could you explain, for each of the five commands, which layer it proves and which layer it does NOT prove? "SYNCED" proves istiod delivered config — it does not prove the config is the RIGHT config. That's exactly the gap 3.8's bottom-up hierarchy exists to close.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.2 — Read a Live SPIFFE Certificate, Not Just Its Status

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Don't just trust istioctl x describe pod's summary — pull the raw certificate Envoy is actually presenting and read its identity yourself, the way a security audit would.

  1. Dump the workload's SDS secrets as JSON: istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -o json
  2. Extract and base64-decode the "default" certificate's raw_bytes field.
  3. Read it with openssl x509 -noout -text and find the URI SAN.
  4. Confirm the URI SAN matches spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api exactly — namespace and service account both correct.
Hint: The certificate is inside the JSON under dynamicActiveSecrets[].secret.tlsCertificate.certificateChain.inlineBytes — that value is base64, and the decoded result is itself a PEM certificate openssl can read directly.
View Solution
decode the live SPIFFE cert
# 1-2. Pull the cert and decode it in one pipeline
istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -o json \
  | jq -r '.dynamicActiveSecrets[] | select(.name=="default") | .secret.tlsCertificate.certificateChain.inlineBytes' \
  | base64 -d > jobpost-api.pem

# 3. Read the identity out of the cert itself
openssl x509 -in jobpost-api.pem -noout -text | grep -A1 "Subject Alternative Name"
# URI:spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api

# bonus: check how much runway is left before Citadel's next rotation
openssl x509 -in jobpost-api.pem -noout -enddate

Check yourself: did the URI SAN read exactly spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api — trust domain, then namespace, then service account, in that order? A cert with the wrong namespace or service account embedded would still show "VALID CERT" in istioctl x describe pod's summary — the summary confirms the cert is well-formed and unexpired, not that it carries the identity you assumed. This is why 3.2 calls SPIFFE identity cryptographic rather than just "encrypted": you just proved the claim yourself instead of trusting a status string.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.3 — Match the Symptom to One of the Six Repeat Offenders

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

For each observation below, name which of 3.7's six repeat offenders it matches (or say "none of the six") and the exact first command you'd run — before proposing any fix:

  1. A pod shows 2/2 READY, but every call to it returns a plaintext-caller TCP connection RESET instead of an HTTP 403.
  2. A pod has been Running for 10 minutes but kubectl get pods still shows 0/2, and describe shows no container start events for istio-proxy at all.
  3. A teammate says "mTLS suddenly broke mesh-wide" — every service reports handshake failures citing an untrusted issuer.
  4. A newly scaled-up replica of skills-service is 2/2 Running, but istioctl proxy-status doesn't list it at all, even 5 minutes later.
Hint: "Not listed in proxy-status at all" is a different failure mode than "listed but STALE" — one means the proxy never established a control-plane connection in the first place.
View Solution
#OffenderFirst command
1□4 — plaintext caller gets TCP RESET, not 403istioctl x describe pod <pod> — check effective mTLS mode is STRICT
2□5 — CrashLoopBackOff / stuck in Initkubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy -n anihpj — read why istio-proxy never started
3□6 — mTLS errors: unknown identity / certificate expiredistioctl proxy-config secret deploy/<name> -n anihpj — check CA/root cert status mesh-wide
4None of the six — this is the injection webhook path, not synckubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels then kubectl get mutatingwebhookconfiguration istio-sidecar-injector — a proxy istiod never heard from was likely never injected against a live webhook

Check yourself: did you correctly separate #4 from the six? The six repeat offenders in 3.7's table all assume a sidecar already exists and is at least attempting to talk to istiod. "Never appears in proxy-status" is a step earlier than any of them — it belongs to the INJECTION phase of the golden debugging order, not SYNC. Conflating "never connected" with "connected but STALE" is one of the most common mistakes on the ICA troubleshooting domain.

🔬 Practice Drill 3.4 — Prove Which Injection Mechanism Your Cluster Actually Uses

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Don't assume — prove, with two commands, whether a live cluster runs the default istio-init path (3.5) or the istio-cni plugin (3.10) for injected Pods.

  1. Check whether the CNI DaemonSet exists and is fully scheduled: kubectl get daemonset -n istio-system istio-cni-node
  2. Pick any meshed Pod and list its initContainers by name: kubectl get pod <pod> -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.initContainers[*].name}'
  3. State the rule connecting the two outputs, then predict what you'd see on a cluster enforcing Pod Security "restricted" without CNI enabled.
Hint: The two commands should agree with each other — if the DaemonSet exists and is fully scheduled, no injected Pod should list istio-init among its init containers, and vice versa.
View Solution
istio-init vs istio-cni, proven not assumed
# 1. Is the CNI DaemonSet installed and healthy?
kubectl get daemonset -n istio-system istio-cni-node
# DESIRED = CURRENT = READY = node count  → CNI mode is active
# "not found"                             → default istio-init mode

# 2. Does this Pod carry an istio-init init container?
kubectl get pod <pod> -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.initContainers[*].name}'
# "istio-init"   → istio-init mode (privileged per-Pod init container)
# (empty)        → istio-cni mode (rules already written by the node DaemonSet)

Check yourself: a cluster with Pod Security "restricted" enforced and NO istio-cni DaemonSet would show every new injected Pod stuck with an istio-init entry that fails on NET_ADMIN/NET_RAW denial — exactly 3.10's real day-27 incident. Predicting that failure BEFORE it happens, from these two commands alone, is the actual skill — not memorizing that "istio-cni exists."

🔬 Practice Drill 3.5 — Sketch the 6-Waypoint Journey, Timed

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

In 5 minutes, from memory, sketch the UTH's 6-waypoint diagram — Client through Gateway Envoy, network filters, HTTP filters, cluster selection, to the Django container — labeling each waypoint L4 or L7. Do NOT reopen the UTH until you finish.

Hint: Waypoints 3 and 4 are the pair most people merge into one step — network filters (L4, mTLS/authz) and HTTP filters (L7, routing/retries) are two SEPARATE waypoints that always run in that order.
View Solution

Compare your sketch against the UTH's 6-waypoint diagram. The waypoint most people drop entirely: upstream cluster selection (waypoint 5) — it feels like part of "routing" but is actually a separate CDS+EDS+load-balancing step that happens AFTER the HTTP router filter picks a route, not during it.

Check yourself: did you correctly mark network filters (waypoint 3) as running BEFORE HTTP filters (waypoint 4), never the reverse? This ordering is why mTLS/AuthorizationPolicy denials never reach application logs — they're rejected at L4, before HTTP parsing (and therefore before any L7 logging) ever happens.

🖼️ Chapter 3 in One Picture — The Whole Chapter, One Request
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ kubectl apply -f virtualservice.yaml                               │
│         │                                                          │
│         ▼                                                          │
│ 🧠 CONTROL PLANE (3.1-3.3): istiod's Pilot/Citadel/Galley/injector │
│    convert the CRD and push LDS/RDS/CDS/EDS/SDS over xDS gRPC      │
│         │                                                          │
│         ▼                                                          │
│ 🔷 SIDECAR ALREADY LANDED (3.4-3.5, 3.10): mutating webhook added  │
│    istio-proxy; iptables (or istio-cni) redirect 15001/15006       │
│         │                                                          │
│         ▼                                                          │
│ 📦 CLUSTER INVENTORY + LIVE READS (3.6-3.8): every pod istiod      │
│    runs, and what istioctl proxy-status/proxy-config inspect       │
│         │                                                          │
│         ▼                                                          │
│ 🔒 FILTER CHAIN ENFORCES IT (3.9): mTLS + rbac, then HTTP          │
│    filters, router always last -- routed AND secured               │
│         │                                                          │
│         ▼                                                          │
│ ⚙️ pilot-agent (3.11) kept certs + Envoy's bootstrap fresh the     │
│    whole time, underneath every hop above                          │
│         │                                                          │
│         ▼                                                          │
│ ✅ jobpost-api request returns -- encrypted, routed, measured       │
│         │                                                          │
│         └──▶ still wrong? loop back to 3.7's golden debug order    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Chapter 3 pried open the black box Chapter 2 left closed: a YAML change wakes up the control plane (3.1-3.3), whose istiod sub-components — Pilot, Citadel, Galley, and the sidecar injector — convert that CRD and push it over xDS to sidecars that only exist because injection and iptables wired them in ahead of time (3.4-3.5, 3.10).

The next packet then walks that sidecar's filter chain and comes out the other side encrypted, authorized, and measured (3.9), kept alive the whole time by pilot-agent underneath (3.11), on top of the exact component inventory 3.6 named — and whenever any of that breaks, 3.7-3.8 hand you the ordered checklist to find out which hop failed. Nothing here changed jobpost-api's Django code; what changed is that "the mesh is broken" now decomposes into eleven concrete, checkable hops instead of one unsolvable coin flip.

Chapter 4: Installing and Configuring Istio

Chapter 3 opened the hood on istiod and Envoy and showed you the theory: the control plane pushes xDS, iptables redirects traffic, and a sidecar rides shotgun with every app container. Chapter 4 is where that theory has to survive contact with a real cluster. Every one of anihpj's seven services — jobpost-api, user-service, skills-service, location-service, notification-service, auth-service, search-service — has to be labeled, injected, verified, and PROVEN to route traffic through Envoy before any of Chapter 3's architecture matters in practice. Pick the wrong profile and you either strand a lab cluster without an egress gateway or waste a production node group's CPU on gateways nobody asked for — and no profile, not even demo, ever installs Kiali or Jaeger for you; skip the separate `samples/addons/` step and every dashboard command fails regardless of profile. Skip the port-naming convention on a single Service and that one service silently falls back to raw TCP with no retries, no canary weights, and no per-route metrics — a bug that looks like "Istio isn't working" but is really "Istio never got the chance to work."

"You understand istiod and Envoy on paper — but does a real cluster with anihpj's 7 services actually come up clean, or does it half-install and leave you debugging a webhook timeout at 2am?" This chapter turns istioctl, Helm, IstioOperator, ambient mode, the CNI plugin, and Pod Security Admission into one coherent decision: how do you stand up a mesh for anihpj that is both correct today and defensible under a security or platform review tomorrow.

🟢→🟡 Beginner to Intermediate ⏱️ ~3 hours 🛠️ Hands-On 🎯 Installation

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Install Istio on a cluster with istioctl using the correct profile for the scenario (demo, default, minimal, ambient)
  • ✅ Enable and verify sidecar injection for the anihpj namespace, confirming 2/2 READY across all 7 services
  • ✅ Run istioctl proxy-status, istioctl analyze, and a live curl test to PROVE the mesh is routing traffic — not just that pods are Running
  • ✅ Install the identical control plane using Helm's three-chart pipeline (base → istiod → gateway) and explain when Helm beats istioctl
  • ✅ Stand up ambient mode for anihpj, label the namespace correctly, and read the 1/1-vs-2/2 signal to tell which data plane is active
  • ✅ Decide when the Istio CNI plugin and Pod Security Admission's restricted level are required, and in what order to roll them out
  • ✅ Diagnose the 5 most common install failures (Pending pods, webhook timeout, 1/1 instead of 2/2, analyze warnings, STALE proxy-status) from the symptom alone

💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 4
  • "Install Istio with ALL observability tools" = istioctl install --set profile=demo -y THEN kubectl apply -f samples/addons/ — two steps, no single flag does it
  • "Enable injection" = kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled
  • "Verify injection" = pods show 2/2 under READY
  • "Check config for errors" = istioctl analyze -n <namespace>
  • Port naming is CRITICAL: must start with "http", "grpc", "tcp", or "tls"
  • "Check compatibility before installing/upgrading, read-only" = istioctl x precheck
  • "Remove Istio completely, CRDs included" = istioctl uninstall --purge -y then delete the istio-system namespace

4.1 Prerequisites & Cluster RequirementsWhat does my cluster need before installing Istio?Kubernetes 1.28+, kubectl pointed at the cluster, and ~1.2 CPU / 2.9Gi RAM of overhead for anihpj's 7 sidecars.
4.2 Installing istioctl (The CLI)How do I get the Istio command-line tool?Download via istio.io/downloadIstio, add its bin/ to PATH, verify with istioctl version.
4.3 Istio Installation ProfilesWhich built-in preset should I install?7 profiles — demo for learning/labs, default for production, ambient for sidecar-free.
4.4 Step-by-Step: Install for anihpjWhat's the exact command sequence to stand up the mesh?7 steps: verify cluster → install → verify pods → label namespace → deploy → verify 2/2 → open dashboards.
4.5 Verifying Istio is WorkingHow do I prove the install worked, not just that pods are Running?istioctl proxy-status (SYNCED), istioctl analyze (no issues), and a live curl through the mesh.
4.6 The anihpj Deployment with IstioWhat YAML rules does Istio require of my Deployment/Service?app + version labels, and http/grpc/tcp/tls-prefixed port names — get either wrong and Istio silently falls back to raw TCP.
4.7 Profiles — Which One for Which ScenarioGiven this scenario, which profile is correct?Match the ask to the preset: learning=demo, production=default, CI/CD=minimal, sidecar-free=ambient.

4.9 Troubleshooting Installation IssuesThe install or injection looks broken — where do I look first?Work bottom-up: scheduler → control plane → webhook → sidecar → config → traffic; kubectl describe first.
4.10 Installing Istio with HelmHow do I install the identical mesh with Helm instead of istioctl?Three charts in strict order: base (CRDs only) → istiod (control plane) → gateway (data plane).
4.11 Installing Istio in Ambient ModeHow do I install a sidecar-free mesh, and how do I know it took?profile=ambient plus the dataplane-mode=ambient label; pods stay 1/1 while a shared ztunnel does the work.

4.2 Installing istioctl (The Istio CLI)

istioctl is Istio's command-line tool — like kubectl but for Istio operations. You'll use it to install, analyze, debug, and open dashboards.

bash — Installing istioctl 

# Linux / macOS
curl -L https://istio.io/downloadIstio | sh -
cd istio-1.22.*
export PATH=$PWD/bin:$PATH

# Windows (PowerShell)
Invoke-WebRequest https://istio.io/downloadIstio -OutFile istio.zip
Expand-Archive istio.zip
# Add .\istio-1.22.*\bin to your PATH

# Verify installation
istioctl version
# → client version: 1.22.0
📥
istioctl install

Install Istio on cluster. Use --set profile=demo for learning.

🔍

📋

Check if all proxies are SYNCED with istiod. STALE = problem.

Inspect Envoy config: cluster, listener, route, endpoint.

None of the 7 profiles below ever install Kiali, Jaeger, Prometheus, or Grafana — those are observability add-ons, always installed by a separate kubectl apply -f samples/addons/ step regardless of which profile you chose (4.7 covers this in full).

📖 Profile Deep Dive

remote: For multi-cluster — connects to an external control plane. No local istiod. empty: Nothing pre-configured — you add every component manually via IstioOperator. ambient: Sidecar-free mesh using ztunnel (per-node) + waypoint proxies. preview: Experimental features for testing upcoming releases — NEVER use in production.

⚠️ Important

demo profile is for LEARNING only — NOT production! It installs an ingress AND egress gateway with no resource limits, which is convenient for a lab but wasteful at scale. It still does NOT include Kiali/Jaeger/Prometheus/Grafana — that's a separate samples/addons/ apply no matter which profile you use. Use default for production.

4.4 Step-by-Step: Install Istio for anihpj

Follow these 7 steps to go from zero to a fully operational Istio mesh with anihpj running inside it.

1
Verify Cluster

kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes

2
Install Istio + Addons

istioctl install
+ samples/addons/

3
Verify Pods

kubectl get pods
-n istio-system

4
Label Namespace

istio-injection=enabled

5
Deploy anihpj

kubectl apply -f
anihpj/k8s/

Verify 2/2

-n anihpj

Dashboards

kiali

bash — Complete Installation 

# Step 1: Verify cluster is ready
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes

# Step 2a: Install Istio with demo profile (istiod + ingress + egress ONLY — 3 pods)
istioctl install --set profile=demo -y

# Step 2b: Addons are a SEPARATE step — no profile installs them
kubectl apply -f samples/addons/
# installs Kiali, Jaeger, Prometheus, and Grafana as their own Deployments

# Step 3: Verify installation (should show 7 pods running, from 2a + 2b combined)
kubectl get pods -n istio-system
kubectl get svc -n istio-system      # ← Check services too!
# NAME                                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
# istiod-7d7f9c7b8c-x4k2z               1/1     Running   0
# istio-ingressgateway-6d99ff9d4-9xklq   1/1     Running   0
# istio-egressgateway-7f9ddb899-z2p8k    1/1     Running   0
# grafana-6b7857866c-bj84p               1/1     Running   0
# jaeger-7f78b6fb65-hlfgp                1/1     Running   0
# kiali-7c9d5c754f-9cwq5                 1/1     Running   0
# prometheus-64fd8ccd65-nv98w            2/2     Running   0

# Step 4: Create and label anihpj namespace
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled
kubectl get namespace anihpj --show-labels  # ← Verify label applied
# NAME     STATUS   AGE   LABELS
# anihpj   Active   10s   istio-injection=enabled,...

# Step 5: Deploy anihpj (see Appendix B for full YAML)
kubectl apply -f anihpj/k8s/ -n anihpj

# Step 6: Verify sidecars injected (should show 2/2)
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
# NAME                            READY   STATUS    RESTARTS
# jobpost-api-7d4f8b9c-x2k4z    2/2     Running   0
# user-service-6c9d8f7b-m3j5y    2/2     Running   0

# Step 7: Open dashboards (only work because step 2b was run)
istioctl dashboard kiali
istioctl dashboard grafana
istioctl dashboard jaeger
🧬 HOW SIDECAR INJECTION WORKS — The Mutating Webhook
1
You Deploy

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

2
API Server

Receives Pod creation request

3
Check Label

Namespace has istio-injection=enabled?

4
Webhook

MutatingWebhookConfiguration intercepts

5
Inject

Adds istio-proxy + istio-init containers

6
Schedule

Scheduler places modified Pod on a Node

7
Run

istio-init runs first → sets iptables → app starts

💡 Key Insight: Injection is NOT retroactive. If you label a namespace AFTER pods exist, existing pods WON'T get sidecars. You must delete and recreate them. The webhook only fires on Pod creation events.

📖 Manual vs Automatic Injection

Automatic (recommended): Label the namespace → all future pods get sidecars automatically. This is what kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled does.

Manual: Use istioctl kube-inject -f deployment.yaml | kubectl apply -f -. This reads the YAML, adds the sidecar container definitions, and pipes the modified YAML to kubectl. Useful when you don't want to label a namespace or need per-pod control.

4.5 Verifying Istio is Working

✅
Proxy Sync Status

istioctl proxy-status
All pods must show SYNCED next to istiod. If any show STALE, the proxy isn't receiving config.

🔍
Inspect Proxy Config

istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj
Shows what upstream services Envoy knows about.

🩺
Validate Config

istioctl analyze -n anihpj
Catches 80% of configuration errors — missing subsets, port mismatches, VS without DR.

🧪
Traffic Test

kubectl exec -it deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- curl user-service/users/
Should return HTTP 200. Check Kiali to see the traffic flow.

✅ POST-INSTALL VERIFICATION CHECKLIST — Is Everything Working?
1️⃣
Pods Running

kubectl get pods -n istio-system
→ 3 pods Running from demo alone (istiod, ingress, egress); 7 total once samples/addons/ is also applied

2️⃣
Services Created

kubectl get svc -n istio-system
→ istiod, ingressgateway always; kiali/jaeger/prometheus/grafana ONLY if you also ran kubectl apply -f samples/addons/

3️⃣
Sidecars Injected

kubectl get pods -n anihpj
→ Every pod shows 2/2 READY

4️⃣
Proxies Synced

istioctl proxy-status
→ All proxies show SYNCED

5️⃣
Config Valid

istioctl analyze -n anihpj
→ No validation issues found

6️⃣
Traffic Flows

kubectl exec -it deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- curl -s user-service/users/
→ Returns HTTP 200 with data

💡 ICA Exam Tip

If the exam asks "verify the installation is working", run ALL of the above — in order. Start from the bottom (pods) and work up (traffic). Each step validates the layer below it. A pod showing 2/2 but proxy-status showing STALE means istiod can't reach the proxy (check port 15012).

4.6 Understanding the anihpj Deployment with Istio

Your Deployment YAML needs specific labels and port naming conventions for Istio to work correctly. Here's the annotated version:

yaml — jobpost-api Deployment (Istio-ready) 

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api      # ← Istio uses "app" label
      version: v1           # ← REQUIRED for canary subsets!
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: jobpost-api
        version: v1          # ← DestinationRule subsets match this
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: jobpost
        image: anihpj/jobpost:v1
        ports:
        - name: http          # ← MUST be "http" (Istio protocol detection)
          containerPort: 8000 # ← Port naming matters more than number
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: jobpost-api          # ← Matches Deployment label
  ports:
  - name: http                # ← MUST be "http"
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8000
⚠️ Critical Rules for ICA Exam

(1) Port names MUST start with protocol prefix: "http", "grpc", "tcp", or "tls". (2) Pods MUST have app and version labels. (3) Service selectors MUST match Deployment pod labels. Wrong port names = Istio ignores the port entirely.

4.7 Installation Profiles — Which One for Which Scenario

A profile is a named, pre-configured IstioOperator spec shipped inside istioctl — a preset that decides which components are installed and how they are tuned. The wrong profile either wastes resources (demo's extra egress gateway in production) or strands you without an ingress path (minimal in a lab that needs one) — and no profile at all saves you from the separate addons step, so "no Kiali pods found" happens regardless of which profile you picked if you skipped samples/addons/.

📖 KEY TERM — Profile

The exam's most-repeated noun in this chapter. All 7 built-ins: default, demo, minimal, remote, empty, ambient, preview. Exam tell: any ask for "all the observability tools" or "Kiali + Jaeger + Prometheus + Grafana in one install" means profile=demo AND a separate kubectl apply -f samples/addons/ — no single profile flag bundles the dashboards, on this exam or in real Istio.

ProfileInstallsUse it when…
defaultistiod + ingressgatewayProduction baseline; add tools via Helm
demoistiod + ingress + egress (addons are a separate samples/addons/ apply)Learning, labs, ICA practice — NEVER prod
minimalistiod onlyCI/CD pipeline tests, edge/IoT, tight RAM
remoteinjection webhook only (no local istiod)Secondary cluster using an external istiod
emptynothing at allBase for fully custom IstioOperator builds
ambientistiod + ztunnel + CNI (no sidecars)Sidecar-free mesh; big RAM savings per pod
previewdefault + experimental features enabledTesting upcoming features — never prod
bash — Explore Profiles Before Choosing 

istioctl profile list              # names of all 7 profiles
istioctl profile dump demo         # full IstioOperator preset
istioctl profile diff default demo # exactly what demo adds
demo

3 pods: istiod, ingressgateway, egressgateway
~700m CPU / 2.25Gi RAM
Use: Learning, evaluation, ICA exam labs — add samples/addons/ for dashboards

default

2 pods: istiod, ingressgateway
~600Mi RAM
Use: Production baseline, add tools separately

minimal

1 pod: istiod only
~300Mi RAM
Use: Resource-constrained, edge/IoT

⚠️ Important

demo profile is for LEARNING only — NOT production! It installs an ingress AND egress gateway with no resource limits, convenient for a lab but wasteful at scale. Use default for production. Neither profile installs observability tools — that's always a separate samples/addons/ apply.

📖 Real anihpj Scenario

The dev cluster runs demo plus kubectl apply -f samples/addons/ (all dashboards, 100% trace sampling); production runs default with Kiali, Prometheus and Grafana installed separately via Helm with proper persistence and HA, and trace sampling dialed down to 1%.
