5.1 What is an Istio Gateway?

A Gateway is the entry point for traffic FROM OUTSIDE the mesh. It replaces (or works alongside) a standard Kubernetes Ingress but is far more powerful. The Gateway is deployed as its own Pod — istio-ingressgateway — which is an Envoy proxy instance dedicated to edge traffic.

🗺️ GATEWAY POSITION — Internet → LB → Edge Envoy Pod → Mesh (vs Plain K8s Ingress)
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ISTIO GATEWAY PATH (anihpj)          PLAIN K8S INGRESS PATH       │
│  ───────────────────────────          ──────────────────────       │
│  🌐 Internet                          🌐 Internet                  │
│      │ GET https://api.anihpj.com         │ any Host header        │
│      ▼                                    ▼                        │
│  Cloud LoadBalancer (TCP :443)        Cloud LoadBalancer           │
│      │                                    │                        │
│      ▼                                    ▼                        │
│  🔷 istio-ingressgateway POD          📦 ingress-controller POD    │
│     (standalone Envoy proxy)          (nginx / traefik / ...)      │
│     programmed by Gateway CRD         programmed by Ingress        │
│      │ decrypt TLS, match host            │ host/path rules        │
│      ▼                                    ▼                        │
│  ═══ ENTERS THE MESH 🔒 ═══           K8s Service (kube-proxy)     │
│      │ VirtualService routing,            │                        │
│      │ retries, mTLS, metrics             ▼                        │
│      ▼                                Pod (no sidecar powers)      │
│  jobpost-api Pod 🔷 (sidecar)                                      │
│                                                                    │
│  → SAME position in the network path — but the Istio edge pod      │
│    is a FULL Envoy: every mesh feature applies from hop one        │
│  → a K8s Ingress pod is only an HTTP router — mesh policy stops    │
│    at its door — no mTLS, no weights, no fault injection           │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📦
Kubernetes Ingress
  • ✅ Simple host/path routing
  • ❌ No header manipulation
  • ❌ No mTLS termination
  • ❌ No weighted routing
  • ❌ Limited TLS options
  • ❌ No egress control
🌐
Istio Gateway
  • ✅ Same host/path routing + MORE
  • ✅ Full header control
  • ✅ mTLS at the edge
  • ✅ Weight-based traffic split
  • ✅ Advanced TLS/SNI
  • ✅ Egress gateway for outbound
📖 Two Types of Gateways

IngressGateway: External traffic INTO the mesh (what we focus on). Deployed as istio-ingressgateway Pod.

EgressGateway: Controlled traffic OUT of the mesh to external APIs. Deployed as istio-egressgateway Pod. Covered in Chapter 8.

⚠️ The Gateway CRD Is Pure Configuration

The thing that actually moves packets is the istio-ingressgateway Pod — an Envoy instance. The Gateway CRD's selector labels just bind this configuration to that Pod. Wrong labels = kubectl apply accepts the YAML but NO Envoy ever receives it — a silent failure, and the classic Gateway gotcha you'll verify away in 5.2. The Gateway resource itself may live in ANY namespace; istio-system is merely a common convention, not a requirement.

5.2 Gateway YAML — Accepting Traffic for anihpj

Here's the complete annotated Gateway resource for anihpj. It accepts HTTP on port 80 and HTTPS on port 443 for anihpj.example.com.

yaml — anihpj-gateway.yaml 

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1     # ← GA API since Istio 1.22
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: anihpj-gateway          # ← name this gateway
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway       # ← which Envoy pod handles this
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 80               # ← accept HTTP on port 80
      name: http
      protocol: HTTP
    hosts:
    - "anihpj.example.com"     # ← only accept this hostname
  - port:
      number: 443              # ← accept HTTPS on port 443
      name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
    tls:
      mode: SIMPLE            # ← TLS termination at gateway
      credentialName: anihpj-tls-cert  # ← K8s secret with cert
    hosts:
    - "anihpj.example.com"
💡 Key Gateway Fields

selector.istio: ingressgateway — This targets the istio-ingressgateway Pod that Istio creates during installation. That Pod has the label istio: ingressgateway.

TLS mode SIMPLE — Standard one-way TLS. The gateway holds the certificate, client verifies it. For mutual TLS at the edge, use MUTUAL.

credentialName — References a Kubernetes Secret containing tls.crt and tls.key, read by SDS from the ingress gateway WORKLOAD's own namespace (istio-system for the default shared gateway) — NOT necessarily this Gateway resource's own namespace.

Applying the YAML is only half the job — always verify the config actually reached the edge Envoy:

🔎 VERIFY THE GATEWAY LANDED IN THE EDGE ENVOY — Two-Step Check
# step 1 — resource accepted? (necessary, NOT sufficient)
kubectl get gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpj
# NAME             AGE
# anihpj-gateway   12s   ← exists in etcd, says nothing more

# step 2 — did the edge Envoy get it? (the real test)
istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/istio-ingressgateway \
    -n istio-system
# ADDRESS  PORT  MATCH  DESTINATION
# 0.0.0.0  8080  ALL    Route: http.80   ← :80 server pushed
# 0.0.0.0  8443  SNI    Route: https.443 ← :443 + TLS pushed
# (pod ports 8080/8443 sit behind service ports 80/443)

# step 2 empty? → selector matched no pod. Check the labels:
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway
📖 kubectl get vs istioctl proxy-config — Two Different Questions

kubectl get gateway proves the API server ACCEPTED the object, nothing more — a Gateway with a wrong selector still shows up here. istioctl proxy-config listener proves the edge Envoy is actually LISTENING — the test that matters. On the ICA exam, treat a bare kubectl get as unverified until the second command confirms it.

5.3 How Gateway Connects to VirtualService

The Gateway and VirtualService work as a mandatory pair. The Gateway says "I accept this traffic" and the VirtualService says "now route it like this." They are linked by the gateways field in VirtualService.

🔗 GATEWAY + VIRTUALSERVICE — The Mandatory Two-Resource Pattern
1️⃣
STEP 1: Gateway

"I accept this traffic"

  • Listen on port 80/443
  • For host: anihpj.example.com
  • On: istio-ingressgateway Pod
2️⃣
STEP 2: VirtualService

"Now route it like this"

  • gateways: [anihpj-gateway]
  • hosts: [anihpj.example.com]
  • match: uri /jobs/*
  • route: to jobpost-api:8000
⚠️ CRITICAL RULE

Gateway WITHOUT VirtualService = traffic DROPPED. The Gateway accepts the connection but has no routing rules, so the request goes nowhere.

VirtualService without Gateway = mesh-internal routing only. The VS only applies to service-to-service calls within the mesh, not external traffic.

📖 Real anihpj Scenario — Launch Morning

The team applied the Gateway, DNS cutover went live... and every request to api.anihpj.com returned 404. kubectl showed the Gateway healthy. The cause: the VirtualService was still sitting in a git branch — the Gateway was accepting traffic with ZERO routing rules. The fix took 30 seconds: kubectl apply the VirtualService with gateways: [anihpj-gateway] — the 404s stopped instantly. Lesson: a Gateway alone NEVER routes; treat Gateway + VS as one deployment unit and always apply them together.

5.4 Common Gateway Patterns — Production-Ready Configurations

DEFINITION: a Gateway "pattern" is a ready-made spec.servers[] recipe — the three below cover ~95% of real clusters and are the exact configs the ICA exam asks you to write from scratch.

Why it matters: Gateways fail silently (wrong selector, missing secret, absent VirtualService) → starting from a known-good pattern removes whole classes of launch-day surprises for anihpj.

How it works: every pattern is just a different combination of port.protocol and the tls: block inside ONE Gateway resource:

  • Pattern 1 HTTP-only → dev clusters, quick demos
  • Pattern 2 HTTPS SIMPLE → the production baseline
  • Pattern 3 HTTP→HTTPS → production + automatic 301 upgrade

All YAML below uses apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1 — the GA API since Istio 1.22; prefer it for everything you write today.

🌐
Pattern 1: HTTP Only

Port 80, no TLS. Simple dev setup. Not for production.

port: {number:80, name:http, protocol:HTTP}
hosts: ["api.anihpj.com"]
🔒
Pattern 2: HTTPS + TLS

Port 443 with SIMPLE TLS. Production standard.

port: {number:443, name:https, protocol:HTTPS}
tls: {mode:SIMPLE, credentialName:cert}
hosts: ["api.anihpj.com"]
🔄
Pattern 3: HTTP→HTTPS Redirect

Two servers: port 80 redirects to 443.

servers:
- port:80 → redirect to 443
- port:443 → HTTPS + TLS
💡 ICA Exam Pattern

The exam frequently asks you to configure a Gateway that accepts HTTPS on port 443 for a specific hostname. Remember: selector: istio: ingressgateway is MANDATORY — without it, the Gateway config has no Envoy to bind to. The TLS secret must be in the SAME namespace as the ingress gateway WORKLOAD — istio-system for the default shared gateway — regardless of which namespace the Gateway resource itself lives in. anihpj's own Gateway lives in namespace anihpj (5.2), but its credentialName secret still belongs in istio-system, where the actual istio-ingressgateway Pod runs.

⏱️ Redirect Round-Trip — What Actually Goes Over the Wire (Pattern 3)
T=0ms:  GET http://api.anihpj.com/jobs/  ──────▶ gateway :80
T=1ms:  ◀────── 301 Moved Permanently
        Location: https://api.anihpj.com/jobs/
T=2ms:  client re-issues the request over TLS ──▶ gateway :443
T=5ms:  TLS handshake (SIMPLE) → VirtualService → jobpost-api
✅ one extra round trip on FIRST contact; browsers cache the 301
🔧 Under the Hood — httpsRedirect Skips Routing Entirely

Pilot compiles that HTTP server's tls.httpsRedirect into the listener's own route config with requireTls set, so the edge Envoy answers the 301 straight from local route state — no Cluster lookup, no RDS hand-off to a VirtualService, and no hit against jobpost-api's request metrics. The real work only happens on the second request, the one that lands on :443.

5.5 Deep Dive — TLS Handshake: SIMPLE vs MUTUAL vs PASSTHROUGH

DEFINITION: tls.mode on a Gateway server decides WHERE the TLS tunnel ends and WHO must prove their identity with a certificate.

Why it matters: pick wrong and you either break every client (MUTUAL without client certs), lose end-to-end encryption guarantees, or double-terminate TLS — the ICA tests all modes.

How it works: the gateway Envoy either TERMINATES the handshake itself (SIMPLE / MUTUAL — needs a cert secret) or forwards the still-encrypted bytes onward (PASSTHROUGH — no secret at all).

📖 Key Term — TLS Termination

The point in the connection path where an encrypted TLS tunnel is decrypted. tls.mode picks that point for a Gateway server — SIMPLE and MUTUAL terminate AT the gateway Envoy; PASSTHROUGH pushes termination all the way to the jobpost-api Pod, leaving the mesh hop encrypted the whole way.

🔐 GATEWAY TLS MODES — What Happens at Each Handshake
  SIMPLE (One-way TLS):
  Client ──SYN──▶ Gateway          Gateway presents cert → Client verifies server
  Client ◀──CERT─ Gateway          Gateway does NOT verify client identity
  Client ──DATA─▶ Gateway          ✅ Most common for public HTTPS websites

  MUTUAL (Two-way mTLS):
  Client ──SYN──▶ Gateway          Gateway presents cert → Client verifies server
  Client ◀──CERT─ Gateway          Gateway REQUESTS client certificate
  Client ──CERT─▶ Gateway          Client presents cert → Gateway verifies client
  Client ──DATA─▶ Gateway          ✅ B2B/partner APIs, high security, zero-trust

  PASSTHROUGH:
  Client ──SYN──▶ Gateway          Gateway SNI reads hostname (NO termination)
  Client ──TLS──▶ Gateway──▶Backend  TLS passes through untouched to backend
                                    ✅ End-to-end encryption, no cert at Gateway
⚠️ ICA Exam: Secret Requirements by Mode

SIMPLE: Secret needs tls.crt (server cert) + tls.key (private key), type kubernetes.io/tls (kubectl create secret tls ...). MUTUAL: Secret needs tls.crt + tls.key + ca.crt (CA bundle to verify client certs) — created as type generic (kubectl create secret generic ...), since the 3-key shape doesn't fit the kubernetes.io/tls type. The secret MUST be in the SAME namespace as the ingress gateway WORKLOAD (istio-system for the default shared gateway), NOT necessarily the Gateway resource's own namespace. For PASSTHROUGH, no secret is needed — the Gateway just forwards raw TLS bytes to the backend.

TLS ModeCert on Gateway?Client Verified?Secret Required?Use Case
SIMPLEYesNotls.crt + tls.keyPublic HTTPS APIs
MUTUALYesYestls.crt + tls.key + ca.crtZero-trust / partner APIs
PASSTHROUGHNoNoNoneEnd-to-end TLS to backend
AUTO_PASSTHROUGHNoNoNoneGateway detects SNI, auto-forwards
🧭 SNI Routing — How PASSTHROUGH Routes Without Decrypting
1. client opens TCP to gateway :443, sends TLS ClientHello
   → the SNI field ("api.anihpj.com") is UNENCRYPTED by design
2. gateway Envoy peeks at the SNI — nothing else is readable
3. SNI matched against Gateway servers[].hosts
4. VirtualService tls: rules match on sniHosts → pick the destination
5. the encrypted stream is piped to the jobpost-api pod byte-for-byte
   — the POD's own certificate finishes the handshake 🔒
# VirtualService snippet used with PASSTHROUGH:
tls:
- match:
  - port: 443
    sniHosts: ["api.anihpj.com"]     # ← route key = SNI
  route:
  - destination:
      host: jobpost-api
      port:
        number: 8000
🎯 ICA Exam Note — TLS Is Taught Here, Graded Under a Different Domain

"Securing Edge Traffic with TLS" is graded under the Securing Workloads domain (25%), NOT Traffic Management — but it is TAUGHT here in 5.2 (credentialName + TLS block) and here in 5.5 (SIMPLE/MUTUAL/PASSTHROUGH modes) because the Gateway resource is where edge TLS actually lives. If the exam asks you to secure edge traffic, come back to 5.2/5.5, not the mesh-internal mTLS chapter — that covers MESH-INTERNAL mTLS between sidecars, a different problem.

5.6 Deep Dive — Kubernetes Gateway API vs Istio APIs: The Future Standard

DEFINITION: the Kubernetes Gateway API (gateway.networking.k8s.io) is the vendor-neutral SIG-Network standard for ingress + routing — one CRD set implemented by Istio, Envoy Gateway, nginx, GKE, and others.

Why it matters: Istio treats it as the FUTURE default traffic API; new Istio docs lead with it, and the ICA may show either style.

How it works: install the Gateway API CRDs, create a Gateway with gatewayClassName: istio, then attach HTTPRoute resources to it via parentRefs — Istio programs Envoy from those resources. The big behavioral difference: an istio-class Gateway API Gateway AUTO-PROVISIONS its own Envoy Deployment + Service — you no longer pre-install a shared istio-ingressgateway pod.

🔄 ISTIO APIs vs KUBERNETES GATEWAY API — Side-by-Side
ConceptIstio APIKubernetes Gateway API
GatewayGateway (networking.istio.io)Gateway (gateway.networking.k8s.io)
HTTP routingVirtualService.httpHTTPRoute
TCP routingVirtualService.tcpTCPRoute
TLS routingVirtualService.tlsTLSRoute
gRPC routingVirtualService.http (match on gRPC)GRPCRoute
Traffic splitweight in VS routebackendRefs.weight
Header manipulationheaders.request.addfilters: RequestHeaderModifier
DeploymentSeparate Gateway + Deployment/ServiceGateway auto-provisions Deployment+Service
📝 Gateway API Example — HTTPRoute
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: anihpj-gw
  namespace: istio-ingress
spec:
  gatewayClassName: istio  # Links to Istio's implementation
  listeners:
  - name: http
    hostname: "*.anihpj.com"
    port: 80
    protocol: HTTP
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: All  # ← this listener's namespace-scoping knob — the Gateway API's
                     # own equivalent of 5.8's hosts[] "ns/" prefix. "All" lets the
                     # HTTPRoute below attach from a DIFFERENT namespace (anihpj);
                     # "Same" would restrict it to istio-ingress only
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: jobpost-route
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: anihpj-gw
    namespace: istio-ingress
  hostnames: ["api.anihpj.com"]
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /api
    backendRefs:
    - name: jobpost-api
      port: 80
      weight: 90
    - name: jobpost-api-v2
      port: 80
      weight: 10
    filters:
    - type: RequestHeaderModifier
      requestHeaderModifier:
        add:
        - name: x-gateway-version
          value: "k8s-gwapi"
📖 What "Auto-Provisions" Actually Creates

The moment that Gateway resource is applied, Istio's controller creates real, named Kubernetes objects for you: Deployment/anihpj-gw-istio and Service/anihpj-gw-istio in namespace istio-ingress — the <gateway-name>-istio suffix is the naming convention to look for. Confirm it landed with kubectl get deploy,svc -n istio-ingress | grep anihpj-gw — no manual istio-ingressgateway install step required.

💡 ICA Exam: Key Differences

1. Gateway API Gateway auto-provisions its own Deployment/Service (with gatewayClassName: istio). 2. Different protocol types are separate resources (HTTPRoute, TCPRoute, etc.) — not combined in one VirtualService. 3. Gateway API uses parentRefs to bind routes to gateways (vs gateways: [name] in VS). 4. Mesh traffic config: set parentRefs.kind: Service to apply HTTPRoute to in-cluster traffic. 5. Prerequisite: Gateway API CRDs must be installed separately.

Adoption guidance for anihpj (and for the exam):

  • Gateway API CRDs are NOT bundled with Istio or Kubernetes — apply the release manifest from the gateway-api repo BEFORE creating any Gateway of class istio
  • Both API families coexist happily in one mesh — migrate the edge hostname-by-hostname, no big-bang rewrite required
  • DestinationRule-level policy (circuit breaking, LB algorithm, subsets) still comes from Istio APIs — keep them alongside
  • Mesh-internal (east-west) routing with HTTPRoute exists too: set parentRefs to kind: Service (the GAMMA initiative)
  • Rule of thumb: NEW clusters → start with Gateway API at the edge; existing anihpj configs → migrate opportunistically

5.7 Completing the TLS Mode Set — ISTIO_MUTUAL and OPTIONAL_MUTUAL

DEFINITION: two more tls.mode values exist beyond 5.5's four — ISTIO_MUTUAL secures the gateway with certificates Istio's own CA issues and auto-rotates, and OPTIONAL_MUTUAL runs the same handshake as MUTUAL but still accepts clients that send no certificate at all.

Why it matters: ISTIO_MUTUAL is the mode real multi-cluster and east-west gateways run in production — confusing it with MUTUAL is a documented exam trap because both modes REQUIRE a client cert, yet only MUTUAL needs a credentialName secret at all. OPTIONAL_MUTUAL lets anihpj roll out partner client-certs gradually instead of a hard cutover that breaks old callers.

How it works: ISTIO_MUTUAL skips credentialName entirely — Envoy fetches its cert/key over the same SDS (Secret Discovery Service) channel every sidecar uses, signed by istiod's own CA, and expects the PEER to present a cert from that same CA back. OPTIONAL_MUTUAL still requests a client cert during the handshake but never rejects a connection that omits one.

tls.modeGW cert?Client cert?Secret data keys
ISTIO_MUTUALautoauto (mesh)none (Istiod CA)
OPTIONAL_MUTUALYesoptionaltls.crt + tls.key
  • ISTIO_MUTUAL → east-west / multi-cluster gateways trusting the mesh's own CA — no manual certs to issue
  • OPTIONAL_MUTUAL → a public API that wants client certs from registered partners but must keep serving anonymous callers during the migration
⚠️ anihpj Gotcha

ISTIO_MUTUAL on the PUBLIC ingress gateway means only callers holding an Istio-issued mesh certificate can connect — that excludes every browser and external client, so it belongs on internal/east-west gateways, never on the public edge api.anihpj.com sits behind.

5.8 Namespace-Scoped Hosts and Cross-Namespace Gateway Binding

DEFINITION: two independent namespace rules govern a shared Gateway — the hosts[] entry's optional "namespace/" prefix picks WHICH namespace's VirtualServices may claim a hostname, and a VirtualService's own gateways[] field decides WHICH Gateway (and in what namespace) it is even asking to bind to.

Why it matters: production clusters rarely dedicate one istio-ingressgateway per team — anihpj's real cluster has several teams sharing the SAME edge Envoy; skip the hosts[] namespace prefix and ANY team's VirtualService can claim ANY hostname mesh-wide, and a copy-pasted gateways: [anihpj-gateway] silently points at the WRONG Gateway the moment a VirtualService moves to a different namespace.

How it works: hosts[] accepts <namespace>/<dnsName> — the namespace half is a literal name, "." (this Gateway's own namespace only), or "*" (any namespace) — and when NO prefix is written at all, Istio silently defaults to "*/", i.e. any namespace may bind. gateways[] resolves a bare name against the VirtualService's OWN namespace, so cross-namespace references must be written <gateway namespace>/<gateway name>.

🧠 Analogy — Paging a Coworker by First Name

A bare gateways: [anihpj-gateway] reference works like paging a coworker by first name over an office intercom — it reaches "anihpj-gateway" on YOUR OWN floor (namespace) without asking further. Move to a different floor and the same page reaches nobody; only "floor + name" — gateways: [anihpj/anihpj-gateway] — still gets through.

hosts[] syntaxWhich VirtualServices May Bind
ns1/*.example.comOnly VS living IN namespace ns1
./api.anihpj.comOnly VS in the GATEWAY's own namespace
*/api.anihpj.comVS in ANY namespace (explicit)
api.anihpj.com (no prefix)ANY namespace — same as */, default
🔀 GATEWAYS[] FIELD — Why a Bare Name Is Namespace-Relative
SCENARIO A — VS and Gateway share a namespace (works)
  Gateway            anihpj/anihpj-gateway
  VirtualService     anihpj/jobpost-vs
  gateways: [anihpj-gateway]
    → resolves to anihpj/anihpj-gateway  (correct)

SCENARIO B — VS lives in a DIFFERENT namespace (breaks silently)
  Gateway            anihpj/anihpj-gateway
  VirtualService     jobpost-team/jobpost-vs
  gateways: [anihpj-gateway]
    → looks for jobpost-team/anihpj-gateway — NOT FOUND
    → route never attaches, kubectl shows no error at all

FIX — always namespace-qualify cross-namespace references:
  gateways: [anihpj/anihpj-gateway]   # explicit, always correct
💡 anihpj Rule of Thumb

Lock down hosts[] with an explicit namespace prefix on every shared production Gateway, and always write cross-namespace gateways[] references in full ns/name form — never rely on the silent "*/" default.

5.9 Advanced Server Fields — name, bind, and Selector Scope

DEFINITION: three lesser-known knobs round out the Gateway CRD — Server.name (a label for stats and logs), Server.bind (pins a listener to one IP or a Unix domain socket instead of every interface), and PILOT_SCOPE_GATEWAY_TO_NAMESPACE (an istiod environment variable that changes how far a Gateway's selector search reaches).

Why it matters: without Server.name, every server in a multi-port Gateway shows up in istioctl/Prometheus output as an anonymous port number — debugging which listener a stat belongs to becomes guesswork. Server.bind matters on dual-homed or host-network edge nodes. PILOT_SCOPE_GATEWAY_TO_NAMESPACE is the difference between "any namespace's Gateway can bind the shared istio-ingressgateway" (the cluster-wide default) and a locked-down mesh where only Gateways inside istio-system itself may.

How it works: name must be unique across the Servers in one Gateway and is purely cosmetic — Envoy uses it to prefix stats and logs. bind takes an IP literal or unix:///path/to/uds and overrides the "listen on every interface" default. The PILOT flag lives on the istiod Deployment — false (the default) searches ALL namespaces for selector-matching pods, true restricts that search to the Gateway's own configuration namespace.

FieldDefaultWhy You'd Set It
Server.nameunsetStats/log prefix (unique per GW)
Server.bindall interfacesPin listener to one IP or UDS
PILOT_SCOPE_...false (all ns)Restrict selector to own namespace
🔧 Checking & Using name / bind / the Pilot Scope Flag
# is PILOT_SCOPE_GATEWAY_TO_NAMESPACE already set on istiod?
kubectl get deploy istiod -n istio-system -o yaml \
  | grep -A1 PILOT_SCOPE_GATEWAY_TO_NAMESPACE

# Server.name + Server.bind inside a real Gateway server:
servers:
- port:
    number: 443
    name: https-api        # ← appears in proxy-config listener
    protocol: HTTPS
  bind: 10.0.0.5            # ← pin to one NIC, dual-homed node
  hosts: ["api.anihpj.com"]
💡 anihpj Rule of Thumb

Name every server the moment a Gateway has more than one port — it is the only thing that makes istioctl proxy-config listener and Envoy access logs readable once http, https, and a redirect server all share one Gateway.

🔧 Under the Hood — From YAML to a Live Listener: the xDS Pipeline Behind Every Gateway
🗺️ One Pipeline, Six Steps — What Every Fact in 5.1-5.9 Is Really Describing

Every fact in 5.1-5.9 is really one pipeline seen from different angles. Here it is end to end, for one real request: an HTTPS GET to api.anihpj.com hitting the Pattern-2 Gateway from 5.4.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. kubectl apply -f anihpj-gateway-https.yaml                       │
│    → apiserver stores the object in etcd (5.2's "necessary, NOT     │
│      sufficient" step — nothing is listening yet)                   │
│                                                                     │
│ 2. istiod's Pilot WATCHES Gateway objects cluster-wide (or just one │
│    namespace if PILOT_SCOPE_GATEWAY_TO_NAMESPACE=true, 5.9)         │
│    → resolves spec.selector {istio: ingressgateway} against live    │
│      Pods — the exact match 5.1 warned can fail silently on a       │
│      typo'd label                                                   │
│                                                                     │
│ 3. Pilot compiles the matched Gateway into xDS resources:           │
│    • LDS: a listener on 0.0.0.0:8443, named from Server.name if     │
│      you set one (5.9) — otherwise an anonymous port number         │
│    • SDS: fetches the TLS cert — from the credentialName secret for │
│      SIMPLE/MUTUAL, or istiod's own CA for ISTIO_MUTUAL (5.7)       │
│    • RDS: the HTTP route table 5.3's VirtualService will attach to, │
│      keyed by its gateways: reference                               │
│                                                                     │
│ 4. Pilot pushes all three over a gRPC xDS STREAM to every Envoy pod  │
│    the selector matched — a hot reload, zero restart, zero dropped  │
│    connections                                                      │
│                                                                     │
│ 5. istioctl proxy-config listener (5.2) reads this exact in-memory  │
│    state — it is not guessing, it IS the live truth                 │
│                                                                     │
│ 6. a real ClientHello for api.anihpj.com now arrives at :8443:      │
│    Envoy inspects the SNI at L4 FIRST, before any TLS work, to pick  │
│    the right filter chain if multiple Gateways share the port →     │
│    THEN terminates TLS per the tls.mode matrix (5.5, 5.7) → THEN    │
│    the HTTP Connection Manager hands off to the RDS route table     │
│    5.3 wired to jobpost-api                                         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 ICA Insight: kubectl apply only ever proves step 1 of this pipeline — istiod's Pilot must still match the selector (step 2), compile LDS/SDS/RDS (step 3), and push them over the xDS stream (step 4) before proxy-config listener (step 5) shows anything real. When a Gateway "exists" but routes nothing, the break is almost always step 2 (selector/label typo) or step 4 (STALE proxy, blocked port 15012) — never step 1, because kubectl already told you that part succeeded.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Gateway is the mesh's entry point for external traffic — deployed as its own Envoy pod (istio-ingressgateway), far more capable than plain Kubernetes Ingress (header manipulation, weighted splits, advanced TLS/SNI, egress control).
  • The Gateway CRD is pure configuration — its selector binds it to a real Envoy pod. A typo'd label means the YAML is accepted but no Envoy ever receives it, a silent failure.
  • kubectl get gateway proves acceptance, not delivery — only istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system proves the edge Envoy actually got the config.
  • Gateway and VirtualService are a mandatory pair — a Gateway with no VirtualService drops traffic entirely; a VirtualService with no Gateway only applies to mesh-internal service-to-service calls.
  • Three production patterns cover ~95% of real clusters: HTTP-only (dev), HTTPS SIMPLE (prod baseline), HTTP→HTTPS redirect via httpsRedirect: true.
  • Five tls.mode values, each a different trust model: SIMPLE (public, server-only), MUTUAL (B2B/zero-trust, both sides), PASSTHROUGH (SNI-routed, no termination at the edge), ISTIO_MUTUAL (mesh CA, east-west), OPTIONAL_MUTUAL (gradual client-cert rollout).
  • An unprefixed hosts[] entry silently defaults to "*/" — any namespace's VirtualService may bind that hostname unless you explicitly namespace-scope it.
  • A bare gateways: [name] reference resolves relative to the VirtualService's OWN namespace, not the Gateway's — cross-namespace references must be fully qualified as ns/name.
  • The Kubernetes Gateway API is Istio's own stated future default — Gateway/HTTPRoute replace Gateway/VirtualService, and an istio-class Gateway API Gateway auto-provisions its own Envoy Deployment instead of reusing a shared istio-ingressgateway.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "Applying a Gateway means it's live." No — kubectl apply only proves the API server accepted the object into etcd. istiod's Pilot must still match the selector and push xDS before any Envoy actually listens.
  • "A Gateway without a VirtualService still routes somewhere reasonable." No — the Gateway accepts the TCP/TLS connection but has zero routing rules, so the request goes nowhere. Treat Gateway + VS as one deployment unit.
  • "The TLS secret must be in the same namespace as the Gateway resource." Not quite — it must be in the SAME namespace as the ingress gateway WORKLOAD (istio-system for the default shared gateway), which is often a DIFFERENT namespace than the Gateway custom resource itself.
  • "An unprefixed hosts[] entry is scoped to the Gateway's own namespace." No — it silently defaults to "*/", meaning ANY namespace's VirtualService can claim that hostname.
  • "gateways: [anihpj-gateway] always finds the right Gateway." No — a bare name resolves against the VirtualService's OWN namespace. Move the VS to a different namespace and the same reference silently points nowhere, with no error from kubectl.
  • "ISTIO_MUTUAL is just MUTUAL with a shorter config." No — ISTIO_MUTUAL skips credentialName entirely and uses istiod's own CA over SDS; MUTUAL requires a manually-provisioned secret with ca.crt. Confusing the two is a documented exam trap.
  • "The Kubernetes Gateway API works exactly like Istio's Gateway CRD, just renamed." No — it auto-provisions its own Envoy Deployment/Service per Gateway, and splits routing across HTTPRoute/TCPRoute/TLSRoute/GRPCRoute instead of one VirtualService covering all protocols.

💼 Chapter 5 — Daily Work Takeaways

  • Never trust kubectl get gateway alone — always confirm with istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system before declaring a Gateway "done."
  • Apply Gateway and VirtualService together, as one unit — a Gateway that outlives its VirtualService (or vice versa) is a common launch-day 404.
  • Default to SIMPLE + credentialName for public hosts; reach for MUTUAL/PASSTHROUGH only when the requirement explicitly demands a client certificate or pod-owned TLS.
  • Namespace-scope hosts[] explicitly on every shared production Gateway — don't rely on the silent "*/" default once more than one team shares the edge.
  • Fully qualify cross-namespace gateways[] references as ns/name — a bare name is a namespace-relative reference, not a cluster-wide lookup.
  • Name every Server the moment a Gateway carries more than one port — unnamed servers show up as anonymous port numbers in Envoy stats and logs.
  • For the ICA exam: "accept external traffic" = Gateway; "TLS at the edge" = SIMPLE + credentialName; "Gateway isn't routing" = check the VirtualService's gateways field first.
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 5

Seven quick-fire phrase-to-answer mappings — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Accept external HTTPS traffic" = Gateway with tls.mode: SIMPLE + credentialName
  • "Gateway isn't routing anything" = check the VirtualService's gateways field FIRST — a Gateway alone never routes
  • "Verify the Gateway config actually landed" = istioctl proxy-config listener, never just kubectl get gateway
  • "Client must present a certificate" = tls.mode: MUTUAL (manual secret with ca.crt) or ISTIO_MUTUAL (mesh CA, no secret)
  • "End-to-end encryption all the way to the pod" = tls.mode: PASSTHROUGH — no termination at the edge
  • "Restrict which namespace can bind a hostname" = hosts[] with an explicit ns/ prefix
  • "Vendor-neutral, future-default routing API" = the Kubernetes Gateway API (Gateway + HTTPRoute)

🧠 Chapter 5 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Name three capabilities an Istio Gateway has that a plain Kubernetes Ingress does not.
Show Answer
Answer

Any three of: full header manipulation, mTLS termination at the edge, weight-based traffic splitting, advanced TLS/SNI routing, and a dedicated egress gateway for outbound traffic.

Explanation

Ingress covers simple host/path routing only. Istio's Gateway is a full Envoy instance — everything Envoy can do at L4-L7 is available at the edge, not just basic routing.

Q2
Which two commands together prove a Gateway is fully working, and what does EACH one individually prove?
Show Answer
Answer
CommandProves
kubectl get gatewayThe API server accepted the object into etcd — necessary, NOT sufficient
istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-systemThe edge Envoy is actually listening — the real test
Explanation

A Gateway with a wrong selector still shows up under kubectl get — the object exists, it just binds to no Pod. Only the proxy-config command reads the live Envoy state.

Q3
What happens to traffic when a Gateway exists but no VirtualService references it?
Show Answer
Answer

Traffic is DROPPED. The Gateway accepts the connection (and terminates TLS if configured) but has no routing rules, so the request goes nowhere.

Explanation

This is the exact "Launch Morning" scenario in 5.3 — a Gateway can be perfectly healthy while every request still 404s, because the VirtualService that was supposed to route it never got applied.

Q4
Name all five tls.mode values and one distinguishing fact about each.
Show Answer
Answer
ModeDistinguishing fact
SIMPLEServer-only cert, most common for public HTTPS
MUTUALBoth sides present certs; needs a manual secret with ca.crt
PASSTHROUGHNo termination at the edge — SNI-routed, backend pod owns the cert
ISTIO_MUTUALMesh CA-issued certs via SDS — no credentialName at all
OPTIONAL_MUTUALRequests a client cert but still accepts connections without one
Explanation

SIMPLE/MUTUAL/PASSTHROUGH are the "TLS Modes I" set (5.5); ISTIO_MUTUAL/OPTIONAL_MUTUAL complete the set (5.7). AUTO_PASSTHROUGH is a 6th value for auto-detected SNI routing.

Q5
What secret data keys does SIMPLE need vs MUTUAL?
Show Answer
Answer

SIMPLE: tls.crt + tls.key, type kubernetes.io/tls. MUTUAL: tls.crt + tls.key + ca.crt (to verify client certs), type generic. Both live in the SAME namespace as the ingress gateway WORKLOAD (istio-system by default) — not necessarily the Gateway resource's own namespace.

Explanation

The extra ca.crt is what lets the gateway verify an incoming client certificate — without it, MUTUAL has no way to know which CA to trust for client identity.

Q6
What does an unprefixed hosts[] entry (e.g. just api.anihpj.com, no namespace prefix) default to?
Show Answer
Answer

It silently defaults to "*/api.anihpj.com" — ANY namespace's VirtualService may bind that hostname.

Explanation

On a shared production edge, this means any team's VirtualService can accidentally (or maliciously) claim a hostname it shouldn't. Always write the namespace prefix explicitly.

Q7
A VirtualService in namespace jobpost-team writes gateways: [anihpj-gateway], referencing a Gateway that actually lives in namespace anihpj. Does this work?
Show Answer
Answer

No. A bare name in gateways[] resolves relative to the VirtualService's OWN namespace — Istio looks for jobpost-team/anihpj-gateway, which doesn't exist. The route silently never attaches, with no error from kubectl.

Explanation

The fix is to fully qualify it: gateways: [anihpj/anihpj-gateway]. This is exactly 5.8's Scenario B — a copy-pasted bare reference that worked in the original namespace breaks the moment the VS moves.

Q8
What does Server.name control, and what does Server.bind control?
Show Answer
Answer

Server.name — a purely cosmetic label used to prefix stats and logs for that server; without it, multi-port Gateways show anonymous port numbers. Server.bind — pins the listener to one specific IP or a Unix domain socket instead of every interface (useful on dual-homed nodes).

Explanation

Neither field changes routing behavior — both exist purely for operational clarity and network placement, which is exactly why they're easy to skip until a multi-port Gateway becomes hard to debug.

Q9
What does setting PILOT_SCOPE_GATEWAY_TO_NAMESPACE=true on istiod change?
Show Answer
Answer

It restricts a Gateway's selector search to its OWN configuration namespace. The default (false) searches ALL namespaces for selector-matching Pods.

Explanation

This is the difference between "any namespace's Gateway can bind the shared istio-ingressgateway" (cluster-wide default) and a locked-down mesh where only Gateways inside istio-system itself may bind it.

Q10
In the Kubernetes Gateway API, what CRD replaces VirtualService for HTTP routing, and what's the biggest deployment-model difference from Istio's own Gateway CRD?
Show Answer
Answer

HTTPRoute replaces VirtualService for HTTP. The biggest difference: an istio-class Gateway API Gateway AUTO-PROVISIONS its own Envoy Deployment + Service — you no longer pre-install a shared istio-ingressgateway Pod that multiple Gateways bind to via selector.

Explanation

Different protocols get their own resource too — TCPRoute, TLSRoute, GRPCRoute — instead of all being folded into one VirtualService's http/tcp/tls blocks.

⚙️ Chapter 5 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
kubectl get gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpj shows the object exists, but istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system shows no listener for it. Task: Name the most likely root cause and write the exact command to confirm it, then the fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# Most likely cause: selector doesn't match any live pod
kubectl get gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'
# Compare against the actual ingress pod's labels:
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway
# If the second command returns nothing, the selector value is wrong —
# fix the Gateway's spec.selector to match the real Pod label exactly
Explanation

The Gateway CRD is pure configuration — a typo'd selector value means kubectl apply succeeds (etcd doesn't validate against live Pods) but istiod's Pilot never finds a Pod to push the config to.

Q2
Every request to api.anihpj.com returns 404 immediately after a DNS cutover. kubectl get gateway shows it Healthy. Task: Name the most likely cause, the command to confirm it, and the fix — without touching the Gateway itself.
Show Answer
Answer
# Most likely cause: no VirtualService references this Gateway yet
kubectl get virtualservice -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 gateways
# If empty or missing anihpj-gateway, that's the whole problem

# Fix: apply the VirtualService that was supposed to ship with it
kubectl apply -f anihpj-vs.yaml -n anihpj
Explanation

A healthy Gateway with zero routing rules still returns 404 for everything — the connection is accepted, TLS may even terminate correctly, but there's nowhere to send the request. Always deploy Gateway + VirtualService together.

Q3
Write a complete Gateway YAML named notify-gateway in namespace anihpj that accepts HTTPS on :443 for host notify.anihpj.com, terminating SIMPLE TLS with a secret named notify-tls-cert.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: notify-gateway
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 443
      name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
    tls:
      mode: SIMPLE
      credentialName: notify-tls-cert
    hosts:
    - "notify.anihpj.com"

Verify with: istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system | grep 8443

Explanation

Note the secret name is a plain string, not a namespace-qualified reference — credentialName is resolved by SDS against the ingress gateway WORKLOAD's own namespace (istio-system for the default shared gateway), NOT this Gateway resource's own namespace (anihpj). Create notify-tls-cert in istio-system, even though the Gateway CR itself lives in anihpj.

Q4
Write the kubectl create secret command for a MUTUAL TLS gateway that needs to verify client certificates issued by a company CA.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl create secret generic partner-mtls-cert \
  --from-file=tls.crt=server.crt \
  --from-file=tls.key=server.key \
  --from-file=ca.crt=company-ca.crt \
  -n istio-system
Explanation

MUTUAL needs three files, not two — ca.crt is what lets the gateway Envoy verify an incoming client certificate's chain of trust. Omitting it means the secret is only valid for SIMPLE mode, and MUTUAL handshakes will fail. Note the namespace: -n istio-system, the ingress gateway workload's own namespace — not wherever the Gateway CR referencing it happens to live.

Q5
A VirtualService in namespace skills-team has gateways: [anihpj-gateway], but the Gateway actually lives in namespace anihpj. Routing silently doesn't work and there's no error anywhere. Task: Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# Diagnose: a bare gateways[] name is namespace-relative to the VS itself
# Istio is looking for skills-team/anihpj-gateway — which doesn't exist
kubectl get gateway anihpj-gateway -n skills-team
# NotFound — confirms the theory

# Fix: fully qualify the cross-namespace reference
kubectl patch virtualservice skills-vs -n skills-team --type='json' \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/gateways/0","value":"anihpj/anihpj-gateway"}]'
Explanation

This is 5.8's Scenario B exactly — a bare name that worked when copy-pasted from a same-namespace example silently fails cross-namespace, with zero error output from kubectl or istioctl analyze catching it as invalid syntax.

Q6
A shared production Gateway's hosts[] has no namespace prefix. A different team's VirtualService, in a different namespace, unexpectedly starts serving api.anihpj.com. Task: Explain why this was possible and write the fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# Before (vulnerable) — no namespace prefix:
hosts:
- "api.anihpj.com"    # silently means "*/api.anihpj.com" — any namespace

# After (locked down):
hosts:
- "anihpj/api.anihpj.com"   # only VirtualServices IN anihpj may bind this
Explanation

An unprefixed host is exactly equivalent to explicitly writing "*/api.anihpj.com" — Istio never scopes it to the Gateway's own namespace by default. On a multi-team cluster this is a real hostname-hijack risk, not just a style nitpick.

Q7
Write a Pattern-3 Gateway (HTTP→HTTPS redirect) for host api.anihpj.com: port 80 redirects, port 443 serves SIMPLE TLS with secret api-tls-cert.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: api-gateway
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 80
      name: http
      protocol: HTTP
    hosts: ["api.anihpj.com"]
    tls:
      httpsRedirect: true    # ← 301, no routing lookup at all
  - port:
      number: 443
      name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
    tls:
      mode: SIMPLE
      credentialName: api-tls-cert
    hosts: ["api.anihpj.com"]
Explanation

httpsRedirect: true is compiled directly into the listener's route config — the edge Envoy answers the 301 from local state with no Cluster lookup and no RDS hand-off, so it works even before any VirtualService exists.

Q8
You need an east-west gateway for cross-cluster traffic that trusts only certificates issued by the mesh's own CA — no manually managed certs. Task: Name the correct tls.mode and write the relevant Gateway server block.
Show Answer
Answer
servers:
- port:
    number: 15443     # conventional east-west gateway port
    name: tls
    protocol: TLS
  tls:
    mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL   # ← NO credentialName — istiod's own CA via SDS
  hosts: ["*.local"]
Explanation

ISTIO_MUTUAL is the documented exam trap for this exact scenario — picking MUTUAL instead would require manually provisioning and rotating certs, defeating the point of "trusts only the mesh's own CA." Never use ISTIO_MUTUAL on the PUBLIC edge — it would reject every browser.

Q9
A Gateway has three servers (HTTP redirect, HTTPS API, HTTPS admin) all sharing one Gateway resource. Envoy stats and access logs show only raw port numbers, making it impossible to tell which server a given stat belongs to. Task: Fix this without changing any routing behavior.
Show Answer
Answer
servers:
- port: {number: 80, name: http-redirect, protocol: HTTP}
  # ...
- port: {number: 443, name: https-api, protocol: HTTPS}
  # ...
- port: {number: 8443, name: https-admin, protocol: HTTPS}
  # ...
Explanation

Server.name is purely cosmetic but directly controls the stats/log prefix Envoy uses — it's the single field that turns "port 443" into "https-api" in every debugging session from here on. Add it the moment a Gateway has more than one server.

Q10
Migrate search.anihpj.com from Istio's Gateway/VirtualService to the Kubernetes Gateway API's Gateway/HTTPRoute, keeping the same 90/10 canary split between search-v1 and search-v2.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: search-gw
  namespace: istio-ingress
spec:
  gatewayClassName: istio
  listeners:
  - name: https
    hostname: "search.anihpj.com"
    port: 443
    protocol: HTTPS
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: search-route
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: search-gw
    namespace: istio-ingress
  hostnames: ["search.anihpj.com"]
  rules:
  - backendRefs:
    - name: search-v1
      port: 80
      weight: 90
    - name: search-v2
      port: 80
      weight: 10
Explanation

Note this Gateway needs NO pre-installed istio-ingressgateway Pod — the gatewayClassName: istio Gateway auto-provisions its own Envoy Deployment and Service the moment it's applied. Weighting moves from VirtualService's weight field to HTTPRoute's backendRefs[].weight, same concept, different CRD.

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 5
  • Default to SIMPLE + credentialName for every public host — it is correct ~95% of the time; reach for MUTUAL/PASSTHROUGH only when the requirement explicitly says "client cert" or "the app owns TLS."
  • Write hosts[] with an explicit namespace prefix (ns/host or ./host) on day one — retrofitting it later means finding every VirtualService that silently relied on the "*/" default.
  • Wildcard hosts ("*.anihpj.com") save a Gateway server block per subdomain, but one wildcard SNI can't serve multiple unrelated certs on the same port — one cert per wildcard.
  • The #1 exam-day failure mode is a Gateway/VirtualService mismatch: grep both for the SAME host string and the SAME gateway name before moving on — a typo compiles fine, it just never routes.
  • istioctl proxy-config listener beats kubectl get gateway whenever you're unsure the config landed — get only proves etcd saw it, not that Envoy did.
  • Name every Server the moment a Gateway has more than one port (5.9) — future-you debugging Envoy stats will thank present-you.

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 5)

Chapter 5 is where the Gateway's YAML, its verification, and its TLS secrets all come together — these commands cover applying, proving delivery, and catching namespace/host mismatches early.

CommandWhat It Checks / Does in Chapter 5
APPLY / INSPECT THE GATEWAY
kubectl apply -f anihpj-gateway.yaml -n anihpjApply the Gateway resource (5.2)
kubectl get gateway -n anihpjAccepted != delivered — necessary, not sufficient (5.2)
kubectl describe gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpjFull resource detail — selector + servers (5.2)
VERIFY IT REACHED THE EDGE ENVOY
istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-systemThe REAL test — not kubectl get (5.2)
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgatewayConfirm the selector matches a live pod (5.1)
TLS SECRETS, NAMESPACE SCOPING & MISMATCH-CATCHING
kubectl create secret tls anihpj-tls-cert --cert=server.crt --key=server.key -n istio-systemCorrect type + keys for SIMPLE/MUTUAL TLS — same namespace as the ingress gateway WORKLOAD, not the Gateway CR (5.2, 5.4)
kubectl get deploy istiod -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A1 PILOT_SCOPE_GATEWAY_TO_NAMESPACECheck the selector-search-scope flag (5.9)
istioctl analyze -n anihpjCatch Gateway/VirtualService host or name mismatches early (5.8)

🔬 Practice Drill 5.1 — Write and Verify a Production-Shaped Gateway

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Write and verify a production-shaped Gateway for a new anihpj hostname right now — don't just read this, do it:

  1. Write a Gateway named search-gateway in namespace anihpj that accepts HTTPS on :443 for host search.anihpj.com, tls.mode: SIMPLE, credentialName: search-anihpj-tls-cert (5.2, 5.4).
  2. Add an HTTP :80 server on the SAME Gateway with tls.httpsRedirect: true so plaintext requests 301 to HTTPS (5.4 Pattern 3).
  3. kubectl apply it, then run kubectl get gateway search-gateway -n anihpj — remember this only proves acceptance, not delivery.
  4. Prove delivery with istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system — you should see both an 8080 and an 8443 listener for the new host.
  5. Namespace-scope it defensively: add a "./" prefix to hosts[] so only VirtualServices inside anihpj can bind search.anihpj.com (5.8).
Hint: Steps 3 and 4 are the whole point — kubectl get only proves acceptance, istioctl proxy-config proves delivery. If you see both an 8080 and 8443 listener for search.anihpj.com, you've independently verified the entire 5.2/5.4/5.8 skill set in under 8 minutes.
View Solution

Step 4's listener output should show TWO entries for the new host — an 8080 listener answering with a 301 (Pattern 3's redirect), and an 8443 listener with an SNI match for search.anihpj.com terminating SIMPLE TLS. If either is missing, re-check step 1's selector and step 3's namespace before assuming istiod is broken.

Check yourself: did you genuinely see the 8080/8443 pair in your own terminal, not just write the YAML and assume it worked? The whole point of this drill is proving delivery, not just acceptance.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.2 — Break the Selector, Diagnose It Live

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

On a cluster with a working Gateway, deliberately break it and fix it using ONLY the two verification commands from 5.2 — no guessing.

  1. Patch your Gateway's spec.selector to a value that matches no live Pod (e.g. istio: wrong-label).
  2. Confirm kubectl get gateway still shows the object as present — note that it does NOT report the break.
  3. Confirm istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system now shows the listener MISSING.
  4. Restore the correct selector and confirm the listener reappears.
Hint: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=ingressgateway tells you the exact label value a correct selector needs to match.
View Solution

kubectl get gateway should show the object Healthy/present through the entire drill — that field never reflects selector-match failures, because the API server has no concept of "did this bind to a real Pod." Only the proxy-config command's listener list changes.

Check yourself: could you now explain to a teammate why "the Gateway looks fine in kubectl" and "traffic is completely broken" are not contradictory statements?

🔬 Practice Drill 5.3 — Match the Symptom to the Broken Layer

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

For each observation, name the single most likely cause and the one command you'd run to confirm it — before proposing any fix:

  1. A Gateway and VirtualService both apply cleanly, but requests get a TCP connection reset instead of an HTTP response.
  2. HTTPS works for api.anihpj.com but a teammate's new VirtualService for api.anihpj.com in a DIFFERENT namespace also starts serving traffic, unintentionally.
  3. A VirtualService moved from namespace anihpj to namespace anihpj-v2 during a refactor; its routes silently stopped working with zero error output.
  4. An east-west gateway configured with tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL rejects every connection from public internet clients.
Hint: Two of these four are the SAME root cause family (namespace scoping), just triggered from opposite directions — one over-permits, one under-permits.
View Solution
#CauseConfirm with
1PASSTHROUGH or a protocol mismatch — likely the Gateway is expecting SNI-routed TLS but the client sends plain HTTPkubectl get gateway -o yaml — check tls.mode against what the client actually sends
2Unprefixed hosts[] defaulted to "*/"kubectl get gateway -o yaml | grep -A3 hosts — look for a bare hostname with no namespace prefix
3A bare gateways[] reference is namespace-relative — it silently stopped resolving after the movekubectl get gateway anihpj-gateway -n anihpj-v2 — confirm it returns NotFound
4Working as designed, not a bug — ISTIO_MUTUAL requires a mesh-issued client cert that no public browser hasistioctl x describe pod on the gateway — confirm ISTIO_MUTUAL is intentional for this listener, then move public traffic to a SIMPLE listener instead

Check yourself: did you correctly identify #4 as "not a bug"? ISTIO_MUTUAL doing exactly what it's designed to do — rejecting non-mesh clients — is a config-placement mistake (using it on a public listener), not a broken mechanism.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.4 — Namespace-Scope a Shared Gateway, Live

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Prove to yourself, with two namespaces on a real cluster, that hosts[] scoping actually blocks a cross-namespace hijack.

  1. Create a Gateway in namespace team-a with an UNPREFIXED host shared.anihpj.com.
  2. From namespace team-b, apply a VirtualService that also claims shared.anihpj.com and routes to a team-b Service.
  3. Confirm — via istioctl proxy-config route — that BOTH VirtualServices are now live for the same host (the vulnerability).
  4. Fix the Gateway's hosts[] to "team-a/shared.anihpj.com" and re-check — team-b's VirtualService should no longer bind.
Hint: istioctl proxy-config route deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system --name http.443 -o json shows exactly which VirtualServices contributed routes for a given host.
View Solution

Before the fix, both namespaces' VirtualServices legitimately compile into the route table — this isn't a bug, it's the documented behavior of the "*/" default working exactly as specified. After scoping hosts[] to team-a/, team-b's VirtualService reference is rejected at the Gateway boundary, not silently ignored — istioctl analyze will now flag it.

Check yourself: did you verify the BEFORE state actually showed the vulnerability, not just assume it would? Reproducing the actual hijack, even briefly and safely, is what makes the fix's necessity concrete instead of theoretical.

🔬 Practice Drill 5.5 — Sketch the Six-Step xDS Pipeline, Timed

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

In 5 minutes, from memory, write the UTH's 6-step pipeline from kubectl apply to a live ClientHello being served — name what istiod compiles at each xDS step (LDS/SDS/RDS). Do NOT reopen the UTH until you finish.

Hint: Step 3 is really three sub-steps happening together (LDS + SDS + RDS) — most people only remember one of the three.
View Solution

Compare against the UTH diagram. The step most people drop: step 6's ordering — Envoy inspects SNI at L4 FIRST (before any TLS work) to pick the right filter chain when multiple Gateways share a port, THEN terminates TLS, THEN hands off to RDS. Reversing "inspect SNI" and "terminate TLS" is a common conceptual error.

Check yourself: did you correctly separate "kubectl apply succeeds" (step 1, proves nothing about delivery) from "istiod's Pilot matches the selector" (step 2, the actual first real step)? Conflating these two is exactly what 5.2's "necessary, not sufficient" warning exists to prevent.

🌐 Chapter 5 in One Picture — From Sealed Mesh to Scoped, Production-Ready Front Door

│ 🌐 Gateway exists, unverified                                     │

Chapter 5 took anihpj from a sealed mesh to a scoped, production-ready front door in five moves: define what a Gateway even is and how its selector binds to a real Envoy pod (5.1), write and VERIFY its YAML instead of trusting kubectl's silent acceptance (5.2), pair it with a VirtualService because a Gateway alone never routes anything (5.3), choose a battle-tested pattern for HTTP, HTTPS, or a redirect (5.4), and pick exactly the right TLS mode for the situation from the full five-mode set spread across 5.5 and 5.7.

The last two sections made that Gateway safe to share: namespace-scoped hosts and fully-qualified gateway references stop one anihpj team's VirtualService from silently hijacking another's hostname (5.8), and naming servers plus understanding PILOT_SCOPE_GATEWAY_TO_NAMESPACE keep a multi-port, multi-team edge debuggable (5.9). Every later chapter in Part 5 — VirtualService's routing, DestinationRule's load balancing, ServiceEntry's egress — only matters once this front door is open, verified, and locked down correctly.

Chapter 6: VirtualService — Smart Traffic Routing

The VirtualService is Istio's traffic routing brain. It overrides Kubernetes' default round-robin and lets you control EXACTLY where each request goes — based on URI path, headers, weights, or any combination. Think of it as the GPS for your traffic: "turn left here, go 90% this way, 10% that way."

"Where does a request go once it's already inside the mesh?" Chapter 5's Gateway only gets a request through anihpj's front door — it says nothing about which of jobpost-api's pods answers it, whether a canary version sees any traffic at all, or what happens the instant user-service or auth-service has a bad five seconds. VirtualService is the resource that answers all of that, and it is the single CRD you will touch the most in this entire guide: every canary release, every A/B test, every retry policy, every timeout, and every chaos-engineering fault injection in anihpj is one YAML block inside a VirtualService's http: list. Get the weighted canary split wrong here and real users hit an untested jobpost-api:v2; get the retry/timeout math wrong here and a 200ms blip in skills-service turns into a page-wide 504.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~3 hours 🚦 Routing 🎯 ICA 35%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Explain what a VirtualService governs (WHERE traffic goes) versus what a DestinationRule governs (HOW it behaves once it arrives, Chapter 7)
  • ✅ Write a weighted canary split (e.g. 90/10) between jobpost-api:v1 and :v2, and reason correctly about how Envoy normalizes the weights
  • ✅ Route by HTTP header (A/B testing) and by URI prefix/exact/regex (path-based routing), ordering rules so the specific ones fire first
  • ✅ Configure retries (attempts, perTryTimeout, retryOn) and a request timeout whose numbers never conflict with each other's math (6.12)
  • ✅ Inject delay and abort faults to prove resilience features actually work, and explain why fault + retries/timeout can't share one route
  • ✅ Predict, for any multi-rule VirtualService, exactly which single rule Envoy matches first — and debug a real "my route isn't firing" bug
  • ✅ Scope an Envoy's visibility with the Sidecar CRD and pick the ONE owner (app code or mesh) for a given timeout/retry to avoid a conflict
🎓 ICA Relevance
Traffic Management 35%
Graded ICA sub-skillCovered in this chapter
Configuring Traffic Shifting6.3
Configuring Routing within a Service Mesh6.4, 6.5, 6.9
Using Resilience Features6.6, 6.7, 6.11, 6.12

💡 Its own named subtopic: "Using Fault Injection" is graded separately from the resilience features (retries/timeouts) it's used to test — see 6.8. VirtualService is graded across nearly every Traffic Management sub-skill except pure ingress/egress wiring (Gateway/ServiceEntry, Ch5/Ch8) and destination-only policy (DestinationRule, Ch7).

💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 6
  • "Route traffic by URI" = match: uri: prefix: /jobs/ in VirtualService
  • "Canary traffic split" = weight: 90 + weight: 10 on route destinations (need DestinationRule subsets)
  • "Add retries" = retries: {attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 2s} in VirtualService http section
  • "Add timeout" = timeout: 5s — total request budget including all retries
  • "Test resilience" = fault: {delay: {percentage: {value: 50}, fixedDelay: 5s}} — inject delays
  • "Multiple match conditions" = AND within one match block, OR across separate match blocks
  • Exam hands-on: Write VirtualService with weights, retries, timeouts, and fault injection from scratch

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 6 Learning Arc

Sections 6.1 through 6.15 read as one continuous argument in five groups: first DEFINE the VirtualService and prove you can PIN traffic to one version, then learn the three ways to CHOOSE a different route, then make that route SURVIVE FAILURE, then master the ORDERING and SCOPE rules that keep multiple routes from fighting each other, and finally layer on the ADVANCED in-flight editing and non-HTTP capabilities most exam-takers forget exist.
