Read it as a sentence: define the CRD and prove you can pin traffic to one version (6.1-6.2), learn the three ways to choose a different route (6.3-6.5), make that route survive failure (6.6-6.8), master the ordering and scoping rules that keep multiple routes from fighting each other (6.9-6.12), and finally layer on the advanced in-flight editing and non-HTTP capabilities most exam-takers forget exist (6.13-6.15).

SectionAnswers the question…One-line takeaway
6.1 What is a VirtualService?What does a VirtualService actually control?WHERE traffic goes — a routing table compiled into Envoy, not a proxy itself; DestinationRule governs HOW (Ch7).
6.2 Basic RoutingHow do I pin 100% of traffic to one version?A route with no match block and one destination sends everything to that subset.
6.3 Weight-Based Traffic SplittingHow do I run a canary release?Weighted destinations split traffic by any ratio — Envoy normalizes weights that don't sum to 100.
6.4 Header-Based RoutingHow do I route by who's asking?Match a header value to send specific callers (premium users, QA, canary testers) to a specific subset.
6.5 URI/Path-Based RoutingHow do I route by which path was requested?prefix/exact/regex on uri — most specific first, the no-match catch-all last.
6.6 RetriesHow does Envoy recover from a transient 5xx?attempts + perTryTimeout + retryOn — safe only for idempotent (GET) requests.
6.7 TimeoutsHow do I stop a slow call from hanging forever?timeout: Ns returns a fast 504 instead of blocking a caller thread.
6.8 Fault InjectionHow do I prove my resilience features actually work?Inject delay or abort on a percentage of requests, then watch retries/timeouts absorb it — or not.
6.9 Route Matching PrecedenceWhich rule does Envoy actually pick?Top-to-bottom, first match wins — a catch-all above a specific rule makes that rule dead code.
6.10 Sidecar CRDHow do I stop every Envoy from knowing the whole mesh?Sidecar's egress hosts trims one proxy's scope — smaller config, faster pushes, less memory.
6.11 App vs Mesh-Level Failure RecoveryWho owns this timeout — my code or Istio?Pick ONE owner per concern; a tighter app timeout races the mesh's retry and wins before it can help.
6.12 Deep Dive — Retry Budget MathWill my retries actually fit before the timeout fires?timeout ≥ (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout, or the last retry gets cut off mid-flight.
6.13 Header ManipulationHow do I add or strip headers with zero app code changes?headers.request/response set/add/remove, applied per-route in flight by Envoy.
6.14 CORS PolicyWhy does my SPA's browser fetch() fail with a CORS error?corsPolicy answers the browser's OPTIONS preflight on the API's behalf — no app code involved.
6.15 TCP and TLS Route BlocksWhat about traffic that isn't HTTP at all?tcp: routes raw connections by port; tls: routes by SNI hostname without ever decrypting.

6.1 What is a VirtualService?

A VirtualService defines WHERE traffic goes, HOW MUCH traffic, and under WHAT conditions. It works for both external traffic (via Gateway) and internal service-to-service calls within the mesh. It attaches to a Kubernetes Service by name and overrides K8s' default simple round-robin.

📖 VirtualService vs DestinationRule — The Golden Rule

VirtualService = WHERE (the GPS route — which road to take). DestinationRule = HOW (the driving rules — speed limit, lane choice). VirtualService decides the destination first, then DestinationRule applies policies to that destination.

💡 A Routing Table, Not a Proxy

A VirtualService is not itself a running process — it's a routing TABLE that istiod compiles and pushes into each relevant Envoy's own config via RDS. Adding rules to it costs ZERO extra network hops; Envoy already holds the compiled table in memory before the request ever arrives, and simply looks it up.

6.2 Basic Routing — Send All Traffic to One Version

jobpost-api has v1 and v2 running simultaneously. By default, Kubernetes alternates between both. A VirtualService can pin ALL traffic to v1:

yaml — Basic route: 100% to v1 

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - jobpost-api              # ← the K8s Service name
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v1           # ← 100% to v1 (subset defined in DestinationRule)

6.3 Weight-Based Traffic Splitting (Canary Deployments)

Deploy jobpost-api:v2 and gradually shift traffic: 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%. Roll back instantly by changing one number — zero downtime.

yaml — Canary: 90% v1, 10% v2 

spec:
  hosts:
  - jobpost-api
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v1           # ← stable version
      weight: 90             # ← 90% to v1
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v2           # ← canary version
      weight: 10             # ← 10% to v2
⚖️ CANARY DEPLOYMENT — Gradual Traffic Shift
Phase 1
v1: 100% · v2: 0%
Deploy v2, no traffic
Phase 2
v1: 95% · v2: 5%
Smoke test v2
Phase 3
v1: 75% · v2: 25%
Monitor metrics
Phase 4
v1: 50% · v2: 50%
Halfway confidence
Phase 5
v1: 0% · v2: 100%
Full migration ✅
🔧 Under the Hood — Every Draw Is Independent

Envoy's weight draw is STATELESS and per-REQUEST — a fresh random number every time, with no memory of what the same user got last time. That means a single browser session can bounce between v1 and v2 across its own requests during a canary. If you need "same user, same pod" — e.g. a per-user cache that only warms on one version — that's a DIFFERENT feature: DestinationRule's consistentHash load balancing (Chapter 7), not anything a weighted VirtualService route provides.

6.4 Header-Based Routing (A/B Testing)

Route users to different versions based on HTTP headers. Premium users see the new UI, everyone else stays on stable.

Incoming request to jobpost-api — Which version?
Header: x-user-type = premium?
✅ jobpost-api:v2 (new UI)
No matching header?
✅ jobpost-api:v1 (stable)

🧪 A/B Testing Use Cases for anihpj

Header / ConditionRoute To
x-user-type: premiumjobpost-api:v2 (premium UI)
x-canary: "true"jobpost-api:v2 (canary)
x-internal-user: "1"skills-svc:v2 (beta features)
user-agent: contains "Mobile"jobpost-api mobile-optimized
cookie: session=stagingall services:v2 staging
yaml — Header-based A/B testing for jobpost-api 

spec:
  http:
  - match:                          # ← check this FIRST
    - headers:
        x-user-type:
          exact: premium            # ← if header matches "premium"
    route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v2                  # ← premium users → v2 (new UI)
  - route:                          # ← default (no header match)
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v1                  # ← everyone else → v1 (stable)
💡 Match Order Matters!

VirtualService evaluates rules top-to-bottom, first match wins. Always put specific matches (header-based) BEFORE the default catch-all route. If you reverse the order, the default route matches first and your A/B test never triggers.

6.5 URI-Based and Path-Based Routing

Route different URL paths to different microservices — all through ONE VirtualService:

yaml — Path-based routing for all anihpj services 

spec:
  http:
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /jobs/        # → jobpost-api:8000
    route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /users/       # → user-service:8080
    route:
    - destination:
        host: user-service
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /skills/      # → skills-service:8090
    route:
    - destination:
        host: skills-service
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /locations/   # → location-service:8070
    route:
    - destination:
        host: location-service
  - route:                    # ← default (no match)
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api     # fallback

6.6 Retries — Automatic Failure Recovery

Without Istio: if user-service returns a 503, Django fails immediately. With Istio retries: Envoy automatically retries up to 3 times before giving up. No code changes needed.

🔄 RETRY TIMELINE — How Envoy Absorbs Transient Failures
❌ WITHOUT Retries

T=0ms: jobpost-api → user-service → 503
T=1ms: Envoy returns 503 to Django
T=2ms: Django returns 500 to browser
💥 User sees error (service recovers 200ms later)

✅ WITH Retries (attempts: 3)

T=0ms: Attempt 1 → 503 ❌
T=100ms: Attempt 2 → 503 ❌
T=200ms: Attempt 3 → 200 ✅
T=201ms: Django gets success
✅ User never sees an error!

yaml — Retry configuration 

spec:
  http:
  - retries:
      attempts: 3              # ← try up to 3 times
      perTryTimeout: 2s        # ← each attempt has 2s timeout
      retryOn: 5xx,gateway-error,reset  # ← what errors trigger retry
    route:
    - destination:
        host: user-service
⚠️ Retries Are Only Safe for Idempotent Requests

GET requests are idempotent — retrying is safe. POST/PUT/DELETE are NOT — retrying could double-charge a payment or create duplicate records. Always set retryOn to only retry on safe status codes.

6.7 Timeouts — Don't Wait Forever

Without timeouts, a slow service can block Django threads for 30-60 seconds, causing thread pool exhaustion. Istio timeouts return a fast 504, protecting your application.

⏱️ TIMEOUT — Fast Failure vs Slow Hang
❌ Without Timeout

T=0s: Django calls slow skills-service
T=10s: Still waiting...
T=30s: Still waiting... thread BLOCKED
T=60s: Django default timeout → error
💥 Thread pool exhaustion!

✅ With Timeout (3s)

T=0s: Django calls skills-service
T=3s: Envoy returns 504 Gateway Timeout
T=3.01s: Django gets fast 504 → graceful degradation
✅ Thread pool protected!

💡 Combined Retry + Timeout Pattern

timeout: 10s (total budget) + retries: attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 3s = 3 attempts × 3s = 9s max, under the 10s budget. ✅ Always ensure retries × perTryTimeout < timeout.

6.8 Fault Injection — Testing Resilience

Intentionally inject failures to verify your timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers actually work. Two types: delay (slow responses) and abort (error responses).

🐌
Delay Injection

"Delay 30% of requests to user-service by 7 seconds"

Tests: Do timeouts fire correctly? Does the app degrade gracefully? Are retries configured properly?

💥
Abort Injection

"Return HTTP 500 for 10% of requests to auth-service"

Tests: Does outlier detection eject the failing host? Does the fallback mechanism work? Are error messages user-friendly?

yaml — Fault injection examples 

# Delay: 30% of requests delayed by 7 seconds
spec:
  http:
  - fault:
      delay:
        fixedDelay: 7s
        percentage:
          value: 30
    route:
    - destination:
        host: user-service
---
# Abort: 10% of requests return HTTP 500
spec:
  http:
  - fault:
      abort:
        httpStatus: 500
        percentage:
          value: 10
    route:
    - destination:
        host: auth-service

6.9 Route Matching Precedence — How Envoy Chooses Routes

When multiple VirtualService rules could match a request, Envoy uses specific precedence. Understanding this prevents "my route isn't working" confusion.

🏆 ROUTE MATCHING PRECEDENCE — First Match Wins (Top→Bottom)
1
Exact Match

uri: exact: /health
Matches ONLY /health

2
Prefix Match

uri: prefix: /api/v1/
Matches /api/v1/jobs, /api/v1/users...

3
Regex Match

uri: regex: ^/api/v[12]/.*
Matches v1 or v2 API paths

4
Default Route

No match block — catch-all.
Must be LAST in the list.

⚠️ Order Matters!

VirtualService http routes are evaluated top to bottom. Always put most specific rules FIRST. If the catch-all (no match) route comes before a specific route, the specific route will NEVER be reached. This is the #1 VirtualService misconfiguration.

📋 COMMON VIRTUALSERVICE PATTERNS — Copy-Paste Templates

PatternUse CaseKey Fields
Weight-based canary90% v1, 10% v2weight: 90 + weight: 10
Header-based A/BPremium users → v2headers: {x-user-type: exact: premium}
Path-based routing/api/* → service-Auri: prefix: /api/
Retry + Timeout3 retries, 5s totalretries: {attempts:3, perTryTimeout:1s} + timeout: 5s
Fault injectionTest resiliencefault: {delay: {percentage: {value:50}, fixedDelay: 5s}}
Traffic mirrorTest v2 silentlymirror: {host: svc, subset: v2}

6.10 Sidecar CRD — Controlling Proxy Scope and Performance

The Sidecar CRD lets you fine-tune what each Envoy proxy can reach. By default, every Envoy knows about EVERY service in the mesh — which means huge memory usage in large deployments (500+ services). The Sidecar resource lets you limit this scope for performance and security.

⚠️
Without Sidecar Resource

Every Envoy proxy knows about ALL services in the mesh. 500 services = 500 clusters in EACH Envoy's config. Memory per sidecar: 300MB+. Config push time: seconds per change. Not scalable.

✅
With Sidecar Resource

Limit each Envoy to only the services it actually calls. jobpost-api only needs: user-service, skills-service, auth-service. Config size: 90% smaller. Memory: 50MB. Production-ready.

yaml — Sidecar: Limit jobpost-api's scope to only 3 services 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Sidecar
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  egress:
  - hosts:
    - "./user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"   # Only these
    - "./skills-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local" # services are
    - "./auth-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"   # visible to Envoy
    - "istio-system/*"                            # Always allow istiod
💡 When to Use Sidecar on the ICA Exam

If a question mentions "reduce memory usage per sidecar" or "limit which services a pod can reach," the answer is Sidecar CRD. In production with 100+ services, Sidecar resources are mandatory for performance. Without them, each Envoy's config grows unboundedly, causing high memory usage and slow config propagation.

⚠️ Sidecar Is a Performance Knob, Not a Security Control

Scoping egress.hosts narrows what an Envoy can ROUTE to — it is not an access-control mechanism, and should never be presented as one on the exam. A service left out of the list simply has no CDS cluster to route through (calls to it fail as unroutable); it isn't cryptographically or authoritatively DENIED the way an AuthorizationPolicy denial is. For actual access control, pair Sidecar scoping with AuthorizationPolicy (Chapter 9) — "limit visibility" and "enforce authorization" are two different problems with two different CRDs.

6.11 Application vs Mesh-Level Failure Recovery — Avoiding Conflicts

A critical concept from the official docs: your application code and Istio handle failures independently. They don't know about each other — and this can cause conflicts.

⚠️ CONFLICT EXAMPLE — App Timeout vs Istio Timeout
Your Django code:
  requests.get('http://user-service/users/', timeout=2)  # ← 2s timeout

Istio VirtualService:
  timeout: 3s        # ← 3s timeout (applied by Envoy)
  retries:
    attempts: 1
    perTryTimeout: 2s

What ACTUALLY happens:
  T=0s    Django sends request
  T=2s    Django's OWN timeout fires → raises Timeout exception
          Envoy NEVER gets to apply its retry!
          The 3s VirtualService timeout is useless.

🔑 Golden Rule: App timeout MUST be >= (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout + buffer
   (the same 6.12 retry-budget formula — the "+1" is the initial attempt)
   Fix: Set Django timeout to 5s (or remove it and let Istio handle it)
⚠️ Important: Fault Injection + Retries/Timeout

The official Istio docs state: fault injection and retry/timeout config CAN syntactically coexist on the same route — kubectl apply won't reject it — but timeouts and retries will NOT be enabled when a fault is present on that route. The fault silently wins; your retry/timeout numbers become inert, not erroring, just ignored. If you need to test resilience with real retries/timeout still active, create a separate VirtualService for the fault.

6.12 Deep Dive — Retry Budget Math: Why Your Timeouts Fail

The #1 VirtualService misconfiguration: setting retries that exceed the timeout budget. Here's the formula you MUST know for the ICA exam:

🧮 RETRY BUDGET FORMULA
  timeout ≥ (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout

  Example: attempts=2, perTryTimeout=1s
  Budget: (2 + 1) × 1s = 3s → timeout MUST be ≥ 3s

  ❌ timeout=2s, retries=2, perTry=1s → 3s needed but only 2s budget → 504!
  ✅ timeout=4s, retries=2, perTry=1s → 3s fits in 4s budget → works!

  The "+1" is for the INITIAL attempt (which is NOT a retry). Many forget this!
⚠️ ICA Exam Trap

Questions often give you: attempts=3, perTryTimeout=2s, timeout=5s. Quick math: (3+1)×2=8s needed, only 5s budget → retries will be cut short. The 3rd retry never completes. Answer: increase timeout to ≥8s or reduce attempts to 1.

6.13 Header Manipulation — Rewriting Requests and Responses In Flight

The headers field on an HTTP route adds, overwrites, or strips HTTP headers with zero application code changes. headers.request edits BEFORE the call reaches the upstream; headers.response edits BEFORE the reply reaches the caller. Each side supports three operations: set (a map of key → value that overwrites or creates the header), add (appends WITHOUT removing an existing header — can produce duplicate header lines, so use set unless duplicates are wanted, e.g. multi-value headers), and remove (a plain list of header names, deleted outright).

yaml — anihpj hides an internal header, adds a trace tag 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: user-service-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - user-service
  http:
  - headers:
      request:
        set:
          x-request-source: mesh   # ← stamped on every call
        remove:
        - x-internal-debug-token   # ← app header, drop it
      response:
        remove:
        - x-powered-by             # ← don't leak stack info
    route:
    - destination:
        host: user-service

🔀 Request/Response Header Editing — Where Each Operation Applies

headers.* fieldDirectionApplied by
request.set / addcaller → upstream, before deliveryoutbound
request.removecaller → upstream, before deliveryoutbound
response.set / addupstream → caller, before returninbound
response.removeupstream → caller, before returninbound
⚠️ Header Edits Are Per-Route, Not Conditional on the Outcome

The same headers block can sit next to a match, so different rules stamp different headers per route — for example, only the /jobs/ prefix rule adds x-cache-tier: hot. Header manipulation still runs even on a request a match rejects for OTHER reasons — it is applied per-ROUTE, not conditional on the rest of that route's outcome.

6.14 CORS Policy — Browser Cross-Origin Access Control

corsPolicy on an HTTP route makes Envoy answer Cross-Origin Resource Sharing preflight (OPTIONS) requests and stamp CORS headers on real responses — on the caller's BEHALF, with no application code involved. anihpj's SPA frontend lives on a different origin (app.anihpj.example) than the API (api.anihpj.example); the BROWSER blocks the fetch() unless the API's response carries Access-Control-Allow-Origin — without corsPolicy, Django would otherwise need django-cors-headers wired into every service separately.

🌐 CORS Preflight — The Browser Asks Permission Before the Real Request
1. Browser JS on app.anihpj.example calls:
   fetch("https://api.anihpj.example/jobs/")

2. Browser sends an OPTIONS preflight FIRST (not the real GET):
   OPTIONS /jobs/  Origin: https://app.anihpj.example

3. Envoy answers using corsPolicy — NEVER reaches jobpost-api:
   200 OK
   Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.anihpj.example
   Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST
   Access-Control-Max-Age: 86400

4. Browser is satisfied → sends the REAL GET /jobs/ request,
   which now reaches jobpost-api normally
yaml — anihpj SPA calling the jobpost-api origin 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - jobpost-api
  http:
  - corsPolicy:
      allowOrigins:
      - exact: https://app.anihpj.example
      allowMethods: ["GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"]
      allowHeaders: ["authorization", "content-type"]
      maxAge: "24h"             # ← cache the preflight, skip retest
      allowCredentials: true    # ← cookies/auth headers allowed
    route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
⚠️ Wildcard Origin + Credentials Don't Mix

allowOrigins with exact: "*" is NOT the same as allowing credentials from anywhere — browsers reject a wildcard origin combined with allowCredentials: true. Be explicit per origin instead.

💡 ICA Exam Cue

"The API works with curl but the SPA's browser fetch() fails with a CORS error" → check corsPolicy, not AuthorizationPolicy. curl never sends a preflight and never enforces CORS — only browsers do.

6.15 TCP and TLS Route Blocks — Routing Beyond HTTP

Besides http:, a VirtualService can carry tcp: and tls: blocks. tcp: routes raw L4 connections by port/source with NO awareness of what's inside them. tls: routes by the SNI hostname of a TLS handshake WITHOUT decrypting the traffic. Not everything in the anihpj mesh is HTTP — a raw Postgres connection, a Redis connection, or a plain-TLS legacy endpoint the sidecar should route but never terminate.

BlockMatch fieldsNotes
tcp:destinationSubnets, port, sourceLabels, sourceNamespace, gatewaysNo uri/headers — there's no HTTP request to inspect
tls:sniHosts (required), destinationSubnets, port, sourceLabels, sourceNamespace, gatewaysEnvoy peeks at the unencrypted SNI field of the ClientHello, then forwards the still-encrypted bytes untouched
🔀 Block Selection — How Envoy Picks http: vs tcp: vs tls:
New connection arrives at the sidecar
          │
          ▼
Is the payload HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, or gRPC?
   YES ──────────────────────────▶ use the  http:  block
   NO, but it's a TLS ClientHello ─▶ use the  tls:  block
          (routes on SNI, payload stays encrypted)
   NO, plain TCP ──────────────────▶ use the  tcp:  block
          (routes on port / source only, opaque bytes)
🐘
TCP Route — anihpj's Postgres Connection
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: postgres-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - postgres-primary
  tcp:
  - match:
    - port: 5432
    route:
    - destination:
        host: postgres-primary
        port:
          number: 5432
🔒
TLS Route — Split by SNI, Never Decrypted
spec:
  hosts:
  - "*"
  tls:
  - match:
    - port: 443
      sniHosts:
      - legacy.anihpj.example   # routes by SNI only
    route:
    - destination:
        host: legacy-tls-service
        port:
          number: 443

📋 HTTP vs TCP vs TLS — What Each Block Type Can and Cannot Do

Capabilityhttp:tcp:tls:
uri/header matchyesnono
sniHosts matchnonoyes
weighted routingyesyesyes
retries/timeoutyesnono
fault injectionyesnono
corsPolicyyesnono
sees payloadyesnono (encrypted)
⚠️ hosts: Is Usually "*" for a tls: Block

A VirtualService's hosts: for a tls: block is usually "*" — the SNI value in sniHosts does the real routing, not hosts:. The 6.9 route-precedence rule (first-match-wins, top-to-bottom) applies independently WITHIN each block — http:, tcp:, and tls: are evaluated as separate rule lists, not merged together.

🔧 Under the Hood — How VirtualService Route Matching Actually Works: HTTP Match Conditions, Route Precedence Rules, Weight Distribution, and How Precedence/Weight/Retry/Timeout Bundle Per Rule
🗺️ VirtualService Route Matching — How Envoy Selects the Right Backend
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ROUTE MATCHING PRIORITY — First Match Wins (Order Matters!)                    │
│                                                                              │
│  REQUEST ARRIVES: GET /api/v1/users/123  (Host: api.anihpj.com)               │
│       │                                                                       │
│       ▼                                                                       │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ CHECK ROUTE 1: match: prefix: "/api/v2/"                              │   │
│  │ → "/api/v2/" NOT in "/api/v1/users/123" → SKIP                      │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│       │                                                                       │
│       ▼                                                                       │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ CHECK ROUTE 2: match: prefix: "/api/v1/" + headers: canary: "true"   │   │
│  │ → PREFIX match! But header "canary: true" not present → SKIP         │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│       │                                                                       │
│       ▼                                                                       │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ CHECK ROUTE 3: match: prefix: "/api/v1/" (weight: 90% v1, 10% v2)   │   │
│  │ → PREFIX match! No header requirement → MATCH!                         │   │
│  │ → Envoy generates random number (0-100) → 73 → routes to v1 (0-89)    │   │
│  │ → RESULT: Forward to v1 subset                                         │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  CRITICAL RULE: Envoy evaluates routes in ORDER — first match WINS.          │
│  Put MORE SPECIFIC routes BEFORE less specific routes!                        │
│  ❌ BAD:  prefix: / → prefix: /api/  (first route catches everything!)      │
│  ✅ GOOD: prefix: /api/ → prefix: /  (specific → general)                  │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 Match Condition Types — What VirtualService Can Match On
Match TypeYAML KeyExampleUse Case
URI Prefixuri.prefix"/api/v1/"Path-based routing, API versioning
URI Exacturi.exact"/healthz"Health check, specific endpoint
URI Regexuri.regex"/users/\\d+"Pattern-based routing (costly!)
Headersheaderscanary: "true"A/B testing, canary header routing
Query ParamsqueryParamsversion: "v2"?version=v2 in URL
MethodmethodGET / POST / PUTRESTful API method routing
Authorityauthority"api.anihpj.com"Host-based routing

🔀 Weight Distribution — How Traffic Splitting Works in Envoy
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WEIGHTED ROUTING — Behind the Scenes of 90/10 Canary Splits                    │
│                                                                              │
│  VirtualService spec:                                                          │
│    - route:                                                                    │
│      - destination: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v1}  weight: 90              │
│      - destination: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v2}  weight: 10              │
│                                                                              │
│  HOW ENVOY IMPLEMENTS WEIGHTS:                                                 │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ 1. Envoy normalizes weights: total = 90+10 = 100                       │   │
│  │ 2. Creates ranges: v1 = [0, 90), v2 = [90, 100)                       │   │
│  │ 3. For EACH request: generates random number 0-99                      │   │
│  │ 4. Selects destination based on which range the number falls into     │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Request 1: random=23  →  in [0,90)  → v1                              │   │
│  │ Request 2: random=87  →  in [0,90)  → v1                              │   │
│  │ Request 3: random=94  →  in [90,100)→ v2                              │   │
│  │ Request 4: random=5   →  in [0,90)  → v1                              │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ Over 1000 requests: ~900 to v1, ~100 to v2 (± statistical variance)  │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  WEIGHT PRECISION: Weights are integers 1-100. Total does NOT need to = 100. │
│  Envoy NORMALIZES to percentages internally.                                  │
│  weight: 3 + weight: 1 = 75% / 25% (normalized from 3+1=4 total)           │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧩 The Rule Bundle — Precedence + Weight + Retry + Timeout, Together

6.12 already showed the retry-budget formula in isolation; this closing insight shows what happens when precedence (6.9), weight (6.3), retries (6.6) and timeout (6.7) all fire together for ONE real request — because in production they never fire alone.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ONE REQUEST, ONE RULE'S BUNDLE — jobpost-api-vs has 3 http rules:        │
│                                                                          │
│   RULE 1  match: header x-user-type=premium                              │
│           route: subset v2 | retries: 2, perTryTimeout 1s | timeout 3s   │
│   RULE 2  match: uri prefix /jobs/                                       │
│           route: 90% v1 / 10% v2 | retries: 3, perTryTimeout 2s |        │
│                  timeout 10s                                             │
│   RULE 3  (catch-all, no match block)                                    │
│           route: subset v1 | (no retries/timeout block set)              │
│                                                                          │
│ REQUEST A: GET /jobs/42, header x-user-type: premium                     │
│   step 1  Envoy walks rules top -> bottom (6.9 precedence)               │
│   step 2  RULE 1's header match succeeds -> STOP. RULE 2 and RULE 3      │
│           are never evaluated for this request at all                    │
│   step 3  destination is a single subset (v2) -- no weight draw needed,  │
│           RULE 2's 90/10 split is 100% irrelevant here                   │
│   step 4  RULE 1's OWN resilience bundle arms: up to 2 retries, 1s per   │
│           try, 3s total -- RULE 2's numbers (3 / 2s / 10s) never apply   │
│                                                                          │
│ REQUEST B: GET /jobs/42, no special headers                              │
│   step 1  RULE 1 match fails (header absent) -> skip                     │
│   step 2  RULE 2's uri prefix matches -> STOP                            │
│   step 3  NOW the weight draw runs: random 0-99, 0-89 -> v1, 90-99 -> v2 │
│   step 4  RULE 2's OWN bundle arms: up to 3 retries, 2s per try, 10s     │
│           total -- a completely different budget than REQUEST A got      │
│                                                                          │
│ THE SYNTHESIS: match, weight, retries and timeout are NOT independent    │
│ mesh-wide settings that blend together -- they are all bolted onto the   │
│ SAME winning rule and travel as one bundle. A request inherits exactly   │
│ one rule's whole bundle, never a mix of two rules' numbers. Misreading   │
│ this (assuming 'the' timeout for a VirtualService) is the #1 reason a    │
│ person debugging jobpost-api reads the wrong retries/timeout pair.       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 ICA Insight: VirtualService route matching is evaluated in ORDER — first match wins. ALWAYS put specific routes before catch-all routes. Key matching types: prefix (most common), exact, regex (expensive — avoid in production), headers (A/B testing), queryParams. Weights are normalized — 90+10 and 9+1 produce the SAME ratios. The random number for weight selection is generated per-request by Envoy — not based on connection or session ID unless CONSISTENT_HASH is used in DestinationRule. A request inherits exactly ONE rule's whole bundle — match, weight, retries, and timeout travel together; there is no mesh-wide default that blends two rules' numbers.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • VirtualService = WHERE, DestinationRule = HOW (Chapter 7) — VirtualService picks the destination and subset; DestinationRule decides load balancing, circuit breaking, and connection limits once a subset is chosen.
  • A route with no match: block and one destination pins 100% of traffic to that subset — the simplest possible VirtualService.
  • Weights don't need to sum to 100 — Envoy normalizes any ratio (9:1 produces the same 90/10 split as 90:10).
  • Rules are evaluated top-to-bottom, first match wins — a catch-all (no match block) placed above a specific rule makes that specific rule permanently dead code.
  • Retries are only safe for idempotent requests — GET is safe to retry; POST/PUT/DELETE risk double-charging or duplicate records unless retryOn is scoped carefully.
  • The retry budget formula: timeout ≥ (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout — the "+1" accounts for the initial attempt, which is not itself a retry.
  • Fault injection and retries/timeout CAN syntactically coexist on the same VirtualService route, but retries/timeout go inert when a fault is present — test resilience on a separate VirtualService if you need real retries/timeout still active.
  • The Sidecar CRD scopes what one Envoy can see — without it, every proxy knows about every service mesh-wide, which becomes a real memory and config-push-latency problem past ~100 services.
  • App-level and mesh-level failure recovery are independent — a Django-side timeout tighter than Istio's own can fire first and prevent Envoy's retry from ever getting a chance to help.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "Weights must sum to exactly 100." No — Envoy normalizes whatever ratio you give it; weight: 3 + weight: 1 produces a 75/25 split.
  • "Route order in the YAML doesn't matter, Envoy picks the best match." No — it's strictly top-to-bottom, first match wins. A catch-all above a specific rule means the specific rule NEVER fires.
  • "Retries are always safe to add." No — only for idempotent methods. Retrying a POST that already partially succeeded can create duplicate records.
  • "More retry attempts is always safer." No — if (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout exceeds the route's timeout, the last retry gets cut off mid-flight, and you've made latency worse, not resilience better.
  • "Fault injection plus real retries/timeout tests resilience end-to-end." No — the config is accepted, but Istio silently disables retries/timeout on any route that also has a fault block; test faults on a dedicated VirtualService instead if you need the real resilience config active too.
  • "Every Envoy proxy only knows about the services it actually calls, by default." No — the DEFAULT is every Envoy knows about the WHOLE mesh; the Sidecar CRD is what scopes it down, and it's opt-in, not automatic.
  • "Setting a timeout in my VirtualService means my app code doesn't need one." Not necessarily — if your app-level timeout is tighter than Istio's, YOUR timeout fires first and Istio's retries never get invoked at all.

💼 Chapter 6 — Daily Work Takeaways

  • Always order match rules most-specific-first — the #1 VirtualService misconfiguration is a catch-all sitting above a targeted rule.
  • Run 6.12's retry-budget formula against your own numbers before shipping — timeout ≥ (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout, every single time.
  • Test fault injection on its own VirtualService, never combined with the real retries/timeout config on that same route.
  • Reach for the Sidecar CRD once the mesh crosses roughly 50-100 services — the memory and config-push savings become real, not theoretical.
  • Pick exactly ONE owner per timeout/retry concern — app code or the mesh, never both fighting silently.
  • Verify with istioctl proxy-config route, not just kubectl describe vs — only the proxy-config command shows what Envoy actually holds.
  • For the ICA exam: route-order bugs, retry-budget math, and the fault-injection/retry conflict are the three most commonly tested VirtualService traps.
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 6

Seven quick-fire phrase-to-answer mappings — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Route traffic by URI" = match.uri.prefix (or exact/regex)
  • "Canary split" = weight fields on route destinations — Envoy normalizes automatically
  • "A/B test by caller" = match.headers with an exact/prefix/regex value
  • "Add resilience" = retries + timeout block, budget-checked against 6.12's formula
  • "Test resilience" = fault.delay / fault.abort — on a SEPARATE VirtualService from real retries/timeout
  • "My route never fires" = check rule ORDER first — a catch-all above the specific rule is the #1 cause
  • "Reduce sidecar memory / limit visibility" = the Sidecar CRD's egress.hosts

🧠 Chapter 6 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
In one sentence each, what does VirtualService govern versus what does DestinationRule govern?
Show Answer
Answer

VirtualService decides WHERE a request goes — which subset, by weight/header/path. DestinationRule decides HOW it gets there once chosen — load balancing, circuit breaking, connection pools.

Explanation

The two CRDs are always a pair for any subset-based routing — a VirtualService referencing a subset that no DestinationRule defines produces 503 "no healthy upstream," not a routing error.

Q2
Do VirtualService weights need to sum to 100?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Envoy normalizes whatever ratio you give it — weight: 3 + weight: 1 produces the same 75/25 split as weight: 75 + weight: 25.

Explanation

Pick numbers that are easy to reason about under time pressure rather than numbers that merely happen to add to 100 — the exam doesn't require the sum-to-100 form.

Q3
A VirtualService has a catch-all rule (no match block) as its FIRST http rule, followed by a header-matched rule. What happens to the header-matched rule?
Show Answer
Answer

It never fires. Rules are evaluated top-to-bottom, first match wins — the catch-all matches every request immediately, so nothing below it is ever reached.

Explanation

This is the #1 VirtualService misconfiguration according to the chapter's own repeated warnings — always put the most specific rules first, catch-all last.

Q4
Why are retries only safe for idempotent requests like GET?
Show Answer
Answer

Because a POST/PUT/DELETE that already partially succeeded (e.g. the database write committed, but the response was lost) would be repeated by a retry — potentially double-charging a payment or creating a duplicate record.

Explanation

GET requests don't change state, so repeating one is always safe. retryOn should be scoped carefully for any route handling non-idempotent methods.

Q5
State the retry budget formula, and explain what the "+1" accounts for.
Show Answer
Answer

timeout ≥ (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout. The "+1" accounts for the INITIAL attempt, which is not itself a retry — a config with attempts: 2 actually makes up to 3 total tries (1 initial + 2 retries).

Explanation

Forgetting the "+1" is the single most common exam trap in this chapter — attempts=3/perTryTimeout=2s/timeout=5s LOOKS fine at a glance but actually needs 8s, not 5s.

Q6
Can a single VirtualService route combine fault injection with retries and a timeout?
Show Answer
Answer

They CAN be written on the same route — Istio won't reject the YAML — but per the official docs, timeouts and retries will NOT be enabled when a fault is present on that route. The fault silently overrides them. If you need real retries/timeout active during a resilience test, use two separate VirtualServices.

Explanation

This is a documented Istio limitation, not a bug — it exists because fault injection and resilience testing measuring the SAME mechanism on the SAME route would produce confusing, self-canceling results.

Q7
What problem does the Sidecar CRD solve, and what's the default behavior without one?
Show Answer
Answer

Without a Sidecar resource, EVERY Envoy proxy knows about EVERY service in the mesh — in a 500-service mesh that's 500 clusters loaded into each sidecar's config, costing real memory and slow config pushes. The Sidecar CRD's egress.hosts limits one Envoy's visibility to only the services it actually calls.

Explanation

This isn't optional at scale — production meshes with 100+ services treat Sidecar resources as mandatory for performance, not a nice-to-have.

Q8
Django sets a 2s client timeout on a call; the VirtualService sets a 3s timeout with 1 retry at perTryTimeout 2s. What ACTUALLY happens?
Show Answer
Answer

Django's OWN 2s timeout fires FIRST — it raises a Timeout exception before Envoy's 3s VirtualService timeout or its retry ever gets a chance to help. The mesh-level resilience config is effectively useless here.

Explanation

App-level and mesh-level failure recovery are independent — neither knows about the other. The golden rule: the app timeout must be ≥ the mesh's own retry budget plus a buffer, or removed entirely and left to Istio.

Q9
An SPA's browser fetch() call to the API fails with a CORS error, but the identical request works fine via curl. What should you check, and why doesn't curl reproduce the problem?
Show Answer
Answer

Check corsPolicy on the VirtualService, not AuthorizationPolicy. curl never sends a CORS preflight and never enforces CORS — CORS is a BROWSER security mechanism, not a server-side or network-level restriction.

Explanation

Without corsPolicy, Envoy never answers the browser's OPTIONS preflight with the right Access-Control-Allow-* headers, so the browser blocks the real request before it's even sent.

Q10
What's the difference between a VirtualService's tcp: block and its tls: block, and which one can still route by hostname?
Show Answer
Answer

tcp: routes raw L4 connections by port/source only — no awareness of hostname. tls: routes by the unencrypted SNI field of the TLS ClientHello — it CAN route by hostname (sniHosts) without ever decrypting the traffic.

Explanation

Neither block supports uri/header matching, retries, timeout, fault injection, or corsPolicy — those are all HTTP-layer features that only the http: block can use.

⚙️ Chapter 6 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
A VirtualService's premium-header rule stopped firing after a teammate "cleaned up" the YAML. All traffic, premium or not, goes to v1. Task: Diagnose the most likely cause and write the fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# Diagnose: dump the route order
kubectl get vs jobpost-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 "match:\|route:"
# Most likely: the catch-all rule (no match: block) got moved ABOVE
# the header-matched rule during the "cleanup"

# Fix: reorder http[] so the header match comes FIRST, catch-all LAST
kubectl apply -f jobpost-api-vs-fixed.yaml -n anihpj
Explanation

This is the exact "cleanup that isn't" scenario the chapter warns about — reordering YAML blocks looks harmless but silently changes matching behavior, since order is semantically meaningful in VirtualService.

Q2
Write a VirtualService for jobpost-api that sends x-canary: "true" requests to subset v2, and everything else 95/5 between v1 and v2.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - jobpost-api
  http:
  - match:
    - headers:
        x-canary:
          exact: "true"
    route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v2
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v1
      weight: 95
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v2
      weight: 5
Explanation

The header-matched rule MUST come first — if the weighted catch-all were first, it would match every request (including canary ones) before the header rule ever got evaluated.

Q3
Your team sets attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 2s, timeout: 5s on a route. Requests are getting cut off mid-retry. Task: Run the retry budget formula and fix it.
Show Answer
Answer
# Budget check: (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout = (3+1) × 2s = 8s needed
# Configured timeout is only 5s → 3s short, 3rd retry gets cut off

# Fix option A: raise the timeout to cover the full budget
#   timeout: 8s

# Fix option B: reduce attempts to fit the existing 5s budget
#   attempts: 1  →  (1+1) × 2s = 4s, fits inside 5s
Explanation

Either fix is valid depending on the real requirement — raising the timeout preserves retry resilience but costs latency; reducing attempts keeps latency tight but weakens the retry safety net.

Q4
A teammate wants to test that auth-service's timeout and retry config actually protects callers under a real failure. They add a fault.abort block directly on the SAME route that already has retries and timeout set. Task: Explain why this won't work and write the correct approach.
Show Answer
Answer

Istio accepts fault injection and retry/timeout config on the SAME route without error, but retries/timeout will NOT be enabled once a fault is present — they silently go inert, not erroring, just ignored. The correct approach: create a SEPARATE VirtualService (or a separate route matched by a test-only header) carrying only the fault block, applied temporarily during the resilience test.

Explanation

A common pattern: gate the fault-injection VirtualService behind a header like x-chaos-test: true so it only affects deliberate test traffic, never production requests.

Q5
The mesh has grown to 300 services and istiod's config-push latency has become noticeable. Task: Write a Sidecar resource limiting jobpost-api's Envoy visibility to only user-service, skills-service, and istiod itself.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Sidecar
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  egress:
  - hosts:
    - "./user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
    - "./skills-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
    - "istio-system/*"
Explanation

Note what egress.hosts actually scopes: it's the DATA-PLANE routing table — which service clusters THIS Envoy can send application traffic to. It does NOT control the proxy's own xDS connection to istiod — that control-plane channel is set up independently at bootstrap and isn't affected by Sidecar scoping either way. istio-system/* is included here as Istio's own documented convention, so the proxy can still route to any istio-system-hosted service the app might call directly (e.g. a telemetry or addon endpoint) — not because omitting it would break config delivery.

Q6
Verify that a VirtualService's retry config actually reached the live Envoy for jobpost-api — write the command, not just kubectl describe.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl proxy-config route deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -o json | grep -A4 retryPolicy
Explanation

kubectl describe vs only shows what you APPLIED — it proves nothing about whether Envoy actually received and compiled it. istioctl proxy-config route reads Envoy's live in-memory route table, the same distinction Chapter 5 taught for Gateways.

Q7
Write a VirtualService rule that adds a header x-request-source: mesh to every outbound request to user-service and strips x-powered-by from the response.
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  hosts:
  - user-service
  http:
  - headers:
      request:
        set:
          x-request-source: mesh
      response:
        remove:
        - x-powered-by
    route:
    - destination:
        host: user-service
Explanation

request.set edits before the call reaches user-service; response.remove edits before the reply reaches the original caller. Both happen with zero Django code changes.

Q8
anihpj's SPA at app.anihpj.example calls the API at api.anihpj.example with credentials (cookies). Write the corsPolicy that allows this specific origin with credentials.
Show Answer
Answer
http:
- corsPolicy:
    allowOrigins:
    - exact: https://app.anihpj.example
    allowMethods: ["GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE"]
    allowHeaders: ["authorization", "content-type"]
    allowCredentials: true
  route:
  - destination:
      host: jobpost-api
Explanation

Note allowOrigins uses an EXACT origin, not a wildcard — browsers reject allowCredentials: true combined with a wildcard "*" origin outright, so credentialed cross-origin requests always need an explicit origin list.

Q9
Write a VirtualService tls: block that routes traffic for SNI hostname legacy.anihpj.example on port 443 to a service named legacy-tls-service, without terminating the TLS connection.
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  hosts:
  - "*"
  tls:
  - match:
    - port: 443
      sniHosts:
      - legacy.anihpj.example
    route:
    - destination:
        host: legacy-tls-service
        port:
          number: 443
Explanation

hosts: ["*"] is normal for a tls: block — the real routing decision is made by sniHosts, not hosts. Envoy reads the unencrypted SNI field and forwards the still-encrypted bytes untouched.

Q10
A request to /api/v1/users/123 should match a specific v1-API rule, but a colleague's newly-added rule for /api/ (prefix) is catching it first. Task: Explain the fix and the general principle it demonstrates.
Show Answer
Answer

Fix: move the more specific /api/v1/ prefix rule ABOVE the broader /api/ prefix rule. Principle: Envoy has no concept of "most specific prefix wins" — it is PURELY ordinal, top-to-bottom, first match wins, regardless of how specific each rule's match condition looks.

Explanation

This is worth memorizing as a hard rule, not an inference: prefix: /api/ placed above prefix: /api/v1/ will ALWAYS win for any /api/v1/* request, no matter how much more specific the lower rule looks on paper.

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 6
  • Weights don't need to sum to 100 — Envoy normalizes any ratio (9:1 is the same split as 90:10), so pick numbers that are easy to reason about under exam pressure, not numbers that merely add up cleanly.
  • Memorize 6.12's formula cold: timeout ≥ (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout — the exam will hand you numbers that look fine at a glance and fail it.
  • Before debugging "my route never fires," check order first — a catch-all (no match: block) sitting above a specific rule is the #1 cause, not a typo inside the match condition itself.
  • fault: and retries:/timeout: on the SAME route silently disable each other per the docs — if you need both, use two VirtualServices, not one.
  • Delete an app-level timeout (or size it generously above the mesh's) before trusting Istio's retries — a tighter app timeout races the mesh and wins before Envoy's retry ever gets a chance to help.
  • Run istioctl analyze before kubectl apply — an undefined subset (missing DestinationRule) is a free catch that saves real exam minutes.

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 6)

Every command below already appeared earlier in this chapter — grouped here as one reference for applying, inspecting, and validating a VirtualService.

CommandWhat It Does / Checks in Chapter 6
kubectl apply -f jobpost-api-vs.yaml -n anihpjCreate/update a VirtualService (6.2)
kubectl get vs -n anihpjList VirtualServices (vs short name) (6.1)
kubectl describe vs jobpost-api-vs -n anihpjSee routes, matches, and weights (6.3)
kubectl delete -f jobpost-api-vs.yamlRemove a VirtualService — the fault-injection swap pattern (6.11)
istioctl analyze -n anihpjValidate before apply — catches undefined subsets (6.3)
istioctl proxy-config route deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -o json | grep -A4 retryPolicyConfirm the live retry config Envoy actually holds (6.6)
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | wc -lCount what this Envoy can reach — verify Sidecar scoping (6.10)

🔬 Practice Drill 6.1 — Build, Order, and Verify a Production VirtualService

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Build and verify a real jobpost-api-vs, right now — don't just read this, do it:

  1. Write a VirtualService that sends 90% of jobpost-api traffic to subset v1 and 10% to subset v2 (reuse 6.3's YAML as your starting point).
  2. Add a header-based rule ABOVE the weighted rule: requests carrying x-user-type: premium always go to v2 — and confirm your rule ORDER follows 6.9 (the specific match sits before the weighted catch-all).
  3. Attach retries (attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 2s, retryOn: 5xx) and a timeout to the weighted rule, then run 6.12's formula against your own numbers: does (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout fit inside your timeout?
  4. kubectl apply -f jobpost-api-vs.yaml -n anihpj, then run istioctl proxy-config route deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -o json | grep -A4 retryPolicy and confirm Envoy actually holds the numbers you wrote.
  5. Break it on purpose — move the catch-all rule to the top — and watch your premium-header rule stop firing, then put the order back.
Hint: Steps 1-2 test 6.3 and 6.4's patterns together with 6.9's ordering rule; steps 3-4 are 6.12's retry-budget formula applied for real; step 5 is the #1 VirtualService misconfiguration (6.9) reproduced on purpose so you recognize it instantly on exam day.
View Solution

After step 4, the JSON output should show a retryPolicy block with numRetries: 3 and a perTryTimeout matching what you wrote — if it's missing entirely, istioctl analyze first to rule out a YAML error before assuming a delivery problem. Step 5 should make the premium-header rule stop firing completely, not partially — that binary behavior (works / totally dead) is the tell for a route-ordering bug specifically, versus a gradual degradation which would point elsewhere.

Check yourself: did you verify step 3's math BEFORE applying, or after? Catching a retry-budget mismatch on paper is faster than discovering it via cut-off requests in step 4's live output.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.2 — Prove the Fault-Injection/Retry Conflict Yourself

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Don't take 6.11's warning on faith — reproduce the fault-injection/retry conflict on a live cluster.

  1. Apply a VirtualService with BOTH a fault.abort block (50% of requests, HTTP 500) AND a retries block (attempts: 3) on the SAME route.
  2. Send 20 requests and count how many client-visible errors you actually see.
  3. Split them into two separate VirtualServices — one with only fault.abort gated behind a test header, one with only retries — and repeat the 20-request test.
  4. Compare the error counts between step 2 and step 3.
Hint: Use istioctl proxy-config route to inspect what Envoy actually compiled for the combined route in step 1 — one of the two blocks won't appear the way you expect.
View Solution

In the combined config, the retry policy does not protect against the injected fault the way you'd expect from the two features working together — confirming they don't compose on one route. The split configuration in step 3 behaves as each feature independently documents.

Check yourself: could you now explain this to a teammate using YOUR OWN request counts, not just quoting the docs? That's the difference this drill is built to create.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.3 — Match the Symptom to the Broken Layer

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

For each observation, name the most likely cause and the ONE command you'd run to confirm it — before proposing any fix:

  1. A canary VirtualService with weight: 90/weight: 10 is somehow sending roughly 50/50 traffic in Kiali.
  2. A retries block with attempts: 5, perTryTimeout: 1s, timeout: 3s is producing MORE 504s than before it was added.
  3. A header-based A/B rule works for curl -H "x-user-type: premium" but never fires from the real browser SPA.
  4. A tcp: block's fault-injection-style config (borrowed from an http: example) silently does nothing.
Hint: Two of these four are actually the SAME root cause wearing different clothes — a feature that only exists in the http: block being used somewhere it can't apply.
View Solution
#CauseConfirm with
1A SECOND VirtualService (or a different rule) is also matching this host with different weights, and precedence is picking the wrong onekubectl get vs -n anihpj -o yaml — look for more than one VS touching the same host
2Retry budget math: (5+1)×1s = 6s needed, only 3s available — retries are firing then getting cut off by the outer timeout, converting transient errors into hard 504sRun 6.12's formula by hand against the actual config
3The real browser sends different header casing/values than curl, or a corsPolicy preflight is stripping the custom headeristioctl proxy-config route + browser devtools network tab — compare actual request headers sent
4Not a bug, a feature limit — fault: is an http:-only field; tcp: blocks have no concept of HTTP status codes to abort withRe-read 6.15's capability table — fault injection is listed as unsupported for tcp:

Check yourself: did you correctly identify #4 as "working as designed," not a bug to chase? A tcp: block silently ignoring an HTTP-only field is the documented behavior, not a defect.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.4 — Scope a Sidecar Resource, Then Prove It Worked

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

On a cluster with several meshed services, prove Sidecar scoping actually shrinks an Envoy's config — don't just apply it and assume.

  1. Before any Sidecar resource exists, count jobpost-api's Envoy clusters: istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | wc -l.
  2. Apply a Sidecar resource scoping jobpost-api to only 2 real dependencies plus istio-system/*.
  3. Re-run the cluster count command and compare.
  4. Confirm jobpost-api can still actually reach its 2 real dependencies (a live curl), and that a call to a service you DIDN'T list now fails differently than before.
Hint: Include istio-system/* in the egress hosts list, matching Istio's own documented convention — egress.hosts scopes DATA-PLANE routing only, not the proxy's own xDS connection to istiod (that's independent of Sidecar scoping either way).
View Solution

The cluster count should drop substantially — often by 90%+ in a mesh with many services. The un-scoped dependency call should now fail at the CDS layer (no cluster exists for it) rather than reaching the destination and failing for an application reason — a meaningfully different failure signature you can point to as proof the scoping is real, not just configured.

Check yourself: did you verify the ALLOWED dependencies still work, not just that the blocked one now fails? Scoping too narrowly and breaking a real dependency is the actual production risk this drill is rehearsing against.

🔬 Practice Drill 6.5 — Sketch the Rule-Bundle Diagram, Timed

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

In 5 minutes, from memory, sketch the UTH's "Rule Bundle" diagram: a 3-rule VirtualService (header match / weighted prefix match / catch-all), and for TWO different incoming requests, trace which single rule wins and which retry/timeout numbers travel with it. Do NOT reopen the UTH until you finish.

Hint: The trap most people fall into: assuming a VirtualService has ONE timeout/retry setting that applies mesh-wide. It doesn't — each rule carries its own bundle.
View Solution

Compare against the UTH's REQUEST A / REQUEST B trace. The detail most people drop: RULE 2's 90/10 weight draw is 100% IRRELEVANT for REQUEST A, because RULE 1 already matched and stopped evaluation — weight only matters for requests that fall through to the rule that HAS a weight split.

Check yourself: did you correctly show that a request inherits exactly ONE rule's whole bundle (match + weight + retries + timeout), never a mix of two different rules' numbers? This is the single most-tested conceptual point in the whole chapter.

🚦 Chapter 6 in One Picture — One anihpj Request's Whole VirtualService Life
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ REQUEST arrives for jobpost-api (VS already applied, 6.1-6.2)     │
│          │                                                        │
│          ▼ walked top → bottom, FIRST match wins (6.9)            │
│ 🎯 MATCH RULES                                                    │
│    ├─ header x-user-type: premium?  → subset v2  (A/B test, 6.4) │
│    ├─ uri prefix /jobs/ + weight draw → 90% v1 / 10% v2 (6.3,6.5)│
│    └─ no match → catch-all v1                                     │
│          │                                                        │
│          ▼ the WINNING rule's own bundle arms                     │
│ 🛡️ RESILIENCE BUNDLE (6.6, 6.7, 6.11, 6.12)                       │
│    retries: N attempts @ perTryTimeout  |  timeout: total budget  │
│    (a fault: block on this route disables retries/timeout          │
│     instead, 6.8 — test faults on a SEPARATE VirtualService)      │
│          │                                                        │
│          ▼ in-flight edits                                        │
│ ✏️ HEADERS rewritten (6.13); CORS preflight answered if the       │
│    caller is a browser on another origin (6.14)                   │
│          │                                                        │
│          ▼                                                        │
│ ✅ Envoy delivers to the chosen pod — non-HTTP traffic (Postgres, │
│    a raw TLS endpoint) skips ALL of the above and uses the        │
│    separate tcp:/tls: rule lists instead, matched by port or      │
│    SNI only (6.15)                                                 │
│                                                                    │
│    (running underneath everything: the Sidecar CRD, 6.10, already │
│     decided which destinations THIS Envoy was even told about)    │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Every arrow above is a decision this chapter taught you to make deliberately instead of by accident. A request is matched exactly once (6.1, 6.9), routed by weight, header, or path depending on which rule wins (6.2-6.5), handed the winning rule's OWN retry/timeout bundle rather than some mesh-wide default (6.6-6.7, 6.11-6.12), spared from testing tools bleeding into production traffic (6.8), optionally rewritten and CORS-annotated in flight (6.13-6.14), and — for traffic that was never HTTP to begin with — handled by a completely separate tcp:/tls: pipeline that ignores everything else in this list (6.15). Chapter 7 picks up exactly where this diagram's last arrow lands: once Envoy knows WHERE a request goes, DestinationRule decides HOW it actually gets there.

Quick recap — 🎯 Match: header / URI / query, top-to-bottom, first match wins · ⚖️ Weight: canary splits Envoy normalizes for you · 🔄 Retries + ⏱️ Timeout: one bundle per winning rule, budgeted with 6.12's formula · 🐌 Delay / 💥 Abort: fault injection tests the bundle on purpose, never in prod · ✏️ Headers + 🌐 CORS: in-flight edits, zero app code · 🔌 tcp:/tls:: a separate pipeline for traffic that was never HTTP.

Chapter 7: DestinationRule — Traffic Policies and Load Balancing

The DestinationRule defines HOW traffic is sent AFTER VirtualService decides WHERE it goes. It configures load balancing algorithms, circuit breakers, connection pools, TLS mode, and named subsets for canary routing.

Chapter 6's VirtualService can say "send 90% of /jobs/ traffic to subset: v1" all day, but that instruction means nothing until something defines what "subset: v1" actually IS and decides how a request reaches it once chosen — that something is this chapter's DestinationRule. Without it, jobpost-api's canary split has no pods to land on, user-service has no sticky-session guarantee for its per-user cache, and — most importantly — a single misbehaving auth-service pod has nothing stopping it from doing exactly what Chapter 1's cascade failure showed: blocking every caller's threads until all of anihpj goes down with it. DestinationRule's outlierDetection is the one setting in this entire guide that turns "one slow dependency takes down the whole system" into "one bad pod gets ejected in milliseconds while the rest of anihpj keeps serving." Every canary you will ever ship, and every circuit breaker anihpj ever trips in production, is configured right here.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~3 hours ⚙️ Policies 🎯 ICA 35%
