7.1 What is a DestinationRule?

DestinationRule applies post-routing policies. VirtualService picks the destination (which service, which subset), then DestinationRule applies: load balancing, TLS mode, circuit breaker settings, and connection pool limits.

🔀 VIRTUALSERVICE + DESTINATIONRULE — How They Work Together
1
Request

GET /jobs/ arrives

2
VirtualService

WHERE? → match /jobs/* → jobpost-api, subset v1 (90%)

3
DestinationRule

HOW? → subset v1 = pods with version:v1 label

4
Load Balancer

LEAST_CONN → pick pod with fewest active connections

5
Circuit Breaker

Check: has pod failed 5 times? → CLOSED ✅

6
mTLS

ISTIO_MUTUAL → encrypt connection to pod

7
Pod

Request delivered to jobpost-api-v1-abc

📖 The Golden Rule

VirtualService = WHERE (the GPS route). DestinationRule = HOW (the driving rules — speed limit, lane choice, seatbelt). VS decides the destination; DR applies policies to that destination.

7.2 Defining Subsets (Required for Canary)

Subsets link Pod labels to route targets. The VirtualService says "send to subset v1" and DestinationRule resolves "subset v1 = pods with label version: v1".

🏷️ SUBSET RESOLUTION — Labels → Subsets → Routing
Pod: jobpost-v1-abc

labels:
app: jobpost-api
version: v1

✅ Matches subset v1

Pod: jobpost-v2-xyz

labels:
app: jobpost-api
version: v2

✅ Matches subset v2

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE

If pods are missing the version label, the subset resolves to ZERO endpoints → 503 errors! Always add labels: version: v1 to ALL your Deployments.

🔧 Under the Hood — Subsets Don't Create Pods, They Filter Endpoints

A subset doesn't create new Pods or new network paths — Istiod is already watching the Kubernetes Endpoints behind the jobpost-api Service. A subset's label selector is applied on top of that existing endpoint list, and the filtered result is pushed to every Envoy sidecar as an EDS (Endpoint Discovery Service) update. No pods match the label → EDS pushes an empty list to Envoy — which is exactly why the COMMON MISTAKE above produces 503s instead of a config error.

7.3 Load Balancing Algorithms

AlgorithmBehaviorBest Foranihpj Use
ROUND_ROBINEach pod in turnUniform workloadsskills-service
LEAST_CONNFewest active connectionsVariable-duration requestsjobpost-api
RANDOMRandom selectionVery fast, statelessauth-service
CONSISTENT_HASHSame user → same podSession affinity / cachinguser-service
PASSTHROUGHBypass Envoy LBCustom load balancing—

🎯 Decision Guide — Which Algorithm for Each anihpj Service?

ServiceAlgorithmWhy
jobpost-apiLEAST_CONNMix of fast/slow Django views
user-serviceCONSISTENT_HASHPer-user cache warmth (hash on x-user-id header)
skills-serviceROUND_ROBINUniform stateless queries
auth-serviceRANDOMVery fast, stateless, uniform latency
search-serviceLEAST_CONNVariable search complexity per query
📖 Naming Update — LEAST_CONN Is a Legacy Alias

LEAST_CONN above is the legacy alias — modern Istio calls the same algorithm LEAST_REQUEST, and LEAST_REQUEST (not ROUND_ROBIN) is Istio's ACTUAL default when you configure no loadBalancer at all — istio.io documented this default by Istio 1.17, well before the v1 API GA'd at Istio 1.22. Envoy's own default is ROUND_ROBIN — that's why older docs call it "the default"; Istio overrides it per-cluster. Sticky sessions at scale get two extra algorithm choices, RING_HASH and MAGLEV — the full 7-algorithm tour is in 7.8.

7.4 Circuit Breaking (Outlier Detection)

A circuit breaker prevents cascading failures. When a service starts failing, the breaker opens and stops ALL requests to it — giving it time to recover.

🔌 CIRCUIT BREAKER STATE MACHINE
CLOSED
Normal

Requests flow ✅
Counting errors...

5 errs
→ OPEN

All requests fail immediately ❌
Service protected

30s
→ HALF-OPEN

One test request allowed
If OK → CLOSED

yaml — Circuit breaker configuration 

trafficPolicy:
  outlierDetection:
    consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5   # after 5 errors, eject host
    interval: 30s                 # check every 30 seconds
    baseEjectionTime: 30s         # keep ejected for 30 seconds
    maxEjectionPercent: 50        # never eject more than 50% of hosts

7.5 Connection Pool Settings

Control how many concurrent connections Envoy allows per service. This prevents a slow service from being overwhelmed by queued requests consuming Envoy memory.

🏊 CONNECTION POOL — Request Queuing Visualization
Incoming requests ──▶ [=====QUEUE=====|100 max|] ──▶ skills-service

Scenario A (normal):  50 requests → queue at 50% — ✅ OK
Scenario B (busy):   100 requests → queue FULL → 503 returned
Scenario C (spike):  200 requests → 100 queued, 100 fast-rejected

WHY: Without limit, 1000 requests queue up consuming memory
until the service falls over. With limit: fast 503 → caller can retry.
🧠 Mental Model — The Coffee Shop Connection Pool

Think of skills-service's connection pool like a small coffee shop: maxConnections is the number of tables inside (a hard cap on how many customers are served at once), and http1MaxPendingRequests is the line forming outside the door. As long as there's room in that line, new customers wait their turn — but once the line itself is full, the shop turns people away at the door (a fast 503) instead of making them stand outside forever while skills-service quietly falls over.

7.6 Complete DestinationRule for anihpj

yaml — Complete DestinationRule for jobpost-api 

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: jobpost-api
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      simple: LEAST_CONN          # smart load balancing
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 100
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 50
        http2MaxRequests: 100
    outlierDetection:             # circuit breaker
      consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50
    tls:
      mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL          # enforce mTLS
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1                 # stable version
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2                 # canary version

7.7 Deep Dive — Circuit Breaker States: CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN (a Teaching Analogy)

A circuit breaker is a per-pod health switch inside Envoy — it counts failures for every backend pod and "trips" (stops sending that pod traffic) once failures cross a threshold.

📖 KEY TERM — outlierDetection

outlierDetection is Istio's config field name for what this chapter calls a "circuit breaker." Same mechanism, two names: the docs say circuit breaker, the YAML field is outlierDetection — the ICA exam expects you to know both. But note: CLOSED/OPEN/HALF-OPEN are NOT literal Envoy/Istio terminology — they're this chapter's teaching analogy for a real mechanism that's actually just two states: in-the-pool (healthy) and EJECTED (removed, timed backoff). Don't expect to see these three words in any istioctl output or Envoy log.

Why it matters: without one, every caller keeps hammering a dying pod — requests queue behind it, caller threads block, and the failure cascades upstream: one sick auth-service pod leaves jobpost-api's workers stuck waiting, jobpost-api runs out of workers, and ALL of anihpj goes down. Envoy's outlierDetection analysis runs every interval, ejects pods that crossed the error threshold, and re-admits them after a cooling-off period — the classic CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN pattern. Repeat offenders sit out longer: ejection time = baseEjectionTime × times-ejected (30s → 60s → 90s → ...). Envoy reality check: there is no literal probe request — in HALF-OPEN the pod simply rejoins the pool and the next few REAL requests are the probe; 5 more errors send it straight back to OPEN.

🔌 CIRCUIT BREAKER STATE MACHINE — Transitions and the Canonical anihpj Parameters
STATE 1: CLOSED   (normal — pod is in the load-balancing pool)
  • every request is forwarded; Envoy counts errors per pod
  • consecutive-error counter: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 = threshold!
  • any single success resets the counter back to 0
           │
           │  TRIP CONDITION: consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5
           │  (5 straight 502/503/504 or TCP connect failures)
           ▼
STATE 2: OPEN     (tripped — pod EJECTED from the pool)
  • Envoy sends this pod NOTHING; remaining pods take over
  • callers never block on the sick pod → no cascade upstream
  • guard rail: maxEjectionPercent: 50 → with 4 pods, at most
    2 are ever OPEN at once — 2 always keep serving
           │
           │  COOL-OFF: baseEjectionTime: 30s expires
           │  (2nd ejection waits 60s, 3rd waits 90s, ...)
           ▼
STATE 3: HALF-OPEN (probation — pod quietly re-admitted)
  • pod rejoins the pool; live traffic is the probe
  • requests succeed → error count stays 0 → back to CLOSED ✅
  • 5 more failures → re-ejected → back to OPEN, for longer ❌

Sweep cadence: the outlier analysis runs every interval: 30s

📋 Outlier Detection Tuning — Meaning, Safe Value, Symptom If Wrong

FieldMeaningSafe ValueSymptom If Wrong
consecutiveGatewayErrors502/503/504 + TCP connect failures count toward the trip51-2: pods flap on one blip; 50: it never trips at all
consecutive5xxErrorsApp 5xx only — TCP connection failures are NOT counted(off)A connection-refused pod is never ejected
intervalHow often the ejection-analysis sweep runs30s300s: a sick pod serves errors for 5 whole minutes
baseEjectionTimeLength of the 1st ejection (×2, ×3... on repeats)30s1h: capacity stays down long after the pod recovers
maxEjectionPercentCap on % of the pool ejected at the same time50100: the breaker can eject EVERY pod — a self-made outage
minHealthPercentBelow this healthy %, ejection is suspended entirely(off)Set high on small pools: ejection quietly disables
⏱️ REAL SCENARIO TIMELINE — skills-service Bad Deploy vs the Breaker
Fleet: 4 skills-service pods behind :8090; mesh baseline 847 req/s,
2.1% errors, p99 234ms. Pod 3 ships a bad deploy.

T=0s     pod 3 starts timing out; service-wide numbers hit
         8.1% errors / p99 1240ms — dashboards go red
T=4s     pod 3 returns its 5th consecutive 503
         → circuit OPENS: pod 3 ejected (1/4 = 25% ≤ 50% cap)
T=4-34s  3 healthy pods absorb the load; caller-visible
         errors drop back under 1%
T=34s    baseEjectionTime: 30s expires → HALF-OPEN:
         pod 3 re-admitted, live requests probe it
T=35s    still broken → 5 fast failures → OPEN again
         (2nd ejection = 60s this time)
T=95s    the bad deploy is rolled back; pod 3 restarts clean
T=97s    probes succeed → CLOSED ★ users never saw an outage

7.8 Load Balancing — All 7 Algorithms

From the official Istio docs, DestinationRules support 7 load balancing algorithms. The default is LEAST_REQUEST — Envoy picks 2 random hosts and sends to the one with fewer active requests. Here's every option:

AlgorithmHow It WorksBest ForSession Affinity?
LEAST_REQUESTPick 2 random hosts, send to one with fewer active requests (LEAST_CONN is a deprecated alias for this exact same algorithm — not a 8th option)General purpose (DEFAULT)No
RANDOMRandomly pick a healthy hostStateless services, no hot spotsNo
ROUND_ROBINCycle through hosts in order: 1,2,3,1,2,3...Equal-capacity nodesNo
PASSTHROUGHSkip Envoy's LB entirely — forward straight to whatever the original destination address/port wasOriginal-destination routing, egress passthroughNo
CONSISTENT_HASHHash HTTP header/cookie → always same hostSession stickiness without cookies✅ Soft (via hash)
RING_HASHKetama consistent hashing ringMinimal disruption when hosts added/removed✅ Soft (via ring)
MAGLEVGoogle's Maglev hash algorithm (faster than Ketama)High-throughput, many backends✅ Soft (via table)
📝 DestinationRule LB Examples
# Simple LB: Round Robin for v1 subset
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-dr
spec:
  host: jobpost-api
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1
    trafficPolicy:
      loadBalancer:
        simple: ROUND_ROBIN

# Consistent Hash: Session affinity by HTTP header
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2
    trafficPolicy:
      loadBalancer:
        consistentHash:
          httpHeaderName: "x-session-id"  # Same session → same pod
💡 ICA Exam: LB Algorithm Selection

Default = LEAST_REQUEST (not round-robin!). Session affinity: Use CONSISTENT_HASH with HTTP header or cookie. Equal-capacity pods: ROUND_ROBIN. Long-lived gRPC streams: LEAST_CONN (balances connections, not requests). Minimal rebalancing: RING_HASH or MAGLEV (when hosts are frequently added/removed). The LB algorithm is set in the DestinationRule's trafficPolicy.loadBalancer field.

7.9 Deep Dive — Locality Load Balancing: Region → Zone → Sub-Zone Failover

From the official Istio tasks: Locality Load Balancing routes traffic based on geographic location — keeping requests within the same region/zone when possible and failing over to distant zones only when local endpoints are unhealthy.

🌍 LOCALITY HIERARCHY — Region → Zone → Sub-Zone
  REGION: us-east          ← Coarse: large geographic area
    ZONE: us-east-1a       ← Medium: availability zone
    ZONE: us-east-1b
  REGION: eu-west
    ZONE: eu-west-1a
    ZONE: eu-west-1b
      SUB-ZONE: rack-12    ← Fine: same rack (custom Istio label)

  LOCALITY MATCHING (in order):
  1. Same Region + Same Zone + Same Sub-Zone  = 🥇 PRIORITY (local)
  2. Same Region + Same Zone                   = 🥈
  3. Same Region                               = 🥉
  4. Different Region                          = 🏁 LAST RESORT (failover only)
FeatureDescriptionK8s Label
RegionGeographic area (us-east, eu-west)topology.kubernetes.io/region
ZoneAvailability zone within regiontopology.kubernetes.io/zone
Sub-ZoneCustom subdivision (rack, row)topology.istio.io/subzone (Istio-only)
📝 Locality Failover Configuration
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-dr
spec:
  host: jobpost-api
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      localityLbSetting:
        enabled: true  # Default is already true!
        distribute:
        - from: us-east/us-east-1a/*
          to:
            us-east/us-east-1a/*: 80    # 80% stays local
            us-east/us-east-1b/*: 15    # 15% to same region, other zone
            eu-west/*: 5                # 5% to other region
    outlierDetection:  # REQUIRED for automatic failover
      consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50   # the canonical anihpj values from 7.4 — always set explicitly
💡 ICA Exam: Locality LB Key Facts

Default: enabled=true in mesh config. Automatic failover: requires outlierDetection in DestinationRule — Envoy detects unhealthy endpoints and fails over to next locality. Weighted distribution: use distribute field to control cross-region traffic percentages. No K8s sub-zone: sub-zone uses Istio's custom label topology.istio.io/subzone. Hosted cloud providers auto-label region and zone; self-managed clusters need manual labeling.

7.10 Connection Pool — The Complete Field Reference

connectionPool has exactly two sub-blocks — tcp (TCPSettings) and http (HTTPSettings). 7.5 introduced only 4 of the real 13 fields; this section completes the reference. The fields 7.5 skipped are exactly the ones that bite in production: maxRequestsPerConnection controls HTTP keep-alive recycling, idleTimeout silently closes connections Envoy thinks are dead, and h2UpgradePolicy decides whether Envoy-to-backend traffic gets promoted to HTTP/2. Every field you don't set falls back to its own Istio/Envoy default below — connectionPool ships permissive (near-unlimited) until you deliberately tighten it.

TCPSettings FieldDefaultWhat It Controls
maxConnections2³²-1Hard cap on HTTP/1.1 + TCP connections
connectTimeout10sTCP handshake timeout to the backend
tcpKeepalive(unset)SO_KEEPALIVE: probes / time / interval sub-fields
maxConnectionDuration(unset)Force-close a connection after this long
idleTimeout1 hourClose an idle connection; 0s = disabled
HTTPSettings FieldDefaultWhat It Controls
http1MaxPendingRequests2³²-1Pending-request queue depth
http2MaxRequests2³²-1Max active HTTP/2 requests
maxRequestsPerConnection0 (max 2²⁹)Requests per connection before recycle
maxRetries2³²-1Max retries in flight at once
idleTimeout1 hourIdle connection-pool timeout
h2UpgradePolicyDEFAULTHTTP/1 → HTTP/2 upgrade policy
useClientProtocolfalseMirrors the client's own protocol
maxConcurrentStreams2³¹-1HTTP/2 streams per connection
⚠️ maxRequestsPerConnection: 1 Disables Keep-Alive Entirely

Setting maxRequestsPerConnection: 1 is the one value that fully DISABLES HTTP keep-alive — every request gets a brand-new TCP connection. Only worth it for legacy backends that can't multiplex; expensive (extra handshakes) everywhere else.

💡 tcpKeepalive — Detect a Dead Backend Faster Than the OS Default

tcpKeepalive has its own probes / time / interval sub-fields. Left unset, Envoy inherits whatever the OS-level socket defaults are (commonly probes: 9, time: 7200s, interval: 75s on Linux) — set it explicitly to detect a dead backend faster than a 2-hour OS default.

7.11 portLevelSettings — Per-Port Traffic Policy Overrides

portLevelSettings lets ONE DestinationRule apply different loadBalancer / connectionPool / outlierDetection / tls settings to different ports on the SAME host — the top-level trafficPolicy becomes the fallback for any port not explicitly listed. A real anihpj service often exposes more than one port — search-service serves REST on :8080 and an internal gRPC API on :9090; those two ports have completely different traffic shapes and deserve different tuning, not one-size-fits-all.

⚠️ The Critical Gotcha — portLevelSettings Does NOT Inherit

Unlike subset-level trafficPolicy (7.12), portLevelSettings does NOT inherit from the destination-level trafficPolicy — it is a full replacement. Any field you omit on a port falls back to Istio's own default, NOT to the value you set at the top level.

yaml — search-service: per-port override, and the trap 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: search-service-ports
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: search-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:                    # ← fallback for any port below
    loadBalancer:
      simple: LEAST_REQUEST
    outlierDetection:
      consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50
    portLevelSettings:
    - port:
        number: 8080                # ← REST API port
      loadBalancer:
        simple: ROUND_ROBIN         # ← overrides the fallback above
      connectionPool:
        http:
          http1MaxPendingRequests: 50
      # ⚠ outlierDetection is NOT inherited by ports below —
      #   reverts to OFF (Istio default) for port 8080
    - port:
        number: 9090                # ← internal gRPC port
      connectionPool:
        http:
          h2UpgradePolicy: UPGRADE

🔀 Inheritance Rules — portLevelSettings vs Subset trafficPolicy

ScopeInherits Parent?Gotcha
Subset trafficPolicy (7.12)YES — field-level mergeOnly the fields you set override
portLevelSettingsNO — full replaceOmitted fields fall back to the Istio default, not your top-level value
💡 Rule of Thumb

If you add portLevelSettings for ONE field (say, just loadBalancer), copy the rest of the top-level trafficPolicy block into it too — otherwise you silently lose your circuit breaker and connection pool limits on that port.

7.12 Subset-Level trafficPolicy — Per-Subset Overrides

A subset (7.2) can carry its OWN trafficPolicy block. Subsets INHERIT the destination-level trafficPolicy, and the subset's own fields MERGE over it, overriding only what they explicitly set — the opposite inheritance model from portLevelSettings (7.11). An untested v2 canary should not get the same trust as the stable v1 — a canary deserves a smaller connection pool (limit its blast radius) and a faster-tripping circuit breaker (its own bugs shouldn't need 5 strikes to notice). Envoy builds one cluster per subset; each cluster starts from the destination-level trafficPolicy, then applies the subset's trafficPolicy fields on top.

yaml — jobpost-api: v1 inherits, v2 overrides 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: jobpost-api
  trafficPolicy:                  # ← baseline, applies to ALL subsets
    loadBalancer:
      simple: LEAST_REQUEST
    outlierDetection:
      consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1                 # ← no override: uses baseline as-is
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2
    trafficPolicy:                 # ← MERGES over the baseline above
      connectionPool:
        http:
          http1MaxPendingRequests: 10   # canary: throttle harder
      outlierDetection:
        consecutiveGatewayErrors: 2     # canary: trip 5x faster
        interval: 10s
        baseEjectionTime: 30s
        maxEjectionPercent: 100         # ok to eject all of a canary
⚠️ Merge Happens at the Block Level, Not the Sibling-Field Level

v2's outlierDetection block above replaces the baseline outlierDetection wholesale — all 4 fields must be re-specified together. Istio merges at the FIELD level between trafficPolicy blocks, not by mixing individual sibling values from two different outlierDetection objects.

7.13 consistentHash — The Complete Field Reference

Every field below lives under trafficPolicy.loadBalancer.consistentHash (or its nested ringHash / maglev sub-message). 7.3 and 7.8 showed httpHeaderName and maglev.tableSize; four more real fields exist and are exam-relevant. httpHeaderName only works when the CALLER already sends a stable header — for browser traffic with no custom headers, httpCookie or useSourceIp are the practical choices for the same sticky-session outcome. Whichever key field you set (header, cookie, source IP, or query param) is fed into the SAME ring-hash or Maglev table selected by consistentHash's ringHash/maglev sub-message — the key source and the hash algorithm are independent choices.

FieldMeaningDefault
httpHeaderNameHash one HTTP header value—
httpCookieMint / read a session cookie—
useSourceIpHash the caller's source IPfalse
httpQueryParameterNameHash one URL query parameter—
ringHash.minimumRingSizeKetama ring size1024
maglev.tableSizeLookup table size (prime)65537
yaml — user-service: session affinity with no custom header 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: user-service-cookie-affinity
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      consistentHash:
        httpCookie:
          name: anihpj-session   # ← Envoy MINTS this if not present
          path: /
          ttl: 3600s             # ← cookie lifetime = 1 hour
💡 httpCookie Is Special — Envoy Sets It, the Client Doesn't Have To

Unlike httpHeaderName (which only reads a header the client already sends), httpCookie is special: if the browser has no cookie yet, ENVOY ITSELF sets one on the response — the very next request from that browser is then sticky, with no client changes required.

7.14 TunnelSettings — Tunneling TCP/TLS Through a Proxy

trafficPolicy.tunnel wraps outbound TCP or TLS traffic inside an HTTP CONNECT (or POST) tunnel toward an intermediate proxy before it reaches the real destination — an advanced, low-frequency field, but a real, documented part of DestinationRule. Some anihpj partner integrations only accept connections that arrive through a corporate forward proxy (firewall allow-listing, audit logging at the proxy) — tunnel lets Envoy speak to that proxy without the application ever knowing a proxy is involved. Envoy opens a connection to targetHost:targetPort (the intermediate proxy), issues an HTTP CONNECT (or POST) to establish the tunnel, then relays the original TCP/TLS bytes through it — usable ONLY on TCP or TLS routes, never on HTTP routes.

yaml — routing through an intermediate proxy 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: legacy-proxy-tunnel
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: legacy-mainframe.partner.internal
  trafficPolicy:
    tunnel:
      protocol: CONNECT       # ← wrap traffic in an HTTP CONNECT
      targetHost: proxy.partner.internal
      targetPort: 3128        # ← the intermediate proxy's port

  # tunnel: valid on TCP/TLS routes only — not usable for HTTP
📖 KEY TERM — protocol: CONNECT vs POST

protocol accepts CONNECT (the standard HTTP proxy tunnel method) or POST (for proxies that only forward POST bodies). targetHost and targetPort are both required — they identify the intermediate proxy itself, not the final backend.

7.15 exportTo — Scoping a DestinationRule Across Namespaces

exportTo controls which namespaces can SEE and USE this DestinationRule; the default (when omitted) is "*" — exported to every namespace in the mesh, exactly like the exportTo behavior on ServiceEntry (Chapter 8). In a multi-team anihpj-style cluster, a DestinationRule with aggressive tuning (say, a canary's throttled connectionPool from 7.12) written for one team's testing should not silently apply everywhere that host is reachable from — exportTo is the fix. Istiod filters which proxies receive this DestinationRule's config based on exportTo — proxies outside the allowed namespaces never see it, so their traffic to the same host falls back to Istio's defaults.

yaml — keep a DestinationRule private to anihpj 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: jobpost-api
  exportTo:
  - "."                      # ← visible ONLY inside anihpj
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      simple: LEAST_REQUEST
exportTo ValueVisible From
"*" (the default)Every namespace in the mesh
"."Only the DestinationRule's own namespace
["team-a","team-b"]Only the namespaces listed
💡 Not a DestinationRule-Only Feature

The same rule applies to VirtualService and ServiceEntry — exportTo is a mesh-wide visibility mechanism, not a DestinationRule-only feature. anihpj's convention is exportTo: ["."] on every team-owned DestinationRule unless cross-namespace sharing is a deliberate, documented decision.

🔧 Under the Hood — How DestinationRule Actually Shapes Traffic: Load Balancing Algorithm Selection, Circuit Breaker State Machine, Connection Pool Tuning, and How Multiple Resources Cooperate on One Request

🔬 Outlier Detection's Real Lifecycle — "CLOSED/OPEN/HALF-OPEN" as a Teaching Analogy

Terminology check: Envoy's actual outlier-detection code has no fields or states literally named "CLOSED," "OPEN," or "HALF-OPEN" — those are borrowed from the general Hystrix-style circuit-breaker pattern as a teaching analogy. Envoy's REAL model is two-state: a host is either in the load-balancing pool (healthy) or EJECTED (removed, for a timed backoff period). There is no gated "probe" request — when the ejection timer expires, the host is simply placed back in the pool and the very next REAL request routed to it is what proves whether it recovered.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  OUTLIER DETECTION'S REAL 2-STATE LIFECYCLE (using CLOSED/OPEN as labels)        │
│                                                                              │
│       ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐          │
│       │                "CLOSED" — Healthy, in the pool            │          │
│       │  • All requests forwarded to this backend normally        │          │
│       │  • Envoy counts consecutive 5xx errors PER HOST            │          │
│       │  • Counter: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 (threshold!)          │          │
│       │  • A single SUCCESS resets the counter to 0                │          │
│       └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘          │
│                                │ consecutive5xxErrors reached                │
│                                ▼                                              │
│       ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐          │
│       │              "OPEN" — EJECTED from the pool               │          │
│       │  • This host receives ZERO traffic; other pods absorb it  │          │
│       │  • No literal "rejection" happens — Envoy just never      │          │
│       │    picks this host during load balancing                 │          │
│       │  • Timer starts: baseEjectionTime × (times ejected so far)│          │
│       └────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘          │
│                                │ ejection timer expires                      │
│                                ▼                                              │
│       ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐          │
│       │        Re-admitted — back in the pool, being watched      │          │
│       │  • NO synthetic/gated probe — the pool just includes it   │          │
│       │    again, and normal live traffic is what tests it         │          │
│       │  • New requests succeed → stays in the pool ("CLOSED")    │          │
│       │  • 5 more consecutive errors → ejected again ("OPEN"),     │          │
│       │    this time for a LONGER backoff period                  │          │
│       │  • maxEjectionPercent caps how many hosts can be ejected  │          │
│       │    at once, mesh-wide safety valve                        │          │
│       └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘          │
│                                                                              │
│  CRITICAL PARAMETERS:                                                          │
│  consecutive5xxErrors: 5   ← How many failures before ejecting                │
│  interval: 30s              ← How often the ejection sweep runs               │
│  baseEjectionTime: 60s     ← Length of the FIRST ejection (backs off after)   │
│  maxEjectionPercent: 50    ← Max % of the pool ejected at once                │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 7 Load Balancing Algorithms — Which One for Which Scenario
AlgorithmHow It WorksConnection AffinityBest For
ROUND_ROBINEach backend in turn (1→2→3→1)NoStateless services, uniform load
LEAST_REQUESTBackend with fewest active requests (LEAST_CONN is a deprecated alias for this — not a separate algorithm)NoGeneral purpose (DEFAULT)
RANDOMRandom backend selectionNoSimple, low overhead
PASSTHROUGHBypass Envoy's LB, forward to the original destinationNoOriginal-destination / egress passthrough
CONSISTENT_HASHHash of header/cookie/source IPYES (sticky)Sessions, caching, sharding
RING_HASHConsistent ring hash (like Maglev)YESMinimal disruption on backend change
MAGLEVGoogle's consistent hash algorithmYES (strong)Large backend pools, fast lookup
🔗 One Request, Three Resources Cooperating

7.7 walked through the circuit breaker alone; 7.9 walks through locality failover alone. In production, anihpj's resources never act alone — a single request routinely exercises a VirtualService's subset choice, a DestinationRule's label resolution, AND a completely different service's circuit breaker, all in the same few milliseconds. Here is what that looks like end to end.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ONE REQUEST, THREE RESOURCES — POST /jobs/42/apply under partial failure│
│                                                                         │
│ (1) VirtualService jobpost-api-vs (Ch6) matches POST /jobs/*/apply,    │
│     rolls the canary weight, and this time picks subset: v2 (10% slice)│
│              │                                                          │
│              ▼                                                          │
│ (2) DestinationRule jobpost-api-dr (7.2) resolves subset v2 = pods     │
│     labeled version: v2, then loadBalancer: LEAST_REQUEST (7.3/7.8)    │
│     picks pod jobpost-api-v2-7f8 out of that pool                       │
│              │                                                          │
│              ▼                                                          │
│ (3) jobpost-api-v2-7f8's own code calls auth-service to check the       │
│     caller's session token — a second, independent Envoy hop           │
│              │                                                          │
│              ▼                                                          │
│ (4) auth-service's DestinationRule already tripped ITS OWN             │
│     outlierDetection 40s ago: pod auth-3 hit consecutiveGatewayErrors: │
│     5 and sits EJECTED / OPEN (7.4, 7.7) — auth-3 is NOT in the pool   │
│              │                                                          │
│              ▼                                                          │
│ (5) LEAST_REQUEST can only choose among the 3 healthy auth-service      │
│     pods — request lands on auth-1, succeeds in 40ms                   │
│              │                                                          │
│              ▼                                                          │
│ (6) jobpost-api-v2-7f8 returns 201 Created. The caller never learns     │
│     auth-3 exists, is unhealthy, or was ever a candidate at all        │
│                                                                         │
│ WHAT JUST COOPERATED: VirtualService chose a subset by NAME, the       │
│ DestinationRule turned that name into real PODS and picked one, and a  │
│ completely separate DestinationRule's circuit breaker had already      │
│ pre-filtered a THIRD service's pool before this request ever arrived.  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
WITHOUT outlierDetection on auth-serviceWITH outlierDetection (this chapter's config)
auth-3 stays in the LB pool while sickauth-3 ejected after 5 gateway errors (7.4)
~1-in-4 requests still routed to auth-30-in-4 requests routed to auth-3
caller blocks for connectTimeout (7.10)caller never notices auth-3 exists
VS retry (Ch6) doubles latency, or failsp99 latency unaffected by the sick pod
enough pile-up reproduces Ch1's cascaderest of anihpj stays fully served
🔑 ICA Insight: DestinationRule is where TRAFFIC QUALITY is configured (VirtualService = ROUTING, DestinationRule = POLICY). Outlier detection (what this chapter nicknames "circuit breaking," using CLOSED/OPEN/HALF-OPEN as a memorable but NON-literal analogy for Envoy's real healthy/ejected model) is a guaranteed ICA exam topic — know the exact field names: consecutiveGatewayErrors, interval, baseEjectionTime, maxEjectionPercent. Default maxEjectionPercent=10 is often too LOW for a small pool — always set it explicitly (50 is the anihpj convention) so you know exactly how much capacity you're willing to eject. The LB algorithm is per-DestinationRule and overridable per-subset (7.12) or per-port (7.11, which does NOT inherit). CONSISTENT_HASH requires a hash key (header/cookie/source IP) — without one, it falls back to non-hash-based distribution. And no DestinationRule setting acts alone in production: a single request's subset choice, pod selection, and a completely unrelated service's already-tripped outlier detection all cooperate in the same request path — debug the WHOLE chain, not just the DestinationRule in front of you.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • DestinationRule = HOW, VirtualService = WHERE — VS picks the destination/subset; DR decides load balancing, circuit breaking, TLS, and connection pools once that destination is chosen.
  • Subsets filter existing Endpoints by Pod label — they don't create pods or new network paths. No matching label = zero endpoints = 503, not a config error.
  • LEAST_REQUEST is Istio's real default, not ROUND_ROBIN — only write loadBalancer when you need something else.
  • Outlier detection (nicknamed "circuit breaking") is really a 2-state mechanism: healthy (in the pool) or EJECTED (removed, timed backoff) — the CLOSED/OPEN/HALF-OPEN labels are a teaching analogy, not literal Envoy terminology, and there's no synthetic gated "probe" — live traffic tests a re-admitted host.
  • Repeat ejections back off exponentially: ejection time = baseEjectionTime × times-ejected (30s → 60s → 90s...).
  • portLevelSettings fully REPLACES the top-level trafficPolicy per port — it never merges, unlike subset-level trafficPolicy which DOES merge.
  • Locality load balancing silently does nothing without outlierDetection — automatic zone failover requires ejection to be configured at all.
  • exportTo defaults to "*" (visible mesh-wide) — anihpj's convention is "." (private to the owning namespace) unless cross-namespace sharing is deliberate.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "Envoy's circuit breaker literally has CLOSED/OPEN/HALF-OPEN states." No — that's this chapter's teaching analogy. Envoy's real model is 2-state: in-the-pool (healthy) or ejected. There's no gated "probe" request; a re-admitted host is tested by ordinary live traffic.
  • "A missing subset label produces a clear error." No — it silently resolves to ZERO endpoints, producing 503s that look like a routing bug, not a labeling bug.
  • "ROUND_ROBIN is Istio's default load balancer." No — LEAST_REQUEST is the real default when no loadBalancer is set; ROUND_ROBIN is Envoy's OWN bare default, which Istio overrides per-cluster.
  • "portLevelSettings inherits the top-level trafficPolicy, just like subsets do." No — it's a full REPLACEMENT per port. Any field you don't repeat falls back to Istio's own default, not your top-level value.
  • "Locality load balancing works automatically once configured." No — localityLbSetting is silently inert without outlierDetection also configured; failover needs a way to detect unhealthy endpoints first.
  • "maxEjectionPercent's default is fine to leave alone." Its real default (10%) is actually often too CONSERVATIVE — during a real multi-pod incident it may cap ejection well below what's needed to protect the rest of anihpj. Always set it explicitly (50 is the canonical anihpj value) so the cap is a deliberate decision, not an accident either direction.
  • "CONSISTENT_HASH always provides session stickiness." Only if you also configure a hash key (header, cookie, or source IP) — without one, there's nothing to hash on and stickiness silently doesn't happen.

💼 Chapter 7 — Daily Work Takeaways

  • Always pair a VirtualService subset reference with a matching DestinationRule subset — a name that only exists on one side is a 503, not a routing decision.
  • Start outlierDetection from the canonical anihpj values (5 / 30s / 30s / 50%) and tune from there rather than inventing numbers under pressure.
  • Remember portLevelSettings does NOT inherit — copy the whole trafficPolicy block in if you're overriding even one field per-port.
  • Verify live ejection state with pilot-agent request GET clusters | grep outlier_detection, not just that the YAML applied cleanly.
  • Give an untested canary subset its own tighter trafficPolicy — smaller connection pool, faster-tripping outlier detection — since it hasn't earned the same trust as stable.
  • Scope aggressive tuning with exportTo: ["."] so one team's canary settings never silently apply mesh-wide.
  • For the ICA exam: know both vocabularies — "circuit breaker" (docs/conversational) and outlierDetection (the actual YAML field) — and the real healthy/ejected mechanism underneath the CLOSED/OPEN/HALF-OPEN analogy.
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 7

Seven quick-fire phrase-to-answer mappings — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Define subsets for canary" = subsets: [{name, labels: {version: ...}}], matching VirtualService's subset references exactly
  • "Pick a load-balancing algorithm" = trafficPolicy.loadBalancer.simple — remember LEAST_REQUEST is the real default
  • "Circuit breaker" / "outlier detection" = outlierDetection with consecutiveGatewayErrors/interval/baseEjectionTime/maxEjectionPercent — always cap maxEjectionPercent below 100
  • "Sticky sessions" = loadBalancer.consistentHash — needs a hash key (header/cookie/sourceIP) or there's nothing to hash on and stickiness silently doesn't happen
  • "Per-port override" = portLevelSettings — REPLACES, never merges
  • "Per-subset override" = subset-level trafficPolicy — MERGES over the destination-level baseline
  • "Subset resolves to nothing / 503 no healthy upstream" = check Pod labels FIRST with kubectl get pods --show-labels

🧠 Chapter 7 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
In one sentence each, what does DestinationRule control versus what does VirtualService control?
Show Answer
Answer

VirtualService picks WHERE a request goes (which subset, by weight/header/path). DestinationRule decides HOW it's delivered once chosen — load balancing, circuit breaking (outlier detection), connection pools, and TLS mode.

Explanation

Neither is useful alone: a VirtualService referencing a subset with no matching DestinationRule produces 503s, and a DestinationRule with subsets nobody routes to just sits unused.

Q2
What happens when a DestinationRule subset's label selector matches zero Pods?
Show Answer
Answer

The subset resolves to ZERO endpoints, and requests routed to it get 503 errors — NOT a configuration error at apply time.

Explanation

A subset doesn't create Pods — it filters the Service's EXISTING Kubernetes Endpoints by label. No matching Pods means EDS pushes an empty list to Envoy, which is indistinguishable at the YAML level from "working but temporarily no healthy pods."

Q3
What is Istio's REAL default load-balancing algorithm when no loadBalancer is configured?
Show Answer
Answer

LEAST_REQUEST — not ROUND_ROBIN. Envoy picks 2 random hosts and sends to whichever has fewer active requests.

Explanation

ROUND_ROBIN is Envoy's own bare default absent any config — Istio overrides it per-cluster to LEAST_REQUEST, which is why older docs and some engineers still assume ROUND_ROBIN incorrectly.

Q4
Does Envoy's outlier detection literally have "CLOSED," "OPEN," and "HALF-OPEN" states in its code? What's the real mechanism?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Those are a teaching analogy borrowed from the general circuit-breaker pattern. Envoy's real model is 2-state: a host is either in the load-balancing pool (healthy) or EJECTED (removed, for a timed backoff period). There's no synthetic "probe" request — a re-admitted host is simply tested by the next real requests routed to it.

Explanation

This matters on the exam because a question describing REAL Envoy behavior ("a pod is ejected and later starts receiving live traffic again") should be recognized as the SAME mechanism this chapter calls CLOSED/OPEN/HALF-OPEN — don't expect the literal words in any istioctl output.

Q5
A pod gets ejected 3 times in a row for repeated failures, with baseEjectionTime: 30s. How long is the 3rd ejection?
Show Answer
Answer

90 seconds. Ejection time = baseEjectionTime × times-ejected — 30s → 60s → 90s for the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd ejections respectively.

Explanation

This exponential backoff means a genuinely broken pod gets progressively longer timeouts, reducing wasted traffic to a pod that keeps failing, while a pod that recovers after one ejection only paid the base 30s cost.

Q6
What's the difference between how portLevelSettings and subset-level trafficPolicy handle inheritance from the destination-level baseline?
Show Answer
Answer

portLevelSettings does NOT inherit — it's a full replacement per port; omitted fields fall back to Istio's own default, not your top-level value. Subset trafficPolicy DOES inherit — the subset's fields MERGE over the destination-level baseline, overriding only what's explicitly set.

Explanation

This is one of the most exam-relevant gotchas in the chapter: adding a single-field portLevelSettings override for one port silently drops your circuit breaker and connection pool on that port unless you copy those fields in too.

Q7
Why does locality load balancing (region/zone-aware routing) require outlierDetection to actually work?
Show Answer
Answer

Locality LB needs a way to know when local endpoints are UNHEALTHY before it will fail over to a more distant zone. Without outlierDetection configured, Istio has no unhealthy-endpoint signal to trigger failover on — localityLbSetting is silently inert.

Explanation

This is a real "it's configured but doing nothing" trap — the YAML applies cleanly, istioctl analyze shows no errors, and yet cross-zone failover never happens during a real outage.

Q8
What does exportTo default to when omitted, and what's anihpj's own convention?
Show Answer
Answer

Default (omitted) = "*" — visible to every namespace in the mesh. anihpj's convention = ["."] — private to the DestinationRule's own namespace, unless cross-namespace sharing is a deliberate, documented decision.

Explanation

The same exportTo mechanism applies to VirtualService and ServiceEntry too — it's a mesh-wide visibility control, not unique to DestinationRule.

Q9
Name the field that lets Envoy route TCP/TLS traffic through an intermediate corporate proxy, and state one thing it CANNOT be used for.
Show Answer
Answer

trafficPolicy.tunnel — wraps outbound TCP/TLS traffic in an HTTP CONNECT or POST tunnel toward an intermediate proxy. It CANNOT be used on HTTP routes — only TCP/TLS routes.

Explanation

This is a low-frequency but real, documented field — useful when a partner integration only accepts connections arriving through a specific corporate forward proxy for firewall allow-listing or audit logging.

Q10
CONSISTENT_HASH is configured with no hash key set (no httpHeaderName, httpCookie, or useSourceIp). What actually happens to load balancing?
Show Answer
Answer

Session affinity silently doesn't happen — CONSISTENT_HASH without a key source (no header, cookie, or source IP configured) has nothing to hash on, so Envoy can't compute a consistent target and effectively distributes requests without stickiness instead.

Explanation

This is a real "looks configured, isn't working" trap similar to locality LB without outlierDetection — the YAML is valid, istioctl analyze shows no error, but the sticky-session behavior a team is expecting simply never happens.

⚙️ Chapter 7 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
jobpost-api's canary VirtualService routes 10% of traffic to subset: v2, but every v2 request returns 503 "no healthy upstream." Task: Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# Diagnose: check the DestinationRule's v2 subset label selector
kubectl get destinationrule jobpost-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 "name: v2"

# Compare against real pod labels:
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=jobpost-api --show-labels
# Most likely: no pods carry the "version: v2" label the subset expects

# Fix: add the missing label to the v2 Deployment's pod template
kubectl patch deployment jobpost-api-v2 -n anihpj --type='json' \
  -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/metadata/labels/version","value":"v2"}]'
Explanation

This is 7.2's #1 mistake in practice — the subset resolves silently to zero endpoints, which LOOKS like a routing bug but is actually a labeling bug.

Q2
Write a DestinationRule for user-service that uses CONSISTENT_HASH session affinity based on a cookie, with a 1-hour TTL.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: user-service-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: user-service
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      consistentHash:
        httpCookie:
          name: anihpj-session
          path: /
          ttl: 3600s
Explanation

httpCookie is special among the hash-key options — Envoy itself MINTS the cookie on the first response if the browser doesn't already have one, so no client-side changes are needed for stickiness to kick in.

Q3
auth-service has been failing intermittently. Write an outlierDetection block using the canonical anihpj values, then write the command to confirm the ejection counters are live on a real Envoy.
Show Answer
Answer
trafficPolicy:
  outlierDetection:
    consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5
    interval: 30s
    baseEjectionTime: 30s
    maxEjectionPercent: 50
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/jobpost-api -c istio-proxy -- \
  pilot-agent request GET clusters | grep -A1 outlier_detection
Explanation

kubectl apply succeeding proves nothing about whether Envoy is actually enforcing the policy — the pilot-agent request command reads Envoy's own live ejection counters, the same "verify delivery, not just acceptance" pattern taught since Chapter 5's Gateway section.

Q4
search-service exposes REST on :8080 and gRPC on :9090. The team wants ROUND_ROBIN + a tight connection pool on :8080, while keeping the destination-level circuit breaker active on :8080 too. They write a portLevelSettings block with only loadBalancer and connectionPool for port 8080. Task: Explain what actually happens to the circuit breaker on port 8080.
Show Answer
Answer

It's LOST on port 8080. portLevelSettings does not inherit the top-level trafficPolicy — it's a full replacement. Since outlierDetection wasn't repeated in the port 8080 block, that port reverts to Istio's default (no ejection at all) even though the destination-level block still has it configured.

Explanation

The fix: copy the full outlierDetection block into the port 8080 portLevelSettings entry too — the rule of thumb is "if you override ANY field per-port, copy the whole trafficPolicy block in with it."

Q5
Give jobpost-api's v2 canary subset a smaller connection pool and a faster-tripping circuit breaker than the stable v1 baseline, while v1 keeps inheriting the destination-level defaults unchanged.
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  host: jobpost-api
  trafficPolicy:
    outlierDetection:
      consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2
    trafficPolicy:
      connectionPool:
        http:
          http1MaxPendingRequests: 10
      outlierDetection:
        consecutiveGatewayErrors: 2
        interval: 10s
        baseEjectionTime: 30s
        maxEjectionPercent: 100
Explanation

v1 needs NO override at all — subset trafficPolicy MERGES, so leaving v1's subset block empty of trafficPolicy means it simply inherits the destination-level baseline. v2's whole outlierDetection block is replaced wholesale (Istio merges at the block level, not by mixing individual sibling fields from two different blocks).

Q6
A team configured localityLbSetting.enabled: true expecting automatic zone failover during an outage, but during a real zone failure, traffic did NOT fail over — it kept timing out against the dead zone. Task: Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# Diagnose: check whether outlierDetection exists on this DestinationRule
kubectl get destinationrule <name> -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 outlierDetection
# If missing entirely — that's the root cause
# Fix: add outlierDetection — locality LB requires it to detect unhealthy zones
trafficPolicy:
  outlierDetection:
    consecutive5xxErrors: 3
    interval: 30s
    baseEjectionTime: 60s
Explanation

Locality LB has no independent health signal of its own — it relies entirely on outlierDetection to know a zone's endpoints are unhealthy before routing around them. Without it, Envoy keeps sending traffic to the "preferred" zone even after every pod there stops responding.

Q7
Write a DestinationRule field reference check: for connectionPool, what field disables HTTP keep-alive entirely, and why would you ever want that?
Show Answer
Answer
connectionPool:
  http:
    maxRequestsPerConnection: 1   # every request gets a brand-new TCP connection

Only worth setting for legacy backends that can't multiplex requests over a single connection — everywhere else it's expensive (extra handshakes per request).

Explanation

This is one of the 9 "extra" connectionPool fields 7.10 covers beyond 7.5's basic 4 — exactly the kind of field-reference detail the exam expects you to recognize even if you rarely use it.

Q8
Verify which load-balancing algorithm Envoy is ACTUALLY running for jobpost-api's calls to user-service — not what the YAML claims, what's live.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj \
  --fqdn user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local -o json | grep -i lbPolicy
Explanation

Same verification discipline as every prior chapter: kubectl get/describe proves the API server accepted your YAML, never that Envoy compiled and applied it. The proxy-config command reads the live cluster config.

Q9
A DestinationRule with an aggressive, canary-only connection pool tuning was applied in namespace anihpj with no exportTo set. A completely different team's namespace starts seeing their OWN calls to jobpost-api unexpectedly throttled. Task: Explain why, and fix it.
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  host: jobpost-api
  exportTo:
  - "."          # ← scope visibility to anihpj's own namespace only
Explanation

Omitted exportTo defaults to "*" — visible and applied mesh-wide. The aggressive canary tuning meant for one team's testing was silently affecting every other namespace's calls to the same host. Setting exportTo: ["."] is anihpj's own stated convention for exactly this reason.

Q10
A partner integration requires all outbound connections to a legacy mainframe to route through a corporate forward proxy at proxy.partner.internal:3128, using HTTP CONNECT. Write the DestinationRule field for this.
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  host: legacy-mainframe.partner.internal
  trafficPolicy:
    tunnel:
      protocol: CONNECT
      targetHost: proxy.partner.internal
      targetPort: 3128
Explanation

targetHost/targetPort identify the INTERMEDIATE proxy, not the final mainframe destination (that's spec.host). This only works on TCP/TLS routes — never HTTP.

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 7
  • Name subsets identically to how VirtualService references them — a typo'd subset: v2 vs subset: V2 resolves to zero endpoints, not an error message.
  • Start outlierDetection with the canonical anihpj values (5 / 30s / 30s / 50%) from 7.4 and only tune from there — inventing numbers under exam time pressure wastes minutes.
  • Remember portLevelSettings does NOT inherit (7.11) — if you add it for one field, copy the whole trafficPolicy block in with it.
  • On the exam, istioctl analyze catches a broken subset label reference before you waste time debugging a 503 by hand.
  • Reach for LEAST_REQUEST by doing nothing — it is Istio's real default (7.8); only write loadBalancer when you need something else.
  • If locality LB (7.9) "isn't working," check outlierDetection first — without it, Istio silently ignores localityLbSetting.

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 7)

Every command below already appeared earlier in this chapter — grouped here as one reference for applying, inspecting, and validating a DestinationRule.

CommandWhat It Does / Checks in Chapter 7
kubectl apply -f jobpost-api-dr.yaml -n anihpjCreate/update the DestinationRule (7.6)
kubectl get destinationrule -n anihpjList every DestinationRule in the namespace (7.1)
kubectl describe destinationrule jobpost-api-dr -n anihpjResolved subsets, trafficPolicy, Istiod events (7.2)
kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labelsConfirm pods carry version: v1/v2 — 7.2's #1 mistake
istioctl analyze -n anihpjCatch a broken subset reference before you apply it
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj --fqdn user-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local -o json | grep -i lbPolicyConfirm which LB algorithm Envoy is really running (7.8)
kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/jobpost-api -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request GET clusters | grep -A1 outlier_detectionLive ejection counters for the circuit breaker (7.4/7.7)
istioctl proxy-statusConfirm the DestinationRule reached every sidecar (SYNCED)

🔬 Practice Drill 7.1 — Circuit-Break auth-service, Then Prove It Live

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Build and verify a real circuit breaker for auth-service, right now — don't just read this, do it:

  1. kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=auth-service --show-labels — confirm you have real version: labels to work with.
  2. Write auth-service-dr.yaml: host: auth-service, outlierDetection with the canonical values from 7.4 (consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5, interval: 30s, baseEjectionTime: 30s, maxEjectionPercent: 50).
  3. kubectl apply -f auth-service-dr.yaml -n anihpj.
  4. kubectl describe destinationrule auth-service-dr -n anihpj — confirm the outlierDetection block is present and no Istiod warnings appear.
  5. kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/jobpost-api -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request GET clusters | grep -A1 outlier_detection — confirm the ejection counters exist and read 0 (healthy baseline).
Hint: Steps 1-2 test 7.2's label-matching requirement together with 7.4's canonical outlierDetection numbers; steps 3-5 prove the config actually reached Envoy — don't trust that kubectl apply succeeding means Envoy is enforcing it.
View Solution

Step 5's grep should show ejection-related counters (e.g. outlier_detection.ejections_active: 0) present in the live cluster dump — their mere presence, even at zero, proves the policy compiled and reached Envoy. A completely empty grep result means the DestinationRule never made it to this proxy (check istioctl proxy-status for SYNCED).

Check yourself: did you check step 1's labels BEFORE writing the YAML in step 2, or after applying and getting a silent zero-endpoint subset? Catching a label mismatch before you apply is the habit this drill is building.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.2 — Reproduce the portLevelSettings Non-Inheritance Trap

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Don't take 7.11's warning on faith — reproduce the non-inheritance behavior on a live cluster.

  1. Apply a DestinationRule with a destination-level outlierDetection block AND a portLevelSettings entry for one port that sets ONLY loadBalancer (no outlierDetection repeated).
  2. istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/<svc> -n anihpj --port <that-port> -o json | grep -A5 outlier_detection — check what's actually active on that port's cluster.
  3. Compare against the SAME grep run for a port that has NO portLevelSettings override at all.
  4. Add the missing outlierDetection block into the portLevelSettings entry and re-run step 2.
Hint: Istio's clusters are per-port — istioctl proxy-config cluster lists one cluster entry per port your Service exposes, so you can inspect each port's compiled policy independently.
View Solution

Step 2's output should show default (empty/absent) outlier detection on the overridden port, while step 3's un-overridden port still shows the destination-level values — confirming portLevelSettings replaced rather than merged. Step 4's re-run should show the values back once explicitly repeated.

Check yourself: could you now explain to a teammate, using your own proxy-config cluster output, exactly which fields got dropped and why? That's the difference between memorizing the rule and having verified it.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.3 — Match the Symptom to the Broken Layer

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

For each observation, name the most likely cause and the ONE command you'd run to confirm it — before proposing any fix:

  1. A canary subset with a correct label selector is returning 100% 503s the moment it's referenced by a VirtualService.
  2. CONSISTENT_HASH is configured for session stickiness, but users keep landing on a different pod every request.
  3. A localityLbSetting.enabled: true block was applied, but a real zone outage caused total downtime instead of failover.
  4. An outlierDetection block with maxEjectionPercent: 100 ejected every single pod in a pool during a bad deploy, causing a full outage instead of a partial one.
Hint: Two of these four are actually the SAME root cause wearing different clothes — a field silently missing that another feature depends on to function.
View Solution
#CauseConfirm with
1The subset's label selector doesn't actually match any live Pod (typo'd value or the Deployment never got the label) — zero endpoints, not a routing bugkubectl get pods --show-labels compared against the DestinationRule's subset selector
2No hash key configured (no httpHeaderName/httpCookie/useSourceIp) — CONSISTENT_HASH has nothing to hash on, so stickiness silently doesn't happenkubectl get destinationrule -o yaml — check for a populated consistentHash key field
3Missing outlierDetection — locality LB has no health signal to trigger failover without itSame YAML check for an outlierDetection block on the same DestinationRule
4Not a bug, a misconfiguration — 100% was set EXPLICITLY (likely copy-pasted from a canary example, where ejecting the whole canary is fine) onto a stable production service, where it isn'tRe-check 7.4's canonical value (50%) against what was actually applied

Check yourself: did you correctly identify #1 and #2 as "missing key field" bugs versus #3 and #4 as "missing/wrong outlierDetection" bugs? Grouping symptoms by root-cause family is faster triage than treating each as unique.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.4 — Scope Aggressive Tuning With exportTo, Then Prove Isolation

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

On a cluster with more than one namespace calling the same Service, prove exportTo actually isolates a DestinationRule's effect — don't just apply it and assume.

  1. Before any exportTo is set, apply an aggressive canary DestinationRule (tiny connection pool, fast-tripping outlierDetection) for jobpost-api in namespace anihpj.
  2. From a DIFFERENT namespace's pod, run istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/<other-svc> -n <other-ns> --fqdn jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local -o json — confirm the aggressive settings leaked mesh-wide.
  3. Add exportTo: ["."] to the DestinationRule and re-apply.
  4. Re-run step 2's command from the other namespace and compare.
Hint: The default (omitted) exportTo is "*" — mesh-wide visibility — so step 2 should show the leak clearly before the fix.
View Solution

Step 2 (before the fix) should show the aggressive connection pool and outlierDetection values applied even from the OTHER namespace's view of jobpost-api. Step 4 (after adding exportTo: ["."]) should show the other namespace falling back to Istio's plain defaults for that cluster — proof the scoping is real, not just configured.

Check yourself: did you verify from the OTHER namespace's pod, not just re-check the YAML in anihpj? A working exportTo is only provable from the perspective it's supposed to exclude.

🔬 Practice Drill 7.5 — Sketch the Full Request Path Through a DestinationRule

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking back at 7.6's example YAML, sketch (on paper or in a text file) the decision path a single request takes from VirtualService match through to a delivered response, for a DestinationRule with: 2 subsets (v1/v2), a destination-level LEAST_REQUEST + outlierDetection, and a v2-subset-level connectionPool override.

  1. Label each decision point: subset selection, load-balancer algorithm choice, connection-pool check, outlier-detection eligibility.
  2. Mark which settings v1 uses (inherited) versus which v2 uses (merged override).
  3. Mark the ONE point where a request could be silently dropped to zero endpoints, and why.
Hint: This is a paper/whiteboard drill — the point is retrieving the mental model from memory under light time pressure, the same way the exam expects you to reason about a YAML file without running it.
View Solution

v1 should show ALL destination-level settings applied unchanged (LEAST_REQUEST, outlierDetection) since its subset trafficPolicy is empty. v2 should show the SAME LEAST_REQUEST + outlierDetection (inherited/merged) PLUS its own connectionPool override layered on top — subset trafficPolicy merges, it doesn't replace. The silent-drop point is the subset label match itself: if v2's label selector doesn't match any live Pod, the request never reaches load balancing or outlier detection at all — it just resolves to zero endpoints upstream of both.

Check yourself: did your sketch correctly distinguish "merges" (subset trafficPolicy) from "replaces" (portLevelSettings, tested in Drill 7.2) using the same diagram? Confusing these two is 7.11-7.12's single most common exam trap.

│                                     │                                 │

│ single biggest defense against the cascade failure that opened      │
│ this guide                                                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Chapter 7 took anihpj from "VirtualService knows WHERE to send traffic" to "DestinationRule knows HOW to deliver it and survive when it fails": 7.1-7.2 defined subsets so a canary split has real pods to land on; 7.3-7.4-7.5 picked a load-balancing algorithm, wired up outlier detection (nicknamed "circuit breaking," taught via the CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN analogy), and capped connection pools; 7.6 combined all three into one production-ready YAML; 7.7-7.9 went deep on the breaker's internals and on zone-aware failover; and 7.10-7.15 supplied the complete field reference — per-port overrides, per-subset overrides, every consistentHash field, proxy tunneling, and cross-namespace scoping — for every one of those settings. The result, jobpost-api-dr.yaml, is anihpj's single biggest structural defense against the exact cascade failure that opened this guide back in Chapter 1.

Quick recap — 🏷️ Subsets: label selectors turn a VirtualService's named destination into real pods · ⚖️ Load Balancing: LEAST_REQUEST is the real default, not ROUND_ROBIN · 🔌 Circuit Breaker: healthy↔ejected with backoff (taught via the CLOSED→OPEN→HALF-OPEN analogy), tuned by outlierDetection · 🏊 Connection Pool: a proactive cap that complements the breaker's reactive one · 🌍 Locality LB: same-zone first, but silently inert without outlierDetection · 🔀 Overrides: portLevelSettings replaces, subset trafficPolicy merges · 🔒 exportTo: keep aggressive tuning from leaking mesh-wide.

Chapter 8: ServiceEntry — Connecting to External Services

Istio's actual default is ALLOW_ANY — every external call passes through uncontrolled, with no mTLS, no metrics, no policy. Production meshes like anihpj's switch to REGISTRY_ONLY, which then blocks ALL external traffic that isn't explicitly registered. Your anihpj app needs to call Stripe for payments, SendGrid for emails, and S3 for file uploads. ServiceEntry registers these external services so Istio knows about them — and can apply policies to them.

"Ch5-7 got traffic INTO and AROUND the mesh — can the mesh leave itself at all?" Chapters 5-7 solved three questions about traffic already inside the anihpj mesh — who may enter (Gateway), where it goes (VirtualService), and how it's delivered (DestinationRule) — but none of them can get jobpost-api's payment call to api.stripe.com out the door, because that traffic is trying to leave the mesh entirely. By default, Istio's REGISTRY_ONLY posture treats api.stripe.com exactly like a mistyped hostname: unknown to the registry, blackholed, 502. ServiceEntry is the one CRD in this Part that answers the direction none of the other three touch — can the mesh leave itself at all, and if so, through which door and under whose audit? Register the host and every tool you already trust from Chapters 5-7 — retries, timeouts, TLS, circuit breakers — becomes available for the call to Stripe too, not just the call to user-service. Skip this chapter and anihpj is stuck between two bad defaults: REGISTRY_ONLY silently kills every payment and password-reset email, or ALLOW_ANY ships every outbound call unaudited and in the clear.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🌍 External 🎯 ICA 35%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Explain why REGISTRY_ONLY blackholes api.stripe.com by default, and what changes under ALLOW_ANY vs a mandatory Egress Gateway (8.1)
  • ✅ Write a complete ServiceEntry that registers an external host with hosts, ports, location: MESH_EXTERNAL, and resolution (8.2)
  • ✅ Wire the mandatory Gateway + two-match VirtualService pair that detours traffic through istio-egressgateway, and name the one resource that stays optional (8.3, 8.5)
  • ✅ Stack REGISTRY_ONLY + egress gateway + AuthorizationPolicy into the three-layer egress defense pattern PCI auditors expect (8.4)
  • ✅ Pick the correct resolution mode — NONE, STATIC, DNS, DNS_ROUND_ROBIN, or DYNAMIC_DNS — for a given external dependency (8.7)
  • ✅ Choose endpoints vs workloadSelector for a MESH_INTERNAL ServiceEntry, and scope its visibility with exportTo (8.8, 8.9)
  • ✅ Pin an external server's certificate identity with subjectAltNames and prove traffic is really detouring through the egress gateway instead of bypassing it (8.5, 8.10)
🎓 ICA Relevance
Traffic Management 35%

ServiceEntry sits inside Traffic Management, the 35%-weighted domain that decides more exam points than any other single topic — and within that 35%, egress is graded as concretely as ingress. Expect a live cluster, a real external host, and a scoring check for whether traffic actually left through the door you built, not just whether your YAML parses:

Graded skillWhere Chapter 8 teaches it

Note the split from 8.4's audit table: registering and routing the ServiceEntry is graded here under Traffic Management, while the AuthorizationPolicy that pins api.stripe.com to one ServiceAccount is graded under the separate Securing Workloads domain (25%), and reading the egress gateway's access log to PROVE the detour worked is a Troubleshooting-domain skill (20%) — one feature, three exam domains, all worth points.

💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 8
  • "Register external API" = ServiceEntry with hosts:, location: MESH_EXTERNAL, resolution: DNS
  • "No ServiceEntry in REGISTRY_ONLY" = 502 Bad Gateway — external calls BLOCKED
  • "Apply policies to external" = Once registered, create VirtualService/DestinationRule targeting the ServiceEntry host
  • "Switch to REGISTRY_ONLY" = Create ServiceEntries FIRST, then switch mode — never switch first
  • "Egress Gateway" = Central exit point — single source IP, central audit, PCI compliance
  • "Wildcards" = hosts: ["*.amazonaws.com"] — register entire domains
  • Exam hands-on: Write ServiceEntry YAML from scratch + attach VirtualService timeout

8.1 The Problem: Calling External APIs from Within the Mesh

anihpj needs to call several real external dependencies from inside the mesh: Stripe for payments, SendGrid for transactional emails, S3 for uploaded media, and a third-party job-board API. Without a ServiceEntry, every one of those calls hits an HTTP 502 — not a network failure, a deliberate mesh-level rejection.

🎓 ICA Exam Note — Both Directions

"Connecting In-Mesh Workloads to External Workloads and Services" covers BOTH directions of traffic crossing the mesh boundary. This chapter teaches mesh → external (ServiceEntry, below). For the reverse direction — an external VM joining the mesh via WorkloadEntry — see Chapter 16.2.

🚫 BLOCKED TRAFFIC — REGISTRY_ONLY, No ServiceEntry Yet
  REGISTRY_ONLY mode, NO ServiceEntry for api.stripe.com yet:

  [jobpost-api Pod]
   app ── "POST https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges" ──▶ (sidecar)

   [Envoy sidecar] looks up its cluster table:
     outbound|443||api.stripe.com ............ NOT FOUND ❌
     → the request falls into Envoy's BlackHoleCluster

   plain HTTP call → Envoy answers 502 Bad Gateway
   HTTPS/TCP call  → connection dropped — no bytes leave the pod

   api.stripe.com ......... never contacted (mesh = walled garden)

  FIX: apply a ServiceEntry → istiod pushes a new Envoy cluster
       via xDS → the very same call now reaches Stripe ✅
🔧 Under the Hood — BlackHoleCluster Is Real

BlackHoleCluster isn't a made-up error state — it's a real, statically-configured Envoy cluster every sidecar ships with. REGISTRY_ONLY routes any unmatched host straight into it, and its handler is deliberately minimal: HTTP gets an immediate 502, raw TCP/TLS just gets reset — no upstream connection is ever attempted. That's why 8.2's fix works instantly: istiod's next xDS push simply swaps the host onto a real cluster instead of this dead-end one.

🌍 ISTIO OUTBOUND TRAFFIC MODES
ALLOW_ANY (default)

All external traffic passes uncontrolled. No policies. Still Istio's actual default today.

REGISTRY_ONLY

Only registered ServiceEntry hosts allowed. Recommended for production.

Egress Gateway

All external traffic through one Pod. Central audit. Required for strict compliance.

anihpj's own posture: REGISTRY_ONLY mesh-wide + ServiceEntry for each real external dependency, PLUS an egress gateway specifically for payment traffic (PCI compliance).

🧠 Analogy — the Loading-Dock Warehouse

Picture anihpj's outbound traffic as a warehouse with a dozen loading-dock doors. ALLOW_ANY is every door propped open — trucks roll out whichever way is closest, unlogged. REGISTRY_ONLY padlocks every door except the ones already on the shipping manifest (api.stripe.com, api.sendgrid.com); an unlisted truck just finds its door welded shut. The Egress Gateway posture goes further: even manifested trucks must exit through ONE dock, past a guard who logs every load.

📖 Real Incident — anihpj's First REGISTRY_ONLY Rollout

Password-reset emails silently stopped. Sidecar access logs showed 502s against cluster BlackHoleCluster for api.sendgrid.com — nobody had registered SendGrid before the mode switch. A ServiceEntry was applied and the mail queue drained within seconds. Lesson: create every ServiceEntry FIRST, then switch to REGISTRY_ONLY — never the other order.

Check which mode your own mesh runs before assuming anything:

bash — check and switch the outbound traffic mode 
# check the current mode
kubectl get configmap istio -n istio-system -o yaml \
    | grep -A1 outboundTrafficPolicy
# outboundTrafficPolicy:
#   mode: REGISTRY_ONLY            ← anihpj production setting

# switch (only AFTER ServiceEntries exist — see 8.4):
istioctl install --set \
    meshConfig.outboundTrafficPolicy.mode=REGISTRY_ONLY -y

8.2 ServiceEntry YAML — Registering External Services

yaml — ServiceEntry for anihpj external services 

# Stripe payments API
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: stripe-payments
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL       # tells Istio this is external
  resolution: DNS
---
# SendGrid email API
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: sendgrid-email
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.sendgrid.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
---
# AWS S3 (wildcard for all regions)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: aws-s3
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - "*.amazonaws.com"           # wildcard
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: NONE               # wildcard hosts can't use DNS (see 8.7)

8.3 Egress Gateway — Controlled Exit from the Mesh

🔀 EGRESS GATEWAY — Centralized Outbound Traffic
❌ WITHOUT

jobpost-api → direct → api.stripe.com
user-service → direct → api.stripe.com
3 different source IPs, no audit

✅ WITH Egress Gateway

All Pods → egressgateway → external
✅ One fixed source IP
✅ Central audit log
✅ Block all by stopping gateway

istio-egressgateway is a standalone Envoy Deployment in istio-system with NO app container — its only job is forwarding mesh traffic outward under central control. Deploying the Pod alone changes NOTHING: traffic only detours through it once a Gateway + VirtualService are wired (8.5). Like ingress Gateways, the egress Gateway resource may live in ANY namespace — istio-system is convention, not a requirement.

bash — install the egress gateway and confirm it's running 
# the "default" istioctl profile ships WITHOUT an egress gateway:
istioctl install -y \
    --set "components.egressGateways[0].enabled=true" \
    --set "components.egressGateways[0].name=istio-egressgateway"

kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway
# NAME                                    READY   STATUS
# istio-egressgateway-6c9b57d9d4-x2krw    1/1     Running

# emergency kill switch (blocks all routed egress):
kubectl scale deploy/istio-egressgateway -n istio-system \
    --replicas=0

8.4 External Service Security Patterns — Production Best Practices

🛡️
Pattern 1: Whitelist-Only

Switch to REGISTRY_ONLY mode. Create ServiceEntries ONLY for APIs you need. All other external traffic is blocked by default. This is zero-trust for egress.

istioctl install --set meshConfig.outboundTrafficPolicy.mode=REGISTRY_ONLY -y
🚪
Pattern 2: Egress Gateway

Route ALL external traffic through a single egress gateway pod. Single source IP for firewall rules. Central audit. Block all egress by stopping one pod.

Gateway(type:egress) → VirtualService → ServiceEntry
🔐
Pattern 3: AuthorizationPolicy

Pin the egress gateway's AuthorizationPolicy to the caller's ServiceAccount — only jobpost-api's SA may route through the gateway to api.stripe.com. Blocks lateral abuse even if another workload reaches the gateway.

principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"]

A compromised anihpj pod with open egress can ship the PostgreSQL user table to any server on the internet — egress control is your LAST line of defense AFTER a breach. The full AuthorizationPolicy that implements Pattern 3, pinning api.stripe.com access to only the jobpost-api ServiceAccount:

yaml — AuthorizationPolicy on the egress gateway 
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-stripe-payments-only
  namespace: istio-system          # lives WITH the gateway pods
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      istio: egressgateway         # enforced AT the egress Envoy
  action: ALLOW                    # anything unmatched → denied
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals:                # SPIFFE identity, mTLS-proven
        - cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api
    to:
    - operation:
        hosts: ["api.stripe.com"]  # this door opens ONLY to Stripe,
                                    # for ONLY that ServiceAccount
Audit RequirementMesh Mechanism That Satisfies It
"Deny-by-default outbound"outboundTrafficPolicy: REGISTRY_ONLY
"Documented external dependencies"One ServiceEntry per external API
"Single controlled egress point / fixed source IP"istio-egressgateway = fixed source IP for Stripe's firewall allowlist
"Log every outbound call"Envoy access logs on the egress gateway
"Least privilege — only the payment app reaches Stripe"AuthorizationPolicy on the egress gateway, keyed on SPIFFE principal
"Emergency kill switch"Scale istio-egressgateway to 0 replicas
🔄 EXTERNAL TRAFFIC POLICY DECISION — Which Mode for Production?
Production security requirements?
Basic: allow everything
→ ALLOW_ANY (default, NOT recommended)
Standard: whitelist-only
→ REGISTRY_ONLY + ServiceEntries
✅ Recommended for most production
Strict: full audit + single IP
→ REGISTRY_ONLY + Egress Gateway
✅ Required for PCI/HIPAA compliance

8.5 Deep Dive — Egress Gateway Traffic Path Step-by-Step
