When you configure an Egress Gateway, traffic takes a specific 4-hop path. Understanding this flow is critical for the ICA exam:

🔀 EGRESS GATEWAY TRAFFIC FLOW — 4 Hops to the Internet
HOP 1: Pod → Sidecar Envoy (outbound :15001)
  App calls api.stripe.com:443 → iptables redirects to Envoy :15001
  Envoy matches VirtualService: "route to egress gateway"

HOP 2: Sidecar Envoy → istio-egressgateway Pod
  Traffic forwarded to istio-egressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local:443
  mTLS between sidecar and egress gateway (SPIFFE certs)

HOP 3: Egress Gateway → External API (api.stripe.com)
  Gateway matches its own VS rules: "route to api.stripe.com"
  Performs DNS resolution, establishes TLS to Stripe

HOP 4: Response flows back through same path
  Stripe → Egress Gateway → Sidecar Envoy → App container
  Headers, status codes, body — all proxied transparently
💡 Why Egress Gateway Matters

Single source IP: Stripe sees all requests from ONE IP (the egress gateway Node IP) — simpler firewall rules. Central audit: All external calls logged in ONE place. Kill switch: Stop the egress gateway pod = ALL external traffic blocked instantly. Required for PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC2 compliance.

📖 Which Resources Are Mandatory?

ServiceEntry — MANDATORY, registers the external host. Gateway (egress) — MANDATORY, opens the listener on the istio: egressgateway Envoy. VirtualService — MANDATORY, ONE VS with TWO match blocks: mesh→gateway, then gateway→external. DestinationRule — OPTIONAL, only for TLS origination (app speaks plain HTTP, gateway upgrades to HTTPS) or to tune the sidecar→gateway hop. Mis-wiring ONE resource makes traffic silently bypass the gateway — calls still succeed, but the audit trail is empty, the worst failure mode: the invisible one.

The Gateway resource that opens the door on the egress Envoy:

yaml — egress Gateway resource 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: egress-stripe
  namespace: istio-system        # convention (ANY ns works)
spec:
  selector:
    istio: egressgateway         # binds to the EGRESS Envoy,
                                  # NOT istio: ingressgateway!
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 443
      name: tls
      protocol: TLS               # passthrough listener (HTTPS)
    hosts:
    - api.stripe.com
    tls:
      mode: PASSTHROUGH           # app's TLS stays intact

The two-match VirtualService — the heart of the egress detour, with one match for each hop:

yaml — the two-match VirtualService 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: stripe-through-egress
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts: [api.stripe.com]
  gateways:
  - mesh                         # reserved word: every sidecar
  - istio-system/egress-stripe   # the egress Gateway above
  tls:
  - match:                       # BLOCK 1: sidecar → gateway
    - gateways: [mesh]
      port: 443
      sniHosts: [api.stripe.com]
    route:
    - destination:
        host: istio-egressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local
        port: {number: 443}
  - match:                       # BLOCK 2: gateway → internet
    - gateways: [istio-system/egress-stripe]
      port: 443
      sniHosts: [api.stripe.com]
    route:
    - destination:
        host: api.stripe.com     # the ServiceEntry host
        port: {number: 443}

The optional DestinationRule — only needed when the app sends plain HTTP and you want the GATEWAY to upgrade the call to HTTPS toward Stripe:

yaml — optional DestinationRule: TLS origination at the gateway 
# ONLY needed when the app sends plain HTTP on port 80 and you
# want the GATEWAY to upgrade the call to HTTPS toward Stripe:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: stripe-originate-tls
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  host: api.stripe.com
  trafficPolicy:
    portLevelSettings:
    - port: {number: 443}
      tls:
        mode: SIMPLE             # gateway originates TLS

# for plain HTTPS passthrough (the Gateway above) SKIP this resource
⚠️ Prove the Detour Works — the Access Log Is the Proof

The call MUST appear in the egress gateway's own access log — an empty log means traffic is bypassing it, even if the curl call itself returned 200.

bash — verifying the detour 
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- \
    curl -s https://api.stripe.com/v1 -o /dev/null

kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway \
    --tail=3 | grep stripe
# [2026-07-02T10:14:07Z] "- - -" ... outbound|443||api.stripe.com
#                          ← the hop-3 entry: detour confirmed

8.6 Deep Dive — DNS Proxying & Protocol Selection: How Istio Routes Without HTTP Headers

Two critical operational features from the official docs that every ICA candidate must understand:

🌐 DNS Proxying — ServiceEntry Resolution Without Custom DNS

By default, Kubernetes DNS doesn't know about ServiceEntry hosts. DNS Proxying makes the Envoy sidecar intercept DNS queries from the application and resolve ServiceEntry addresses locally — no external DNS changes needed.

  WITHOUT DNS Proxying:
  App → DNS query: "api.stripe.com" → kube-dns → ❌ NXDOMAIN (unknown)

  WITH DNS Proxying:
  App → DNS query: "api.stripe.com" → Sidecar intercepts → Checks ServiceEntry registry
  → Returns: 240.240.0.1 (auto-allocated VIP) → App sends request to VIP
  → Envoy routes VIP → ServiceEntry → api.stripe.com:443
# Enable DNS Proxying (sidecar mode)
apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: IstioOperator
spec:
  meshConfig:
    defaultConfig:
      proxyMetadata:
        ISTIO_META_DNS_CAPTURE: "true"  # Enable DNS interception
# Or per-pod annotation:
# proxy.istio.io/config: proxyMetadata.ISTIO_META_DNS_CAPTURE: "true"
# Ambient mode: enabled by default from Istio 1.25+
💡 Address Auto-Allocation

For ServiceEntries without explicit spec.addresses, Istio auto-allocates VIPs from the 240.240.0.0/16 range (Class E, non-routable). Each ServiceEntry gets a unique VIP. Envoy routes based on this VIP to distinguish multiple TCP services on the same port. Opt-out: networking.istio.io/enable-autoallocate-ip: "false" label on ServiceEntry.

🔌 Protocol Selection — How Istio Knows HTTP vs TCP

Istio can proxy ANY TCP traffic, but L7 features (routing, metrics, retries) require protocol identification. Two methods:

MethodHowExamplePriority
appProtocol (K8s 1.18+)Service port fieldappProtocol: https🥇 HIGHEST
Port namename: <protocol>[-suffix]name: http-web or grpc-api🥈 Second
Auto-detectionEnvoy inspects trafficDetects HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2🥉 Fallback (→ TCP if unknown)
kind: Service
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 443
    name: https-api      # ← Protocol detected: HTTPS
    appProtocol: https   # ← Explicit (takes precedence)
  - port: 9090
    name: grpc-metrics   # ← Protocol detected: gRPC (HTTP/2)
  - port: 5432
    name: tcp-postgres   # ← Protocol detected: TCP
⚠️ ICA: Port Name is MANDATORY for L7 Features

If a port is named myapp-port instead of http-myapp, Istio treats it as opaque TCP — no VirtualService routing, no metrics labels, no retries. The protocol prefix in the port name is NOT optional for L7 features. Supported prefixes: http, http2, grpc, grpc-web, tcp, tls, https, plus the experimental database prefixes mongo, mysql, redis — the prefix IS the contract. Also: Gateways don't auto-detect at all — a Gateway server speaks EXACTLY the protocol its YAML declares, no sniffing, ever.

📖 Real Incident — the Server-First Protocol Trap

anihpj's PostgreSQL port was once left unnamed — psql connections just hung. Envoy's auto-detection sniffer waits for the CLIENT to send bytes first to identify the protocol, but PostgreSQL is a server-first protocol (the server speaks first) — the sniffer waited forever for bytes that were never coming from that side. Lesson: always name database ports with an explicit tcp- prefix — never rely on auto-detection for server-first protocols like PostgreSQL.

8.7 Deep Dive — resolution Has Five Modes, Not Three

Section 8.2 taught DNS, STATIC, and NONE as ServiceEntry's resolution field — but the real spec ships five values: NONE, STATIC, DNS, DNS_ROUND_ROBIN, and DYNAMIC_DNS.

🔄 DNS vs DNS_ROUND_ROBIN — Behavior Under IP Rotation
DNS mode — a CDN rotates its 4 answer IPs every 30 seconds:
  connection 1 opens → resolves [a,b,c,d] → picks IP-a
  30s later: DNS rotates → Envoy re-resolves → pool reshuffled
  in-flight connections MAY be redistributed / drained  ⚠️

DNS_ROUND_ROBIN mode — same CDN, same 30s rotation:
  connection 1 opens → resolves → uses ONLY the 1st IP returned
  30s later: DNS rotates → only NEW connections see the new IP
  connection 1 stays OPEN on IP-a — no drain, no cycling  ✅
ModeConnection Behavioranihpj Use Case
NONETrusts an already-resolved destination IP (iptables/eBPF)Wildcard SNI passthrough
STATICFixed IPs from spec.endpoints, never re-checkedInternal VM cluster, fixed IP list
DNSRe-resolves the full answer set; connections may reshuffle/churnapi.stripe.com — the 90% cloud-API case
DNS_ROUND_ROBINUses only the 1st IP returned; open connections survive DNS rotationCDN-fronted host with many rotating IPs
DYNAMIC_DNSResolves the SNI/Host header AT REQUEST TIME (ambient mode)Ambient-mode wildcard waypoint hosts (rare)
💡 Why Trade Load Balance for Stability?

Plain DNS mode re-resolves the FULL answer set and can reshuffle load behind LIVE connections — for large web-scale hosts fronted by huge, fast-rotating DNS answer sets (CDNs, hyperscale SaaS APIs), that constant reshuffling wastes connection-pool churn. DNS_ROUND_ROBIN trades perfect load distribution for connection stability: identical wiring to DNS mode — only the resolution: value changes. Neither DNS nor DNS_ROUND_ROBIN can be used with wildcard hosts or Unix-domain-socket endpoints.

📖 DYNAMIC_DNS — the Newest Mode

Resolves the hostname carried in the SNI or HTTP Host header AT REQUEST TIME, so ONE wildcard host entry stands in for many real subdomains without enumerating them. Valid ONLY for wildcard hosts — works in sidecar mode for both MESH_INTERNAL and MESH_EXTERNAL, but in ambient mode only for MESH_EXTERNAL (bound to a waypoint proxy); does NOT work for raw TCP (no SNI/Host header to recover the real hostname). ICA exam note: DYNAMIC_DNS is ambient-mesh-era and not yet common exam material — know it EXISTS as the 5th value.

8.8 Deep Dive — WorkloadEntry: the Real YAML Behind endpoints and workloadSelector

endpoints is a ServiceEntry field holding a list of WorkloadEntry-shaped objects (address, ports, labels, weight…) that back STATIC resolution — this is the actual syntax behind 8.2's "STATIC → PostgreSQL VM at 10.0.1.50:5432" row. workloadSelector is the alternative: instead of hardcoding IPs inline, label-select standalone kind: WorkloadEntry objects that carry matching labels — valid ONLY when location: MESH_INTERNAL. The two fields are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE — only one may be set per ServiceEntry.

yaml — endpoints: the real YAML behind STATIC resolution 

# STATIC resolution — the endpoints field, spelled out in full
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-postgres-vm
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - postgres.anihpj.internal
  location: MESH_INTERNAL
  ports:
  - number: 5432
    name: tcp-postgres
    protocol: TCP
  resolution: STATIC
  endpoints:
  - address: 10.0.1.50        # the VM's real IP
    ports:
      tcp-postgres: 5432      # port NAME → real port
yaml — workloadSelector: label-selecting a standalone WorkloadEntry 

# MESH_INTERNAL + workloadSelector — label-select real VMs
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-legacy-workers
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - legacy-workers.anihpj.internal
  location: MESH_INTERNAL     # workloadSelector needs this
  ports:
  - number: 8080
    name: http-worker
    protocol: HTTP
  resolution: STATIC
  workloadSelector:
    labels:
      app: legacy-worker      # matches labels below
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: WorkloadEntry            # a SEPARATE, standalone object
metadata:
  name: legacy-worker-vm1
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  address: 10.0.2.11
  labels:
    app: legacy-worker         # the selector match
  serviceAccount: legacy-worker-sa
FieldShapeBest For
endpointsInline address/ports/labels list, in THIS ServiceEntry objectA handful of fixed IPs (one DB VM, one legacy host)
workloadSelectorLabel-selects SEPARATE kind: WorkloadEntry objects by matching labelsA fleet of VMs that scales/rotates on its own timeline
💡 An Endpoint's ports Map Is Optional

Omit it and that endpoint inherits the SAME port numbers already declared in the ServiceEntry's own ports list — no need to repeat them for the common case.

8.9 Deep Dive — exportTo Beyond "*" and ".": Naming Specific Namespaces

exportTo also accepts an explicit LIST of namespace names — 8.2 only showed the two extremes, "*" (every namespace) and "." (private to the ServiceEntry's own namespace). anihpj's platform team owns shared ServiceEntries (Stripe, SendGrid) that the anihpj-billing team also needs, but NOT every namespace in the mesh — a named list is least-privilege without going fully private.

yaml — sharing stripe-payments with ONE more team 

# 8.2's stripe-payments ServiceEntry, shared with ONE more team
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: stripe-payments
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
  exportTo:
  - anihpj              # its own namespace (equivalent to '.')
  - anihpj-billing       # ALSO visible here — nowhere else

# any OTHER namespace (anihpj-notifications, default, ...) still
# gets 'host not found' — exactly as if this ServiceEntry didn't
# exist for them at all
exportTo ValueWho Can Route to Itanihpj Example
"*"Every namespace in the mesh (unset = this)The DEFAULT — no exportTo field at all
"."ONLY the ServiceEntry's own namespaceAn anihpj-only DB ServiceEntry
[ns1, ns2]ONLY the namespaces named in the liststripe-payments shared anihpj + billing only
⚠️ The Silent-Failure Gotcha

A consumer left off the list doesn't get a clear error — it gets a routing failure that looks IDENTICAL to "the ServiceEntry was never created," which makes exportTo mistakes hard to diagnose unless you check this field first.

8.10 Deep Dive — subjectAltNames: Pinning the External Server's Identity

subjectAltNames is an optional ServiceEntry field that gives Envoy an EXPLICIT allow-list of certificate SAN values (or spiffe:// URIs) to accept from the remote peer, layered on top of whatever standard TLS chain validation already applies. For wildcard MESH_EXTERNAL hosts (like *.amazonaws.com), it turns a fuzzy "any cert under this wildcard" trust into a documented, audit-friendly allow-list. Pair it with the DestinationRule TLS settings from 8.5 — the DestinationRule originates or forwards the handshake, and subjectAltNames is the extra allow-list Envoy checks the peer certificate against.

📖 The MESH_INTERNAL + workloadSelector Case

For a MESH_INTERNAL ServiceEntry built with workloadSelector (8.8), you usually don't need to set subjectAltNames by hand at all — the matching WorkloadEntry's own serviceAccount field is AUTOMATICALLY folded into the SAN verification Envoy performs. This wildcard-trust-narrowing pattern here is specifically for MESH_EXTERNAL hosts, where there's no WorkloadEntry/ServiceAccount to derive an identity from in the first place.

🔒 NARROWING WILDCARD TRUST TO NAMED IDENTITIES
hosts: ["*.amazonaws.com"] ServiceEntry, WITHOUT subjectAltNames:
  any CA-trusted cert matching *.amazonaws.com is accepted —
  s3.amazonaws.com, ec2.amazonaws.com, ANY AWS service all pass

SAME ServiceEntry, WITH subjectAltNames: [s3.amazonaws.com]:
  only a cert presenting s3.amazonaws.com in its SAN passes
  a cert for ec2.amazonaws.com (still otherwise valid) is
  REJECTED — explicit, auditable, least-privilege trust  ✅
yaml — pinning stripe-payments to its expected certificate identity 

# 8.2's stripe-payments ServiceEntry + certificate identity pin
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: stripe-payments
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
  subjectAltNames:
  - api.stripe.com        # MUST match the cert's real SAN entry
bash — confirm the real SAN before hardcoding it 
# confirm the real SAN BEFORE hardcoding it:
openssl s_client -connect api.stripe.com:443 2>/dev/null \
    | openssl x509 -noout -ext subjectAltName
⚠️ Gotcha

Values must match the certificate's ACTUAL SAN entries exactly (case-sensitive DNS names, or a spiffe://... URI for MESH_INTERNAL peers) — confirm real values with openssl s_client before hardcoding; this field NARROWS trust, it doesn't replace normal TLS validation.

🔧 Under the Hood — The Full Outbound-Call Decision Model: Five Gates from a Blocked 502 to an Audited, Certificate-Pinned Egress Call
🗺️ Five Gates, One Request — jobpost-api Calls api.stripe.com

Five gates decide exactly what happens to a real outbound call — this is the model 8.1-8.10 built piece by piece, assembled here as ONE decision path.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  GATE 1 — IS THE HOST REGISTERED? (8.1, 8.2)                                  │
│    no ServiceEntry  → outboundTrafficPolicy decides: ALLOW_ANY passes         │
│                       it through blind — no mTLS, no metrics, no AuthZ!      │
│                       REGISTRY_ONLY → 502, done                               │
│    ServiceEntry exists → continue to Gate 2                                   │
│                                                                                │
│  GATE 2 — HOW DOES ENVOY FIND THE IP? (8.7, 8.8)                              │
│    resolution: DNS            → re-resolves periodically (Stripe's case)      │
│    resolution: STATIC         → fixed endpoints/workloadSelector (8.8)        │
│    resolution: NONE           → wildcard passthrough, already-resolved IP     │
│    resolution: DNS_ROUND_ROBIN/DYNAMIC_DNS → CDN- or ambient-specific         │
│                                                                                │
│  GATE 3 — DIRECT EXIT OR THROUGH THE EGRESS GATEWAY? (8.3, 8.5)               │
│    no egress Gateway/VS wired → sidecar dials api.stripe.com directly         │
│                                  (registered, but unaudited)                   │
│    Gateway + 2-match VS wired → 4-hop detour: app → sidecar →                 │
│                                  istio-egressgateway → api.stripe.com          │
│                                                                                │
│  GATE 4 — TLS: PASSTHROUGH OR ORIGINATED AT THE EDGE? (8.5)                   │
│    app already speaks HTTPS → Gateway tls.mode: PASSTHROUGH (Stripe)          │
│    app speaks plain HTTP    → DestinationRule tls.mode: SIMPLE                │
│                                originates TLS at the gateway (SendGrid)        │
│                                                                                │
│  GATE 5 — WHO ELSE MAY SEE OR TRUST THIS HOST? (8.4, 8.9, 8.10)               │
│    AuthorizationPolicy on the egress gateway → pins the caller's SA           │
│    exportTo                                  → scopes which namespaces        │
│                                                  may reference the host        │
│    subjectAltNames                           → pins the exact cert            │
│                                                  identity Envoy accepts        │
│                                                                                │
│  RESULT for jobpost-api → api.stripe.com: registered (DNS) → routed          │
│  via egress gateway → TLS PASSTHROUGH → AuthorizationPolicy allows            │
│  only jobpost-api's ServiceAccount → subjectAltNames pins Stripe's            │
│  certificate identity. Five gates, one line in an exam scenario:              │
│  "make this external call, and prove it's controlled."                        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 Port Name Protocol Detection — How Istio Knows TCP vs HTTP
Port Name PrefixDetected ProtocolL7 Features Available
http-HTTP/1.1VS routing, retries, metrics, tracing
http2-HTTP/2VS routing, retries, metrics, tracing
grpc-gRPC (HTTP/2)VS routing, retries, metrics, tracing
grpc-web-gRPC-WebBrowser-compatible gRPC
tcp-TCP (opaque)❌ NO L7 routing or metrics
tls-TLS (SNI inspected)SNI routing only
https-HTTPS (TLS+HTTP)TLS termination then HTTP features
No prefixTCP (default)❌ NO L7 — even if it IS HTTP!
🔑 ICA Insight: Every external call anihpj makes passes through the SAME five gates, whether the exam scenario spells them all out or not: registration, resolution, routing (direct vs egress gateway), TLS posture, and identity/scope controls. When a scenario says "make this external call, and prove it's controlled," it is really asking you to answer all five gates in order — miss one and the call either fails outright or succeeds unaudited, which on a PCI-style exam scenario is graded as a fail even though the curl command returned 200.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • REGISTRY_ONLY treats an unregistered host as a BlackHoleCluster — instant 502, no upstream ever attempted, not a network-level failure.
  • ServiceEntry alone only REGISTERS a host — it doesn't force traffic through any particular door. Without a Gateway + 2-match VirtualService, a registered call still dials out directly from the sidecar, unaudited.
  • The 2-match VirtualService pattern is mandatory for a real egress detour: one match routes mesh→gateway, a second routes gateway→external — skip either half and traffic silently bypasses the gateway while still succeeding.
  • An empty egress-gateway access log after a "successful" call means the detour didn't happen — the call still worked (direct dial-out), it just wasn't audited. This is the single most exam-relevant verification habit in the chapter.
  • resolution has 5 modes, not 3: NONE/STATIC/DNS are the common ones; DNS_ROUND_ROBIN trades load distribution for connection stability under IP rotation, DYNAMIC_DNS resolves SNI/Host at request time for wildcard hosts (ambient-era, rare on today's exam).
  • endpoints and workloadSelector are mutually exclusive — inline a handful of fixed IPs with endpoints, or label-select separate scaling WorkloadEntry objects with workloadSelector, never both on one ServiceEntry.
  • Port-name protocol prefix is mandatory for L7 features — an unprefixed or wrongly-prefixed port name makes Istio treat real HTTP traffic as opaque TCP: no routing, no metrics, no retries.
  • subjectAltNames narrows trust, it doesn't replace TLS validation — it's an additional allow-list Envoy checks the peer certificate against, layered on top of normal chain validation, not a substitute for it.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "A ServiceEntry alone routes traffic through the egress gateway." No — it only REGISTERS the host with Envoy. Without a Gateway + 2-match VirtualService wired to it, the sidecar dials out directly, registered but unaudited.
  • "If the curl call succeeds, the egress gateway detour worked." No — a successful call only proves the destination was reachable. Check the egress gateway's own access log; an empty log after a "successful" call means the detour was bypassed.
  • "resolution: DNS and DNS_ROUND_ROBIN are basically the same." No — plain DNS re-resolves the FULL answer set and can reshuffle live connections; DNS_ROUND_ROBIN uses only the first IP returned and lets open connections survive a DNS rotation untouched.
  • "endpoints and workloadSelector can be combined for flexibility." No — they're mutually exclusive. Pick inline fixed IPs (endpoints) OR label-selected separate WorkloadEntry objects (workloadSelector), never both on the same ServiceEntry.
  • "A port named myapp-port still gets HTTP routing since the traffic IS HTTP." No — Istio only detects HTTP from an explicit appProtocol field or a correctly prefixed port name (http-, http2-, grpc-, etc.). An unprefixed name is treated as opaque TCP regardless of what's actually flowing over it.
  • "exportTo only supports '*' (everyone) or '.' (just me)." No — it also accepts an explicit namespace list for least-privilege sharing with specific teams, without going fully private or fully mesh-wide.
  • "A consumer left off an exportTo list gets a clear permission-denied error." No — it gets a routing failure indistinguishable from "the ServiceEntry doesn't exist at all," which makes exportTo mistakes genuinely hard to diagnose unless you check this field first.

💼 Chapter 8 — Daily Work Takeaways

  • Always register a ServiceEntry BEFORE switching outboundTrafficPolicy to REGISTRY_ONLY — flip the mode first and every unregistered call anihpj makes starts 502ing immediately, including ones nobody remembered to inventory.
  • Check the egress gateway's access log, not just the response code, whenever you need to PROVE a call was audited — a 200 response proves reachability, not compliance.
  • Prefer resolution: DNS for the 90% cloud-API case (Stripe, SendGrid, most SaaS) — reach for DNS_ROUND_ROBIN only when a CDN's fast IP rotation is visibly churning your connection pool.
  • Confirm real certificate SAN values with openssl BEFORE hardcoding subjectAltNames — a typo'd or stale SAN value silently rejects every legitimate call.
  • Name ports with the correct protocol prefix from day one — retrofitting a wrongly-named port after a service is already in production is a silent, hard-to-diagnose loss of retries/metrics/routing.
  • Scope shared ServiceEntries with an explicit exportTo namespace list, not the mesh-wide default — a platform-owned Stripe/SendGrid ServiceEntry doesn't need to be visible to every team's namespace.
  • For the ICA exam: remember the three-domain split — registering/routing is Traffic Management, the AuthorizationPolicy pin is Securing Workloads, and reading the access log to prove the detour worked is Troubleshooting. One feature, three scored domains.
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 8

Seven quick-fire phrase-to-answer mappings — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Register an external API" = ServiceEntry with hosts, location: MESH_EXTERNAL, resolution: DNS
  • "Force traffic through one audited exit" = Gateway (type: egress) + a 2-match VirtualService detouring through istio-egressgateway
  • "PCI/HIPAA-grade egress posture" = REGISTRY_ONLY + Egress Gateway + AuthorizationPolicy, all three layers stacked
  • "Fixed external IPs, not DNS-resolved" = resolution: STATIC with either endpoints (inline) or workloadSelector (separate WorkloadEntry objects)
  • "Share with one more team, not the whole mesh" = exportTo: [ns1, ns2] — an explicit namespace list
  • "Pin the external server's cert identity" = subjectAltNames — confirm real values with openssl s_client first
  • "Prove the detour actually worked" = check the egress gateway's own access log, not just the response code

🧠 Chapter 8 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
In REGISTRY_ONLY mode, what exactly happens when jobpost-api calls a host with no matching ServiceEntry?
Show Answer
Answer

Envoy routes the request to its internal BlackHoleCluster — an immediate 502, with no upstream connection ever attempted.

Explanation

This is a config-level rejection, not a network-level failure — no DNS lookup, no TCP handshake, nothing reaches the actual destination. That distinction matters for diagnosis: a real network problem and a missing ServiceEntry look identical from a plain curl, but very different in Envoy's own cluster stats.

Q2
Does applying a ServiceEntry, by itself, route traffic through the egress gateway?
Show Answer
Answer

No. A ServiceEntry only REGISTERS the host so Envoy will consider the call at all. Without a Gateway + 2-match VirtualService also wired to that host, the sidecar dials out directly — registered, but completely unaudited.

Explanation

This is the #1 exam trap in this chapter — a call that "succeeds" after only a ServiceEntry was applied looks identical to one that's actually routed through the audited gateway, unless you specifically check the gateway's access log.

Q3
Name all 5 valid values for ServiceEntry's resolution field, and which one is newest.
Show Answer
Answer

NONE, STATIC, DNS, DNS_ROUND_ROBIN, and DYNAMIC_DNS — the newest is DYNAMIC_DNS, which resolves the SNI/Host header at request time for wildcard hosts (ambient-mode era).

Explanation

Most study material only covers the first three — the ICA exam expects you to know all 5 exist, even if DNS_ROUND_ROBIN and DYNAMIC_DNS are rarer in practice.

Q4
What's the practical difference between resolution: DNS and resolution: DNS_ROUND_ROBIN when the upstream DNS answer set rotates?
Show Answer
Answer

DNS re-resolves the FULL answer set periodically and can reshuffle load behind already-open connections. DNS_ROUND_ROBIN uses only the first IP returned per new connection — open connections are never disturbed by a later rotation.

Explanation

This is a real production trade-off, not just trivia: DNS mode gives better load distribution across a CDN's rotating IP pool, DNS_ROUND_ROBIN gives better connection stability — pick based on which one your specific external dependency needs more.

Q5
What's the difference between the endpoints and workloadSelector fields, and can both be set on one ServiceEntry?
Show Answer
Answer

endpoints inlines a list of fixed addresses directly in the ServiceEntry. workloadSelector instead label-selects separate, standalone kind: WorkloadEntry objects. They are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE — only one may be set per ServiceEntry.

Explanation

endpoints suits a handful of fixed IPs (one DB VM); workloadSelector suits a fleet of VMs that scales or rotates on its own timeline, since new WorkloadEntry objects can be added without touching the ServiceEntry itself.

Q6
A Service port is named myapp-port and genuinely carries HTTP traffic. What routing/observability features does Istio provide for it?
Show Answer
Answer

None of the L7 ones — no VirtualService routing, no per-request metrics labels, no retries. Istio treats it as opaque TCP because the port name carries no recognized protocol prefix, regardless of what's actually flowing over the wire.

Explanation

The fix is either renaming the port with a supported prefix (http-myapp) or, on Kubernetes 1.18+, setting the Service's own appProtocol field explicitly — which takes priority over the port-name convention.

Q7
What does subjectAltNames actually protect against, and what does it NOT replace?
Show Answer
Answer

It narrows trust for a wildcard host (like *.amazonaws.com) down to an explicit allow-list of certificate SAN values — so only certs presenting one of those exact names pass, even though other certs under the same wildcard would otherwise be CA-trusted. It does NOT replace standard TLS chain validation — it's an ADDITIONAL check layered on top.

Explanation

Always confirm the real SAN value with openssl s_client ... | openssl x509 -noout -ext subjectAltName before hardcoding it — a typo'd or outdated value silently rejects legitimate traffic with no obvious YAML-level error.

Q8
What happens to a namespace that's left off an exportTo list when it tries to reference that ServiceEntry?
Show Answer
Answer

It gets a routing failure that looks IDENTICAL to "the ServiceEntry was never created" — not a clear permission-denied error.

Explanation

This is exactly why exportTo mistakes are hard to diagnose in production — the symptom gives no hint that the resource exists at all. Always check exportTo scoping FIRST when a "the ServiceEntry doesn't exist" report comes in from a team that didn't create it.

Q9
Which egress resource is OPTIONAL in the mandatory-vs-optional breakdown from 8.5, and what is it used for when present?
Show Answer
Answer

DestinationRule is optional. When present, it's used for TLS origination (the app speaks plain HTTP, and the gateway upgrades the connection to HTTPS before it leaves) or to tune the sidecar-to-gateway hop specifically.

Explanation

ServiceEntry, the egress Gateway, and the 2-match VirtualService are all mandatory for a working, audited egress path — DestinationRule is the one piece you add only when you have a specific TLS-origination or tuning need.

Q10
An egress call to a registered host succeeds (curl returns 200), but the ICA exam scenario is graded as a fail. What's the most likely reason?
Show Answer
Answer

The call succeeded by dialing out directly rather than through the audited egress gateway — the ServiceEntry registered the host, but the Gateway/VirtualService detour was never wired, missing, or misconfigured, so there's no audit trail even though the request worked.

Explanation

PCI-style exam scenarios grade on CONTROL, not just connectivity — "prove it's controlled" means checking the egress gateway's own access log for the call, not just confirming the response code.

⚙️ Chapter 8 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
jobpost-api's payment call to api.stripe.com is returning 502 in a REGISTRY_ONLY mesh. Task: Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# Diagnose: check whether a ServiceEntry exists for the host
kubectl get serviceentry -n anihpj | # look for api.stripe.com
# Fix: register the host
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: stripe-payments
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
kubectl apply -f stripe-serviceentry.yaml
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep stripe
Explanation

The 502 is Envoy's BlackHoleCluster response, not a network error — confirmed by the missing ServiceEntry, and the last command proves Envoy actually received the new cluster after applying the fix.

Q2
A ServiceEntry for api.checkr.com is applied and curl calls succeed, but the egress gateway's access log shows nothing for this host. Task: Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# Diagnose: check for the Gateway + VirtualService detour
kubectl get gateway,virtualservice -n anihpj | grep checkr
# Most likely: missing entirely, or the VirtualService lacks the 2nd match block
# Fix: mandatory Gateway (egress)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: checkr-egress-gw
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    istio: egressgateway
  servers:
  - port: {number: 443, name: tls, protocol: TLS}
    hosts: ["api.checkr.com"]
    tls: {mode: PASSTHROUGH}
Explanation

ServiceEntry only registers the host — it never forces traffic through any particular door. Without the Gateway + 2-match VirtualService, the sidecar dials directly, which still "succeeds" from curl's point of view but leaves zero audit trail.

Q3
Write a ServiceEntry for a legacy on-prem VM at a fixed IP (10.0.5.20:8443), reachable only from inside the mesh, using endpoints (not workloadSelector).
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: legacy-onprem-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - legacy-api.anihpj.internal
  location: MESH_INTERNAL
  ports:
  - number: 8443
    name: https-legacy
    protocol: HTTPS
  resolution: STATIC
  endpoints:
  - address: 10.0.5.20
    ports:
      https-legacy: 8443
Explanation

location: MESH_INTERNAL is correct here (an internal-only VM, not a public external service) and endpoints is the right choice for ONE fixed IP — workloadSelector would be overkill for a single, non-scaling VM.

Q4
anihpj-billing needs to call the shared stripe-payments ServiceEntry (owned by the platform team in namespace anihpj), but no other namespace should be able to. Task: Scope it correctly.
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  # ...
  exportTo:
  - anihpj            # its own namespace
  - anihpj-billing     # the one additional team
Explanation

Omitting exportTo defaults to "*" (every namespace) and "." only covers the ServiceEntry's own namespace — neither fits "exactly these 2 namespaces, nobody else." The explicit list is the only correct answer.

Q5
A ServiceEntry for *.amazonaws.com is registered with resolution: DNS. Applying it fails validation. Task: Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  hosts:
  - "*.amazonaws.com"
  resolution: NONE   # wildcard hosts can't use DNS or DNS_ROUND_ROBIN
Explanation

Wildcard hosts are incompatible with DNS-based resolution modes since there's no single hostname to actually resolve — NONE (trusting an already-resolved destination IP) or, in ambient mode, DYNAMIC_DNS, are the valid choices for a wildcard.

Q6
Verify that a curl call from jobpost-api to a newly-registered external host is actually reaching Envoy's compiled config, before troubleshooting further.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep stripe
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://api.stripe.com/v1
Explanation

The proxy-config check comes FIRST — a missing cluster proves the ServiceEntry never reached this specific Envoy (a sync problem), while a failed curl on top of a PRESENT cluster points to a completely different layer (DNS, TLS, the actual remote API).

Q7
Emergency: a security incident requires blocking ALL egress traffic immediately, without touching individual ServiceEntries. What's the fastest command?
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl scale deploy/istio-egressgateway -n istio-system --replicas=0
Explanation

This only works if egress is ALREADY forced through the gateway (this chapter's Pattern 2/3) — any ServiceEntry with no gateway detour wired to it dials out directly and is unaffected by this kill switch, which is exactly why Pattern 3 (gateway + AuthorizationPolicy) matters for real incident response.

Q8
Write a WorkloadEntry-backed ServiceEntry for a fleet of 3 legacy worker VMs that scales independently, using workloadSelector.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-legacy-workers
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - legacy-workers.anihpj.internal
  location: MESH_INTERNAL
  ports:
  - number: 8080
    name: http-worker
    protocol: HTTP
  resolution: STATIC
  workloadSelector:
    labels:
      app: legacy-worker
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: WorkloadEntry
metadata:
  name: legacy-worker-vm1
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  address: 10.0.2.11
  labels:
    app: legacy-worker
  serviceAccount: legacy-worker-sa
# repeat as vm2, vm3 — add/remove WorkloadEntry objects independently,
# the ServiceEntry itself never needs to change
Explanation

This is exactly the scenario workloadSelector is for — a fleet that scales on its own timeline. Adding VM #4 later means adding one more WorkloadEntry object, not editing the ServiceEntry.

Q9
A ServiceEntry for *.amazonaws.com has no subjectAltNames field. What's the practical trust risk, and how do you narrow it for just S3?
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  hosts:
  - "*.amazonaws.com"
  # ...
  subjectAltNames:
  - s3.amazonaws.com
Explanation

Without subjectAltNames, ANY CA-trusted certificate matching the wildcard is accepted — a cert for ec2.amazonaws.com would pass just as easily as one for s3.amazonaws.com, even though only S3 access was ever intended. The explicit SAN list narrows this to exactly the identity expected.

Q10
A team reports "our ServiceEntry seems to not exist" for a host that platform team confirms was created and applied successfully in namespace anihpj. Task: Diagnose the most likely cause.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl get serviceentry <name> -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 exportTo
Explanation

An exportTo list that doesn't include the reporting team's namespace produces exactly this symptom — a routing failure indistinguishable from non-existence. This is the exportTo silent-failure gotcha from 8.9, reproduced as a real diagnostic scenario.

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 8
  • MESH_EXTERNAL is for real external hosts (Stripe, SendGrid); MESH_INTERNAL is only for VM-mesh-expansion ServiceEntries backed by WorkloadEntry — mixing them up makes a ServiceEntry silently do nothing.
  • Before wiring an egress gateway, check outboundTrafficPolicy first — you can't tell REGISTRY_ONLY from ALLOW_ANY by staring at ServiceEntry YAML alone.
  • An empty istio-egressgateway access log after a "successful" call means traffic bypassed your detour, not that nothing happened — always check the log before trusting the demo.
  • Wildcard hosts (*.amazonaws.com) can't use resolution: DNS or DNS_ROUND_ROBIN — reach for NONE (or DYNAMIC_DNS in ambient mode) or the ServiceEntry won't apply at all.
  • A STATIC endpoint with no ports map just inherits the ServiceEntry's own port numbers — no need to repeat them for the common case.
  • On exam day, verify with istioctl proxy-config cluster BEFORE curl-ing — a missing cluster proves the ServiceEntry never reached Envoy; a failed curl could mean five different things.

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 8)

Every command below already appeared earlier in this chapter — grouped here as one reference for registering, routing, and auditing external traffic.

CommandWhat It Does / Checks in Chapter 8
kubectl get configmap istio -n istio-system -o yaml | grep -A1 outboundTrafficPolicyCheck ALLOW_ANY vs REGISTRY_ONLY (8.1)
istioctl install --set meshConfig.outboundTrafficPolicy.mode=REGISTRY_ONLY -ySwitch outbound mode mesh-wide (8.1)
kubectl apply -f stripe-serviceentry.yaml / kubectl get serviceentry -n anihpjRegister an external host, then confirm it landed (8.2)
istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj | grep stripeConfirm Envoy actually received the new cluster (8.2)
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://api.stripe.com/v1Prove a real call leaves the mesh (8.2)
istioctl install -y --set components.egressGateways[0].enabled=true / kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l istio=egressgatewayInstall the egress gateway, then confirm the Pod is Running (8.3)
kubectl scale deploy/istio-egressgateway -n istio-system --replicas=0Emergency kill switch for ALL routed egress (8.3)
kubectl logs -n istio-system -l istio=egressgateway --tail=3 | grep stripeProve the detour worked, not just that the call succeeded (8.5)
openssl s_client -connect api.stripe.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -ext subjectAltNameConfirm real SAN values BEFORE hardcoding subjectAltNames (8.10)

🔬 Practice Drill 8.1 — Register and Audit a New External Dependency

⏱️ Target Time: 7 minutes
Scenario

anihpj is integrating a fictional background-check API, api.checkr.com, for auth-service. Do this now, on a real (or kind) cluster with Istio installed:

  1. (2 min) Write and apply a ServiceEntry named checkr-verify in anihpj: hosts: [api.checkr.com], port 443 HTTPS, location: MESH_EXTERNAL, resolution: DNS.
  2. (1 min) Confirm it landed: kubectl get serviceentry -n anihpj, then istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/auth-service -n anihpj | grep checkr.
  3. (2 min) Write an egress Gateway (selector istio: egressgateway) plus the two-match VirtualService that detours auth-service's calls to api.checkr.com through istio-egressgateway.
  4. (1 min) Generate one real call from auth-service and confirm it appears in the egress gateway's access log — an empty log means the detour didn't work.
  5. (1 min) Add exportTo: ["."] to checkr-verify so only anihpj can reference it, and say out loud what error a different namespace would now see.
Hint: Steps 1-2 reuse 8.2's registration pattern; step 3 reuses 8.5's two-match VirtualService verbatim, just with a new host; step 5 reuses 8.9's exportTo list form on a ServiceEntry that previously had none.
View Solution

Step 2's proxy-config cluster output should show a new cluster entry for api.checkr.com once the ServiceEntry is applied — its absence means the ServiceEntry never reached this proxy, a sync problem to chase before anything else. Step 4's access log check is the real pass/fail gate: a logged request proves the gateway detour is live, while a "successful" curl with an empty log means traffic bypassed the gateway entirely. Step 5's out-loud answer: a namespace left off the list gets a routing failure that looks identical to the ServiceEntry never having existed.

Check yourself: did you check the access log BEFORE declaring success, or did a 200 response from curl alone satisfy you? That's exactly the trap 8.5's "invisible failure mode" warning is built to catch.

🔬 Practice Drill 8.2 — Prove ServiceEntry Alone Doesn't Route Through the Gateway

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Don't take 8.2/8.3's warning on faith — reproduce the "registered but unaudited" gap yourself, live.

  1. Apply ONLY a ServiceEntry for a test host (no Gateway, no VirtualService detour) and confirm a curl call from a real pod succeeds.
  2. Check the egress gateway's access log for this call.
  3. Now add the Gateway + 2-match VirtualService detour and repeat the same curl call.
  4. Check the access log again and compare.
Hint: Use istioctl proxy-config cluster before and after step 3 too — the cluster the sidecar routes to changes once the detour is wired, even though the curl command itself never changes.
View Solution

Step 1's curl should succeed with ONLY a ServiceEntry applied — proving registration alone is enough for connectivity. Step 2's log check should come back empty. Step 4's log check (after wiring the detour) should show the same call now logged at the gateway — same curl command, same result code, completely different audit posture.

Check yourself: could you now explain to a teammate, using your own before/after log output, exactly why "the call succeeded" is not the same claim as "the call was audited"? That's the core lesson this drill is built to prove, not just state.

🔬 Practice Drill 8.3 — Match the Symptom to the Broken Layer

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

For each observation, name the most likely cause and the ONE command you'd run to confirm it — before proposing any fix:

  1. A ServiceEntry for *.amazonaws.com with resolution: DNS fails validation on apply.
  2. A team reports their ServiceEntry "doesn't exist," but the platform team confirms it was applied successfully in a different namespace.
  3. A ServiceEntry with both endpoints and workloadSelector set fails validation.
  4. A port named myapp-port carries real HTTP traffic, but no VirtualService rule targeting it ever matches.
Hint: Two of these four are actually the SAME root cause wearing different clothes — a field that's mutually exclusive with another, or a naming convention Istio silently depends on.
View Solution
#CauseConfirm with
1Wildcard hosts are incompatible with DNS/DNS_ROUND_ROBIN resolution — there's no single hostname to resolveRe-check 8.7's resolution-mode table for wildcard compatibility
2The reporting team's namespace is missing from the ServiceEntry's exportTo list — a routing failure indistinguishable from non-existencekubectl get serviceentry -o yaml | grep -A3 exportTo
3endpoints and workloadSelector are mutually exclusive — only one may be setRe-check 8.8's field reference
4The port name has no recognized protocol prefix (should be http-myapp), so Istio treats it as opaque TCP with no L7 routingkubectl get svc -o yaml | grep -A2 "name: myapp-port"

Check yourself: did you correctly identify #2 and #4 as "silent, no obvious error" failure modes versus #1 and #3 as "loud, apply-time rejection" failure modes? Knowing WHICH kind of failure you're looking at narrows the diagnosis fast.

🔬 Practice Drill 8.4 — Build the Three-Layer Egress Defense, Then Break Each Layer On Purpose

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Build 8.4's full PCI-style three-layer posture for a test host, then break each layer one at a time to see what actually stops working:

  1. Set outboundTrafficPolicy.mode: REGISTRY_ONLY, register the test host with a ServiceEntry, wire the egress gateway detour, and add an AuthorizationPolicy pinning the gateway to ONE caller's ServiceAccount.
  2. Confirm a call from the authorized ServiceAccount succeeds end-to-end (registered → routed → allowed).
  3. Remove ONLY the AuthorizationPolicy and try the same call from a DIFFERENT ServiceAccount — does it now succeed or fail?
  4. Re-add the AuthorizationPolicy, then try the same different-ServiceAccount call again.
Hint: Step 3 is the point of the whole drill — without the AuthorizationPolicy layer, ANY workload that can reach the egress gateway can route through it to the external host, not just the one you intended.
View Solution

Step 3 (AuthorizationPolicy removed) should show the different-ServiceAccount call SUCCEEDING — proving that registration + routing alone don't restrict WHO can use the detour, only WHETHER a detour exists at all. Step 4 (AuthorizationPolicy restored) should show that same call now REJECTED.

Check yourself: did you correctly predict step 3's outcome BEFORE running it, or did the "lateral abuse" risk only become concrete once you saw it happen? Reasoning about a missing layer in advance is the actual exam skill; watching it fail live is just confirmation.

🔬 Practice Drill 8.5 — Sketch the Five Gates From Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking back at the UTH's diagram, sketch (on paper or in a text file) the five gates a real outbound call passes through, from a blocked 502 to an audited, certificate-pinned egress call.

  1. Name all 5 gates in order.
  2. For each gate, name the ONE field or resource that decides its outcome.
  3. Pick any one gate and describe what happens to the request if that gate is misconfigured.
Hint: This is a paper/whiteboard drill — the point is retrieving the mental model from memory under light time pressure, the same way the exam expects you to reason about a scenario without a diagram in front of you.
View Solution

The 5 gates: (1) Is the host registered? — ServiceEntry / outboundTrafficPolicy. (2) How does Envoy find the IP? — resolution. (3) Direct exit or through the egress gateway? — Gateway + 2-match VirtualService. (4) TLS passthrough or originated at the edge? — DestinationRule tls.mode. (5) Who else may see or trust this host? — AuthorizationPolicy / exportTo / subjectAltNames.

Check yourself: did your sketch correctly separate gate 3 (ROUTING through the gateway) from gate 5 (AUTHORIZING who may use it)? Confusing "does a detour exist" with "who's allowed to use it" is the single most common conceptual gap this chapter tests.

🌍 Chapter 8 in One Picture — From Blocked Call to Audited Egress
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 8.1 THE PROBLEM: jobpost-api → api.stripe.com → ❌ 502                    │
│     (REGISTRY_ONLY, no ServiceEntry yet)                                 │
│                                     │                                    │
│                                     ▼                                    │
│ 8.2 REGISTER: ServiceEntry(api.stripe.com, MESH_EXTERNAL, DNS)           │
│     → istiod → new Envoy cluster pushed mesh-wide                       │
│                                     │                                    │
│                                     ▼                                    │
│ 8.3 ROUTE: Gateway + 2-match VirtualService → detour through            │
│     istio-egressgateway                                                  │
│                                     │                                    │
│                                     ▼                                    │
│ 8.4 SECURE: REGISTRY_ONLY + egress gateway + AuthorizationPolicy        │
│     (jobpost-api ServiceAccount only)                                    │
│                                     │                                    │
│                                     ▼                                    │
│ 8.5-8.10 THE INTERNALS: traffic path · DNS/protocol · 5 resolution      │
│     modes · WorkloadEntry YAML · exportTo scoping · subjectAltNames     │
│     pinning                                                              │
│                                     │                                    │
│                                     ▼                                    │
│ RESULT: jobpost-api → egress gateway → api.stripe.com — registered,     │
│ routed, audited, and pinned to one certificate identity ✅                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Chapter 8 took jobpost-api from a hard-blocked 502 against api.stripe.com to a fully governed outbound call: 8.1 showed why REGISTRY_ONLY blocks unknown hosts by default, 8.2 registered Stripe (and SendGrid, and S3) as a ServiceEntry so Envoy would even consider the call, 8.3 added an egress gateway as the one audited door external traffic must use, and 8.4 stacked REGISTRY_ONLY, the gateway, and an AuthorizationPolicy into the three-layer defense PCI auditors expect. The six deep dives in 8.5-8.10 filled in exactly how that machinery works — the 4-hop egress path, DNS proxying and protocol selection, all five resolution modes, the real YAML behind endpoints and workloadSelector, exportTo's namespace-list form, and subjectAltNames pinning — so that by the end of this chapter you can not only make anihpj call the outside world, but prove, log, and lock down exactly how it does.

Quick recap — 🌍 ServiceEntry: register the host, or it's a BlackHoleCluster · 🚪 Egress Gateway: one audited door, Gateway + 2-match VS, DR optional · 🛡️ Three-Layer Defense: REGISTRY_ONLY + gateway + AuthorizationPolicy · 🔍 Resolution: 5 modes, not 3 — DNS_ROUND_ROBIN and DYNAMIC_DNS for CDN/ambient cases · 🖥️ WorkloadEntry: endpoints (inline) vs workloadSelector (separate objects), mutually exclusive · 🔒 exportTo + subjectAltNames: scope who sees it, pin whose cert you trust.

💼 Chapters 5-8 — Daily Work Takeaways (Traffic Management)

  • Write Gateway YAML to accept external traffic into the mesh
  • Write VirtualService YAML for path-based and weight-based routing
  • Do canary deployments: deploy v2 → route 5% → monitor → ramp up
  • Roll back any deployment instantly by changing one YAML weight
  • Add retries + timeouts to VirtualService (no code changes!)
  • Configure circuit breakers via DestinationRule outlierDetection
  • Set up intelligent load balancing: LEAST_CONN for variable workloads, CONSISTENT_HASH for sticky sessions
  • Register external APIs (Stripe, SendGrid, S3) via ServiceEntry
  • Know the VS+DR mandatory pattern: VirtualService = WHERE to route, DestinationRule = HOW to route
  • Remember: port names MUST start with "http", "grpc", "tcp", or "tls" or Istio ignores them!
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapters 5-8 (Traffic Management — 35%)

This is 35% of the exam, the single biggest domain. You MUST master these:

  • Gateway: accept external traffic → hosts, ports, TLS
  • VirtualService: route traffic → match URI, weight, headers, retries, timeout, fault
  • DestinationRule: policies → subsets, loadBalancer, outlierDetection, tls mode
  • ServiceEntry: external services → hosts, ports, location: MESH_EXTERNAL

📝 Chapters 5-8 — ICA Exam Questions (Traffic Management)

Q1
Create a VirtualService that routes 90% of jobpost-api traffic to subset v1 and 10% to subset v2.
Show Answer
Answer

spec.http[].route: one destination {host: jobpost-api, subset: v1} with weight: 90, plus a second destination {host: jobpost-api, subset: v2} with weight: 10. The two weights in one route block must sum to 100.

Explanation

This is the mandatory VS+DR canary pattern from Chapters 6-7: VirtualService picks the WHERE and the weight, but subsets v1/v2 must already exist in jobpost-api's DestinationRule (7.2) — reference a subset that isn't defined there and every request in that slice gets 503, not a routing error.

Q2
How do you add a 5-second timeout to calls from jobpost-api to user-service?
Show Answer
Answer

In the VirtualService for user-service, add timeout: 5s inside the http section, alongside the route block.

Explanation

Timeouts are a VirtualService field (6.7), not a DestinationRule field — they cap how long Envoy waits for a response before returning a fast 504, protecting the calling Django thread from hanging indefinitely.

Q3
What DestinationRule field enables circuit breaking?
Show Answer
Answer

outlierDetection, with fields consecutiveGatewayErrors (or consecutive5xxErrors), interval, and baseEjectionTime.

Explanation

outlierDetection lives under trafficPolicy in a DestinationRule (7.4) — it is the ONE field that turns "one slow dependency takes down the whole system" into "one bad pod gets ejected in milliseconds."

Q4
How do you register an external API (api.stripe.com) in the mesh?
Show Answer
Answer

Create a ServiceEntry with hosts: [api.stripe.com], ports: [{number: 443, protocol: HTTPS}], location: MESH_EXTERNAL, resolution: DNS.

Explanation

Every field here is mandatory for a working external registration (8.2) — omit location: MESH_EXTERNAL and Istio doesn't know the host lives outside the mesh; omit resolution and Envoy has no way to find the IP.

Q5
What's the difference between VirtualService retries and a DestinationRule circuit breaker?
Show Answer
Answer

Retries attempt to recover from transient failures — try again. Circuit breaker stops ALL requests to a failing pod to prevent cascade — stop trying.

Explanation

They solve opposite problems and live on different CRDs: retries (VirtualService, 6.6) assume the failure is transient and worth another attempt; outlierDetection (DestinationRule, 7.4) assumes the pod is genuinely broken and stops sending it traffic at all, which is exactly what stops a retry storm from making things worse.

Q6
Security requires ALL jobpost-api → api.stripe.com traffic to exit via the egress gateway. Which resources do you create, and which are mandatory?
Show Answer
Answer

Mandatory: ServiceEntry (registers api.stripe.com), Gateway with selector istio: egressgateway, and ONE VirtualService with TWO match blocks — {gateways: [mesh]} routing to istio-egressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local, then {gateways: [<egress-gw>]} routing to api.stripe.com. DestinationRule is OPTIONAL — only needed for TLS origination at the gateway.

Explanation

This is the classic 8.5 mandatory-vs-optional trap: three resources are required for the detour to happen at all, and the DestinationRule only shows up when the app speaks plain HTTP and the gateway needs to originate TLS on the way out.

Q7
You must move production from ALLOW_ANY to REGISTRY_ONLY. Give the safe order of operations.
Show Answer
Answer

1) Audit real egress via Envoy access logs/Kiali. 2) Create a ServiceEntry for EVERY external host found. 3) Test while STILL in ALLOW_ANY. 4) istioctl install --set meshConfig.outboundTrafficPolicy.mode=REGISTRY_ONLY -y. 5) Re-test.

Explanation

Switching first is an outage: it produces instant 502s on every unregistered external call, and ServiceEntries created AFTER the switch don't retroactively fix calls that already failed — always register, then switch, per 8.1's ordering rule.

Q8
hosts: ["*.amazonaws.com"] — what does the wildcard cover, and what are its limits?
Show Answer
Answer

It covers any subdomain ending in .amazonaws.com (s3.amazonaws.com, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com) but NOT the bare apex amazonaws.com — list that separately. * is legal only as the LEFTMOST label (api.*.com is invalid), and a wildcard host cannot be DNS-resolved — pair it with resolution: NONE (passthrough) or SNI routing on an egress gateway.

Explanation

Wildcards follow DNS wildcard rules — one label, leftmost position only — and their resolution constraint (8.7) is the same rule that blocks DNS/DNS_ROUND_ROBIN on wildcard ServiceEntries.

Q9
When do you choose resolution DNS vs STATIC vs NONE in a ServiceEntry?
Show Answer
Answer

DNS = Envoy re-resolves the hostname periodically (cloud APIs like api.stripe.com — the 90% case). STATIC = fixed IPs listed as endpoints (anihpj's PostgreSQL VM at 10.0.1.50:5432). NONE = no lookup at all; Envoy connects to whatever IP the app already resolved — the required pattern for wildcard hosts.

Explanation

This 3-mode summary is 8.2's baseline; 8.7 extends it to five real modes (adding DNS_ROUND_ROBIN and DYNAMIC_DNS) for CDN-fronted and ambient-mode edge cases.

Q10
Make jobpost-api's Stripe calls resilient: 3s total timeout, 2 retries on 5xx, and eject Stripe endpoints after 5 consecutive 5xx. Which resources do you write?
Show Answer
Answer

A VirtualService on hosts: [api.stripe.com] with http.timeout: 3s and retries: {attempts: 2, perTryTimeout: 1s, retryOn: 5xx} (budget: 3 tries × 1s = 3s ≤ 3s ✅), plus a DestinationRule host: api.stripe.com with outlierDetection: {consecutive5xxErrors: 5, interval: 30s, baseEjectionTime: 60s}.

Explanation

This works ONLY because the ServiceEntry (8.2) already made Stripe a registry member — once registered, external hosts take the FULL VirtualService/DestinationRule surface, exactly like an internal service.

Q11
anihpj is onboarding a B2B partner that must present a client certificate before reaching partner.anihpj.com. You set the Gateway's port-443 server to tls.mode: MUTUAL and reuse the TLS secret already created for SIMPLE mode (kubectl create secret tls ..., holding only tls.crt + tls.key). Partner integration tests fail: every connection drops mid-handshake. What's missing, and how do you fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

MUTUAL needs a THIRD secret key, ca.crt — the CA that signed the PARTNER's client certificates — so the gateway has something to verify incoming client certs against. kubectl create secret tls only ever writes tls.crt + tls.key, so verification has nothing to check and the handshake fails before any HTTP is exchanged. Rebuild the secret as a generic one carrying all three keys:

kubectl create secret generic partner-mtls-cert \
    --from-file=tls.crt=server.crt \
    --from-file=tls.key=server.key \
    --from-file=ca.crt=partner-ca.crt \   # ← the missing piece
    -n istio-system

# Gateway YAML needs NO change — mode and name already correct:
# tls: {mode: MUTUAL, credentialName: partner-mtls-cert}
Explanation

MUTUAL mode always needs three secret keys — tls.crt, tls.key, AND ca.crt — but kubectl create secret tls only ever writes the first two. This is the #1 mTLS Gateway trap on the ICA exam (5.5): the Gateway YAML itself often needs no change at all, only the underlying Secret.

Q12
The new admin portal needs its own hostname, admin.anihpj.com, with its own certificate (admin-tls-cert) — but ops wants it served from the SAME istio-ingressgateway Pod and the SAME port 443 that already terminates SIMPLE TLS for api.anihpj.com (anihpj-tls-cert). How do you add it without touching the existing api.anihpj.com server?
Show Answer
Answer

Add a SECOND servers[] entry to the same Gateway, same port number 443, with its own hosts + credentialName — Envoy reads the TLS SNI field to pick the right certificate per connection, so one port can safely terminate many certs as long as each server's hosts list is distinct and each server has a unique name.

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata: {name: anihpj-gateway-https, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  selector: {istio: ingressgateway}
  servers:
  - port: {number: 443, name: https, protocol: HTTPS}       # existing
    tls: {mode: SIMPLE, credentialName: anihpj-tls-cert}
    hosts: ["api.anihpj.com"]
  - port: {number: 443, name: https-admin, protocol: HTTPS}  # NEW
    tls: {mode: SIMPLE, credentialName: admin-tls-cert}
    hosts: ["admin.anihpj.com"]      # SNI picks this cert
Explanation

One Gateway port can safely terminate many certificates because Envoy reads the TLS SNI field to pick the right certificate per connection — but never merge two hostnames under one tls: block; one server = one certificate (5.7).

Q13
The platform team created Gateway anihpj-gateway in namespace istio-system. Your team's VirtualService lives in namespace anihpj and references it with gateways: [anihpj-gateway]. kubectl apply succeeds and kubectl get gateway -n istio-system shows it healthy — but every request still 404s. What's wrong?
Show Answer
Answer

An unqualified gateway name resolves inside the VirtualService's OWN namespace (anihpj), not the Gateway's — Istio looks for a Gateway named anihpj-gateway INSIDE anihpj, finds nothing, and the VS binds to no gateway at all. Qualify it with the Gateway's namespace instead: gateways: ["istio-system/anihpj-gateway"].

Explanation

Rule of thumb: whenever Gateway and VirtualService live in different namespaces, always use the <namespace>/<name> form — an unqualified name silently looks in the wrong namespace and fails with no error, not a warning (5.8).

Q14
After migrating the edge to Gateway API, the jobpost squad creates HTTPRoute jobpost-route in their OWN namespace jobpost-team, with parentRefs pointing at Gateway anihpj-gw (namespace anihpj, listener allowedRoutes: {namespaces: {from: Same}}). Requests never reach jobpost-api, and the HTTPRoute's status shows Accepted: False, reason: NotAllowedByListeners. Name two valid fixes.
Show Answer
Answer

from: Same restricts the listener to routes living in the Gateway's OWN namespace (anihpj) — a route from jobpost-team is rejected before routing is even attempted. Fix 1 — widen the listener:

listeners:
- name: http
  ...
  allowedRoutes:
    namespaces:
      from: All              # was: Same

Fix 2 — simplest: create jobpost-route in namespace anihpj instead, so it satisfies the existing Same restriction. Either way, re-check status: Accepted: True confirms the fix landed.

Explanation

This is the Gateway API's version of the classic Gateway/VirtualService binding gotcha from Chapter 5 — a route from a different namespace is rejected at the listener level before routing is even attempted; check allowedRoutes.namespaces.from whenever a cross-team HTTPRoute reports NotAllowedByListeners (5.6).

Q15
Support tickets say beta testers sending header x-beta-tester: "true" always land on search-service v1, even though this VirtualService was meant to send them to v2. Find the bug and fix it: 
❌ BROKEN — catch-all placed first:
http:
- route:                              # no match = catch-all
  - destination: {host: search-service, subset: v1}
- match:                              # NEVER reached
  - headers: {x-beta-tester: {exact: "true"}}
  route:
  - destination: {host: search-service, subset: v2}
Show Answer
Answer

Rule order, not the header match, is broken. Envoy walks http[] TOP to BOTTOM and stops at the FIRST match; rule 1 has no match block at all (a catch-all) and sits FIRST, so it swallows 100% of traffic before rule 2's header check ever runs. Fix: move the header-matched rule ABOVE the catch-all —

✅ FIXED — specific rule first, catch-all last:
http:
- match:
  - headers: {x-beta-tester: {exact: "true"}}
  route:
  - destination: {host: search-service, subset: v2}
- route:                              # catch-all LAST
  - destination: {host: search-service, subset: v1}
Explanation

Envoy's http[] array is evaluated top to bottom and stops at the FIRST match — a route with no match block at all is a catch-all, and it must always sit LAST or it silently swallows every request before more specific rules ever run (6.9's core rule).

Q16
Write a complete VirtualService for skills-service that sends requests carrying header x-internal-user: "1" to subset v2 (beta features) and routes everyone else to subset v1.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: skills-service-beta
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - skills-service
  http:
  - match:                        # specific rule FIRST
    - headers:
        x-internal-user:
          exact: "1"
    route:
    - destination:
        host: skills-service
        subset: v2               # beta features
  - route:                        # catch-all LAST
    - destination:
        host: skills-service
        subset: v1
Explanation

Same discipline as Q15: specific match first, catch-all last (6.9). Remember subsets v1/v2 must already exist in a DestinationRule (7.2) — this VS applies cleanly even if they don't, but every request then 503s with "no healthy upstream."

Q17
jobpost-api's public API is versioned at /api/v2/, but the Django app itself only knows plain resource paths (/jobs/, /users/) with no version prefix. Write the VirtualService that lets external clients call https://api.anihpj.com/api/v2/jobs/ while jobpost-api receives just /jobs/.
Show Answer
Answer

Match the prefix, then rewrite it away before the route forwards:

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.anihpj.com
  gateways:
  - anihpj-gateway
  http:
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /api/v2/
    rewrite:
      uri: /                 # strips /api/v2/, replaces with /
    route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        port: {number: 8000}
Explanation

rewrite fires AFTER the match but BEFORE the request leaves Envoy, so the backend never sees the version prefix at all. Confirm the rewrite actually applied with istioctl proxy-config route or a live curl -v against the gateway — don't just trust the YAML (6.5).

Q18
Before a peak-traffic day, QA must validate skills-service's resilience config — timeout: 3s, retries {attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 1s} — and then PROVE it survives a real stall using fault injection, without touching the production VirtualService. Walk through both steps.
Show Answer
Answer

Step 1 — budget check (6.12 formula): timeout ≥ (attempts + 1) × perTryTimeout → needed = (3+1) × 1s = 4s, but timeout is only 3s ⚠️ broken — the 3rd retry gets cut off mid-flight. Fix: raise timeout to 4s (or drop attempts to 2, needing only (2+1)×1s = 3s).

Step 2 — prove it without risking prod: per 6.11's two-VS pattern, apply a SEPARATE fault-only VirtualService, run the test, remove it:

# fault-only VS — a TEST-window resource, never combined with the
# retry/timeout VS from Step 1 (fault + retry/timeout in ONE
# VirtualService don't interact):
http:
- fault:
    delay: {fixedDelay: 2s, percentage: {value: 20}}
  route:
  - destination: {host: skills-service}

# expected: p99 rises but errors stay ~stable (retries absorb the
# delay); if errors spike instead, the fixed config isn't actually
# deployed — recheck BEFORE the traffic day
$ kubectl delete -f skills-fault-test.yaml   # always remove after
Explanation

The retry-budget formula from 6.12 catches a broken config before it ever reaches production. And 6.11's two-VS pattern lets you PROVE resilience with fault injection without ever risking the real timeout/retry VirtualService — apply a separate fault-only VS, test, then delete it.

Q19
You add a v3 canary for jobpost-api. The DestinationRule already has a subsets: - name: v3, labels: {version: v3} entry, and the VirtualService sends it 10% of traffic. The v3 Deployment is Running and Ready, but that 10% gets 100% 503s. kubectl get pods --show-labels shows the v3 pods still carrying version: v2. Diagnose AND fix it — including how you'd confirm the fix without waiting for real user traffic.
Show Answer
Answer

A DestinationRule subset is only a label selector — it does not create endpoints, it narrows the existing pool. With the pods mislabeled, subset v3 selects ZERO pods, so Envoy has nowhere to send that 10% and returns 503 immediately.

# fix: patch the Deployment's pod-template label to match the
# subset selector
kubectl patch deployment jobpost-api-v3 -n anihpj --type=json \
    -p '[{"op":"replace",
          "path":"/spec/template/metadata/labels/version",
          "value":"v3"}]'

# confirm: does the v3 cluster have ANY endpoints yet?
istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj \
  --cluster "outbound|8000|v3|jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
# empty  = diagnosis confirmed (this is why it 503s)
# listed = fix confirmed, no need to wait for live traffic
Explanation

A DestinationRule subset is only a label selector, not an endpoint creator (7.2's classic trap) — it narrows the existing pool, and a mislabeled Deployment gives that subset ZERO endpoints, which Envoy answers with 503, not a warning. Confirm the fix at the Envoy level (istioctl proxy-config endpoint) instead of waiting for live traffic to prove it.

Q20
search-service dashboards show p99 climbing to 890ms while the median holds at 120ms (mesh baseline: 847 req/s, 2.1% errors, p99 234ms). The current DestinationRule sets loadBalancer: {simple: ROUND_ROBIN}, and kubectl top pods shows one pod pegged at 95% CPU while its siblings sit near 20%. What's the likely cause, and what one-line fix would you try first?
Show Answer
Answer

ROUND_ROBIN sends every Nth request to a pod in fixed turn regardless of how busy it already is — a pod stuck on a few expensive searches keeps getting NEW requests queued behind them, exactly the "hot pod, high p99, low median" signature. Fix: trafficPolicy.loadBalancer.simple: LEAST_REQUEST. Verify with istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj --fqdn search-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local -o json | grep lbPolicy → "LEAST_REQUEST" confirms Envoy picked it up.

Explanation

ROUND_ROBIN ignores how busy a pod already is — the classic "hot pod, high p99, low median" signature. LEAST_REQUEST (Istio's real default per 7.8) is the correct fix whenever request durations vary a lot.

Q21
auth-service runs only 2 replicas with the canonical outlierDetection block (consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5, interval: 30s, baseEjectionTime: 30s, maxEjectionPercent: 50). Under light packet loss, on-call sees repeated 30-second outages: one pod ejects, HALF-OPENs, fails again, re-ejects — over and over, each cycle dropping 50% of capacity. What would you tune, and why NOT just disable the breaker?
Show Answer
Answer

With a 2-pod pool, ejecting even ONE pod already hits the maxEjectionPercent: 50 ceiling — the breaker is working as designed, the FLEET is too small for it. Tuning options, cheapest first: (1) raise baseEjectionTime (30s→90s) so a flapping pod sits out longer instead of re-probing into more failures every 30s, (2) raise consecutiveGatewayErrors (5→10) so a few blips don't trip it at all, (3) the real fix — scale auth-service to 4+ replicas so a 50% ejection still leaves 2 healthy pods serving.

Explanation

With only 2 replicas, ejecting even ONE pod already hits maxEjectionPercent: 50 — the breaker is working exactly as designed, the FLEET is too small for it. Never disable outlierDetection as the fix: with it off, a truly dead pod keeps receiving 100% of ITS share of traffic instead of a bounded, self-healing 50%.

Q22
Ops configures localityLbSetting.distribute on skills-service to keep 70% of eu-west-1a traffic in-zone, and ships the DestinationRule WITHOUT an outlierDetection block ("we'll add circuit breaking later"). All eu-west-1a pods later crash together. What happens to eu-west-1a callers, and what's the one-block fix?
Show Answer
Answer

Nothing fails over — Istio silently IGNORES localityLbSetting on any DestinationRule that lacks outlierDetection (no health signal means Envoy has no trigger to spill traffic outward), so eu-west-1a callers keep getting routed to the dead local pods forever, with zero automatic recovery. Fix: add the canonical breaker block to the SAME DestinationRule:

outlierDetection:
  consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5
  interval: 30s
  baseEjectionTime: 30s
  maxEjectionPercent: 50

Once present, the 5-error trip ejects the dead 1a pods and Envoy walks the locality preference outward to 1b/1c automatically.

Explanation

7.9's hard requirement: Istio silently IGNORES localityLbSetting on any DestinationRule that lacks outlierDetection, because there's no health signal to trigger a locality failover. "We'll add circuit breaking later" quietly means "locality LB does nothing" until that block exists.

Q23
notification-service opens long-lived connections to an internal Redis cache on port 6379. The Service port is defined as {port: 6379, name: "redis"} with no appProtocol set. Under load, some connections hang for several seconds before finally going through; packet captures show Envoy waiting before forwarding the first bytes. Explain the cause and fix it.
Show Answer
Answer

Protocol selection (8.6) fell through to auto-detection because the port name carries no recognized prefix (http-, grpc-, tcp-, tls-, https-), and Redis's RESP protocol is neither HTTP/1.1 nor HTTP/2 — Envoy's sniffer waits for CLIENT bytes to decide, and that wait is exactly the hang. Fix — name the port so Envoy skips sniffing entirely: ports: [{port: 6379, name: tcp-redis}] (or set appProtocol: tcp, which outranks the name if both are present).

Explanation

This is the same server-first-protocol trap 8.6 flagged for PostgreSQL — Envoy's auto-detection sniffer waits for CLIENT bytes to decide the protocol, and any protocol where the SERVER speaks first (Redis RESP, PostgreSQL) hangs during that wait. Naming the port with a recognized prefix (or setting appProtocol) turns the sniffing gamble into a guarantee.

Q24
notification-service currently calls SendGrid directly over plain HTTP. Compliance now requires ALL of that traffic to exit through istio-egressgateway, upgraded to HTTPS at the gateway (TLS origination) instead of staying plaintext end-to-end. The SendGrid ServiceEntry from 8.2 already exists (hosts: [api.sendgrid.com], port 443 HTTPS). Write every ADDITIONAL resource needed, and name which one actually performs the HTTP→HTTPS upgrade.
Show Answer
Answer

Three more resources — an egress Gateway, a two-match VirtualService, and the DestinationRule that does the real work:

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata: {name: egress-sendgrid, namespace: istio-system}
spec:
  selector: {istio: egressgateway}
  servers:
  - port: {number: 80, name: http, protocol: HTTP}
    hosts: ["api.sendgrid.com"]
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata: {name: sendgrid-through-egress, namespace: anihpj}
spec:
  hosts: [api.sendgrid.com]
  gateways: [mesh, istio-system/egress-sendgrid]
  http:
  - match: [{gateways: [mesh], port: 80}]     # BLOCK 1: app→gw
    route:
    - destination:
        host: istio-egressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local
        port: {number: 80}
  - match:                                    # BLOCK 2: gw→net
    - gateways: [istio-system/egress-sendgrid]
      port: 80
    route:
    - destination:
        host: api.sendgrid.com
        port: {number: 443}      # DR below originates TLS here
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata: {name: sendgrid-originate-tls, namespace: istio-system}
spec:
  host: api.sendgrid.com
  trafficPolicy:
    portLevelSettings:
    - port: {number: 443}
      tls:
        mode: SIMPLE   # ← THIS is what upgrades HTTP to HTTPS
Explanation

The Gateway only opens the door and the VirtualService only steers traffic through it — neither touches encryption. It's the DestinationRule's tls.mode: SIMPLE (the same TLS-origination pattern 8.5 used for Stripe) that actually performs the HTTP→HTTPS upgrade at the gateway edge.

Chapter 9: Metrics — Measuring Every Request
