Istio gives you automatic observability — metrics, traces, and access logs for every request, with ZERO code changes. This chapter covers the three pillars of observability and how Istio makes them available without touching your Django code.

"Somewhere in the mesh a number is moving — can you see it before a user opens a ticket?" jobpost-api's healthy baseline is 847 req/s, 2.1% errors, p99 234ms; if skills-service quietly drifts to 8.1% errors and a 1,240ms p99, nothing in Django's own code and no kubectl get pods output will tell you. Metrics are the FIRST of the three observability pillars this Part introduces — the layer that catches the drift the instant it happens, using only three numbers per service: rate, errors, duration. Chapter 10's traces can only tell you WHERE a slow request lost its time once you already suspect skills-service, and Chapter 11's Kiali graph can only light up red once metrics and traces both exist to feed it — everything downstream of this chapter starts here. None of it costs a line of Django code: Envoy's sidecar already counts every request in and out of all seven anihpj services, and Prometheus is already scraping it.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~3 hours 📊 Observability 🎯 Feeds TS 20%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Name the three observability pillars (metrics, traces, logs) and state which parts of each Istio gives you automatically (9.1)
  • ✅ Define RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) and read it straight off a Grafana panel for any anihpj service (9.2, 9.4)
  • ✅ Trace one request's metrics from Envoy's raw :15090 stats through the merged :15020 scrape endpoint into a Prometheus time series (9.3)
  • ✅ Pick the correct PromQL function for a counter, a gauge, or a histogram — rate()/increase(), raw/avg_over_time(), histogram_quantile() — without guessing (9.8)
  • ✅ Add a low-cardinality custom dimension to istio_requests_total with a Telemetry resource, and explain why a user_id dimension would melt Prometheus (9.5, 9.9, 9.11)
  • ✅ Read a default Envoy access-log line field by field and pull a request's trace ID out of it (9.6, 9.12)
  • ✅ Tell proxy-level, service-level, and control-plane metrics apart, and name the one istiod metric that means "a proxy just rejected a config push" (9.7)
🎓 ICA Relevance
Troubleshooting FEEDS 20%

Metrics have no line item of their own on the official ICA blueprint — Observability sits outside all four graded domains. What IS graded is 🎯 Troubleshooting (Domain 4, 20%), and almost every troubleshooting scenario opens with a symptom phrased in exactly this chapter's vocabulary: "users report an elevated error rate," "p99 latency spiked," "a service stopped receiving traffic." The exam will never literally say "run this PromQL query" — it expects the reflex: reach for istioctl dashboard prometheus/grafana, spot the RED-metric anomaly in seconds, and use it to decide which config object (VirtualService, DestinationRule, PeerAuthentication) is worth inspecting next.

Troubleshooting skill this chapter feedsWhere Chapter 9 teaches it
Spot a RED-metric anomaly in seconds9.2, 9.4
Pick the right PromQL function without guessing9.8
Read one specific request's full detail, not an average9.6, 9.12
Recognize a control-plane (istiod) problem vs an app problem9.7

Skip this chapter and you lose no single graded question directly — you lose the minutes every Domain 4 task assumes you already have.

💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 9
  • "Check RED metrics" = Grafana Istio Service Dashboard
  • "Validate Istio config" = istioctl analyze -n <ns>
  • "A raw counter graph keeps climbing" = you forgot rate() or increase() — not a real problem
  • "Add a custom metric dimension" = Telemetry API tagOverrides — LOW cardinality only, never user/request IDs
  • "What happened to THIS one request" = access log line, not an aggregate metric
  • Exam hands-on: write a RED-trio PromQL query (rate / error% / p99) from memory

9.1 The Observability Pillars: Metrics, Traces, Logs

Observability has three pillars that work together to give you a complete picture of your system. Istio provides Metrics and Traces automatically — zero code changes needed in your Django app.

Istio's Envoy proxy measures RED metrics for EVERY service, EVERY request — with zero Prometheus instrumentation in your Django code.

How many requests per second?

❌
ERRORS

What % are failing? Usually scoped to 5xx (server-side) — 4xx is tracked separately as client-error rate.

⏱️

How long do requests take?

9.3 Prometheus + Istio — How Metrics Are Collected

Istio configures Envoy to emit Prometheus-format metrics. Prometheus scrapes every Envoy proxy every 15 seconds — no application changes needed.

🔄 METRICS PIPELINE — From Request to Dashboard
1
Request

User hits GET /jobs/

2
Envoy Records

istio_requests_total{dst="user-service"}++
istio_request_duration_milliseconds = 87ms

3
Prometheus Scrapes

GET :15020/stats/prometheus (every 15s)
Scrapes ALL pods in mesh

4
Grafana Queries

PromQL: rate(istio_requests_total[5m])
histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)

5
Dashboard

jobpost-api: 847rps, 2.1% err, p99=234ms

⚠️ Scrape-Port Clarification (Exam-Accurate)

Prometheus does NOT scrape Envoy directly by default — it scrapes the istio-agent on :15020, which serves MERGED app + Envoy metrics. :15020/stats/prometheus is the DEFAULT scrape target (injected pods carry the prometheus.io/port: "15020" annotation); :15090/stats/prometheus is the RAW Envoy stats endpoint, served by the Envoy process itself — Envoy metrics ONLY, no app data. When a diagram says "Envoy exposes stats on :15090," read it as "the Envoy metrics ORIGINATE at :15090" — the scrape itself lands on the agent's merged :15020 endpoint.

🔌 Sidecar Metrics Ports — :15020 (Merged) vs :15090 (Raw Envoy)

PortServed ByWhat You Get
:15020istio-agent (pilot-agent)MERGED app + Envoy stats — ✅ DEFAULT scrape target
:15090Envoy process directlyRAW Envoy stats only (debugging, no app data)
:8000Django app (your code)App's own custom metrics (merged INTO :15020)
🔀 MERGE FLOW — How One Scrape Collects Everything
  Django app :8000/metrics ──────┐
                                  ├──► istio-agent :15020
  Envoy :15090/stats/prometheus ─┘         │  (one merged page)
                                            ▼
                              Prometheus scrape (every 15s)

9.5 Custom Metrics & Telemetry API

Beyond RED metrics, you can add custom dimensions and labels using Istio's Telemetry API — without touching application code. DEFINITION: the Telemetry API is the CRD (telemetry.istio.io/v1) that tunes WHAT Envoy reports — metrics, access logs, trace sampling — per mesh, per namespace, or per workload. No app code changes, no Envoy restart.

📖 KEY TERM — Telemetry API Scope

ONE CRD, THREE possible blast radii, decided only by WHERE you point it: mesh-wide (apply in istio-system), namespace-wide (apply in anihpj — this section's example), or a single workload (add spec.selector). Same fields every time — only metadata.namespace and selector change.

anihpj scenario: product wants req/s split by job category, so ops adds a job_category label sourced from the x-job-category header that jobpost-api already sends downstream. istiod translates the Telemetry resource into Envoy stats config and pushes it over xDS — allow ~30s end-to-end (istiod ~5s → xDS push ~5s → next scrape 15s).

yaml — Telemetry: Add custom metric dimensions 
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1    # v1 since Istio 1.22
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-custom-metrics
  namespace: anihpj                  # every workload in anihpj
spec:
  metrics:
  - providers:
    - name: prometheus                # the built-in stats provider
    overrides:
    - match:
        metric: REQUEST_COUNT         # istio_requests_total
        mode: CLIENT_AND_SERVER       # see REPORTER note below
      tagOverrides:
        job_category:                 # NEW Prometheus label
          value: request.headers["x-job-category"]
        user_region:                  # 2nd custom dimension
          value: request.headers["x-user-region"]
⚠️ REPORTER Note — Why mode Matters

Every request yields TWO copies of each metric — the client sidecar reports reporter="source", the server sidecar reports reporter="destination". mode: CLIENT_AND_SERVER applies the tagOverride to BOTH copies; use CLIENT or SERVER to touch only one side. In PromQL, always pin one side (reporter="destination") or your req/s doubles — 847 req/s becomes a phantom 1,694.

Verify the new dimension is actually live — don't just trust that kubectl apply succeeded:

bash — apply, drive traffic, query 
kubectl apply -f telemetry-custom.yaml
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- \
    curl -s -H "x-job-category: devops" \
    http://skills-service:8090/api/skills/

istioctl dashboard prometheus
# PromQL:
# sum(rate(istio_requests_total{
#   job_category="devops",
#   reporter="destination"}[5m]))
# → non-empty result = the custom dimension is live

# NOTE: allow ~30s — istiod push (~10s) + next scrape (15s)

9.6 Access Logs — Auditing Every Request

From the official docs: Istio can generate access logs for every request flowing through the mesh. Unlike metrics (aggregate data) and traces (sampled requests), access logs provide a full record of every single request — source, destination, latency, status, headers, and more.

📝 ISTIO ACCESS LOG — Anatomy of a Log Entry
[2026-06-02T09:31:27.360Z] "GET /api/jobs/123 HTTP/1.1" 200 - "-" 0 135 5 2 "-"
"curl/7.60.0" "d209e46f-9ed5-9b61-bbdd-43e22662702a"
"jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:8000"
"10.244.1.5:8000"
inbound|8000|http|jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local -

BREAKDOWN:
  Timestamp: 2026-06-02T09:31:27.360Z
  Method:    GET /api/jobs/123
  Protocol:  HTTP/1.1
  Status:    200 (success)
  Latency:   5ms total (DURATION) · 2ms was spent in the upstream app
             (UPSTREAM_SERVICE_TIME) · 5-2=3ms was Envoy/proxy overhead
  Bytes:     0 sent, 135 received
  Client:    curl/7.60.0
  Trace ID:  d209e46f-9ed5-9b61-bbdd-43e22662702a  ← links to Jaeger!
  Target:    jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:8000
  Direction: inbound (receiving traffic)
  TLS:       mutual_tls (if mTLS enabled)
yaml — Telemetry API: Configure access logs 
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-access-logs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessLogging:
  - providers:
    - name: envoy
    # Optional: filter to only log errors
    # filter:
    #   expression: response.code >= 400
💡 Access Logs vs Metrics vs Traces — When to Use Each

Metrics: "What percentage of requests are failing?" (aggregate). Traces: "Why was THIS specific request slow?" (sampled). Access Logs: "What exactly happened at 9:31:27 AM?" (every request, full detail). Access logs are essential for security audits and debugging specific errors.

⚠️ Volume Warning — Full Logging Adds Up Fast

At jobpost-api's 847 req/s baseline, FULL access logging writes roughly 73 million lines/day for that ONE service alone (847 × 86,400 seconds). Keep the errors-only filter (response.code >= 400, shown commented out above) active in production — logging every 200 OK response mesh-wide is expensive storage with little diagnostic value.

9.7 Control Plane Metrics — Monitoring istiod Health

From the official docs: Istio's control plane (istiod) also exports self-monitoring metrics. These are separate from service-level metrics — they tell you about Istio's own health, not your services' health.

🕹️ KEY CONTROL PLANE METRICS — What to Monitor

Metric CategoryWhat It Tells YouExample
xDS Push LatencyHow fast istiod pushes config to Envoypilot_xds_push_time
Config Sync StatusHow many proxies are SYNCED vs STALEpilot_proxy_convergence_time
CSR HandlingCertificate signing request ratescitadel_server_csr_count
Memory/CPUistiod resource consumptionprocess_resident_memory_bytes, process_cpu_seconds_total
Connected ProxiesNumber of Envoy sidecars connectedpilot_xds gauge
Config Rejects (xDS)Envoy rejected a config push from istiodpilot_total_xds_rejects
Config Rejects (Admission)Invalid CRDs rejected at the API server webhookgalley_validation_failed
📖 Proxy-Level vs Service-Level vs Control-Plane Metrics

Proxy-level: Raw Envoy stats (cluster health, connection errors, SSL errors). Service-level: Istio's standard metrics (istio_requests_total, istio_request_duration_milliseconds). Control-plane: istiod's own health metrics. On the ICA exam, service-level metrics are the most commonly tested — they're what you see in Grafana dashboards.

9.8 Deep Dive — Counters, Gauges, Histograms in PromQL

Istio emits three Prometheus metric TYPES — using the wrong PromQL function on the wrong type produces a meaningless graph. During the skills-service incident, the on-call engineer first graphed istio_requests_total raw and saw a line climbing forever → panic. Wrapped in rate(), it showed a steady 89 req/s — traffic was normal all along; the 8.1% error rate was the real problem.

📊 METRIC TYPES
COUNTER

Only increases (resets to 0 on pod restart). istio_requests_total. Use rate() or increase(). NEVER query raw — shows meaningless massive number.

GAUGE

Goes up/down. pilot_xds, envoy_cluster_upstream_cx_active. Query raw or avg_over_time(). Shows current state at scrape moment.

HISTOGRAM

Cumulative "le" buckets — the buckets themselves are counters. istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket. Use histogram_quantile() for p50/p95/p99 percentiles.

PromQL — the RED trio for jobpost-api 
# RATE — requests per second (COUNTER + rate)
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{reporter="destination",
  destination_service=~"jobpost-api.*"}[5m]))
# → 847 req/s

# ERRORS — share of 5xx responses
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{reporter="destination",
  destination_service=~"jobpost-api.*",
  response_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
/ sum(rate(istio_requests_total{reporter="destination",
  destination_service=~"jobpost-api.*"}[5m])) * 100
# → 2.1 (%)

# DURATION — p99 latency (HISTOGRAM + histogram_quantile)
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(
  istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket{
    destination_service=~"jobpost-api.*"}[5m])) by (le))
# → 234 (ms)
⚠️ Cardinality Warning — Labels Multiply Time Series

istio_requests_total already carries ~25 labels. anihpj today: 10 workloads × 10 services × 10 response codes × 2 protocols × 2 TLS modes ≈ 4,000 time series — fine. Add ONE bad tagOverride — user_id from the x-user-id header — and 50,000 users × 4,000 = 200,000,000 time series → Prometheus eats RAM → OOMKilled → NO metrics for anyone. Rule: only add LOW-cardinality dimensions (category, region, tier); NEVER user IDs, request IDs, session tokens, or full URLs.

9.9 Standard Dimensions — Full Label Reference for istio_requests_total

Istio's proxy extension attaches roughly 25 labels — the standard dimensions — to every istio_requests_total (and istio_request_duration_milliseconds, istio_request_bytes, istio_response_bytes) sample automatically, before any Telemetry API customization ever runs. 9.5's tagOverrides ADD labels on top of this set — you can't design a good custom dimension, or explain an empty PromQL result, without knowing what's already there. Every dimension below is recorded TWICE per request — once by the caller's sidecar (reporter="source") and once by the callee's sidecar (reporter="destination").

📤 Source-Identity Dimensions — Who Sent the Request

LabelWhat It Captures
reporterSide that recorded it: source | destination
source_workloadCalling Deployment, e.g. jobpost-api
source_workload_namespaceNamespace the caller runs in
source_principalCaller SPIFFE ID (mTLS identity)
source_appapp label of the caller Pod
source_versionversion label of the caller Pod

📥 Destination-Identity Dimensions — Who Received It

LabelWhat It Captures
destination_workloadCalled Deployment, e.g. skills-service
destination_workload_namespaceNamespace the callee runs in
destination_principalCallee SPIFFE ID (mTLS identity)
destination_appapp label of the callee Pod
destination_versionversion label of the callee Pod
destination_serviceFQDN dialed, e.g. skills-svc.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
destination_service_nameShort Service name, e.g. skills-service
destination_service_namespaceNamespace of the Service object

📨 Request/Response Dimensions — What Happened

LabelWhat It Captures
request_protocolhttp | grpc | https | tcp
response_codeHTTP status: 200, 404, 500 ...
grpc_response_statusgRPC status code (grpc traffic only)

🔒 Security & Topology Dimensions — How + Where

LabelWhat It Captures
connection_security_policymutual_tls | none | unknown
response_flagsEnvoy outcome code: UH, UO, NR, DC, "-"
source_canonical_service / _revisionStable service name/revision, survives version bumps
destination_canonical_service / _revisionStable service name/revision of the callee
source_cluster / destination_clusterMulticluster: which cluster the caller/callee runs in
PromQL — anihpj security audit: find plaintext hops into skills-service 
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{
  reporter="destination",
  destination_workload="skills-service",
  connection_security_policy!="mutual_tls"}[5m]))
by (source_workload, connection_security_policy)
# → any non-zero result names the exact caller still sending
#   plaintext — fix its DestinationRule/PeerAuthentication (Ch6)

9.10 TCP Metrics — Measuring Raw (Non-HTTP) Connections

TCP metrics are the 4 counters Istio's proxy extension emits for connections it can only see as bytes — Postgres, Redis, raw gRPC without HTTP framing detected, or any protocol the mesh treats as plain TCP. Sections 9.2-9.8 all assume HTTP (response_code, path, RED) — a TCP hop has none of that, yet anihpj's Postgres connection is real mesh traffic that still needs metrics.

🔧 Under the Hood — How Istio Decides HTTP vs TCP

The sniff happens once, at connection setup, entirely inside Envoy's own process — it inspects the first bytes for HTTP framing (a request line, or the HTTP/2 preface) before a single byte reaches the upstream app. Guess HTTP: the connection gets the full istio_requests_total treatment for its whole lifetime. Guess TCP (or skip the guess entirely because the Service port already carries a tcp- name prefix): it's locked onto only the 4 counters below, for skills-service's Postgres hop and everything like it.

🔌 The Four TCP Metrics — for Raw (Non-HTTP) Traffic

Metric NameType + Meaning
istio_tcp_connections_opened_totalCOUNTER — a new TCP connection was opened
istio_tcp_connections_closed_totalCOUNTER — a TCP connection was closed
istio_tcp_sent_bytes_totalCOUNTER — bytes sent, proxy to downstream
istio_tcp_received_bytes_totalCOUNTER — bytes received from downstream
🐘 anihpj SCENARIO — skills-service → PostgreSQL (Raw TCP, Not HTTP)
skills-service opens a plain TCP connection to postgres:5432 (a DB driver
speaks the Postgres wire protocol — not HTTP — so Envoy can only see bytes
and connection events: no path, method, or response_code)

1. CONNECTION OPENS
   istio_tcp_connections_opened_total{
     destination_service="postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"} += 1

2. DATA FLOWS (recorded continuously, every 15s by default —
   interval name: tcpReportingDuration, per the official docs)
   istio_tcp_sent_bytes_total{...}     += bytes proxy→downstream
   istio_tcp_received_bytes_total{...} += bytes downstream→proxy

3. CONNECTION CLOSES
   istio_tcp_connections_closed_total{
     destination_service="postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"} += 1
   (final byte counters flush on close too)
PromQL — throughput, churn, and active connections to postgres 
# throughput — bytes/sec flowing to postgres (COUNTER + rate)
sum(rate(istio_tcp_sent_bytes_total{
  destination_service=~"postgres.*"}[5m]))

# connection churn — opens vs closes should track each other;
# opens without matching closes = a connection leak
sum(rate(istio_tcp_connections_opened_total{
  destination_service=~"postgres.*"}[5m]))

# active connections right now (GAUGE-style via subtraction)
sum(istio_tcp_connections_opened_total{destination_service=~
  "postgres.*"}) - sum(istio_tcp_connections_closed_total{
  destination_service=~"postgres.*"})
💡 A Narrower Label Set

TCP metrics still carry destination_service, source_workload, reporter, and connection_security_policy — but NEVER response_code, request_protocol, or grpc_response_status. There is no status code to read in raw bytes.

9.11 The Telemetry API Deep Dive — Full Resource Structure

Recap from 9.5: Telemetry (telemetry.istio.io/v1) is the CRD that tunes metrics, access logs, and tracing per mesh/namespace/workload. This section is the FULL field map — not just the single tagOverrides slice 9.5 showed.

🗂️ Telemetry spec — the Four Top-Level Fields

spec: FieldWhat It Configures
selectorLabel-match workloads in THIS namespace
targetRefsNewer alternative: point at a Gateway/Service
metrics[]Providers + overrides for metrics (9.5, 9.11)
accessLogging[]Providers + filter for access logs (9.6)
tracing[]Providers + sampling % for traces (Chapter 10)

🔢 match.metric — the IstioMetric Enum

match: metric: ValueTargets This Real Metric
ALL_METRICSEvery Istio default metric at once
REQUEST_COUNTistio_requests_total
REQUEST_DURATIONistio_request_duration_milliseconds
REQUEST_SIZEistio_request_bytes
RESPONSE_SIZEistio_response_bytes
TCP_OPENED_CONNECTIONSistio_tcp_connections_opened_total
TCP_CLOSED_CONNECTIONSistio_tcp_connections_closed_total
TCP_SENT_BYTESistio_tcp_sent_bytes_total
TCP_RECEIVED_BYTESistio_tcp_received_bytes_total
GRPC_REQUEST_MESSAGESistio_request_messages_total
GRPC_RESPONSE_MESSAGESistio_response_messages_total

🏷️ MetricsOverrides + TagOverride — Full Field Map

FieldMeaning
overrides[].matchMetricSelector: metric + mode (9.5)
overrides[].disabledbool — true STOPS this metric being emitted
overrides[].tagOverridesmap<label name, TagOverride>
tagOverrides.X.operationUPSERT (default) or REMOVE
tagOverrides.X.valueAttribute expr, UPSERT only (9.5 example)

anihpj scenario: RESPONSE_SIZE for jobpost-api is disabled (nobody dashboards on it, and it's a full histogram of cardinality-multiplying series) AND the source_canonical_revision tag is REMOVEd mesh-wide (anihpj ships canary-free, so that tag is dead weight on every series):

yaml — Telemetry: disable one metric, strip a dead-weight tag mesh-wide 
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1    # v1 since Istio 1.22
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-trim-metrics
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  metrics:
  - providers:
    - name: prometheus
    overrides:
    - match:
        metric: RESPONSE_SIZE   # disable one metric
        mode: SERVER            # only the callee side
      disabled: true            # drop it for jobpost-api
    - match:
        metric: ALL_METRICS     # every remaining metric
      tagOverrides:
        source_canonical_revision:
          operation: REMOVE     # anihpj has no canary
                                 # rollouts — cut cardinality
📖 OLD Way vs NEW Way

Before the Telemetry API, ANY metric customization meant hand-writing an EnvoyFilter patch against Envoy's stats config (Lua or WASM, redeploy every matching proxy). The Telemetry API replaced that for tagging, disabling, and re-scoping — but EnvoyFilter is still the ONLY way to invent a brand-new metric NAME from scratch; the Telemetry API can only shape Istio's own default metrics. Since Istio 1.18 the Prometheus EnvoyFilter is no longer installed by default (meshConfig.defaultProviders drives it instead) — and a hand-written EnvoyFilter targeting the SAME stats as a Telemetry resource is NOT supported together; pick one mechanism per metric.

AspectEnvoyFilter (OLD WAY)Telemetry API (NEW)
How you scope itPatches the proxy, error-proneselector / targetRefs (namespace)
New custom metricYes — Lua/Wasm, full controlNo — relabels EXISTING metrics only
Add a dimensionLua/Wasm, redeploy proxiestagOverrides UPSERT, no restart
Drop a dimensionLua/Wasm, redeploy proxiestagOverrides REMOVE, no restart
Disable a metricHand-edit stats configoverrides[].disabled: true
Mix the twoNot supported together (1.18+)The documented, recommended path

9.12 Access Log Format Reference — Every Default Field, Field by Field

Recap from 9.6: this section gives the COMPLETE default TEXT format string verbatim (9.6 only walked through the fields visible in one example line), plus the JSON alternative. A meshConfig field, not the Telemetry API, decides the FORMAT — the Telemetry API's accessLogging only turns logging on/off and picks the provider.

📝 meshConfig.accessLogFormat's DEFAULT Value, Verbatim
[%START_TIME%] "%REQ(:METHOD)% %REQ(X-ENVOY-ORIGINAL-PATH?:PATH)%
%PROTOCOL%" %RESPONSE_CODE% %RESPONSE_FLAGS% %RESPONSE_CODE_DETAILS%
%CONNECTION_TERMINATION_DETAILS% "%UPSTREAM_TRANSPORT_FAILURE_REASON%"
%BYTES_RECEIVED% %BYTES_SENT% %DURATION%
%RESP(X-ENVOY-UPSTREAM-SERVICE-TIME)% "%REQ(X-FORWARDED-FOR)%"
"%REQ(USER-AGENT)%" "%REQ(X-REQUEST-ID)%" "%REQ(:AUTHORITY)%"
"%UPSTREAM_HOST%" %UPSTREAM_CLUSTER_RAW% %UPSTREAM_LOCAL_ADDRESS%
%DOWNSTREAM_LOCAL_ADDRESS% %DOWNSTREAM_REMOTE_ADDRESS%
%REQUESTED_SERVER_NAME% %ROUTE_NAME%

🔖 The Default Text Access Log — Every Macro, in Order

Envoy Log MacroMeaning
%START_TIME%Request start timestamp, UTC
%REQ(:METHOD)%HTTP method: GET, POST ...
%REQ(X-ENVOY-ORIGINAL-PATH?:PATH)%The request path
%PROTOCOL%HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, ...
%RESPONSE_CODE%HTTP status code
%RESPONSE_FLAGS%Envoy outcome: UH, UO, NR, DC, "-"
%RESPONSE_CODE_DETAILS%Why: via_upstream, route_not_found...
%CONNECTION_TERMINATION_DETAILS%Why the connection closed, usually "-"
%UPSTREAM_TRANSPORT_FAILURE_REASON%TLS/transport failure reason, or "-"
%BYTES_RECEIVED%Request body size, bytes
%BYTES_SENT%Response body size, bytes
%DURATION%Total request time, ms
%RESP(X-ENVOY-UPSTREAM-SERVICE-TIME)%Upstream-only time, ms
%REQ(X-FORWARDED-FOR)%Caller IP chain
%REQ(USER-AGENT)%Client user-agent string
%REQ(X-REQUEST-ID)%Correlation id — paste into Jaeger
%REQ(:AUTHORITY)%:authority / Host header
%UPSTREAM_HOST%Backend ip:port that served the request
%UPSTREAM_CLUSTER_RAW%Envoy cluster: direction|port|subset|svc
%UPSTREAM_LOCAL_ADDRESS%Proxy's own ip:port dialing upstream
%DOWNSTREAM_LOCAL_ADDRESS%ip:port the client connected to
%DOWNSTREAM_REMOTE_ADDRESS%The calling client's ip:port
%REQUESTED_SERVER_NAME%SNI hostname (TLS handshake)
%ROUTE_NAME%Matched VirtualService route name
📖 Three meshConfig Fields Control Access Logs

Independent of the Telemetry API's on/off switch: accessLogFile — destination path, default EMPTY (disabled); the demo install profile sets it to /dev/stdout for you — the default/production profiles do not, by design. accessLogEncoding — TEXT (default, shown above) or JSON. accessLogFormat — replace the ENTIRE default string above with your own macros (add/drop/reorder fields).

yaml — Telemetry: turn access logs on; JSON encoding is a meshConfig field 
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-json-logs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessLogging:
  - providers:
    - name: envoy
# meshConfig.accessLogEncoding: JSON  # set mesh-wide at install time
# (Telemetry API turns logging ON/OFF and picks the provider; the
#  TEXT vs JSON *encoding* choice itself is still a meshConfig field)
📋 Resulting anihpj Log Line (JSON Encoding)
{"start_time":"2026-06-02T10:30:45.360Z","method":"GET",
 "path":"/api/jobs/123","response_code":200,
 "response_flags":"-","bytes_received":0,"bytes_sent":4523,
 "duration":45,"upstream_service_time":"43",
 "upstream_cluster":"inbound|8000||",
 "request_id":"d209e46f-9ed5-9b61-bbdd-43e22662702a",
 "authority":"anihpj.example.com"}

Keys mirror the TEXT macros, lower-cased — one JSON object per request, easy for Loki/EFK to index.

🔧 Under the Hood — One Incident, Five Hops: Counter to Red Panel
🗺️ The skills-service Incident — From One Counter to a Red Grafana Panel

9.8 taught you the three PromQL metric types and 9.11 mapped the full Telemetry CRD — this is neither. This is the clock: exactly how long it takes the skills-service incident to travel from one Envoy counter to a red rectangle on a human's screen, and why every hop above takes the time it takes.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HOP 1 — ENVOY COUNTS IT THE INSTANT IT HAPPENS (in-process, no network)     │
│    istio_requests_total{destination_service="skills-service",               │
│      response_code="500"} += 1                                              │
│    istio_request_duration_milliseconds{...} = 1240                          │
│                                                                              │
│  HOP 2 — THE COUNTER SITS ON THE SIDECAR, STALE UNTIL SOMEONE SCRAPES IT     │
│    origin: Envoy :15090 raw stats → merged onto istio-agent :15020 (9.3)     │
│    — nothing has left the Pod yet; this is a number sitting in memory        │
│                                                                              │
│  HOP 3 — PROMETHEUS'S SCRAPE TICK PULLS IT INTO THE TIME-SERIES DB          │
│    scrape_interval: 15s (9.3) → worst case 15s of lag before Prometheus      │
│    has even SEEN the bad request exists                                     │
│                                                                              │
│  HOP 4 — PromQL TURNS RAW CUMULATIVE COUNTERS INTO A REAL PERCENTAGE (9.8)   │
│    sum(rate(istio_requests_total{destination_service=~"skills-service.*",    │
│      response_code=~"5.."}[5m])) /                                          │
│    sum(rate(istio_requests_total{destination_service=~"skills-service.*"}    │
│      [5m])) * 100                                                           │
│    → as bad requests fill the 5m window: 2.1% baseline climbs to 8.1%        │
│                                                                              │
│  HOP 5 — GRAFANA RE-RUNS THAT SAME QUERY ON ITS OWN PANEL REFRESH TIMER      │
│    Istio Service Dashboard (9.4), skills-service panel turns red             │
│    → total time, first 500 to human sees red:                               │
│       scrape lag (≤15s) + Grafana refresh (10-30s typ.) = under a minute     │
│                                                                              │
│  — this is the automatic engine behind 9.2's dashboard mockup: nobody        │
│    ran a query by hand — the pipeline above was already running before      │
│    the incident even started                                                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 RED Metrics — The Three Pillars, With Alert Thresholds
MetricPromQL QueryAnswersAlert Threshold
RATEsum(rate(istio_requests_total[5m]))"Is it getting traffic?"Drop > 50% in 5min
ERRORSsum(rate(istio_requests_total{response_code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(istio_requests_total[5m]))"Is it failing?"> 1% error rate
DURATIONhistogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))"Is it slow?"P99 > 500ms

Why HOP 4's percentage needs BOTH sides merged: the sidecar only sees DESTINATION-side metrics (response_code, latency); an ingress/egress gateway sees SOURCE-side metrics (caller identity, source IP). Prometheus's federation/relabeling merge (the same "istio-HA" pattern behind multi-replica Prometheus setups) combines both into one complete istio_requests_total series — without it, a query scoped to only one reporter side silently under-counts the real rate.

🔑 ICA Insight: Metrics aren't graded as their own domain, but every Domain 4 (Troubleshooting, 20%) scenario assumes you already have this pipeline running in your head: a bad request is counted the INSTANT it happens (no network round-trip), sits stale on the sidecar until the next 15s scrape, and only becomes a human-readable percentage once PromQL wraps it in rate(). Total lag from first 500 to a red Grafana panel is typically under a minute — know that number so you never blame "metrics are slow" when the real problem is a service.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Metrics, traces, and access logs are the three observability pillars — Istio gives you metrics and traces automatically (zero code), access logs need one Telemetry resource to switch on.
  • RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) is the smallest useful signal — three numbers, all from Envoy, that answer "is this service unwell?" before you reach for anything fancier.
  • Prometheus scrapes the MERGED istio-agent endpoint on :15020, not raw Envoy on :15090 — :15090 is where Envoy's OWN stats originate, but the actual scrape target combines app + Envoy metrics on :15020.
  • Always wrap a counter in rate() or increase() — a raw istio_requests_total graph is a meaningless ever-climbing staircase, not a real problem.
  • Counters, gauges, and histograms each need a DIFFERENT PromQL function — rate()/increase() for counters, raw or avg_over_time() for gauges, histogram_quantile() for histograms. Using the wrong one produces a graph that LOOKS valid but means nothing.
  • Only add LOW-cardinality custom dimensions — a user_id or request_id tagOverride can multiply a mesh's time-series count by 50,000x and OOMKill Prometheus.
  • TCP (non-HTTP) traffic gets only 4 counters — opened/closed connections, sent/received bytes — never response_code or request_protocol, since raw bytes carry no status.
  • Control-plane metrics (istiod's own health) are separate from service-level metrics — a climbing pilot_total_xds_rejects means Istio itself is the problem, not anihpj's app code.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "Prometheus scrapes Envoy directly on :15090." No — the default scrape target is the istio-agent's MERGED endpoint on :15020. Port :15090 is where Envoy's raw stats originate, not where the actual scrape lands.
  • "A raw istio_requests_total graph shows real traffic volume." No — counters only ever increase (and reset to 0 on pod restart), so an un-wrapped counter graph is always a misleading upward staircase. Always wrap it in rate() or increase().
  • "Any PromQL function works on any metric type." No — histogram_quantile() on a counter, or raw-querying a counter, both produce numbers that LOOK plausible but are meaningless. Match the function to the type: counter → rate/increase, gauge → raw/avg_over_time, histogram → histogram_quantile.
  • "Adding a custom metric dimension is always safe." No — a single HIGH-cardinality tagOverride (user_id, request_id, session token) can multiply the mesh's time-series count by tens of thousands, exhausting Prometheus's memory and taking down metrics for every service, not just the one you customized.
  • "TCP metrics include a response_code, just like HTTP metrics do." No — raw TCP traffic has no status code to read. TCP metrics are limited to 4 counters: opened/closed connections and sent/received bytes.
  • "The Telemetry API can create a brand-new custom metric name." No — it can only shape (tag, disable, re-scope) Istio's own EXISTING default metrics. Inventing a genuinely new metric name still requires a hand-written EnvoyFilter with Lua/WASM.
  • "Forgetting the reporter label just gives a slightly-off number." No — omitting reporter="destination" (or "source") can silently DOUBLE every count, since the same request is recorded once by each side's sidecar.

💼 Chapter 9 — Daily Work Takeaways

  • Start every investigation with the RED trio before reaching for traces or logs — most "what's wrong" questions die right there, in seconds.
  • Never eyeball a raw counter graph — reflexively wrap every _total metric in rate() before drawing any conclusion from it.
  • Pin the reporter label explicitly in every query you write — an omitted reporter silently doubles your numbers and wastes an on-call engineer's time chasing a phantom traffic spike.
  • Review a proposed custom dimension for cardinality BEFORE applying it — multiply out workloads × services × response codes × your new label's real-world value count; if it's unbounded (any user-supplied value), reject it.
  • Check control-plane metrics before blaming the app — a climbing pilot_total_xds_rejects or STALE proxy count means the investigation belongs with istiod, not with anihpj's Django code.
  • Use istioctl dashboard grafana/prometheus instead of hunting down Service names and ports by hand — it's the faster path to the same UI every time.
  • For the ICA exam: practice writing the RED-trio PromQL query from memory — rate, error percentage, and p99 duration — since the exam expects the reflex, not a lookup.
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 9

Seven quick-fire phrase-to-answer mappings — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Check RED metrics" = Grafana Istio Service Dashboard, or the raw PromQL trio (rate/errors/duration)
  • "A counter keeps climbing forever" = not a bug — you forgot to wrap it in rate() or increase()
  • "Add a custom metric dimension" = Telemetry API tagOverrides, LOW cardinality only
  • "What happened on THIS one request" = access log line, not an aggregate metric — check %REQ(X-REQUEST-ID)% to jump to its trace
  • "Percentile latency (p99)" = histogram_quantile() on the _bucket series — never on a raw counter or gauge
  • "Is istiod itself the problem?" = check control-plane metrics (pilot_xds_push_time, pilot_total_xds_rejects), separate from service-level metrics
  • "Metrics for a non-HTTP (raw TCP) hop" = the 4 TCP counters only — opened/closed connections, sent/received bytes

🧠 Chapter 9 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Name the three observability pillars, and state which ones Istio gives you automatically with zero app code changes.
Show Answer
Answer

Metrics and traces are automatic — Istio's Envoy sidecar produces both with zero Django code changes. Access logs are only PARTIAL — Istio can generate them, but you must explicitly enable logging via a Telemetry resource.

Explanation

This matters because "Istio gives you observability for free" is only half-true — the access-log pillar specifically requires one deliberate configuration step (9.6), unlike metrics and traces which are on by default.

Q2
What are the three RED metrics, and which single Istio metric name backs BOTH Rate and Errors?
Show Answer
Answer

Rate, Errors, Duration. Both Rate and Errors come from the SAME metric, istio_requests_total — Rate is the overall count wrapped in rate(), Errors is the same metric filtered to response_code=~"5.." and divided by the unfiltered total.

Explanation

Duration is the ONLY one of the three backed by a different metric entirely (istio_request_duration_milliseconds, a histogram) — recognizing that Rate and Errors share one counter is what makes the RED-trio PromQL fast to write from memory.

Q3
Which port does Prometheus actually scrape by default, and what does that endpoint contain that the "other" metrics port doesn't?
Show Answer
Answer

Port :15020, served by the istio-agent — it contains MERGED app + Envoy metrics in one response. Port :15090 (served by the Envoy process directly) has ONLY Envoy's raw stats, no application-level data.

Explanation

This is a genuinely common exam trap — many diagrams (including this chapter's own pipeline diagram) show ":15090" near "Prometheus scrapes," which is easy to misread as the actual scrape TARGET rather than where Envoy's OWN stats originate.

Q4
A dashboard shows istio_requests_total as a raw, ever-climbing number instead of a rate. What's wrong, and what's the fix?
Show Answer
Answer

Nothing is actually broken — istio_requests_total is a COUNTER, which only ever increases (until a pod restart resets it to 0). Querying it raw always produces a climbing staircase. The fix is wrapping it in rate() or increase(), which converts the cumulative count into a real per-second (or per-window) rate.

Explanation

This exact scenario played out in 9.8's on-call story: an engineer panicked seeing a raw counter climb forever, then found a steady 89 req/s once wrapped in rate() — the real problem was the 8.1% error rate, not the shape of the raw graph.

Q5
Which PromQL function is correct for reading p99 latency, and why would rate() be the wrong choice for that same metric?
Show Answer
Answer

histogram_quantile() is correct — latency is exposed as a HISTOGRAM (istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket), and only histogram_quantile() can compute a percentile from cumulative "le" buckets. rate() is for COUNTERS, not histograms — using it here would produce a number with no percentile meaning at all.

Explanation

The histogram's underlying buckets ARE technically counters (each bucket counts observations ≤ that bucket's boundary), which is why histogram_quantile() internally still uses rate() on the buckets — but you never call rate() alone and expect a percentile out of it.

Q6
A team adds a tagOverride pulling x-user-id into a new Prometheus label. What happens to the mesh, and why?
Show Answer
Answer

Prometheus's memory usage explodes and it eventually OOMKills, taking down metrics for the ENTIRE mesh — not just the one service that added the tag. A high-cardinality dimension like user_id multiplies the existing time-series count by the number of distinct users (potentially tens of thousands), turning ~4,000 series into hundreds of millions.

Explanation

This is why the rule is "only LOW-cardinality dimensions" (category, region, tier) — never user IDs, request IDs, session tokens, or full URLs, all of which have effectively unbounded distinct values.

Q7
skills-service's connection to PostgreSQL shows no response_code label anywhere in its metrics. Is this a bug?
Show Answer
Answer

No — this is expected. PostgreSQL is raw TCP, not HTTP, so Envoy can only see bytes and connection events. TCP metrics are limited to 4 counters (opened/closed connections, sent/received bytes) — there is no status code to read in raw bytes.

Explanation

This is the same "not a bug, a feature limit" pattern seen with other HTTP-only fields elsewhere in this guide — recognizing when a missing field is EXPECTED (vs. a real misconfiguration) is a recurring exam skill.

Q8
What's the difference between proxy-level, service-level, and control-plane metrics, and which does the ICA exam test most often?
Show Answer
Answer

Proxy-level: raw Envoy stats (cluster health, connection errors, SSL errors). Service-level: Istio's standard metrics (istio_requests_total, istio_request_duration_milliseconds). Control-plane: istiod's own self-monitoring health metrics. Service-level metrics are the most commonly tested — they're what you see in Grafana dashboards.

Explanation

Recognizing WHICH category a metric name belongs to helps you route a troubleshooting scenario correctly — a climbing control-plane metric points at istiod itself, not at any one application service.

Q9
A PromQL query filtered only to reporter="destination" is being compared against the same query with no reporter filter at all. Which one is correct, and why might the unfiltered one be misleading?
Show Answer
Answer

The reporter="destination"-filtered query is correct. Every request is recorded TWICE — once by the caller's sidecar (reporter="source") and once by the callee's sidecar (reporter="destination"). An unfiltered query sums BOTH recordings together, silently doubling the real count.

Explanation

This is one of the highest-value habits in the whole chapter: forgetting the reporter label doesn't produce an obviously-wrong number — it produces a plausible-looking number that's exactly 2x too high, which is much harder to catch by eye.

Q10
What is the ONLY way to invent a brand-new Prometheus metric name that doesn't already exist in Istio's default set, and why can't the Telemetry API do it?
Show Answer
Answer

A hand-written EnvoyFilter with Lua or WASM. The Telemetry API can only shape (tag, disable, re-scope) Istio's EXISTING default metrics — it has no mechanism to define an entirely new metric name from scratch.

Explanation

This is why EnvoyFilter hasn't been fully replaced by the Telemetry API despite being the "OLD way" for tagging/disabling — the two mechanisms serve different jobs, and a hand-written EnvoyFilter targeting the SAME stats as a Telemetry resource is explicitly NOT supported together.

⚙️ Chapter 9 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
skills-service's Grafana panel shows an 8.1% error rate. Task: Write the exact PromQL to confirm this number yourself, from scratch.
Show Answer
Answer
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{reporter="destination",
  destination_service=~"skills-service.*",
  response_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
/ sum(rate(istio_requests_total{reporter="destination",
  destination_service=~"skills-service.*"}[5m])) * 100
Explanation

Both the numerator (5xx-only) and denominator (all responses) MUST be wrapped in rate() and MUST both pin reporter="destination" — mixing a raw numerator with a rated denominator, or omitting the reporter filter on just one side, produces a wrong percentage that still looks plausible.

Q2
Confirm which port Prometheus is actually scraping on jobpost-api's pod, live — don't just assume from the docs.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- \
    curl -s localhost:15020/stats/prometheus | head -5
# confirm this returns BOTH app metrics (if any) and istio_ metrics merged

kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- \
    curl -s localhost:15090/stats/prometheus | head -5
# confirm this returns Envoy-only stats, no app-level data
Explanation

Running BOTH commands and comparing their output is the only way to actually verify the merge behavior rather than just trusting a diagram — :15020's output should be a superset of what a bare Django /metrics endpoint plus :15090's raw Envoy stats would show separately.

Q3
Write a Telemetry resource that adds a request_tier custom dimension (from header x-request-tier) to jobpost-api's REQUEST_COUNT metric only.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-tier-dimension
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  metrics:
  - providers:
    - name: prometheus
    overrides:
    - match:
        metric: REQUEST_COUNT
      tagOverrides:
        request_tier:
          value: request.headers["x-request-tier"]
Explanation

The selector scopes this to jobpost-api ONLY (not mesh-wide) — omitting it would apply the tagOverride to every workload in the namespace. request_tier (e.g. "free"/"pro"/"enterprise") is a textbook LOW-cardinality dimension, unlike a user_id.

Q4
A team wants access logs enabled for anihpj, but ONLY for 5xx responses, to avoid drowning the log pipeline in 200s. Write the Telemetry resource.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-errors-only-logs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessLogging:
  - providers:
    - name: envoy
    filter:
      expression: "response.code >= 400"
Explanation

The filter.expression field is exactly what 9.6's commented-out example hinted at — it's a real, functioning field, not a placeholder. This is the difference between "log everything" (expensive) and "log only what's actionable" (the anihpj production pattern).

Q5
jobpost-api's error rate looks fine in Grafana (2.1%), but a customer reports a specific failed request at 09:31:27 AM. Task: Find that ONE request's full detail.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl logs deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -c istio-proxy \
    --since-time=2026-06-02T09:31:00Z | grep "09:31:27"
Explanation

This is exactly the "aggregate metric vs one-request access log" distinction the chapter teaches — a 2.1% aggregate error rate can't tell you anything about ONE specific customer's request; only the access log line (with its trace ID, status, and full timing breakdown) can.

Q6
istiod's pilot_total_xds_rejects metric is climbing steadily. A teammate says "jobpost-api must be misconfigured." Task: Explain why they're wrong and what to check instead.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl exec deploy/istiod -n istio-system -- \
    curl -s localhost:15014/metrics | grep pilot_total_xds_rejects
Explanation

pilot_total_xds_rejects is a CONTROL-PLANE metric — it measures istiod's own health (config pushes istiod itself rejected), completely separate from any application-level service metric. A climbing value means some CRD in the mesh is malformed and istiod is refusing to push it — the investigation belongs with recently-applied config objects, not with jobpost-api's application code.

Q7
Write the PromQL to detect any service still sending plaintext (non-mTLS) traffic to skills-service, broken down by which caller is responsible.
Show Answer
Answer
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{
  reporter="destination",
  destination_workload="skills-service",
  connection_security_policy!="mutual_tls"}[5m]))
by (source_workload, connection_security_policy)
Explanation

Any non-zero result names the exact caller still sending plaintext — the fix belongs in that caller's DestinationRule or a mesh-wide PeerAuthentication policy (Chapter 6), not in skills-service itself.

Q8
Write a Telemetry resource that DISABLES the RESPONSE_SIZE metric for jobpost-api's server side only, without affecting any other metric or any other workload.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-disable-response-size
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  metrics:
  - providers:
    - name: prometheus
    overrides:
    - match:
        metric: RESPONSE_SIZE
        mode: SERVER
      disabled: true
Explanation

mode: SERVER scopes this to only the CALLEE side of jobpost-api's traffic — its CLIENT-side RESPONSE_SIZE metric (when jobpost-api calls other services) stays enabled. Omitting mode would disable both directions.

Q9
A postgres connection pool from skills-service seems to be leaking connections. Write the PromQL to confirm this from TCP metrics alone.
Show Answer
Answer
sum(istio_tcp_connections_opened_total{destination_service=~
  "postgres.*"}) - sum(istio_tcp_connections_closed_total{
  destination_service=~"postgres.*"})
Explanation

This computes "active connections right now" via subtraction (opens minus closes) — a GAUGE-style read built from two counters. A steadily GROWING result over time (not just a stable non-zero number) is the actual leak signature; opens and closes should track each other closely under normal operation.

Q10
A dashboard built on istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket is producing a p99 that looks impossibly low compared to what users report. What's the most likely PromQL mistake?
Show Answer
Answer
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(
  istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket{
    destination_service=~"jobpost-api.*"}[5m])) by (le))
# the "by (le)" grouping is REQUIRED — histogram_quantile needs the
# bucket boundary label preserved, or the calculation is wrong
Explanation

Forgetting by (le) on the inner sum() is the single most common histogram_quantile mistake — without it, the bucket-boundary label collapses and the quantile calculation silently produces a nonsensical number instead of erroring out.

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 9
  • Reach for the RED trio first (rate / errors / duration) before anything fancier — most "what's wrong" questions die right there.
  • Wrap every counter in rate() or increase() before you look at it — a raw istio_requests_total graph is always a misleading staircase.
  • Pin reporter="destination" (or "source") in every query — forget it and every number silently doubles (847 becomes a phantom 1,694).
  • istioctl dashboard grafana/prometheus opens the right port-forward for you — faster than hunting down the Service name and port.
  • RED is for services; USE (Utilization/Saturation/Errors) is for the node a service runs on — don't reach for CPU graphs when it's a service's error rate that moved.
  • A flat citadel_server_csr_count or a climbing pilot_total_xds_rejects (9.7) means istiod is the problem, not anihpj — check control-plane metrics before you blame the app.

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 9)

Every command below already appeared earlier in this chapter — grouped here as one reference for collecting, reading, and debugging Istio's metrics.

CommandWhat It Does / Checks in Chapter 9
istioctl dashboard prometheusPrometheus UI, port-forward handled for you (9.3)
istioctl dashboard grafanaIstio Service / Mesh / Workload dashboards (9.4)
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- curl -s localhost:15020/stats/prometheusMerged app + Envoy metrics — the DEFAULT scrape target (9.3)
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- curl -s localhost:15090/stats/prometheusRaw Envoy-only stats, no app data — debugging only (9.3)
kubectl exec deploy/istiod -n istio-system -- curl -s localhost:15014/metrics | grep pilot_Control-plane health: xDS pushes/rejects/convergence (9.7)
kubectl logs -f deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -c istio-proxyLive Envoy access logs for one workload (9.6)
kubectl apply -f telemetry-custom.yamlPush a Telemetry resource: custom metric dims or an access-log on/off switch (9.5, 9.11)

🔬 Practice Drill 9.1 — Confirm an Incident Live in Grafana and Prometheus

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Do this now, on a real (or kind) cluster with Istio, Prometheus, and Grafana installed:

  1. (2 min) istioctl dashboard grafana → open the Istio Service Dashboard, service = skills-service.
  2. (1 min) Read the Rate panel — near the 9.2 baseline of 89 req/s?
  3. (1 min) Read the Error Rate panel — 8.1% (incident) or back to 0.3-2%?
  4. (2 min) Switch service to jobpost-api — compare p99 to the 234ms baseline vs the 1,240ms incident number from 9.2.
  5. (2 min) istioctl dashboard prometheus → run this by hand: 
    sum(rate(istio_requests_total{reporter="destination",
  destination_service=~"skills-service.*",
  response_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
    Your own number should match the Grafana panel from step 3.
Hint: Steps 1-4 reuse 9.4's Grafana dashboards verbatim; step 5 reuses 9.8's RED-trio PromQL pattern, just filtered to skills-service's 5xx responses.
View Solution

Step 5's hand-run PromQL number should match the Grafana panel from step 3 to within rounding — if it doesn't, the most likely cause is a missing or mismatched reporter filter between what Grafana's dashboard query uses internally and what you typed by hand.

Check yourself: did you compare the RAW numbers, or did you round both to "about 8%" and call it a match? Catching a small discrepancy here is exactly the skill that catches a reporter-filter bug before it wastes an hour later.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.2 — Prove the :15020 vs :15090 Scrape-Port Distinction Yourself

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Don't take 9.3's port clarification on faith — confirm it live on a real pod.

  1. kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- curl -s localhost:15020/stats/prometheus | wc -l — count the merged endpoint's total metric lines.
  2. kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- curl -s localhost:15090/stats/prometheus | wc -l — count the raw Envoy-only endpoint's lines.
  3. Grep both outputs for a metric name that ONLY exists in Django's own app code (not an istio_/envoy_ prefixed one) — does it appear on :15020, :15090, or both?
  4. Check the pod's own annotations for prometheus.io/port to confirm which port Prometheus was actually TOLD to scrape.
Hint: If jobpost-api doesn't expose its own /metrics endpoint, step 3 will show zero app-specific lines on EITHER port — that's still useful data, confirming the merge behavior applies only when there's something to merge.
View Solution

:15020's line count should be greater than or equal to :15090's (it's a superset — Envoy stats plus, if present, app metrics). Step 4's annotation check should show "15020", confirming that's the port Prometheus was actually configured to scrape — not :15090.

Check yourself: could you now explain to a teammate, pointing at your own terminal output, exactly why a diagram showing ":15090" near "Prometheus scrapes" is easy to misread? That's the concept this drill is built to cement.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.3 — Match the Symptom to the Right PromQL Fix

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

For each broken query below, name what's wrong and rewrite it correctly — before running anything:

  1. istio_requests_total{destination_service=~"jobpost-api.*"} — graphed raw, shows an ever-climbing line with no useful shape.
  2. rate(istio_request_duration_milliseconds_bucket{...}[5m]) — used directly as "the p99 latency," with no further wrapping.
  3. sum(rate(istio_requests_total{response_code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(istio_requests_total{}[5m])) — computed anihpj-wide, no reporter filter, number always looks exactly double what Grafana shows.
Hint: Each one is a genuine, distinct PromQL mistake from this chapter's own teaching — not a trick question with a hidden trap.
View Solution
#ProblemFix
1Querying a COUNTER raw — always climbs, never useful on its ownWrap in rate(...[5m])
2rate() alone on histogram buckets isn't a percentile — it's just the per-bucket increase rateWrap the whole expression in histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(...)) by (le))
3Missing reporter="destination" — every request counted TWICE (once per side)Add reporter="destination" to both the numerator and denominator

Check yourself: did you catch that #3's symptom ("always exactly double") is a specific, recognizable signature of the missing-reporter bug, not just "a wrong number"? Recognizing that exact 2x pattern is faster than re-deriving the whole query from scratch under exam pressure.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.4 — Build and Apply a Cardinality-Safe Custom Dimension

⏱️ Target Time: 7 minutes
Scenario

anihpj wants to dashboard traffic by subscription tier. Build this for real:

  1. Before writing any YAML, list the realistic distinct values for a "subscription tier" dimension (e.g. free/pro/enterprise) and estimate the resulting time-series multiplication against 9.8's ~4,000-series baseline.
  2. Write and apply a Telemetry resource adding tagOverrides.subscription_tier from header x-subscription-tier, scoped to jobpost-api only.
  3. Generate a request carrying that header and confirm the new label appears: kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -c istio-proxy -- curl -s localhost:15020/stats/prometheus | grep subscription_tier.
  4. Now repeat steps 1-2 for a hypothetical x-user-id dimension instead — but STOP before step 3. Explain out loud why you're stopping.
Hint: Step 1's estimate should be a small, bounded multiplier (3-5x); step 4's estimate should be effectively unbounded — that contrast IS the point of the drill.
View Solution

Step 3's grep should show the new subscription_tier label attached to istio_requests_total samples for jobpost-api. Step 4 should never reach application — user_id has effectively unlimited distinct values, and applying it would multiply the baseline by tens of thousands, risking an OOMKill for the whole mesh's Prometheus instance.

Check yourself: did you actually do the multiplication in step 1 with real numbers, or just recite "low cardinality good, high cardinality bad" without quantifying it? Doing the math is what makes this a judgment call you can defend on the exam, not a memorized rule.

🔬 Practice Drill 9.5 — Sketch the Full Metrics Pipeline From Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking back at the UTH's diagram, sketch (on paper or in a text file) every hop a single bad request takes from the moment Envoy counts it to the moment a human sees a red Grafana panel.

  1. Name all 5 hops in order.
  2. For each hop, name the ONE mechanism or timing figure that governs it (e.g. scrape interval, refresh timer).
  3. Give a rough total-lag estimate, first-500 to red-panel.
Hint: This is a paper/whiteboard drill — the point is retrieving the mental model from memory under light time pressure, the same way the exam expects you to reason about "why is this taking so long to show up" without a diagram in front of you.
View Solution

The 5 hops: (1) Envoy counts it instantly, in-process, no network round-trip. (2) The counter sits stale on the sidecar until scraped. (3) Prometheus's scrape tick (every 15s) pulls it into the time-series DB. (4) PromQL's rate() turns the raw cumulative counter into a real percentage. (5) Grafana re-runs that query on its own panel-refresh timer (10-30s typical). Total lag, first bad request to a red panel: typically under a minute.

Check yourself: did your sketch correctly separate "Envoy counts it" (instant, hop 1) from "a human sees it" (up to ~45s later, hops 2-5)? Confusing these two is why some engineers wrongly assume metrics are real-time when they're actually near-real-time with a bounded, knowable lag.

📊 Chapter 9 in One Picture — One Request, Every Metric It Leaves Behind
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ① REQUEST: GET /api/jobs/ → jobpost-api                                  │
│    (mesh baseline: 847 req/s, 2.1% errors, p99 234ms)                    │
│                                     │                                     │
│                                     ▼                                    │
│ ② ENVOY SIDECAR records it, all in one pass:                             │
│    • HTTP RED counters + duration histogram ............ 9.2, 9.8       │
│    • ~25 standard dimensions stamped on every sample ..... 9.9          │
│    • 4 TCP counters for any raw hop (e.g. → postgres) .... 9.10         │
│    • one access-log line, full default field set ..... 9.6, 9.12        │
│                                     │                                     │
│                                     ▼                                    │
│ ③ COLLECTION: :15090 raw stats merge onto :15020 (istio-agent)           │
│    → Prometheus scrapes every 15s ........................... 9.3       │
│                                     │                                     │
│                                     ▼                                    │
│ ④ SHAPING (optional): Telemetry API adds/drops dimensions,               │
│    flips access logs on — no restart, ~30s to take effect .. 9.5, 9.11  │
│                                     │                                     │
│                                     ▼                                    │
│ ⑤ READING: PromQL turns counters/histograms into a real                  │
│    rate / error% / p99 → Grafana renders the panel ........ 9.4, 9.8    │
│                                     │                                     │
│                                     ▼                                    │
│ ⑥ WATCHING THE WATCHER (parallel path, always on): istiod's own          │
│    :15014 metrics confirm the pipeline ITSELF is healthy .... 9.7       │
│                                     │                                     │
│                                     ▼                                    │
│ ⑦ OUTCOME: skills-service flagged — 8.1% errors, p99 1240ms              │
│    → the ONE clue that sends you to Chapter 10 to find WHERE            │
│       in its call chain the 1,240ms is actually lost                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Chapter 9 gave anihpj its first real eyes on the mesh: 9.1 named the three observability pillars and showed metrics and traces arrive with zero Django code changes, 9.2 introduced RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) as the three numbers that answer "is it getting traffic, is it failing, is it slow," and 9.3-9.4 traced those numbers from Envoy's raw stats through Prometheus's scrape into Grafana's pre-built dashboards. 9.5-9.6 added the two ways to go beyond the defaults — Telemetry API custom dimensions, and full-detail access logs for the ONE request metrics average away — while 9.7 pointed the same toolkit at istiod itself. The five deep dives in 9.8-9.12 filled in the reference material every one of those sections assumes: which PromQL function fits which metric type, the full ~25-label reference for istio_requests_total, the four counters that cover raw TCP hops, the complete Telemetry CRD field map, and the full default access-log format string, field by field.

Quick recap — 📊 RED: Rate/Errors/Duration, wrap counters in rate() · 🔥 Prometheus: scrapes the merged :15020 endpoint every 15s (raw stats originate at :15090) · 📈 Grafana: 4 pre-built dashboards, Service is your daily driver · ⚙️ Telemetry API: custom dimensions + access-log on/off, no restart · 🏷️ ~25 standard dimensions, always LOW cardinality · 🔌 TCP metrics: 4 counters for non-HTTP hops · 📝 Access logs: full per-request detail, the trace ID links straight to Jaeger · ✅ Zero code: all of it comes from Envoy, not Django.

Chapter 10: Distributed Tracing — Follow Any Request Across All Services

A single GET /jobs/ triggers 5+ service calls. Without tracing, you have no idea which service is the bottleneck. Jaeger distributed tracing shows every hop, every duration, in one Gantt chart.

"Chapter 9's metrics just named skills-service as a suspect — but where, exactly, inside that request, is it slow?" Chapter 9's RED metrics can tell an anihpj on-call engineer that skills-service's p99 latency just jumped to 1,240ms — that names WHAT looks wrong. But a Grafana panel cannot show you the one GET /jobs/ request that took 342ms, or which of its downstream hops — user-service, auth-service, skills-service, location-service — actually burned the time. Distributed tracing closes exactly that gap: it follows ONE real request as it crosses every service boundary in the anihpj mesh and renders the result as a Gantt-style waterfall where the widest bar IS the answer. In this chapter's running incident, a 342ms trace through jobpost-api exposes a single 195ms skills-service span as the bottleneck — a fact no dashboard of averages could ever surface on its own. By the end of this chapter you will be able to go from "users say the site feels slow" to "the skills-service call inside trace 7f3e9a12b4c06d8e is the culprit" in about the time it takes to open one dashboard.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 🔭 Tracing 🎯 Feeds Troubleshooting
