10.1 What is Distributed Tracing?

🔍
Trace

The entire journey of ONE request across all services. Contains multiple spans linked by a Trace ID.

📏
Span

One unit of work — one service call. Has start time, duration, and parent-child relationships.

🔭 DISTRIBUTED TRACE — anihpj GET /jobs/ (342ms total)
Trace ID: 7f3e9a12b4c06d8e    Duration: 342ms

▶ jobpost-api (GET /jobs/)                                 0ms → 342ms
  ▶ user-service (GET /users/42/)                         12ms → 87ms
    ▶ auth-service (POST /validate-token/)               15ms → 45ms
  ▶ skills-service (GET /skills/?ids=1,2,3)               92ms → 287ms
    ← 195ms ← SLOW! This is the bottleneck ⚠️
  ▶ location-service (GET /locations/7/)                 295ms → 320ms

🔍 skills-service call took 195ms — investigate database query!

10.2 How Istio Enables Tracing (Almost Automatically)

Envoy automatically injects tracing headers into every request. Your Django code just needs to forward them between services.

python — Django header propagation (required!) 

# Add this to your Django views that call other services:
ISTIO_HEADERS = [
    'x-request-id',
    'x-b3-traceid',        # ← links all spans together
    'x-b3-spanid',
    'x-b3-parentspanid',
    'x-b3-sampled',
    'x-b3-flags',
]

def get_jobs(request):
    # Forward tracing headers to propagate trace context:
    headers = {
        h: request.META.get('HTTP_' + h.upper().replace('-', '_'))
        for h in ISTIO_HEADERS
        if request.META.get('HTTP_' + h.upper().replace('-', '_'))
    }
    users = requests.get('http://user-service/users/', headers=headers)
    skills = requests.get('http://skills-service/skills/', headers=headers)
    # ...
⚠️ CRITICAL — No Header Propagation = Broken Traces

If you don't forward the x-b3-* headers, each service call becomes a separate, disconnected trace. You won't see the full call chain — just isolated spans. This is the #1 tracing mistake.

10.3 Jaeger — Visualizing Traces

Jaeger is the default tracing backend. Open with istioctl dashboard jaeger. Key features: trace search, service dependency graph, latency histograms.

💡 How to Find Bottlenecks in Jaeger

1. Open Jaeger → Search → sort by Longest Duration. 2. Click the slowest trace. 3. Look at the Gantt chart — the widest bar is the bottleneck. 4. Click that span to see tags: HTTP method, URL, status code. 5. Cross-reference with logs at that timestamp.

10.4 Tracing Sampling Rate

Tracing every request adds overhead. Istio defaults to 1% sampling — trace 1 out of 100 requests.

🟢 Dev: 100%

Trace everything. Useful for debugging locally.

🟡 Prod: 1-5%

Enough for statistical analysis without overhead. 100% is too expensive in production.

10.5 Deep Dive — The B3 Header Propagation Contract

DEFINITION: B3 is the trace-context header format (born in Zipkin; "B3" is its internal codename "BigBrotherBird") that carries trace identity between services as plain HTTP headers. A trace survives only if EVERY hop carries the same context — the x-b3-* headers ARE that context; drop them once and the chain snaps into disconnected spans.

📖 How It Works — Three Rules

The FIRST Envoy in the chain (usually the ingress gateway) mints x-b3-traceid and makes the sampling decision. Every later Envoy creates a child span and UPDATES x-b3-spanid / x-b3-parentspanid for its own hop. Your app's only job: copy the headers from the inbound request onto every outbound call, UNCHANGED. x-request-id rides along too — not a B3 header, but Envoy's per-request UUID — forward it so access logs in every service can be joined to the trace afterwards.

📋 The B3 Header Contract — 5 B3 Headers + x-request-id

HeaderPurposeWho Sets It
x-b3-traceid64/128-bit trace ID — the glue on ALL spansFirst Envoy (gateway)
x-b3-spanidID of THIS hop's spanEvery Envoy, each hop
x-b3-parentspanidspanId of the caller — builds the call treeEvery Envoy
x-b3-sampled1 = trace, 0 = skip (the sampling verdict)First Envoy
x-b3-flags1 = debug — FORCES sampling (beats the %)You, manually (curl -H)
x-request-idEnvoy request UUID for log-to-trace joinsFirst Envoy
🔗 DIVISION OF LABOUR — Envoy Does 80%, Your Code Does 20%
ENVOY SIDECAR — automatic (the 80%)                YOUR DJANGO CODE — manual (the critical 20%)
✅ creates span context (traceId, spanId, timing)  □ read x-b3-* + x-request-id from the inbound request
✅ injects x-b3-* headers into requests             □ attach them, UNCHANGED, to every outbound HTTP call
✅ updates spanid/parentspanid at every hop
✅ reports finished spans to the tracing backend

❌ skip the 20% → every hop starts a NEW trace: Jaeger shows five 1-span traces instead of one 5-span
   call chain — the #1 tracing failure in the field

Per-view forwarding (10.2) works, but relies on every developer remembering it in every view — the production answer is a Django MIDDLEWARE that captures the headers once per request, automatically. Never generate your own IDs — Envoy owns span creation; your code is only the courier.

python — anihpj/middleware.py: capture once, use everywhere 
TRACE_HEADERS = [
    'x-request-id',      'x-b3-traceid',   'x-b3-spanid',
    'x-b3-parentspanid', 'x-b3-sampled',   'x-b3-flags',
]

class IstioTracingMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        request.trace_headers = {      # ← UNCHANGED copy
            h: request.META['HTTP_' +
                             h.upper().replace('-', '_')]
            for h in TRACE_HEADERS
            if 'HTTP_' + h.upper().replace('-', '_')
                in request.META
        }
        return self.get_response(request)

# settings.py
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'anihpj.middleware.IstioTracingMiddleware',
    # ... the rest ...
]

# any views.py — no per-view header plumbing needed:
requests.get('http://skills-service:8090/skills/',
             headers=request.trace_headers)
⚠️ Real anihpj Incident

SREs suddenly saw five 1-span traces per GET /jobs/ instead of one 5-span chain — user-service had swapped its HTTP client library and silently stopped forwarding the headers, so every hop began a brand-new trace. Envoy CREATES spans automatically, but it cannot see INSIDE your process — only your code can tie inbound to outbound.

10.6 Deep Dive — Tracing Providers: Zipkin, Jaeger, OpenTelemetry

DEFINITION: a tracing provider is the backend Envoy ships finished spans to; Istio can speak several dialects — Zipkin, OpenTelemetry (OTLP), Datadog, and more. "Jaeger" in the demo profile is really Envoy speaking the ZIPKIN protocol to a Jaeger collector on port 9411 — knowing which protocol and port are in play is half of every "no traces appearing" debug session.

Declare providers once under meshConfig.extensionProviders, then a Telemetry resource selects WHICH provider is active (plus its sampling rate) — mesh-wide from istio-system or per namespace. The industry direction is OpenTelemetry: Envoy sends OTLP to one collector, and the collector fans out to Jaeger, Tempo, or a vendor APM — swap backends without touching Envoy again.

yaml — extensionProviders + a Telemetry resource selecting one 
# IstioOperator excerpt (istioctl install -f iop.yaml):
meshConfig:
  extensionProviders:
  - name: jaeger-zipkin
    zipkin:
      service: zipkin.istio-system.svc.cluster.local
      port: 9411               # ← Zipkin v2 span API
  - name: otel
    opentelemetry:
      service: otel-collector.istio-system.svc.cluster.local
      port: 4317               # ← OTLP over gRPC
---
# A Telemetry resource picks the ACTIVE provider:
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: mesh-tracing
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  tracing:
  - providers:
    - name: otel               # ← switch backends HERE
    randomSamplingPercentage: 1.0
🔀 OTEL COLLECTOR PIPELINE — One Receiver, Many Exporters
anihpj Envoy sidecars (every namespace, every sidecar pod)
                       │
                       │ OTLP gRPC :4317
                       ▼
          ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
          │ otel-collector (istio-system)    │
          │   receivers:  [otlp]             │
          │   processors: [batch]            │
          │   exporters:  [jaeger, tempo]     │
          └───────┬─────────────────┬────────┘
                  │                 │
                  ▼                 ▼
          Jaeger (today's UI)   Grafana Tempo / vendor APM

Swap or add a backend = edit ONLY the collector config —
Envoy keeps sending OTLP :4317 to the same address

📊 Header Formats — B3 (Zipkin) vs W3C traceparent (OTel)

B3 (Zipkin-style)W3C Trace Context
Headersx-b3-traceid, -spanid, -parentspanid, -sampled, -flagstraceparent + tracestate (2 headers total)
FormatFive separate headers (or the compact single "b3")One combined value: 00-<traceid>-<spanid>-<flags>
Used byClassic Zipkin / Jaeger path (demo)OTel SDKs and the otel provider
Standard?De-facto (Zipkin)Official W3C rec
💡 Migration Guidance — Zipkin/B3 → OpenTelemetry, the Safe Order

1. Deploy an OTel collector; add the "otel" provider in meshConfig NEXT TO the existing Zipkin one (they coexist). 2. Point the collector's exporter at the EXISTING Jaeger — same UI, new pipeline; verify traces still assemble. 3. Flip the Telemetry provider for the anihpj namespace first, watch for broken chains, then go mesh-wide. 4. Teach apps to forward traceparent + tracestate IN ADDITION to x-b3-* during the transition; drop B3 only after every service and client has switched.

⚠️ Gotcha — A Mixed Mesh Snaps the Chain

A mixed mesh where jobpost-api forwards only B3 and skills-service forwards only traceparent → the chain snaps at that boundary. Forwarding BOTH during migration is the fix (10.8).

10.7 Deep Dive — Custom Tags & the Telemetry API vs Legacy MeshConfig

DEFINITION: Istio has TWO ways to declare "how tracing behaves," one legacy and one current — the legacy path is a single meshConfig.defaultConfig.tracing block (a hold-over from before the Telemetry API existed); the current path is meshConfig.extensionProviders (WHO to send spans to) plus a Telemetry resource (WHICH provider + WHAT sampling rate).

⚠️ Leaving Both Populated Does NOT Merge Them

The official install docs have you explicitly zero out the legacy block (tracing: {}) so there is only ONE source of truth. Skip that step and anihpj SREs will "fix" sampling in a Telemetry resource and see nothing change, because the legacy block is still winning.

How it works: step 1 — declare the backend under extensionProviders (10.6). Step 2 — explicitly empty the legacy block so it cannot conflict: defaultConfig.tracing: {}. Step 3 — turn tracing on mesh-wide: enableTracing: true. Step 4 — apply a Telemetry resource that references the provider BY NAME and sets the sampling rate.

yaml — disable legacy tracing, the migration step teams skip 
# IstioOperator excerpt (istioctl install -f iop.yaml):
meshConfig:
  enableTracing: true
  defaultConfig:
    tracing: {}       # ← empties the LEGACY sampling path
  extensionProviders:
  - name: "jaeger"
    opentelemetry:
      service: jaeger-collector.istio-system.svc.cluster.local
      port: 4317
---
# Telemetry resource is now the ONLY sampling source:
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: mesh-default
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  tracing:
  - providers:
    - name: "jaeger"
    randomSamplingPercentage: 1.00

Custom tags: a Telemetry resource can stamp EXTRA key/value pairs onto every span anihpj generates — three sources exist, and specifying customTags on a namespace/workload resource REPLACES the parent's tags entirely (no field-by-field merge):

  • literal — a fixed string, same on every span
  • environment — reads a proxy environment variable (e.g. the pod's cluster ID), with an optional fallback defaultValue
  • header — copies a value straight off the inbound request (e.g. a caller-supplied user ID), with an optional default
yaml — custom tags: three sources, one Telemetry resource 
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-span-tags
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  tracing:
  - providers:
    - name: "jaeger"
    randomSamplingPercentage: 100.00
    customTags:
      "app_version":
        literal:
          value: "anihpj-v2.4.1"
      "cluster_id":
        environment:
          name: ISTIO_META_CLUSTER_ID
          defaultValue: "Kubernetes"
      "caller_user_id":
        header:
          name: "x-user-id"
          defaultValue: "anonymous"

🏷️ Custom Tag Types — Source, Syntax, anihpj Use Case

TypeReads Fromanihpj Example
literalA fixed string in the CRD"app_version": "anihpj-v2.4.1"
environmentA proxy env var + defaultValueISTIO_META_CLUSTER_ID
headerAn inbound header + defaultValuex-user-id → "caller_user_id"
📖 Field Length Guard

extensionProviders also accepts maxTagLength (default 256) to cap how much of a long URL or header value gets stamped onto a tag — raise it if anihpj's /jobs/?filter=... query strings are getting truncated in Jaeger.

10.8 Deep Dive — W3C Trace Context & the Complete Header Checklist

DEFINITION: W3C Trace Context is the vendor-neutral trace header standard — two headers, traceparent and tracestate — that OpenTelemetry SDKs and Istio's "otel" extension provider speak natively, alongside (not instead of) B3.

10.5 covered the 5 B3 headers; official Istio guidance is that EVERY anihpj service should be ready to forward BOTH families at once during any migration — dropping either one snaps the trace at that hop, exactly like dropping a B3 header does. traceparent packs everything into ONE value — version-traceid-parentid-traceflags — where parentid is the sender's own span ID (the same role x-b3-spanid plays in B3); tracestate carries extra vendor-specific state and is mostly opaque to your code — just copy it through unmodified.

🧬 TRACEPARENT ANATOMY — One Header, Four Dash-Separated Fields
traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01

  00                                ← version (always 00)
  4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736    ← trace-id (32 hex chars)
  00f067aa0ba902b7                    ← parent-id (16 hex chars)
  01                                  ← trace-flags (01 = sampled)

tracestate: rojo=00f067aa0ba902b7,congo=t61rcWkgMzE
  ← opaque vendor key=value list — forward it UNCHANGED

The COMPLETE list: every header an anihpj service must be ready to read on the way in and copy on the way out — this is the checklist to paste into a code-review template.

✅ Complete Header Propagation Checklist — B3 + W3C + Envoy

HeaderFamilyRequired For
x-request-idEnvoy (own header)ALWAYS — every hop
x-b3-traceidB3 multi-headerZipkin/Jaeger backends
x-b3-spanidB3 multi-headerZipkin/Jaeger backends
x-b3-parentspanidB3 multi-headerZipkin/Jaeger backends
x-b3-sampledB3 multi-headerZipkin/Jaeger backends
x-b3-flagsB3 multi-headerZipkin/Jaeger backends
b3B3 single-headerAlternative to the 5 above
traceparentW3C Trace Contextotel provider, OTel SDKs
tracestateW3C Trace Contextotel provider, OTel SDKs

During a Zipkin → OpenTelemetry migration (10.6, step 4), forward the B3 block AND traceparent/tracestate together — only drop B3 once every anihpj service and every client has cut over.

python — anihpj/middleware.py: B3 AND W3C, forwarded together 
TRACE_HEADERS = [
    'x-request-id',
    'x-b3-traceid',   'x-b3-spanid',  'x-b3-parentspanid',
    'x-b3-sampled',   'x-b3-flags',   'b3',
    'traceparent',    'tracestate',    # ← W3C, added here
]

class IstioTracingMiddleware:
    def __init__(self, get_response):
        self.get_response = get_response

    def __call__(self, request):
        request.trace_headers = {
            h: request.META['HTTP_' +
                             h.upper().replace('-', '_')]
            for h in TRACE_HEADERS
            if 'HTTP_' + h.upper().replace('-', '_')
                in request.META
        }
        return self.get_response(request)

10.9 Deep Dive — Sampling Precedence & the "Zero Traces" Runbook

DEFINITION: sampling percentage can be set in THREE places at once — a Telemetry resource, a per-pod annotation, and the legacy MeshConfig — and Istio defines an explicit precedence order for which one wins when they disagree.

⚠️ Real anihpj Incident — 20 Minutes Lost to a Forgotten Telemetry Resource

An anihpj on-call engineer once bumped a proxy.istio.io/config pod annotation to 100% on skills-service to debug a P1, saw NO change, and lost 20 minutes before finding a mesh-wide Telemetry resource from an old experiment still pinning sampling to 1% — the Telemetry resource was outranking the pod annotation, exactly as the precedence order says it should.

🥇 SAMPLING PRECEDENCE — Three Knobs, One Winner
#1  Telemetry API           (namespace or workload)  ← HIGHEST
       ↓ overrides #2 and #3
#2  Pod annotation          (proxy.istio.io/config)
       ↓ overrides #3
#3  MeshConfig               (defaultConfig.tracing.sampling — legacy)
                                                       ← LOWEST

Custom OTel sampler configured on the provider → BEATS ALL THREE,
and locks randomSamplingPercentage to 100 (not configurable)
yaml — per-pod override: annotation beats MeshConfig, loses to Telemetry 
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: skills-service
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        proxy.istio.io/config: |
          tracing:
            sampling: 20   # ← this Deployment only, 20%

The runbook — work top to bottom the moment Jaeger shows zero (or too few) anihpj traces:

🚑 Zero-Traces Runbook — Symptom → Likely Cause → Fix

SymptomLikely CauseFix
No traces at allTracing disabled / no providerEnable + wire provider (10.6)
Traces need 100+ reqs1% default — working as intendedRaise % for dev only (10.4)
Raised % but no changeA higher-precedence Telemetry resource is already set elsewhere (mesh or namespace)Check kubectl get telemetry -A for a resource outranking the one you just touched
Many 1-span tracesApp not forwarding headersApply 10.8 checklist/middleware
One service missingStill points at OLD collectorRepoint to new service:port
🔧 Under the Hood — How Distributed Tracing Actually Works in Istio: B3 Header Propagation, Span Context, Jaeger Integration, and the Complete Header Lifecycle, One Hop at a Time
🗺️ Distributed Tracing Architecture — From Request to Trace
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TRACING PIPELINE — How Istio Builds a Complete Call Chain                       │
│                                                                              │
│  REQUEST: GET /api/jobs/ → anihpj-web → jobpost-api → postgres              │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 1: INGRESS GATEWAY CREATES ROOT SPAN                                     │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Gateway Envoy receives request (no trace headers yet)                  │   │
│  │ → Creates NEW trace: traceID=abc123, spanID=001, parentSpanID=null    │   │
│  │ → Injects B3 headers into request:                                     │   │
│  │   x-b3-traceid: abc123                                                │   │
│  │   x-b3-spanid: 001                                                     │   │
│  │   x-b3-parentspanid: (none — root span!)                              │   │
│  │   x-b3-sampled: 1 (yes, trace this)                                   │   │
│  │ → Reports span to Jaeger (zipkin.istio-system:9411)                   │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 2: SIDECAR CREATES CHILD SPAN                                           │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ anihpj-web sidecar receives request WITH B3 headers                    │   │
│  │ → Creates CHILD span: traceID=abc123, spanID=002, parentSpanID=001    │   │
│  │ → UPDATES x-b3-spanid: 002, x-b3-parentspanid: 001                   │   │
│  │ → Reports span to Jaeger                                               │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 3: YOUR APP MUST FORWARD HEADERS! (The #1 Pitfall)                      │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ anihpj-web APP receives request from sidecar                           │   │
│  │ → Reads B3 headers from request.META                                   │   │
│  │ → Makes HTTP call to jobpost-api:                                      │   │
│  │   ❌ WITHOUT forwarding: NEW trace starts — broken chain!              │   │
│  │   ✅ WITH forwarding: copies x-b3-* headers → chain continues         │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ DJANGO FIX (5 headers to forward):                                     │   │
│  │ headers = {                                                            │   │
│  │   'x-b3-traceid': request.headers.get('x-b3-traceid'),                │   │
│  │   'x-b3-spanid': request.headers.get('x-b3-spanid'),                   │   │
│  │   'x-b3-parentspanid': request.headers.get('x-b3-parentspanid'),      │   │
│  │   'x-b3-sampled': request.headers.get('x-b3-sampled', '1'),            │   │
│  │   'x-b3-flags': request.headers.get('x-b3-flags', ''),                 │   │
│  │ }                                                                       │   │
│  │ requests.get('http://jobpost-api:8000/api/process', headers=headers)  │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 4: JAEGER ASSEMBLES THE TRACE                                           │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ Jaeger receives spans from ALL Envoys (via Zipkin protocol)            │   │
│  │ → Groups spans by traceID=abc123                                       │   │
│  │ → Orders by parentSpanID → builds call tree                            │   │
│  │ → Displays: Gateway(200ms) → anihpj-web(80ms) → jobpost-api(45ms)     │   │
│  │ →            → postgres(15ms)                                           │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 B3 Header Contract — The 5 Headers That Make Tracing Work
HeaderPurposeWho Sets ItRequired?
x-b3-traceidUnique trace ID (64 or 128 bits)First Envoy in chain (Gateway)✅ Yes — the glue that connects all spans
x-b3-spanidCurrent span ID (64 bits)Every Envoy (UPDATED each hop)✅ Yes — identifies THIS span
x-b3-parentspanidParent span IDEvery Envoy (previous spanID)✅ Yes — builds the call tree
x-b3-sampled0=don't trace, 1=traceFirst Envoy (sampling decision)⚠️ Recommended — saves resources
x-b3-flagsDebug flag (force trace)Manual (for debugging only)❌ Optional
⏱️ The Complete Header Lifecycle — One Incident, One Hop at a Time

10.5-10.9 each zoomed into ONE piece of the tracing puzzle — the B3 contract, providers, custom tags, W3C headers, sampling precedence. Here they are stitched into a single walkthrough: the exact header lifecycle of the anihpj incident this chapter keeps returning to, as ONE request crosses the jobpost-api → skills-service hop that produced the 195ms span.

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STEP 1 -- jobpost-api INBOUND Envoy (request enters the mesh)         │
│   reads:  nothing (this IS the first hop)                             │
│   mints:  x-b3-traceid + the sampling verdict x-b3-sampled (10.9)     │
│                                                                       │
│ STEP 2 -- jobpost-api Django, IstioTracingMiddleware (10.5)           │
│   reads:    every x-b3-*, x-request-id, traceparent/tracestate (10.8) │
│   forwards: all of it UNCHANGED onto the outbound call -- mints       │
│             nothing, pure courier                                     │
│                                                                       │
│ STEP 3 -- jobpost-api OUTBOUND Envoy (dialing skills-service)         │
│   reads:    request.trace_headers set in step 2                       │
│   mints:    new x-b3-spanid; x-b3-parentspanid = its own span id;     │
│             stamps 10.7 custom tags; translates protocol per the      │
│             10.6 provider config (e.g. Zipkin -> OTLP)                │
│   forwards: x-b3-traceid + x-b3-sampled UNCHANGED                     │
│                                                                       │
│ STEP 4 -- skills-service INBOUND Envoy (span: 92ms -> 287ms = 195ms)  │
│   reads:  all headers carried from step 3                             │
│   mints:  its own span; forwards x-request-id for log-to-trace joins  │
│                                                                       │
│ STEP 5 -- Jaeger / OTel backend                                       │
│   receives the finished spans from steps 3 and 4, stitches them       │
│   under ONE traceId (7f3e9a12b4c06d8e) -- the 342ms trace from 10.3   │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 ICA Insight: Istio does span CREATION automatically, but header PROPAGATION is YOUR responsibility. The #1 ICA tracing scenario: "Jaeger shows isolated spans" → fix: forward B3 headers in application code. The 5 B3 headers are: traceid (the glue), spanid (current hop), parentspanid (who called me), sampled (trace it?), flags (debug). Istio uses the Zipkin protocol to send spans to Jaeger (zipkin.istio-system:9411) by default, or OTLP to an OpenTelemetry collector (10.6). Sampling rate controls resource usage — 100% (dev) vs 1% (prod), with an explicit precedence order when Telemetry API, a pod annotation, and legacy MeshConfig all try to set it at once (10.9). Underneath every row of the lifecycle above: exactly ONE actor mints new IDs at each hop (Envoy), exactly ONE actor is a pure courier with zero mint responsibility (your Django code), and the moment that courier fails to forward even ONE header, the next Envoy has nothing correct to mint from — which is precisely how a 5-span trace becomes five 1-span traces.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • A trace is the whole journey; a span is one timed hop — every span in a trace shares the same Trace ID, which is the glue linking them into one Gantt waterfall.
  • Envoy does 80% automatically (create/inject/report); your app does the critical 20% (forward) — the single most common tracing failure is your code silently dropping the B3 headers between hops.
  • The widest bar in a Jaeger Gantt chart IS the bottleneck — sort by Longest Duration, open the slowest trace, and the answer is visual, not computed.
  • Sampling is 100% for dev, 1-5% for production — and x-b3-flags: 1 force-samples ONE request without touching any YAML.
  • Sampling precedence is Telemetry API > pod annotation > legacy MeshConfig — a stale, forgotten Telemetry resource from an old experiment is the #1 reason a pod-annotation or MeshConfig sampling change appears to do nothing; the Telemetry API always wins regardless of scope.
  • The legacy MeshConfig tracing block must be explicitly zeroed out (defaultConfig.tracing: {}) when migrating to the Telemetry API — leaving both populated does NOT merge them, the legacy block silently keeps winning.
  • B3 and W3C traceparent/tracestate are different header families for different backends — during any Zipkin→OpenTelemetry migration, forward BOTH; dropping either snaps the chain at whichever service switched first.
  • A 200 status code on the widest span means SLOW, not FAILING — go straight to the database query plan or downstream call, not the error logs.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "Istio's automatic tracing means I don't need to touch my app code." No — Envoy creates spans automatically, but it cannot see INSIDE your process. Your code must explicitly forward the B3 (or W3C) headers, or every hop starts a brand-new, disconnected trace.
  • "Raising the sampling percentage to 100% will always show more traces." Not if you raised it via a pod annotation or the legacy MeshConfig block while a HIGHER-precedence Telemetry resource elsewhere still pins a lower rate — the Telemetry API always wins (Telemetry API > pod annotation > MeshConfig), so check for a competing Telemetry resource before assuming your change didn't apply.
  • "Setting the new Telemetry sampling rate is enough during a provider migration." No — leaving the legacy defaultConfig.tracing block populated means it keeps winning; it must be explicitly zeroed (tracing: {}) or the new setting silently does nothing.
  • "B3 and W3C headers are interchangeable, pick either one." No — a mixed mesh where one service forwards only B3 and another forwards only traceparent snaps the trace at that exact boundary. Forward BOTH during any migration.
  • "A slow span with a 200 status code must be a metrics or dashboard glitch." No — 200 means the request succeeded, just slowly. The next step is the actual downstream call or database query behind that span, not the error logs.
  • "x-b3-flags forcing a trace also changes the mesh-wide sampling rate." No — it forces sampling for that ONE request and its downstream hops only; the configured percentage is unchanged for every other request.
  • "tracestate is safe to drop since it's vendor-specific." No — even though its contents are mostly opaque to your code, it must still be forwarded UNCHANGED alongside traceparent, or vendor-specific trace correlation breaks for whichever backend relies on it.

💼 Chapter 10 — Daily Work Takeaways

  • Reach for a Django middleware, not per-view header copying — capturing trace headers once per request in one place is far less error-prone than relying on every developer remembering it in every view.
  • Check header propagation BEFORE touching sampling whenever traces look broken or fragmented — 100% sampling with dropped headers still produces disconnected 1-span traces, not the connected story you need.
  • Use x-b3-flags: 1 to force-sample a single production request during a live investigation — no config change, no waiting for the next sampled request to happen to be the right one.
  • Never leave 100% sampling on in production — it's a dev-only setting; keep it in the 1-5% range in production and force-sample individual requests instead.
  • Work the Zero-Traces runbook top to bottom instead of guessing — no traces / traces need 100+ requests / raised % but no change / many 1-span traces / one service missing, each with a distinct likely cause and fix.
  • Confirm real SAN-equivalent facts live: use istioctl proxy-config bootstrap ... | grep -i trac to confirm which tracing provider/collector Envoy actually has configured, rather than trusting the YAML alone.
  • For the ICA exam: practice reciting the 5 B3 headers and their roles from memory (traceid/spanid/parentspanid/sampled/flags) — the exam's #1 tracing scenario is diagnosing a header-propagation gap.
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 10

Seven quick-fire phrase-to-answer mappings — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Why are traces broken/isolated?" = Missing B3 header propagation — your app code must forward x-b3-* headers
  • "Find the bottleneck" = Jaeger → sort Longest Duration → widest Gantt bar
  • "No traces appearing" = Work the Zero-Traces runbook: provider wired? sampling > 0%? headers forwarded?
  • "Force ONE trace without touching YAML" = curl -H "x-b3-flags: 1"
  • "Raised sampling, nothing changed" = Check for a higher-precedence Telemetry resource elsewhere (kubectl get telemetry -A) — the Telemetry API always wins over a pod annotation or MeshConfig
  • "Switching Zipkin → OpenTelemetry" = Forward BOTH B3 and W3C traceparent/tracestate during the migration
  • "Add custom span metadata" = Telemetry API customTags — literal, environment, or header source

🧠 Chapter 10 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
In one sentence each, what's the difference between a trace and a span?
Show Answer
Answer

A trace is the entire journey of ONE request across every service it touches. A span is one timed unit of work — one service call — within that journey. Every span in a trace shares the same Trace ID.

Explanation

This distinction matters because "the trace is 342ms" and "the skills-service span is 195ms" are answering different questions — the trace tells you something is slow, individual spans tell you WHERE.

Q2
What percentage of tracing work does Envoy handle automatically, and what's the one piece left to your application code?
Show Answer
Answer

Roughly 80% — Envoy creates span context, injects the B3 headers, updates spanid/parentspanid at every hop, and reports finished spans to the tracing backend. The remaining 20%: your application code must READ the inbound trace headers and FORWARD them, unchanged, on every outbound call it makes.

Explanation

Envoy cannot see inside your process — it has no way to know your Django view is about to make a downstream HTTP call, so it can't inject headers into a request it never observes being created.

Q3
A team forgets to forward B3 headers in one service. What does Jaeger show instead of one connected trace?
Show Answer
Answer

Multiple DISCONNECTED, isolated 1-span traces instead of one multi-span call chain — each hop starts a brand-new trace because the service that dropped the headers gave the next Envoy nothing correct to build on.

Explanation

This is the single most common tracing failure mode and the #1 ICA tracing scenario — recognizing "many 1-span traces" as a header-propagation symptom (not a sampling or provider problem) is the fast path to the right fix.

Q4
Name the 5 B3 headers and, for each, who is responsible for setting/updating it.
Show Answer
Answer

x-b3-traceid (first Envoy, the glue for the whole trace), x-b3-spanid (every Envoy, updated each hop), x-b3-parentspanid (every Envoy, builds the call tree), x-b3-sampled (first Envoy, the sampling verdict), x-b3-flags (you, manually, to force sampling).

Explanation

Your application code never MINTS any of these — it only reads what's inbound and copies it, unchanged, onto outbound calls. The only header a human ever sets by hand is x-b3-flags, for on-demand debugging.

Q5
What's the recommended sampling percentage for development versus production, and how do you trace ONE specific production request without changing that percentage?
Show Answer
Answer

100% in development, 1-5% in production. To trace one specific production request without touching the configured percentage, send x-b3-flags: 1 on that request — it forces sampling regardless of the current rate.

Explanation

100% sampling in production is expensive at real traffic volumes — the force-flag gives you the debugging power of 100% sampling for exactly the one request you care about, with none of the overhead.

Q6
Sampling can be set in three different places. Name all three and their precedence order.
Show Answer
Answer

Telemetry API (highest) > pod annotation (proxy.istio.io/config) > legacy MeshConfig (defaultConfig.tracing.sampling, lowest). A custom OTel sampler configured on the provider beats all three and locks sampling to 100%.

Explanation

Knowing this order cold is what turns a 20-minute "why isn't my sampling change working" investigation into a 30-second check of the next-highest-precedence source.

Q7
What protocol does Envoy speak to send spans to a "Jaeger" backend by default, and what's the alternative for OpenTelemetry?
Show Answer
Answer

By default, Envoy speaks the ZIPKIN protocol (port 9411) to a Jaeger collector. For OpenTelemetry, Envoy sends OTLP over gRPC (port 4317) to an OTel collector, which can then fan out to Jaeger, Tempo, or a vendor APM.

Explanation

"Jaeger" in casual conversation usually refers to the UI, not the wire protocol — Envoy is actually speaking Zipkin's protocol underneath, which is why knowing the protocol/port distinction matters for debugging "no traces appearing."

Q8
What are the three sources for a custom span tag via the Telemetry API, and what happens if you set customTags at both the mesh level and a namespace level?
Show Answer
Answer

Three sources: literal (a fixed string), environment (a proxy environment variable, with an optional default), and header (an inbound request header, with an optional default). Setting customTags at the namespace level REPLACES the mesh-level tags entirely — there's no field-by-field merge.

Explanation

The "replace, not merge" behavior is a real trap — a team adding one namespace-specific tag can accidentally lose every mesh-wide tag they expected to still be present, unless they explicitly re-declare them too.

Q9
What are the two W3C Trace Context headers, and what does each one carry?
Show Answer
Answer

traceparent packs version, trace-id, parent-id, and trace-flags into ONE dash-separated value. tracestate carries extra vendor-specific state and is mostly opaque to your code — just copy it through unmodified.

Explanation

Unlike B3's five separate headers, W3C Trace Context compresses the core identity into a single header — but the propagation OBLIGATION is identical: forward both headers unchanged on every outbound call.

Q10
A trace shows a span with a 200 HTTP status code as the widest bar in the Gantt chart. Is this a bug in the tracing setup?
Show Answer
Answer

No — this is expected and exactly what tracing is FOR. A 200 status means the request succeeded; the width of the bar means it was SLOW. The next step is investigating that specific call's downstream dependency (a database query, an external API), not the error logs — there was no error.

Explanation

Confusing "slow" with "failing" wastes investigation time in the wrong place (error logs) instead of the right one (the widest span's own tags and downstream calls).

⚙️ Chapter 10 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
Jaeger shows five separate 1-span traces for a single GET /jobs/ request instead of one 5-span chain. Task: Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# Diagnose: check whether the app is forwarding B3 headers on outbound calls
kubectl logs deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -c istio-proxy --tail=20 | grep -i b3
# Most likely: application code (or a swapped HTTP client library) stopped
# copying inbound x-b3-* headers onto outbound calls
# Fix: add (or restore) header-forwarding middleware
class IstioTracingMiddleware:
    def __call__(self, request):
        request.trace_headers = {
            h: request.META['HTTP_' + h.upper().replace('-', '_')]
            for h in TRACE_HEADERS
            if 'HTTP_' + h.upper().replace('-', '_') in request.META
        }
        return self.get_response(request)
Explanation

This is 10.5's exact real-anihpj-incident scenario — user-service swapped its HTTP client library and silently stopped forwarding headers. A middleware approach (capture once, use everywhere) is more resilient to this than per-view header copying.

Q2
An on-call engineer bumps a proxy.istio.io/config pod annotation to 100% sampling on skills-service during an incident but sees no change in Jaeger. Task: Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# Diagnose: check for a Telemetry resource outranking the pod annotation
kubectl get telemetry -A
# Fix: update (or remove) the stale higher-precedence Telemetry resource
kubectl edit telemetry mesh-default -n istio-system
Explanation

This mirrors 10.9's own real anihpj incident: a forgotten mesh-wide (or namespace-wide) Telemetry resource from an old experiment was still pinning sampling to a low rate, and it OUTRANKED the pod annotation the engineer just changed — exactly per the documented precedence order (Telemetry API > pod annotation > MeshConfig). A pod annotation can never outrank a Telemetry resource, no matter how specific the annotation's scope looks — always check kubectl get telemetry -A first when a lower-precedence change appears to do nothing.

Q3
Write a Telemetry resource enabling 100% sampling for the anihpj namespace only, for local development.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-dev-tracing
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  tracing:
  - providers:
    - name: "jaeger"
    randomSamplingPercentage: 100.00
Explanation

Scoping to namespace: anihpj (rather than istio-system) keeps this dev-friendly 100% rate from accidentally applying mesh-wide to other teams' production traffic.

Q4
A team migrating from Zipkin to OpenTelemetry wants both providers active simultaneously during the transition. Write the extensionProviders block.
Show Answer
Answer
meshConfig:
  extensionProviders:
  - name: jaeger-zipkin
    zipkin:
      service: zipkin.istio-system.svc.cluster.local
      port: 9411
  - name: otel
    opentelemetry:
      service: otel-collector.istio-system.svc.cluster.local
      port: 4317
Explanation

Both providers can be declared side by side — a Telemetry resource then picks which one is ACTIVE by name. This lets a team flip the active provider per-namespace first, verify traces still assemble, then go mesh-wide.

Q5
anihpj wants every span tagged with a fixed app version, the cluster ID from an env var, and the caller's user ID from a header. Write the Telemetry resource.
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  tracing:
  - providers:
    - name: "jaeger"
    randomSamplingPercentage: 100.00
    customTags:
      "app_version":
        literal:
          value: "anihpj-v2.4.1"
      "cluster_id":
        environment:
          name: ISTIO_META_CLUSTER_ID
          defaultValue: "Kubernetes"
      "caller_user_id":
        header:
          name: "x-user-id"
          defaultValue: "anonymous"
Explanation

Each tag type maps directly to its source: literal for constants, environment for proxy env vars (with a fallback), header for per-request caller data (also with a fallback for when the header is absent).

Q6
A team applies a new Telemetry resource for sampling, but the legacy MeshConfig tracing block is still populated from an old install. Task: Diagnose and fix the underlying conflict.
Show Answer
Answer
# IstioOperator excerpt (istioctl install -f iop.yaml):
meshConfig:
  enableTracing: true
  defaultConfig:
    tracing: {}       # explicitly empty the LEGACY block
Explanation

Leaving both the legacy block AND a Telemetry resource populated does NOT merge them — the legacy block keeps winning silently. Explicitly zeroing it (tracing: {}) is a required migration step, not optional cleanup.

Q7
Confirm which tracing provider and collector address Envoy actually has configured on a live jobpost-api pod — don't just trust the YAML.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl proxy-config bootstrap deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -o json | grep -i trac
Explanation

This is the same "verify delivery, not just acceptance" discipline used throughout this guide — a Telemetry resource applying cleanly doesn't prove Envoy actually received and is using that config.

Q8
Write the middleware TRACE_HEADERS list needed to forward BOTH B3 and W3C headers during a provider migration.
Show Answer
Answer
TRACE_HEADERS = [
    'x-request-id',
    'x-b3-traceid',   'x-b3-spanid',  'x-b3-parentspanid',
    'x-b3-sampled',   'x-b3-flags',   'b3',
    'traceparent',    'tracestate',    # ← W3C, added here
]
Explanation

Both header families are forwarded UNCHANGED, identically — the middleware doesn't need to understand either format, just copy whatever is present on the inbound request to every outbound call.

Q9
Force-sample exactly one production request to skills-service without changing any Telemetry resource.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- \
    curl -s -H "x-b3-flags: 1" http://skills-service:8090/skills/
Explanation

x-b3-flags: 1 overrides the sampling percentage for this ONE request and its downstream hops only — no YAML change, no risk of accidentally raising the mesh-wide sampling rate.

Q10
Jaeger shows zero traces for anihpj entirely, not even fragmented ones. Task: Work the runbook — what's the FIRST thing to check, and why first?
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl get telemetry -A
# confirm tracing is enabled and a provider is actually wired at all
Explanation

ZERO traces (not fragmented, not missing-one-service) points at the top of the runbook: tracing disabled or no provider configured at all — check this BEFORE sampling rate, header propagation, or anything downstream, since none of those matter if tracing was never turned on in the first place.

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 10
  • Traces missing or arriving as disconnected 1-span fragments? Check header propagation (10.5/10.8) BEFORE touching sampling — 100% sampling with dropped headers still produces five 1-span traces, not the one connected story you need.
  • Raised the sampling % and nothing changed? Per the Zero-Traces Runbook, check for a leftover proxy.istio.io/config pod annotation first — a stale annotation from an old debug session is the most common reason a Telemetry change appears to do nothing (10.9).
  • Need one traced request in prod without touching any config? Send x-b3-flags: 1 — it forces sampling for that request and every downstream hop, no YAML required (10.4).
  • Never leave 100% sampling on in production — it is a dev-only setting; 1-5% is the production range this chapter recommends (10.4).
  • Migrating providers? Forward BOTH B3 and W3C headers during the transition (10.6/10.8) — dropping either family snaps the chain at whichever service switched first.
  • A 200 status code on the widest span means SLOW, not FAILING — go straight to the database query plan, not the error logs (10.3).

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 10)

Every command below already appeared earlier in this chapter — grouped here as one reference for driving Jaeger, sampling, and tracing-provider debugging.

CommandWhat It Does / Checks in Chapter 10
istioctl dashboard jaegerOpens the Jaeger UI, port-forward handled for you (10.3)
kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- curl -s -H "x-b3-flags: 1" http://skills-service:8090/skills/Force-samples ONE prod request, bypassing the % (10.4)
kubectl apply -f dev-tracing.yamlNamespace-scoped Telemetry, e.g. 100% sampling in anihpj (10.4)
kubectl get telemetry -ALists every Telemetry resource mesh-wide — find who set what (10.7, 10.9)
kubectl get deploy skills-service -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 proxy.istio.io/configReveals a pod-annotation sampling override (10.9 runbook)
istioctl proxy-config bootstrap deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -o json | grep -i tracConfirms which tracing provider/collector Envoy actually has (10.6)

🧪 Practice Drill 10.1 — Find the 195ms Span

⏱️ Target Time: 5-10 minutes
Scenario

Do this now, timed, on your own anihpj cluster:

  1. (1 min) Run istioctl dashboard jaeger and let it open in your browser.
  2. (1 min) Search Service: jobpost-api.anihpj, Operation: GET /jobs/, Sort: Longest Duration.
  3. (2 min) Open the slowest trace and find the WIDEST bar in the Gantt waterfall — confirm it is the ~195ms skills-service span.
  4. (2 min) Click that span and read its tags — confirm http.status_code is 200 (slow, not failing), then note the upstream_cluster value.
  5. (2 min, stretch) Force-sample one fresh request with x-b3-flags: 1 (10.4's command) and watch it appear in Jaeger's search results within seconds.
Hint: Steps 1-2 reuse 10.3's Jaeger search workflow; step 3 is the same widest-bar reflex from 10.1's trace diagram; step 5 proves you can force a trace on demand without touching any Telemetry YAML — the same reflex a Domain 4 troubleshooting task expects cold.
View Solution

Step 4's http.status_code: 200 confirms the span is slow, not failing — the investigation belongs with the downstream call/query, not the error logs. Step 5's forced request should appear in Jaeger's search results within a few seconds of the curl command, well before the next natural sampling window would have caught it.

Check yourself: did you actually read the span's tags in step 4, or did you stop once you found the widest bar? The width tells you WHERE; the tags tell you WHAT was happening there — both are needed for a real diagnosis.

🧪 Practice Drill 10.2 — Reproduce a Broken Trace, Then Fix It

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Don't take 10.5's header-propagation warning on faith — break it and fix it yourself.

  1. Temporarily remove (or comment out) the header-forwarding logic in a test service's outbound call.
  2. Generate a request through that service and search for it in Jaeger.
  3. Confirm you see MULTIPLE disconnected 1-span traces instead of one connected chain.
  4. Restore the header-forwarding logic and repeat the same request.
  5. Confirm Jaeger now shows ONE connected multi-span trace for the same call path.
Hint: If your test service uses a middleware pattern (10.5), the fastest way to break this is to comment out the middleware registration in settings.py rather than editing every view.
View Solution

Step 3 should show exactly as many 1-span traces as there are hops downstream of the broken service — each one missing its parent relationship. Step 5's restored trace should show the SAME number of spans, now correctly nested under one shared Trace ID.

Check yourself: could you now explain to a teammate, using your own before/after Jaeger screenshots, exactly what "disconnected" looks like versus "connected"? That's the difference between reciting the rule and having verified it.

🧪 Practice Drill 10.3 — Match the Symptom to the Broken Layer

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

For each observation, name the most likely cause and the ONE command you'd run to confirm it — before proposing any fix:

  1. Jaeger shows ZERO traces for anihpj at all — not even fragmented ones.
  2. A namespace Telemetry resource was raised to 50% sampling, but ONE specific workload's traces are still capped at 1%.
  3. A service migrating to OpenTelemetry stops appearing in traces the moment a downstream partner service switches providers.
  4. A custom span tag defined mesh-wide in istio-system is completely missing on every span from one specific namespace.
Hint: Two of these four share the exact same root-cause SHAPE — something more specific silently overriding something broader, even though the broader one looks like it should apply.
View Solution
#CauseConfirm with
1Tracing disabled entirely, or no extensionProvider wired — the top of the Zero-Traces runbookkubectl get telemetry -A and check meshConfig.enableTracing
2A workload-scoped Telemetry resource is outranking the namespace-scoped one for that specific workload — specificity matters WITHIN the Telemetry API itselfkubectl get telemetry -n <namespace> -o yaml \| grep -B5 selector
3Mixed-protocol mesh — the partner switched providers/header families and the chain snaps at that boundaryCheck whether both services forward BOTH B3 and W3C headers (10.8)
4A namespace-level Telemetry resource REPLACED the mesh-level customTags instead of merging with themkubectl get telemetry -n <namespace> -o yaml \| grep -A5 customTags

Check yourself: did you correctly identify #2 and #4 as the same "more-specific-silently-wins" shape — BOTH resolved entirely WITHIN the Telemetry API's own workload > namespace > mesh specificity rule, not a cross-mechanism precedence question? That's a genuinely different pattern from a pod annotation vs. Telemetry API question (which is a flat, mechanism-based rule with no specificity involved at all) — confusing the two is the real trap here.

🧪 Practice Drill 10.4 — Migrate a Namespace From Zipkin to OpenTelemetry, Safely

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Follow 10.6's safe migration order for real, on a test namespace:

  1. Confirm the CURRENT active provider for anihpj via istioctl proxy-config bootstrap.
  2. Add an "otel" extensionProvider NEXT TO the existing Zipkin one (don't remove Zipkin yet).
  3. Update the middleware/header-forwarding code to forward BOTH B3 and W3C headers (10.8), if not already doing so.
  4. Flip the Telemetry resource's active provider to "otel" for the anihpj namespace ONLY (not mesh-wide).
  5. Generate a request and confirm a trace still assembles correctly end-to-end.
Hint: Step 3 is easy to skip since traces might still work if EVERY service in the chain happens to already be forwarding W3C headers — don't assume, verify it's actually in the code before flipping providers.
View Solution

Step 5's trace should assemble with no gaps — if it doesn't, the most likely cause is a service in the chain that's still B3-only meeting a downstream hop that's now OTel-only, snapping the chain at that exact boundary (10.6's mixed-mesh gotcha).

Check yourself: did you flip the provider namespace-first (as the drill specifies) rather than mesh-wide? Testing the blast radius small before going wide is the actual production discipline this drill is rehearsing, not just the mechanical YAML change.

🧪 Practice Drill 10.5 — Sketch the Header Lifecycle From Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking back at the UTH's diagram, sketch (on paper or in a text file) what happens to trace headers across a 2-hop request: jobpost-api → skills-service.

  1. At jobpost-api's INBOUND Envoy: what gets minted, what gets read?
  2. At jobpost-api's Django code: what gets read, what gets forwarded, what gets minted?
  3. At jobpost-api's OUTBOUND Envoy (dialing skills-service): what gets minted, what stays unchanged?
Hint: Exactly ONE of the three steps should have "mints: nothing" as its answer — that's the step your app code is responsible for, and it's the one this whole chapter's core lesson is about.
View Solution

Step 1 (inbound Envoy, first hop): mints x-b3-traceid + the sampling verdict. Step 2 (Django code): reads everything inbound, forwards it UNCHANGED, mints NOTHING — pure courier. Step 3 (outbound Envoy): mints a new x-b3-spanid and sets x-b3-parentspanid to its own span id, forwards traceid/sampled unchanged.

Check yourself: did your sketch correctly show step 2 minting nothing? This is the single most tested concept in the chapter — Envoy mints IDs at both Envoy hops, your code is a pure courier in between, never a minter.

🔭 Chapter 10 in One Picture — One Request, Every Hop It Crosses
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1 request: GET /jobs/ -> jobpost-api -> user-service -> auth-service  │
│                       -> skills-service -> location-service           │
│         (10.1: trace = the whole journey, span = one timed hop)       │
│                                  │                                    │
│                                  ▼                                    │
│ Envoy auto-creates spans + injects x-b3-* headers (10.2) -- YOUR CODE │
│ must forward them unchanged, hop to hop (10.5 B3 + 10.8 W3C headers)  │
│                                  │                                    │
│                                  ▼                                    │
│ Jaeger renders the Gantt waterfall (10.3) -- widest bar = the 195ms   │
│ skills-service span = the bottleneck                                  │
│                                  │                                    │
│                                  ▼                                    │
│ How much of this gets recorded? Sampling (10.4) -- precedence order   │
│ is Telemetry API > pod annotation > MeshConfig (10.9)                 │
│                                  │                                    │
│                                  ▼                                    │
│ When it breaks: check the provider/protocol (10.6), audit custom      │
│ tags (10.7), then run the Zero-Traces runbook top to bottom (10.9)    │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Chapter 10 took anihpj from "users say the site feels slow" to "the skills-service call inside trace 7f3e9a12b4c06d8e is the culprit," in about the time it takes to open one dashboard: 10.1-10.3 introduced trace vs span, Envoy's near-automatic header injection, and Jaeger's Gantt waterfall as the tool that turns spans into a single visual bottleneck; 10.4 added the sampling knob that decides how many requests ever reach that waterfall; and 10.5-10.9 supplied the troubleshooting toolkit underneath — the exact B3 header contract and its 80/20 Envoy-vs-your-code split, the Zipkin/Jaeger/OpenTelemetry provider landscape, custom span tags via the Telemetry API (and why the legacy MeshConfig block must be zeroed out first), the W3C traceparent/tracestate alternative to run alongside B3 during any migration, and the sampling-precedence order that resolves exactly the kind of "I raised it to 100% and nothing changed" incident this chapter opened with.

Quick recap — 🔍 Trace vs 📏 Span: whole journey vs one timed hop, linked by a shared Trace ID (10.1) · 🔗 Header propagation: Envoy does 80% (create/inject/report), your Django code does the critical 20% (forward) (10.2, 10.5) · 🔭 Jaeger: search → sort Longest Duration → widest bar = bottleneck (10.3) · 🎯 Sampling: 100% dev / 1-5% prod, force ONE request with x-b3-flags: 1 (10.4) · 🔀 Providers: Envoy speaks Zipkin (:9411) or OTLP (:4317) — pick one behind a Telemetry resource (10.6) · 🏷️ Custom tags: literal / environment / header, three sources on one Telemetry CRD (10.7) · 🧬 W3C: traceparent + tracestate, forward alongside B3 during migration (10.8) · 🥇 Precedence: Telemetry API > pod annotation > MeshConfig, worked top to bottom by the Zero-Traces runbook (10.9). Chapter 11 (Kiali) now takes this same incident and turns it into a picture you can read in seconds.

Chapter 11: Kiali — Visualizing Your Entire Service Mesh

Kiali is the "control panel" for your Istio mesh. It shows a live service topology graph, validates your Istio configuration, and even generates YAML from a UI. Think of it as Google Maps for your microservices.

"Forget the numbers and the spans for a second — just show me the whole mesh, at a glance." By this point in Part 6, Grafana has already flagged a WHAT (skills-service's p99 climbing to 1,240ms, Chapter 9) and Jaeger has already found a WHY (a 195ms skills-service span inside a 342ms trace, Chapter 10). Kiali is where those two answers finally become ONE picture: run istioctl dashboard kiali and the same skills-service incident that took two chapters to diagnose lights up as a single red edge on a graph of all seven anihpj services. Metrics told you a number moved and traces told you which hop it moved on, but only Kiali shows you the shape of the whole mesh at once — which services are healthy, which edges are failing, and whether a broken VirtualService is the cause before you even open a trace. It also closes a loop the earlier two chapters could not: Kiali validates the live Istio YAML behind every edge, so the same graph that shows you a red connection can tell you, on the same screen, that a DestinationRule subset typo is why. That is why Kiali is the capstone of Part 6, not a third tool bolted onto the first two — it is the one screen you actually leave open all day.

11.1 What is Kiali?

DEFINITION: Kiali is the open-source management console for the Istio mesh — it merges Prometheus metrics, Istio config, and Kubernetes state into one live, clickable picture. Kiali provides four main capabilities: service topology graph, RED metrics visualization, Istio config validation, and YAML wizards. Open with istioctl dashboard kiali.

Why it matters: "which anihpj service is unhealthy RIGHT NOW?" is answered in seconds by looking at colored nodes and edges. Kiali stores nothing itself — it is a read-mostly UI over data that already exists, so deleting Kiali loses no telemetry. The four capabilities you will use daily:

🗺️
Topology

Live service graph built from real traffic.

💓
Health

RED metrics per node (service) and edge (call path).

✅
Validation

Catches broken VirtualService/DestinationRule YAML.

🧙
Wizards

Generate correct Istio YAML from the UI.

🗺️ KIALI OVERVIEW PAGE — First Screen After istioctl dashboard kiali

11.3 Validating Istio Configuration

Kiali validates your VirtualService and DestinationRule YAML and shows errors inline. How it works: Kiali cross-checks every Istio object against the live service registry and against every OTHER Istio object — most real mistakes are dangling references between two objects that are each valid on their own. Common issues detected:

Missing Subset

VS references subset not in DR

Port Mismatch

Gateway port not open in pod

Conflicting Rules

Multiple VS claiming same host

🧠 ANALOGY — The Office Directory

A VirtualService that still points at a renamed subset is like calling a coworker's old desk extension after they moved to a new desk: the extension number you dialed is still perfectly valid, and the coworker still works at the company — the two facts just no longer point at each other. Kiali's validation is the office directory that catches the mismatch before you pick up the phone and hear silence.

⚠️ Real anihpj Story — KIA1107

A DestinationRule renamed subset "v2" to "canary" but the VirtualService still said "v2" → every canary request failed → Kiali flagged KIA1107 seconds after the apply, long before anyone read a log.

📋 Kiali Config Validation — Three Real anihpj Errors, Annotated
  Istio Config — Namespace: anihpj          ❌ 2 errors  ⚠️ 1 warning

  ❌ VirtualService/jobpost-api          KIA1107
     route[0].destination.subset: "v2"
     └─▶ subset not found in any DestinationRule
         (DR "jobpost-api" only defines subsets: v1, canary)

  ❌ Gateway/anihpj-gateway              KIA0302
     selector: istio: eastwest-gateway
     └─▶ no workload matches this selector in the namespace
         (anihpj's ingress pods use istio: ingressgateway)

  ⚠️ VirtualService/jobpost-api-legacy   KIA1106
     hosts: ["jobpost-api"]
     └─▶ two VirtualServices define routes for the same host —
         rules may conflict; merge them into a single VS

The Speed Tips at the end of this chapter reference KIA1106 directly — it's this exact warning: two VirtualServices both claiming the jobpost-api host. Unlike the two ❌ errors above (which reliably break traffic), this ⚠️ warning is sometimes an intentional in-progress migration, not a bug — read it in context before assuming it needs an immediate fix.

⚖️ Kiali Validation vs istioctl analyze — Pick the Right Tool

AspectKiali Validationistioctl analyze
InterfaceWeb UI, visualCLI, text output
RunsContinuously, liveOn demand
ScopeAll namespaces-n <ns> or -A
Offline YAML check❌ live only✅ file.yaml
CI/CD pipelines❌ not scriptable✅ exit code ≠ 0
Best forDiscovery, triageAutomation, pre-apply gate
💡 ICA Exam Tip

If asked to "validate configuration," run BOTH istioctl analyze -n <ns> (CLI) AND check Kiali's Validation tab (UI). Different code prefixes (KIA1107 vs IST0101) — same class of checks. Kiali catches the same errors but presents them visually.

11.4 Kiali Wizards — Generate Istio YAML From UI

DEFINITION: a Kiali wizard is a form that outputs standard VirtualService/DestinationRule objects — nothing proprietary; kubectl can read, edit, or delete them like any YAML you wrote. Kiali can generate correct VirtualService + DestinationRule YAML without you writing a single line. Wizards available for:

⚖️
Traffic Shifting

Slide percentage bars → Kiali creates VS with weights + DR with subsets.

🔀
Request Routing

Set header match rules via form → Kiali generates the complete A/B testing YAML.

🐌
Fault Injection

Checkboxes for delay/abort → Kiali creates VirtualService with fault blocks.

⏱️
Request Timeouts

Set HTTP timeout + retry policy per route without hand-typing YAML.

🚫
Traffic Suspension

Click to block traffic → Kiali creates a route with an HTTP 503 response.

💡 Why Wizards Matter

Hand-written canary YAML is the #1 source of subset typos — the wizard reads LIVE pod labels, so the subsets it generates always match running pods. Update or delete wizard-created rules later from the same Actions menu — Kiali labels the objects it manages.

What the Traffic Shifting wizard actually writes — slide the form to 90/10 on jobpost-api, and this is the exact YAML it generates:

yaml — wizard output: Traffic Shifting 90/10 on jobpost-api 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api            # named after the service
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - jobpost-api
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v1
      weight: 90                # slider position → weight
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v2
      weight: 10                # weights must sum to 100
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: jobpost-api
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1                # read from LIVE pod labels
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2

11.5 The Observability Debug Flow — From Alert to Root Cause

DEFINITION: the debug flow is a fixed four-step route through the observability stack: Grafana → Kiali → Jaeger → logs. Without a fixed route you tab-hop between dashboards for an hour; with it, most anihpj incidents go from alert to root cause in minutes. Each tool answers exactly ONE question — never skip a step, or you end up grepping seven services blind instead of one service, one timestamp.

🔍 OBSERVABILITY DEBUG FLOW — 4-Step Pattern
1
Grafana

"WHAT is wrong?"
Which service has high latency?
→ skills-service p99=1,240ms ⚠️

2
Kiali

"WHERE is it?"
Which edge is red?
→ jobpost→skills edge = 🔴 8.1% errors

3
Jaeger

"WHY is it slow?"
Which span is wide?
→ skills-service span = 195ms of 342ms!

4
Logs

"HOW to fix?"
Check app logs at timestamp
→ "Missing index on user_id"

✅ Result: Found root cause (missing DB index) in under 2 minutes using 3 dashboards.

⏱️ WORKED INCIDENT — anihpj p99 Alert, From Page to Fix

TimeTool / ActionFinding
T+0minPagerDuty fires"anihpj p99 > 500ms for 5 minutes"
T+1minGrafanajobpost-api p99 = 234ms ✅ … skills-service p99 = 1240ms 🔴 → suspect found
T+2minKialiEdge jobpost-api → skills-service is red: 89 req/s at 8.1% errors (rest of mesh green)
T+4minJaegerSort by duration, open top trace (342ms): span "SELECT … FROM skills WHERE user_id" = 195ms
T+6minLogskubectl logs deploy/skills-service -n anihpj → psql EXPLAIN: Seq Scan — no index on user_id
T+9minFixpsql: CREATE INDEX idx_skills_user_id ON skills(user_id);
T+12minVerifyGrafana p99 falls 1240ms → 87ms; the Kiali edge turns green; incident closed in 12 minutes
🔍 Deep Dive — Kiali Diagnostic Workflow: A Second Worked Example (6 Steps, Alert → Root Cause)

Same 4-step pattern, a different incident — this time the red edge traces to an external dependency, not a missing index:

  Step 1: Open Kiali → Filter namespace → OBSERVE COLORS
    🟢 Green nodes = healthy (200s, low latency) → SKIP
    🟡 Yellow nodes = degraded (some errors or high latency) → INVESTIGATE
    🔴 Red nodes = failing (high error rate, timeouts) → PRIORITY

  Step 2: HOVER over red node → Quick metrics popup
    RPS: 142 req/s  |  Error %: 37% (was 0.2% before)  →  SOMETHING CHANGED

  Step 3: FOLLOW RED EDGES upstream (who calls the failing service?)
    Click edge jobpost-api → payment-svc: Error % 82%  →  payment-svc is DOWN

  Step 4: DRILL INTO payment-svc node → View detailed metrics
    5xx Rate: 142/min  |  Latency p99: 12s (normally 200ms)  →  TIMEOUT pattern

  Step 5: Click Span → Open Jaeger traces for payment-svc
    Trace shows: payment-svc → Stripe API timing out at 10s  →  EXTERNAL DEPENDENCY

  Step 6: CHECK ISTIO CONFIG → "Istio Config" tab
    Are there validation errors on payment-svc's DestinationRule? →  FIX YAML
🧠 ICA Exam: Kiali Diagnostic Shortcuts

Kiali's Istio Config tab validates ALL of your YAML in one view — it catches: missing subsets, mismatched hosts, expired certs, invalid TLS config. On the ICA exam, if you're told "something is broken," open Kiali FIRST, check the Config tab for validation errors (red X marks), then follow the workflow above.

11.6 Deep Dive — How Kiali Builds the Service Graph

DEFINITION: the service graph is COMPUTED, never configured — Kiali assembles it on every refresh from three live sources. When the graph looks wrong, fix the SOURCE: an empty graph means Prometheus is down or not scraping; missing versions mean pods lack app/version labels; no config badges mean Kiali cannot reach the Istio config.

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  KIALI DATA SOURCES — How the Graph Comes Alive                                 │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │                        KIALI SERVER                                     │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐ │   │
│  │  │ PROMETHEUS       │  │ K8s API          │  │ ISTIO API            │ │   │
│  │  │ (istio_requests_) │  │ (Pods, Services, │  │ (CRD validation)     │ │   │
│  │  │                  │  │  Deployments)    │  │                      │ │   │
│  │  │ Provides:        │  │ Provides:        │  │ Provides:            │ │   │
│  │  │ • Traffic volume │  │ • Pod status     │  │ • YAML validity      │ │   │
│  │  │ • Error rates    │  │ • Label mappings │  │ • Config warnings    │ │   │
│  │  │ • Latency data   │  │ • Service→Pods   │  │ • Best practices     │ │   │
│  │  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘ │   │
│  │           │                      │                      │               │   │
│  │           └──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┘               │   │
│  │                                  ▼                                       │   │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │   │
│  │  │                    SERVICE GRAPH ENGINE                            │  │   │
│  │  │                                                                   │  │   │
│  │  │ 1. Merge: Prometheus flows → build SOURCE→DEST edges              │  │   │
│  │  │ 2. Enrich: K8s API → add pod names, versions, health status       │  │   │
│  │  │ 3. Validate: Istio API → check CRD configs for errors              │  │   │
│  │  │ 4. Score: Compute HEALTH = f(error_rate, latency, availability)   │  │   │
