│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  merged on EVERY refresh (60s default) — nothing here is a one-time snapshot  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🎨 Kiali Health Legend — One Legend for Nodes AND Edges

ColorMeaning — Nodes and Edges
🟢 GreenHealthy — errors under threshold, pods ready
🟠 OrangeDegraded — a small but non-zero error rate (Kiali's own default starts near 0.1%)
🔴 RedFailing — no healthy pods, or error rate above Kiali's default failure threshold (~10%)
⚪ GrayIdle — no traffic in the selected time window
📖 anihpj Gotcha — Zero Traffic Shows Gray, Not Green

Edge thickness is proportional to request volume, and a 🔒 lock icon marks mTLS on that hop. Thresholds are tunable in Kiali's health config — anihpj sets "failing" at 5% errors, which is why skills-service (8.1%) shows RED in this chapter's graphs. A service with zero traffic shows GRAY (idle), not green — edges come from Prometheus counters, so no requests means no edges, even when pods are perfectly fine.

11.7 Installing Kiali — Demo Add-on vs Production-Ready Setup

DEFINITION: Kiali is NOT a core Istio control-plane component — it is an optional observability integration that ships and is installed separately from istiod and the data plane. Three real install paths exist; only two of them are supported for anything beyond a demo cluster. The anihpj kind cluster you study on and a real anihpj production cluster should almost never use the same install method — the quick-start YAML is not hardened.

Install PathProduction-ready? / anihpj uses it for…
samples/addons/kiali.yaml (kubectl apply)❌ Demo only — Istio's own docs call this "not tuned for performance or security" → anihpj: local kind cluster, exam study
kiali-operator (Kubernetes Operator)✅ Production-ready — the Kiali project's own recommended install path → anihpj: staging + production clusters
Helm chart (kiali/kiali-server)✅ Production-ready — fits teams already managing every other Istio addon via Helm → anihpj: same lifecycle as the rest

If you expose the sample install without anonymous auth, update the signing_key value in Kiali's ConfigMap first — every sample install ships with the identical default key.

🔧 Under the Hood — What signing_key Actually Protects

The signing_key is not an Istio or mTLS certificate — it is a secret Kiali's own web server uses to sign the session cookie your browser gets after login, fully separate from anything in the data plane. Because every sample install ships the identical key, anyone who copies it can forge a valid Kiali session against a cluster they never ran kubectl against — rotating it secures only the web console's front door, not mesh traffic or mTLS certificates.

anihpj note: istioctl dashboard kiali behaves the same regardless of which path installed it — the command just port-forwards to whatever Service named kiali it finds, so this is not a decision you need to relearn for the exam.

11.8 Kiali's Validation Categories — What Gets Checked Beyond VS/DR

11.3 showed three real errors, but VirtualService/DestinationRule mistakes are only two of roughly a dozen categories Kiali validates on every refresh. Every Istio object kind Kiali understands has its own set of checks, each with a severity (❌ error, ⚠️ warning, or an informational note) and its own code prefix.

📖 KEY TERM — Validation Category

A group of checks for ONE Istio object kind (Gateway, Sidecar, PeerAuthentication…), sharing a code prefix (KIA0xxx-KIA12xx) and severity; 11.3's two errors came from just ONE category out of roughly a dozen.

Why it matters: exam and real-world misconfigurations don't only hide in VirtualServices — a missing ServiceAccount on an AuthorizationPolicy, an unnamed Service port, or a stale Sidecar egress host are just as common, and each lives on a different tab than the "Istio Config" list you already know. How it works: open a namespace → Istio Config → the object list groups warnings by kind; click any row to jump straight to the offending line, same as the VS/DR examples in 11.3.

📋 Kiali Validation Categories — a Representative Check per Kind

CategoryExample Check Kiali RunsSeverity
AuthorizationPolicyKIA0106 — rule's ServiceAccount principal not found anywhere in the mesh❌ error
DestinationRuleKIA0203 — subset selector labels match zero live pods (a typo'd version: label)❌ error
GatewayKIA0302 — selector matches no workload in this namespace❌ error
PeerAuthenticationKIA0501 — namespace sets STRICT mTLS but no DestinationRule enables ISTIO_MUTUAL to match⚠️ warning
PortsKIA0601 — Service port name skips the required protocol prefix (http-, grpc-, tcp-…)⚠️ warning
ServicesKIA0701 — a Deployment has no Service exposing a matching containerPort⚠️ warning
SidecarKIA1004 — an egress host in a Sidecar resource has no match in the service registry⚠️ warning
VirtualServiceKIA1105 — the same host+subset pair is targeted by two different route rules⚠️ warning
ServiceEntryKIA1211 — two ServiceEntries define the exact same host+port combination⚠️ warning
⚠️ anihpj Gotcha — A Number Isn't a Protocol

skills-service's container port was named "8090" instead of "http-skills" — Istio's protocol sniffing depends on the http-/grpc-/tcp- prefix convention, not the number, so requests were silently treated as raw TCP (no retries, no HTTP-aware routing) until KIA0601 flagged it.

11.9 Graph Types & Traffic Animation — Reading the Graph Correctly

DEFINITION: the Service Graph shown in 11.2 is only ONE of four graph types Kiali can render — Graph Settings lets you change the "altitude" of the picture without leaving the page. Picking the wrong graph type can hide the answer: an App Graph merges v1 and v2 into a single node, so a canary regression that only affects v2 traffic is invisible until you switch to the Versioned App Graph.

🔎 Kiali Graph Types — Pick the Right Altitude for the Question

Graph TypeOne Node =Best anihpj Use Case
App GraphOne app, all versions merged into one nodeDaily morning health scan (fewest nodes, fastest read)
Versioned App GraphOne app VERSION (v1, v2 shown separately)Confirming a canary's v2 slice is healthy before shifting to 100%
Workload GraphOne Kubernetes workload (Deployment/StatefulSet)A specific pod is crash-looping — 1:1 with kubectl get deploy
Service GraphOne Kubernetes Service (highest altitude)The default 11.2 topology view; ideal for onboarding a new engineer

Traffic animation: Graph Settings → Traffic Animation overlays moving dots on every edge so you can watch requests flow without clicking anything. Dot density approximates request volume, a dot that stutters or pauses mid-edge flags a latency spike on that exact hop, and dot color always matches the edge's health color from 11.6's legend.

🎬 TRAFFIC ANIMATION — Reading the Dots on a Live Edge
  Graph Settings → ✅ Traffic Animation

  [jobpost-api]  ··●···●····●··  [skills-service]
                 dots = live requests flowing right now

  Dot spacing → requests/sec (dense dots = high volume)
  Dot stutter → this hop's edge latency just spiked
  Dot color   → matches the edge health color (11.6's legend)

  anihpj tip: turn animation OFF on a >20-service graph — the
  redraw cost makes the whole tab lag; turn it back on only
  for the one edge you are actively debugging
🔧 Under the Hood — Part 6's Hidden Thread: The Coordinates That Carry One Incident Across Three Tools (Ch9 → Ch10 → Ch11 → Fixed)
🧵 One Incident, Three Tools, Five Coordinates

Ch9-11 look like three unrelated tools, but the skills-service incident only closes in 12 minutes (11.5) because ONE small set of coordinates travels with you from screen to screen. Lose one and a 12-minute fix becomes an hour of blind tab-hopping.

┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ① GRAFANA (Ch9) narrows the whole mesh to ONE coordinate:             │
│    service=skills-service, window=last 15 min, p99=1240ms. That is    │
│    the only thing you carry forward — a name and a time window, not   │
│    a saved query.                                                     │
│                                                                       │
│ ② KIALI (Ch11) takes that coordinate as a namespace filter and        │
│    instantly adds a SECOND coordinate Grafana never had: the exact    │
│    CALLER. Grafana graphed skills-service alone; Kiali's graph shows  │
│    the red edge is specifically jobpost-api -> skills-service, 8.1%  │
│    errors — every other inbound edge to skills-service is still       │
│    green, which rules out a mesh-wide problem in one glance.          │
│                                                                       │
│ ③ JAEGER (Ch10) receives both coordinates (the edge, the window) as   │
│    a service+operation search and returns a THIRD coordinate: the     │
│    exact span — SELECT ... FROM skills WHERE user_id, 195ms.         │
│                                                                       │
│ ④ THE WIRE BETWEEN ② AND ③: Kiali's edge panel has a "View Traces"    │
│    button (11.5, step 2->3) that pre-fills Jaeger's search with the  │
│    coordinates Kiali already holds — you never retype a namespace or  │
│    a service name by hand.                                            │
│                                                                       │
│ ⑤ THE FIX (psql CREATE INDEX) happens OUTSIDE all three tools — but   │
│    it is CONFIRMED inside Kiali, because Kiali is the only one of     │
│    the three that redraws itself automatically (11.6) without you    │
│    re-running anything: the SAME red edge from step ② turns green,    │
│    closing the loop back to Grafana's p99 panel from step ①.          │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 ICA Insight: Ch9-11 are not three skills to memorize separately — they are one coordinate system (service → edge → span) that gets more precise at each stop, and Kiali is both the SECOND stop (finds the edge) and the LAST stop (confirms the fix). That dual role is why Kiali closes Part 6 instead of just extending it.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Kiali stores nothing itself — it's a read-mostly UI merging Prometheus, the Kubernetes API, and Istio config into one live picture; deleting Kiali loses no telemetry.
  • The graph is COMPUTED, never configured — when it looks wrong, fix the SOURCE (Prometheus down, missing pod labels, unreachable Istio config), not the graph itself.
  • Zero traffic shows GRAY, not green — edges come from Prometheus counters, so a healthy service with no requests in the time window is indistinguishable from an unmonitored one at a glance.
  • Kiali Validation and istioctl analyze check the same class of problems but aren't interchangeable — Kiali is live/visual/all-namespaces but not scriptable; analyze is CLI/on-demand/scoped but CI/CD-friendly. Use both.
  • Wizard-generated YAML reads LIVE pod labels — it can never typo a subset's version: label the way hand-written YAML can, because it's reading the label directly off running pods.
  • The debug flow is a fixed 4-step route, never skip a step: Grafana (WHAT) → Kiali (WHERE) → Jaeger (WHY) → logs (HOW) — skipping ahead means grepping every service blind instead of one service at one timestamp.
  • The wrong graph "altitude" can hide the answer — an App Graph merges all versions into one node, so a canary-only regression is invisible until you switch to the Versioned App Graph.
  • Kiali is not a core control-plane component — it ships and installs separately from istiod; the sample add-on is demo-only, kiali-operator or Helm are the production-ready paths.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "A gray node means the service is unhealthy." No — gray means IDLE (no traffic in the selected time window), not failing. A perfectly healthy service with zero recent requests still shows gray.
  • "Kiali's Validation tab replaces istioctl analyze." No — they check similar things but serve different jobs: Kiali is live and visual (great for discovery/triage), analyze is scriptable (the only one that fits a CI/CD pre-apply gate). Use both, not either/or.
  • "The App Graph is always the right graph to look at." No — it merges every version of an app into one node, which HIDES a canary-only regression. Switch to the Versioned App Graph when you need to isolate one version's traffic specifically.
  • "Rotating Kiali's signing_key secures mesh traffic." No — signing_key only signs Kiali's own web session cookie. It's completely separate from mTLS certificates and data-plane traffic; rotating it secures the console's front door only.
  • "Kiali validates only VirtualService and DestinationRule." No — roughly a dozen categories are checked on every refresh (AuthorizationPolicy, Gateway, PeerAuthentication, Ports, Sidecar, ServiceEntry, and more), each with its own KIA code prefix.
  • "The sample add-on install is fine for production since it's still 'real' Kiali." No — Istio's own docs explicitly call it "not tuned for performance or security." kiali-operator or the Helm chart are the only supported production paths.
  • "A named port like '8090' is close enough to a protocol prefix." No — protocol detection depends on the http-/grpc-/tcp- STRING prefix convention, not the port number. An unprefixed numeric name gets silently treated as raw TCP — no retries, no HTTP-aware routing.

💼 Chapter 11 — Daily Work Takeaways

  • Open Kiali FIRST when told "something is broken" — scan for red, check the Istio Config tab for validation errors, THEN follow the 4-step debug flow — don't start by grepping logs blind.
  • Default to the App Graph for a fast morning scan, and switch to Versioned App only when isolating one canary version specifically — picking the wrong altitude wastes time re-reading the same graph twice.
  • Prefer the wizard over hand-typed canary YAML whenever the wizard covers the case — it eliminates the #1 source of subset typos by reading live pod labels directly.
  • Run istioctl analyze before opening Kiali, not instead of it — it's instant and scriptable, telling you within seconds whether a problem is CONFIG (analyze catches it) or RUNTIME (it won't) before the graph even finishes loading.
  • Treat ⚠️ warnings and ❌ errors differently — a "two VirtualServices, same host" warning is often an intentional in-progress migration; only errors reliably block traffic. Don't burn incident-response minutes chasing every icon.
  • Turn Traffic Animation off on large graphs and back on only for the one edge under active investigation — it's a real render-time cost, not a free visual.
  • For the ICA exam: know both validation surfaces (Kiali's Validation tab AND istioctl analyze) and their different code-prefix conventions (KIA1107 vs IST0101) — the exam may reference either.
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 11

Seven quick-fire phrase-to-answer mappings — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Which service is unhealthy?" = 🔴 RED nodes/edges in the Kiali graph — not gray (that's idle, not failing)
  • "Validate Istio configuration" = BOTH istioctl analyze -n <ns> AND Kiali's Validation tab
  • "Generate canary/routing YAML fast" = Right-click the service node → the matching wizard (Traffic Shifting/Request Routing/Fault Injection/Timeouts)
  • "Isolate one canary version's health" = Switch from App Graph to Versioned App Graph
  • "Confirm mTLS is active on a connection" = Enable Security display → look for the 🔒 lock icon on the edge
  • "Something's broken, where do I start?" = Kiali FIRST (Config tab for errors), then the 4-step Grafana→Kiali→Jaeger→logs flow
  • "What's checked beyond VS/DR?" = ~12 validation categories, each its own KIA code prefix (AuthorizationPolicy, Gateway, Sidecar, ServiceEntry...)

🧠 Chapter 11 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What does Kiali actually store, and what happens to your telemetry if you delete it?
Show Answer
Answer

Kiali stores NOTHING itself — it's a read-mostly UI over data that already exists in Prometheus, the Kubernetes API, and Istio's own config. Deleting Kiali loses zero telemetry; you just lose the visualization layer.

Explanation

This matters operationally — Kiali can be safely reinstalled, upgraded, or temporarily removed without any data-loss risk, unlike Prometheus (which owns the actual metrics) or Jaeger (which owns the actual spans).

Q2
A service has had zero traffic in the selected time window. What color does its node show in Kiali, and why isn't it green?
Show Answer
Answer

GRAY — idle, not green. Kiali's edges and health scores are computed from Prometheus request counters; no requests means no data to compute a health color from at all, regardless of how healthy the underlying pods actually are.

Explanation

This is a common misread — an engineer scanning quickly might assume gray means "fine" (confusing it with green) or investigate it as broken (confusing it with red), when it actually means "no data in this window."

Q3
Name one thing Kiali's Validation tab can do that istioctl analyze cannot, and one thing analyze can do that Kiali cannot.
Show Answer
Answer

Kiali can validate across ALL namespaces simultaneously in one continuously-live view. istioctl analyze can check an OFFLINE YAML file before it's ever applied, and can be scripted into a CI/CD pipeline via its exit code — Kiali is not scriptable and has no offline mode.

Explanation

This asymmetry is why the ICA exam tip says "if asked to validate configuration, run BOTH" — each tool covers a gap the other has.

Q4
Why can a wizard-generated canary VirtualService never have a subset-label typo, when a hand-written one commonly does?
Show Answer
Answer

The wizard reads the subset's label selector directly off LIVE, currently-running pods — it isn't possible for it to reference a label value that doesn't exist on a real pod, because it never invents the value, it copies it.

Explanation

A hand-written YAML file has no such guardrail — a human can type version: v2 when the actual running pods are labeled version: V2 or canary, and nothing catches it until traffic silently resolves to zero endpoints.

Q5
What are the four steps of the observability debug flow, in order, and what question does each one answer?
Show Answer
Answer

Grafana ("WHAT is wrong?") → Kiali ("WHERE is it?") → Jaeger ("WHY is it slow?") → logs ("HOW do I fix it?"). Each tool answers exactly ONE question in the chain.

Explanation

Skipping a step (e.g. going straight from an alert to grepping logs) means searching blind across every service instead of the one service and timestamp the earlier steps would have already narrowed you to.

Q6
An App Graph shows jobpost-api as one healthy green node, but a specific canary (v2) rollout is actually failing. Why didn't the graph show it?
Show Answer
Answer

The App Graph merges ALL versions of an app into a single node — v1's healthy traffic and v2's failing traffic get averaged together, and if v1 carries most of the volume, the combined node can still read green. Switching to the Versioned App Graph would show v1 and v2 as separate nodes, exposing v2's problem directly.

Explanation

This is exactly why 11.9 warns that picking the wrong graph "altitude" can hide the answer — the App Graph's fewer-nodes convenience is a real tradeoff, not a strictly better default.

Q7
What does Kiali's signing_key actually protect, and what does it NOT protect?
Show Answer
Answer

It signs Kiali's own web session cookie — the secret that proves a browser is legitimately logged into the Kiali console. It does NOT protect mesh traffic, mTLS certificates, or anything in the data plane — it's entirely a web-console concern.

Explanation

Since every sample install ships with the SAME default key, anyone who has ever seen that default can forge a valid session against any cluster running the unrotated sample install — a real, low-effort exposure if the console is reachable.

Q8
Which install path is production-ready for Kiali, and which is explicitly NOT — per Istio's own documentation?
Show Answer
Answer

kiali-operator and the Helm chart (kiali/kiali-server) are both production-ready. The sample add-on (samples/addons/kiali.yaml) is explicitly demo-only — Istio's own docs describe it as "not tuned for performance or security."

Explanation

istioctl dashboard kiali behaves identically regardless of which path installed it — it's not a decision that changes your daily workflow, only your install-time risk posture.

Q9
A Service's container port is named "8090" instead of "http-skills." What does Kiali flag, and what's the real runtime consequence?
Show Answer
Answer

Kiali flags this via the Ports validation category (e.g. KIA0601 — missing protocol prefix). The real consequence: Istio's protocol detection depends on the http-/grpc-/tcp- STRING prefix, not the port number, so this traffic gets silently treated as raw TCP — no retries, no HTTP-aware routing, no L7 metrics.

Explanation

This is the same port-naming rule taught in the Traffic Management chapters, now reappearing as a Kiali VALIDATION category — reinforcing that Kiali's checks aren't Kiali-specific rules, they're the same real Istio behavior surfaced visually.

Q10
How often does Kiali's graph refresh, and what does that refresh interval let you do that a one-time snapshot tool couldn't?
Show Answer
Answer

Every 15 seconds by default. This lets you apply a fix (like a database index) and watch the SAME red edge turn green on its own, live, without re-running any command — Kiali confirms the fix worked in near-real-time, closing the loop back to the original alert.

Explanation

This is exactly the mechanism behind the chapter's worked incident: the graph that first showed the red edge is the SAME graph, refreshed automatically, that later confirms the fix — no separate "did it work" tool is needed.

⚙️ Chapter 11 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
A teammate reports "the mesh looks broken" with no other detail. Task: Name your exact first three actions, in order, with commands.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl analyze -n anihpj
istioctl dashboard kiali

1. Run istioctl analyze first (instant, scriptable — rules config in/out). 2. Open Kiali and check the Istio Config tab for ❌ errors. 3. Scan the Graph tab for red nodes/edges.

Explanation

This ordering (CLI check → Kiali config check → Kiali graph scan) means you know within seconds whether you're chasing a CONFIG problem or a RUNTIME problem before you've spent any real time in the UI.

Q2
A DestinationRule's subset was renamed from "v2" to "canary" but the VirtualService still references "v2." Task: Predict what Kiali shows, then confirm live.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl get destinationrule jobpost-api-dr -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 "name: v2\|name: canary"
kubectl get virtualservice jobpost-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml | grep subset
Explanation

Kiali's Validation tab flags this as a dangling-reference error (11.3's real KIA1107 example) — the VS's "v2" subset reference points at nothing, since the DR no longer defines a subset by that name. Every request routed to that subset fails.

Q3
Use a Kiali wizard (conceptually — describe the exact clicks) to shift 20% of jobpost-api traffic to a v2 canary, without writing any YAML by hand.
Show Answer
Answer

Right-click the jobpost-api node → Traffic Shifting wizard → set the weight slider to 80% v1 / 20% v2 → Apply. Kiali generates a VirtualService with the weighted routes and a DestinationRule with the v1/v2 subsets, reading the subset labels off the live pods.

Explanation

The generated YAML is standard, kubectl-editable Istio config — nothing proprietary. You could achieve the identical result hand-typing YAML; the wizard just removes the label-typo risk.

Q4
Confirm which Service Kiali's dashboard command is actually forwarding to, regardless of how Kiali was installed.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl get svc kiali -n istio-system
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=kiali
Explanation

istioctl dashboard kiali doesn't care whether Kiali came from the sample add-on, kiali-operator, or Helm — it just port-forwards to whatever Service named kiali it finds. This command works identically across all three install paths.

Q5
A sample-add-on Kiali install is about to be exposed outside the cluster for the first time. Task: Name the one config change required first, and why.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl edit configmap kiali -n istio-system
# update the signing_key value — every sample install ships the identical default
Explanation

Without rotating signing_key, anyone who knows the well-known default value (published in every copy of the sample YAML) can forge a valid Kiali session cookie against your specific cluster.

Q6
skills-service's node is RED with 8.1% errors. Walk the debug flow to find root cause — name each tool and what you look for.
Show Answer
Answer

1. Grafana: confirm skills-service's p99/error-rate panel shows the anomaly. 2. Kiali: find the specific red EDGE (which caller is affected) and its live RED metrics. 3. Jaeger: search skills-service, sort by duration, find the widest span. 4. Logs: kubectl logs at that span's timestamp for the actual error detail.

Explanation

Each step narrows the search: Grafana finds the SERVICE, Kiali finds the EDGE (which caller), Jaeger finds the SPAN (which operation), logs find the ROOT CAUSE (why). Skipping any step means re-deriving what that step would have told you, the hard way.

Q7
A namespace-wide PeerAuthentication sets STRICT mTLS, but Kiali flags a KIA0501 warning. What's the likely cause?
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl get destinationrule -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A3 tls

Likely cause: no DestinationRule enables ISTIO_MUTUAL TLS mode to actually match the namespace's STRICT PeerAuthentication policy — the two settings need to correspond for mTLS to function as configured.

Explanation

PeerAuthentication (server-side, what the workload REQUIRES) and DestinationRule TLS mode (client-side, what the caller SENDS) are two different resources that both need to agree — Kiali's KIA0501 exists specifically to catch this mismatch.

Q8
You need to confirm a fix actually worked without re-running any command. What Kiali behavior makes this possible?
Show Answer
Answer

Kiali's graph auto-refreshes every 60 seconds by default (tunable, and can be triggered manually) — after applying a fix, simply wait one refresh cycle and watch the same edge/node transition from red to green live, with zero manual re-querying.

Explanation

This is the exact mechanism behind the chapter's own worked incident (11.5) — the SAME graph that first showed the red edge is what confirms the fix, closing the loop without ever leaving the tab.

Q9
A canary rollout needs isolated health visibility for v2 only, separate from v1's traffic. Which graph type do you switch to, and why?
Show Answer
Answer

Versioned App Graph — it shows each app VERSION as a separate node (v1 and v2 shown independently), unlike the App Graph which merges all versions into one node and would hide a v2-only problem.

Explanation

Graph Settings lets you switch altitude without leaving the page — no need to reconfigure Kiali or apply any new YAML, just a UI toggle.

Q10
Two ServiceEntries accidentally define the exact same host+port combination. Which Kiali validation category catches this, and what severity?
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl get serviceentry -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A2 hosts

The ServiceEntry validation category (e.g. KIA1211), flagged as a ⚠️ warning — not a hard error, but worth resolving since it can lead to unpredictable resolution behavior.

Explanation

This is one of roughly a dozen validation categories beyond VirtualService/DestinationRule (11.8) — each Istio object kind Kiali understands has its own dedicated set of checks and code-prefix range.

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 11
  • Scan for red first: on a graph with 20+ nodes, ignore every green and gray node and jump straight to the one red edge — Kiali's whole value is that you read ONE broken connection, not all seven anihpj services.
  • Trust the wizard over hand-typed YAML: a wizard-generated subset can never typo a version: label because it reads that label off LIVE pods (11.4) — reserve hand-written VirtualServices for the cases a wizard does not cover.
  • Read ⚠️ warnings differently from ❌ errors: a KIA1106 "two VirtualServices, same host" warning is often an intentional in-progress migration, not a bug — only ❌ errors reliably block traffic, so do not burn exam-clock minutes chasing every icon.
  • Run istioctl analyze -n anihpj before opening Kiali: it is scriptable and instant, so you already know whether a problem is CONFIG (analyze catches it) or RUNTIME (analyze will not) before the graph even loads.
  • Default to the App Graph for a fast morning scan (fewest nodes, fastest read) and switch to the Versioned App Graph only when you need to isolate one canary version's traffic (11.9).
  • Turn Traffic Animation off on any graph bigger than ~20 services and back on only for the one edge you are actively debugging (11.9) — it is a nice-to-have that costs render time mid-incident.

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 11)

Every command below already appeared earlier in this chapter — grouped here as one reference for driving Kiali install, validation, and edge-debugging tasks.

istioctl dashboard kialiOpen Kiali; port-forwards to the kiali Service (11.1, 11.7)

🧪 Practice Drill 11.1 — Turn the Red Edge Green

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Run this against your own anihpj kind cluster right now:

  1. (2 min) istioctl dashboard kiali, select the anihpj namespace, and open the Graph tab.
  2. (2 min) Find the red edge jobpost-api → skills-service, click it, and write down its req/s, error %, and p99.
  3. (2 min) Open the Istio Config tab and confirm whether any ❌ errors are present right now.
  4. (1 min) Apply 11.5's fix — CREATE INDEX idx_skills_user_id ON skills(user_id); — against skills-service's database.
  5. (1 min) Wait one Kiali refresh cycle (60 seconds by default, 11.6 — or trigger a manual refresh) and confirm the same edge has turned green.
Hint: Steps 1-2 reuse 11.2's graph-reading reflex; step 3 is the same validation check from 11.3/11.8; steps 4-5 prove Kiali is a LIVE picture, not a snapshot — the same 15-second-refresh fact 11.6 explains, and the same reflex a Domain 4 troubleshooting task expects cold.
View Solution

Step 5 should show the edge transitioning from red to green with NO manual re-query — if it doesn't within 1-2 refresh cycles, the index creation likely didn't target the right table/column, or you're looking at a cached browser tab that needs a manual reload.

Check yourself: did you write down the BEFORE numbers in step 2, or only look at the AFTER state? Without a concrete before/after comparison, you can't actually prove the fix worked — you can only observe that the color changed.

🧪 Practice Drill 11.2 — Reproduce the Gray-vs-Green Confusion Yourself

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Don't take 11.6's "zero traffic shows gray, not green" claim on faith — confirm it live.

  1. Identify a healthy anihpj service that's currently receiving traffic — confirm its node is green.
  2. Scale that service's callers to 0 (or otherwise stop traffic to it) and wait for the current time window to roll past the last real request.
  3. Refresh the Kiali graph and observe the node's new color.
  4. Restore traffic and confirm the node returns to green once new requests start flowing.
Hint: If Kiali's time window is set to "Last 1 hour," you may need to wait, or narrow the window to "Last 1 minute," to see the transition to gray happen quickly.
View Solution

Step 3 should show the node turn GRAY, not stay green — confirming that Kiali's health color is entirely traffic-derived, not a static "is this pod running" check. Step 4 should show it return to green as soon as new traffic starts flowing again.

Check yourself: could you now explain to a teammate, using your own before/during/after screenshots, why a perfectly healthy but idle service is NOT the same as a green service in Kiali's model? That's the distinction this drill is built to make concrete.

🧪 Practice Drill 11.3 — Match the Symptom to the Broken Layer

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

For each observation, name the most likely cause and the ONE command or click you'd use to confirm it — before proposing any fix:

  1. A service's node is gray even though you're certain real traffic is flowing to it right now.
  2. The App Graph shows jobpost-api as fully green, but users report canary-specific errors.
  3. Kiali's graph loads with zero nodes or edges at all for a namespace you know has running pods.
  4. A newly-applied ServiceEntry doesn't show any validation warning, even though it duplicates an existing host+port pair.
Hint: One of these four is NOT actually a Kiali bug at all — it's working exactly as designed, and the "problem" is a misunderstanding of what triggers a check.
View Solution
#CauseConfirm with
1The Kiali time-window filter is set too narrow, or Prometheus itself isn't scraping/reachable — check the source, not the graphWiden the time window; separately confirm Prometheus is up
2App Graph merges all versions into one node — the canary's errors are averaged away by v1's healthy volumeSwitch to Versioned App Graph
3Kiali can't reach Prometheus, the K8s API, or both — the graph engine has no source data to mergeCheck Kiali pod logs and its ConfigMap's Prometheus URL
4Not a bug — the validation may simply not have run yet, or the specific KIA check for duplicate ServiceEntry hosts may be a warning-only category that's easy to miss in a long listManually check kubectl get serviceentry -A -o yaml \| grep -A2 hosts for real duplicates

Check yourself: did you correctly identify #4 as "working as designed, easy to overlook" rather than assuming Kiali silently failed? Distinguishing a real tool failure from a check you simply didn't notice is a genuine diagnostic skill.

🧪 Practice Drill 11.4 — Install Kiali the Production Way, Then Prove the Demo Path Would Have Been Wrong

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Compare the demo add-on and a production install path side by side, conceptually and where possible live:

  1. Read the sample add-on YAML (samples/addons/kiali.yaml) and identify what's missing compared to a hardened install (auth config, resource limits, the shared default signing_key).
  2. Install via kiali-operator or the Helm chart on a test cluster instead.
  3. Compare: does istioctl dashboard kiali behave any differently depending on which path you used?
  4. Confirm the ConfigMap's signing_key differs between a fresh Helm/operator install and a fresh sample-add-on install.
Hint: Step 3's answer should be "no" — this is the whole point of 11.7's note that istioctl dashboard kiali doesn't care how Kiali was installed, it just finds the Service.
View Solution

Step 1 should surface the shared default signing_key as the most exam-relevant gap. Step 3 should confirm the dashboard command's behavior is identical either way — the install path is purely a security/production-readiness decision, not a workflow decision.

Check yourself: did you check the ACTUAL signing_key value in step 4, or just assume Helm/operator installs randomize it? Verifying assumptions instead of trusting documentation summaries is the actual habit this drill is rehearsing.

🧪 Practice Drill 11.5 — Sketch the Three-Tool Coordinate Handoff From Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking back at the UTH's diagram, sketch (on paper or in a text file) what "coordinate" each tool adds to the skills-service incident, and how it hands off to the next tool.

  1. What's the ONE coordinate Grafana narrows the whole mesh down to?
  2. What SECOND coordinate does Kiali add that Grafana never had?
  3. What THIRD coordinate does Jaeger add, and what carries the first two coordinates INTO Jaeger's search?
  4. Which tool CONFIRMS the fix, and how, without you re-running anything?
Hint: This is a paper/whiteboard drill — the point is retrieving the mental model from memory under light time pressure, the same way the exam expects you to reason about a multi-tool incident without three dashboards open in front of you.
View Solution

(1) Grafana narrows to a service name + time window (service=skills-service, p99=1240ms). (2) Kiali adds the exact CALLER — the specific red edge (jobpost-api → skills-service), ruling out a mesh-wide problem. (3) Jaeger adds the exact SPAN (the 195ms skills-service span inside the 342ms trace) — Kiali's "View Traces" button carries the edge/window into Jaeger's search automatically, no retyping. (4) Kiali confirms the fix — because it's the only one of the three that redraws itself automatically without you re-running anything, the same red edge from step 2 turning green closes the loop.

Check yourself: did your sketch correctly identify Kiali's DUAL role (second stop AND last stop)? Missing that it appears twice in the flow is the most common gap in recalling this diagram from memory.

💼 Chapters 9-11 — Daily Work Takeaways (Observability)

  • Check Grafana every morning: RED metrics for all anihpj services
  • Know which service is slowest, which has the most errors, at a glance
  • Use Jaeger to trace a slow request across ALL services in one view
  • Find bottlenecks: "skills-service span takes 195ms of a 342ms trace → add index"
  • Use Kiali service graph as your daily dashboard — see live topology
  • Validate Istio config with istioctl analyze before applying
  • Kiali can catch: missing subsets, port mismatches, VS without DR
  • Remember: metrics = WHAT, traces = WHY, logs = DETAILS
  • Propagate Istio tracing headers in your Django code (x-b3-* headers)
  • Set tracing sampling: 100% in dev, 1-5% in production
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapters 9-11 (Observability — feeds Troubleshooting 20%)

Observability is not its own graded domain; it is how you FIND the root cause tested by Troubleshooting (20%). Skipping this chapter cluster costs you there instead:

  • "Check RED metrics for a service" = Grafana Istio dashboards
  • "Find why a request is slow across services" = Jaeger distributed tracing
  • "See live service topology" = Kiali service graph
  • "Validate Istio config" = istioctl analyze -n <namespace>

📝 Chapters 9-11 — ICA Exam Questions (Observability)

Q1
How do you open the Kiali dashboard?
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl dashboard kiali
Explanation

This single command port-forwards to whichever Service named kiali is running, regardless of which install path (11.7) put it there — the same reflex as istioctl dashboard grafana/jaeger/prometheus from Chapters 9-10.

Q2
What are the three RED metrics Istio captures automatically?
Show Answer
Answer

Rate (requests/sec), Errors (4xx/5xx %), Duration (latency p50/p95/p99).

Explanation

RED is the three-number vocabulary every dashboard in Part 6 speaks — Grafana panels, Kiali node/edge colors, and Jaeger span tags are all just different VIEWS onto the same three Envoy-collected numbers (9.2, 11.2).

Q3
How does Istio enable distributed tracing without code changes?
Show Answer
Answer

Envoy automatically injects tracing headers (x-b3-traceid, x-b3-spanid) into every request. Your app just needs to propagate these headers.

Explanation

Envoy does the 80% — creating spans and injecting headers — automatically; your Django code's only remaining job is the critical 20%: forward the headers unchanged on every outbound call (10.5). Skip that and Jaeger shows disconnected 1-span traces instead of one chain.

Q4
Jaeger shows ZERO traces for the anihpj namespace. Walk the debug chain that finds the cause.
Show Answer
Answer

Check, cheapest first:

1) Generate traffic — traces only exist for sampled requests:

for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null http://$GATEWAY_IP/api/jobs/
done

2) Sampling too low? kubectl get telemetry -A — at the default 1% you need ~100 requests to see a single trace.
3) Tracing provider configured? Check meshConfig.extensionProviders + a Telemetry resource that references it.
4) App dropping headers? Verify x-b3-* propagation (see Q10).

Explanation

No sampling, no provider, or dropped headers all produce an empty Jaeger — this order tests them fastest.

Q5
EXAM TASK: set trace sampling to 100% for the anihpj namespace only, leaving the mesh-wide default untouched.
Show Answer
Answer

Apply a namespace-scoped Telemetry resource:

apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: full-sampling
  namespace: anihpj   # ← scope = this ns
spec:
  tracing:
  - randomSamplingPercentage: 100
Explanation

A Telemetry object in a workload namespace overrides the mesh default only there — dev debugging gets every trace while production namespaces keep their cheap 1-5%.

Q6
EXAM TASK: add a "request_host" label to istio_requests_total for anihpj workloads, without touching application code.
Show Answer
Answer

Use the Telemetry API's tagOverrides:

apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: custom-labels
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  metrics:
  - providers:
    - name: prometheus
    overrides:
    - match:
        metric: REQUEST_COUNT  # requests_total
      tagOverrides:
        request_host:
          value: request.host  # CEL expression
Explanation

Envoy stamps the new label on every sample; Prometheus picks it up from the merged metrics endpoint (istio-agent :15020) on the next scrape — zero app redeploys.

Q7
EXAM TASK: enable Envoy access logs for the anihpj namespace only, then read jobpost-api's access log.
Show Answer
Answer

Apply namespace-scoped access logging:

apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: access-logs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessLogging:
  - providers:
    - name: envoy

Then read the log:

kubectl logs deploy/jobpost-api -c istio-proxy -n anihpj
Explanation

A namespace-scoped Telemetry beats mesh-wide meshConfig.accessLogFile — you pay the log volume only in the namespace you are debugging.

Q8
Kiali shows a red edge from jobpost-api to skills-service. Give the triage sequence.
Show Answer
Answer

1) Click the edge → per-hop RED metrics: 89 req/s, 8.1% errors, p99 1240ms.
2) Check OTHER inbound edges to skills-service — all red means a callee (skills-service) problem; only this one red means a caller (jobpost-api) problem.
3) Edge panel → "View Traces" → Jaeger opens pre-filtered on this hop; open the widest span.
4) Confirm in the proxy log:

kubectl logs deploy/skills-service -c istio-proxy \
  -n anihpj | grep " 503 "
Explanation

Edge → traces → logs narrows topology → request → cause without ever guessing.

Q9
Alert: "istiod config push latency high, proxies STALE." What do you check, in order?
Show Answer
Answer

1) Grafana → Istio Control Plane Dashboard: istiod CPU/memory, push latency, connected proxy count.
2) istioctl proxy-status — any proxy not SYNCED for CDS/LDS/EDS/RDS is running on stale routing config.
3) kubectl top pod -n istio-system -l app=istiod (at its limit?).
4) Fix — scale out or raise limits:

kubectl scale deploy/istiod -n istio-system --replicas=2
Explanation

STALE proxies silently ignore new VirtualServices — a routing change that "does nothing" is often an istiod push problem, not a YAML problem.

Q10
Jaeger shows every anihpj service as its own one-span trace instead of one connected chain. Fix it in the Django code.
Show Answer
Answer

The apps are dropping trace context between inbound and outbound calls. Propagate the B3 headers:

# anihpj/tracing.py
TRACE_HEADERS = ["x-request-id", "x-b3-traceid",
    "x-b3-spanid", "x-b3-parentspanid",
    "x-b3-sampled", "x-b3-flags"]

def trace_headers(request):
    return {h: request.headers[h]
            for h in TRACE_HEADERS
            if h in request.headers}

# jobpost/views.py — pass context downstream
requests.get(
    "http://skills-service:8090/api/skills/",
    headers=trace_headers(request))
Explanation

Envoy creates a span per hop, but only the APP can link an inbound request to its outbound calls — forwarding x-b3-* joins the per-hop spans into one end-to-end trace.

Chapter 12: Mutual TLS (mTLS) — Encrypting Everything

Inside a Kubernetes cluster, traffic is plain HTTP by default. Any compromised pod can sniff passwords, tokens, and PII from other services. Istio's mTLS encrypts ALL service-to-service traffic automatically — without changing a single line of code.

"Every anihpj pod says 'trust me' over the wire — who, cryptographically, is actually calling?" Parts 5 and 6 made anihpj's traffic fast and visible — Gateways, canary VirtualServices, circuit-breaking DestinationRules, Kiali graphs, Jaeger traces — but every one of those beautifully instrumented hops still travels as plain, unauthenticated HTTP between pods, and any pod that lands on the same node can tcpdump the lot. Chapter 12 is the first time anihpj gets a REAL identity: not a Pod name, not an IP, but an unforgeable SPIFFE X.509 certificate that says exactly which ServiceAccount issued this request, minted and rotated by istiod without touching a line of Django. By 12.13 every one of jobpost-api, user-service, skills-service, location-service, notification-service, auth-service, and search-service will hold — and prove — its own cryptographic identity on every single hop. Chapter 13 then spends that identity to decide who may call whom; none of that is possible until Chapter 12 establishes WHO everyone is.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔒 Security 🎯 ICA 25%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Explain why plaintext service-to-service HTTP is a sniffing, impersonation, and lateral-movement risk — even "internal" traffic
  • ✅ Configure PeerAuthentication in PERMISSIVE, STRICT, DISABLE, and UNSET modes at mesh, namespace, and workload scope, and predict which one wins when scopes overlap
  • ✅ Trace the full certificate lifecycle: CSR at pod startup, istiod (Citadel CA) issuance, SDS delivery to Envoy, and grace-period-ratio rotation around the 12-hour mark
  • ✅ Read a SPIFFE ID (spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api) and name which segment is the trust domain, namespace, and ServiceAccount
  • ✅ Tell an mTLS failure (TCP reset, no HTTP code at all) apart from an AuthorizationPolicy failure (HTTP 403 RBAC) using istioctl x describe pod and istioctl proxy-config secret
  • ✅ Explain the DestinationRule/PeerAuthentication TLS contract and why a stale tls.mode: DISABLE causes 503s the moment STRICT is enabled
  • ✅ Describe auto mTLS (Istio 1.5+) and identify when an external CA (plug-in certs, SPIRE, cert-manager) should replace istiod's built-in CA
🎓 ICA Relevance
Security 25%
💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 12
  • "Encrypt all service traffic" = PeerAuthentication mode: STRICT (12.3, 12.6)
  • TCP reset with no HTTP code = mTLS problem; HTTP 403 "RBAC: access denied" = AuthorizationPolicy problem (Chapter 13) — never debug the wrong CRD (12.7)
  • 503 (flag UC) right after flipping STRICT = 9 times out of 10 a stale DestinationRule with tls.mode: DISABLE (12.8)
  • "Why does mTLS work with zero DestinationRules?" = auto mTLS — Pilot wires ISTIO_MUTUAL automatically whenever both sidecars exist (12.12)
  • Certificate rotation timing = ~12 hours (the 0.5 grace-period ratio of a 24h cert), NOT "5 minutes before expiry" (12.13)
  • Remember: mTLS = identity (WHO); AuthorizationPolicy = permissions (WHAT) — Chapter 13 picks up right where this chapter ends

🧭 Section Map — the Chapter 12 Learning Arc

Sections 12.1 through 12.13 read as one continuous build in four groups: first you name WHY plaintext traffic fails and WHAT mTLS actually proves, then you turn it on and learn how its certificates are born, then you harden that identity against impersonation and learn to troubleshoot it, and finally six deep dives — difficulty steps up to 🔴 from 12.10 on — go under the hood on everything left: the DR/PA contract, external CAs, the UNSET mode, SPIFFE anatomy, auto mTLS, and the real rotation numbers.
