Read it as one sentence: 12.1-12.2 name the problem and the concept, 12.3-12.4 turn mTLS on and explain how its certificates are born, 12.5-12.7 harden that identity against impersonation and teach you to troubleshoot it, and 12.8-12.13 go under the hood on everything left — the DR/PA contract, external CAs, the UNSET mode, SPIFFE anatomy, auto mTLS, and rotation timing.

SectionAnswers the question…One-line takeaway
12.1 The Security Problem Without mTLSWhat can a compromised pod do on plaintext anihpj traffic?Sniff JWTs/PII, impersonate a service, or move laterally — one foothold reaches the whole mesh.
12.2 What is Mutual TLS?How is mTLS different from the TLS your browser already uses?BOTH sides present a SPIFFE X.509 cert, not just the server.
12.3 PeerAuthentication — mTLS ModesHow do I actually turn mTLS on?PERMISSIVE for migration, STRICT to enforce, DISABLE to debug.
12.4 Certificate LifecycleWho issues and renews every workload's certificate?istiod's CSR→sign→SDS pipeline, rotated at the ~12h grace-period mark, not moments before expiry.
12.5 Secure NamingCan a valid certificate alone let an attacker impersonate a service?No — istiod's secure-naming map also checks the SPIFFE ID matches the service being dialed.
12.6 PeerAuthentication Policy HierarchyWhich PeerAuthentication wins when mesh, namespace, and workload overlap?Narrowest scope always wins: workload beats namespace beats mesh.
12.7 mTLS TroubleshootingIs this a TCP reset or an HTTP 403 — and does that matter?TCP reset = mTLS; HTTP 403 RBAC = AuthorizationPolicy (Ch13) — never debug the wrong CRD.
12.8 Deep Dive — The DR/PA TLS ContractWhy does STRICT mode suddenly cause 503s?A stale DestinationRule tls.mode disagrees with the server's PeerAuthentication mode.
12.9 Deep Dive — External CAs: SPIRE & Plug-in CAWhen should istiod's built-in CA be replaced?FIPS/HSM/PKI-federation requirements point to plug-in CA certs, SPIRE, or cert-manager (istio-csr).
12.10 The Fourth Mode — UNSETWhat does an empty mtls.mode field actually mean?UNSET = inherit the parent scope; the mechanism behind 12.6's hierarchy.
12.11 SPIFFE Identity AnatomyWhat do the four parts of a SPIFFE ID mean?scheme + trust domain + namespace + ServiceAccount — bound to the SA, never the Pod.
12.12 Auto mTLSWhy does mTLS work with zero hand-written DestinationRules?Pilot auto-fills ISTIO_MUTUAL client-side whenever the destination has a sidecar.
12.13 Certificate TTL and Rotation InternalsWhen exactly does a workload cert rotate?~12 hours in (the 0.5 grace-period ratio), plus jitter — never "5 minutes before expiry."

12.1 The Security Problem Without mTLS

Without Istio, your Kubernetes cluster has three critical attack vectors open right now:

🔴 WITHOUT ISTIO — 3 Attack Vectors Open
👃
ATTACK 1: Sniffing

Rogue pod on same node runs tcpdump → captures all plain HTTP between services. JWT tokens, passwords, PII — all visible in plaintext.

🎭
ATTACK 2: Impersonation

Attacker deploys a pod named "user-service" → jobpost-api connects to the fake service → returns fake data, steals real requests.

🦶
ATTACK 3: Lateral Movement

Compromised skills-service calls user-service → exfiltrates ALL user data. Any service can call any other service.

🟢 WITH ISTIO — All 3 Attacks Blocked
🔒
DEFENSE 1: mTLS

All traffic encrypted. Rogue pod sees only binary garbage. SPIFFE certificates auto-issued by istiod.

🪪
DEFENSE 2: SPIFFE Identity

Fake service has no valid certificate. Envoy rejects: "Not spiffe://.../ns/anihpj/sa/user-service".

🚫
DEFENSE 3: AuthzPolicy

AuthorizationPolicy: ALLOW from jobpost-api ONLY → skills-service request → 403 Forbidden.

Bundle those gaps together and a single foothold on the node/network — with mTLS off — buys an attacker four separate capabilities, side by side:

🧰 ATTACKER'S TOOLKIT — 4 Things a Foothold Buys You Without mTLS
1. 🔍 Sniffing

tcpdump reads plaintext body + creds ❌

2. 🎭 Fake Svc

fake pod claims "user-service" — no ID check ❌

3. 😈 MITM

intercept + modify traffic undetected ❌

4. 🚪 Lateral

foothold = full mesh reach, no extra ID ❌

The real question is scope: how far does ONE compromised pod's damage spread? Compare anihpj's blast radius before Istio's STRICT mTLS is on vs after:

💥 BLAST RADIUS — One Compromised Pod, Before vs After STRICT mTLS
SCENARIO: attacker gets remote code execution inside the skills-service
pod (e.g. a vulnerable dependency) — the SAME compromised pod in both
panels below

BEFORE — no PeerAuthentication STRICT mode (blast radius = WHOLE mesh)

  😈 skills-service (compromised)
       │   plaintext HTTP, zero identity check on any hop
       ├──▶ jobpost-api    ✅ reachable — traffic readable & spoofable
       ├──▶ user-service   ✅ reachable — traffic readable & spoofable
       └──▶ postgres       ✅ reachable — DB creds sniffed in cleartext

  BLAST RADIUS: every anihpj service the attacker can now read or spoof

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

AFTER — PeerAuthentication mode: STRICT (blast radius = ONE identity)

  😈 skills-service (compromised)
       │   every hop now demands mTLS + a valid SPIFFE certificate
       ├──▶ jobpost-api    ✅ its own, already-allowed call — unchanged
       ├──▶ user-service   ✅ its own, already-allowed call — unchanged
       └──▶ postgres       ❌ tries "I am jobpost-api" — but its Envoy
            can only present ONE cert: spiffe://.../ns/anihpj/sa/
            skills-service (SDS-issued, can't be faked). AuthzPolicy:
            ALLOW postgres callers = jobpost-api ONLY → ❌ 403 REJECTED

  BLAST RADIUS: only what skills-service's own identity could already
  reach — it can never borrow jobpost-api's or user-service's identity

12.2 What is Mutual TLS (mTLS)?

Regular TLS: server proves identity to client (like HTTPS websites). Mutual TLS: BOTH sides prove identity to each other. Istio issues X.509 SVID certificates (SPIFFE standard) to every workload automatically.

🤝 mTLS HANDSHAKE — What Happens in Every Service Call
1
Envoy(jobpost)

"Hello, I am jobpost-api"
Presents SPIFFE cert (SVID)

2
Envoy(user)

"I am user-service"
Presents SPIFFE cert (SVID)

3
Verify

Both verify with istiod
Cert: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api

4
Encrypt

mTLS tunnel established 🔒
GET /users/42 sent encrypted

✅
Done!

Zero code change in Django!
Certs auto-rotate every 24h

📖 SPIFFE Identity Format

Each certificate contains: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api-serviceaccount. This identifies the service, not the node or IP. Even if an attacker gets the same IP, they can't get the same SPIFFE identity without the certificate.

12.3 PeerAuthentication — Configuring mTLS Mode

PeerAuthentication is the Istio CRD that controls mTLS. Three modes: PERMISSIVE (migration), STRICT (enforce), DISABLE (debug only).

yaml — PeerAuthentication for anihpj 

# Enforce STRICT mTLS for entire anihpj namespace
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT       # ALL traffic must use mTLS
                       # Plain HTTP will be REJECTED

# Per-workload: only user-service requires STRICT
---
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: user-service-mtls
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: user-service
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT
🔄 MIGRATION PATH — PERMISSIVE → STRICT
Week 1
PERMISSIVE
Accept both HTTP + mTLS
No disruption
Week 2
STRICT per namespace
Non-sidecar → connection reset (never 403)
Fix: inject sidecars
RESULT
All traffic encrypted ✅
Kiali shows lock icons
Zero Django code changes

12.4 Certificate Lifecycle — How istiod Issues Certs

Every pod gets an X.509 certificate at startup from istiod's built-in CA. Certs default to a 24-hour TTL but rotate around the 12-hour mark — no manual renewal needed. (The exact mechanics — grace-period ratio and jitter — are 12.13's deep dive.)

🔄 CERTIFICATE LIFECYCLE — Full Flow for anihpj
T=0
Pod Deployed

kubectl apply → Pod created

0.1s
Sidecar Injected

Webhook adds istio-proxy

0.3s
CSR Sent

Proxy → istiod:15012
spiffe://.../sa/jobpost-api

0.5s
Cert Issued

istiod validates SA → signs X.509 cert (24h expiry)

0.7s
mTLS Ready

Cert in-memory. All calls now use mTLS!

~12h
Auto-Rotate

Grace-period ratio (0.5) reached → new CSR → new cert → seamless!

Certificate delivery rides SDS (Secret Discovery Service) — a gRPC streaming API istio-agent exposes to its own sidecar over a local Unix Domain Socket, not a file istiod writes to disk. Envoy holds the cert and private key in memory only, and SDS PUSHES the replacement the instant istio-agent gets a new one — which is why rotation is a live swap, zero pod restart required.

💡 Cert Anatomy

Subject: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api-serviceaccount

Issuer: istiod (cluster.local root CA) · Valid: 24 hours · SANs: SPIFFE URI

Rotation: default 24h TTL, renewed once the grace-period ratio (0.5) elapses — around the 12-hour mark, NOT moments before expiry. Zero downtime. You never need to manually renew certificates. (Full numbers, including the ±15-minute jitter added since Istio 1.24: see 12.13.)

12.5 Secure Naming — Preventing Service Impersonation

Secure naming is a critical Istio security concept from the official docs. It answers: "Is this SPIFFE identity allowed to run this service?" Without it, an attacker with a valid certificate for one service could impersonate another.

How the map itself gets built and enforced: istiod watches every Service and the ServiceAccounts behind it, compiles a secure-naming map of "which SPIFFE identities are authorized to serve which service names," and pushes that map to every client Envoy over xDS — the SAME discovery channel that delivers routing and cluster config. When a client Envoy receives a peer's SVID during the handshake, it compares the presented identity against this pushed map before trusting the connection, not just checking that the certificate is validly signed.

🎭 IMPERSONATION ATTACK — How Secure Naming Defeats It
ATTACK SCENARIO:
  Attacker compromises test-team's service account → gets valid SPIFFE cert
  Attacker deploys fake user-service pod with test-team's cert
  DNS spoofing redirects jobpost-api traffic to fake user-service

WITHOUT Secure Naming:  ❌ Attack succeeds
  jobpost-api Envoy sees valid SPIFFE cert → trusts it → sends data

WITH Secure Naming:     ✅ Attack BLOCKED
  jobpost-api Envoy checks: "Is spiffe://.../sa/test-team authorized
  to run user-service?"
  → istiod's secure naming map says: NO. Only spiffe://.../sa/user-service
    is authorized to run user-service.
  → Connection REJECTED — authentication fails!

🔑 Secure Naming Map (maintained by istiod):
  spiffe://.../sa/jobpost-api  → jobpost-api  ✅
  spiffe://.../sa/user-service → user-service ✅
  spiffe://.../sa/test-team    → test-service ✅
  spiffe://.../sa/test-team    → user-service ❌ NOT AUTHORIZED
💡 ICA Exam Relevance

While secure naming is automatic in Istio (istiod maintains the mapping, Envoy enforces it), understanding it helps answer questions about "why can't an attacker impersonate a service even with a valid certificate?" The answer: Secure naming — the SPIFFE identity must match the service name in istiod's registry.

12.6 PeerAuthentication Policy Hierarchy — Mesh → Namespace → Workload

From the official docs: PeerAuthentication policies follow a strict narrowest-match-wins hierarchy. Understanding this prevents configuration surprises:

ScopeSelectorApplies ToPriority
Mesh-wideNo selector, root namespaceALL workloads in meshLowest (fallback)
Namespace-wideNo selector, specific namespaceAll workloads in that namespaceMedium
Workload-specificselector.matchLabels: setOnly matching podsHighest (overrides all)
⚠️ Key Rules from Official Docs

Only ONE mesh-wide and ONE namespace-wide PeerAuthentication can exist. If you create multiple, newer ones are IGNORED. Workload-specific policies can coexist — the oldest one wins when multiple match. This is different from RequestAuthentication, where ALL matching policies are combined.

🥇 POLICY PRECEDENCE — Narrowest Match Wins, Worked Example
  Pod: user-service-6b9c…  (app: user-service, ns: anihpj)

  candidate policies:                            mode
  ① MESH-WIDE   istio-system, no selector       PERMISSIVE
  ② NAMESPACE   anihpj, no selector             STRICT
  ③ WORKLOAD    selector app: user-service      DISABLE
                (legacy port exemption)

  precedence:  ③ beats ② beats ①
  → effective mode for THIS pod:  DISABLE   (from ③)
  → every other anihpj pod:       STRICT    (from ②)
  → pods in other namespaces:     PERMISSIVE (from ①)

  delete ③ → pod falls back to ②  (STRICT)
  delete ② → namespace falls back to ①  (PERMISSIVE)
  delete ① → Istio built-in default:  PERMISSIVE

The same three scopes, side by side as one manifest set — same CRD, three different reaches:

yaml — 3-scope PeerAuthentication: mesh, namespace, workload 
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1   # v1 GA since Istio 1.22
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: istio-system    # root namespace = MESH-WIDE
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: PERMISSIVE          # mesh-level fallback
---
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: anihpj          # no selector = NAMESPACE-WIDE
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT              # all of anihpj must use mTLS
---
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: legacy-batch-exempt
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: legacy-batch        # selector = WORKLOAD scope
  mtls:
    mode: PERMISSIVE          # this ONE app may still get
                               # plaintext (overrides STRICT)

12.7 mTLS Troubleshooting — Common Scenarios and Solutions

Three golden rules cut most mTLS incidents down to a single command before you touch any YAML:

⚠️ Golden Rule 1 — TCP Reset, Not HTTP 403

STRICT mode rejects plaintext at the TCP layer — the caller sees "connection reset by peer," never an HTTP status code at all. If you see a 403 "RBAC: access denied" instead, the problem is an AuthorizationPolicy (Chapter 13), not mTLS.

⚠️ Golden Rule 2 — The Stale DestinationRule

A 503 (response flag UC) minutes after enabling STRICT almost always means a stale DestinationRule still says tls.mode: DISABLE on the client side — the full contract is 12.8's deep dive.

⚠️ Golden Rule 3 — Measure Before Guessing

Four modern probes, fastest first: istioctl x describe pod, istioctl proxy-config secret, Kiali's lock icons, and a raw openssl s_client handshake.

🔴 Symptom🔍 Root Cause✅ Fix
503 (flag UC) right after enabling STRICTStale DestinationRule with tls.mode: DISABLE (client)Set tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL or delete the tls block entirely
curl: "connection reset by peer" — NOT an HTTP 403!Plaintext hit a STRICT port — mTLS rejects at the TCP layerInject sidecar into the caller pod; or PERMISSIVE while migrating
Sidecar-less pod can't reach anihpj servicesSTRICT demands a client SVID cert it does not haveLabel namespace istio-injection=enabled + rollout restart
Calls OK from namespace A, fail from namespace BPeerAuthentication scope differs between namespacesAlign PeerAuthentication; check istioctl x describe pod
HTTP 403 "RBAC: access denied"NOT mTLS! An AuthorizationPolicy denied the callerFix the AuthorizationPolicy (Chapter 13)
TLS handshake fails, cert expiredistiod down >24h — no CSR renewals happenedRestore istiod; restart pod for a fresh CSR + cert
bash — mTLS verification toolbox (modern commands only) 
# 1 — one-shot mTLS posture of a pod (BEST first move)
istioctl x describe pod jobpost-api-7d9f4b-x2v4c -n anihpj
#   → prints effective PeerAuthentication + DR TLS mode

# 2 — inspect the live SPIFFE cert Envoy holds in memory
istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj
#   → shows "default" cert + ROOTCA, ~24h validity window

# 3 — Kiali: Graph → Display → Security
#   → every encrypted edge shows a 🔒 padlock icon

# 4 — raw probe: openssl against the service port
openssl s_client -connect user-service.anihpj:8080
#   → shows the presented chain; SAN = SPIFFE URI
📖 A Deprecated Command to Forget

istioctl authn tls-check was removed from istioctl long ago. If an old runbook or study note still mentions it, mentally substitute istioctl x describe pod — it prints the same effective-mode answer in one call.

12.8 Deep Dive — The DR/PA TLS Contract (Why 503s Happen)

mTLS is a contract between two independent configs: DestinationRule's trafficPolicy.tls.mode controls what the CLIENT Envoy sends (ISTIO_MUTUAL, MUTUAL, SIMPLE, DISABLE); PeerAuthentication's mtls.mode controls what the SERVER Envoy accepts (STRICT, PERMISSIVE, DISABLE). A 503 is born the moment the two sides disagree — the client-side Envoy fails to open the upstream connection and synthesizes the 503 itself (flag UC); the server never even logs a request. Best practice: write no tls block in DestinationRules at all — sidecar-to-sidecar traffic then auto-negotiates mTLS ("auto mTLS," 12.12) and tracks the PeerAuthentication mode with zero extra configuration.

DR tls.modePA: STRICTPA: PERMISSIVEPA: DISABLE
ISTIO_MUTUAL (mesh certs)✅ mTLS 🔒✅ mTLS 🔒❌ handshake fails
DISABLE (plaintext)❌ TCP reset, client sees 503✅ works (unencrypted)✅ works (unencrypted)
(no tls block — safest DR)✅ auto mTLS✅ auto mTLS✅ plaintext
⚠️ THE 3 CLASSIC TRAPS — Memorize These Before the Exam
TRAP 1 — the invisible DISABLE:
  a DR written pre-Istio with tls.mode: DISABLE sits harmless under
  PERMISSIVE for months... the day PA flips to STRICT, every call
  through it dies with 503 UC.
  → audit BEFORE enabling STRICT:
     kubectl get destinationrules -A -o yaml | grep -B5 "mode: DISABLE"

TRAP 2 — ISTIO_MUTUAL ≠ MUTUAL:
  ISTIO_MUTUAL = mesh's auto-issued SPIFFE certs (normal)
  MUTUAL       = certs YOU mount yourself (external TLS)
  picking MUTUAL without providing certs = broken handshake

TRAP 3 — blaming the server:
  the 503 is generated CLIENT-side (Envoy could not open the upstream
  TLS connection) — the server never saw the request; its access log
  stays empty. Read the CALLER's logs and response flags (UC/UF) first
💡 Debug Command

istioctl authn tls-check is gone from modern istioctl — use istioctl x describe pod to see the effective DR + PA modes for a pod in one call (12.7).

12.9 Deep Dive — External CAs: SPIRE Integration and Plug-in CA Certificates

By default, Istio uses its built-in CA (istiod) to issue SPIFFE X.509 SVID certificates. But for enterprise environments requiring FIPS 140-2 compliance, hardware security modules (HSM), or centralized PKI, you can replace istiod's CA with SPIRE — the CNCF SPIFFE Runtime Environment. Exam signals that point here: "FIPS compliance required," "use existing PKI," "HSM integration," "multi-trust-domain federation."

🔐 DEFAULT CA (istiod) vs EXTERNAL CA (SPIRE) — Architecture
Default: istiod CA
  • istiod generates a self-signed root CA at install
  • Stores root cert in cacerts Kubernetes secret
  • Auto-rotates workload certs every 24 hours
  • Simple, zero-config, no external dependencies
  • ✅ Best for most deployments
External: SPIRE
  • SPIRE Server + SPIRE Agents on each node
  • Plugs into enterprise PKI, Vault, HSM backends
  • Can integrate with FIPS 140-2 validated HSM/KMS backends
  • Multi-cluster, multi-cloud identity federation
  • ✅ Best for regulated industries (finance, government)
🔄 SPIRE CERTIFICATE FLOW — How Workloads Get Identity
  1. SPIRE Agent on Node → registers workload with SPIRE Server
  2. SPIRE Server → validates workload identity (K8s SA, labels)
  3. SPIRE Server → issues SPIFFE SVID → pushes to Agent
  4. SPIRE Agent → writes SVID to Unix Domain Socket (UDS)
  5. Envoy → reads SVID from UDS via SDS (Secret Discovery Service)
  6. Envoy → presents SVID to peers for mTLS handshake

  SVID format: spiffe://example.org/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api
  (trust domain = example.org, not cluster.local)
💡 ICA Exam: When to Use SPIRE

The ICA exam may ask about external CA scenarios. Key signals: "FIPS compliance required," "use existing PKI," "HSM integration," "multi-trust-domain federation." Default answer for most scenarios: istiod's built-in CA is sufficient. SPIRE is for specific enterprise requirements.

Plug-in Your Own CA Certificates — Enterprise PKI Integration

Instead of using istiod's self-signed root CA, you can plug in your own enterprise root CA, intermediate CA certs, and signing key. This is a separate concept from SPIRE — here you're still using istiod as the CA, but with your own certificate chain.

🏛️ CA HIERARCHY — Multi-Cluster with One Root CA
  ROOT CA (Offline, HSM-protected)
  │  Signs intermediate CAs for each cluster
  ├── Intermediate CA: cluster1  → istiod signs workload certs for cluster1
  ├── Intermediate CA: cluster2  → istiod signs workload certs for cluster2
  └── Intermediate CA: cluster3  → istiod signs workload certs for cluster3

  RESULT: All clusters share the same root of trust → cross-cluster mTLS works

  SECRET STRUCTURE (cacerts secret in istio-system):
  ca-cert.pem     = Intermediate CA certificate (istiod signs with this)
  ca-key.pem      = Intermediate CA private key
  root-cert.pem   = Root CA certificate (distributed to all workloads)
  cert-chain.pem  = Full chain: intermediate → root
# Step 1: Generate root CA
make -f tools/certs/Makefile.selfsigned.mk root-ca
# Output: root-cert.pem, root-key.pem

# Step 2: Generate intermediate CA for each cluster
make -f tools/certs/Makefile.selfsigned.mk cluster1-cacerts
# Output: cluster1/{ca-cert.pem, ca-key.pem, cert-chain.pem, root-cert.pem}

# Step 3: Create cacerts secret (MUST be named "cacerts")
kubectl create secret generic cacerts -n istio-system \
  --from-file=cluster1/ca-cert.pem \
  --from-file=cluster1/ca-key.pem \
  --from-file=cluster1/root-cert.pem \
  --from-file=cluster1/cert-chain.pem

# Step 4: Install Istio — it detects cacerts secret automatically
istioctl install --set profile=demo -y
💡 ICA: cacerts Secret Name is MAGIC

The secret MUST be named cacerts in the istio-system namespace. Istio automatically detects it at startup. If present, istiod uses these certs instead of generating a self-signed root. For multi-cluster: share the SAME root-cert.pem across all clusters — this is what enables cross-cluster mTLS with a unified trust domain.

A Third Path — cert-manager (istio-csr)

istiod can also become a Registration Authority and forward every CSR to cert-manager, which signs via Vault, Venafi, or a private ACME CA. One line to remember for the exam: install istio-csr, point istiod at it, and every workload certificate is now audited and managed like the rest of your enterprise PKI — no more istiod self-signed root at all.

12.10 The Fourth Mode — UNSET and PeerAuthentication Inheritance

mtls.mode actually has four legal values, not three: STRICT, PERMISSIVE, DISABLE, and UNSET. UNSET is the implicit default whenever a PeerAuthentication (or a single portLevelMtls entry) omits mode entirely. 12.6 already showed workload beats namespace beats mesh — UNSET is the MECHANISM that makes that hierarchy possible. A policy that is UNSET does not mean "no mTLS setting" — it means "look at my parent scope and copy it":

  • UNSET at workload scope → inherit the namespace-wide policy
  • UNSET at namespace scope → inherit the mesh-wide policy
  • UNSET at mesh scope (or no mesh-wide policy exists at all) → Istio's hard-coded fallback is PERMISSIVE
  • portLevelMtls entries follow the SAME rule at port granularity: an UNSET port inherits the workload's own mtls.mode instead of the namespace/mesh chain
ModeMeaning
UNSETInherit from parent scope; if there is no parent (the mesh-wide policy itself is UNSET), treated as PERMISSIVE
DISABLEConnection is not tunneled — plaintext only
PERMISSIVEConnection can be EITHER plaintext or mTLS
STRICTConnection MUST be an mTLS tunnel — client cert required, plaintext rejected
yaml — portLevelMtls: UNSET on one legacy port 
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-mixed
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT        # workload default: STRICT
  portLevelMtls:
    8888:
      mode: UNSET        # port 8888 (health probe) instead
                          # inherits anihpj's namespace policy
⚠️ Two Exam Traps

portLevelMtls only applies once a workload selector is set, and the port number is the CONTAINER port, not the Kubernetes Service port — a common exam trap. Deletion cascade (ties back to 12.6): delete the workload policy → its pods fall to UNSET → they now inherit namespace; delete that too → namespace falls to UNSET → mesh; delete the mesh-wide policy too → Istio's built-in UNSET fallback is PERMISSIVE, never STRICT — "secure by default" is something YOU configure, not something Istio assumes.

12.11 SPIFFE Identity Anatomy — Reading a Cert Like the Exam Wants

Every workload identity in the mesh is a SPIFFE ID with exactly four parts: spiffe://<trust-domain>/ns/<namespace>/sa/<service-account>. SPIFFE IDs are the noun every other security feature operates on — secure naming (12.5) matches against them, AuthorizationPolicy source.principals (Chapter 13) filters on them, and istioctl/Kiali display them verbatim.

📖 Key Term — SPIFFE ID vs. SVID

The ID is the URI STRING itself (e.g. spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api); the SVID is the signed X.509 CERTIFICATE that carries that ID inside its SAN field. The exam uses both words on purpose — one is a name, the other is the document that proves it.

ComponentMeaning
spiffe://Fixed scheme — always this literal
cluster.localTRUST DOMAIN — the mesh's identity root (default "cluster.local"; your own domain under SPIRE federation, see 12.9)
/ns/anihpjLiteral "/ns/" + the Kubernetes NAMESPACE the workload runs in
/sa/jobpost-apiLiteral "/sa/" + the Kubernetes ServiceAccount the Pod runs as — THIS is the actual "who," not the Pod name
ServiceSPIFFE ID
jobpost-apispiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api
user-servicespiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/user-service
skills-servicespiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/skills-service
istio-ingressgateway (mesh-wide, not anihpj-owned)spiffe://cluster.local/ns/istio-system/sa/istio-ingressgateway-service-account

The identity is bound to the ServiceAccount, NOT the Pod name, NOT the IP, NOT the Deployment — scale jobpost-api to 20 pods and every single one presents the IDENTICAL SPIFFE ID, because they all run under the same ServiceAccount. Two anihpj Pods can therefore never be told apart by identity alone if they share a ServiceAccount — if you need per-Pod granularity in an AuthorizationPolicy, you need a DIFFERENT ServiceAccount per workload, not just a different Pod.

💡 Where You Will SEE This String in Real Tooling

istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj lists the "default" workload cert + "ROOTCA" by name — to read the SPIFFE URI itself, decode the cert bytes (openssl s_client ... | openssl x509 -noout -text, look under X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: URI:spiffe://...) or check istioctl x describe pod's identity output. Kiali → click an edge → the "mTLS" panel shows both principals. AuthorizationPolicy source.principals (Chapter 13) is a list of these exact strings.

12.12 Auto mTLS — Zero-Config Client-Side TLS Since Istio 1.5

Auto mTLS is the Pilot feature (default ON since Istio 1.5) that automatically sets the CLIENT Envoy's TLS behavior to match what the destination can accept — WITHOUT you writing a DestinationRule tls block.

🧠 Analogy — the Automatic Transmission

Auto mTLS is a car's automatic transmission: Django just says "go" — a plain http:// call — and Pilot, like the transmission, silently picks the right gear (ISTIO_MUTUAL or plaintext) by reading road conditions (does the destination's Envoy have a sidecar?). A manual DestinationRule tls block is shifting gears by hand — it works, but forgetting to update it when PeerAuthentication moves to STRICT is exactly how 12.8's 503s get born.

Why it matters: before Istio 1.5, every mesh needed a hand-written ISTIO_MUTUAL DestinationRule per hardened service; forget one and that service silently kept sending/receiving plaintext even though PeerAuthentication said STRICT. Auto mTLS removes that entire failure mode for standard in-mesh traffic. How it works: every sidecar-injected Pod's Endpoint carries an internal label recording that it has a sidecar; istiod's Pilot component reads that label through service discovery and knows, for each destination, whether it has a sidecar; when building the CLIENT'S Envoy config, if the caller did NOT write an explicit tls block in a DestinationRule, Pilot fills one in FOR them — ISTIO_MUTUAL if the destination has a sidecar, plaintext if it does not. An explicit tls block in a DestinationRule ALWAYS overrides auto mTLS — this is 12.8's Trap 1 in reverse: auto mTLS is the safe default, a leftover explicit block is the trap.

🤖 AUTO mTLS DECISION — What Pilot Fills In When a DR Has No tls Block
  jobpost-api Envoy about to call user-service.anihpj:8080
  DestinationRule for user-service: NO tls block

       Does user-service's endpoint have a sidecar?
              │                          │
            YES                          NO
              │                          │
              ▼                          ▼
   Pilot injects:                Pilot injects:
   tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL        (nothing — plaintext origin)
   → 🔒 mTLS automatically         → talks plaintext to a
                                     non-mesh / VM / legacy
                                     endpoint, e.g. a payment
                                     gateway outside anihpj
yaml — disabling auto mTLS mesh-wide (rare) 
apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: IstioOperator
spec:
  meshConfig:
    enableAutoMtls: false   # default is true
💡 Exam Framing

"Why does jobpost-api get mTLS to user-service with ZERO DestinationRule anywhere in anihpj?" → auto mTLS, not magic — Pilot saw both sidecars and wired ISTIO_MUTUAL in. Turning enableAutoMtls off does NOT turn off mTLS itself — PeerAuthentication STRICT still rejects plaintext on the SERVER side; it only means every DestinationRule now needs an explicit tls block, because Pilot stops filling one in automatically.

12.13 Certificate TTL and Rotation Internals — the Real Numbers

Two DIFFERENT certificates live in an Istio mesh, with two very different lifetimes — the WORKLOAD cert (what 12.4 covers) and the ROOT/intermediate CA cert that signs it. The exam expects you to know rotation is NOT "wait until 5 minutes before expiry" — it happens much earlier, and mixing up workload-cert TTL with root-cert TTL is a common wrong answer on certificate-lifetime questions.

CertificateDefault TTLRotation Trigger
Workload cert (per-Pod SVID, what Envoy presents in a handshake)24 hoursistio-agent requests renewal once the grace-period ratio (0.5) elapses — around the 12-hour mark, plus a small random jitter (default ratio 0.01, roughly ±15 minutes since Istio 1.24) so hundreds of replicas started together don't all hit istiod at once
Root / intermediate CA cert (signs every workload cert)10 years (self-signed default)Lives in the istio-ca-secret in istio-system; NOT rotated on the same schedule as workload certs — root rotation is a deliberate, rare, operator-driven procedure with old and new roots trusted side-by-side during the transition
🔄 CORRECTED ROTATION TIMELINE — Replaces "5 Minutes Before Expiry"
  T=0h:      cert issued, 24h validity window opens
  T≈12h:     grace-period ratio (0.5) reached — istio-agent requests
             a NEW cert (± ~15 min jitter since 1.24)
  T≈12h+j:   new CSR signed by istiod → new cert swapped into Envoy
             via SDS → OLD cert is simply discarded early, it was
             still technically valid
  T=24h:     original cert's validity window would have ended —
             irrelevant, it was replaced 12 hours earlier

The old cert keeps working right up to its own real expiry — the swap is seamless, no dropped connections. Both numbers are configurable on istiod, but the exam only expects you to know the DEFAULTS and the RELATIONSHIP: workload certs rotate WAY before they expire (roughly the halfway point), and the root CA cert does not rotate on any per-Pod schedule at all.

⚠️ istiod Down for >24h

If istiod is down for longer than the workload cert's TTL (24h by default), NO renewals can happen — existing certs expire and handshakes start failing mesh-wide until istiod is restored (this is 12.7's Golden Rule 3 scenario, "cert expired").

🔧 Under the Hood — One anihpj Call, Start to Finish: jobpost-api → user-service Through Every mTLS Gate
🧵 Four Gates, One HTTP Call

Chapter 12 looks like 13 separate topics, but a single real call — jobpost-api calling user-service hours after both pods booted — passes through every one of them in sequence. Miss any single gate and the call never completes.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PHASE 1 — IDENTITY IS BORN (pod boot — ties 12.4's pieces together)         │
│   T=0.0s  jobpost-api Pod scheduled; istio-proxy sidecar injected           │
│   T=0.3s  sidecar sends a CSR to istiod: "I am sa/jobpost-api, ns/anihpj"   │
│   T=0.5s  istiod (Citadel CA) verifies the ServiceAccount token, signs a    │
│           24h X.509 SVID: spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api   │
│   T=0.7s  cert lands in Envoy via SDS — jobpost-api can now PROVE itself    │
│                                                                             │
│ PHASE 2 — THE CALL (hours later, e.g. T=6h — well inside the 24h cert)     │
│   ①  Django calls http://user-service:8080/users/42 — the app has NO       │
│      idea mTLS exists (12.12: auto mTLS wires this up silently)            │
│   ②  jobpost-api's Envoy checks secure naming (12.5): the istiod-pushed    │
│      map says only .../sa/user-service may answer for user-service:8080    │
│   ③  TLS 1.3 ClientHello sent; user-service's Envoy answers with ITS SVID: │
│      spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/user-service                      │
│   ④  jobpost-api's Envoy verifies: signed by the mesh root? SAN matches    │
│      the secure-naming map from step ②? not expired? — all checks pass     │
│   ⑤  jobpost-api's Envoy presents ITS OWN SVID in return — this is the     │
│      "mutual" in mTLS; user-service now knows the caller's identity too    │
│   ⑥  user-service's Envoy checks its OWN effective PeerAuthentication      │
│      mode (12.6/12.10): namespace anihpj = STRICT — a valid client cert    │
│      is mandatory, this one qualifies — tunnel accepted                    │
│   ⑦  encrypted tunnel established; "GET /users/42" travels inside it;      │
│      user-service's access log records the caller's principal for          │
│      Chapter 13's AuthorizationPolicy to filter on next                    │
│                                                                             │
│ RESULT: one HTTP call, zero Django code touched — yet it crossed FOUR      │
│ independent gates (a live cert from Phase 1, a secure-naming check, a      │
│ two-way identity exchange, and a PeerAuthentication mode gate) and every   │
│ single one had to say yes before byte one of /users/42 could move.        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 ICA Insight: mTLS is not one feature, it's four independently-configured gates that happen to fire in one call: (1) a certificate must already exist and be valid (12.4, 12.13), (2) the client's Envoy must find the destination's identity legitimate via secure naming (12.5), (3) both sides must actually exchange and verify SVIDs (12.2), and (4) the server's effective PeerAuthentication mode must accept what was presented (12.6, 12.10) — and none of the four gates requires a DestinationRule tls block, because auto mTLS (12.12) wires gate 3 up for free. Debugging a failure means identifying WHICH gate rejected the call, not just that "mTLS is broken."

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • mTLS proves identity in BOTH directions — regular TLS only proves the server's identity; Istio's mTLS has both Envoys present a SPIFFE X.509 cert to each other.
  • A failed mTLS handshake is a TCP-layer reset, never an HTTP status code — "connection reset by peer" with NO HTTP code at all means mTLS; an HTTP 403 "RBAC: access denied" means AuthorizationPolicy (Chapter 13). Confusing the two wastes real debugging time.
  • Certificates rotate around the 12-hour mark, not moments before 24h expiry — the grace-period ratio (0.5) triggers renewal at the halfway point, plus jitter since Istio 1.24, specifically so hundreds of replicas don't all hit istiod simultaneously.
  • A valid certificate alone isn't enough — secure naming also checks the SPIFFE ID is AUTHORIZED to run the specific service being dialed, closing the gap a stolen-but-valid cert would otherwise exploit.
  • PeerAuthentication resolution is narrowest-scope-wins: workload beats namespace beats mesh — and UNSET (the 4th, implicit mode) is the actual mechanism that makes inheritance up that chain possible.
  • A 503 right after flipping STRICT is almost always a stale DestinationRule with an explicit tls.mode: DISABLE that silently worked under PERMISSIVE for months — the safest DestinationRule for mTLS purposes is one with NO tls block at all.
  • Auto mTLS (default since Istio 1.5) fills in ISTIO_MUTUAL automatically whenever a DestinationRule has no explicit tls block — an explicit block always overrides it, which is exactly how the "invisible DISABLE" trap happens.
  • SPIFFE identity is bound to the ServiceAccount, never the Pod — scale a Deployment to 20 replicas and every pod presents the identical SPIFFE ID, because they share one ServiceAccount.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "An HTTP 403 means mTLS is misconfigured." No — mTLS failures never produce an HTTP status code at all (it's a TCP-layer reset). A 403 "RBAC: access denied" is always an AuthorizationPolicy problem (Chapter 13), never mTLS.
  • "Certificates rotate 5 minutes before they expire." No — the grace-period ratio (0.5) triggers renewal around the HALFWAY point of the 24h TTL (~12 hours), specifically to spread renewal load and avoid a last-minute scramble.
  • "Only ONE PeerAuthentication can exist per namespace, period." Partially true — only ONE mesh-wide and ONE namespace-wide policy are honored (newer duplicates are ignored); but MULTIPLE workload-specific policies can coexist, with the OLDEST one winning on overlap.
  • "Disabling auto mTLS also disables mTLS enforcement." No — enableAutoMtls: false only stops Pilot from auto-filling DestinationRule TLS settings. PeerAuthentication STRICT still rejects plaintext on the server side regardless; you'd just need to write every tls block by hand.
  • "ISTIO_MUTUAL and MUTUAL are the same thing, just different names." No — ISTIO_MUTUAL uses the mesh's own auto-issued SPIFFE certs; MUTUAL requires YOU to mount external certs yourself. Picking MUTUAL without providing certs breaks the handshake.
  • "A 503 after enabling STRICT means the server is broken." No — the 503 is generated CLIENT-side (the client's Envoy couldn't open the upstream TLS connection); the server's own access log stays completely empty. Always check the CALLER's logs and response flags first.
  • "The mesh's UNSET fallback defaults to STRICT for safety." No — Istio's built-in UNSET fallback, all the way up the chain with no policy set anywhere, is PERMISSIVE, never STRICT. "Secure by default" is something you configure, not something Istio assumes.

💼 Chapter 12 — Daily Work Takeaways

  • Migrate PERMISSIVE → STRICT namespace-by-namespace, never mesh-wide in one shot — flip each namespace only after Kiali confirms every inbound edge is already showing a lock icon.
  • Audit for stale tls.mode: DISABLE DestinationRules BEFORE flipping to STRICT, not after — kubectl get destinationrules -A -o yaml | grep -B5 "mode: DISABLE" takes seconds and prevents a real outage.
  • Reach for istioctl x describe pod FIRST on any mTLS investigation — it prints the effective PeerAuthentication mode AND DestinationRule TLS mode in one call, faster than reasoning through the hierarchy by hand.
  • Never write an explicit DestinationRule tls block unless you have a specific reason to — let auto mTLS handle the common case; an explicit block is exactly the kind of leftover config that causes a 503 months later when PeerAuthentication changes.
  • When rotating root/intermediate CAs, treat it as a deliberate, rare, operator-driven procedure — trust old and new roots side-by-side during the transition; never treat root rotation like routine workload-cert rotation.
  • Decode a cert's SPIFFE URI with openssl x509 -noout -text and jump straight to the SAN field — ignore the Subject/Issuer CN noise, the URI is the actual identity.
  • For the ICA exam: know the DR/PA contract table (12.8) cold — which combination of DR tls.mode and PA mtls.mode produces mTLS, plaintext, or a broken handshake is a guaranteed exam pattern.
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 12

Seven quick-fire phrase-to-answer mappings — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Encrypt all service traffic" = PeerAuthentication mode: STRICT
  • "TCP reset, no HTTP code at all" = mTLS problem; "HTTP 403 RBAC" = AuthorizationPolicy problem (Ch13) — never confuse the two
  • "503 right after flipping STRICT" = 9 times out of 10, a stale DestinationRule with tls.mode: DISABLE
  • "mTLS works with zero DestinationRules" = auto mTLS — Pilot wires ISTIO_MUTUAL automatically whenever both sidecars exist
  • "Certificate rotation timing" = ~12 hours (the 0.5 grace-period ratio of a 24h cert), NOT "5 minutes before expiry"
  • "FIPS/HSM/existing-PKI requirement" = replace istiod's built-in CA with SPIRE, plug-in CA certs, or cert-manager (istio-csr)
  • "Read a workload's identity" = the SPIFFE ID's /sa/<name> segment — bound to the ServiceAccount, never the Pod name

🧠 Chapter 12 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What's the difference between regular TLS (like HTTPS on a website) and mutual TLS?
Show Answer
Answer

Regular TLS: only the SERVER proves its identity to the client. Mutual TLS: BOTH sides present a certificate and prove their identity to each other.

Explanation

This is why mTLS defeats impersonation attacks that regular TLS wouldn't catch — even if an attacker's fake service could somehow present a valid-looking response, it has no way to present a legitimate CLIENT certificate proving it's an authorized caller.

Q2
A caller gets "connection reset by peer" with no HTTP status code at all. Is this an mTLS problem or an AuthorizationPolicy problem?
Show Answer
Answer

mTLS. STRICT mode rejects plaintext at the TCP layer — there's no HTTP exchange to even produce a status code. An AuthorizationPolicy denial, by contrast, always produces an HTTP 403 "RBAC: access denied."

Explanation

This distinction is the fastest triage step in the whole chapter — the PRESENCE or ABSENCE of an HTTP status code alone tells you which of two completely different CRDs (PeerAuthentication vs AuthorizationPolicy) to go debug.

Q3
When exactly does a 24-hour workload certificate actually rotate?
Show Answer
Answer

Around the 12-hour mark — when the grace-period ratio (0.5) of the 24h TTL elapses — plus a small random jitter (since Istio 1.24) so many replicas started together don't all request renewal at the exact same moment. NOT "5 minutes before expiry."

Explanation

Rotating at the halfway point (rather than near expiry) gives a wide safety margin — even if istiod is briefly unavailable right when a renewal is due, there's still ~12 hours of validity left on the old cert to retry.

Q4
An attacker has a valid SPIFFE certificate for their own ServiceAccount and deploys a fake pod pretending to be user-service. Why does secure naming block this?
Show Answer
Answer

Because istiod's secure-naming map only authorizes SPECIFIC SPIFFE IDs to serve SPECIFIC services. The attacker's certificate is valid (it's real and signed by the mesh CA) but is NOT in the map as authorized to serve user-service — the calling Envoy checks this map and rejects the connection even though the cert itself passes normal validation.

Explanation

This is the gap a "just check the cert is validly signed" approach would miss — secure naming is the extra check that a valid cert is being presented by the RIGHT identity for THIS specific service.

Q5
Mesh-wide, namespace-wide, and workload-specific PeerAuthentication policies all exist and disagree. Which one wins?
Show Answer
Answer

Workload-specific wins — the hierarchy is narrowest-scope-wins: workload beats namespace beats mesh.

Explanation

This mirrors a pattern seen elsewhere in Istio (like Sidecar CRD scoping) — the most SPECIFIC configuration always overrides the more general one, letting you set a safe mesh-wide default while carving out exceptions for individual workloads.

Q6
A DestinationRule has no tls block at all. Does mTLS still work between two sidecar-injected services?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes — this is auto mTLS (default since Istio 1.5). Pilot detects that the destination has a sidecar and automatically fills in tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL for the client, with zero DestinationRule configuration required.

Explanation

This is actually the SAFEST state a DestinationRule can be in for mTLS purposes — an explicit tls block, even a "correct" one today, is a future 503 risk if it ever falls out of sync with PeerAuthentication changes.

Q7
What's the difference between the DestinationRule TLS modes ISTIO_MUTUAL and MUTUAL?
Show Answer
Answer

ISTIO_MUTUAL uses the mesh's own auto-issued SPIFFE certificates — the normal in-mesh case. MUTUAL requires YOU to mount external certificates yourself, typically for TLS to something outside Istio's own certificate management.

Explanation

Picking MUTUAL without actually providing certs is a real exam trap — it looks similar to ISTIO_MUTUAL but silently breaks the handshake since there's no cert source configured.

Q8
A PeerAuthentication's mtls.mode field is left empty (UNSET) at the workload level, and there's no namespace-wide policy either. What mode actually applies?
Show Answer
Answer

PERMISSIVE. UNSET means "inherit from the parent scope" — workload inherits namespace, namespace inherits mesh, and if even the mesh-wide policy is UNSET (or doesn't exist), Istio's hard-coded fallback is PERMISSIVE, never STRICT.

Explanation

This is why "secure by default" is a common exam misconception — Istio's actual out-of-the-box behavior with no PeerAuthentication configured anywhere is permissive, not strict; security is something you deliberately configure.

Q9
What's the difference between a SPIFFE ID and an SVID?
Show Answer
Answer

The SPIFFE ID is just the URI string (e.g. spiffe://cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api). The SVID is the signed X.509 certificate document that carries that ID inside its SAN field — the ID is a name, the SVID is the proof.

Explanation

The exam uses both terms deliberately — confusing "the identity string" with "the certificate that proves it" is exactly the kind of precision gap a well-written distractor answer exploits.

Q10
Which certificate rotates roughly every 12 hours, and which one does NOT follow that same schedule?
Show Answer
Answer

The WORKLOAD certificate (per-Pod SVID) rotates around the 12-hour mark. The ROOT/intermediate CA certificate (which signs every workload cert) does NOT rotate on that schedule at all — it defaults to a 10-year self-signed lifetime and is rotated only via a deliberate, rare, operator-driven procedure.

Explanation

Mixing up these two certificates' lifetimes is a common wrong answer on exam certificate-lifecycle questions — they're two genuinely different objects with two genuinely different rotation models.

⚙️ Chapter 12 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
Immediately after enabling STRICT mTLS for the anihpj namespace, jobpost-api starts getting 503s (flag UC) calling user-service. Task: Diagnose and fix.
Show Answer
Answer
# Diagnose: look for a stale DestinationRule disabling TLS
kubectl get destinationrules -A -o yaml | grep -B5 "mode: DISABLE"
# Fix: remove the stale tls block, or set it to ISTIO_MUTUAL explicitly
kubectl edit destinationrule user-service-dr -n anihpj
Explanation

This is 12.8's Trap 1 exactly — a DestinationRule written pre-Istio (or during PERMISSIVE testing) with an explicit tls.mode: DISABLE sat harmless for months, then broke the moment PeerAuthentication flipped to STRICT.

Q2
Write a PeerAuthentication enforcing STRICT mTLS for the entire anihpj namespace.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT
Explanation

Naming it default in a namespace-scoped PeerAuthentication is the conventional pattern — only ONE namespace-wide policy is honored, so this name signals "this IS the namespace default," matching istiod's own naming convention.

Q3
Confirm the EFFECTIVE PeerAuthentication mode and DestinationRule TLS mode for a specific running pod, in one command.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl x describe pod jobpost-api-7d9f4b-x2v4c -n anihpj
Explanation

This should be your FIRST command in any mTLS investigation — it resolves the entire PeerAuthentication hierarchy (mesh/namespace/workload) AND the DestinationRule TLS settings for you, rather than manually reasoning through 12.6's precedence rules by hand.

Q4
Only skills-service (not the whole anihpj namespace) needs to run with mTLS temporarily disabled for a legacy debugging session. Write the PeerAuthentication.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: skills-service-debug
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: skills-service
  mtls:
    mode: DISABLE
Explanation

The selector field scopes this to ONLY skills-service — workload-specific policies win over the namespace default (12.6), so this narrowly overrides STRICT for just this one workload without touching the rest of anihpj.

Q5
A health-check port (8888) on jobpost-api needs to stay accessible without mTLS, while the rest of the workload's traffic stays STRICT. Write the PeerAuthentication.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-health-port
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT
  portLevelMtls:
    8888:
      mode: PERMISSIVE
Explanation

portLevelMtls uses the CONTAINER port number (not the Kubernetes Service port) and only takes effect once a workload selector is set — both are real exam traps from 12.10.

Q6
Read the SPIFFE URI directly off a live certificate Envoy is presenting for user-service.
Show Answer
Answer
openssl s_client -connect user-service.anihpj:8080 2>/dev/null \
    | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep -A1 "Subject Alternative Name"
Explanation

The SPIFFE URI lives under the SAN field, NOT the Subject or Issuer CN — those fields are mostly noise for Istio's own certs. This is the same technique used to confirm an external ServiceEntry's real certificate identity in Chapter 8.

Q7
A team reports "istioctl authn tls-check shows command not found." Task: Give the modern equivalent.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl x describe pod <pod> -n anihpj
Explanation

istioctl authn tls-check was removed from istioctl long ago — a real, current gotcha for anyone following an old runbook or outdated study material. istioctl x describe pod prints the same effective-mode answer in one call.

Q8
anihpj needs FIPS 140-2 compliant certificate issuance instead of istiod's built-in self-signed CA. Name the recommended replacement and why.
Show Answer
Answer

SPIRE (the CNCF SPIFFE Runtime Environment) — it plugs into enterprise PKI, Vault, or HSM backends and can integrate with FIPS 140-2 validated key-storage backends, plus multi-cluster/multi-cloud identity federation that istiod's built-in CA doesn't offer.

Explanation

The exam signal phrases to recognize: "FIPS compliance required," "use existing PKI," "HSM integration," "multi-trust-domain federation" — all point to SPIRE (or, for a lighter-weight enterprise-PKI-only need without SPIRE's full runtime, plug-in CA certs or cert-manager/istio-csr).

Q9
Install a custom root/intermediate CA for anihpj's cluster instead of using istiod's self-signed default.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl create secret generic cacerts -n istio-system \
  --from-file=cluster1/ca-cert.pem \
  --from-file=cluster1/ca-key.pem \
  --from-file=cluster1/root-cert.pem \
  --from-file=cluster1/cert-chain.pem
Explanation

The secret name MUST be exactly cacerts in istio-system — istiod auto-detects it at startup and uses these certs instead of generating a self-signed root. For multi-cluster, share the SAME root-cert.pem across every cluster to enable cross-cluster mTLS.

Q10
istiod has been down for 30 hours. What happens to mTLS across the mesh, and what's the fix?
Show Answer
Answer

Since 30 hours exceeds the 24-hour workload-cert TTL, no renewals could happen during the outage — existing certs have expired and handshakes are failing mesh-wide. Fix: restore istiod, then restart affected pods to force a fresh CSR and get a new valid certificate.

Explanation

This is 12.7's Golden Rule 3 scenario in a concrete form — "TLS handshake fails, cert expired" traces back to istiod being unavailable for longer than the cert TTL, not a config error on any individual service.

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 12
  • Migrate PERMISSIVE → STRICT namespace-by-namespace, never mesh-wide in one shot — flip the namespace-wide PeerAuthentication only after Kiali shows every inbound edge already locked.
  • 503 (flag UC) right after flipping STRICT is 9 times out of 10 a stale DestinationRule with tls.mode: DISABLE — grep for it BEFORE you flip.
  • TCP reset with no HTTP code = mTLS problem; HTTP 403 "RBAC: access denied" = AuthorizationPolicy problem (Ch13) — never debug the wrong CRD.
  • istioctl x describe pod is your first command, not proxy-config secret — it prints the EFFECTIVE PA mode + DR TLS mode in one shot.
  • To read a cert fast: pipe openssl s_client into openssl x509 -noout -text and jump straight to "Subject Alternative Name" — that URI IS the identity, ignore the Subject/Issuer CN noise.
  • "istioctl authn tls-check" is gone — if a runbook mentions it, mentally substitute istioctl x describe pod.

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 12)

Every command below already appeared earlier in this chapter — grouped here as one reference for driving PeerAuthentication, cert inspection, and mTLS-debugging tasks.

CommandWhat It Does in Chapter 12
kubectl apply -f peerauth.yamlSets PA mode: PERMISSIVE/STRICT/DISABLE (12.3, 12.6)
istioctl x describe pod <pod> -n anihpjEffective PA mode + DR TLS mode, ONE call (12.7)
istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/<name> -n anihpjLive SPIFFE cert + ROOTCA in Envoy's memory (12.7, 12.11)
openssl s_client -connect <svc>.anihpj:<port>Raw handshake; prints the presented cert chain (12.7)
openssl x509 -noout -textDecode a cert; read the SPIFFE URI under SAN (12.11)
kubectl get destinationrules -A -o yaml | grep -B5 "mode: DISABLE"Find stale DRs before flipping to STRICT (12.8)
kubectl create secret generic cacerts -n istio-system ...Install your own root/intermediate CA (12.9)
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpjForce pods to re-CSR after a CA or PA change (12.9)

🧪 Practice Drill 12.1 — Flip anihpj from PERMISSIVE to STRICT and Prove It

⏱️ Target Time: 8-10 minutes
Scenario

Run this against your own anihpj kind cluster right now:

  1. (1 min) kubectl get peerauthentication -n anihpj -o yaml — confirm today's mode (likely PERMISSIVE from the Week-1 migration in 12.4).
  2. (2 min) Apply a namespace-wide PeerAuthentication with mtls.mode: STRICT for the anihpj namespace (the YAML in 12.3 is ready to reuse).
  3. (2 min) istioctl x describe pod on a jobpost-api pod — confirm the EFFECTIVE mode now reads STRICT, not just "applied."
  4. (2-3 min) From a NON-sidecar pod (or curl with no mesh identity), hit user-service:8080 — expect "connection reset by peer," not a 403 — that confirms you're seeing mTLS enforcement, not AuthorizationPolicy.
  5. (2 min) Open Kiali's graph, enable the Security display — every anihpj edge should now show a 🔒 padlock; any edge without one is a sidecar-less straggler to fix before calling this done.
Hint: Step 1 reuses 12.6's policy-hierarchy reflex; steps 2-3 reuse 12.3's YAML and 12.7's "measure before guessing" rule; step 4 proves 12.7's Golden Rule 1 (TCP reset, not 403) with your own hands; step 5 is the same Kiali lock-icon check 12.1's diagram already promised.
View Solution

Step 4's curl should fail with a connection-level error (no HTTP status line at all) — if you see an HTTP 403 instead, you're actually looking at an AuthorizationPolicy from a later chapter, not mTLS enforcement; re-check that no AuthorizationPolicy already exists in anihpj. Step 5's padlocks should appear on EVERY edge except any sidecar-less straggler — that's a real gap to fix, not an expected result.

Check yourself: did you verify the FAILURE mode in step 4 (no HTTP code) as carefully as you verified the success in step 5? A quick "it errored, good enough" skips exactly the diagnostic signal (TCP reset vs 403) this whole chapter is built around.

🧪 Practice Drill 12.2 — Reproduce the Stale-DestinationRule 503 Trap Yourself

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Don't take 12.8's Trap 1 on faith — build and trigger it live.

  1. While anihpj is still PERMISSIVE, apply a DestinationRule for skills-service with an explicit tls.mode: DISABLE.
  2. Confirm calls to skills-service still work fine under PERMISSIVE.
  3. Flip anihpj's namespace-wide PeerAuthentication to STRICT.
  4. Repeat the same call to skills-service and observe what happens.
  5. Fix it by removing the DestinationRule's tls block entirely (not just changing its value).
Hint: Step 4 should reproduce the exact 503 (flag UC) symptom from 12.8 — if it doesn't, double check the DestinationRule's selector actually targets skills-service.
View Solution

Step 4 should show a 503 with response flag UC — and critically, skills-service's OWN access log should show NOTHING for this request, since the client-side Envoy never even opened the upstream connection. Step 5's fix (removing the block, not just editing its value) lets auto mTLS take back over.

Check yourself: did you check skills-service's access log in step 4 and confirm it was EMPTY? That empty log is the concrete proof that this is a client-side failure, not a server-side one — the single most important diagnostic fact in 12.8's whole Trap 3.

🧪 Practice Drill 12.3 — Match the Symptom to the Broken Layer

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

For each observation, name the most likely cause and the ONE command you'd run to confirm it — before proposing any fix:

  1. A non-sidecar pod trying to reach an anihpj service gets "connection reset by peer."
  2. A team raised a namespace PeerAuthentication to STRICT but a specific workload still accepts plaintext.
  3. An mTLS handshake fails with a certificate-expired error mesh-wide, all at once.
  4. A curl to a service returns HTTP 403 "RBAC: access denied" right after mTLS was enabled.
Hint: One of these four is NOT actually an mTLS problem at all, despite happening right after an mTLS change — the timing is a coincidence, not a cause.
View Solution
#CauseConfirm with
1Expected behavior — STRICT demands a client SVID cert the non-sidecar pod doesn't haveConfirm no sidecar: kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].name}'
2A workload-specific PeerAuthentication (higher precedence) is overriding the namespace policy for that one workloadistioctl x describe pod on that specific workload
3istiod was down long enough (>24h) for renewals to stop happening mesh-wideCheck istiod's own uptime/restart history: kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod
4NOT an mTLS problem — this is an AuthorizationPolicy denial (Chapter 13), coincidentally discovered right after enabling mTLSCheck for an AuthorizationPolicy: kubectl get authorizationpolicy -A

Check yourself: did you correctly identify #4 as a DIFFERENT CRD entirely, not an mTLS misconfiguration? The HTTP 403 itself is the tell — mTLS failures never produce an HTTP status code.

🧪 Practice Drill 12.4 — Set Up an External CA Conceptually, Then Prove You Understand the Handoff

⏱️ Target Time: 7 minutes
Scenario

anihpj's compliance team requires FIPS 140-2 certificate issuance. Work through the decision and setup conceptually:

  1. Name which of the three external-CA options (SPIRE, plug-in CA certs, cert-manager/istio-csr) best fits a pure FIPS-compliance requirement versus a "we already have enterprise PKI" requirement versus a "we want centralized cert-manager-style auditing" requirement.
  2. For the plug-in CA certs path specifically, write the exact kubectl create secret command that installs a custom root/intermediate CA.
  3. Explain what happens if the secret is named anything other than exactly cacerts.
  4. For a 3-cluster mesh, explain what MUST be shared across all three clusters for cross-cluster mTLS to work.
Hint: Step 3's answer should make you realize this is a "magic string" convention, not a configurable field name — istiod is looking for that EXACT name at startup.
View Solution

(1) FIPS/HSM → SPIRE; existing enterprise PKI without a full SPIRE runtime → plug-in CA certs; centralized cert-manager-style auditing → cert-manager/istio-csr. (2) kubectl create secret generic cacerts -n istio-system --from-file=... (the 4 files: ca-cert.pem, ca-key.pem, root-cert.pem, cert-chain.pem). (3) If misnamed, istiod never detects it and silently falls back to generating its own self-signed root — no error, just unexpected default behavior. (4) The SAME root-cert.pem must be shared across all three clusters' cacerts secrets — that's what establishes one unified trust domain across all of them.

Check yourself: did you correctly distinguish "plug-in CA certs" (still using istiod as the CA, just with your own cert chain) from "SPIRE" (replacing istiod's CA function entirely)? These are two genuinely different architectures that solve overlapping but distinct problems.

🧪 Practice Drill 12.5 — Sketch the Four-Gate Call Path From Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking back at the UTH's diagram, sketch (on paper or in a text file) the four independent gates a single jobpost-api → user-service call passes through, hours after both pods booted.

  1. Name all 4 gates in order.
  2. For each gate, name the ONE mechanism/section that governs it.
  3. Name the ONE gate that does NOT require any DestinationRule configuration at all, and why.
Hint: This is a paper/whiteboard drill — the point is retrieving the mental model from memory under light time pressure, the same way the exam expects you to reason about a failed call without a diagram in front of you.
View Solution

The 4 gates: (1) A certificate must already exist and be valid — governed by the certificate lifecycle (12.4, 12.13). (2) The client's Envoy must find the destination's identity legitimate via secure naming (12.5). (3) Both sides must actually exchange and verify SVIDs — the mTLS handshake itself (12.2). (4) The server's effective PeerAuthentication mode must accept what was presented (12.6, 12.10). Gate 3 requires no DestinationRule configuration — auto mTLS (12.12) wires it up automatically whenever both sidecars exist.

Check yourself: did your sketch correctly separate gate 2 (secure naming — is this identity ALLOWED to be here) from gate 4 (PeerAuthentication — does the mode accept what was presented)? Both are "acceptance checks" but at genuinely different layers, and conflating them is the most common gap in recalling this diagram.

Chapter 12 took anihpj from every hop being plaintext and every identity being an easily-spoofed IP, to every one of jobpost-api, user-service, skills-service, location-service, notification-service, auth-service, and search-service holding an unforgeable SPIFFE certificate that is issued at boot, checked on every handshake, hardened against impersonation, and silently rotated roughly every 12 hours — all without a single Django code change. What Chapter 12 deliberately does NOT do is decide who is ALLOWED to call whom once identity is proven; that authorization decision, layered on top of the identity this chapter builds, is exactly where Chapter 13's AuthorizationPolicy picks up.

Quick recap — 🔓 Plaintext (12.1): any rogue pod can sniff, impersonate, or move laterally · 🤝 mTLS the concept (12.2): BOTH sides present a SPIFFE cert, not just one · 🔐 PeerAuthentication (12.3): PERMISSIVE → STRICT switches enforcement on · 📜 Certificate Lifecycle (12.4): istiod issues + rotates SVIDs around the 12h mark · 🪪 Secure Naming (12.5): a valid cert alone isn't enough, the NAME must match too · 🏛️ Policy Hierarchy (12.6): workload beats namespace beats mesh · 🔧 Troubleshooting (12.7): TCP reset = mTLS, HTTP 403 RBAC = AuthorizationPolicy · 🤝 DR/PA Contract + External CAs (12.8-12.9): the contract behind every 503, plus SPIRE/plug-in CA/cert-manager · ⚙️ UNSET + Inheritance (12.10): the mechanism behind 12.6's hierarchy · 🆔 SPIFFE Anatomy (12.11): reading spiffe://.../ns/.../sa/... on demand · 🤖 Auto mTLS (12.12): Pilot wires ISTIO_MUTUAL with zero DestinationRules · ⏱️ TTL & Rotation (12.13): ~12h renewal, never "5 minutes before expiry." Chapter 13 picks up right here: AuthorizationPolicy decides WHO may call WHOM once identity is proven.

Chapter 13: Authorization Policies — Who Can Call What

mTLS proves identity, but doesn't restrict access. Without AuthorizationPolicy, any service with a valid cert can call any other service. AuthorizationPolicy is Istio's Layer 7 firewall — you define exactly WHO can call WHAT, using WHICH methods, on WHICH paths.

Chapter 12 spent thirteen sections proving WHO is calling — every anihpj pod now carries an unforgeable SPIFFE certificate and every hop is encrypted end to end. But identity alone is a dead end: with only mTLS switched on, a compromised skills-service still authenticates perfectly AS skills-service, then walks straight into user-service and dumps every row of PII — the request was 100% encrypted and 100% authenticated the whole way, and nothing stopped it. That is exactly the trap Part 7's own analogy warns about: a badge system that only checks whether the badge is real, never whether THIS badge should open THIS door, is theater — cryptographically perfect, and useless. Chapter 13 is where anihpj closes that gap: AuthorizationPolicy is the doorman who actually reads the badge and decides. By 13.11 you will trace one real request through FOUR simultaneous decision layers — CUSTOM, AUDIT, DENY, ALLOW — the single most exam-critical sequence in the whole Securing Workloads domain, because getting the order wrong either 403s legitimate traffic or silently lets an attacker straight through.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🛡️ Access Control 🎯 ICA 25%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Explain why mTLS (identity) and AuthorizationPolicy (authorization) are two separate controls, and why anihpj needs BOTH
  • ✅ Write a deny-all AuthorizationPolicy and layer explicit ALLOW rules on top of it without causing a traffic outage
  • ✅ Wire RequestAuthentication + requestPrincipals together so a MISSING JWT, not just an invalid one, becomes a real 403
  • ✅ Use exclusion fields (notPaths, notPrincipals) to carve out an exception like /healthz without weakening the rest of a policy
  • ✅ Lock down a non-HTTP TCP port (postgres:5432) with a ports-only ALLOW rule, and explain why paths/methods can never match there
  • ✅ Rehearse a risky policy with istio.io/dry-run before enforcing it, and read the shadow verdict across logs, metrics, and traces
  • ✅ Trace one request through the full CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW order (with AUDIT as a non-blocking side-channel) and predict the verdict
🎓 ICA Relevance
Securing Workloads 25%
💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 13
  • "Deny all traffic" = AuthorizationPolicy with empty spec: {} — no rules = nothing allowed
  • "Allow specific caller" = ALLOW rule with principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"]
  • "First ALLOW policy changes the default" = the moment ANY AuthorizationPolicy targets a workload, it flips from allow-by-default to implicit-deny
  • Evaluation order: CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW, with AUDIT running independently the whole time as a log-only side-channel that never blocks anything
  • 401 vs 403: 401 = RequestAuthentication rejected a present-but-broken JWT; 403 = AuthorizationPolicy rejected it (including a missing token, once requestPrincipals is required)
  • TCP workloads (postgres, kafka) only match on ports/principals/namespaces/ipBlocks — paths/methods are silently dropped, never enforced
