SectionAnswers the question…One-line takeaway
13.1 The Need for Service-Level AuthorizationIs a valid certificate alone enough?No — mTLS proves WHO, not WHAT they may do. Zero-trust denies by default.
13.2 AuthorizationPolicy — The Istio FirewallWhat CRD enforces authorization?AuthorizationPolicy, compiled into an Envoy RBAC filter and pushed via xDS.
13.3 Building a Zero-Trust PolicyHow do I roll this out without an outage?ALLOW rules first, deny-all last (or shadow it with dry-run).
13.4 RequestAuthentication — JWT VerificationHow do I verify the END USER, not just the service?RequestAuthentication validates the JWT; AuthorizationPolicy + requestPrincipals turns a missing token into a 403 too.
13.5 Exclusion Matching — NOT ConditionsHow do I carve out an exception like /healthz?Every positive field has a negated "not" twin — notPaths, notPrincipals, and so on.
13.6 TCP AuthorizationCan I protect a raw TCP port like postgres:5432?Yes — but only ports/principals/namespaces/ipBlocks apply; paths/methods never match TCP.
13.7 Deep Dive — Policy Evaluation with Real RequestsWhat actually happens, request by request?CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW → default; DENY always beats ALLOW.
13.8 Deep Dive — Dry-Run AuthorizationHow do I test a risky policy safely?istio.io/dry-run: "true" shadow-evaluates — logs, never enforces.
13.9 The AUDIT ActionHow do I log matches without blocking anything?AUDIT is a 4th action — visibility only, never gates ALLOW/DENY.
13.10 CUSTOM Action — ext-authzWhat if no built-in field covers my check?CUSTOM delegates to an external authorizer over ext_authz (HTTP/gRPC).
13.11 The Complete Evaluation OrderHow do all four actions interact on ONE request?CUSTOM first (can only deny) → DENY → ALLOW → default, AUDIT watching throughout.
13.12 The Complete when Condition Key ReferenceWhat keys can a when: clause actually match on?A fixed vocabulary — source.principal, request.auth.claims[x], connection.sni, and more.

13.1 The Need for Service-Level Authorization

mTLS ensures the caller IS who they claim to be. But should a compromised skills-service be allowed to call user-service and read all user data? With zero-trust, the answer is NO. Every call must be explicitly authorized.

🎭 OVERLY-PERMISSIVE MESH vs ZERO-TRUST MESH
WITHOUT AuthorizationPolicy — mTLS-only 'permissive' mesh:

  😈 compromised skills-service (attacker inside the pod)
     ├──✅──▶ user-service      GET /api/users/*  → dumps user PII
     ├──✅──▶ auth-service      probes /validate  → forges sessions
     └──✅──▶ location-service  maps the internal network

  mTLS happily says: 'this really IS skills-service' — then lets
  every call through. Identity ✅  Encryption 🔒  Permissions ❌

WITH zero-trust (deny-all + explicit ALLOW policies):

  😈 compromised skills-service
     ├──❌──▶ user-service      403 RBAC: access denied
     ├──❌──▶ auth-service      403 (not on the allow-list)
     └──❌──▶ location-service  403

  jobpost-api ──✅──▶ skills-service  (explicitly allowed, GET)

  Blast radius of one hacked pod: EVERYTHING → almost nothing
⚠️ CRITICAL — mTLS ≠ Authorization

Even with STRICT mTLS, without AuthorizationPolicy, ANY service can call ANY other service. mTLS proves identity but doesn't restrict permissions. You need BOTH: mTLS for encryption + identity, AuthorizationPolicy for access control.

13.2 AuthorizationPolicy — The Istio Firewall

AuthorizationPolicy works at Layer 7 (HTTP). You can allow/deny based on: source identity (SPIFFE), HTTP method (GET/POST/DELETE), HTTP path, headers, and source namespace.

🔍 AUTHORIZATION POLICY EVALUATION — How Istio Decides
1
Request

skills-service → GET /users/42 → user-service

2
CUSTOM?

Custom policy exists? Evaluate first

3
DENY?

Matching DENY policy? → DENY ❌

4
ALLOW?

Matching ALLOW policy? → ALLOW ✅

5
Default

No matching ALLOW → DENY ❌

Result
403

skills-service NOT in allow-list for user-service

yaml — Complete AuthorizationPolicy for anihpj 

# Step 1: Deny ALL traffic in anihpj namespace
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all
  namespace: anihpj
spec: {}                        # ← empty spec = deny everything
---
# Step 2: Allow ingress → jobpost-api (GET/POST only)
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-ingress-to-jobpost
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals:
        - "cluster.local/ns/istio-system/sa/istio-ingressgateway"
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
---
# Step 3: Allow jobpost-api → user-service (GET only)
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-jobpost-to-users
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: user-service
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals:
        - "cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET"]
        paths: ["/api/users/*"]
🔧 Under the Hood — From YAML to Envoy RBAC Filter

Applying this YAML doesn't make kube-apiserver start checking requests — istiod compiles the AuthorizationPolicy's rules into an Envoy RBAC filter and pushes it to every matching sidecar over xDS, the same channel that already delivers listeners, routes, and certs. The ALLOW/DENY check then runs entirely inside each pod's own Envoy sidecar, request by request — no round trip back to istiod or the API server is ever made.

13.3 Building a Zero-Trust Policy for anihpj

Step-by-step: deny everything → allow specific paths only. Here's the complete policy matrix:

🔐 ZERO-TRUST POLICY MATRIX — anihpj

SourceTargetAllowed Methods
istio-ingressgatewayjobpost-apiGET, POST
jobpost-apiuser-serviceGET only
jobpost-apiskills-serviceGET only
jobpost-apilocation-serviceGET only
user-serviceauth-serviceGET, POST
PrometheusALL servicesGET /metrics
ANY OTHERANY❌ DENIED
💡 ICA Exam Tip

If ANY AuthorizationPolicy targets a workload, all requests NOT explicitly ALLOWed are DENIED. The default "allow all" only applies when ZERO policies target that workload.

⚠️ Rollout Order Matters — ALLOWs First, Deny-All LAST

Apply the ALLOW policies from the matrix above FIRST, and the deny-all LAST (or shadow it with dry-run — see 13.8). Applying deny-all before the ALLOWs exist 403s every live call for as long as the gap lasts. Each ALLOW policy lives next to its TARGET service: the policy selecting user-service governs traffic INTO user-service, not traffic it sends out.

🚀 ROLLOUT & VERIFY — Applying the Matrix Without an Outage
# 1. Apply every ALLOW policy from the matrix (rows above)
$ kubectl apply -f authz/ -n anihpj      # 6 ALLOW policies

# 2. Apply deny-all in DRY-RUN mode first (see 13.8)
#    metadata.annotations: "istio.io/dry-run": "true"
$ kubectl apply -f deny-all-dryrun.yaml

# 3. Watch shadow-denies across live traffic (847 req/s)
#    → zero legitimate flows would be denied? proceed

# 4. Enforce: remove the dry-run annotation
$ kubectl annotate authorizationpolicy/deny-all -n anihpj \
    istio.io/dry-run-

# 5. Verify one allowed and one denied path
$ kubectl exec deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -- \
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
    http://user-service:8080/api/users/42        → 200 ✅
$ kubectl exec deploy/skills-service -n anihpj -- \
    curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' \
    http://user-service:8080/api/users/42        → 403 ❌

13.4 RequestAuthentication — JWT Verification at the Mesh Level

While PeerAuthentication (Chapter 12) verifies service-to-service identity via SPIFFE mTLS, RequestAuthentication verifies end-user identity using JSON Web Tokens (JWT). This is how you authenticate human users or external API clients at the mesh level — no application code changes needed. anihpj use case: only requests carrying a valid JWT issued by auth-service should reach user-service or jobpost-api.

🪪 REQUEST AUTHENTICATION FLOW — JWT Validation at the Gateway
  1. User sends request with: Authorization: Bearer <JWT_TOKEN>
  2. Ingress Gateway Envoy intercepts request
  3. RequestAuthentication policy tells Envoy: "Validate JWT for issuer X using JWKS at URL Y"
  4. Envoy fetches public keys from JWKS endpoint → validates signature
  5. If valid: forward to backend with request.auth.principal populated
  6. If invalid/missing: by default, STILL forwards (401 only if AuthorizationPolicy enforces it)

  ⚠️ CRITICAL: RequestAuthentication alone does NOT reject requests!
  It only VALIDATES. To REJECT, you need an AuthorizationPolicy that requires requestPrincipals (or a DENY action).
PeerAuthentication (Ch 12)
  • Service-to-service identity
  • Uses SPIFFE X.509 certificates
  • Modes: STRICT / PERMISSIVE / DISABLE / UNSET
  • source.principal populated
  • No JWT involved
RequestAuthentication (Ch 13)
  • End-user / API client identity
  • Uses JWT tokens (OIDC/OAuth2)
  • Validates: issuer, audience, expiry, signature
  • request.auth.principal populated
  • Requires a JWKS endpoint (public key set)
📝 RequestAuthentication YAML Example
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: RequestAuthentication
metadata:
  name: jwt-auth
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      istio: ingressgateway  # Apply to ingress gateway
  jwtRules:
  - issuer: "https://auth.anihpj.com"
    jwksUri: "https://auth.anihpj.com/.well-known/jwks.json"
    audiences: ["jobpost-api"]
    fromHeaders:
    - name: Authorization
      prefix: "Bearer "
    forwardOriginalToken: true  # Pass JWT to backend
🔗 JWT + AuthorizationPolicy — Requiring Valid Tokens
# Step 1: RequestAuthentication VALIDATES the JWT
# (Above policy)

# Step 2: AuthorizationPolicy REJECTS requests without valid JWT
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-jwt
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      istio: ingressgateway
  action: DENY
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        notRequestPrincipals: ["*"]  # No valid JWT → DENY
JWT StatusRequestAuthentication+ AuthZ Policy (above)
No token✅ 200 (passes through)❌ 403 (DENY: no principal)
Valid token✅ 200 (principal set)✅ 200 (has principal)
Invalid/expired token❌ 401 (validation fails)❌ 401 (same)
⚠️ ICA Exam: The 60-Second JWT Clock Skew

Istio allows 60 seconds of clock skew for JWT validation. A token becomes valid 60 seconds BEFORE its nbf (not before) time and remains valid 60 seconds AFTER its exp (expiry) time. If a question shows a token expiring at T+5s and still working at T+65s — that's the 60s skew, not a bug.

🎯 Additional Pattern — Claim-Based Access Control

The require-jwt policy above turns a missing token into a 403. A different, equally common pattern: allow the request only if a valid JWT carries a specific claim value — for example, restricting a write endpoint to admins:

# Verify JWTs issued by anihpj's own auth-service
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: RequestAuthentication
metadata:
  name: jwt-auth
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  jwtRules:
  - issuer: "auth-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
    jwksUri: "http://auth-service/.well-known/jwks.json"
---
# Allow only requests with a valid JWT containing role=admin
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-admin-jwt
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - when:
    - key: request.auth.claims[role]
      values: ["admin"]

Both patterns compose: require-jwt guarantees SOME valid token exists; a claims-based ALLOW then decides WHICH tokens are good enough for a specific action. RequestAuthentication only ever validates — the AuthorizationPolicy layered on top is what actually turns a claim into a decision.

13.5 Exclusion Matching — "NOT" Conditions in AuthorizationPolicy

From the official docs: AuthorizationPolicy supports exclusion matching using notPaths, notValues, notIpBlocks, notPrincipals, and their less-common siblings notServiceAccounts, notRemoteIpBlocks, and notTrustDomains. This allows you to say "apply this policy to everything EXCEPT..." — a powerful pattern for health checks and public endpoints. Real policies always need carve-outs: "require a JWT on every path EXCEPT /healthz" cannot be expressed with positive matches alone — a request matches an exclusion rule only if it does NOT match any excluded value, and exclusions sit inside the same from/to/when blocks and combine with positive fields.

🔥 anihpj War Story — The Day require-jwt Restart-Looped Every Pod

The day require-jwt went live, kubelet liveness probes — which carry no JWT — started failing. jobpost-api pods restart-looped until /healthz was exempted with notPaths. The fix is Pattern 1 below.

🩺
Pattern 1: Skip JWT for Health Checks
rules:
- to:
  - operation:
      notPaths: ["/healthz", "/ready"]
  from:
  - source:
      requestPrincipals: ["*"]

Requires JWT for ALL paths EXCEPT /healthz and /ready. Health probes bypass auth.

🚫
Pattern 2: Deny External to Admin
action: DENY
rules:
- to:
  - operation:
      paths: ["/admin"]
  from:
  - source:
      notNamespaces: ["anihpj"]

Denies /admin access from ANY namespace EXCEPT anihpj.

✅
Pattern 3: Allow All Except /admin
action: ALLOW
rules:
- to:
  - operation:
      notPaths: ["/admin"]
  from:
  - source:
      requestPrincipals: ["*"]
- to:  # /healthz: no auth needed
  - operation:
      paths: ["/healthz"]

Any valid JWT reaches everything EXCEPT /admin; /healthz needs no JWT at all (no from: clause = anyone).

📋 EXCLUSION MATCHING FIELDS — What You Can Negate

Exclusion FieldRule Matches When…Example
notPathsURL path is NOT one of thesenotPaths: ["/healthz", "/ready"]
notPrincipalsCaller SPIFFE identity is NOT in the listnotPrincipals: ["cluster.local/..."]
notNamespacesCaller namespace is NOT in the listnotNamespaces: ["external"]
notIpBlocksSource IP is NOT inside these CIDRsnotIpBlocks: ["10.0.0.0/8"]
notMethodsHTTP method is NOT one of thesenotMethods: ["DELETE"]
notHostsHost header is NOT one of thesenotHosts: ["internal.anihpj.com"]
notRequestPrincipalsAll JWT principals EXCEPT thesenotRequestPrincipals: ["*"]
notValuesAll when: values EXCEPT thesenotValues: ["hack"]
notServiceAccountsCaller K8s service account is NOT in the listnotServiceAccounts: ["cluster.local/ns/prod/sa/legacy"]
notRemoteIpBlocksOriginal client IP (from X-Forwarded-For) is NOT inside these CIDRsnotRemoteIpBlocks: ["10.0.0.0/8"]
notTrustDomainsCaller's SPIFFE trust domain is NOT one of thesenotTrustDomains: ["cluster.local"]

Also available: notPorts. Every one of these is the exact negated twin of its positive-match field — same location in the rule, opposite logic.

13.6 TCP Authorization — Protecting Non-HTTP Workloads

From the official docs: AuthorizationPolicy works for any plain TCP protocol (MongoDB, Redis, MySQL, Kafka, PostgreSQL), not just HTTP. The difference: HTTP-only fields (hosts, methods, paths, requestPrincipals) are ignored for TCP traffic. Only ports, principals, namespaces, and ipBlocks apply. Identity still works on TCP: principals come from the mTLS SPIFFE certificate exchanged in the TLS handshake — Istio's auto-mTLS (12.12) upgrades sidecar-to-sidecar traffic to mTLS by default even under PERMISSIVE, so principals populate without needing STRICT.

⚠️ The TCP Trap — HTTP-Only Fields Are Silently Dropped, Not Rejected

Putting paths or methods on a TCP-target policy is the bug, not a feature — and Istio does NOT reject the YAML for it:

  • In an ALLOW rule: the rule can never match (paths/methods never apply to TCP) — so the traffic you MEANT to allow is DENIED instead.
  • In a DENY rule: Istio drops only the HTTP-only fields and enforces the rest — the policy may DENY MORE than you wrote (the field you thought was scoping it down was never active).
🧠 ANALOGY: A TCP-only checkpoint is a parking-garage gate arm: it reads your access card and answers GO or NO-GO, full stop — it cannot ask "which floor" or "what's your business here" the way an HTTP-aware policy's staffed lobby desk can (paths, methods, headers). Taping paths: ["/admin/*"] onto a postgres:5432 rule is like stickering "floor 4 only" on a gate arm that can't read floors — it changes nothing; you still only get GO or NO-GO.
yaml — TCP AuthZ: Only jobpost-api can access MongoDB on port 27017 
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: mongodb-policy
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: mongodb
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"]
    to:
    - operation:
        ports: ["27017"]          # ← ONLY port-level control for TCP
⚠️ Important: mTLS Dependency for Principal-Based Rules

From the official docs: if you use principals, namespaces, or source.principal in AuthorizationPolicy, mTLS MUST be enabled. These fields derive from SPIFFE certificates — without mTLS, they're empty or spoofable. STRICT only matters here to reject non-mesh plaintext callers outright; under PERMISSIVE such a caller is simply let through with no principal set, silently failing any principals-based ALLOW rule. Always pair principal-based AuthZ with PeerAuthentication STRICT.

13.7 Deep Dive — Policy Evaluation with Real Requests

Understanding the EXACT evaluation order is critical for the ICA exam. For every request, the target's sidecar evaluates policies in a FIXED order: CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW → default. Two defaults to memorize: if NO ALLOW policy targets the workload, the mesh behaves as if authorization does not exist (allow-by-default); the moment ANY ALLOW policy targets it, everything not explicitly matched by an ALLOW rule gets 403 (implicit deny). DENY always beats ALLOW — a matching DENY ends evaluation immediately; no ALLOW further down can rescue the request. Let's walk through 3 real requests and see how Istio decides ALLOW or DENY.

🔍 EVALUATION ORDER — CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW (DENY always beats ALLOW)
REQUEST 1: jobpost-api → GET /api/users/42 → user-service
  Step 1: CUSTOM policies? → None
  Step 2: DENY policies? → "deny-skills" checks: source=skills-service? → NO match
  Step 3: ALLOW policies? → "allow-jobpost" checks: source=jobpost-api? → YES ✅
  Step 4: All conditions met? → YES → ALLOW ✅ (200 OK)

REQUEST 2: skills-service → GET /api/users/42 → user-service
  Step 1: CUSTOM policies? → None
  Step 2: DENY policies? → "deny-skills" checks: source=skills-service? → YES ❌
  RESULT: DENY (403 Forbidden) — evaluation STOPS here, ALLOW never checked

REQUEST 3: notification-service → GET /api/users/9 → user-service
  Step 1: CUSTOM? → None. Step 2: DENY? → no match → continue.
  Step 3: ALLOW? → "allow-jobpost" exists but source ≠ jobpost-api
  RESULT: ❌ 403 IMPLICIT deny — an ALLOW policy targets user-service, so
          anything unmatched is rejected (with ZERO ALLOW policies this
          would have been 200 — the "no policies at all" default)
⚠️ CRITICAL: The First ALLOW Policy Changes the Default

The moment you create the FIRST AuthorizationPolicy with action: ALLOW targeting a workload, the default switches from ALLOW-ALL to DENY-ALL for that workload. Only explicitly ALLOWed requests pass. Always create a deny-all (spec: {}) FIRST, then add selective ALLOW policies — or better, apply the ALLOWs first and shadow the deny-all with dry-run (13.3, 13.8).

13.8 Deep Dive — Dry-Run Authorization: Test Policies Without Breaking Traffic

From the official docs: Dry-run authorization lets you test an AuthorizationPolicy before enforcing it. Add the annotation istio.io/dry-run: "true" and Istio will shadow-evaluate the policy — logging what WOULD be denied while still allowing all traffic through. Why it matters: the first ALLOW policy flips a workload to implicit-deny; one missing rule 403s real users. Dry-run rehearses the change against live traffic (anihpj's 847 req/s) with zero user impact.

🧪 DRY RUN AUTHZ — Test Before You Enforce
  WITHOUT Dry Run (risky):
  Apply DENY policy → 5 minutes later → "Why is production broken?!" → PANIC ROLLBACK

  WITH Dry Run (safe):
  Apply DENY policy with dry-run annotation → Traffic still flows normally →
  Check 3 output channels → Adjust policy → Remove annotation → Enforce safely

  OUTPUT CHANNELS:
  1. Proxy Logs:  "shadow denied, matched policy ns[foo]-policy[name]-rule[0]"
  2. Prometheus:  envoy_http_inbound_*_rbac{authz_dry_run_result="denied"}
  3. Zipkin Trace: istio.authorization.dry_run.deny_policy.result: "denied"
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: test-deny-headers
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    istio.io/dry-run: "true"  # ← Shadow mode: evaluate but don't enforce
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  action: DENY
  rules:
  - to:
    - operation:
        paths: ["/admin"]    # Would block /admin... but only logs it!
🎭 Parallel Evaluation — One Request, Two Policies, One Verdict

The real (enforcing) policy and the dry-run (shadow) policy both evaluate the SAME request at the SAME time — but only the real policy's verdict ever touches the connection:

                Incoming request to jobpost-api (evaluated by the Envoy sidecar)
                                      │
       Envoy evaluates BOTH policies on the SAME request, at the SAME time
                                      │
              ┌───────────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
              ▼                                                 ▼
  REAL POLICY (enforcing)                          DRY-RUN POLICY (shadow)
  name: allow-jobpost-read                         name: deny-admin-paths
  action: ALLOW                                    istio.io/dry-run: "true"
  → REAL verdict: ALLOW or DENY                     → SHADOW verdict: ALLOW or DENY
              │                                                 │
       ENFORCED on the real connection            RECORDED to logs, metrics & traces only
              │                                                 │
              └───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                                      ▼
             Request proceeds based ONLY on the REAL policy's verdict —
             the dry-run result NEVER wins, NEVER blocks

A bug in the shadow policy's YAML cannot cause a real outage; the worst it can do is write a noisy line to the three channels below.

📡 QUICK-REFERENCE — the Three Output Channels, Side by Side

ChannelWhat to Look ForWhy It Matters
Envoy access / proxy logsrbac:debug log line: "shadow denied/allowed, matched policy ns[anihpj]-policy[NAME]-rule[N]"Names the EXACT rule that would fire — best for pinpointing which rule needs a fix
Prometheus metricsRBAC filter's dry-run-labeled counters (authz_dry_run_action / authz_dry_run_result)Aggregate, mesh-wide view — spot a spike in would-be denies before it ships live
Distributed traces (Zipkin/Jaeger)istio.authorization.dry_run.deny_policy.name/.result span tagsTies ONE shadow verdict to ONE exact request — correlate with a specific user's report
🛤️ SAFE ROLLOUT SEQUENCE — Ship a Stricter Policy With Zero Risk First
STEP 1
Deploy dry-run
Add istio.io/dry-run: "true"
Risk: ZERO (observe only)
STEP 2
Watch & verify
Logs + metrics + traces,
one full traffic cycle
STEP 3
Flip to enforce
Remove annotation (or "false")
Now enforced with confidence

Step 2 is where the real decision gets made: unexpected DENYs in the shadow verdict send you back to fix the rule and repeat Step 1, before the annotation ever comes off.

⚠️ ICA Exam: Dry Run Limitations

1. Only ALLOW and DENY actions are shadowed — CUSTOM is never dry-run (13.10). 2. ALLOW and DENY dry-run results are logged separately — check BOTH. 3. Requires proxy debug logging: istioctl proxy-config log deploy/X --level rbac:debug. 4. Experimental annotation — not for production API contracts, re-verify after Istio upgrades. 5. To enforce: remove the annotation or set it to "false" — a forgotten annotation is a toothless policy.

13.9 The AUDIT Action — Logging Requests Without Blocking Them

AUDIT is a fourth AuthorizationPolicy action alongside ALLOW, DENY, and CUSTOM — it logs a request that matches its rules but never changes whether the request is allowed or denied. The docs are explicit: "AUDIT policies do not affect whether requests are allowed or denied to the workload. Requests will be allowed or denied based solely on CUSTOM, DENY and ALLOW actions." Why it matters: anihpj's compliance team wants a paper trail of every hit on /admin/* with zero risk of an outage on the admin console — AUDIT gives visibility with no enforcement, the opposite trade-off from dry-run (13.8), which rehearses enforcement that IS about to go live.

⚡ AUDIT AT A GLANCE — The Four Action Types Side by Side

ActionWhat It Does to the Request
ALLOWPermits the request if it matches the rules
DENYRejects the request if it matches any rule
CUSTOMDelegates the verdict to an external authorizer; its answer is ANDed with DENY/ALLOW, never overrides them (13.10)
AUDITLogs a match for visibility only — never allows or denies anything by itself
yaml — anihpj AUDIT policy: watch /admin/* before a DENY exists 
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: audit-admin-access
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  action: AUDIT      # ← logs matches, never blocks anything
  rules:
  - to:
    - operation:
        paths: ["/admin/*"]   # every hit on /admin/* gets logged

How it works: a request matching an AUDIT rule is only "internally marked" as auditable — producing an actual log line requires "a separate plugin... configured and enabled to actually fulfill the audit decision"; with none wired up, the mark is set but nothing observable happens. anihpj's audit-admin-access ships as a standing policy (not a one-time rehearsal like dry-run) and stays in place indefinitely, even after a real DENY or ALLOW policy is later added for the same path.

🆚 AUDIT vs DRY-RUN — Easy to Confuse, Mechanically Different

AspectAUDIT (action: AUDIT)DRY-RUN (istio.io/dry-run: "true")
What it isA 4th, independent action type on its own policyAn annotation on an existing ALLOW/DENY policy
Needs a plugin?YES — a logging plugin must be enabled, or nothing observable happens (request is only "internally marked")NO — proxy logs, Prometheus metrics, and trace tags work out of the box (13.8)
Attaches toIts own standing AuthorizationPolicy + rulesThe SAME rules the real ALLOW/DENY would enforce
Typical useOngoing compliance trail: "who touched /admin"One-time rehearsal before flipping a NEW policy live
🔑 KEY EXAM FACT

AUDIT sits OUTSIDE the CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW pipeline entirely — it is evaluated independently and never gates a response. Don't confuse it with dry-run, which shadow-tests a REAL ALLOW/DENY policy that's about to be enforced; AUDIT is a standing, separate action type with no enforcement intent at all.

13.10 CUSTOM Action — External Authorization with ext-authz

action: CUSTOM delegates the allow/deny decision to an external authorizer over Envoy's ext_authz protocol (HTTP or gRPC). The docs are explicit that the extension "cannot bypass the authorization decision made by ALLOW and DENY action" — a request is allowed if and only if CUSTOM and every ALLOW/DENY policy all agree to allow it. Why it matters: some checks are too dynamic for a static AuthorizationPolicy field — anihpj's fraud-check service scores every POST /api/jobs/ against account age, posting velocity, and an ML risk model; none of that fits into principals/paths/when-conditions alone.

How it works: two-step wiring. (1) Register the authorizer as a MeshConfig extensionProvider (envoyExtAuthzHttp or envoyExtAuthzGrpc) naming its Kubernetes service and port. (2) Point an AuthorizationPolicy's action: CUSTOM + provider.name at that name, scoping which requests are sent to it with rules. anihpj detail: only POST /api/jobs/* is routed to fraud-check — GET calls and every other path skip the external hop entirely, keeping the fast path fast.

yaml — MeshConfig extensionProvider: register fraud-check 
# patch istiod's MeshConfig ("kubectl edit cm istio -n istio-system")
# to register the external authorizer
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: istio
  namespace: istio-system
data:
  mesh: |-
    extensionProviders:
    - name: fraud-check      # this name is what CUSTOM policies cite
      envoyExtAuthzHttp:
        service: "fraud-check.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
        port: "9000"
        timeout: "2s"        # default is 600s, far too slow in prod
        includeRequestHeadersInCheck: ["authorization", "x-user-id"]
        headersToUpstreamOnAllow: ["x-fraud-score"]
        headersToDownstreamOnDeny: ["content-type"]
        failOpen: false      # default; see the table below
yaml — AuthorizationPolicy: action: CUSTOM referencing fraud-check 
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: fraud-check-on-post
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  action: CUSTOM
  provider:
    name: fraud-check   # must match extensionProviders[].name
  rules:
  - to:                  # only these requests go to fraud-check;
    - operation:          # everything else skips it entirely
        methods: ["POST"]
        paths: ["/api/jobs/*"]
Field (envoyExtAuthzHttp)Meaning
serviceK8s DNS name of the authorizer
portPort the authorizer listens on
timeoutMax wait for a verdict (default 600s!)
includeRequestHeadersInCheckHeaders copied INTO the check call
headersToUpstreamOnAllowAuthorizer headers forwarded on to the real backend on ALLOW
headersToDownstreamOnAllowAuthorizer headers returned to the caller on ALLOW
headersToDownstreamOnDenyAuthorizer headers returned to the caller on DENY
failOpentrue = allow through on error; false (default) = deny on error
statusOnErrorHTTP status sent to the caller if the authorizer itself is unreachable
⚠️ Fail-Open vs Fail-Closed — What Happens When fraud-check Is Down

failOpen: false (the default): 403 returned immediately — jobpost-api's business logic never runs. Safe default for a money-moving path: an outage never silently disables fraud protection.
failOpen: true: Request proceeds AS IF fraud-check said ALLOW. Only pick this for non-critical checks where availability beats strict enforcement.

🔑 Limitations (Exam-Relevant)

At most ONE extension provider is allowed per workload — different workloads may each use a different provider, but you cannot stack two on one. A CUSTOM policy is NEVER shadow-evaluated by dry-run (13.8). CUSTOM always runs BEFORE DENY and ALLOW on every request that reaches the sidecar, regardless of policy creation order (this is the mechanism behind 13.11's Q16). failOpen defaults to false — if fraud-check.anihpj is unreachable, jobpost-api fails CLOSED (403), not open; that default must be changed explicitly per-provider if a check is meant to be best-effort rather than mandatory.

13.11 The Complete Evaluation Order — CUSTOM, AUDIT, DENY, and ALLOW Together

With all four action types now covered individually, here is the full per-request pipeline: CUSTOM decides first (and can only ever end in a deny — it cannot rescue a request DENY/ALLOW would otherwise reject) → DENY → ALLOW → workload default, while AUDIT runs the entire time as a side-channel that only writes log/metric/trace evidence and never participates in the allow/deny decision. Real anihpj workloads carry more than one action type at once — 13.7's deny-skills and allow-jobpost, now joined by fraud-check's CUSTOM policy (13.10) and audit-admin-access's AUDIT policy (13.9) — and the exam tests whether you can trace ONE request through all four layers without losing the order.

🔢 FULL EVALUATION ORDER — One anihpj Request, All Four Actions
Incoming request → jobpost-api sidecar

0. AUDIT runs INDEPENDENTLY, the whole time, in parallel —
   audit-admin-access logs a hit if the path is /admin/* —
   this NEVER changes the outcome of steps 1-4 below

1. CUSTOM   fraud-check fires first, only for POST /api/jobs/*
     authorizer says DENY  → STOP here → 403 (steps 2-3 skipped)
     authorizer says ALLOW → continue to step 2

2. DENY     deny-skills: source == skills-service?
     YES → STOP here → 403 (step 3 never runs)
     NO  → continue to step 3

3. ALLOW    allow-jobpost: source + method + path all match?
     YES → 200 OK
     NO  → 403 (an ALLOW policy targets this workload, so
            anything unmatched is implicit-denied)

4. If NO ALLOW policy targets the workload at all → allow by
   default (CUSTOM and DENY above still apply either way)
🧭 THREE-REQUEST WALKTHROUGH — CUSTOM, AUDIT, DENY, ALLOW Together
REQUEST A: jobpost-api's own retry → POST /api/jobs/ (a legit caller,
           not skills-service)
  0. AUDIT: path isn't /admin/* → no log entry
  1. CUSTOM: fraud-check called, returns ALLOW → continue
  3. ALLOW: allow-jobpost matches → 200 OK

REQUEST B: skills-service → POST /api/jobs/ (should never reach
           business logic — it's on the deny list)
  0. AUDIT: path isn't /admin/* → no log entry
  1. CUSTOM: fraud-check STILL runs and is billed/logged for this
     call — CUSTOM cannot be skipped by a later DENY
  2. DENY: deny-skills matches → STOP → 403
  (scope the CUSTOM policy's own selector/from to exclude callers
   you already know are denied, or you pay for the check twice)

REQUEST C: notification-service → GET /admin/reports (never
           explicitly allowed anywhere)
  0. AUDIT: path IS /admin/* → audit-admin-access LOGS the hit
  1. CUSTOM: rule only matches POST /api/jobs/* → skipped
  2. DENY: deny-skills source doesn't match → continue
  3. ALLOW: allow-jobpost exists but source doesn't match → 403
  RESULT: request is BOTH logged by AUDIT and rejected by
  implicit-deny — AUDIT firing changes nothing about the 403
🔑 KEY EXAM FACT

Reordering YAML, reapplying policies in a different sequence, or renaming resources never changes this order — the ACTION TYPE alone fixes the phase (CUSTOM, then DENY, then ALLOW), and AUDIT is not a phase at all, just a parallel observer that never blocks anything.

13.12 The Complete when Condition Key Reference

Every when: entry needs a key drawn from a fixed, documented vocabulary plus either values or notValues — 13.4 already used one of these keys (request.auth.claims[role]); this section is the full list. Why it matters: exam questions routinely swap in a DIFFERENT key from this same family — request.auth.principal instead of requestPrincipals, source.ip instead of source.principal, connection.sni for a TLS-passthrough Gateway — confusing them is the trap. Each key is scoped to HTTP-only or HTTP+TCP, and several require mTLS or TLS to even be populated (source.namespace, source.principal, connection.sni).

🔧 Matching on Any Istio Attribute — the when Clause

Beyond identity/method/path, match on ANY Istio attribute using when. A single rule can combine a header check with a JWT-issuer check:

spec:
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"]
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET"]
    when:
    - key: request.headers[x-api-version]
      values: ["v2", "v3"]  # Only requests with specific header value
    - key: request.auth.claims[iss]
      values: ["https://auth.anihpj.com"]  # Must come from specific issuer

📖 COMPLETE when CONDITION KEY REFERENCE

KeyMatches / Scope
source.ipSource workload IP, single IP or CIDR (HTTP+TCP)
source.namespaceCaller's namespace, needs mTLS (HTTP+TCP)
source.principalCaller's SPIFFE identity, needs mTLS (HTTP+TCP)
remote.ipOriginal client IP via X-Forwarded-For or PROXY protocol (HTTP+TCP)
destination.ipTarget workload IP (HTTP+TCP)
destination.portTarget port, 0-65535 (HTTP+TCP)
connection.sniSNI from the TLS handshake, needs TLS (HTTP+TCP)
request.headers[x]Any HTTP request header (HTTP only)
request.auth.principalJWT "iss/sub" once RequestAuthN validates it (HTTP only)
request.auth.audiencesJWT "aud" claim (HTTP only)
request.auth.presenterJWT "azp" claim (HTTP only)
request.auth.claims[x]Any raw JWT claim, e.g. claims[role] (HTTP only)
🧩 ANIHPJ when: EXAMPLES — Four Conditions, Four Use Cases
# 1. geofence the admin console to the corp VPN egress range
  when:
  - key: remote.ip
    values: ["203.0.113.0/24"]

# 2. scope a rule to only the Prometheus scrape port
  when:
  - key: destination.port
    values: ["15020"]

# 3. TLS-passthrough gateway: only accept anihpj's real domain
  when:
  - key: connection.sni
    values: ["jobs.anihpj.com"]

# 4. require a canary marker header on the canary subset
  when:
  - key: request.headers[x-canary]
    values: ["true"]

Also available: notValues inside any when: block negates the match — the condition-level sibling of the notPaths/notPrincipals family from 13.5. An experimental experimental.envoy.filters.* key also exists for raw Envoy filter metadata but carries no backward-compatibility guarantee — treat it as non-exam material.

📦 Related Advanced Feature — ClusterTrustBundle (Recent Istio Versions)

ClusterTrustBundle is a Kubernetes CRD (certificates.k8s.io/v1alpha1) that recent Istio releases support for distributing trusted CA bundles cluster-wide, as an alternative to manually mounting CA certs on every node — treat the exact version gate as a moving target and check your own installed version's release notes rather than a fixed number:

apiVersion: certificates.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: ClusterTrustBundle
metadata:
  name: anihpj-custom-ca
spec:
  trustBundle: |
    -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
    MIIDXTCCAkWgAwIBAgIJAKl...
    -----END CERTIFICATE-----

Enable with --set values.pilot.env.ENABLE_CLUSTER_TRUST_BUNDLE_API=true (requires K8s 1.27+). This is a trust-distribution mechanism, not a when: condition key — it is listed here because it is the same family of "advanced certificate/identity reference" trivia the exam occasionally pairs with this section.

🔧 Under the Hood — How Istio AuthorizationPolicy Actually Works: Rule Evaluation Order, SPIFFE Principal Matching, JWT Validation, and the RBAC Filter in Envoy
🗺️ AuthorizationPolicy — The Istio Firewall for Service-to-Service Traffic
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AUTHORIZATION POLICY — How Every Request Gets Allowed or Denied               │
│                                                                              │
│  EVALUATION ORDER (for each request):                                          │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ STEP 1: Check CUSTOM actions first                                      │   │
│  │   → External authorizer (ext_authz) evaluates the request               │   │
│  │   → Says DENY → STOP here → 403 (steps 2-3 skipped entirely)          │   │
│  │   → Says ALLOW → does NOT stop — continue to step 2 regardless         │   │
│  │     (CUSTOM can only ever END a request early by denying it; it        │   │
│  │      cannot bypass or short-circuit the DENY/ALLOW steps that follow) │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ STEP 2: Check DENY rules                                                │   │
│  │   → Any DENY rule match? → DENY (immediate) → STOP                    │   │
│  │   → "Blocked paths": /admin, blocked IPs, blocked principals         │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ STEP 3: Check ALLOW rules                                                │   │
│  │   → Any ALLOW rule match? → ALLOW → STOP                               │   │
│  │   → "Explicit allows": GET /api/* by SPIFFE principal X               │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │ STEP 4: Default DENY (if any policy selects the workload)              │   │
│  │   → No rule matched → DENY (default)                                   │   │
│  │   → Empty spec = no rules = everything DENIED                          │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  RULE MATCHING (ALL conditions must be true):                                  │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ rules:                                                                  │   │
│  │ - from:                        # WHO is the caller?                    │   │
│  │   - source:                                                              │   │
│  │       principals: ["spiffe://.../sa/jobpost-sa"]  # SPIFFE identity    │   │
│  │       namespaces: ["anihpj"]                       # Namespace         │   │
│  │   to:                          # WHAT are they trying to do?           │   │
│  │   - operation:                                                           │   │
│  │       methods: ["GET"]                              # HTTP method       │   │
│  │       paths: ["/api/users/*"]                       # URL path          │   │
│  │   when:                        # UNDER WHAT conditions?                │   │
│  │   - key: request.auth.claims[iss]                   # JWT issuer         │   │
│  │     values: ["auth.anihpj.com"]                                         │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  ALL conditions in a SINGLE rule must be TRUE → rule matches.          │   │
│  │  ANY matching rule (across all policies) → ALLOW or DENY.              │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 JWT Validation — How Istio Verifies End-User Tokens
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  JWT AUTHENTICATION — From Token to Verified Identity                           │
│                                                                              │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │                  RequestAuthentication (JWT)                            │   │
│  │                                                                        │   │
│  │  Client sends: Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...                    │   │
│  │       │                                                                 │   │
│  │       ▼                                                                 │   │
│  │  Envoy extracts JWT from Authorization header                           │   │
│  │       │                                                                 │   │
│  │       ▼                                                                 │   │
│  │  Envoy validates:                                                        │   │
│  │  ├── Signature valid? (against JWKS from issuer URL)                   │   │
│  │  ├── Not expired? (exp claim)                                          │   │
│  │  ├── Issuer matches? (iss claim = auth.anihpj.com)                    │   │
│  │  └── Audience matches? (aud claim)                                     │   │
│  │       │                                                                 │   │
│  │       ▼                                                                 │   │
│  │  VALID JWT → Envoy adds to request metadata:                            │   │
│  │    request.auth.claims[iss] = "auth.anihpj.com"                        │   │
│  │    request.auth.claims[sub] = "user-123"                                │   │
│  │    request.auth.claims[role] = "admin"                                  │   │
│  │       │                                                                 │   │
│  │       ▼                                                                 │   │
│  │  AuthorizationPolicy can now use these claims:                           │   │
│  │    when:                                                                 │   │
│  │    - key: request.auth.claims[role]                                     │   │
│  │      values: ["admin"]        # Only admins can POST /admin/           │   │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                              │
│  RequestAuthentication + AuthorizationPolicy = Complete AuthN+AuthZ          │
│                                                                              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 Zero-Trust Building Blocks — The Layer Cake of Istio Security
LayerIstio CRDWhat It DoesQuestion Answered
1. EncryptionPeerAuthenticationmTLS encrypts ALL traffic"Is traffic encrypted?"
2. IdentitySPIFFE (automatic)Every pod has cryptographic ID"WHO is calling?"
3. AuthenticationRequestAuthenticationVerify JWT tokens (end-user auth)"Is the token valid?"
4. AuthorizationAuthorizationPolicyAllow/deny based on identity + claims"Is this caller ALLOWED?"
5. Dry-RunAuthorizationPolicy (annotated)Test policies without breaking traffic"What WOULD this policy block?"
🔑 ICA Insight: AuthorizationPolicy is how you build zero-trust in Istio. Key facts: (1) Evaluation order = CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW → Default Deny, with AUDIT watching independently the whole time (13.9, 13.11). (2) Empty spec = deny everything — this is the zero-trust starting point. (3) ALL conditions in a single rule must be TRUE (from + to + when). (4) SPIFFE principals use the format `spiffe://cluster.local/ns/NAMESPACE/sa/SERVICEACCOUNT`. (5) JWT claims from RequestAuthentication flow into AuthorizationPolicy via `request.auth.claims[key]` — AuthN provides the token verification, AuthZ enforces permissions based on claims.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • mTLS proves WHO, AuthorizationPolicy decides WHAT — even with STRICT mTLS everywhere, without AuthorizationPolicy ANY authenticated service can call ANY other service. You need both, always.
  • The moment ANY AuthorizationPolicy (of ANY action type) targets a workload, the default flips from allow-all to implicit-deny — everything not explicitly matched by an ALLOW rule gets 403. With zero policies, the mesh behaves as if authorization doesn't exist.
  • Evaluation order is fixed by ACTION TYPE, never by YAML order or creation order: CUSTOM first (can only ever end in a deny, never independently allow-and-stop) → DENY (always wins if matched) → ALLOW → workload default. AUDIT runs independently the whole time and never gates the decision.
  • RequestAuthentication only ever VALIDATES a JWT — it never rejects a request by itself. To actually reject a missing or invalid token, you need an AuthorizationPolicy requiring requestPrincipals or using a DENY action.
  • 401 vs 403 is a free diagnostic: 401 means RequestAuthentication rejected a present-but-broken JWT (bad signature, expired, wrong issuer); 403 means AuthorizationPolicy rejected the request (including "no token at all" once required).
  • TCP workloads (postgres, kafka, redis) only match on ports/principals/namespaces/ipBlocks — HTTP-only fields like paths/methods are silently DROPPED, not rejected, which can make a DENY rule block MORE than intended.
  • Dry-run (istio.io/dry-run: "true") shadow-evaluates ALLOW/DENY policies with zero enforcement risk — but CUSTOM policies can NEVER be dry-run; stage those against a canary path instead.
  • Every positive match field has a negated "not" twin (notPaths, notPrincipals, notNamespaces, notIpBlocks, notMethods, notHosts, notRequestPrincipals, notValues, notPorts, notServiceAccounts, notRemoteIpBlocks, notTrustDomains) — the standard way to carve out an exception like /healthz without weakening the rest of a policy.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "A CUSTOM policy that says ALLOW can short-circuit the rest of evaluation." No — CUSTOM can only ever END a request early by DENYING it. If the external authorizer says allow, evaluation continues to DENY and ALLOW policies regardless — CUSTOM cannot bypass or rescue a request they would otherwise reject.
  • "RequestAuthentication rejects requests with missing or invalid JWTs." No — it only VALIDATES. A missing token, by default, still passes through with no principal set. You must pair it with an AuthorizationPolicy requiring requestPrincipals (or a DENY) to actually reject anything.
  • "Applying deny-all first, then adding ALLOW policies, is the safe rollout order." Backwards — deny-all FIRST 403s every live call for as long as the gap lasts before the ALLOWs exist. Apply every ALLOW policy first, then deny-all (ideally shadowed via dry-run first).
  • "A DENY rule with paths on a TCP target is more precise than a plain port-only DENY." No — paths is silently DROPPED for TCP traffic, so the rule enforces only what's left (usually just the principal/port match) — often denying MORE than intended, not less.
  • "AUDIT and dry-run are basically the same feature with different names." No — AUDIT is a standing 4th action type needing a separate logging plugin to produce observable output; dry-run is an annotation on a REAL about-to-be-enforced ALLOW/DENY policy that works out of the box with no plugin. Different mechanisms, different intents (ongoing compliance trail vs. one-time rehearsal).
  • "Principal-based ALLOW rules work fine under PERMISSIVE mTLS." Technically yes if the caller uses mTLS, but a plaintext caller under PERMISSIVE is let through with NO principal set at all, silently failing any principals-based rule — always pair principal-based AuthZ with PeerAuthentication STRICT.
  • "CUSTOM policies get shadow-tested by dry-run just like ALLOW/DENY." No — dry-run only shadows ALLOW and DENY actions. CUSTOM is NEVER dry-run; it always executes for real the moment it's applied.

💼 Chapter 13 — Daily Work Takeaways

  • Always apply ALLOW policies BEFORE deny-all (or dry-run the deny-all first) — never flip a namespace to implicit-deny before its allow-list already exists.
  • Reach for dry-run on every new ALLOW/DENY policy before enforcing it — the risk of a bad policy is zero during rehearsal, and all three output channels (logs, metrics, traces) are free, built-in tooling.
  • When a wave of 403s follows a new policy, check whether it's the FIRST ALLOW targeting that workload — that alone flips the default from allow-by-default to implicit-deny, independent of anything else in the rule.
  • Never put paths or methods on a TCP-target policy — Istio won't reject the YAML, it'll just silently drop those fields and enforce a different (usually broader) policy than you intended.
  • Scope CUSTOM policies to exclude callers you already know are denied elsewhere — CUSTOM always runs first and can't be skipped by a later DENY, so an unscoped external authorizer call gets paid for (latency, cost) even on requests that were always going to be rejected.
  • Use notPaths/notPrincipals for real exceptions (health checks, public endpoints) rather than writing a second overlapping policy — the negated field family is the documented, less error-prone pattern.
  • For the ICA exam: be able to trace a single request through all four action types (CUSTOM/AUDIT/DENY/ALLOW) and state the verdict without hesitation — this is explicitly the most exam-critical sequence in the Securing Workloads domain.
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 13

Seven quick-fire phrase-to-answer mappings — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Deny all traffic" = AuthorizationPolicy with empty spec: {}
  • "Allow only ONE specific caller" = ALLOW rule with from.source.principals: [...] naming its exact SPIFFE ID
  • "Missing JWT should also be rejected" = pair RequestAuthentication with an ALLOW requiring requestPrincipals: ["*"], or a DENY on notRequestPrincipals: ["*"]
  • "Exempt health checks from a policy" = notPaths: ["/healthz", "/ready"]
  • "Protect a raw TCP database port" = ALLOW with only ports + principals — never paths/methods
  • "Test a risky policy safely" = istio.io/dry-run: "true" annotation, check rbac:debug logs + Prometheus + traces
  • "Trace CUSTOM/AUDIT/DENY/ALLOW on one request" = CUSTOM (deny-only, runs first) → DENY (always wins) → ALLOW → default, AUDIT watching independently throughout

🧠 Chapter 13 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
With STRICT mTLS enabled mesh-wide and zero AuthorizationPolicies applied, can skills-service call user-service and read all its data?
Show Answer
Answer

Yes. mTLS proves identity (WHO is calling) but enforces no permissions at all. With zero AuthorizationPolicies, the mesh behaves as allow-by-default — ANY authenticated service can call ANY other service.

Explanation

This is the exact gap Chapter 13 exists to close — a compromised pod that authenticates perfectly can still do unlimited damage without a second, independent control restricting what it may call.

Q2
A team applies their FIRST AuthorizationPolicy for user-service — a single ALLOW rule permitting jobpost-api. What happens to every OTHER caller that was working fine a moment ago?
Show Answer
Answer

They all start getting 403. The moment ANY AuthorizationPolicy targets a workload, the default flips from allow-all to implicit-deny — everything not explicitly matched by an ALLOW rule is now rejected, not just the caller the new rule was written for.

Explanation

This is the single most common cause of a sudden wave of 403s right after a "harmless-looking" new policy — the team only thought about what they were ALLOWING, not that they were also implicitly denying everyone else at the same time.

Q3
Does RequestAuthentication, by itself, reject a request with a missing JWT?
Show Answer
Answer

No. RequestAuthentication only VALIDATES tokens that are present. A request with NO token at all passes through with a 200 by default — no principal gets set, but nothing rejects it. Rejecting a missing token requires a separate AuthorizationPolicy requiring requestPrincipals.

Explanation

This is a genuinely common misconception — RequestAuthentication and AuthorizationPolicy are two separate CRDs doing two separate jobs, and skipping the second one silently leaves the "require a JWT" intent completely unenforced.

Q4
A caller gets a 401. A different caller gets a 403 for a similar-looking request. What's the difference?
Show Answer
Answer

401 means RequestAuthentication rejected a PRESENT but BROKEN JWT (bad signature, expired, wrong issuer). 403 means AuthorizationPolicy rejected the request — including the case of NO token at all, once requestPrincipals is required.

Explanation

This status-code distinction is a free, instant diagnostic — you can tell which of two completely different CRDs to go debug just from the HTTP status code alone, before reading a single log line.

Q5
A DENY policy targets postgres:5432 with paths: ["/admin"] and a principal match. What actually gets enforced?
Show Answer
Answer

Only the principal + port match — paths is silently DROPPED for TCP traffic (it's an HTTP-only field). The DENY rule ends up blocking that principal on port 5432 ENTIRELY, not just requests to a nonexistent "/admin path" within Postgres's wire protocol.

Explanation

This is the TCP trap in its DENY form — Istio doesn't reject the invalid YAML, it just quietly enforces less than what was written, which for a DENY rule means denying MORE than intended.

Q6
What are the three output channels dry-run authorization writes to, and which one lets you correlate a shadow verdict with ONE specific user's report?
Show Answer
Answer

Proxy/access logs (rbac:debug level), Prometheus metrics (authz_dry_run_result), and distributed traces (span tags). Distributed traces are the one that ties a shadow verdict to ONE exact request, since each trace corresponds to a single real call.

Explanation

Logs are best for pinpointing which exact rule fired; metrics give an aggregate mesh-wide view; traces give per-request correlation — each channel answers a different question, which is why the chapter recommends checking all three, not just one.

Q7
Can a CUSTOM policy's ALLOW verdict short-circuit evaluation and skip the DENY/ALLOW checks that follow it?
Show Answer
Answer

No. CUSTOM can only ever END a request early by DENYING it. If the external authorizer says allow (doesn't deny), evaluation continues normally to the DENY and ALLOW steps — CUSTOM cannot bypass or rescue a request those steps would otherwise reject.

Explanation

This is directly from Istio's own documentation: the CUSTOM extension "cannot bypass the authorization decision made by ALLOW and DENY action" — a request is allowed if and only if CUSTOM and every ALLOW/DENY policy all agree to allow it.

Q8
What's the difference between AUDIT and dry-run — both seem to "just log something"?
Show Answer
Answer

AUDIT is a 4th, independent action type on its OWN standing policy, and needs a separate logging plugin enabled or nothing observable happens at all. Dry-run is an ANNOTATION on an existing about-to-be-enforced ALLOW/DENY policy, and works out of the box with no plugin — it's a one-time rehearsal, not a standing compliance trail.

Explanation

They also serve different intents: AUDIT is for ongoing "who touched /admin" visibility with no enforcement plan at all; dry-run is specifically for rehearsing a REAL policy that IS about to go live.

Q9
An AuthorizationPolicy uses principals to match callers, but the namespace is still on PERMISSIVE mTLS. What happens to a plaintext caller?
Show Answer
Answer

It's let through with NO principal set at all — under PERMISSIVE, a plaintext caller isn't rejected at the mTLS layer, but it also has no SPIFFE identity to check. A principals-based ALLOW rule silently fails to match it (which, depending on the rest of the policy, could mean either an unexpected allow or an unexpected deny).

Explanation

This is why the chapter insists on always pairing principal-based AuthorizationPolicy rules with PeerAuthentication STRICT — under PERMISSIVE, the two controls can silently work against each other's assumptions.

Q10
Name at least 4 of the "when:" condition keys and state whether each is HTTP-only or works for both HTTP and TCP.
Show Answer
Answer

Examples: source.ip (HTTP+TCP), source.principal (HTTP+TCP, needs mTLS), connection.sni (HTTP+TCP, needs TLS), destination.port (HTTP+TCP), request.headers[x] (HTTP only), request.auth.claims[x] (HTTP only).

Explanation

The HTTP-only vs HTTP+TCP scoping matters for the same reason as 13.6's ports/paths trap — using an HTTP-only when key against a TCP-target policy silently does nothing, the same "silently dropped, not rejected" failure mode.

⚙️ Chapter 13 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a broken state, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
Write a deny-all AuthorizationPolicy for the anihpj namespace, staged safely with dry-run first.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    istio.io/dry-run: "true"
spec: {}
Explanation

The dry-run annotation is what makes this SAFE to apply even before every ALLOW policy exists — it shadow-evaluates without enforcing, so no live traffic breaks while you verify the allow-list is complete.

Q2
Only istio-ingressgateway may call jobpost-api with GET or POST. Write the ALLOW policy.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-ingress-to-jobpost
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals:
        - "cluster.local/ns/istio-system/sa/istio-ingressgateway"
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
Explanation

The policy lives on jobpost-api's own selector (13.3's rule: each ALLOW policy sits next to its TARGET, governing traffic INTO it, not out of it).

Q3
Require a valid JWT for every path on jobpost-api EXCEPT /healthz and /ready.
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - to:
    - operation:
        notPaths: ["/healthz", "/ready"]
    from:
    - source:
        requestPrincipals: ["*"]
  - to:
    - operation:
        paths: ["/healthz", "/ready"]
Explanation

Two rules in one policy: the first requires a JWT for everything except the health paths, the second explicitly allows the health paths with no from: block (meaning anyone, no auth required).

Q4
Only jobpost-api may connect to postgres on port 5432. Write and verify the policy.
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"]
    to:
    - operation:
        ports: ["5432"]
psql "host=postgres.anihpj port=5432 ..." -c "SELECT 1;"
# allowed pod: rows returned; blocked pod: connection reset
Explanation

Only ports and principals are used — no paths/methods, since this is a raw TCP target and those fields would be silently dropped anyway.

Q5
jobpost-api's allow-jobpost policy exists, but requests are still getting 403 from a legitimate caller. Task: Diagnose using dry-run tooling.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl proxy-config log deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj --level rbac:debug
kubectl logs deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -c istio-proxy | grep -i rbac
Explanation

Raising the RBAC log level surfaces exactly which rule (or lack thereof) is producing the verdict — faster than guessing at the YAML by eye, especially when multiple policies target the same workload.

Q6
Wire an external fraud-check authorizer for POST /api/jobs/ only, failing closed if fraud-check is unreachable.
Show Answer
Answer
# MeshConfig extensionProvider (patch istiod's ConfigMap)
extensionProviders:
- name: fraud-check
  envoyExtAuthzHttp:
    service: "fraud-check.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
    port: "9000"
    timeout: "2s"
    failOpen: false   # fail CLOSED — the default, explicit here for clarity
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  action: CUSTOM
  provider:
    name: fraud-check
  rules:
  - to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["POST"]
        paths: ["/api/jobs/*"]
Explanation

failOpen: false means a fraud-check outage 403s the request instead of silently letting it through — the correct default for a money-moving path, where availability should never silently disable fraud protection.

Q7
Log every hit on /admin/* without blocking anything, as a standing compliance policy.
Show Answer
Answer
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  action: AUDIT
  rules:
  - to:
    - operation:
        paths: ["/admin/*"]
Explanation

Unlike dry-run, this AUDIT policy stays in place PERMANENTLY as a standing compliance trail — it isn't a rehearsal for something about to be enforced, and requires a logging plugin actually enabled to produce visible output.

Q8
Restrict the admin console to the corporate VPN egress range using a when: condition.
Show Answer
Answer
rules:
- to:
  - operation:
      paths: ["/admin/*"]
  when:
  - key: remote.ip
    values: ["203.0.113.0/24"]
Explanation

remote.ip reads the ORIGINAL client IP (via X-Forwarded-For or PROXY protocol), not the immediate connection's source — the correct key when the real client is behind a load balancer or gateway.

Q9
A request to jobpost-api's POST /api/jobs/ from skills-service (already on a permanent deny list) still triggers a billable call to the external fraud-check authorizer. Is this expected, and how do you stop the wasted cost?
Show Answer
Answer
# scope the CUSTOM policy itself to exclude already-denied callers
spec:
  action: CUSTOM
  provider:
    name: fraud-check
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        notPrincipals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/skills-service"]
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["POST"]
        paths: ["/api/jobs/*"]
Explanation

Yes, expected — CUSTOM always runs FIRST, before DENY, and cannot be skipped by a later DENY rule. The only way to avoid the wasted external call is to scope the CUSTOM policy's own from/selector to exclude callers you already know are denied elsewhere.

Q10
Only requests carrying JWT claim role=admin may POST to /api/jobs/. Write both required resources.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: RequestAuthentication
metadata:
  name: jwt-auth
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  jwtRules:
  - issuer: "auth-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
    jwksUri: "http://auth-service/.well-known/jwks.json"
---
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-admin-jwt
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["POST"]
        paths: ["/api/jobs/*"]
    when:
    - key: request.auth.claims[role]
      values: ["admin"]
Explanation

Two separate CRDs, both required: RequestAuthentication validates the JWT signature/issuer/expiry; the AuthorizationPolicy's when clause is what actually checks the role claim and turns it into a decision.

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 13
  • Apply every ALLOW policy for a workload BEFORE its deny-all goes live (or dry-run the deny-all first) — flipping deny-all before the ALLOWs exist 403s all live traffic for as long as the gap lasts (13.3).
  • A sudden wave of 403s right after ONE new AuthorizationPolicy lands? Check whether it is the FIRST ALLOW targeting that workload — that alone flips the default from allow-by-default to implicit-deny (13.7).
  • 401 vs 403 is a free diagnostic: 401 = RequestAuthentication rejected a present-but-broken JWT; 403 = AuthorizationPolicy rejected it (including "no token at all" once requestPrincipals is required) (13.4).
  • Dry-run every new ALLOW/DENY before enforcing it and read all three channels (rbac:debug proxy logs, Prometheus authz_dry_run_* metrics, trace tags) — CUSTOM can never be dry-run, so stage those against a canary path instead (13.8, 13.10).
  • One phrase covers every ordering question the exam can ask: "CUSTOM can only say no, DENY always wins, ALLOW is the last word, AUDIT never speaks" (13.11).
  • TCP workload (postgres, kafka)? Only ports/principals/namespaces/ipBlocks are valid match fields — paths or methods showing up in a TCP-target policy is the bug, not a feature (13.6).

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 13)

Every command below already appeared earlier in this chapter — grouped here as one reference for rolling out, inspecting, and rehearsing AuthorizationPolicy.

CommandWhat It Does / Checks in Chapter 13
kubectl apply -f authz/ -n anihpjApply the anihpj ALLOW policy set (13.3)
kubectl get authorizationpolicy -n anihpjList every policy in the namespace
kubectl describe authorizationpolicy <name> -n anihpjShow one policy's full rule set
kubectl annotate authorizationpolicy/<name> -n anihpj istio.io/dry-run-Remove dry-run → start enforcing (13.8)
istioctl proxy-config log deploy/<svc> -n anihpj --level rbac:debugRaise RBAC log level, see shadow verdicts (13.8)
kubectl exec deploy/<svc> -n anihpj -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w %{http_code} <url>Quick allow/deny smoke test
psql "host=postgres.anihpj port=5432 ..." -c "SELECT 1;"Verify TCP ALLOW: reset = blocked, rows = OK (13.6)

🧪 Practice Drill 13.1 — Ship Deny-All + One ALLOW, Zero Outage

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Do this now, timed, on your own anihpj cluster:

  1. (1 min) Apply a deny-all AuthorizationPolicy in anihpj, but annotate it istio.io/dry-run: "true" first — nothing is enforced yet.
  2. (1 min) Curl jobpost-api → user-service from inside the mesh right now and confirm it still returns 200 (dry-run enforces nothing).
  3. (2 min) Run istioctl proxy-config log deploy/user-service -n anihpj --level rbac:debug, then watch for "shadow denied" lines.
  4. (2 min) Write and apply one real ALLOW policy on user-service permitting only jobpost-api, GET, /api/users/*.
  5. (2 min) Remove the dry-run annotation (istio.io/dry-run-) and re-run both curls: jobpost-api → 200, skills-service → 403.
Hint: Step 1 reuses 13.8's dry-run annotation; step 3 is the exact rbac:debug reflex 13.8 teaches for reading shadow verdicts; step 4 is 13.3's zero-trust matrix reduced to one row; step 5 proves the CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW order from 13.7/13.11 by watching the SAME two callers land on opposite verdicts.
View Solution

Step 3's log output should show "shadow denied" lines for callers NOT yet in your ALLOW policy, even though their real requests still succeed (200) — that's dry-run doing its job. Step 5 should show a clean split: jobpost-api 200, skills-service 403, proving the ALLOW policy is now actually enforced.

Check yourself: did you check the rbac:debug logs in step 3 BEFORE writing the real ALLOW policy in step 4, or did you skip straight to step 4 and trust the dry-run passively? Actually reading the shadow verdicts is the whole point of rehearsing — skipping that step defeats the drill's purpose.

🧪 Practice Drill 13.2 — Reproduce the TCP Paths-Silently-Dropped Trap Yourself

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Don't take 13.6's TCP trap on faith — build and observe it live.

  1. Apply an ALLOW policy on a TCP-target workload (e.g. postgres) that includes BOTH ports: ["5432"] AND an HTTP-only field like paths: ["/admin"].
  2. Confirm the policy applies with no YAML validation error.
  3. From an allowed principal, connect via psql and confirm the connection succeeds DESPITE never sending any "/admin path."
  4. Use istioctl proxy-config log ... --level rbac:debug to confirm the paths field never appears in the actual matched-rule evaluation.
Hint: Step 3 is the key observation — if paths actually mattered, no plain psql connection (which has no concept of an HTTP path) could ever match, and the connection would fail. It succeeding is the proof the field was ignored.
View Solution

Step 3's psql connection should succeed — proving paths was silently ignored, not enforced. If it had been enforced, no TCP connection (which has no HTTP path concept at all) could ever match the rule, and every connection would fail.

Check yourself: could you now explain to a teammate, using your own psql session as proof, why this ISN'T a bug in Istio but a genuine misunderstanding of what fields apply to TCP? That's the distinction this drill is built to make concrete.

🧪 Practice Drill 13.3 — Match the Symptom to the Broken Layer

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

For each observation, name the most likely cause and the ONE command you'd run to confirm it — before proposing any fix:

  1. A caller with a completely missing Authorization header still gets a 200 from a service with RequestAuthentication configured.
  2. A brand-new ALLOW policy for one caller causes 403s for FIVE other previously-working callers.
  3. A CUSTOM fraud-check policy keeps firing for a caller that's on a permanent DENY list.
  4. An AUDIT policy for /admin/* shows zero log lines even though /admin/* is definitely being hit.
Hint: Two of these four are actually "working exactly as designed" once you know the mechanism — not bugs to fix, but behavior to explain correctly.
View Solution
#CauseConfirm with
1Not a bug — RequestAuthentication only validates PRESENT tokens; a missing token needs a separate AuthorizationPolicy requiring requestPrincipals to actually reject itCheck for an ALLOW/DENY policy referencing requestPrincipals
2The new policy was the FIRST AuthorizationPolicy targeting that workload — it flipped the default from allow-all to implicit-deny for everyone, not just its own target callerkubectl get authorizationpolicy -n <ns> -o yaml — check if this is the only/first policy
3Not a bug — CUSTOM always runs FIRST and cannot be skipped by a later DENY rule; this is expected, wasteful behavior unless the CUSTOM policy is scoped to exclude known-denied callersCheck the CUSTOM policy's own from/selector scope
4Missing logging plugin — AUDIT only "internally marks" a request; producing an actual log line needs a separate plugin configured and enabledCheck whether an audit logging plugin/adapter is actually deployed

Check yourself: did you correctly identify #1 and #3 as "working as designed" rather than bugs to fix? Distinguishing expected mechanism from actual misconfiguration is the real diagnostic skill this drill tests.

🧪 Practice Drill 13.4 — Build the Complete Zero-Trust Stack, Layer by Layer

⏱️ Target Time: 10 minutes
Scenario

Build all three security layers for a test workload, verifying each one before adding the next:

  1. Layer 1 (encryption): confirm PeerAuthentication STRICT is active — istioctl x describe pod.
  2. Layer 2 (authorization): apply a deny-all (dry-run first, per Drill 13.1) then one real ALLOW policy for a specific caller.
  3. Layer 3 (end-user auth): add a RequestAuthentication + an ALLOW requiring requestPrincipals, so a request now needs BOTH a valid service identity AND a valid JWT.
  4. Test all 4 combinations: (a) right service + valid JWT → 200. (b) right service + no JWT → 403. (c) wrong service + valid JWT → 403. (d) wrong service + no JWT → 403.
Hint: Case (c) is the one most people get wrong when predicting the outcome — a valid JWT does NOT rescue a caller that fails the service-identity ALLOW check; both layers must independently pass.
View Solution

All 4 cases in step 4 should produce exactly the stated results — only case (a) succeeds. Case (c) failing despite a valid JWT is the key proof that the layers are independent AND-ed together, not alternatives where passing one is enough.

Check yourself: did you predict all 4 outcomes BEFORE running the tests, or only after? Correctly predicting case (c) in advance is the real signal you understand that these are independent, both-required gates, not a single combined check.

🧪 Practice Drill 13.5 — Sketch the Four-Action Evaluation Order From Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking back at the UTH's diagram, sketch (on paper or in a text file) how a single request is evaluated across all four AuthorizationPolicy action types.

  1. Name the order the four action types are checked in.
  2. For each of CUSTOM and DENY, state exactly what a match does to the rest of evaluation.
  3. State where AUDIT fits into this order, and what happens if it "matches."
Hint: This is a paper/whiteboard drill — the point is retrieving the mental model from memory under light time pressure, the same way the exam expects you to trace a request through all four layers without a diagram in front of you.
View Solution

Order: CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW → workload default. A CUSTOM match (deny only) stops evaluation immediately with a 403 — a CUSTOM "allow" does NOT stop evaluation, it continues to DENY. A DENY match ALWAYS stops evaluation immediately with a 403, no ALLOW rule further down can rescue it. AUDIT is NOT part of this sequence at all — it runs independently, in parallel, the entire time, and a match only produces a log entry (if a plugin is configured) — it never changes the ALLOW/DENY outcome.

Check yourself: did your sketch correctly show CUSTOM's asymmetry — that it can deny-and-stop but cannot allow-and-stop? That asymmetry is the single most tested, most commonly mis-recalled detail in this whole evaluation model.
