Chapter 13 starts from a single gap — mTLS proves identity but enforces nothing — and closes it in stages: first with a blunt deny-all plus a hand-built allow-list for anihpj (13.1-13.3), then with JWT-based end-user identity checks (13.4), then with the carve-outs real production traffic always needs — health probes, TCP databases (13.5-13.6) — then with the tooling to change any of it safely via dry-run (13.7-13.8), and finally with the complete four-action mental model — CUSTOM, DENY, ALLOW, and the log-only AUDIT side-channel, plus the full when: condition-key reference (13.9-13.12) — that the ICA exam expects you to trace for any single request without hesitation.

Quick recap — 🔓 mTLS proves WHO, AuthorizationPolicy decides WHAT (13.1) · 🚫 The CRD: deny-all (spec: {}) + explicit ALLOW rules (13.2) · 🗺️ A real zero-trust matrix for anihpj, rolled out via dry-run (13.3) · 🪪 RequestAuthentication + requestPrincipals turns a MISSING token into a 403 too (13.4) · 🩺 Carve-outs: notPaths for /healthz (13.5) · 🔌 Ports-only rules for TCP targets like postgres:5432 (13.6) · 🔍 Evaluation basics: CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW (13.7) · 🧪 Proven safe to change via istio.io/dry-run shadow testing (13.8) · 📝 AUDIT: a log-only side-channel that never blocks (13.9) · 🌐 CUSTOM: external ext-authz, e.g. fraud-check (13.10) · 🔢 The COMPLETE four-action order, AUDIT always watching (13.11) · 📖 The full when: condition-key reference (13.12). Chapter 13 leaves anihpj with every call both encrypted (Ch12) AND explicitly permitted (Ch13) — nothing left to chance.

💼 Chapters 12-13 — Daily Work Takeaways (Security)

  • Enable STRICT mTLS: every service call encrypted, zero code changes
  • Know that SPIFFE certs auto-rotate around the 12h mark — no manual renewal
  • Build a deny-all AuthorizationPolicy → then allow specific paths
  • Create a zero-trust policy matrix: which service can call which
  • Validate JWT tokens at the mesh level — no auth code in services
  • Migrate safely: PERMISSIVE mode first → verify → then STRICT
  • Check certs: openssl s_client to verify mTLS between pods
  • Remember: mTLS = identity (WHO), AuthzPolicy = permissions (WHAT)
  • Know that without AuthzPolicy, ANY service can call ANY service even with mTLS enabled — mTLS alone is NOT access control!
  • Exempt /healthz probes with notPaths — never disable JWT auth to fix a probe
  • Lock PostgreSQL :5432 with a ports-based ALLOW (verify via psql)
  • Rehearse risky policies with istio.io/dry-run: "true" — read shadow results in proxy logs, Prometheus metrics, and Kiali
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapters 12-13 (Securing Workloads — 25%)

This is 25% of the exam (official domain name: "Securing Workloads" — Authorization, Authentication, and Edge TLS):

  • "Encrypt all service traffic" = PeerAuthentication mode: STRICT
  • "Restrict which service can call which" = AuthorizationPolicy
  • "Validate JWT tokens at mesh level" = RequestAuthentication
  • "Protect a database/TCP port" = AuthorizationPolicy with to.operation.ports — HTTP-only fields NEVER match TCP traffic
  • "Test a policy safely first" = istio.io/dry-run: "true"
  • Evaluation order = CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW; the FIRST ALLOW policy on a workload flips its default to implicit deny
🔧 Bonus Walkthrough — Tracing a Disguised Request Through All Four Actions

13.7 walked three separate requests, each tripping only ONE layer. 13.11 then laid out the clean four-step pipeline. Here is the messy, realistic case the exam loves: a single request that LOOKS like it should hit every layer, but doesn't — because "CUSTOM runs first" only means CUSTOM runs first for requests its OWN rule actually scopes in, not for every request that reaches the sidecar.

Scenario: skills-service (already on deny-skills' block list) tries to dodge the fraud-check CUSTOM policy — scoped only to POST /api/jobs/* — by posting to an admin-side import path instead: POST /admin/api/jobs/bulk-import on jobpost-api.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ REQUEST: skills-service -> POST /admin/api/jobs/bulk-import        │
│ -> jobpost-api sidecar (a disguised lateral-movement attempt)      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
     AUDIT runs independently the whole time — the CUSTOM/DENY/ALLOW
     trunk on the right is evaluated separately, in the same pass
                             │
              ┌──────────────┴──────────────┐
              ▼                             ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────┐  ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ AUDIT (audit-admin-access) │  │ STEP 1 - CUSTOM (fraud-check)│
  │ path matches /admin/*? YES │  │ rule matches POST /api/jobs/*?│
  │ -> LOG the hit, right now  │  │ NO - path is /admin/api/jobs/*│
  │                            │  │ -> SCOPED OUT: does not run;  │
  │                            │  │  "runs first" never fires here│
  └────────────────────────────┘  └────────────────────────────┘
                                              │
                                              ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────┐  ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ AUDIT VERDICT               │  │ STEP 2 - DENY (deny-skills)│
  │ logged to proxy log,        │  │ source == skills-service?  │
  │ metrics, and trace tags —   │  │ YES -> STOP HERE -> 403    │
  │ this NEVER changes the      │  │ (step 3, ALLOW, never      │
  │ ALLOW/DENY outcome          │  │  reached)                  │
  └────────────────────────────┘  └────────────────────────────┘
              │                             │
              └──────────────┬──────────────┘
                             ▼
        ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │ RESULT: 403, reason = DENY (deny-skills)    │
        │ PLUS one AUDIT log line recorded for /admin/*│
        │ — two independent outcomes from one request │
        └────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The lesson: disguising the path did not help the attacker (deny-skills still catches the source identity regardless of URL), but it DID prove that CUSTOM's "runs first" guarantee is conditional on its own rule actually matching — a request can sail past a CUSTOM policy entirely and still be judged, and logged, by the layers behind it.

📝 Chapters 12-13 — ICA Exam Questions (Security)

Q1
How do you enforce STRICT mTLS for the anihpj namespace?
Show Answer
Answer

Create a PeerAuthentication resource with spec.mtls.mode: STRICT in the anihpj namespace.

Explanation

This is the direct exam mapping for "encrypt all service traffic" (12.3).

Q2
What AuthorizationPolicy would allow ONLY jobpost-api to GET /api/users/* on user-service?
Show Answer
Answer
selector: {app: user-service}
action: ALLOW
rules:
- from:
  - source:
      principals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"]
  to:
  - operation:
      methods: ["GET"]
      paths: ["/api/users/*"]
Explanation

ALLOW rules combine WHO (principals) with WHAT (methods/paths) inside ONE rule — all conditions in that rule must be true together (13.2).

Q3
Why is mTLS alone not sufficient for security?
Show Answer
Answer

mTLS provides identity (WHO is calling) but not authorization (WHAT they are allowed to do). Without AuthorizationPolicy, ANY authenticated service can call ANY other service. You need BOTH.

Explanation

The single most repeated distinction across Part 7 — a compromised pod can authenticate perfectly and still do damage if nothing restricts what it may call (13.1).

Q4
anihpj still has two legacy Deployments without sidecars. How do you reach STRICT mTLS without an outage?
Show Answer
Answer

Stage it: apply PeerAuthentication mode: PERMISSIVE to anihpj first (accepts BOTH plaintext and mTLS), confirm every edge shows locks in Kiali and istioctl x describe pod reports mTLS, inject sidecars into the two stragglers, then edit the same resource to mode: STRICT.

Explanation

The safe migration path is always PERMISSIVE → verify → STRICT, never a direct jump (12.3).

Q5
Task: only istio-ingressgateway may call jobpost-api; everything else in anihpj is blocked. Which two AuthorizationPolicies do you apply?
Show Answer
Answer

(1) deny-all: namespace anihpj, spec: {} — empty spec denies all. (2) ALLOW: selector {app: jobpost-api}, action: ALLOW, from.source.principals: ["cluster.local/ns/istio-system/sa/istio-ingressgateway"].

Explanation

The deny-all flips the default to implicit-deny; the ALLOW re-opens exactly one path (13.2, 13.3).

Q6
Only JWTs carrying role=admin may POST /api/jobs/. What do you build?
Show Answer
Answer

A RequestAuthentication (issuer https://auth.anihpj.com, jwksUri https://auth.anihpj.com/.well-known/jwks.json) plus an ALLOW AuthorizationPolicy: from.source.requestPrincipals: ["https://auth.anihpj.com/*"], to.operation {methods: ["POST"], paths: ["/api/jobs/*"]}, when request.auth.claims[role] = admin.

Explanation

RequestAuthentication validates the signature; the claim check lives in the AuthorizationPolicy — two separate CRDs, both required (13.4).

Q7
After turning on STRICT mTLS, every call to user-service returns 503 (upstream connect error). A DestinationRule for user-service exists. Diagnose.
Show Answer
Answer

The DestinationRule likely sets trafficPolicy.tls.mode: DISABLE, so client sidecars send plaintext that the STRICT server resets. Confirm with istioctl x describe pod <user-service-pod> (it flags the PA/DR conflict), then set tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL or delete the stale rule.

Explanation

The DR/PA TLS contract: a mismatch between what the client sends and what the server requires always shows up as a 503, generated client-side (12.8).

Q8
Restrict PostgreSQL at postgres.anihpj:5432 so only jobpost-api and user-service can connect. Write and verify the policy.
Show Answer
Answer

ALLOW policy: selector {app: postgres}, from.source.principals: [".../sa/jobpost-api", ".../sa/user-service"], to.operation.ports: ["5432"]. Use ONLY ports — methods/paths never match TCP and would make the ALLOW rule unmatchable (traffic denied). Verify with psql: allowed pods run SELECT 1; blocked pods get a connection reset.

Explanation

TCP AuthorizationPolicy only understands ports/principals/namespaces/ipBlocks (13.6).

Q9
You must land a deny policy on jobpost-api mid-day with zero risk. How do you test it live, and where do you read the results?
Show Answer
Answer

Annotate it "istio.io/dry-run": "true" — traffic keeps flowing while Envoy shadow-evaluates. Read results in: proxy logs ("shadow denied", after istioctl proxy-config log ... --level rbac:debug), the rbac metric with authz_dry_run_result="denied" in Prometheus/Kiali, and dry-run span tags in tracing. Remove the annotation to enforce.

Explanation

Three output channels, cross-checked together, before flipping enforcement on (13.8).

Q10
Kubelet probes to /healthz return 403 after you required JWTs on jobpost-api. Fix it without weakening auth on the real endpoints.
Show Answer
Answer

Use exclusion matching in the require-jwt ALLOW policy: on the JWT rule set to.operation.notPaths: ["/healthz", "/ready"], and add a second rule with paths: ["/healthz", "/ready"] and no from: block. Probes (no JWT) now pass; every other path still demands a token.

Explanation

This is the exact anihpj war story behind 13.5 — the day require-jwt shipped without this exemption, jobpost-api restart-looped.

Q11
anihpj's namespace-wide PeerAuthentication is STRICT, yet a debug pod's plain curl to notification-service returns 200 OK instead of a connection reset. kubectl get peerauthentication -n anihpj lists a second object, notification-legacy (selector app: notification-service, mode: PERMISSIVE), left over from a debugging session. Explain why plaintext still works, and fix it without touching the namespace-wide default.
Show Answer
Answer

PeerAuthentication precedence is narrowest-scope-wins, not creation order or "namespace beats workload": the workload-scoped notification-legacy (mode PERMISSIVE) beats the namespace-wide default (STRICT) for that one workload only. Fix: kubectl delete peerauthentication notification-legacy -n anihpj — the pod then inherits the namespace default (STRICT). Confirm with istioctl x describe pod, then re-curl plaintext and expect "connection reset by peer," not 200.

Explanation

Precedence is ALWAYS narrowest-match-wins, regardless of when each policy was created (12.6).

Q12
istiod was accidentally scaled to 0 for about 30 hours during a botched Helm upgrade; the data plane kept routing on cached config the whole time. Now that istiod is back, calls between jobpost-api and user-service fail with a hard TLS handshake error — not a 503, not a 403. How do you confirm this is a cert-expiry problem, and fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

SVID certs are valid only ~24h, and with istiod unreachable for over a day neither pod could renew before expiry — a plain PA/DR mismatch produces a 503, not a handshake failure, so suspect expired crypto material instead. Confirm with istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj (the default cert's "Not After" timestamp is in the past) or openssl s_client -connect user-service.anihpj:8080 ("certificate has expired"). Fix: verify istiod is healthy, then force fresh CSRs with kubectl rollout restart deployment jobpost-api user-service -n anihpj — expired certs do not renew themselves without a restart.

Explanation

A TLS handshake failure (not 503, not 403) is the exam's signature for expired certificates, not a PA/DR mismatch (12.4, 12.13).

Q13
Security mandates that every anihpj mesh certificate chain to the company's existing enterprise root CA instead of istiod's self-signed root — but wants the least invasive change: istiod should keep issuing and auto-rotating the workload certs, just under the new root. Which upgrade path do you pick, and what are the exact steps?
Show Answer
Answer

Plug-in CA certs — istiod keeps signing and rotating SVIDs, only the root changes (SPIRE and cert-manager/istio-csr both take issuance away from istiod entirely, more invasive than asked). Steps: (1) generate an intermediate CA under the enterprise root, producing ca-cert.pem, ca-key.pem, root-cert.pem, cert-chain.pem; (2) kubectl create secret generic cacerts -n istio-system --from-file=... — name MUST be cacerts, namespace MUST be istio-system; (3) istioctl install --set profile=default -y so istiod picks up the new root; (4) kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj so every workload requests a fresh CSR under the new chain.

Explanation

Three external-CA upgrade paths exist (plug-in certs, SPIRE, cert-manager); the exam expects you to pick the LEAST invasive one that satisfies the stated requirement (12.9).

Q14
The test-team ServiceAccount (cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/test-team) was compromised and must be blocked from calling search-service immediately — but every other caller in anihpj (jobpost-api, user-service, skills-service, and any service added later) must keep working without you hand-listing every legitimate principal. Write the policy.
Show Answer
Answer
selector: {app: search-service}
action: ALLOW
rules:
- from:
  - source:
      notPrincipals: ["cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/test-team"]

Any principal OTHER than test-team satisfies the rule and is allowed; test-team fails the match and — because this ALLOW policy now targets search-service — falls through to implicit deny (403). Belt-and-suspenders option: add a companion action: DENY rule with from.source.principals: [".../sa/test-team"] so the block survives even if the ALLOW policy is later removed.

Explanation

notPrincipals matches everyone except the named identity — the right tool when you need to block ONE caller without enumerating everyone else (13.5).

Q15
anihpj adds a Kafka broker at kafka.anihpj:9092; only notification-service and search-service should publish to it. A teammate scopes a DENY policy narrowly — blocking skills-service only when it hits an "/admin" path — with rules: [{from: [{source: {principals: [".../sa/skills-service"]}}], to: [{operation: {ports: ["9092"], paths: ["/admin"]}}]}]. After applying it, ALL of skills-service's Kafka traffic is blocked, not just calls to "/admin". Explain the bug and give the corrected policy.
Show Answer
Answer

Kafka on 9092 is raw TCP, and paths is an HTTP-only match field — Istio silently drops it from a DENY rule instead of rejecting the policy, leaving only ports: ["9092"] plus the principal to enforce. The rule actually reads "DENY skills-service on port 9092, full stop," denying MORE than intended. Corrected policy: drop the paths field and own the fact this is an all-or-nothing TCP block: action: DENY, rules: [{from: [{source: {principals: [".../sa/skills-service"]}}], to: [{operation: {ports: ["9092"]}}]}]. If skills-service genuinely needs partial access, split it onto a separate port — AuthorizationPolicy cannot inspect L7 semantics inside a raw TCP stream.

Explanation

The exact TCP DENY trap from 13.6 — HTTP-only fields are silently dropped, not rejected, and can make a DENY rule deny MORE than written.

Q16
anihpj wires an external fraud-detection CUSTOM AuthorizationPolicy in front of jobpost-api's POST /api/jobs/, calling out to fraud-check.anihpj:9000 on every request. A separate DENY policy permanently blocks skills-service from reaching jobpost-api. During a load test, fraud-check.anihpj's logs show it being invoked for requests FROM skills-service — traffic that should never reach business logic. Is this a bug, and does moving the DENY policy ahead of the CUSTOM one fix it?
Show Answer
Answer

Not a bug — it is the fixed Istio evaluation order: CUSTOM always runs first, before DENY and before ALLOW, for every request that reaches the sidecar, and this order cannot be changed by editing YAML or by policy creation order. So the fraud-check CUSTOM provider fires even for skills-service traffic the DENY policy will reject moments later; reordering the DENY policy ahead of it is not possible, and would not help if it were. To cut wasted external calls, scope the CUSTOM policy's own selector/from.source.notPrincipals to exclude skills-service directly, so a caller that is denied anyway never triggers the external fraud-check round trip.

Explanation

The ACTION TYPE fixes the phase (CUSTOM → DENY → ALLOW) — application order and YAML ordering are both irrelevant (13.10, 13.11).

Q17
Comprehensive security drill. Task: (a) Apply STRICT mTLS (PeerAuthentication). (b) Apply deny-all AuthorizationPolicy. (c) Create selective ALLOW policies for all anihpj services. (d) Add JWT validation (RequestAuthentication). (e) Test all paths: allowed → 200, denied by AuthorizationPolicy → 403, missing JWT → also 403 (once requestPrincipals is required), a present-but-invalid JWT → 401. (f) Verify in Kiali: green locks on every edge, graph shows allowed traffic only. (g) Explain the 3 security layers.
Show Answer
Answer

Layer 1: mTLS (encryption + service identity, Ch12). Layer 2: AuthorizationPolicy (service-level access control, 13.2-13.3). Layer 3: RequestAuthentication + JWT (end-user identity, 13.4). All three compose Istio's zero-trust security model — none of them alone is sufficient.

Explanation

Complete security stack: encrypt everything (mTLS) → restrict services (AuthzPolicy) → authenticate users (JWT). This capstone ties every section of Chapters 12-13 together.

Q18
Verify mTLS is working end-to-end, using only current (non-deprecated) tooling.
Show Answer
Answer

istioctl x describe pod <pod> -n anihpj — fastest, prints the EFFECTIVE PeerAuthentication mode + DestinationRule TLS mode in one shot. istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/<name> -n anihpj — most detailed, shows the live SPIFFE cert, ROOTCA, and expiration. Kiali Graph → Display → Security — fastest visual check, every encrypted edge shows a 🔒 lock icon.

Explanation

istioctl authn tls-check is REMOVED (12.7) — if an older runbook mentions it, substitute istioctl x describe pod. Use Kiali for the overview, then drill into x describe pod / proxy-config secret for detail.

Chapter 14: Canary Deployments — Safe Feature Releases

Shipping jobpost-api's next version is risky by default — deploy it, and every job search on the platform is now betting on code nobody has run in production yet. Canary deployments, shadow/mirror testing, and blue-green cut-overs are three disciplined answers to the same question: how do you move real traffic from v1 to v2 with a same-second rollback available at every step, using nothing but the weight and mirror fields Chapter 6 already taught?

"How do I ship a change without betting everything on it?" jobpost-api's matching-logic rewrite (v2) is exactly the kind of change anihpj cannot afford to ship blind — get it wrong and every job search on the platform breaks at once. Chapter 6 already gave you the two YAML fields this entire chapter runs on: a VirtualService's weight field, which splits traffic by percentage, and its mirror field, which copies traffic without ever touching the response a real user sees. Chapter 14 adds no new CRD at all — it asks a harder question about those same two fields: in what SEQUENCE, gated by what SIGNAL, with what ROLLBACK PLAN, do you move weight from 0 to 100? Canary (14.1), shadow/mirror testing (14.2), and blue-green (14.3) are three disciplined answers to that one question, not three different technologies — and 14.4's decision matrix exists because picking the wrong one for a given anihpj change (a schema migration flipped like a canary, or a one-line patch flipped like blue-green) is its own kind of outage. By 14.7 you can also tell apart "canary" applied to jobpost-api (an application decision, yours to make) from "canary" applied to istiod itself (a mesh-operator decision, covered fully in Chapter 17) — two ideas the exam tests as separate questions.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2 hours 🚀 Deployment 🎯 Extends 2 Domains

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Run jobpost-api-v2 through a full canary ramp — mirror → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% — using only VirtualService weight edits, with a same-second rollback available at every single step
  • ✅ Configure mirror + mirrorPercentage so jobpost-api-v2 sees real production traffic while its responses are silently discarded, and explain why a mirrored write still lands in PostgreSQL
  • ✅ Execute an instant blue-green cut-over (and rollback) for a service like user-service, and name the shared-database compatibility trap that comes bundled with it
  • ✅ Use the risk/rollback/cost decision matrix (14.4) to pick canary, blue-green, rolling, or shadow for any anihpj scenario in under 30 seconds
  • ✅ Describe how a metrics-gated automated canary (Flagger, Argo Rollouts) promotes or rolls back jobpost-api v2 without a human staring at Grafana for five days
  • ✅ Ramp mirrorPercentage independently of route weight (1% → 10% → 50% → 100%) and configure a multi-destination mirrors[] rule
  • ✅ Tell an APPLICATION canary (jobpost-api v1/v2 via VirtualService weight) apart from a CONTROL-PLANE canary (istiod stable/canary via istioctl revision) without hesitating
🎓 ICA Relevance
Extends Traffic Mgmt 35% Extends Install/Upgrade 20%

⚠️ Honest framing: Chapter 14 carries no line item of its own on the official ICA blueprint — Part 8 exists to extend Traffic Management (35%) and Installation, Upgrade & Config (20%) to production scale, not to add a ninth domain. In practice this means the exam almost never says "canary deployment" outright; it says "roll out a change gradually," "test a new version without risking real users," or "release with an instant rollback," and expects you to reach for the exact VirtualService weight/mirror pattern Chapter 6 already taught. The one place this chapter draws a hard, independently-graded line is 14.7: a scenario about safely upgrading Istio itself belongs to Chapter 17's Installation/Upgrade domain and is answered with istioctl revisions, not VirtualService weights — confusing the two is a guaranteed wrong answer, not a partial-credit one.

14.1 The Full Canary Deployment Workflow

Phase-by-phase rollout for jobpost-api:v2 — from zero traffic to 100% production:

📈 CANARY LIFECYCLE — jobpost-api:v2 Gradual Rollout
Day 1
v1: 100% · v2: 0%
Deploy v2 only
Check v2 starts OK
Day 2
v1: 95% · v2: 5%
Error rate < 1%? ✅
Proceed
Day 3
v1: 75% · v2: 25%
p99 < 300ms? ✅
Proceed
Day 4
v1: 50% · v2: 50%
v2 errors 5%? ⚠️
❌ ROLLBACK!
Day 7
v1: 0% · v2: 100%
Fix bug, restart
✅ Production!
💡 Instant Rollback

At ANY phase, rollback takes ~2 seconds: change weight to 0% for v2 in VirtualService. v1 handles all traffic instantly. User impact: ZERO. Compare this to a traditional deployment rollback which can take 10+ minutes.

📊 Deployment Strategy Comparison

StrategyTraffic SwitchRollback SpeedBest For
Canary (Istio)Gradual %~2sRisk mitigation, monitoring
Blue-GreenInstant 100%~2sFast switch, staging parity
Rolling UpdatePod-by-podMinutesSimple apps, less control
Shadow/MirrorParallel copyN/AZero-risk production testing

14.2 Shadow / Mirror Traffic Testing

Mirror 100% of live traffic to v2 — but discard v2 responses. Users see v1, but v2 processes real production traffic silently. Best way to test under real load before going live.

yaml — Traffic Mirroring: v2 gets silent copy 

spec:
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v1              # Real users get v1
      weight: 100
    mirror:
      host: jobpost-api
      subset: v2                # v2 gets silent copy
    mirrorPercentage:
      value: 100.0              # Copy 100% to v2

# ✅ Users: 100% served by v1 (zero impact)
# ✅ v2: receives all real production requests
# ✅ Check v2 metrics BEFORE any user sees it

14.3 Blue-Green Deployments with Istio

Maintain two identical environments — blue (current) and green (new). Switch ALL traffic instantly with one YAML change. Rollback is equally instant.

🔵 BLUE (Current)

v1 running, 100% traffic. Green deployed but receives 0%. Both environments fully ready.

🟢 GREEN (New)

Switch: VS weight → v2:100%. Traffic cuts over instantly. If issues: switch back to blue — 2 seconds. No DNS propagation delay.

14.4 Deployment Strategy Decision Matrix — Which to Use When

DEFINITION: a decision matrix maps each release strategy to its risk, rollback speed, and cost — choosing one becomes a lookup, not a debate. The ICA exam (and 2 A.M. on-call reality) hands you a scenario — "high-risk rewrite," "DB migration," "tiny patch" — and expects the matching strategy, every time. How to read it: risk = worst-case user impact mid-rollout; rollback = time to undo; cost = extra infrastructure kept running while the rollout is in flight.

📊 Decision Matrix — Five Strategies Scored for anihpj

StrategyRiskRollbackCostIstio CRDsUse at anihpj for
Canary (weights)🟡 Low — 5% blast radius~2s: v2 weight → 0+ a few v2 podsVS + DR (subsets)jobpost-api v2: risky matching-logic rewrite
Blue-Green (VS flip)🟡 Low — all-or-nothing~2s: flip VS back2× full stack (blue + green)VS + DR (subsets)user-service: PostgreSQL schema migration needing an instant undo
Rolling (K8s only)🔴 High — no % controlMinutes: rolling restart~1× (surge pods)None (K8s native)location-service: trivial stateless patch bump
Shadow / Mirror🟢 Zero — users never hit v2N/A: remove mirror stanza+ v2 podsVirtualService (mirror field)skills-service: prove the 8.1%-error fix under real load, safely
A/B Testing (headers)🟢 Zero — explicit opt-in onlyInstant: remove header match+ a few v2 podsVS (headers match)beta-tester UX experiments via x-canary-user header routing
🧭 Decision Flow — Pick a Strategy in Five Questions
Q1  Must users be 100% shielded while v2 is tested?
      │ YES → SHADOW / MIRROR  (then come back to Q2)
      ▼ no
Q2  All-or-nothing change (DB schema / infra) + instant undo?
      │ YES → BLUE-GREEN
      ▼ no
Q3  Only a specific KNOWN group (beta testers, internal staff) —
    not a random percentage of anonymous users?
      │ YES → A/B TESTING  (header-based match, explicit opt-in)
      ▼ no
Q4  Risky code you want to watch under partial real load?
      │ YES → CANARY  5% → 25% → 50% → 100%
      ▼ no
Q5  Boring, low-risk, stateless patch?
        YES → plain Kubernetes ROLLING UPDATE

📋 Scenario Quick-Reference — Real anihpj Situations

ScenarioBest StrategyWhy
High-risk code change, need monitoringCanarySmall blast radius (5%), gradual ramp, monitor each phase
Database migration, need instant parityBlue-GreenInstant switch, instant rollback, both environments identical
Testing v2 with zero user impactTraffic Mirrorv2 gets real traffic silently, responses discarded, zero risk
New feature for beta testers onlyHeader-based RoutingRoute based on x-user-type: beta → v2, others → v1

Infrastructure change (node pool, K8s version)Blue-GreenDeploy to new cluster, switch DNS/VirtualService instantly

14.5 Deep Dive — Automated Canary: Metrics-Gated Promotion and Rollback

DEFINITION: a metrics-gated canary promotes (or rolls back) v2 automatically, based on Prometheus numbers instead of a human staring at Grafana for five days. Humans miss 3 A.M. error spikes; a controller checking every minute does not — and it rolls back in seconds, before the pager even fires. A loop queries Prometheus, compares v2 against the gates (and against v1's live baseline), and edits the VirtualService weights up on pass, to zero on fail. Set the gates BEFORE the rollout starts — deciding thresholds mid-incident is how bad deploys reach 100%.

🧠 ANALOGY — The Adaptive Cruise Control

Think of the metrics-gated loop like a car's adaptive cruise control: it never asks the driver's permission every second, it just watches one gauge (here: v2's error rate and p99 latency) against a set limit, and brakes — drops v2's weight to 0 — the instant that gauge is crossed. A human can still grab the wheel, but the system never waits for one before reacting.

🚦 Promotion Gates — What jobpost-api v2 Must Prove at Each Step

GateThreshold
1. Error Ratev2 5xx ratio < 1% AND not > 2% above v1's live rate
2. Latencyv2 p99 < 300ms AND not > 2× v1's p99 (baseline 234ms)
3. Soak Time24h clean at the current weight before ramping to the next step

ALL gates pass → promote: 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%. ANY gate fails → rollback: v2 weight → 0 (~2 seconds).

promql — v2 error ratio over the last 5 minutes 
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{destination_service_name=
  "jobpost-api",destination_version="v2",
  response_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
/ sum(rate(istio_requests_total{destination_service_name=
    "jobpost-api",destination_version="v2"}[5m]))
💡 Instant Rollback — the One-Liner to Memorize

kubectl patch vs jobpost-api-vs -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/http/0/route/1/weight","value":0}]' — route/1 is the v2 entry in the VS route list. With v2 at weight 0, Envoy sends ALL traffic to v1 — weights are relative proportions, so v1's number does not need to be edited back to 100. Propagation ~2s. Pods untouched. Users never notice.

🔁 AUTOMATED CANARY LOOP — What a Controller Does Every Minute
T+0m  : set v2 weight = 5, start the clock
T+1m  : query Prometheus → all gates pass? ✅ keep watching
...
T+24h : Gate 3 (soak) satisfied at 5% → promote to weight 25, reset the clock
T+48h : Gate 3 satisfied at 25% → promote to weight 50, reset the clock
T+72h : Gate 3 satisfied at 50% → promote to weight 100 — DONE
ANY minute a gate fails, at ANY step:
  → v2 weight = 0        (automatic — no human in the loop)
  → alert #anihpj-oncall with the failing metric attached
  → rollout marked FAILED; fix v2, start again from MIRROR

Flagger (CNCF, Flux family): you declare a Canary custom resource holding these gates; Flagger then OWNS the VirtualService — it creates it, walks the weights up step by step, runs the Prometheus checks between steps, and flips the weight back to 0 on failure. One page of YAML replaces five days of dashboard-watching.

Argo Rollouts: swaps your Deployment for a Rollout CRD whose strategy.canary.trafficRouting.istio block points at your VS and DR; AnalysisTemplates run PromQL gates between steps and abort automatically on failure. Pairs naturally with Argo CD for GitOps-driven progressive delivery.

🩺 CANARY HEALTH DASHBOARD — Monitor at Each Phase
📊
Grafana Workload

Compare v1 vs v2: RPS, Error %, p50/p95/p99 latency, CPU/Memory

🚦 v2 err > 2% above v1 = ROLLBACK (Gate 1)

🗺️
Kiali Graph

🟢 v2 = healthy | 🟡 = degraded | 🔴 = ROLLBACK NOW

🚦 Red node = Immediate Rollback

🔭
Jaeger Traces

Sort by Longest Duration. Compare v1 vs v2 spans.

🚦 v2 p99 > 2× v1 = ROLLBACK (Gate 2)

14.6 Traffic Mirroring at Partial Percentages and Multi-Destination Mirrors

DEFINITION: mirrorPercentage is NOT locked to 100 — it accepts any float from 0.0 to 100.0, so anihpj can shadow only a slice of live traffic instead of the full firehose. Mirroring at 100% doubles jobpost-api's real compute load on the mirror target; ramping the percentage (1% → 10% → 50% → 100%) gets a valid production sample while v2 is still small, cheap, and easy to kill if it falls over. mirrorPercentage is completely independent of the route's weight fields — v1 keeps serving 100% of real users the whole time, no matter what mirrorPercentage is set to.

⚠️ Omitted mirrorPercentage Means 100%, Not 0%

If mirrorPercentage is omitted entirely, Istio mirrors ALL traffic (100%) by default — always set it explicitly during a ramp so "no field" doesn't silently mean "full load."

yaml — Partial-Percentage Mirror Ramp: Shrinking the Blast Radius 
http:
- route:
  - destination: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v1}
    weight: 100
  mirror: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v2}
  mirrorPercentage: {value: 1.0}    # STEP 1: 1% mirrored
  # ...gate clean 1h, then bump the value...
  # mirrorPercentage: {value: 10.0}   # STEP 2: 10% mirrored
  # mirrorPercentage: {value: 50.0}   # STEP 3: 50% mirrored
  # mirrorPercentage: {value: 100.0}  # STEP 4: full firehose

# v1 weight never changes — real users see ZERO difference
# across all four steps; only v2's mirrored load grows
yaml — Multi-Destination Mirror: the plural "mirrors" field 
http:
- route:
  - destination: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v1}
    weight: 100
  mirrors:
  - destination: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v2}
    percentage: {value: 25.0}  # canary gets 1/4 of traffic
  - destination: {host: jobpost-api-loadtest}
    percentage: {value: 100.0} # sandbox gets everything

# Each entry in mirrors[] is independent: different targets,
# different percentages, all from ONE HTTPRoute rule
📖 Separate Stats, Same Dashboards

Envoy generates separate stats for the mirrored destination, so v2's mirrored-traffic metrics land in Prometheus/Grafana under its own destination_version label — the same dashboards anihpj already uses for the weighted-canary gates in 14.5. HTTPRoute also supports the plural mirrors[] field (HTTPMirrorPolicy) shown above, which mirrors to MULTIPLE destinations at once, each with its own destination and percentage — e.g. mirror to the v2 canary AND a separate load-test sandbox from one rule.

14.7 Istio Control-Plane Canary Upgrades vs Application Canary — Don't Confuse Them

DEFINITION: everything in 14.1-14.6 is APPLICATION canary — a VirtualService weight decides which version of jobpost-api a user's request reaches. Istio also has its own, completely separate CONTROL-PLANE canary: running two istiod versions side by side so a mesh upgrade can be tested before it touches every namespace. The ICA exam tests both, and they are graded independently — a scenario asking "how do you safely test a new Istio version before a mesh-wide upgrade" is answered with istioctl revisions, NOT VirtualService weights.

🎭 Two Different Things That Share the Word "Canary"

APP CANARY (14.1-14.6)CONTROL-PLANE CANARY (Ch 17)
What splitsjobpost-api v1 vs v2istiod stable vs istiod canary
Lives inVirtualService weight / mirror fieldsistioctl revision + namespace label
Blast radius% of USER requests% of NAMESPACES on the new mesh
RollbackEdit VS weight to 0 (~2 seconds)Relabel namespace back to old revision
Who caresjobpost-api developersMesh operators

istioctl install --set revision=canary installs a second, fully independent istiod (its own Deployment, Service, and webhook, all labeled with the revision name) alongside the existing control plane — nothing mesh-wide changes yet. A namespace only picks up the canary control plane once it is labeled istio.io/rev=canary AND its pods are restarted so the sidecar injector re-runs — untouched namespaces stay on the stable revision the entire time.

⚠️ The Legacy Label Takes Precedence

The legacy istio-injection=enabled label takes precedence over istio.io/rev for backward compatibility — it must be REMOVED (istio-injection-) when adding istio.io/rev, or the namespace silently stays on the stable control plane. Also: revision names can't contain "." — use 1-30-2, not 1.30.2.

bash — Control-Plane Canary: Install, Test, Promote 
# 1. Install a second istiod next to the stable one:
istioctl install --set revision=canary

# 2. Point ONE test namespace at it (never anihpj-prod yet):
kubectl label namespace anihpj-staging \
  istio-injection- istio.io/rev=canary
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj-staging

# 3. Watch anihpj-staging on the new control plane; clean?
#    relabel more namespaces the same way, one at a time

# 4. Rollback = relabel to the stable revision + restart —
#    the OLD istiod never left, so this is instant
kubectl label namespace anihpj-staging \
  istio.io/rev=canary- istio.io/rev=stable
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj-staging

# Production pattern: a stable TAG so app teams never
# relabel by hand — promote by moving the tag instead:
istioctl tag set prod-stable --revision 1-29-1
istioctl tag set prod-canary --revision 1-30-2
istioctl tag set prod-stable --revision 1-30-2 --overwrite
#  ^ moves EVERY ns labeled istio.io/rev=prod-stable onto
#    1-30-2 with no relabeling at all
📖 Full Coverage Lives in Chapter 17

The full upgrade workflow, canary-then-promote cadence, and istioctl x precheck live in Chapter 17 — this section exists only so 14's "canary" is never mistaken for 17's.

14.8 Deep Dive — Canary Deployment Patterns: Mirror → Canary → Gradual → Full

The ICA exam tests your understanding of the complete deployment progression. Here's every stage explained:

🔄 DEPLOYMENT PROGRESSION — 5 Stages, Increasing Risk
Stagev1 trafficv2 trafficRiskVS YAML
1. Mirror100% (serves users)Shadow only (responses DISCARDED)Zeromirror: {host: v2}
2. Canary 5%95%5% (real users)Lowweight: v1=95, v2=5
3. Canary 25%75%25%Low-Medweight: v1=75, v2=25
4. Canary 50%50%50%Mediumweight: v1=50, v2=50
5. Full cutover0%100%Highweight: v1=0, v2=100
🧮 HEADER-BASED CANARY — Route by User Identity
  http:
  - match:
    - headers:
        x-canary-user:
          exact: internal-testers    # Internal employees → v2
    route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v2
  - route:                           # Everyone else → v1
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v1
⚠️ ICA: Automated Rollback Criteria

On the exam, you MUST specify WHEN to rollback. Define thresholds BEFORE deployment: (a) Error rate: v2 > 2% above v1 → ROLLBACK. (b) Latency p99: v2 > 2× v1 → ROLLBACK. (c) Any 5xx from v2 that v1 doesn't have → ROLLBACK. Use Grafana/Kiali dashboards to monitor these in real-time.

🔧 Under the Hood — What Envoy Actually Does at Each Weight Shift: xDS Propagation, RDS Hot-Swaps, and Why Rollback Is Provably ~2 Seconds

14.5 already showed the PROMOTION GATES that decide WHEN jobpost-api v2 is allowed to ramp. This is the layer underneath that decision: what literally happens inside Envoy the instant that YAML edit lands, and why "propagation ~2s" in 14.1's rollback box is a specific, provable number and not a hopeful guess.

🗺️ The xDS Propagation Path — From kubectl apply to a Live Envoy Route Table
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  EVERY VIRTUALSERVICE EDIT FOLLOWS THE SAME PATH                             │
│                                                                              │
│  1. kubectl apply/patch  →  Kubernetes API server stores the new weight     │
│  2. istiod's controller (watching that object) recomputes jobpost-api's      │
│     route configuration                                                     │
│  3. istiod pushes it to every subscribed Envoy over the SAME long-lived     │
│     xDS gRPC stream those sidecars have held open since they started —      │
│     no new connection, no restart, no drain                                 │
│  4. Envoy hot-swaps its in-memory route table (RDS) as soon as the push     │
│     lands                                                                   │
│  5. The NEXT request it receives — even one arriving on an already-open,    │
│     kept-alive connection — is weighed against the new split                │
│                                                                              │
│  NOTHING about a weight edit ever touches a running pod.                    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📊 Weight Shift Timeline — Every Canary Stage as Envoy Sees It
StageWeight v1/v2Envoy RDS, via xDSIn-Flight Requests
MIRROR100 / 0v2 added as mirror onlyUntouched
5%95 / 5Clusters [v1:95, v2:5]Unaffected
25%75 / 25Clusters [v1:75, v2:25]Unaffected
50%50 / 50Clusters [v1:50, v2:50]Unaffected
100%0 / 100Clusters [v1:0, v2:100]None on v1
ROLLBACKany → 0v2 dropped from RDSv2 finishes
⏪ Why Rollback Promises ZERO, Not Minimal

Rollback works by the exact same mechanism, run in reverse: patching v2's weight to 0 is one more RDS push, and Envoy simply stops selecting the v2 cluster for any NEW request. Requests already in-flight to v2 are NOT killed — they finish normally and return their response — which is the real reason 14.1's rollback box can promise "user impact: ZERO" instead of "user impact: minimal."

🔑 ICA Insight: A VirtualService weight or mirror edit is never a redeploy — it is a config push over the same long-lived xDS stream every sidecar already holds open, and Envoy hot-swaps its route table (RDS) the moment the push lands. That is WHY "propagation ~2s" is a provable number: it is API-server-write time plus one xDS push, nothing more. Rollback is the identical mechanism run backward, and in-flight v2 requests are allowed to finish rather than being killed — the actual reason 14.1 can promise zero user impact, not just fast recovery.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Canary, shadow/mirror, and blue-green are three disciplined uses of the SAME two VirtualService fields (weight, mirror) already taught in Chapter 6 — Istio adds no dedicated "canary" CRD at all.
  • Rollback is a config push, never a redeploy — provably ~2 seconds because it is one xDS push over an already-open gRPC stream that every sidecar holds open, not a pod restart or a new connection.
  • mirrorPercentage and route weight are fully independent fields — v1 can stay at 100% weight (real users never move) while v2's mirrored share ramps anywhere from 0 to 100 independently.
  • Omitting mirrorPercentage defaults to 100%, not 0% — always set it explicitly during a ramp, or "no field" silently means "full firehose."
  • A mirrored write is a REAL write — a mirrored POST still executes against PostgreSQL. Never mirror a write-heavy endpoint at 100% without a shadow/sandboxed backend behind v2.
  • An automated canary (Flagger, Argo Rollouts) edits the exact same weight field a human would — the only difference is a controller querying Prometheus between steps instead of a person watching Grafana for days.
  • The decision matrix scores every strategy on the same three axes — risk (worst-case blast radius), rollback speed, and cost (extra infra kept running) — turning "which strategy" into a lookup, not a debate.
  • APPLICATION canary and CONTROL-PLANE canary share only a word: jobpost-api's canary is a VirtualService weight decision (this chapter); istiod's own canary is an istioctl revision decision (Chapter 17) — the exam grades them as separate questions.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "Rollback restarts the v1 pods to take over." No — pods are never touched. Rollback is a weight edit propagated over xDS; v1 was already serving traffic the whole time, its share just goes back to 100%.
  • "If I don't set mirrorPercentage, nothing gets mirrored." Backwards — an omitted mirrorPercentage defaults to 100%, the FULL firehose, not zero.
  • "Blue-green needs DNS propagation to cut over." No — Istio's blue-green is the same instant VirtualService weight flip as canary (100/0), not a DNS-layer switch, so there's no propagation delay to wait out.
  • "There's a dedicated Canary or BlueGreen CRD in Istio." No such CRD exists — every strategy in this chapter is built entirely from ordinary VirtualService weight/mirror fields and DestinationRule subsets.
  • "Mirrored traffic is inherently safe because it's just for testing." Only reads are side-effect-free by nature — a mirrored write against a real database is a real write, mirror or not.
  • "The exam will say the word 'canary deployment' outright." Rarely — it says "roll out gradually," "test safely with real traffic," or "instant rollback," and expects you to reach for the matching weight/mirror pattern without the keyword.
  • "Istiod's own canary upgrade also uses a VirtualService weight." No — a control-plane canary (Chapter 17) is a completely separate mechanism: a second istiod Deployment selected via istioctl revision/namespace label, with zero VirtualService involvement.

💼 Chapter 14 — Daily Work Takeaways

  • Ramp jobpost-api v2 through mirror → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%, checking Grafana/Kiali gates between every step, never skipping a stage on a risky rewrite.
  • Roll back with one weight-field patch the instant a gate fails — don't reach for kubectl rollout undo on a canary; the correct reflex is the same kubectl patch vs used to ramp up.
  • Stand up a shadow/mirror test before any risky rewrite ever reaches a real user — mirror at a low percentage first if the mirror target can't absorb a full firehose.
  • Reach for blue-green specifically for all-or-nothing changes needing an instant undo — a schema migration or infra swap, not a routine code patch.
  • Wire Flagger or Argo Rollouts to automate the promotion gate on anything that would otherwise need a human watching dashboards for days.
  • Ramp mirrorPercentage independently of weight whenever a full 100% mirror would overload the mirror target's own compute budget.
  • Before touching istiod itself, confirm whether the scenario is an application canary or a control-plane canary — the tooling, blast radius, and rollback mechanism are completely different.
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 14

Seven quick-fire phrase-to-answer mappings — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Roll out a new version gradually" = VirtualService weight-based canary (14.1)
  • "Test a new version with real traffic, zero risk" = mirror + mirrorPercentage, responses discarded (14.2, 14.6)
  • "Switch to the new version instantly, with instant rollback" = blue-green, the same weight field flipped 100/0 (14.3)
  • "Which strategy fits this scenario" = the 14.4 risk/rollback/cost decision matrix, not a judgment call
  • "Promote or roll back without a human watching" = a metrics-gated controller (Flagger/Argo Rollouts) editing weight automatically (14.5)
  • "Shadow only a slice of traffic, not the whole firehose" = ramp mirrorPercentage independently of route weight (14.6)
  • "Canary" about istiod, revisions, or a mesh-wide upgrade = Chapter 17's control-plane canary (istioctl revision), NEVER a VirtualService weight (14.7)

🧠 Chapter 14 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What two VirtualService fields does this entire chapter build on, both already taught in Chapter 6?
Show Answer
Answer

weight (splits traffic by percentage between subsets) and mirror (copies traffic to a subset without the caller ever seeing its response).

Explanation

Chapter 14 introduces zero new CRDs — canary, shadow/mirror, and blue-green are three disciplined SEQUENCES and SIGNALS for using these same two fields (14.0 intro).

Q2
True or false: with mirror configured, the real user's browser ever sees a response generated by v2?
Show Answer
Answer

False. v2's response to a mirrored request is always discarded — the real user's connection only ever sees v1's response (14.2).

Explanation

This is exactly what makes mirroring zero-risk for READS — v2 can crash, time out, or return garbage and no real user is ever affected.

Q3
You apply a VirtualService with a mirror block but never set mirrorPercentage at all. What percentage of traffic actually gets mirrored?
Show Answer
Answer

100% — an omitted mirrorPercentage defaults to the full firehose, not zero.

Explanation

This is the exact trap 14.6's warning box calls out — always set the field explicitly during a ramp so "no field" doesn't silently become "100%."

Q4
Roughly how long does a canary rollback take, and what mechanism makes that number provable rather than a guess?
Show Answer
Answer

~2 seconds — API-server write time plus one xDS push over the long-lived gRPC stream every Envoy sidecar already holds open. Envoy hot-swaps its in-memory route table (RDS) the instant the push lands; nothing about the edit ever touches a running pod.

Explanation

The UTH walks this exact path (kubectl apply → istiod recomputes → xDS push → RDS hot-swap → next request re-weighed) — knowing WHY it's ~2s, not just the number, is what the ICA actually tests.

Q5
jobpost-api's internal testers must reach v2 via a special header, while everyone else stays on v1. Which VirtualService mechanism does this, and is it weight-based?
Show Answer
Answer

Header-based routing — an http.match.headers rule (e.g. x-canary-user: exact: internal-testers) routed to the v2 subset, with a fallback route (no match) sending everyone else to v1. Not weight-based — it's an explicit opt-in match, not a percentage split.

Explanation

14.4's decision matrix lists this as "A/B Testing" — zero risk because it's explicit opt-in, never a random percentage of anonymous users (14.4, 14.8).

Q6
Name the three axes the 14.4 decision matrix scores every deployment strategy on.
Show Answer
Answer

Risk (worst-case user impact mid-rollout), rollback speed (time to undo), and cost (extra infrastructure kept running while the rollout is in flight).

Explanation

Scoring on fixed axes is what turns "which strategy" into a lookup instead of a debate — the exam and 2 A.M. on-call reality both hand you a scenario and expect the matching strategy on sight (14.4).

Q7
Distinguish an APPLICATION canary from a CONTROL-PLANE canary in one sentence each.
Show Answer
Answer

Application canary: a VirtualService weight decision splitting jobpost-api v1/v2 traffic, owned by app developers. Control-plane canary: an istioctl revision decision running two istiod versions side by side, owned by mesh operators.

Explanation

The ICA exam grades these as separate, independent questions — confusing "canary" applied to jobpost-api with "canary" applied to istiod is a guaranteed wrong answer, not partial credit (14.7).

Q8
Name the two tools this chapter cites for automating a metrics-gated canary promotion.
Show Answer
Answer

Flagger (CNCF, Flux family) and Argo Rollouts. Both own the VirtualService weight edits and query Prometheus between steps, promoting or rolling back without a human watching a dashboard.

Explanation

Flagger owns the VS directly via a Canary CRD; Argo Rollouts swaps in a Rollout CRD whose trafficRouting.istio block points at the same VS/DR pair (14.5).

Q9
Is there a dedicated Istio "Canary" custom resource?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Every strategy in this chapter — canary, shadow/mirror, blue-green — is built entirely from existing VirtualService weight/mirror fields and DestinationRule subsets. (Flagger's own Canary CRD is a THIRD-PARTY controller resource, not an Istio API.)

Explanation

This is why Chapter 14 "carries no line item of its own on the official ICA blueprint" — it's an application of Chapter 6's primitives, not a new domain (front-matter honest framing).

Q10
In a blue-green cutover, what is the ONE field edited to switch all traffic from blue to green?
Show Answer
Answer

The VirtualService weight field — flipped from blue:100/green:0 to blue:0/green:100 in a single edit. Rollback is the same field flipped back.

Explanation

Blue-green is NOT a separate mechanism from canary — it's the same weight field used for an all-or-nothing 100% switch instead of a gradual ramp (14.3).

⚙️ Chapter 14 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a scenario, and you produce the fix with real YAML or commands.

Q1
Write the VirtualService HTTP route block sending 90% of jobpost-api traffic to subset v1 and 10% to subset v2.
Show Answer
Answer
http:
- route:
  - destination: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v1}
    weight: 90
  - destination: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v2}
    weight: 10
Explanation

Two destinations under one route, weights summing to 100 — Envoy splits traffic proportionally on every new request (14.1).

Q2
A canary sitting at v1:50/v2:50 needs an emergency full rollback RIGHT NOW. Give the exact one-liner.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl patch vs jobpost-api-vs -n anihpj --type='json' \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/http/0/route/1/weight","value":0}]'
Explanation

route/1 is the v2 entry; weights are relative proportions, so v1 does not need to be separately patched back to 100 (14.1, 14.5).

Q3
Write a mirror-only VirtualService: real users see 100% v1, v2 gets a full silent copy, zero user impact.
Show Answer
Answer
http:
- route:
  - destination: {host: jobpost-api, subset: v1}
    weight: 100
  mirror:
    host: jobpost-api
    subset: v2
  mirrorPercentage:
    value: 100.0
Explanation

v1's weight stays at 100 for real users the whole time — mirror/mirrorPercentage is an entirely separate, additive field, not a second route (14.2).

Q4
You need to ramp a mirror from 1% to 10% of traffic. Which field changes, and does route weight need to change too?
Show Answer
Answer
mirrorPercentage:
  value: 10.0   # was 1.0
Explanation

Only mirrorPercentage changes. Route weight is untouched and unaffected — real users see zero difference across the entire ramp, only v2's mirrored load grows (14.6).

Q5
jobpost-api is currently 100% v1. Name the steps (not full YAML) to execute a blue-green cutover to v2, with a rollback trigger if p99 exceeds 2× the v1 baseline.
Show Answer
Answer

(1) Deploy v2 (green) at 0% traffic, confirm it starts healthy. (2) Flip the VirtualService weight to v1:0/v2:100 in one edit — instant cutover. (3) Watch Jaeger/Grafana p99 for v2; if it exceeds 2× v1's recorded baseline, immediately flip the weight back to v1:100/v2:0. (4) Once stable, retire the old v1 Deployment.

Explanation

Blue-green's whole appeal is that steps 2 and the rollback in step 3 are the SAME single-field edit run in opposite directions — no DNS, no new connections (14.3, 14.5's gate pattern applied to a blue-green context).

Q6
A teammate wants proof that a weight change you just applied is actually live on Envoy, not just stored in the Kubernetes API. Name the exact command.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj
Explanation

This reads Envoy's actual in-memory RDS route table via the sidecar's admin interface — the only way to confirm the xDS push already landed, not just that kubectl apply succeeded (UTH, 14.1).

Q7
Write the PromQL query an automated canary gate would use to compute v2's 5xx error ratio over the last 5 minutes.
Show Answer
Answer
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{destination_service_name=
  "jobpost-api",destination_version="v2",
  response_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
/ sum(rate(istio_requests_total{destination_service_name=
    "jobpost-api",destination_version="v2"}[5m]))
Explanation

5xx-labeled request rate over total request rate, both windowed to 5 minutes — this is Gate 1 in 14.5's promotion-gate table, checked every minute by the automation loop (14.5).

Q8
Stand up a SECOND istiod to test a mesh upgrade before touching anihpj-prod. Name the minimum 2 commands.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl install --set revision=canary
kubectl label namespace anihpj-staging \
  istio-injection- istio.io/rev=canary
Explanation

The install alone changes NOTHING mesh-wide — a namespace only picks up the canary control plane once explicitly relabeled (and its pods restarted so the injector re-runs). The legacy istio-injection label must be removed or it silently wins (14.7).

Q9
Given a mirrors[] block mirroring 25% to a v2 canary AND 100% to a load-test sandbox, how many total copies does a single matching request produce?
Show Answer
Answer

Up to 3 total: the 1 real response from v1 (the primary route), plus independently, roughly 1-in-4 requests also get mirrored to v2 (25%), and effectively every request gets mirrored to the load-test sandbox (100%). Each entry in mirrors[] is evaluated independently — they are not mutually exclusive.

Explanation

The plural mirrors[] field allows multiple simultaneous mirror targets, each with its own independent percentage — a single request can be mirrored to some, all, or none of them (14.6).

Q10
Per 14.8's 5-stage progression table, at which stage does v2 FIRST receive real user traffic (not just a mirrored copy), and what's the labeled risk level?
Show Answer
Answer

Stage 2 — "Canary 5%" (v1:95/v2:5). Labeled risk: Low. Stage 1 (Mirror) is Zero risk because v2's responses are discarded, not routed to users.

Explanation

This is the exact line the ICA exam expects you to draw: mirroring never counts as "v2 serving users," even at 100% mirror — only a weighted route does (14.8).

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 14
  • Rollback is a weight edit, never a redeploy — if you find yourself reaching for kubectl rollout undo on a canary, stop: the correct one-liner is the same kubectl patch vs from 14.1 (14.1, UTH).
  • mirrorPercentage and route weight are INDEPENDENT fields — check both before assuming "0% traffic" means v2 sees nothing at all (14.6).
  • Never mirror a write endpoint at 100% without a shadow database — the copy is real, not simulated; a mirrored POST still INSERTs (14.2, 14.6).
  • Blue-green's instant switch is only as safe as its shared schema — confirm both versions tolerate the CURRENT PostgreSQL schema before flipping, not after (14.3).
  • On a decision-matrix question, read "instant rollback needed" as blue-green and "watch it under partial load" as canary — the exam rarely uses either word directly (14.4).
  • "Canary" in a question about istiod, revisions, or mesh upgrades is Chapter 17's domain, not this one — don't reach for VirtualService weight on an installation question (14.7).

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 14)

Every command below already appeared earlier in this chapter — grouped here as one reference for driving canary rollouts, verifying live Envoy state, and control-plane canary upgrades.

CommandWhat It Does / Checks in Chapter 14
kubectl apply -f jobpost-api-v2.yaml -n anihpjDeploy v2 at replicas:0 (Phase 1 — zero traffic yet) (14.1)
kubectl get virtualservice jobpost-api-vs -n anihpj -o yamlRead the CURRENT weight / mirror split (14.1, 14.2)
kubectl patch vs jobpost-api-vs -n anihpj --type='json' -p='[...]'Edit ONE weight field — ramp up or roll back (14.1, 14.5)
istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpjConfirm Envoy's live RDS route matches the VS (UTH)
istioctl analyze -n anihpjCatch a bad subset/weight before it ever applies (14.1)
kubectl delete deployment jobpost-api-v1 -n anihpjRetire v1 once v2 is fully promoted (14.1)
kubectl label ns anihpj-staging istio-injection- istio.io/rev=canaryOpt ONE namespace into a CONTROL-PLANE canary (14.7)
istioctl tag set prod-stable --revision 1-30-2 --overwritePromote every ns on that tag at once (14.7)

🧪 Practice Drill 14.1 — Ramp jobpost-api from 10% to 50%, Then Roll It Back

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

Do this now, timed, on your own anihpj cluster:

  1. kubectl get virtualservice jobpost-api-vs -n anihpj -o yaml — confirm the CURRENT split (should read v1:90 / v2:10).
  2. Patch the VirtualService so v1:50 / v2:50 — one weight edit, both destinations.
  3. istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj — confirm the sidecar's live route table already shows 50/50.
  4. Time a rollback: patch v2 back to weight 0 and note how long it takes to see 0% in proxy-config routes again.
  5. Re-run the same istioctl proxy-config routes check — confirm v1 is back to 100% and no pod was ever touched.
Hint: Steps 1-2 reuse 14.1's weight-edit pattern; step 3 is the same live-route-table reflex the UTH walkthrough just proved happens over xDS, not a redeploy; step 4 times the exact ~2s propagation number 14.1's rollback box promises; step 5 confirms the promise — zero pods touched, in-flight v2 requests simply finish on their own.
View Solution

Step 3 should show the live RDS route table already reporting the 50/50 split within a couple seconds of the patch — no pod restart, no "Waiting" state. Step 4's timed rollback should land well under 5 seconds end-to-end (API-server write + one xDS push), and step 5 confirms v1 is back to receiving all requests.

Check yourself: did you actually TIME step 4 with a stopwatch, or estimate it? The whole point of this drill is proving "~2 seconds" is a real, observable number, not a marketing claim — if you skipped the timing, redo the drill and time it for real.

🧪 Practice Drill 14.2 — Build and Verify a Mirror-Only VirtualService

⏱️ Target Time: 7 minutes
Scenario

Prove mirroring is truly zero-impact — don't just read 14.2, watch it happen:

  1. Deploy jobpost-api-v2 at 0 real traffic (weight 100/0), confirm it's healthy but receiving nothing.
  2. Add a mirror block sending 100% of traffic to v2, with NO route weight changes.
  3. Generate 20 real requests against jobpost-api and record every response code the CALLER actually saw.
  4. kubectl logs deploy/jobpost-api-v2 — confirm v2 processed all 20 requests despite the caller never seeing any of its responses.
  5. Deliberately break v2 (e.g. scale it to a bad image) and re-run step 3 — confirm the caller-visible response codes are UNCHANGED.
Hint: Step 4 is the core proof — v2 sees real traffic in its own logs. Step 5 is the more convincing proof — breaking v2 entirely still produces zero visible impact, because its responses were never wired to the caller in the first place.
View Solution

Step 3's 20 response codes should all reflect v1's behavior only, both before and after step 5 breaks v2. Step 4's v2 logs should show 20 processed requests regardless of whether v2 is healthy or broken — mirroring copies the REQUEST, not the outcome.

Check yourself: could you explain to a skeptical teammate why breaking v2 in step 5 didn't page anyone? If your answer isn't "because mirror responses were never routed back to any real caller," re-read 14.2 before moving on.

🧪 Practice Drill 14.3 — Score Three Real anihpj Changes on the Decision Matrix

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking at 14.4's table, pick a strategy (canary / blue-green / rolling / shadow / A-B) for each, and justify it using ONLY risk, rollback speed, and cost:

  1. A PostgreSQL schema migration for user-service that must be instantly undoable if it breaks anything.
  2. A one-line stateless bug fix in location-service with no behavior change to any API contract.
  3. jobpost-api's matching-logic rewrite — the exact scenario this chapter opened with.
Hint: Only ONE of these three should genuinely need gradual, monitored traffic — the other two have a clean, obvious answer once you apply risk/rollback/cost instead of guessing by habit.
View Solution

(1) Blue-green — an all-or-nothing schema change needs an instant, all-or-nothing undo, not a gradual 5%-at-a-time exposure. (2) Rolling update — boring, low-risk, stateless; a full VirtualService/DestinationRule canary setup would be pure overhead. (3) Canary — a risky rewrite is exactly what gradual exposure + monitoring gates exist for.

Check yourself: did you score all three from FIRST PRINCIPLES (the three axes), or did you pattern-match to 14.4's table from memory? On the real exam there's no table to consult — only the reasoning matters.

🧪 Practice Drill 14.4 — Build a Full 3-Stage Metrics-Gated Canary, By Hand

⏱️ Target Time: 10 minutes
Scenario

Simulate what Flagger/Argo Rollouts would do automatically — do it by hand once, so the mechanism is concrete:

  1. Set jobpost-api-vs to v1:95/v2:5. Write down the exact PromQL query (14.5) you'd run to check v2's error ratio.
  2. Run it. If v2's 5xx ratio is under 1% AND not more than 2% above v1's, promote to v1:75/v2:25.
  3. Repeat the same check at 25%, then promote to v1:50/v2:50 if clean.
  4. At 50%, deliberately treat the gate as FAILED (even if it's actually clean) and execute the rollback one-liner from 14.5.
  5. Confirm via proxy-config routes that v2 is back to weight 0.
Hint: Step 4 is deliberate — practicing the ROLLBACK path matters just as much as practicing the promotion path, and it's the one path most people never rehearse until it's a real 3 A.M. incident.
View Solution

Each promotion step is a single weight-field edit gated by the SAME PromQL shape (numerator: 5xx rate, denominator: total rate, both windowed). Step 4's forced rollback should complete in the same ~2 seconds as any other weight patch — the mechanism doesn't care whether the trigger was a real failure or a drill.

Check yourself: did you actually WRITE OUT the PromQL each time, or just wave at "checking the error rate"? The exam expects the literal query shape, not a description of intent.

🧪 Practice Drill 14.5 — Sketch the xDS Propagation Path From Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Close the UTH. On paper or a whiteboard, without looking, write the 5-step path a single kubectl patch vs weight edit takes from the moment you press Enter to the moment the NEXT request is routed by the new weight.

Hint: If your sketch has a pod restart, a new TCP connection, or a "wait for the next deployment" step anywhere in it, it's wrong — none of those happen.
View Solution

(1) kubectl apply/patch → API server stores the new weight. (2) istiod's controller recomputes jobpost-api's route config. (3) istiod pushes it over the SAME long-lived xDS gRPC stream every sidecar already holds open — no new connection. (4) Envoy hot-swaps its in-memory RDS route table the instant the push lands. (5) The NEXT request — even on an already-open kept-alive connection — is weighed against the new split. Nothing touches a running pod at any step.

Check yourself: could you also explain, using this same 5-step path run backward, why rollback promises ZERO user impact rather than just "fast" impact? If not, re-read the UTH's "Why Rollback Promises ZERO, Not Minimal" section.

Chapter 14 starts from two fields you already know from Chapter 6 — weight and mirror — and spends seven sections turning them into disciplined release strategies: a gradual canary (14.1), a zero-risk shadow test (14.2), and an instant blue-green switch (14.3), each scored against the others in a single decision matrix (14.4). The back half goes deeper on the exact same primitives — a metrics-gated loop that promotes or rolls back jobpost-api v2 without a human watching a dashboard (14.5), a mirror that can be ramped or split across multiple destinations instead of firing at 100% (14.6) — before closing on the one distinction the ICA exam grades separately from everything else in this chapter: an application canary is a VirtualService weight decision, a control-plane canary is an istioctl revision decision, and the two are never the same question (14.7).

Quick recap — 📈 Canary: weight ramps mirror → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%, gated at every step, rollback is weight → 0 (14.1) · 🪞 Mirror: mirror + mirrorPercentage copy live traffic with zero user impact — responses discarded (14.2) · 🔵🟢 Blue-Green: the same weight field, used for an instant all-or-nothing switch (14.3) · 🧭 Decision Matrix: risk × rollback × cost — a lookup, not a debate (14.4) · 🔁 Automated Canary: Prometheus gates + Flagger/Argo Rollouts replace a human watching Grafana (14.5) · 📊 Partial Mirrors: mirrorPercentage ramps 0-100 independently of weight; mirrors[] shadows multiple destinations at once (14.6) · 🎭 Two Canaries: application (VirtualService weight, jobpost-api developers) vs control-plane (istioctl revision, mesh operators) — never the same question (14.7). Chapter 15 now asks what stops one caller from taking jobpost-api down, even after this perfectly safe rollout.

Chapter 15: Rate Limiting and Envoy Filters

Protecting jobpost-api from overload is nobody's job by default — a service that has survived a perfectly safe canary rollout (Chapter 14) still has zero defense against a single caller who is technically welcome: a retry storm from search-service during a bad deploy, a scraper hammering /api/jobs/ every few milliseconds, or one batch job that forgot to add backoff. Rate limiting is the layer that catches exactly this, either per-pod (local) or mesh-wide against one shared counter (global) — Envoy rejects the 101st request in a second before Django ever sees it.

"What stops one caller from taking jobpost-api down — even after a perfectly safe rollout?" By the time you reach Chapter 15, jobpost-api has survived Chapter 14's canary rollout and is running v2 for 100% of real users, fully authenticated end-to-end since Chapter 12's mTLS lockdown. None of that protects it from a caller who never technically breaks a rule. And some problems still won't fit any built-in CRD at all — a bespoke auth-token format, a one-off header rewrite, a legacy protocol quirk — which is why this chapter also covers EnvoyFilter and WasmPlugin, the two doors Istio leaves open for running your own code inside Envoy when VirtualService, AuthorizationPolicy, and Telemetry all fall short. Both doors are powerful and both carry real risk: EnvoyFilter edits Envoy's internal xDS config directly, and istio.io's own reference page warns it can destabilize the entire mesh if used carelessly.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2.5 hours 🛡️ Protection 🎯 Extends 2 Domains

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Configure a local (per-pod) rate limit on jobpost-api using EnvoyFilter and Envoy's built-in token bucket
  • ✅ Decide when a requirement ("1000 req/min per IP") demands GLOBAL rate limiting instead of LOCAL, and size the Redis-backed RLS
  • ✅ Shape traffic by client type (e.g. a batch-job header) using fault-injection delay as a deliberate latency brake

💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 15
  • "Protect a service from overload" = EnvoyFilter with local rate limiting
  • "Rate limit across all pods" = Global rate limiting (requires Redis + rate limit service)
  • "Rate limit exceeded" = Envoy returns 429 Too Many Requests — Django never sees it
  • "Different limits per user type" = EnvoyFilter with header match (traffic shaping)
  • Local = independent per pod (no Redis), Global = shared counter (Redis). Different use cases!
  • EnvoyFilter CRD: apiVersion networking.istio.io/v1alpha3 — directly patches Envoy config
  • "Custom auth token / header rewrite no CRD covers" = reach for WasmPlugin (sandboxed, versioned) before a Lua EnvoyFilter (inline, riskier)
  • "Two EnvoyFilters both match one workload" = resolution is namespace scope → priority (lowest first) → creation time → name — never assume, set spec.priority explicitly
