15.1 Local Rate Limiting (Per-Pod)

Each pod has its own independent rate limit bucket. Pod 1 at limit → Pod 2 still serves normally.

🪣 LOCAL RATE LIMITING — Token Bucket per Pod (100 req/s each)
Pod 1

Token bucket: 100 tok/s
████████░░░ 82/100
✅ Serving normally

Pod 2

Token bucket: 100 tok/s
███████████ 100/100
❌ 429 — AT LIMIT!

Pod 3

Token bucket: 100 tok/s
███░░░░░░░ 30/100
✅ Serving normally

Total capacity: 3 pods × 100 = 300 req/s. Each pod's limit is independent — Pod 2 hitting its limit doesn't affect Pods 1 and 3.

yaml — jobpost-api-local-ratelimit: the actual EnvoyFilter 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: EnvoyFilter
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-local-ratelimit
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  workloadSelector:
    labels:
      app: jobpost-api           # ← attach to jobpost-api's sidecar only
  configPatches:
  - applyTo: HTTP_FILTER          # WHERE: the HTTP filter chain
    match:
      context: SIDECAR_INBOUND    # WHEN: only inbound traffic to the pod
      listener:
        filterChain:
          filter:
            name: envoy.filters.network.http_connection_manager
    patch:
      operation: INSERT_BEFORE    # HOW: slot in just before the router
      value:
        name: envoy.filters.http.local_ratelimit
        typed_config:
          "@type": type.googleapis.com/udpa.type.v1.TypedStruct
          type_url: type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.local_ratelimit.v3.LocalRateLimit
          value:
            stat_prefix: jobpost_local_ratelimit
            token_bucket:
              max_tokens: 100        # burst ceiling
              tokens_per_fill: 100   # refilled per interval
              fill_interval: 1s      # the field everyone misreads — see 15.4
            filter_enabled:
              default_value: {numerator: 100, denominator: HUNDRED}
            filter_enforced:
              default_value: {numerator: 100, denominator: HUNDRED}

This is the exact triple 15.6 maps out (HTTP_FILTER + SIDECAR_INBOUND + INSERT_BEFORE) — the same one 15.5's Lua tagger uses, just with a different value: payload. filter_enabled/filter_enforced at 100% mean every matching request is both counted AND actually enforced (setting either below 100% is how you'd shadow-test a limit before enforcing it).

15.2 Global Rate Limiting (Shared Counter)

Rate limit by source IP, user, or API key across ALL pods combined. Requires a Redis-backed rate limit service.

🌐 GLOBAL RATE LIMITING — Architecture
1
Request

IP 203.0.113.42 → jobpost-api

2
Envoy Checks

"Check rate limit for this IP" → gRPC to rate limit service

3
Redis Lookup

IP: 203.0.113.42 count: 987/1000
Under limit ✅

4
Allowed

Request forwarded to Django ✅

1001
Denied

Request #1001: count: 1001/1000
→ 429 Too Many Requests ❌

15.3 Traffic Shaping — Controlling Latency

Apply different rate limits based on request type — protect real users from batch jobs:

👤 Regular User

Header: x-client: browser
No rate limit, full speed
0ms overhead

🤖 Batch Job

Header: x-client: batch-job
EnvoyFilter: 100ms delay
Max 10 req/s

15.4 Deep Dive — Token Bucket Algorithm Explained

DEFINITION: a token bucket is a jar of "permission slips" (tokens) — every request must grab one token to pass; an empty jar means Envoy answers 429 on the spot and Django is never called. The three knobs — maxTokens, tokensPerFill, fillInterval — are the ONLY rate-limit math the exam tests, and misreading fillInterval: 60s as 1s silently turns a "100 req/s" limit into 100 req/MINUTE.

  • fillInterval fires like a metronome → adds tokensPerFill tokens, capped at maxTokens (the bucket never overflows)
  • Each arriving request consumes exactly 1 token → forwarded
  • Bucket empty → instant 429 Too Many Requests, ~0ms cost

Two derived numbers to memorize:

  • Sustained rate = tokensPerFill ÷ fillInterval → 100 ÷ 1s = 100 req/s for each jobpost-api pod
  • Burst ceiling = maxTokens → a full, idle bucket can drain all at once, absorbing a one-off spike of that size
⏱️ TOKEN BUCKET — Millisecond Walkthrough at 100 tok/s
CONFIG: maxTokens: 100  tokensPerFill: 100  fillInterval: 1s

T=0ms:      bucket FULL   [██████████] 100/100 tokens
T=0-300ms:  burst — 100 requests land, each takes 1 token
T=300ms:    bucket EMPTY  [░░░░░░░░░░]   0/100
T=310ms:    request #101 → no token → 429 (Envoy rejects)
T=310-999:  every further request → 429, Django untouched
T=1000ms:   refill tick: +100 tokens, capped at 100 → FULL
T=1001ms:   traffic flows again ✓

BURST TUNING (same 100 req/s sustained, different spikes):
  maxTokens: 100, tokensPerFill: 100 → burst 100, steady 100/s
  maxTokens: 300, tokensPerFill: 100 → burst 300 after a few
    quiet seconds (bucket saves up), still 100/s average
  rule: maxTokens = tokensPerFill  → uniform traffic
        maxTokens > tokensPerFill  → spiky browser traffic

LOCAL vs GLOBAL MATH (identical YAML, different totals):
  LOCAL on 3 jobpost-api pods: 3 × 100 = 300 req/s effective
  HPA scales to 6 pods → silently becomes 600 req/s!
  GLOBAL: 100 req/s TOTAL, no matter how many pods exist
🪣 TOKEN BUCKET — A Second Worked Example (100 req/s, burst 20)
TIME 0s:  Bucket has 20 tokens (maxTokens/burst)
          Request 1 arrives → 1 token consumed → 19 left ✅ 200 OK
          Request 2-20 arrive → tokens consumed → 0 left
          Request 21 arrives → 0 tokens → ❌ 429 Too Many Requests

TIME 1s:  Bucket refills: +10 tokens (tokensPerFill) → 10 tokens
          Now 10 more requests can pass

KEY PARAMETERS:
  maxTokens: 20     = Maximum burst size (bucket capacity)
  tokensPerFill: 10 = Tokens added per fillInterval
  fillInterval: 1s  = How often refill happens
  Effective rate: tokensPerFill / fillInterval = 10 req/s steady
  Burst: Up to maxTokens (20) can pass instantly if bucket is full
💡 ICA Exam: Burst vs Steady Rate

Steady rate: tokensPerFill / fillInterval = 10/s. Burst: maxTokens = 20 can pass at once if bucket is full, then rate drops to 10/s. Set maxTokens to handle traffic spikes without overwhelming the service. For uniform traffic, set maxTokens = tokensPerFill.

📖 Token Bucket vs Leaky Bucket — Know Which One Envoy Uses

Two classic rate-limiting algorithms, easy to mix up on the exam: token bucket (what Envoy actually implements) refills at a fixed rate but lets a full bucket drain in one burst — traffic-friendly for spiky web load. Leaky bucket instead queues requests and releases them at a constant rate, smoothing bursts out entirely rather than allowing them — no maxTokens-style burst capacity. Istio/Envoy's local AND global rate limiting are both token-bucket based; if a question describes "requests queue and drain at a constant rate, no burst allowed," that's leaky bucket phrasing describing behavior Envoy does NOT implement.

15.5 Deep Dive — Extending Envoy: WasmPlugin vs Lua EnvoyFilter

DEFINITION: when no built-in CRD (VirtualService, AuthorizationPolicy, Telemetry) can express your logic, Istio lets you run your OWN CODE inside the sidecar through exactly two doors: the WasmPlugin CRD (extensions.istio.io/v1alpha1), which loads a compiled WebAssembly module into Envoy's sandboxed VM, or a Lua script via EnvoyFilter, which injects a small interpreted function straight into the HTTP filter chain. Custom auth token formats, bespoke request tagging, and odd legacy protocols are the real reasons meshes reach for either — the exam expects you to know WHICH mechanism fits and what each one risks. Both ship differently too: istiod distributes both, but the Wasm module is pulled from an OCI registry by istio-agent (like a container image), while the Lua source travels inline inside the EnvoyFilter YAML itself.

⚠️ Extensions Run on Every Matching Request

Exhaust the built-in CRDs first — custom code is yours to debug at 3 A.M.

yaml — WasmPlugin: the real extension CRD 
apiVersion: extensions.istio.io/v1alpha1    # ← WasmPlugin's home
kind: WasmPlugin
metadata:
  name: jobpost-header-guard
  namespace: anihpj              # plugin scoped to anihpj ns
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api           # ← attach to these sidecars
  url: oci://registry.anihpj.dev/wasm/header-guard:v1.2.0
                                  # ← module pulled like an image
  sha256: 4f2a91c0...             # ← pin the binary (supply chain)
  imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
  phase: AUTHN                   # ← where in the filter chain:
                                  #   AUTHN = before Istio authn
                                  #   AUTHZ = before Istio authz
                                  #   STATS = after authz (metrics)
  priority: 10                   # higher runs earlier in a phase
  failStrategy: FAIL_CLOSE       # plugin crash → block traffic
                                  # (FAIL_OPEN = let traffic pass)
  pluginConfig:                  # ← handed to the module as JSON
    header: x-anihpj-guard
    value: "checked"
yaml — Lua EnvoyFilter: inline script tagging anihpj requests 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: EnvoyFilter
metadata:
  name: jobpost-lua-tag
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  workloadSelector:
    labels:
      app: jobpost-api
  configPatches:
  - applyTo: HTTP_FILTER
    match:
      context: SIDECAR_INBOUND
      listener:
        filterChain:
          filter:
            name: envoy.filters.network.http_connection_manager
            subFilter:
              name: envoy.filters.http.router
    patch:
      operation: INSERT_BEFORE      # run before the router
      value:
        name: envoy.lua
        typed_config:
          "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.lua.v3.Lua
          inline_code: |            # ← the WHOLE program is here
            function envoy_on_request(handle)
              handle:headers():add("x-anihpj-lua", "seen")
            end
            function envoy_on_response(handle)
              handle:headers():add("x-served-by", "anihpj-mesh")
            end

🧩 WasmPlugin vs Lua EnvoyFilter — Choosing Your Extension Mechanism

DimensionWasmPlugin (Wasm module)Lua EnvoyFilter
LanguageRust, Go, C++, AssemblyScript → compiled .wasmLua only, inline in the YAML resource
SafetySandboxed VM — a crash is contained; failStrategy FAIL_CLOSE / FAIL_OPENRuns in Envoy's own process — a bad script stalls worker threads
PerformanceNear-native; small VM overhead per requestInterpreted; fine for tiny header tweaks
Hot-reloadPush new oci:// tag + sha256 → agent re-pulls, no pod restartEdit inline_code → istiod pushes new config, no restart
Best forReal logic: tests, CI/CD, versions, reuse across teams and clustersOne-line tweaks and temporary workarounds you may delete soon

Rule of thumb for anihpj: Lua for a one-line header tweak you might delete next sprint; WasmPlugin for anything with real logic, tests, or versions — or that must NOT be able to crash the proxy (failStrategy: FAIL_CLOSE contains it).

bash — verify: is the Wasm module actually loaded? 
$ kubectl get wasmplugins -n anihpj
NAME                   AGE
jobpost-header-guard   2m           ← CRD accepted

$ istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/jobpost-api \
    -n anihpj -o json | grep -i wasm
"name": "envoy.filters.http.wasm"   ← module live in Envoy

$ curl -sI http://jobpost-api:8000/jobs/ | grep x-anihpj
x-anihpj-guard: checked             ← plugin ran on request

15.6 Deep Dive — EnvoyFilter's Patch Grammar: applyTo, Context, and Operation

DEFINITION: every configPatches entry in an EnvoyFilter is exactly one triple — WHERE to patch (applyTo), WHEN it applies (match.context), and HOW to edit it (patch.operation) — plus a value: payload; nothing about EnvoyFilter is more complicated than reading this triple correctly.

📖 Key Term — The Patch Triple

applyTo = WHERE (HTTP_FILTER, CLUSTER...), match.context = WHEN (SIDECAR_INBOUND, SIDECAR_OUTBOUND, GATEWAY), patch.operation = HOW (INSERT_BEFORE, MERGE...). Every EnvoyFilter in this chapter is just this triple wearing a different value: payload.

15.1's local-ratelimit filter and 15.5's Lua tagger both use the IDENTICAL triple (HTTP_FILTER + SIDECAR_INBOUND + INSERT_BEFORE) — the exam swaps ONE of these three knobs per question to test whether you understand what each knob controls, not just that "EnvoyFilter does something."

🧩 THE PATCH TRIPLE — Mapping Ch15's Own Two Filters to the Triple
15.1 local rate limiter (from earlier in this chapter):
  WHERE (applyTo):   HTTP_FILTER      → HTTP filter chain in the HCM
  WHEN  (context):   SIDECAR_INBOUND  → only traffic inbound to pod
  HOW   (operation): INSERT_BEFORE    → slot in just before router

15.5 Lua request tagger (from earlier in this chapter):
  WHERE (applyTo):   HTTP_FILTER      → same target as above
  WHEN  (context):   SIDECAR_INBOUND  → same direction: inbound
  HOW   (operation): INSERT_BEFORE    → same verb: before router

Same triple, different payload (value:) — that IS EnvoyFilter: the
triple finds the slot, value: fills it in with your custom filter.

📍 applyTo — the WHERE, Full Enum

ValueWhat it patches
LISTENERA listener (add or replace one)
FILTER_CHAINA filter chain inside a listener
NETWORK_FILTERAn L4 filter, e.g. TCP proxy
HTTP_FILTERAn HTTP filter inside the HCM's chain
ROUTE_CONFIGURATIONThe RDS route config (MERGE-only op)
VIRTUAL_HOSTA virtual host in a route config
HTTP_ROUTEOne route inside a matched virtual host
CLUSTERA CDS cluster; also used to ADD new ones
EXTENSION_CONFIGA named ECDS extension-config resource
LISTENER_FILTERA listener filter (runs pre filter chain)
BOOTSTRAPDEPRECATED — patches bootstrap directly
🕐 match.context — the WHEN

ANY: every context: inbound, outbound, gateway
SIDECAR_INBOUND: a sidecar's inbound listener only
SIDECAR_OUTBOUND: a sidecar's outbound listener only
GATEWAY: an ingress/egress Gateway proxy only

🛠️ patch.operation — the HOW

ADD append · REMOVE delete · INSERT_BEFORE/INSERT_AFTER/INSERT_FIRST insert · REPLACE swap a named filter's contents (HTTP/NETWORK filter only) · MERGE deep-merge fields

⚠️ Two Exam Traps Baked Into This Grammar

REPLACE is legal ONLY on HTTP_FILTER and NETWORK_FILTER (it swaps a NAMED filter's contents wholesale). ROUTE_CONFIGURATION accepts ONLY MERGE — pick REPLACE or an INSERT_* there and Istio rejects the config.

Full governance treatment — including WHICH patch wins when two EnvoyFilters both match the same workload, and istio.io's official "use with care" warning — is in 15.9.

15.7 The Global Rate Limiting EnvoyFilter — Wiring Up envoy.filters.http.ratelimit

15.2 covered the ARCHITECTURE of global rate limiting; this section shows the actual EnvoyFilter YAML that wires envoy.filters.http.ratelimit into jobpost-api's chain — the exam can and does ask you to spot a broken field name in exactly this YAML. Global rate limiting always needs TWO EnvoyFilter patches, not one: an HTTP_FILTER patch that inserts the filter into the chain, and a VIRTUAL_HOST (or HTTP_ROUTE) patch that attaches rate_limits actions telling Envoy WHAT to send the RLS server as a "descriptor" (source IP? a header? both?).

yaml — patch 1 of 2: insert envoy.filters.http.ratelimit 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: EnvoyFilter
metadata:
  name: jobpost-global-ratelimit-filter
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  workloadSelector:
    labels:
      app: jobpost-api        # patched onto jobpost-api's sidecar only
  configPatches:
  - applyTo: HTTP_FILTER        # add the ratelimit filter to the HTTP chain
    match:
      context: SIDECAR_INBOUND
      listener:
        filterChain:
          filter:
            name: envoy.filters.network.http_connection_manager
    patch:
      operation: INSERT_BEFORE   # ahead of the router, same as local limit
      value:
        name: envoy.filters.http.ratelimit   # ← the GLOBAL filter name
        typed_config:
          "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.ratelimit.v3.RateLimit
          domain: anihpj-jobpost          # namespaces the descriptors
          failure_mode_deny: true         # RLS unreachable → reject
                                           # (fail-closed; false=fail-open)
          timeout: 0.25s                  # budget inside your p99 latency
          rate_limit_service:
            grpc_service:
              envoy_grpc:
                cluster_name: outbound|8081||ratelimit.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
            transport_api_version: V3
yaml — patch 2 of 2: attach rate_limits actions 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: EnvoyFilter
metadata:
  name: jobpost-global-ratelimit-route
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  workloadSelector:
    labels: {app: jobpost-api}
  configPatches:
  - applyTo: VIRTUAL_HOST        # attach the rate_limits ACTION here
    match:
      context: SIDECAR_INBOUND
      routeConfiguration:
        vhost:
          name: "jobpost-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:8000"
          route: {name: default}
    patch:
      operation: MERGE            # VIRTUAL_HOST only supports MERGE
      value:
        rate_limits:
        - actions:                # each action builds one descriptor
          - remote_address: {}    # key = the client's source IP
          - request_headers:
              header_name: "x-api-key"
              descriptor_key: "API_KEY"  # ← per-key quota, not just IP

The RLS server's OWN config is server-side config for whatever gRPC RLS implementation you deploy (e.g. envoyproxy/ratelimit) — NOT an Istio CRD:

yaml — RLS server config (mounted into the RLS deployment as a ConfigMap) 
domain: anihpj-jobpost         # must match the EnvoyFilter's domain: above
descriptors:
- key: remote_address                 # matches the remote_address action
  rate_limit:
    unit: minute
    requests_per_unit: 1000            # 1000 req/min PER SOURCE IP
- key: API_KEY                        # matches the request_headers action
  rate_limit:
    unit: day
    requests_per_unit: 100000          # free-tier daily quota per key
⚠️ failure_mode_deny Is the Field to Watch on the Exam

true = RLS unreachable → reject traffic (fail-closed, safe but can cause an outage if the RLS pod dies); false = fail-open (traffic flows unlimited if RLS is down). anihpj's choice depends on whether the limit protects a paying customer's quota (fail-closed) or is just a soft guardrail (fail-open).

⚖️ LOCAL vs GLOBAL EnvoyFilter — Side by Side

DimensionLOCAL (15.1)GLOBAL (this section)
Filter name...http.local_ratelimit...http.ratelimit
StateIn-process token bucketExternal RLS + Redis/store
applyTo usedHTTP_FILTER onlyHTTP_FILTER + VIRTUAL_HOST
Extra infraNoneRLS deployment + backing store
ScopePer podWhole mesh, one counter
Extra hop~0ms (in-process)~1-5ms gRPC check per request

15.8 Deep Dive — WasmPlugin's Full CRD Field Reference & Module Distribution

DEFINITION: 15.5 introduced WasmPlugin with the fields you'll touch most (selector, url, sha256, phase, priority, failStrategy, pluginConfig); this section completes the picture with every remaining field the CRD defines, plus exactly how a Wasm module physically gets from your laptop into Envoy's sandboxed VM. The exam's WasmPlugin questions increasingly probe the fields 15.5 didn't cover — targetRefs (Gateway API-style targeting), the url scheme defaulting rules, and the imagePullPolicy/sha256 interaction — because these are the fields people get wrong in real clusters.

📋 WasmPlugin — the Complete Field Reference

FieldWhat it does
selectorWorkloadSelector: label-match which pods get the plugin
targetRefsGateway-API-style alternative to selector; targets a named Gateway/ServiceEntry-like resource instead of labels
urlWasm module or OCI image location; no scheme given defaults to oci://; also supports file:// and http(s)://
sha256Checksum verifying the Wasm module/OCI image (supply chain)
imagePullPolicyIfNotPresent or Always; unspecified = IfNotPresent, BUT a :latest tag forces Always; sha256 set forces IfNotPresent
imagePullSecretCredentials (Secret name) for pulling from a private OCI registry
pluginConfigArbitrary Struct (JSON) handed to the module at load time
pluginNameName used inside Envoy config; was called rootID before
phasePluginPhase: UNSPECIFIED_PHASE, AUTHN, AUTHZ, or STATS
priorityint32; same-phase plugins run in DESCENDING priority order
failStrategyFAIL_CLOSE (5xx on crash), FAIL_OPEN (bypass plugin), or FAIL_RELOAD (spin up a fresh instance per request)
vmConfigWasm VM env vars / runtime settings (e.g. v8 vs wasmtime)
matchTrafficSelector[]; restricts which requests reach the plugin
typePluginType of the Wasm extension (defaults to HTTP)

targetRefs vs selector: pick exactly ONE. selector label-matches ordinary sidecar workloads (jobpost-api); targetRefs is the Gateway-API-style pointer used when the plugin belongs to a Gateway or other named resource, not a labeled Pod:

yaml — targetRefs example, an alternative to selector 
apiVersion: extensions.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: WasmPlugin
metadata:
  name: anihpj-gateway-header-guard
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  targetRefs:                    # ← Gateway-API style, an alt to selector
  - kind: Gateway                # ← attach straight to a named Gateway
    group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
    name: anihpj-ingress
  url: oci://registry.anihpj.dev/wasm/header-guard:v1.2.0
  sha256: 4f2a91c0...
  phase: AUTHN
  pluginConfig:
    header: x-anihpj-guard
    value: "checked"

# NOTE: use targetRefs when the plugin belongs to a Gateway/waypoint
# resource, not a labeled workload; use selector (15.5) for ordinary
# sidecars like jobpost-api. Only one of selector/targetRefs is set.
📦 WASM MODULE DISTRIBUTION — Push Once, Reference Everywhere
1. Build   header-guard.wasm  (Rust/Go/C++/AssemblyScript → compiled)

2. Push to an OCI registry → SAME registry you already use for
   container images:
   $ oras push registry.anihpj.dev/wasm/header-guard:v1.2.0 \
       header-guard.wasm:application/vnd.oci.image.layer.v1.tar

3. Reference it from WasmPlugin.spec.url:
     url: oci://registry.anihpj.dev/wasm/header-guard:v1.2.0
     sha256: 4f2a91c0...        # pin it → forces IfNotPresent pulls

4. istio-agent on each matched pod pulls the OCI artifact like a
   container image, verifies sha256, loads it into the Wasm VM

5. Roll out a new version: bump the tag + sha256, kubectl apply →
   istio-agent re-pulls, NO pod restart, NO proxy restart needed
⚠️ imagePullPolicy's Hidden Rule — a Genuine Exam Trap

Unspecified defaults to IfNotPresent — UNLESS the url tag is literally :latest, in which case Istio silently switches to Always; and if you set sha256 at all, Istio forces IfNotPresent regardless of what imagePullPolicy says, because a pinned digest never needs re-pulling.

15.9 EnvoyFilter Ordering & Governance — priority, Multi-Filter Precedence, and "Use With Care"

DEFINITION: EnvoyFilter has its OWN top-level spec.priority: int32 field (separate from WasmPlugin's priority) that, together with namespace scope and creation time, decides which patch wins when two or more EnvoyFilters touch the same workload. anihpj's platform team and an app team could both ship an EnvoyFilter patching jobpost-api's HTTP_FILTER chain (say, 15.1's local-ratelimit filter and 15.5's Lua tagger) — istiod does NOT reject the collision, it silently applies both in a defined order; the exam expects you to compute that order.

🔀 ENVOYFILTER RESOLUTION ORDER — When Multiple Filters Match One Workload
STEP 1 — namespace scope (broadest first):
  all EnvoyFilters in the config ROOT namespace (usually istio-system)
  applied first, THEN all matching EnvoyFilters in the workload's OWN
  namespace (e.g. anihpj)

STEP 2 — within the same namespace scope, patch sets sort by:
  1. priority          ← spec.priority (int32); LOWEST value first
  2. creation time      ← older EnvoyFilter objects applied first
  3. fully-qualified name ← final tiebreaker, alphabetical

anihpj example: jobpost-api-local-ratelimit (priority unset=0) and
jobpost-lua-tag (priority: 5) both patch jobpost-api's HTTP_FILTER
chain → the priority:0 filter's patch set is evaluated first
⚠️ Why the Exam Treats EnvoyFilter as a Last Resort — Verbatim From istio.io

"This feature must be used with care, as incorrect configurations could potentially destabilize the entire mesh." "The behavior is undefined if multiple EnvoyFilter configurations conflict with each other." "Some aspects of this API are deeply tied to the internal implementation ... any envoy configuration provided through this mechanism should be carefully monitored across Istio proxy version upgrades." Translation for anihpj: reach for VirtualService / AuthorizationPolicy / Telemetry FIRST; EnvoyFilter is the escape hatch, not the front door.

✅ anihpj Governance Checklist — Practical Mitigations, Not Just Theory

PracticeWhy (anihpj-specific rationale)
Always set workloadSelector or targetRefsUnscoped EnvoyFilters hit every sidecar in the namespace, not just jobpost-api
Set spec.priority explicitlyDon't rely on creation-time tiebreaks that silently reorder after a re-apply/CI re-run
Name filters descriptivelyFully-qualified name is the LAST tiebreaker and shows up in istioctl analyze output
Keep one Git-tracked YAML per concernUndefined behavior on conflicts means two teams editing the same patch is a real outage
Re-validate after every Istio minor upgradeEnvoyFilter is tied to Envoy's internal xDS shape, which can change between releases
Prefer WasmPlugin/native CRDs before EnvoyFilterExhaust VirtualService, AuthorizationPolicy, Telemetry, WasmPlugin — in that order

anihpj rule of thumb closing this chapter: EnvoyFilter and WasmPlugin are both "you write the logic" escape hatches — but EnvoyFilter edits Envoy's raw xDS config with NO stability guarantee across Istio versions, while WasmPlugin runs your code inside a sandboxed VM with a versioned, documented CRD surface; when either mechanism CAN solve the problem, WasmPlugin is the one that survives your next Istio upgrade unscathed.

🔧 Under the Hood — Local + Global Rate Limiting Both Live: Which EnvoyFilter Checks First, and Why the Answer Depends on an Alphabetical Accident Unless You Fix It

15.9 already showed the RESOLUTION ORDER that decides which EnvoyFilter patch compiles into the chain first. This is that rule run against a real anihpj scenario: what happens, request by request, when 15.1's local limiter and 15.7's global limiter are BOTH live on jobpost-api at once.

🗺️ Request-by-Request Walkthrough — Local + Global Ratelimit Both Live
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SETUP: two teams, two EnvoyFilters, one workload                            │
│                                                                              │
│  Platform team ships 15.1's jobpost-api-local-ratelimit (100 tok/s per pod,  │
│  no priority set). App team separately ships 15.7's two-patch global        │
│  filter, jobpost-global-ratelimit-filter (1000 req/min per IP via           │
│  RLS+Redis, no priority set either). Both patch the SAME SIDECAR_INBOUND    │
│  HTTP_FILTER chain with INSERT_BEFORE the router — a collision 15.9 says    │
│  istiod will NOT reject.                                                    │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 1  Resolve WHICH patch compiles into the chain first (15.9's rule):   │
│          same namespace (anihpj), same priority (both default to 0) →       │
│          tiebreak = alphabetical name. "jobpost-api-local..." sorts         │
│          before "jobpost-global..." ('a' < 'g') → LOCAL compiles first     │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 2  Envoy always runs HTTP filters in chain order, so every request    │
│          hits envoy.filters.http.local_ratelimit FIRST:                     │
│            bucket EMPTY → instant 429, RLS/Redis NEVER contacted (free)     │
│            bucket OK    → 1 token consumed → falls through to STEP 3        │
│                                                                              │
│  STEP 3  envoy.filters.http.ratelimit (global) runs SECOND:                 │
│            gRPC check to RLS (~1-5ms) → Redis counter for source IP         │
│            over 1000/min  → 429 + Retry-After: 60                           │
│            under 1000/min → forwarded to Django (both gates passed)         │
│                                                                              │
│  THE ACCIDENT: this cheap-check-first order exists ONLY because             │
│  "jobpost-api-local-ratelimit" happens to sort before "jobpost-global-      │
│  ratelimit-filter". Rename or re-create the global filter as, say,          │
│  "aaa-global-ratelimit", and the order FLIPS — every request now pays       │
│  the RLS/Redis round trip BEFORE the free local check, wasting RLS          │
│  capacity exactly when jobpost-api is already under the heaviest load.      │
│                                                                              │
│  THE FIX: never rely on the accident — set spec.priority explicitly         │
│  (local: priority 0, global: priority 10 — LOWEST runs first, per 15.9)     │
│  so the free check always guards the expensive one, no matter what          │
│  either filter is named or which team applies their YAML first.             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 ICA Insight: Two EnvoyFilters can legally patch the same workload — istiod applies both rather than rejecting the collision. Resolution order is namespace scope (root namespace first) → spec.priority (lowest first) → creation time → fully-qualified name (alphabetical). Never let the tiebreaker be an accident: set spec.priority explicitly so the cheap, in-process check (local rate limit) always runs before the expensive gRPC/Redis check (global rate limit), no matter what either filter happens to be named.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Local rate limiting is per-pod and free (in-process token bucket, zero extra infra); global rate limiting is a shared mesh-wide counter via an external RLS + Redis — pick local for "protect one pod," global for "cap this IP/user/API-key across the whole mesh."
  • Token bucket math, memorize both derived numbers: sustained rate = tokensPerFill ÷ fillInterval; burst ceiling = maxTokens. Misreading fillInterval: 60s as 1s silently turns "100 req/s" into "100 req/minute" — a 60× error.
  • Local rate limiting's TOTAL capacity scales with replica count — 3 pods × 100/s = 300/s effective, and HPA scaling to 6 pods silently doubles that ceiling to 600/s. Global rate limiting doesn't have this problem: one counter, mesh-wide, regardless of pod count.
  • WasmPlugin and Lua EnvoyFilter are the two doors for logic no built-in CRD covers — exhaust VirtualService/AuthorizationPolicy/Telemetry first. WasmPlugin is sandboxed, versioned, and OCI-distributed; Lua runs inline in Envoy's own process with no crash containment.
  • Every EnvoyFilter patch is one triple: applyTo (WHERE) + match.context (WHEN) + patch.operation (HOW) — the exam swaps exactly one of these three knobs per question to test whether you understand what each one controls.
  • Global rate limiting always needs TWO EnvoyFilter patches — an HTTP_FILTER patch to insert envoy.filters.http.ratelimit into the chain, and a VIRTUAL_HOST (or HTTP_ROUTE) patch to attach its rate_limits actions. Ship only one and the other half silently does nothing.
  • istiod does NOT reject colliding EnvoyFilters — it silently applies both, resolved by namespace scope → spec.priority (lowest first) → creation time → fully-qualified name. Never let the tiebreaker be an alphabetical accident; set priority explicitly.
  • EnvoyFilter's apiVersion is still networking.istio.io/v1alpha3, and WasmPlugin's is still extensions.istio.io/v1alpha1 — unlike VirtualService/DestinationRule/Gateway/ServiceEntry/AuthorizationPolicy, NEITHER has been promoted to v1 GA.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "fillInterval: 60s and fillInterval: 1s are close enough." No — misreading this field turns a "100 req/s" limit into "100 req/minute," a 60× weaker limit than intended. Always read fillInterval first in any token-bucket YAML.
  • "Local rate limiting caps jobpost-api at exactly the configured rate, mesh-wide." No — it's PER POD. Total effective capacity is the per-pod limit × replica count, and HPA scaling silently changes that total without touching the EnvoyFilter YAML at all.
  • "EnvoyFilter and WasmPlugin use apiVersion v1 now, since VirtualService/DestinationRule/AuthorizationPolicy are all GA." No — both are still stuck at v1alpha3/v1alpha1 respectively. Neither has ever been promoted, unlike most of the other CRDs in this guide.
  • "Two EnvoyFilters targeting the same workload — Istio rejects the invalid one." No — istiod applies BOTH, in a defined order (priority → creation time → name). There's no validation error for the collision itself; the danger is silent, not loud.
  • "ROUTE_CONFIGURATION supports INSERT_BEFORE just like HTTP_FILTER does." No — ROUTE_CONFIGURATION accepts ONLY MERGE. Picking REPLACE or any INSERT_* operation there gets the config rejected outright.
  • "Lua EnvoyFilter carries roughly the same risk as WasmPlugin, just a different language." No — Lua runs directly in Envoy's own process (a bad script can stall worker threads); WasmPlugin runs in a sandboxed VM where a crash is contained by failStrategy.
  • "failure_mode_deny: true is always the safer choice." Depends on the stake, not a universal default — true (fail-closed) protects a paying customer's quota at the cost of a full outage if the RLS pod dies; false (fail-open) never blocks legitimate traffic but lets abuse through while RLS is unreachable.

💼 Chapter 15 — Daily Work Takeaways

  • Reach for LOCAL rate limiting first for any "protect one pod" ask — zero extra infrastructure, answers the requirement instantly.
  • Compute sustained rate and burst from any token-bucket YAML yourself before trusting a teammate's claim about its real limit — read fillInterval's unit first.
  • Before shipping a new EnvoyFilter, check whether VirtualService, AuthorizationPolicy, Telemetry, or WasmPlugin already solves the problem — EnvoyFilter is istio.io's own documented "last resort."
  • Always set workloadSelector (or targetRefs) AND spec.priority explicitly on every EnvoyFilter/WasmPlugin shipped — skipping either invites a silent namespace-wide match or an alphabetical-tiebreak accident.
  • When wiring global rate limiting, verify BOTH patches actually landed — HTTP_FILTER AND VIRTUAL_HOST/HTTP_ROUTE. One without the other is a silent no-op for the missing half, not a loud error.
  • Map failure_mode_deny to the actual business stake, not a reflex default — a paying customer's quota usually wants fail-closed; a soft internal guardrail usually wants fail-open.
  • Re-validate every EnvoyFilter after an Istio minor-version upgrade — it's tied to Envoy's internal xDS shape, which can change between releases with no deprecation warning.
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 15

Seven quick-fire phrase-to-answer mappings — the same shorthand the practice questions below exercise in full scenarios:

  • "Protect a service from overload, per pod" = EnvoyFilter with local_ratelimit (15.1)
  • "Rate limit across all pods by IP / user / API key" = global rate limiting via RLS + Redis (15.2, 15.7)
  • Any question quoting a fillInterval value = stop and compute tokensPerFill ÷ fillInterval yourself before trusting the label (15.4)
  • "Custom logic no CRD covers" = WasmPlugin first, a Lua EnvoyFilter only for a quick, temporary one-line tweak (15.5)
  • "What does applyTo/context/operation mean" = WHERE/WHEN/HOW — one triple, memorize the enum values (15.6)
  • A global-rate-limit YAML sample with only ONE EnvoyFilter patch = incomplete — it needs both HTTP_FILTER AND VIRTUAL_HOST/HTTP_ROUTE (15.7)
  • "Two EnvoyFilters both match one workload" = priority (lowest first) → creation time → name — never assume, set spec.priority explicitly (15.9)

🧠 Chapter 15 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
What's the core scope difference between local and global rate limiting?
Show Answer
Answer

Local rate limiting is PER POD — each pod has its own independent token bucket. Global rate limiting is mesh-wide — ALL pods share ONE counter via an external Redis-backed rate limit service (RLS).

Explanation

This is why local's total capacity scales with replica count while global's does not — global's whole point is capping a client regardless of how many pods are currently running (15.1, 15.2).

Q2
A local rate limit is meant to cap traffic at 100 req/s, but someone typed fillInterval: 60s instead of 1s (with tokensPerFill: 100). What's the ACTUAL effective limit?
Show Answer
Answer

100 requests per 60 seconds — roughly 1.67 req/s, not 100 req/s. That's a 60× weaker limit than intended.

Explanation

Sustained rate = tokensPerFill ÷ fillInterval = 100 ÷ 60s. This exact misreading is called out as the chapter's single most common exam trap (15.4, Speed Tips).

Q3
Write the two formulas a token bucket's maxTokens/tokensPerFill/fillInterval fields let you derive.
Show Answer
Answer

Sustained rate = tokensPerFill ÷ fillInterval. Burst ceiling = maxTokens (a full, idle bucket can drain all at once).

Explanation

Setting maxTokens equal to tokensPerFill gives uniform traffic with no burst headroom; setting it higher absorbs spiky browser-style traffic while keeping the same steady-state rate (15.4).

Q4
True or false: a WasmPlugin module is pulled onto each matched pod the same way a container image is.
Show Answer
Answer

True. istio-agent pulls the OCI artifact named in spec.url like a container image, verifies its sha256, and loads it into Envoy's sandboxed Wasm VM.

Explanation

This is also why rolling out a new version needs no pod or proxy restart — bump the tag + sha256, apply, and istio-agent re-pulls (15.5, 15.8).

Q5
Name the WHERE/WHEN/HOW triple every EnvoyFilter configPatches entry is built from.
Show Answer
Answer

applyTo = WHERE (e.g. HTTP_FILTER, CLUSTER), match.context = WHEN (SIDECAR_INBOUND, SIDECAR_OUTBOUND, GATEWAY), patch.operation = HOW (INSERT_BEFORE, MERGE, etc.).

Explanation

Every EnvoyFilter in this chapter is the same triple wearing a different value: payload — the exam typically changes exactly one of the three per question (15.6).

Q6
Does applyTo: ROUTE_CONFIGURATION support patch.operation: INSERT_BEFORE?
Show Answer
Answer

No. ROUTE_CONFIGURATION accepts ONLY MERGE. Any INSERT_* or REPLACE operation there gets the config rejected.

Explanation

This is one of "Two Exam Traps Baked Into This Grammar" — the other is that REPLACE is legal only on HTTP_FILTER/NETWORK_FILTER (15.6).

Q7
How many EnvoyFilter patches does global rate limiting need, and what does each one do?
Show Answer
Answer

Two. Patch 1 (HTTP_FILTER) inserts envoy.filters.http.ratelimit into the chain. Patch 2 (VIRTUAL_HOST or HTTP_ROUTE) attaches rate_limits actions telling Envoy what descriptor to send the RLS (source IP, a header, or both).

Explanation

Shipping only patch 1 inserts a filter with nothing telling it what to rate-limit on — a common incomplete-YAML exam distractor (15.7).

Q8
Two teams each ship an EnvoyFilter that patches the same workload's HTTP_FILTER chain. What does istiod do?
Show Answer
Answer

It does NOT reject the collision — it applies BOTH, resolved by namespace scope (root namespace first) → spec.priority (lowest first) → creation time → fully-qualified name (alphabetical).

Explanation

This is exactly the scenario the UTH walks through request-by-request — leaving the tiebreaker to chance means renaming a filter can silently reorder which check runs first (15.9, UTH).

Q9
What is the current, correct apiVersion for the EnvoyFilter CRD?
Show Answer
Answer

networking.istio.io/v1alpha3 — EnvoyFilter has never been promoted to a v1 GA apiVersion, unlike VirtualService, DestinationRule, Gateway, ServiceEntry, and AuthorizationPolicy elsewhere in this guide.

Explanation

WasmPlugin is in the same position — still extensions.istio.io/v1alpha1. Both CRDs' own instability is part of why istio.io calls them a last resort (15.9, Key Takeaways).

Q10
failure_mode_deny: true vs false on the global rate limit filter — what's the tradeoff?
Show Answer
Answer

true (fail-closed): if the RLS is unreachable, traffic is REJECTED — safe for a quota, but can cause an outage if the RLS pod dies. false (fail-open): traffic flows unlimited if RLS is down — never blocks legitimate traffic, but lets abuse through during an RLS outage.

Explanation

anihpj's choice depends on what the limit protects — a paying customer's quota usually wants fail-closed; a soft internal guardrail usually wants fail-open (15.7).

⚙️ Chapter 15 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a scenario, and you produce the fix with real YAML or commands.

Q1
Write the token-bucket fields for a local rate limit capping jobpost-api at a steady 50 req/s per pod, with a burst ceiling of 100.
Show Answer
Answer
token_bucket:
  max_tokens: 100
  tokens_per_fill: 50
  fill_interval: 1s
Explanation

Sustained rate = tokensPerFill ÷ fillInterval = 50 ÷ 1s = 50 req/s. Burst = maxTokens = 100 — twice the steady rate, letting a full idle bucket absorb a one-off spike (15.4).

Q2
jobpost-api runs a LOCAL rate limit of 100 req/s per pod at 3 replicas. HPA scales it to 6 replicas under load. What's the new effective TOTAL capacity, and did anyone have to edit the EnvoyFilter?
Show Answer
Answer

600 req/s total (6 × 100), up from 300 req/s at 3 replicas. No — the EnvoyFilter YAML never changed; the effective ceiling moved silently because local rate limiting is per-pod, not mesh-wide.

Explanation

This is the exact trap 15.4's "LOCAL vs GLOBAL MATH" box calls out — if the requirement is a hard mesh-wide ceiling regardless of replica count, GLOBAL rate limiting is the correct tool, not local (15.4).

Q3
Name the applyTo value used by EACH of global rate limiting's two required EnvoyFilter patches.
Show Answer
Answer
patch 1: applyTo: HTTP_FILTER        # inserts envoy.filters.http.ratelimit
patch 2: applyTo: VIRTUAL_HOST       # attaches rate_limits actions
Explanation

Patch 2 could also target HTTP_ROUTE instead of VIRTUAL_HOST depending on scope — but it must use operation: MERGE either way, since both are route-config-family targets (15.7, 15.6's ROUTE_CONFIGURATION trap).

Q4
A colleague's EnvoyFilter sets applyTo: ROUTE_CONFIGURATION with patch.operation: INSERT_BEFORE. What's wrong, and what should the operation be?
Show Answer
Answer

Broken — ROUTE_CONFIGURATION accepts ONLY MERGE. INSERT_BEFORE is legal on HTTP_FILTER/NETWORK_FILTER, not on a route configuration. The fix is operation: MERGE.

Explanation

Istio rejects the config outright with the wrong operation for a given applyTo — this is one of the two "exam traps baked into the grammar" (15.6).

Q5
Write a WasmPlugin pulling a module from an OCI registry, pinned by sha256, running in the AUTHZ phase, failing closed on a crash.
Show Answer
Answer
apiVersion: extensions.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: WasmPlugin
metadata:
  name: jobpost-authz-guard
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: jobpost-api}
  url: oci://registry.anihpj.dev/wasm/authz-guard:v1.0.0
  sha256: 9c1b4e2a...
  phase: AUTHZ
  failStrategy: FAIL_CLOSE
Explanation

Setting sha256 also forces imagePullPolicy to IfNotPresent regardless of what's written there — a pinned digest never needs re-pulling (15.8).

Q6
Two EnvoyFilters both patch jobpost-api's HTTP_FILTER chain with no spec.priority set. One is named "aaa-limiter", the other "zzz-limiter". Which patch compiles into the chain first, and why?
Show Answer
Answer

"aaa-limiter" — with priority unset (defaults to 0) on both and the same namespace scope, the tiebreaker falls to creation time, and if that also ties, to fully-qualified name, alphabetically. "aaa..." sorts before "zzz..." ('a' < 'z').

Explanation

This is exactly the "alphabetical accident" the UTH warns about — a rename could silently flip this order. The fix is always to set spec.priority explicitly rather than depend on naming (15.9, UTH).

Q7
Write the command to confirm a local rate limit filter actually compiled into jobpost-api's live Envoy listener (not just that kubectl apply succeeded).
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/jobpost-api \
  -n anihpj -o json | grep -i ratelimit
Explanation

This reads Envoy's ACTUAL compiled listener config via the sidecar's admin interface — the only way to confirm the EnvoyFilter patch really landed in the live filter chain (Commands Cheat-Card).

Q8
A WasmPlugin has both sha256 set AND imagePullPolicy: Always written explicitly. What actually happens?
Show Answer
Answer

Istio forces IfNotPresent regardless — a pinned sha256 always wins over whatever imagePullPolicy says, because a digest-pinned artifact never needs re-pulling to detect changes.

Explanation

This is called out as "a genuine exam trap" — the reverse case also matters: an unpinned :latest tag forces Always even if imagePullPolicy is left unspecified (15.8).

Q9
Write the command sequence to trip a rate limit for real and count how many requests got 200 vs 429.
Show Answer
Answer
for i in $(seq 1 150); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://jobpost-api:8000/jobs/
done | sort | uniq -c
Explanation

150 requests against a 100-token bucket should show roughly 100 200s and 50 429s — proving the limiter is real, not just theoretically applied (Practice Drill 15.1, Commands Cheat-Card).

Q10
Per the UTH's "alphabetical accident" scenario, write the spec.priority values that GUARANTEE the free local check always runs before the expensive global check, regardless of either filter's name.
Show Answer
Answer
jobpost-api-local-ratelimit:   priority: 0
jobpost-global-ratelimit-filter: priority: 10
Explanation

LOWEST priority value runs first — setting local to 0 and global to 10 makes the cheap in-process check always guard the expensive RLS/Redis round trip, no matter what either filter is named or which team applies their YAML first (UTH, 15.9).

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 15
  • Default to LOCAL first — zero extra infra, and it answers "protect one pod" questions instantly; reach for GLOBAL only when the requirement names a client (an IP, a user, an API key) across ALL pods at once (15.1, 15.2).
  • Read fillInterval before anything else in a token-bucket YAML — fillInterval: 60s disguised as 1s is this chapter's single most common exam trap ("100 req/s" silently becomes "100 req/min") (15.4).
  • Before writing a new EnvoyFilter, check whether VirtualService, AuthorizationPolicy, Telemetry, or WasmPlugin already solves it — EnvoyFilter is istio.io's own "last resort," and every extra one you ship is another unscoped blast radius to review later (15.9).
  • Always set workloadSelector (or targetRefs) AND spec.priority on every EnvoyFilter/WasmPlugin — skipping either leaves you exposed to 15.9's silent namespace-wide match or an alphabetical-tiebreak accident like the UTH walkthrough above (15.6, 15.9).
  • Prefer WasmPlugin over a Lua EnvoyFilter the moment the logic gets tests, versions, or a second team touching it — sha256-pinned OCI images roll forward/back with zero pod restarts; Lua's inline_code has no such safety net (15.5).
  • Map failure_mode_deny straight to the business stake: true (fail-closed) protects a paying customer's quota at the cost of an outage if RLS dies; false (fail-open) never blocks legitimate traffic but lets abuse through while RLS is down (15.7).

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 15)

Every command below already appeared earlier in this chapter — grouped here as one reference for shipping rate limits, verifying live Envoy state, and debugging EnvoyFilter/WasmPlugin collisions.

CommandWhat It Does / Checks in Chapter 15

kubectl get envoyfilters -n anihpjList every EnvoyFilter patching this namespace (spot 15.9 collisions)
kubectl describe envoyfilter <name> -n anihpjConfirm workloadSelector + priority match what you intended (15.9)

istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -o json | grep -i wasmProve the Wasm module actually loaded into Envoy's sandboxed VM (15.5)

🧪 Practice Drill 15.1 — Cap jobpost-api at 100 req/s per Pod, Right Now

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Do this now, timed, on your own anihpj cluster:

  1. (2 min) Copy 15.1's EnvoyFilter into local-ratelimit.yaml: set workloadSelector labels app: jobpost-api, maxTokens: 100, tokensPerFill: 100, fillInterval: 1s.
  2. (1 min) kubectl apply -f local-ratelimit.yaml -n anihpj
  3. (2 min) Verify it's live: istioctl proxy-config listener deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -o json | grep local_ratelimit
  4. (2 min) Trip it: fire 150 quick requests at jobpost-api's /jobs/ endpoint and tally status codes with sort | uniq -c — confirm roughly 100 200s and 50 429s.
  5. (1 min) Clean up: kubectl delete envoyfilter jobpost-api-local-ratelimit -n anihpj and confirm the limit disappears instantly, no pod restart.
Hint: Step 1 reuses 15.1's exact token-bucket fields — sustained rate = tokensPerFill ÷ fillInterval (15.4's math). Step 3 is the same live-filter-chain reflex 15.6's patch triple is built from. Step 4's ~100/50 split is the token bucket draining then refusing once empty — Django never sees the 429s. Step 5 confirms deleting an EnvoyFilter is the same zero-restart mechanism as every other config push in this mesh.
View Solution

Step 3's listener dump should show envoy.filters.http.local_ratelimit present in the chain within seconds of applying — no pod restart needed. Step 4's 150-request loop should land close to 100 200s and 50 429s (exact numbers can drift a few requests either way depending on timing near the 1-second refill boundary).

Check yourself: did step 4's actual count roughly match the token-bucket math you'd predict from maxTokens: 100, or was it wildly off? If it was off, re-check whether your loop fired fast enough to exhaust the bucket inside one fillInterval window before it refilled.

🧪 Practice Drill 15.2 — Wire Global Rate Limiting's Two Patches, Then Break One On Purpose

⏱️ Target Time: 10 minutes
Scenario

Prove BOTH patches are really required, not just documented as required:

  1. Apply ONLY 15.7's patch 1 (the HTTP_FILTER insert) — no patch 2 yet.
  2. Send several requests. Confirm they all still succeed, no matter how many you send — the filter has nothing telling it what to limit on yet.
  3. Now apply patch 2 (the VIRTUAL_HOST merge attaching rate_limits actions).
  4. Re-send the same volume of requests and confirm SOME now return 429 once the per-IP or per-key threshold is crossed.
  5. istioctl proxy-config listener AND istioctl proxy-config route — confirm which patch shows up in which config dump.
Hint: Step 2 is the whole point — a filter with no rate_limits action attached does nothing observable, which is exactly why "only one patch shipped" bugs are easy to miss in code review.
View Solution

Step 2 should show 100% success regardless of request volume — the filter exists in the chain but has no descriptor-building action, so it never has anything to check against the RLS. Step 4 should show 429s appearing once the RLS-side threshold is crossed. Step 5: patch 1 shows up in the LISTENER dump (it's an HTTP_FILTER), patch 2 shows up in the ROUTE dump (it's a VIRTUAL_HOST/route-config-family target).

Check yourself: could you explain to a teammate why a code reviewer might approve patch-1-only as "looks complete" — and why that review would be wrong? That's the exact gap this drill is built to make visible.

🧪 Practice Drill 15.3 — Reproduce the Alphabetical-Accident Collision Yourself

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

Don't take the UTH's walkthrough on faith — build the collision and watch the order for real:

  1. Ship BOTH 15.1's local limiter and 15.7's global limiter on jobpost-api, neither with spec.priority set, named so one sorts alphabetically before the other.
  2. Trip the local limit only (a burst under the global threshold). Confirm you get 429 WITHOUT any RLS/Redis round trip (check RLS logs for zero hits during this step).
  3. Rename (delete + recreate) the global filter so it now sorts BEFORE the local filter alphabetically.
  4. Repeat step 2's exact same burst. Confirm the RLS now gets queried even for requests that would have been rejected for free by the local check.
  5. Fix it for good: add spec.priority: 0 to local and spec.priority: 10 to global, and confirm the order no longer depends on either filter's name.
Hint: Step 4 is the expensive mistake made visible — every request that COULD have been rejected for free now pays a real RLS/Redis round trip instead, wasting capacity exactly when the service is already under load.
View Solution

Step 2 should show zero RLS log hits — the local filter, compiling first alphabetically, rejects with 429 before the request ever reaches the global filter. Step 4 (after the rename) should show RLS hits for the SAME rejected requests — proof the rename flipped which filter runs first. Step 5's explicit priorities should restore the cheap-check-first behavior permanently, independent of any future rename.

Check yourself: before doing this drill, would you have predicted a simple kubectl delete + re-apply with a new name could change WHICH filter runs first, with no priority field touched at all? If not, that's exactly the "silent accident" this chapter warns about.

🧪 Practice Drill 15.4 — Diagnose Four Broken EnvoyFilter/WasmPlugin Symptoms

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

For each symptom, name the most likely cause and the ONE command you'd run to confirm it — before proposing any fix:

  1. A local rate limit EnvoyFilter is applied with no errors, but istioctl proxy-config listener shows no local_ratelimit filter at all.
  2. A global rate-limit EnvoyFilter's HTTP_FILTER patch is confirmed live, but no request is EVER rejected no matter the volume.
  3. A WasmPlugin YAML applies cleanly, but kubectl get wasmplugins shows it, while proxy-config listener | grep wasm shows nothing.
  4. An EnvoyFilter with applyTo: ROUTE_CONFIGURATION and operation: INSERT_BEFORE is rejected at apply time.
Hint: Two of these four point to a missing or mismatched workloadSelector/selector — the YAML is valid, it's just never being attached to the pod you think it is.
View Solution
#CauseConfirm with
1Most likely a workloadSelector label mismatch — the EnvoyFilter validated but never attached to jobpost-api's actual pod labelskubectl describe envoyfilter <name> -n anihpj and compare selector labels against kubectl get pods --show-labels
2Missing patch 2 (VIRTUAL_HOST/HTTP_ROUTE) — the filter is inserted but has no rate_limits action telling it what descriptor to checkistioctl proxy-config route deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj -o json | grep -i rate_limit
3Likely a selector mismatch on the WasmPlugin, OR the OCI pull failed silently (bad sha256/registry auth)kubectl describe wasmplugin <name> -n anihpj for events/pull errors
4Not a bug — ROUTE_CONFIGURATION only supports MERGE, this is working as designedChange operation to MERGE; no further diagnosis needed

🧪 Practice Drill 15.5 — Sketch the Patch Triple From Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Without looking at 15.6, write out the WHERE/WHEN/HOW triple for THREE different EnvoyFilters from this chapter: 15.1's local rate limiter, 15.7's global rate-limit HTTP_FILTER patch, and 15.7's global rate-limit VIRTUAL_HOST patch.

Hint: Two of the three should have an IDENTICAL WHERE/WHEN/HOW triple — only the value: payload differs between them.
View Solution

15.1 local limiter: HTTP_FILTER + SIDECAR_INBOUND + INSERT_BEFORE. 15.7 patch 1 (global filter insert): HTTP_FILTER + SIDECAR_INBOUND + INSERT_BEFORE — IDENTICAL triple to 15.1, different value: payload (a different named filter). 15.7 patch 2 (global actions): VIRTUAL_HOST + SIDECAR_INBOUND + MERGE — a genuinely different triple, since it's attaching actions to an existing route object rather than inserting a new filter.

Check yourself: could you explain WHY patch 2 can't use INSERT_BEFORE the way the other two do? If your answer isn't "because VIRTUAL_HOST only supports MERGE," re-read 15.6's warning box.

Chapter 15 starts where Chapter 14 leaves off — a jobpost-api that is finally live and healthy — and asks what stops a single caller from ruining that. 15.1-15.3 give you the three levers (local, global, shaping); 15.4 supplies the math that makes all three predictable; 15.5 and 15.8 open a second door for anything none of Istio's CRDs cover, weighing a sandboxed WasmPlugin against a quicker but riskier Lua EnvoyFilter; 15.6 hands you the grammar every EnvoyFilter patch is built from; 15.7 uses that grammar to wire up global rate limiting for real; and 15.9 closes the chapter with the discipline to run more than one EnvoyFilter safely — because, as istio.io itself warns, this is a mechanism that must be used with care.

Quick recap — 🪣 Local: per-pod token bucket, free, no infra (15.1) · 🌐 Global: shared Redis counter via RLS, mesh-wide (15.2) · 🚦 Shaping: header match + fault-injection delay for priority lanes (15.3) · ⏱️ Token Bucket: sustained rate = tokensPerFill ÷ fillInterval, burst = maxTokens (15.4) · 🧩 WasmPlugin vs Lua: sandboxed/versioned vs inline/riskier (15.5) · 🔤 Patch Triple: applyTo + context + operation, one grammar for every EnvoyFilter (15.6) · 🌐 Global RL Wiring: HTTP_FILTER inserts, VIRTUAL_HOST attaches actions — two patches, not one (15.7) · 📋 WasmPlugin Full Reference: targetRefs, imagePullPolicy rules, OCI distribution (15.8) · 🔀 Governance: priority → creation time → name resolves collisions; EnvoyFilter is the escape hatch, not the front door (15.9). Chapter 16 now asks the growth question: what happens when jobpost-api outgrows a single cluster.

Chapter 16: Multi-Cluster and Ambient Mesh — Whatever Shape Production Actually Needs

anihpj no longer fits inside one cluster or one interception model. EU jobseekers hitting jobpost-api from Frankfurt and US jobseekers hitting the same API from Virginia both expect sub-100ms responses, and pinning either region to a single cluster means someone's request crosses an ocean on every call. At the same time, seven sidecar-injected services times every replica is real memory the platform team pays for on every node, and low-traffic services like notification-service and location-service burn a full Envoy sidecar just to say "mTLS, please" a handful of times a minute. Layered on top of both problems, anihpj's original PostgreSQL instance was never containerized — it still runs as a VM with real disks attached, sitting just outside the mesh's mTLS boundary until it gets a WorkloadEntry and joins like any other workload.

"What happens when jobpost-api outgrows a single cluster?" Chapter 16 is where anihpj's mesh stops being "one cluster, one interception model, containers only" and becomes whatever shape the business actually needs: multiple clusters bridged by a shared root of trust (16.1, 16.7), a legacy VM treated as a first-class citizen (16.2, 16.8), and sidecar and sidecar-free namespaces coexisting under one mesh (16.3-16.6, 16.9). None of this introduces a new CRD Chapters 1-15 didn't already teach — VirtualService, DestinationRule, WorkloadEntry, and AuthorizationPolicy all still apply, just at the hardest-mode edge cases the exam and production both throw at them.

💡 ICA Exam Tips for Chapter 16
  • "Multi-cluster production" = Multi-Primary (each cluster has own istiod, no SPOF)
  • "Cross-cluster traffic" = East-west gateway (NOT the same as ingress gateway)
  • "Add a VM to mesh" = WorkloadEntry (IP + labels + serviceAccount) + WorkloadGroup
  • "Reduce resource usage" = Ambient mesh (ztunnel per-node, ~50Mi shared vs ~128Mi per pod)
  • "Enable ambient" = Label namespace istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient (NOT istio-injection)
  • Ambient L4 = always on (ztunnel), L7 = optional (waypoint per namespace)
  • "Cross-cluster mTLS handshake failing" = check the shared root CA FIRST — the single most common multi-cluster failure

16.1 Multi-Cluster Istio — Spanning Kubernetes Clusters

Single mesh across EU + US clusters with locality-based routing — EU users go to EU cluster, auto-failover to US if EU is down. mTLS works seamlessly across clusters.

🌍 MULTI-CLUSTER — anihpj EU + US
🌍 EU Users                                    🌎 US Users
     │                                               │
[EU LoadBalancer]                            [US LoadBalancer]
     │                                               │
┌────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────┐
│                        SINGLE ISTIO MESH                              │
│  CLUSTER 1 (EU — Frankfurt)    │    CLUSTER 2 (US — Virginia)         │
│  istiod (EU primary)           │    istiod (US replica)               │
│  jobpost-api:v1 · user-service │    jobpost-api:v1 · user-service     │
│       │    mTLS cross-cluster ─┼─────────┘                            │
│                                                                       │
│  VirtualService: locality-based failover                              │
│  • EU users → EU cluster (low latency)                               │
│  • EU cluster down → auto failover to US cluster                     │
Primary-Remote

One istiod manages both clusters. Simpler but single point of failure.

Multi-Primary

Each cluster has own istiod. Recommended for production.

External CP

istiod outside any cluster. Advanced setup for managed services.

📖 KEY TERM — East-West Gateway

A dedicated Istio gateway that carries service-to-service traffic BETWEEN clusters ("east-west"), unlike the ingress gateway which carries user traffic INTO the mesh ("north-south"). East-west gateway ≠ the ingress gateway in ROLE, but IS the same Envoy gateway image under the hood — only its Gateway resource differs: it exposes port 15443 in tls AUTO_PASSTHROUGH mode, so it forwards mTLS bytes by SNI, never decrypting them.

Cross-cluster mTLS has a hard requirement: all clusters must share the SAME root CA, so SPIFFE identities stay globally unique and a certificate minted in one cluster validates in the other. No shared root CA → cross-cluster handshakes fail → each cluster becomes an island that can only talk to itself. Service discovery across clusters works because each istiod is given a "remote secret" (a kubeconfig) so it can read the OTHER cluster's API server and learn its endpoints — under the hood, istiod points its normal Kubernetes informer at the other cluster's API server via that borrowed kubeconfig, running the same List/Watch on Services and Endpoints it runs locally. Results merge into ONE internal registry alongside local endpoints, then push to every Envoy/ztunnel over standard xDS — why EU and US pods appear side by side with no visible seam.

🔌 Cross-Cluster Plumbing — What Multi-Cluster Really Requires

RequirementWhy it exists
Shared root CACerts from either cluster validate in the other → mTLS works
East-west gateway :15443 (tls AUTO_PASSTHROUGH)Dedicated gateway carrying service-to-service traffic BETWEEN clusters, unopened
Remote secrets (istioctl create-remote-secret)Lets each istiod read the OTHER cluster's API server to discover its services and endpoints
topology.istio.io/network label per clusterTells Istio which network each cluster is on → route via the east-west gateway when crossing
yaml — Locality Failover: keep EU traffic in EU, fail over to US 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-locality
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: jobpost-api
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      localityLbSetting:
        enabled: true            # prefer local endpoints
        failover:
        - from: eu-central-1     # EU cluster's region
          to: us-east-1          # where EU traffic goes
    outlierDetection:            # REQUIRED for failover!
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5    # marks region unhealthy
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
📖 Where "eu-central-1" Actually Comes From

The failover region/zone names in that DestinationRule aren't invented — Istio derives them from standard Kubernetes NODE labels: topology.kubernetes.io/region, topology.kubernetes.io/zone, and topology.istio.io/subzone (Istio's own finer-grained addition, since Kubernetes itself stops at zone). A pod's locality is whatever region/zone/subzone its NODE is labeled with — mislabel one node and that pod silently reports the wrong locality to every DestinationRule doing locality-weighted routing or failover.

16.2 VM Workloads in the Mesh

Add legacy VMs (databases, monoliths) to the Istio mesh. The VM gets a SPIFFE certificate and is treated like a Pod — full mTLS, metrics, and authorization policies.

🎯 ICA exam note: this is the external → in-mesh direction of "Connecting In-Mesh Workloads to External Workloads and Services." The reverse direction (in-mesh → external, e.g. calling api.stripe.com) is ServiceEntry alone — see Chapter 8.

🖥️ VM IN THE MESH — Legacy PostgreSQL VM Joining anihpj
BEFORE (VM outside mesh):

  [skills-service Pod] ──plain TCP──▶ [PostgreSQL VM: 10.0.5.20]
  No mTLS. No metrics. No circuit breaker. Just raw database.

AFTER (VM inside mesh):

  Step 1: Install Envoy proxy on the VM (istio-proxy binary)
  Step 2: Apply WorkloadEntry in Kubernetes (address, labels)
  Step 3: istiod issues a SPIFFE certificate to the VM's Envoy proxy

  [skills-service Pod] ──mTLS──▶ [PostgreSQL VM: 10.0.5.20]
  ✅ Same mTLS as between pods
  ✅ Metrics visible in Grafana
  ✅ AuthorizationPolicy controls who can query the database
📖 KEY TERM — WorkloadGroup

The "Deployment template" for VMs: it declares the labels, network, and serviceAccount that every VM instance inherits. Think of it this way: WorkloadEntry is to a VM what a Pod is to a container; WorkloadGroup is the Deployment that stamps them out. WorkloadEntry is a real Istio CRD (networking.istio.io) — not a native Kubernetes object. Without one, istiod has no record of the VM: no CSR gets validated, no SPIFFE SVID gets issued, and AuthorizationPolicy can't allow or deny it — Postgres could be perfectly healthy and still be a complete blind spot to the mesh.

The VM earns its identity the same way a pod does: the VM's istio-proxy sends a CSR to istiod:15012 → istiod validates it against the WorkloadGroup → signs and returns a SPIFFE SVID certificate. A ServiceEntry (location: MESH_INTERNAL, resolution: STATIC) then gives the VM a stable DNS name that anihpj pods can call — psql connection strings keep working, now over mTLS.

🔄 VM Onboarding Flow — WorkloadGroup → Proxy → SVID → mTLS
1. Apply WorkloadGroup (template: labels, serviceAccount)
2. Generate VM bootstrap files: istioctl x workload entry configure ...
3. Copy files to the VM, install + start istio-proxy
4. VM proxy sends CSR ──▶ istiod:15012
5. istiod validates vs WorkloadGroup ──▶ signs SPIFFE SVID
6. WorkloadEntry created — by hand, as shown below (16.8 covers
   the alpha auto-registration alternative)
7. ServiceEntry (MESH_INTERNAL, STATIC) gives it a DNS name
──▶ skills-service ══mTLS══▶ postgres VM, psql unchanged
yaml — WorkloadEntry: Register a VM 

# Register legacy PostgreSQL VM in the mesh
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: WorkloadEntry
metadata:
  name: postgres-vm
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  address: 10.0.5.20           # VM IP address
  labels:
    app: postgres              # Labels for policy matching
  serviceAccount: postgres-sa  # For SPIFFE identity

# Result: skills-service → PostgreSQL VM over mTLS!
# VM gets cert from istiod, metrics in Grafana,
# AuthorizationPolicy controls who can query it.
yaml — ServiceEntry: Give the VM a Stable DNS Name 
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: postgres-vm
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - postgres.anihpj.internal
  location: MESH_INTERNAL       # inside the trust boundary, not external
  ports:
  - number: 5432
    name: tcp-postgres
    protocol: TCP
  resolution: STATIC             # we already know the VM's address
  endpoints:
  - address: 10.0.5.20

16.3 Istio Ambient Mesh — Sidecar-Free Mode

New architecture (alpha in v1.18, beta in v1.22, GA since v1.24): no sidecar injection required! ztunnel (per-node) handles L4 mTLS, waypoint proxy handles L7 features per namespace. ~18× less memory for L4-only workloads (see anihpj's own numbers below); adding a waypoint narrows that to ~6×, still a major reduction versus one sidecar per pod.

🏗️ SIDECAR vs AMBIENT

Sidecar ModeAmbient Mode
ArchitectureEnvoy proxy per podztunnel per NODE (shared)
Memory per pod~128Mi~0Mi (shared)
7 anihpj services7 × 128Mi = ~900Mi1 ztunnel = ~50Mi
L7 featuresBuilt-in per sidecarOptional waypoint proxy
Pod startup+50ms (sidecar)No overhead
Pod READY2/2 (app + sidecar)1/1 (app only!)
bash — Enable ambient mode for anihpj 

# Install Istio with ambient profile
istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y

# Enable ambient for namespace (no istio-injection label!)
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient

# Result: pods in anihpj get L4 mTLS via ztunnel automatically
# No 2/2 — pods stay at 1/1!

# L7 features (VS routing, retries, L7 authz) need a waypoint —
# that's a separate, optional step covered fully in 16.4 and 16.9.

16.4 Ambient Mesh Architecture — How ztunnel and Waypoint Work Together

From the official docs: Ambient mesh splits Istio's functionality into two layers — a zero-trust secure overlay (ztunnel for L4) and an optional L7 processing layer (waypoint proxy). This layered approach is what gives ambient its memory savings — anihpj's own numbers show ~18× for services that only need ztunnel's L4 tier, narrowing to ~6× for services that also carry a waypoint.

🧠 ANALOGY — The Front Door vs. the Front Desk

Picture ztunnel and the waypoint proxy as a building's front door versus its front desk. EVERY visitor passes the front-door guard (ztunnel), who checks ID and logs who came and went — no exceptions, nothing to configure. Only a few floors bother staffing an actual front desk (waypoint) that also asks WHY you're visiting and can redirect you based on the answer. Low-traffic services like notification-service never need that second desk at all.

🏗️ AMBIENT MESH ARCHITECTURE — Two-Layer Design
🔒
LAYER 1: ztunnel (L4 — Always On)

One ztunnel pod per Kubernetes Node. Handles: mTLS encryption, simple L4 authorization, TCP metrics, and traffic routing at TCP level. Written in Rust for performance. No per-pod overhead. Every pod on the node shares one ztunnel.

🧠
LAYER 2: Waypoint Proxy (L7 — Optional)

One Envoy-based waypoint deployment per namespace (or per service account). Handles: VirtualService routing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, L7 AuthorizationPolicy, telemetry. Only deploy if you need L7 features.

🔄 AMBIENT TRAFFIC FLOW — How a Request Travels
  L4 ONLY (no waypoint):                     L7 (with waypoint):

  Pod A ──▶ ztunnel(Node1) ──▶ Pod B        Pod A ──▶ ztunnel ──▶ waypoint ──▶ ztunnel ──▶ Pod B
  (app)    (mTLS, L4 authz)  (app)          (app)    (mTLS)    (VS routing,  (mTLS)    (app)
                                                    │          retries, CB)           │
                                                    │                                  │
  ✅ mTLS encryption                          ✅ mTLS + L4 authz                      │
  ✅ L4 authz (basic allow/deny)             ✅ VS weight-based routing               │
  ✅ TCP metrics                             ✅ Retries, timeouts, CB                 │
  ❌ HTTP routing (URI/headers)              ✅ L7 AuthorizationPolicy                │
  ❌ Retries, timeouts, circuit breaker      ✅ Full telemetry (RED metrics)          │

🚀 AMBIENT MIGRATION — Sidecar → Ambient Coexistence

StepActionResult
1Install Istio with ambient profileztunnel DaemonSet runs on all nodes
2Label test namespace: istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambientPods get L4 mTLS via ztunnel, no sidecars
3Verify: kubectl get pods shows 1/1No istio-proxy container needed!
4Deploy waypoint if L7 needed: istioctl waypoint apply -n anihpjPer-namespace Envoy for L7 features
5Gradually migrate namespaces from sidecar to ambientBoth modes coexist seamlessly
6Remove istio-injection=enabled from migrated namespacesClean cutover from sidecar to ambient

16.5 Deep Dive — HBONE: HTTP-Based Overlay Network Environment

From the official Istio ambient mesh architecture docs: HBONE (HTTP-Based Overlay Network Environment) is the secure tunneling protocol that replaces iptables-based traffic interception in ambient mode. It's how ztunnel transparently encrypts and routes traffic without sidecars. The source ztunnel opens ONE mTLS connection to the destination ztunnel and multiplexes many application streams over it as HTTP/2 streams — fewer TCP handshakes, fewer TLS sessions to manage. Identity is preserved end-to-end: the mTLS handshake uses the SPIFFE certificate of the SOURCE POD's service account (not the node!) — AuthorizationPolicy still sees cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api as the caller.

🔗 HBONE TUNNEL — How Traffic Flows Through Ambient Mesh
  SIDECAR MODE (iptables):
  App:3000 → iptables REDIRECT → localhost:15001 → Envoy (mTLS) → network

  AMBIENT MODE (HBONE):
  App:3000 → Node network → ztunnel:15008 (HBONE) → remote ztunnel → App:3000

  HBONE PROTOCOL STACK:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Application Data (HTTP/gRPC/TCP)│  ← Your app's payload
  ├──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  HTTP/2 CONNECT tunnel (HBONE)   │  ← Encapsulation layer
  ├──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  mTLS (SPIFFE certs)             │  ← Identity & encryption
  ├──────────────────────────────────┤
  │  TCP/IP                           │  ← Network transport
  └──────────────────────────────────┘

  KEY FACTS:
  • 15008 = HBONE tunnel port (memorize alongside 15001, 15006, 15020, 15021, 15090, 15443)
  • Uses HTTP/2 CONNECT method to create tunnel (like WebSocket-over-HTTP/2)
  • Encrypts via mTLS using SPIFFE identities (same as sidecar mode)
  • ztunnel terminates HBONE on both ends (source ztunnel → dest ztunnel)
  • No iptables needed — ztunnel captures via eBPF or policy routing
  • Waypoints speak HBONE too — same tunnel, extra L7 hop
  • Transparent to applications — no code changes, no sidecars
💡 Why HBONE Instead of iptables?

iptables requires per-pod rules, root privileges (NET_ADMIN), and init containers — the sidecar model. HBONE uses standard HTTP/2 tunneling between ztunnels on each node — no per-pod rules, no init containers, no root access to pod network namespace. This is what makes ambient mesh so much lighter (~18× for L4-only workloads, ~6× once a waypoint is added): one ztunnel per node handles all pods on that node via HBONE tunnels.

16.6 Sidecar vs Ambient — Decision Guide

There is no single "right" mode — decide per namespace using four questions: per-pod L7 needs, resource budget, upgrade blast radius, and maturity requirements. Both modes coexist inside one mesh, so mixed deployments are normal. Rule of thumb for anihpj: latency-critical public services that rely on canary weights and circuit breakers (jobpost-api, skills-service) → sidecar, or ambient + waypoint; internal low-traffic services that only need mTLS + identity allow/deny (notification-service, location-service) → ambient L4 only. When in doubt, start new namespaces in ambient L4 and add a waypoint the day you actually need L7 — it is a one-command, zero-restart upgrade.

⚖️ Decision Table — Choose the Data-Plane Mode per Namespace

QuestionSidecarAmbient
Per-pod L7 needs (VS, retries, CB, WASM/Lua, fault injection)Full L7 in every pod including per-pod EnvoyFilter/WASM customizationL7 only where a waypoint exists; no EnvoyFilter or WASM per pod
Resource budget~128Mi × every pod (7 anihpj svcs ≈ 900Mi just for mesh)~50Mi per node + ~100Mi/waypoint (≈6× cheaper)
Upgrade blast radiusProxy upgrade means restarting EVERY injected podztunnel upgraded per node — app pods never move
Current maturityBattle-tested for years; every Istio feature supportedGA since 1.24 — newer, a few features lag

          │
      ┌───┴───┐

      │        └──▶ Q1b  Need mTLS + basic L4 identity

      │                        │
