17.8 Production Best Practices Reference

These are the distilled operating rules from official Istio production guidance — defaults you adopt BEFORE the first incident. Most production Istio outages trace back to one of these being skipped: an in-place upgrade, no PDB, missing timeouts. Three cards — Deployment, Traffic, Security — treat each line as a policy for the anihpj mesh, not a suggestion.

Deployment
  • ✅ Revisioned (canary) control planes for EVERY upgrade
  • ✅ 3 istiod replicas + PodDisruptionBudget minAvailable: 2
  • ✅ Resource limits on istiod: ~2Gi RAM / 2 CPU per replica
  • ✅ holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts: true — the app never races its own sidecar at startup
  • ❌ NEVER run an in-place istioctl upgrade in production
Traffic
  • ✅ Every VirtualService carries retries (with a sane retryOn)
  • ✅ Timeouts SHORTER than the app's own timeouts — fail fast
  • ✅ Circuit breaker (outlierDetection) on every upstream DR
  • ✅ Header-based canary routing for testing, weights for rollout
  • ✅ istioctl analyze before every apply — a CI gate, not a habit
Security
  • ✅ STRICT mTLS via PeerAuthentication in every prod namespace
  • ✅ AuthorizationPolicy: default deny-all, then explicit ALLOWs
  • ✅ Plan root CA rotation BEFORE expiry — never discover it
  • ✅ Separate namespaces per team / trust boundary
  • ✅ Lock egress: outboundTrafficPolicy REGISTRY_ONLY + explicit ServiceEntry per external API

17.9 Troubleshooting Configuration — The ICA Exam Topic

"Configuration troubleshooting" on the exam almost always means a VirtualService / DestinationRule / Gateway / AuthorizationPolicy that is syntactically VALID YAML but semantically WRONG — a bad selector, a missing subset, a host that doesn't match anything real. This is the single most common ICA task pattern — "the YAML applied cleanly but traffic isn't doing what it says" — it's a config-reading skill, not a deep networking-debugging skill.

The golden rule: run istioctl analyze BEFORE looking at a single log line — it catches roughly 80% of these errors by statically cross-checking every CRD against the others. analyze loads every Istio CRD in the namespace (or cluster) and re-runs istiod's own semantic checks against them — dangling subset references, hosts with no backing Service, gateways nothing selects, and more.

🩺 CONFIG TROUBLESHOOTING — Symptom to Fix

Symptomanalyze saysCheck this CRDFix
VS never matches — traffic stays 100% on the old versionUsually 0 issues (analyze checks syntax, not intent)VirtualService hosts + http.match/route rulesFix match rules / route weights; re-run analyze
DR subset mismatch — 503, no healthy upstream for the subsetError: referenced subset not foundDestinationRule subsets vs the Pod's actual labelsMake subset labels match Pod labels exactly
Gateway host mismatch — 404 straight from the ingress gatewayWarning: no matching workload / host for Gateway selectorGateway hosts+selector AND VS gateways: fieldAlign Gateway hosts to the VS hosts + gateways: entry
AuthorizationPolicy blocks traffic unexpectedly — 403 RBAC deny0 issues (analyze does not evaluate authz intent)AuthorizationPolicy selector + rules.from/toFix selector scope; add the missing explicit ALLOW rule
🔬 istioctl analyze — How It Catches 80% of Configuration Errors
$ istioctl analyze -n anihpj

WHAT IT CHECKS (6 key validation rules):
  CHECK                            │ EXAMPLE ERROR MESSAGE
  ──────────────────────────────── │ ────────────────────────────────────
  VirtualService destinations      │ "Destination host 'xyz' not found in
  exist in service registry        │  service registry"
                                    │
  DestinationRule subset labels    │ "No pods match subset 'v2' labels:
  match actual pods                │  version=v2"
                                    │
  Gateway selector matches pods    │ "Gateway selector did not match any
                                    │  pod: istio=ingressgateway"
                                    │
  Port name protocol prefix        │ "Port name 'myport' missing protocol
  (http-/grpc-/tcp-)                │  prefix — treated as TCP"
                                    │
  PeerAuthentication consistency   │ "Conflicting mTLS modes: namespace
  across mesh                      │  STRICT vs mesh PERMISSIVE"
                                    │
  AuthorizationPolicy syntax       │ "Invalid principal format — must use
                                    │  spiffe:// prefix"

ICA EXAM TIP: Run istioctl analyze FIRST — before proxy-status or
proxy-config. It catches 80% of errors with zero packet inspection.

→ install-time config issues (webhook, injection, pending pods): full depth in 4.9
→ mTLS / authorization config issues (DR×PA TLS contract, RBAC deny): full depth in 12.7

17.10 Troubleshooting the Mesh Control Plane — The ICA Exam Topic

A control-plane problem means istiod ITSELF is unhealthy, unreachable, or has stopped pushing config (an xDS problem) — it is NOT one app or one Envoy acting up; it's the brain of the mesh. Control-plane incidents are rarer than data-plane ones but far more severe — one broken istiod can freeze config delivery to every proxy in every namespace at once. istiod watches the Kubernetes API (CRDs, Services, Endpoints), computes each proxy's config, and pushes it over xDS on :15012 — if any of those three legs (watch, compute, push) breaks, the symptoms show up mesh-wide, not on one pod.

📖 KEY TERM — xDS

The family of gRPC discovery APIs (CDS/LDS/RDS/EDS) istiod uses to push config to every Envoy — the 'x' is a wildcard for Cluster/Listener/Route/Endpoint; all four ride the same stream on :15012.

🧯 CONTROL PLANE SYMPTOMS — Check, Fix

SymptomCheck commandFix
istiod pod CrashLoopBackOff / OOMKilledkubectl describe pod -n istio-system -l app=istiod; kubectl top pod -n istio-systemRaise istiod memory/CPU limits; check for a config-churn storm (too many VS/DR objects)
istiod unreachable — proxy-status shows STALE / NOT SENT for MANY proxies at onceistioctl proxy-status; kubectl get pods -n istio-systemRestore istiod (scale up / fix crash loop); proxies self-heal once it is reachable
Webhook timeout during pod creation — new pods stuck, no sidecar injectedkubectl describe pod <new-pod> -n anihpj, read the Events sectionConfirm istiod:15017 reachable from the API server; re-run istioctl x precheck
xDS push failures in istiod logs (pilot_total_xds_rejects climbing)kubectl logs -l app=istiod -n istio-system | grep -i rejectFind + fix the rejected config object (bad CRD field), then re-apply
🧭 CONTROL PLANE vs DATA PLANE — Which Is It?
THE CORE DIAGNOSTIC INSTINCT:

Symptom affects MANY services / namespaces at once
→ CONTROL PLANE problem (istiod itself)
   e.g. every proxy goes STALE together, every new pod
   fails injection, config stops propagating mesh-wide

Symptom affects ONE service / ONE pod, rest is fine
→ DATA PLANE problem (that pod's Envoy, or ztunnel in
   ambient mode)
   e.g. only jobpost-api returns 503s while every other
   anihpj service stays healthy

QUICK TEST: istioctl proxy-status — MANY rows STALE /
NOT SENT together = suspect istiod; ONE odd row = that
pod's data plane

→ istiod internals (what actually runs inside the pod): 3.2
→ istiod HA architecture (replicas, PDB, zone spread): 17.3
→ control-plane metrics to watch (pilot_*, citadel_*): 9.7

17.11 Troubleshooting the Mesh Data Plane — The ICA Exam Topic

A data-plane problem means ONE specific Envoy sidecar (or ztunnel, in ambient mode) is misbehaving — wrong routing, dropped connections, a missing sidecar, a cert problem on ONE pod — even though istiod and the rest of the mesh are completely healthy. This is where most day-to-day tickets live — "jobpost-api is throwing 503s" is almost always a data-plane question, answered by reading that ONE proxy's live config. Every istioctl proxy-config command reads what is ACTUALLY loaded in that pod's Envoy right now — proxy-status SYNCED only proves istiod pushed something, not that the pushed config is the config you intended.

🩻 DATA PLANE SYMPTOMS — Check, Fix

SymptomCheck commandFix
Pod stuck 1/1 — no sidecar was ever injectedkubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels; kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath (container names)Label namespace istio-injection=enabled (or istio.io/rev=<rev>); rollout restart
istio-proxy CrashLoopBackOffkubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy -n anihpjRead the crash reason (bad config, cert error); fix the cause, then delete pod to force re-inject
proxy-status says SYNCED but traffic is still wrongistioctl proxy-config route/cluster/endpoint deploy/<name> -n anihpj (the LIVE config, not just the sync flag)SYNCED only means istiod pushed something; verify the pushed rules are the ones you intended
Connection reset (not a clean HTTP error)istioctl x describe pod <pod> -n anihpj; check DR tls.mode vs PeerAuthentication modeAlign client DR tls.mode with server PA mode (or drop the tls block for auto mTLS)
503, response flag UH or UFistioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/<name> -n anihpj — any healthy pod IPs at all?UH: no healthy endpoint (check the actual pod/Service); UF: upstream refused the connection
🔧 Under the Hood — Auto mTLS and the Connection-Reset Symptom

"Auto mTLS" means Istio decides FOR you: a client Envoy checks whether the destination's endpoints advertise a sidecar, and if so upgrades the call to mutual TLS automatically — no tls: block in the DestinationRule required at all. An explicit tls.mode only exists to OVERRIDE that default, which is exactly how a mismatched override becomes the connection-reset symptom above.

⬇️ BOTTOM-UP ENVOY DEBUG ORDER — Fastest Route to Root Cause
Always debug bottom-up — the deepest layer explains the
most common failures fastest (EDS before CDS before RDS
before LDS):

1. EDS (endpoints)  — healthy pod IPs behind the cluster?
2. CDS (clusters)   — does the target cluster exist?
3. RDS (routes)     — is your VirtualService rule present?
4. LDS (listeners)  — is Envoy listening on the right port?

istioctl proxy-config endpoint|cluster|route|listener \
  deploy/<name> -n anihpj      (one command per layer)

→ sidecar debugging checklist (six repeat symptoms): 3.7
→ Envoy config hierarchy in depth (LDS/RDS/CDS/EDS): 3.8
→ the full modern command reference sheet: 17.6

17.12 istioctl bug-report — Collecting a Full Diagnostic Bundle

istioctl bug-report packages cluster-wide Istio diagnostics — istiod and Envoy sidecar logs, Envoy config dumps, and the mesh's Istio CRDs — into one downloadable archive, built for handing an incident to a teammate or an Istio support case without a live cluster walkthrough. Section 17.7's Emergency Diagnostic Checklist is 8 manual commands run by hand during an outage; bug-report captures the equivalent evidence in ONE command, which matters most when the person debugging tomorrow wasn't the person paged tonight. It auto-discovers every istio-system pod and every injected workload pod, pulls each container's CURRENT and PREVIOUS logs, an Envoy config_dump per proxy, and the live Istio CRDs (VirtualService, DestinationRule, Gateway, PeerAuthentication, AuthorizationPolicy), then writes it all to a single .tar.gz.

bash — istioctl bug-report: One Command, the Whole Incident 

# Full diagnostic bundle (default: bug-report.tar.gz)
istioctl bug-report

# Scope to one namespace only (large mesh = smaller archive)
istioctl bug-report --include anihpj

# Custom output directory for the finished archive
istioctl bug-report --output-dir /tmp/anihpj-incident-42

# Cap log volume per container (default can be huge)
istioctl bug-report --tail 500 --duration 1h

📦 What's Inside the Archive

Inside the archiveSource
istio-system logsistiod + istio-proxy logs, current + previous
Envoy config dumpsOne dump per injected pod, no manual loop
Cluster resourcesIstio CRDs (VS/DR/GW/PA/AuthzPolicy), Deploys
Cluster infoK8s version, nodes, istiod Deployment/Pod YAML
🎯 ICA Exam Note

bug-report sits in the exam's Diagnostic Tools surface — know WHAT it collects and WHY (a portable, complete evidence snapshot), even on a task that doesn't literally run it.

→ the 8-step manual version of this same evidence: 17.7

17.13 istioctl x precheck — Pre-Upgrade Compatibility Checks

istioctl x precheck is a READ-ONLY scan that runs BEFORE any upgrade — canary or in-place — and reports whether the live cluster is safe to move to the target Istio version: Kubernetes version support, deprecated Istio API fields, and other known upgrade risks. A canary upgrade means standing up a whole second control plane (17.1); precheck catches "this will break" for the price of one read-only command, before that effort is spent. Run precheck with the istioctl BINARY that matches the TARGET version (the new one about to be installed) — it evaluates the current cluster and Istio config against that version's compatibility checks and prints a pass/warn/fail result per check.

🔍 What Precheck Catches

Check categoryWhat it catches
K8s version supportTarget version incompatible with this K8s
Deprecated API fieldsIstio CRD fields removed since your build
Existing CRD validityLive CRs that fail the new version's schema
Injection webhook stateStale webhooks left over from a prior install
🚦 Precheck in the Upgrade Sequence — Run BEFORE Either Path
STEP 0  istioctl x precheck                (run with the NEW
        istioctl binary -- the one matching the upgrade target)
         -> any FAIL/WARN names the exact deprecated field or
            K8s incompatibility; fix it BEFORE step 1

STEP 1  istioctl install --set revision=1-23 -y      (canary)
        istioctl upgrade -y                          (in-place)

STEP 2  onward = the SAME canary/in-place flow as 17.1

→ full canary/in-place mechanics after this step: 17.1

17.14 Revision Tags — Stable Aliases for Canary Control-Plane Upgrades

A revision TAG (istioctl tag set) is a stable, human-readable alias — e.g. prod-stable — that POINTS AT a real revision (e.g. 1-23); namespaces label onto the TAG name instead of the raw revision, so promoting a canary to become the new default is ONE command instead of relabeling every namespace in the mesh. 17.1's canary flow relabels anihpj directly to istio.io/rev=1-23 — fine for one namespace, but at real scale (dozens of namespaces across teams) tags remove the need to touch every namespace's label twice per upgrade (once onto the canary, once to promote it); istio.io's own canary-upgrade guidance recommends tags over raw revision labels for exactly this reason. istioctl tag set points a mutating webhook configuration at a target revision; any workload that references istio.io/rev=<tag-name> resolves to whichever revision the tag CURRENTLY points at, at injection time — existing running pods never move until restarted, exactly like a raw revision label.

🏷️ Revision Tag Promotion — Relabel the TAG, Never the Namespace
BEFORE promotion:
  istioctl tag set prod-stable --revision 1-22
  kubectl label ns anihpj istio-injection- istio.io/rev=prod-stable
  -> anihpj pods run on istiod REVISION 1-22 (via the tag)

AFTER promotion (namespace label is NEVER touched again):
  istioctl tag set prod-stable --revision 1-23 --overwrite
  kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj
  -> SAME istio.io/rev=prod-stable label now resolves to 1-23

istioctl tag list           # show every tag -> revision mapping
istioctl tag remove prod-canary   # cleanup after burn-in ends

The special tag name "default" (istioctl tag set default --revision 1-23) is what injects any pod with NO istio.io/rev label at all, and covers mesh-wide singleton resources — every mesh always resolves through some tag or revision named "default" unless every namespace is explicitly labeled.

🎯 ICA Exam Note

"Upgrading Istio (Canary, In-Place)" is a named exam subtopic (17.1) — tags are the production-grade refinement of the same canary mechanic, not a separate concept.

→ raw-revision canary steps this replaces: 17.1

17.15 istiod Autoscaling and Resource Requests/Limits for Production HA

Production istiod sizing has TWO separate levers: an autoscaling FLOOR/CEILING (values.pilot.autoscaleMin/Max, an Istio-managed HorizontalPodAutoscaler) and per-pod resource requests/limits (the CPU/memory each istiod pod is guaranteed vs. capped at). Section 17.3 already covers WHY 3 replicas + a PodDisruptionBudget matter for HA; this section is the two knobs an exam TASK actually asks you to SET, and the reason autoscaleMin (not a flat kubectl scale) is the production-correct way to guarantee the floor. autoscaleMin is the replica count the HPA will never scale below — production should set it ≥ 2 (never 1), because a single istiod replica is a single point of failure for the sidecar-injection mutating webhook, which uses failurePolicy: Fail and rejects EVERY pod creation cluster-wide while istiod is down; autoscaleMax caps growth under config-churn or connection-count spikes; resources.requests/limits set the CPU/memory Kubernetes schedules against (requests) and throttles/OOM-kills against (limits).

📐 istiod Production Sizing — The Fields an Exam TASK Sets

IstioOperator fieldControlsanihpj prod
values.pilot.autoscaleMinHPA floor — replicas never drop below this, even idle3
values.pilot.autoscaleMaxHPA ceiling under config / connection load spikes5
values.pilot.resources.requests.cpu/memoryCPU/mem GUARANTEED to each istiod pod500m/512Mi
values.pilot.resources.limits.cpu/memoryCPU/mem CAP before throttle / OOM-kill2000m/2Gi
bash — Set It at Install Time: Declarative, Survives the Next Upgrade 

istioctl install -y \
  --set values.pilot.autoscaleMin=3 \
  --set values.pilot.autoscaleMax=5 \
  --set values.pilot.resources.requests.cpu=500m \
  --set values.pilot.resources.requests.memory=512Mi \
  --set values.pilot.resources.limits.cpu=2000m \
  --set values.pilot.resources.limits.memory=2Gi

kubectl get hpa istiod -n istio-system
  # -> MINPODS 3  MAXPODS 5  REPLICAS scales inside that range
⚠️ Manual Scale vs. Declarative Autoscaling

This differs from 17.3's kubectl scale deployment istiod --replicas=3 in one important way — a manual kubectl scale is NOT persisted in the IstioOperator spec, so the NEXT istioctl install/upgrade re-apply silently resets it back to whatever the base profile says; autoscaleMin/Max IS part of the declarative install config and survives every future upgrade.

→ HA architecture, PDB, zone spread: 17.3
→ sidecar-side resource sizing at scale: 17.2

🔧 Under the Hood — The Three-Way Split, Live: One anihpj Incident Through Configuration, Control Plane, and Data Plane

17.7 already gave you the 8-step Emergency Diagnostic Checklist and the 5-step Golden Debug Sequence. This closing walkthrough does not repeat either — it takes the SAME reflex and runs it, decision by decision, against one concrete anihpj incident, showing exactly where the Configuration / Control Plane / Data Plane question (17.9-17.11) gets asked and answered in the middle of real work.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 🔧 UNDER THE HOOD — ONE anihpj INCIDENT, THE WHOLE GUIDE'S REFLEX   │

│ SCENARIO: Friday 4:58pm — skills-service-v2 goes live behind a      │

│ error rate climbing past 4%, all on calls needing a skill lookup.   │

│         → every proxy SYNCED, including skills-service-v2 —         │

│ STEP 3  ASK: Config, Control Plane, or Data Plane?                  │
│         → only calls that hit skills-service-v2 fail; calls         │
│           to user-service and location-service are fine — ONE       │
│           service, not many — so it's Configuration or Data         │
│           Plane (17.9 vs 17.11), never Control Plane.               │
│ STEP 4  istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj  │
│         istioctl proxy-config endpoint deploy/jobpost-api -n anihpj │
│         → the "v2" subset cluster shows ZERO healthy endpoints      │
│           — no pod IPs behind it at all.                            │
│ STEP 5  ROOT CAUSE: skills-service-v2 Pods carry label              │
│         version: v2-canary; the DestinationRule subset still        │
│         selects version: v2 (the Ch7 subset gotcha, triggered by    │
│         Ch14's canary rollout) — analyze missed it because the      │
│         DR and the Deployment are each independently valid YAML.    │
│ STEP 6  FIX: relabel the Pods (or fix the DR subset selector) so    │
│         they match, re-run analyze + proxy-status, and confirm a    │
│         green, healthy v2 node in Kiali.                            │
│                                                                     │
│ THE INSIGHT: no single Envoy misbehaved (that would be Data         │
│ Plane, 17.11) and istiod pushed everything it was told to push      │
│ (that rules out Control Plane, 17.10) — the ROUTING TARGET          │
│ simply didn't exist. That is Configuration (17.9) end to end.       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔑 ICA Insight: Every anihpj incident in this guide reduces to the same three-way question — Configuration, Control Plane, or Data Plane — and istioctl proxy-status is the single command that splits the search space in half: SYNCED everywhere rules out Control Plane; ONE service failing while the rest of the mesh is healthy rules out Data Plane being mesh-wide and points you at Configuration or one pod's Envoy. istioctl analyze catches syntax, never intent — a subset mismatch created by a routine canary rollout (Ch14) is exactly the kind of "independently valid YAML" error it cannot see, which is why the three-way split, not any single command, is the reflex worth keeping after this guide ends.

🔑 Key Takeaways

  • Canary upgrade (old + new istiod side by side) is production-safe; in-place (istioctl upgrade) is not — a bad canary build only ever reaches namespaces deliberately migrated to it, while in-place is an all-or-nothing rolling update of the ONLY control plane.
  • istiod going down does not take the data plane with it — existing Envoy proxies keep serving on their last cached config; only NEW pods (no sidecar can be injected) and NEW config changes (nothing propagates) are affected.
  • ~128Mi RAM + ~100m CPU per sidecar is the sizing rule of thumb — istiod itself scales from 500m/512Mi under 100 proxies up to horizontal scaling past 2000.
  • istioctl analyze is always step 1, and it catches syntax, never intent — a DestinationRule subset and a Deployment can each be independently valid YAML while still referencing each other incorrectly; analyze cannot see that gap.
  • Every anihpj incident reduces to one three-way question — Configuration (17.9), Control Plane (17.10), or Data Plane (17.11) — and istioctl proxy-status is the single command that splits the search space: SYNCED everywhere rules out Control Plane; ONE service failing rules out Data Plane being mesh-wide.
  • A 403 is never mTLS — mTLS failures reset the TCP connection; only an AuthorizationPolicy returns an HTTP 403. Reach for the right tool based on which symptom you actually see.
  • istioctl x precheck runs BEFORE either upgrade path, with the istioctl binary matching the TARGET version — it's a free, read-only way to catch deprecated fields before standing up a whole second control plane.
  • Revision tags (istioctl tag set) turn a canary promotion into ONE command instead of relabeling every namespace twice — namespaces label onto the stable tag name, and re-pointing the tag IS the promotion.
⚠️ Common Gotchas & Misconceptions
  • "istioctl upgrade is fine for production since it's a named exam command." Being exam-testable and being production-safe are different claims — istioctl upgrade replaces the ONLY control plane in place; canary (a second, parallel control plane) is the production-safe mechanic.
  • "If istiod dies, the whole mesh goes down immediately." No — existing proxies keep serving real traffic on cached config. What breaks is NEW pods (no injection) and NEW config pushes, not traffic already flowing.
  • "istioctl analyze passing means the config is correct." No — it validates syntax and cross-CRD references, never INTENT. A subset selector that simply doesn't match any real pod label is exactly the kind of "independently valid YAML" error it cannot catch.
  • "A manual kubectl scale deployment istiod --replicas=3 is a permanent HA fix." No — it's not persisted in the IstioOperator spec, so the next istioctl install/upgrade silently resets it. Use values.pilot.autoscaleMin for a setting that survives upgrades.
  • "A 403 error means mTLS is misconfigured." No — mTLS failures reset the TCP connection outright; a 403 specifically means an AuthorizationPolicy evaluated and denied the request.
  • "proxy-status showing SYNCED means the traffic behavior is correct." No — SYNCED only proves istiod pushed SOME config to that Envoy; it says nothing about whether the pushed rules are the ones you intended. Read the actual config with proxy-config to confirm.
  • "Revision tags are a separate concept from canary upgrades." No — tags are the production-grade refinement of the exact same canary mechanic from 17.1, not a different upgrade strategy.

💼 Chapter 17 — Daily Work Takeaways (Production Operations)

  • Run 3 istiod replicas for HA with a PDB (minAvailable: 2)
  • Know that existing proxies keep working even if istiod goes down — only new pods and config changes are affected
  • Execute a canary upgrade of Istio itself (old+new istiod in parallel), never an in-place istioctl upgrade in production
  • Size Istio for your cluster: sidecars cost ~128Mi each — plan the total, not just the app's own RAM
  • Tune tracing sampling: 1% in prod (100% = expensive)
  • Troubleshoot in order: istioctl analyze → proxy-status → proxy-config → Envoy logs → dashboards
  • Know the top Istio problems: missing sidecar, mTLS mismatch, VirtualService subsets not matching pod labels
  • Use the production checklist before go-live — pods 2/2, SYNCED, 0 errors, STRICT mTLS, HA, alerts
  • Read Grafana alerts: error rate, p99 latency, circuit breaker status
  • Sleep better: circuit breakers isolate failures, mTLS encrypts everything, retries absorb transient errors — your system heals itself
🎯 ICA Exam Tips — Chapter 17 (Troubleshooting — 20%)

Troubleshooting instinct is tested inside every other domain too, not just this chapter:

  • "Why isn't my VirtualService routing?" = Check DestinationRule subsets match pod labels. Run istioctl analyze -n <namespace>
  • "Why is mTLS failing?" = istioctl x describe pod <pod> — shows the pod's effective mTLS mode (the old istioctl authn tls-check was removed)
  • "Why isn't the sidecar injected?" = Check namespace label: kubectl get namespace <ns> --show-labels
  • "How to upgrade Istio?" = Canary upgrade: run old+new istiod simultaneously, migrate namespaces one by one

🧠 Chapter 17 — Lab Q&A · Concept Check (10)

Quick recall of the mental model — 10 questions, each with a full answer & explanation.

Q1
Name the two Istio upgrade mechanics the ICA exam names, and which one is production-safe.
Show Answer
Answer

Canary (istioctl install --set revision=X, old + new istiod side by side) and in-place (istioctl upgrade, replaces the one istiod). Canary is production-safe; in-place is exam-testable but production-risky.

Explanation

The blast radius is the whole story: a bad canary build only ever reaches namespaces deliberately migrated to it, while in-place risk hits every namespace at once (17.1).

Q2
If istiod goes down completely, does traffic between existing anihpj pods stop?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Existing Envoy sidecars keep serving traffic using their last cached config (routing, mTLS, retries all intact). What breaks is new pod injection and new config propagation.

Explanation

This decoupling of data plane from control plane is exactly why control-plane incidents, while rare, are dangerous mainly for what they PREVENT going forward, not what they immediately break (17.3, 17.10).

Q3
Roughly how much RAM and CPU does one Istio sidecar cost?
Show Answer
Answer

~128Mi RAM and ~100m CPU per sidecar proxy.

Explanation

This is the chapter's golden sizing rule — always add this on top of the app's OWN resource requests, never in place of them (17.2).

Q4
What does istioctl analyze actually check, and what can it never catch?
Show Answer
Answer

It statically cross-checks every Istio CRD against the others — dangling subset references, hosts with no backing Service, Gateways nothing selects, port-name protocol prefixes, and more. It can NEVER catch a semantically wrong-but-syntactically-valid config, like a DestinationRule subset selector that just doesn't match any real pod's labels.

Explanation

"Catches syntax, never intent" is the single most important line to remember about analyze for the exam (17.9).

Q5
A symptom is hitting MANY anihpj services and namespaces at once. Is this Control Plane or Data Plane?
Show Answer
Answer

Control Plane. A symptom affecting many services/namespaces simultaneously points at istiod itself; a symptom confined to ONE service/pod points at that pod's own Envoy (Data Plane).

Explanation

istioctl proxy-status is the one command that tests this directly — many STALE/NOT SENT rows together means istiod, one odd row means that pod (17.10).

Q6
True or false: a 403 error between two anihpj services always means mTLS is broken.
Show Answer
Answer

False. mTLS failures reset the TCP connection outright — they never produce an HTTP 403. A 403 specifically means an AuthorizationPolicy evaluated the request and denied it.

Explanation

This distinction alone resolves a large share of real "why am I getting 403s" tickets — check AuthorizationPolicy, not PeerAuthentication (17.9, 17.11, Speed Tips).

Q7
What does istioctl x precheck do, and when should you run it?
Show Answer
Answer

A read-only scan for Kubernetes-version compatibility and deprecated Istio API fields, run with the istioctl BINARY matching the TARGET version, BEFORE starting either upgrade path (canary or in-place).

Explanation

It catches "this will break" for the cost of one command, before you've spent the effort of standing up a whole second control plane (17.13).

Q8
What's the difference between a raw revision label and a revision TAG?
Show Answer
Answer

A raw revision label (istio.io/rev=1-23) points a namespace directly at one specific istiod revision. A TAG (istio.io/rev=prod-stable) is a stable alias that POINTS AT a revision — namespaces label onto the tag name once, and promoting a canary is just re-pointing the tag, not relabeling every namespace again.

Explanation

At real scale (dozens of namespaces), tags remove the need to touch every namespace's label twice per upgrade (17.14).

Q9
What's the ONE field that must be ≥ 2 for production istiod sizing, and why?
Show Answer
Answer

values.pilot.autoscaleMin. A single istiod replica is a single point of failure for the sidecar-injection mutating webhook, which uses failurePolicy: Fail and rejects EVERY pod creation cluster-wide while istiod is down.

Explanation

autoscaleMin (not a manual kubectl scale) is the production-correct way to guarantee this floor, because it's part of the declarative install config and survives future upgrades (17.15).

Q10
What is the Golden Debug Sequence, in order?
Show Answer
Answer

1. istioctl analyze (YAML valid? ~80% caught here). 2. istioctl proxy-status (config pushed to every Envoy?). 3. istioctl proxy-config (what is REALLY inside Envoy?). 4. kubectl logs -c istio-proxy (what errors does Envoy see?). 5. Kiali/Grafana (visual confirmation of the fix).

Explanation

The golden rule is cheapest layer first, every time — analyze is free and read-only, so it always runs before any deep debugging (17.7).

⚙️ Chapter 17 — Scenario & Command Drills (10)

Exam-style and hands-on — 10 drills that mirror how the ICA actually asks: a scenario, and you produce the fix with real commands.

Q1
What is the FIRST command you should run when Istio isn't working?
Show Answer
Answer

istioctl analyze -n <namespace> — catches 80% of configuration errors.

Explanation

istioctl analyze is always step 1 in the Golden Debug Sequence (17.6-17.7) — it's read-only, free, and clears ~80% of false leads before a single log line.

Q2
How do you check if a specific pod has a valid mTLS configuration?
Show Answer
Answer

istioctl x describe pod <pod-name> -n <namespace> — shows the pod's effective mTLS mode. (The old istioctl authn tls-check was removed.)

Explanation

istioctl x describe pod is the modern replacement, and additionally shows the effective VS/DR/PA in force, not just mTLS (17.6).

Q3
What's the safest way to upgrade Istio in production?
Show Answer
Answer

Canary upgrade — install the new istiod version alongside the old one (using revision labels), migrate namespaces one by one, then remove the old istiod when all namespaces are migrated.

Explanation

Canary is production-safe because a bad new build only ever reaches namespaces deliberately migrated to it; in-place (istioctl upgrade) has no such isolation (17.1).

Q4
TASK — upgrade the mesh from Istio 1.22 to 1.23 with zero downtime and prove the anihpj namespace now runs on the new control plane.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl install --set revision=1-23 -y
kubectl label ns anihpj istio-injection- istio.io/rev=1-23
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj
istioctl proxy-status | grep anihpj   # all SYNCED on 1.23
istioctl uninstall --revision=1-22 -y # only after ALL ns
Explanation

Both istiods run in parallel, so live traffic never loses its control plane; each namespace migrates on its own schedule (17.1).

Q5
TASK — make istiod highly available so a node drain can never drop the control plane below two replicas.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl scale deployment istiod -n istio-system --replicas=3
kubectl create pdb istiod-pdb -n istio-system \
  --selector=app=istiod --min-available=2
Explanation

The PDB blocks voluntary evictions (drains, node upgrades) from dropping istiod below 2; spread replicas across zones (17.3).

Q6
TASK — capacity-plan a 50-pod production cluster: how much extra RAM and CPU does adding Istio sidecars cost?
Show Answer
Answer

Sidecars: 50 × 128Mi ≈ 6.4Gi RAM and 50 × 100m = 5 CPU cores; add istiod (2 replicas at 1c/4Gi) → budget ≈ 8Gi RAM / ~6 CPU.

Explanation

~128Mi + 100m per sidecar is the planning rule of thumb, and pod requests must cover app needs PLUS sidecar overhead (17.2).

Q7
SCENARIO — istioctl proxy-status shows jobpost-api as STALE while every other proxy is SYNCED. Diagnose and fix it.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl logs -l app=istiod -n istio-system --tail=100 \
  | grep -i -e error -e push
kubectl logs <jobpost-api-pod> -c istio-proxy -n anihpj \
  | grep -i -e xds -e error
Explanation

STALE means istiod failed to push the latest config to that Envoy — look for xDS push errors (istiod overloaded / OOM) or the proxy losing its :15012 stream; scale istiod or restart the pod so it reconnects and resyncs (17.7, 17.10).

Q8
TASK — add a CI gate so a broken VirtualService can never merge.
Show Answer
Answer
istioctl analyze -f istio/ --use-kube=false  # pure lint
istioctl analyze -f istio/ -n staging        # vs staging
# non-zero exit code → pipeline fails → PR is blocked
Explanation

analyze exits non-zero on errors, so the pipeline fails the PR before broken config ever reaches the cluster (17.5).

Q9
SCENARIO — after migrating anihpj to revision 1-23, the error rate jumps from 2.1% to 8%. Roll back NOW.
Show Answer
Answer
kubectl label ns anihpj istio.io/rev=1-22 --overwrite
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n anihpj
Explanation

The old istiod is still running (never uninstall it until burn-in ends), so rollback is a relabel + restart — minutes, no reinstall (17.1).

Q10
SCENARIO — all 3 istiod replicas crash at once. What breaks for anihpj, and what keeps working?
Show Answer
Answer

Keeps working: ALL existing traffic — every Envoy keeps serving with its last cached config (routing, mTLS, retries intact). Breaks: new pods start without sidecars, config changes stop propagating, and workload cert rotation halts (certs expire in ~24h, so recovery is urgent but not an instant outage).

Explanation

The control plane and data plane are decoupled by design (17.3, 17.10).

⚡ Speed Tips — Chapter 17
  • In ANY incident, run istioctl analyze -A first — it's free, read-only, and clears ~80% of false leads before you touch a log.
  • Check istioctl proxy-status before istioctl proxy-config — one glance tells you to hunt mesh-wide (Control Plane) or on one pod (Data Plane / Configuration).
  • A 403 is NEVER mTLS. mTLS failures reset the TCP connection; only an AuthorizationPolicy returns an HTTP 403 (17.9 / 17.11).
  • Rolling back a canary upgrade is a relabel, not a reinstall — kubectl label ns ... istio.io/rev=<old> plus a rollout restart, minutes not hours (17.1, Q9).
  • Never skip istioctl x precheck before an upgrade — one read-only command catches deprecated fields before you stand up a whole second control plane (17.13).
  • When in doubt between Control Plane and Data Plane, count the blast radius: many services down together means istiod; one service down alone means that pod's Envoy (17.10).

💻 Commands Cheat-Card (Chapter 17)

Chapter 17 is almost entirely commands, not YAML — this closing reference compresses the ones you reach for most, grouped by the job they do.

CommandWhat It Does / Checks in Chapter 17
UPGRADE & PRECHECK
istioctl x precheckRead-only pre-upgrade scan (17.13)
istioctl install --set revision=1-23 -yCanary: NEW istiod beside old (17.1)
istioctl upgrade -yIn-place: overwrite the ONE istiod (17.1)
kubectl label ns anihpj istio.io/rev=X --overwriteMigrate / roll back a namespace (17.1)

istioctl tag set prod-stable --revision 1-23Stable alias, promote w/o relabel (17.14)
DIAGNOSE — THE GOLDEN DEBUG SEQUENCE (17.7)

istioctl proxy-statusSTEP 2 — SYNCED/STALE, mesh-wide? (17.10)

kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy --tail=50STEP 4 — Envoy's own error log (17.7)

🔬 Practice Drill 17.1 — Break anihpj, Then Run the Reflex

⏱️ Target Time: 8 minutes
Scenario

On any live (or lab) anihpj mesh:

  1. Pick any live anihpj DestinationRule and deliberately break one subset selector (edit version: v2 to version: v2-typo) with kubectl apply.
  2. Run istioctl analyze -n anihpj — confirm it stays silent (0 issues). Write down WHY it doesn't catch this (17.9).
  3. Run istioctl proxy-status — confirm every proxy still shows SYNCED. Say out loud which layer this rules OUT.
  4. Run istioctl proxy-config cluster deploy/<affected-service> -n anihpj and find the subset with zero healthy endpoints.
  5. Revert the label, re-run analyze + proxy-status, and confirm Kiali shows a healthy green node again. Stop at 8 minutes.
Hint: If all five steps pass, you've independently reproduced the exact incident in this chapter's own Under the Hood walkthrough — and proven the three-way split (Configuration / Control Plane / Data Plane) by hand, not just by reading it.
View Solution

Step 2 should stay completely silent — analyze validates that the DestinationRule and Deployment are each independently valid YAML, never whether their labels actually agree with each other. Step 3 should show every proxy SYNCED, ruling OUT Control Plane (istiod is healthy and pushing fine). Step 4 should show the broken subset with 0 healthy endpoints — the Data Plane symptom that's really a Configuration root cause.

Check yourself: could you explain, out loud, WHY this is classified as Configuration (17.9) rather than Data Plane (17.11), even though the symptom shows up as "zero healthy endpoints" in a proxy-config dump? If your answer isn't "because no single Envoy is misbehaving — the routing TARGET itself doesn't exist," re-read the UTH's closing insight.

🔬 Practice Drill 17.2 — Run a Real Canary Upgrade End to End, Then Roll It Back

⏱️ Target Time: 12 minutes
Scenario

On a lab cluster (kind/minikube is fine), simulate a full canary upgrade cycle:

  1. Note the current istiod revision: istioctl version / kubectl get pods -n istio-system.
  2. Install a second istiod as a named revision: istioctl install --set revision=canary -y. Confirm BOTH control planes are Running.
  3. Label ONE test namespace onto the canary: kubectl label ns <test-ns> istio-injection- istio.io/rev=canary, then rollout-restart its deployments.
  4. istioctl proxy-status — confirm the test namespace's pods are SYNCED against the CANARY istiod specifically (not the default).
  5. Roll back: relabel the namespace back to the original revision, rollout-restart, and confirm it reconnects to the original istiod — time how long this takes.
Hint: Step 4 is easy to get wrong — "SYNCED" alone doesn't prove WHICH istiod a proxy is synced to; you have to check which revision's Service the pod's sidecar is actually configured to talk to.
View Solution

Step 2 should show two istiod Deployments running side by side with zero impact on existing traffic. Step 4 confirms isolation — only the labeled namespace's pods point at the canary control plane; everything else is untouched. Step 5's rollback should complete in minutes (relabel + restart), never requiring a reinstall.

Check yourself: if you'd made a mistake and labeled the WRONG namespace in step 3, would step 5's rollback still have been just as fast? If your answer isn't "yes, identical mechanism," you haven't fully internalized why canary is isolation-by-design, not just isolation-by-luck.

🔬 Practice Drill 17.3 — Diagnose 4 Symptoms Using Only the Golden Debug Sequence

⏱️ Target Time: 6 minutes
Scenario

For each symptom, name which of the 5 Golden Debug Sequence steps would surface the root cause FIRST — before proposing any fix:

  1. A brand-new VirtualService has a typo'd host that matches no real Service.
  2. Every proxy in the mesh shows STALE at the same moment.
  3. One specific pod returns 503s while every other pod serving the same Deployment is healthy.
  4. A DestinationRule subset selector doesn't match any live pod's labels.
Hint: Two of these four are caught by step 1 alone; the other two need you to go at least one layer deeper.
View Solution
#First step that surfaces itWhy
1Step 1 — istioctl analyzeA host matching no real Service IS a cross-CRD check analyze performs
2Step 2 — istioctl proxy-statusMesh-wide STALE is the textbook Control Plane signal, visible immediately
3Step 3 or 4 — proxy-config / logs on that ONE podOne-pod symptoms need per-pod Data Plane inspection, not a mesh-wide command
4Step 1 — istioctl analyze (sometimes) or Step 3 — proxy-config clusteranalyze catches THIS specific case (dangling subset), but a similar labels-just-don't-match case can slip through to proxy-config

🔬 Practice Drill 17.4 — Size a Real Cluster From Scratch, Then Check Your Math

⏱️ Target Time: 5 minutes
Scenario

Without looking at 17.2's table, size Istio's overhead for a cluster with 220 injected pods, 3 istiod replicas, and 2 Wasm filters running on every pod:

  1. Compute total sidecar RAM and CPU (include the Wasm filter overhead).
  2. Pick the correct istiod CPU/RAM tier from 17.2's sizing table for 220 proxies.
  3. State the ONE thing this total does NOT include, that you'd still need to budget for.
Hint: Step 3 is the trap most people skip on the real exam.
View Solution

Step 1: base sidecar = 220 × 128Mi ≈ 28.2Gi RAM, 220 × 100m = 22 CPU cores; 2 Wasm filters add 220 × 2 × 30Mi ≈ 13.2Gi more RAM. Step 2: 220 proxies falls in the 100-500 tier → 1 CPU / 1Gi PER istiod replica × 3 replicas = 3 CPU / 3Gi. Step 3: none of this includes the APPLICATION's own RAM/CPU requests — sidecar overhead is always ON TOP of app resource needs, never instead of them.

Check yourself: did you remember the Wasm filter overhead in step 1, or only the base ~128Mi? Forgetting per-filter overhead is exactly the kind of undercount that causes a real production capacity review to run short.

🔬 Practice Drill 17.5 — Sketch the Three-Way Triage From Memory

⏱️ Target Time: 4 minutes
Scenario

Without looking at 17.9-17.11 or the UTH, write from memory: (a) the ONE command that splits Configuration/Data-Plane from Control-Plane, (b) what result rules OUT Control Plane, and (c) what result rules IN a Data-Plane (not Configuration) explanation specifically.

Hint: Part (c) is the one people get wrong — Configuration and Data Plane can look IDENTICAL from proxy-status alone; you need a second signal to tell them apart.
View Solution

(a) istioctl proxy-status. (b) Every proxy SYNCED rules out Control Plane — istiod is healthy and pushing config to everyone. (c) Ruling IN Data Plane (over Configuration) needs a SECOND signal beyond proxy-status: if proxy-config shows the live config is actually correct but the pod still misbehaves (crash, cert error, wrong listener), that's Data Plane; if the live config itself is what's wrong (a subset that matches nothing), that's Configuration — proxy-status alone cannot distinguish the two, since both can show SYNCED.

Check yourself: could you explain why "SYNCED" is necessary but not sufficient to distinguish Configuration from Data Plane? If not, re-read 17.9's and 17.11's opening definitions side by side.

Chapter 17's entire argument, read top to bottom: a production mesh stays healthy not because it never breaks, but because every break routes through the same four moves — upgrade and size it safely, know the tools cold, hold it to a written standard, and diagnose it with one three-way question instead of a guess. The skills-service-v2 incident in this chapter's Under the Hood is not a special case; it is what 17.9's Configuration category looks like on a real Friday, solved with the exact commands in this chapter's cheat-card. This closes the main chapter content of the guide — everything from here on is Appendix reference material: CRD tables, full YAML manifests, and command indexes for anihpj's mesh, not new concepts.

Quick recap — 🔄 Upgrade: canary (old+new istiod parallel) beats in-place, always (17.1) · 📊 Size: ~128Mi/100m per sidecar, istiod scales with proxy count (17.2) · 🏗️ HA: 3 replicas + PDB(minAvailable=2), cached config survives istiod loss (17.3) · 🩺 Debug: analyze → proxy-status → proxy-config → logs → dashboards, cheapest layer first (17.4, 17.6-17.7) · 🔄 CI/CD: analyze as a merge-blocking gate (17.5) · ✅ Best Practices: Deployment / Traffic / Security, three cards, not suggestions (17.8) · 🧭 Triage: Configuration vs Control Plane vs Data Plane — the exam's own three-way split (17.9-17.11) · 🎒 Advanced ops: bug-report, x precheck, revision tags, autoscaling floor (17.12-17.15). From here, the Appendices take over as pure reference material.

📎 Appendix A: Istio CRD Quick Reference

Every Istio CRD used anywhere in this guide, gathered into a single table — grouped not by name or chapter but by which of the five API groups owns it. Reach for this page when you remember what a CRD does but not its exact spec fields; every CRD listed here has a full working manifest ported in Appendix B.

📖 Key Term — Custom Resource Definition (CRD)

A CRD teaches the Kubernetes API a new object type. Istio ships roughly 15 of them across five API groups (networking, security, telemetry, extensions, install); istiod watches every one of them and turns each change into live Envoy configuration pushed over xDS.

CRDAPI GroupPurpose
VirtualServicenetworking.istio.ioTraffic routing rules (URI, headers, weight)
DestinationRulenetworking.istio.ioPolicies: LB, subsets, circuit breaker, mTLS
Gatewaynetworking.istio.ioMesh ingress/egress entry point
ServiceEntrynetworking.istio.ioRegister external services in mesh
EnvoyFilternetworking.istio.ioLow-level Envoy config override
WorkloadEntrynetworking.istio.ioRegister VM/external workload
WorkloadGroupnetworking.istio.ioReusable VM onboarding template (metadata/template/probe) — WorkloadEntry is to a VM what a Pod is to a container; WorkloadGroup is the Deployment that stamps them out
PeerAuthenticationsecurity.istio.iomTLS mode (PERMISSIVE/STRICT/DISABLE)
RequestAuthenticationsecurity.istio.ioJWT validation at mesh level
AuthorizationPolicysecurity.istio.ioAccess control (ALLOW/DENY)
Telemetrytelemetry.istio.ioMetrics, tracing, logging config
Sidecarnetworking.istio.ioSidecar proxy scope/config
ProxyConfignetworking.istio.ioPer-workload proxy configuration

🔢 API-Version Reference (Istio 1.22+)

The table above doesn't show apiVersion — the first line of every manifest. This adds two CRDs the table above doesn't cover (WasmPlugin, IstioOperator) and tells you which apiVersion to type today:

apiVersionCRD(s)Status
networking.istio.io/v1VirtualService, DestinationRule, Gateway, ServiceEntry, Sidecar, WorkloadEntry, WorkloadGroupStable
networking.istio.io/v1beta1ProxyConfigNot yet graduated
security.istio.io/v1PeerAuthentication, RequestAuthentication, AuthorizationPolicyStable
telemetry.istio.io/v1TelemetryStable
extensions.istio.io/v1alpha1WasmPluginAlpha
networking.istio.io/v1alpha3EnvoyFilterAlpha
install.istio.io/v1alpha1IstioOperatorInstallation API

Older v1alpha3/v1beta1 manifests — including the ones ported verbatim in Appendix B — still apply cleanly. v1 is the same schema promoted to stable, not a breaking change.

📎 Appendix B: Complete anihpj Istio YAML Manifests

This is the capstone reference for the whole guide — the anihpj manifests behind its most-used CRDs, rendered here in full, working order, so you never have to reconstruct a YAML from a table cell. Copy it, adapt the names, apply it. B.1–B.3 stand the application up (namespace, image, Deployment/Service); B.4–B.7 wire the traffic layer (Gateway, routing, canary, load balancing); B.8–B.10 lock down security (mTLS, deny-all, allow-rules); and B.11–B.13 cover egress and observability (external services, JWT, telemetry).

B.1 Namespace with istio-injection Label

yaml — Namespace with Istio injection enabled 

apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  labels:
    istio-injection: enabled    # ← KEY: enables auto sidecar injection
    environment: production
---
# Verify:
# kubectl get namespace anihpj --show-labels
# NAME      STATUS   LABELS
# anihpj    Active   istio-injection=enabled,environment=prod

B.2 Dockerfiles for All anihpj Services

dockerfile — anihpj/jobpost/Dockerfile 

FROM python:3.11-slim
WORKDIR /app

# Install dependencies (Docker layer cache optimization)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy application code
COPY . .
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# Health check (required for K8s liveness probe)
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=10s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health/ || exit 1

EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000",
     "--workers", "4", "--timeout", "120",
     "anihpj.wsgi:application"]

# Build: docker build -t anihpj/jobpost-api:v1 .
# Push:  docker push anihpj/jobpost-api:v1

B.3 Deployments + Services (Istio Labels)

yaml — Deployment + Service for jobpost-api 

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
      version: v1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: jobpost-api      # ← REQUIRED for Istio/Kiali
        version: v1           # ← REQUIRED for canary subsets
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: jobpost
        image: anihpj/jobpost-api:v1
        ports:
        - name: http          # ← REQUIRED: Istio uses port name
          containerPort: 8000
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health/
            port: 8000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api           # ← VirtualService references this
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: jobpost-api          # ← matches Deployment label
  ports:
  - name: http                # ← MUST be "http"
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8000
📖 Docker Image Flow — From Code to Kubernetes Pod
1
Django Code

anihpj/jobpost/views.py

2
Docker Build

docker build -t anihpj/jobpost-api:v1 .

3
Push to Registry

docker push → Docker Hub / ECR

4
kubectl apply

K8s pulls image → creates Pod

5
Webhook Fires

Adds istio-proxy + istio-init containers

2/2

kubectl get pods → 2/2 READY

B.4-B.13 — Gateway, VirtualService, DestinationRule, PeerAuthentication, AuthorizationPolicy, ServiceEntry, RequestAuthentication, and Telemetry are covered in detail within their respective chapters.

B.4 Istio Gateway for anihpj.example.com

yaml — anihpj-gateway.yaml 

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: anihpj-gateway
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    istio: ingressgateway
  servers:
  - port:
      number: 80
      name: http
      protocol: HTTP
    hosts:
    - "anihpj.example.com"
  - port:
      number: 443
      name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
    tls:
      mode: SIMPLE
      credentialName: anihpj-tls-cert
    hosts:
    - "anihpj.example.com"

B.5 VirtualService — Path-Based Routing

yaml — path-based routing for all services 

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: anihpj-routes
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  gateways:
  - anihpj-gateway
  hosts:
  - "anihpj.example.com"
  http:
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /jobs/
    route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /users/
    route:
    - destination:
        host: user-service
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /skills/
    route:
    - destination:
        host: skills-service
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api

B.6 VirtualService — Canary (90/10 Split)

yaml — canary deployment for jobpost-api 

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-vs
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - jobpost-api
  http:
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v1
      weight: 90
    - destination:
        host: jobpost-api
        subset: v2
      weight: 10

B.7 DestinationRule — Subsets, LB, Circuit Breaker

yaml — DestinationRule for jobpost-api 

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: jobpost-api-dr
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  host: jobpost-api
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      simple: LEAST_CONN
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 100
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 50
    outlierDetection:
      consecutiveGatewayErrors: 5
      interval: 30s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50
    tls:
      mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2

B.8 PeerAuthentication — STRICT mTLS

yaml — PeerAuthentication for anihpj 

apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT

B.9 AuthorizationPolicy — Deny-All Baseline

yaml — deny-all policy 

apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-all
  namespace: anihpj
spec: {}

B.10 AuthorizationPolicy — Allow Rules

yaml — allow ingress → jobpost + jobpost → users 

# Allow ingress → jobpost-api (GET/POST)
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-ingress-to-jobpost
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: jobpost-api
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals:
        - "cluster.local/ns/istio-system/sa/istio-ingressgateway"
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET", "POST"]
---
# Allow jobpost-api → user-service (GET only)
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-jobpost-to-users
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: user-service
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        principals:
        - "cluster.local/ns/anihpj/sa/jobpost-api"
    to:
    - operation:
        methods: ["GET"]
        paths: ["/api/users/*"]

B.11 ServiceEntry — External Payment API

yaml — ServiceEntry for Stripe 

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: stripe-payments
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  hosts:
  - api.stripe.com
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS

B.12 RequestAuthentication — JWT Validation

yaml — JWT validation for API endpoints 

apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: RequestAuthentication
metadata:
  name: jwt-auth
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  jwtRules:
  - issuer: "auth-service.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
    jwksUri: "http://auth-service/.well-known/jwks.json"

B.13 Telemetry — Sampling + Metrics Labels

yaml — Telemetry resource 

apiVersion: telemetry.istio.io/v1
kind: Telemetry
metadata:
  name: anihpj-telemetry
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  tracing:
  - randomSamplingPercentage: 1.0
  metrics:
  - providers:
    - name: prometheus
    overrides:
    - match:
        metric: REQUEST_COUNT
      tagOverrides:
        job_category:
          value: request.headers["x-job-category"]
Apply Order — how B.1–B.13 fit together
B.1 namespace → B.2 images → B.3 deploy+svc        (app up, 2/2 containers)
     │
     ▼  traffic layer
B.4 Gateway → B.5 routes → B.7 DR subsets → B.6 canary 90/10
                 (apply the DestinationRule BEFORE the canary VirtualService —
                  a VS that names a missing subset returns 503)
     │
     ▼  security layer
B.8 STRICT mTLS → B.9 deny-all → B.10 allow pairs → B.12 JWT
     │
     ▼  egress + observability
B.11 ServiceEntry (Stripe) → B.13 Telemetry (1% sampling)

The 13 manifests above don't need to land in numeric order — they need to land in this dependency order. First bring the application itself up (B.1 namespace, B.2 image, B.3 Deployment/Service) until kubectl get pods shows 2/2. Then build the traffic layer: a Gateway (B.4) and route rules (B.5) before touching subsets, and — critically — the DestinationRule's subsets (B.7) BEFORE the canary VirtualService (B.6), since a VirtualService that references a subset the DestinationRule hasn't defined yet returns a 503. Only once traffic flows correctly do you tighten security: STRICT mTLS (B.8) first, then a deny-all baseline (B.9), then the specific allow pairs that let the mesh talk to itself again (B.10), then JWT validation (B.12) on top. Egress and observability — the Stripe ServiceEntry (B.11) and the Telemetry sampling config (B.13) — are independent of the other three layers and can be applied whenever needed.

⚠️ Exam Trap — Commands That No Longer Exist

Old tutorials — and some stale exam-prep material — still reference istioctl authn tls-check. That command was removed from istioctl years ago and does not exist on a current cluster; running it on the exam just burns minutes on an "unknown command" error. Learn the modern replacements below.

🗑️ REMOVED / RENAMED COMMANDS — do not use on the exam

StatusCommandUse Instead
🔴 GONEistioctl authn tls-check <pod> -n <ns>Removed years ago — use istioctl x describe pod <pod> -n <ns> (effective mTLS) or istioctl proxy-config secret <pod> -n <ns> (live certs), or check Kiali's graph lock icons / openssl s_client against the pod's port
🔴 GONEistioctl register / istioctl deregisterRemoved — use WorkloadEntry + WorkloadGroup CRDs for VM workloads
🟡 MOVEDistioctl experimental <cmd>Renamed to istioctl x <cmd> — "x" is the alias; some x commands later graduate to top level
🟠 RISKYistioctl upgrade (in-place)Still exists, but prefer the canary upgrade: install a new revision, relabel namespaces with istio.io/rev, restart workloads, then uninstall the old revision
🟡 DEPRECATEDistioctl verify-installSuperseded by istioctl x precheck (pre-install check) and istioctl analyze -n <ns> (post-install check)
💡 ICA Exam Tip

The 3 most important istioctl commands for the exam: istioctl analyze -n <ns> (validate config), istioctl proxy-status (check sync), istioctl proxy-config cluster <pod> -n <ns> (inspect Envoy). Know these by heart — and remember istioctl authn tls-check is a trap, not a real command.

📎 Appendix D: Common Istio Errors & Solutions

Something in the mesh just broke. This is the triage page: symptom in, likely cause and fix out — reach for this before re-reading a whole chapter, then go back to the chapter covering the matching CRD or component only if you need the underlying "why."

Error / SymptomLikely CauseFix
Pod shows 1/1 not 2/2Sidecar not injectedLabel ns: istio-injection=enabled
503 RBAC: access deniedAuthorizationPolicy blockingAdd explicit ALLOW policy
503 upstream connect errorDR mTLS mode mismatchMatch PeerAuthentication mode
VS not routingSubset not in DestinationRuleAdd matching subset to DR
Traffic to all podsMissing version labelAdd version label to Deployment
analyze: "host not found"Service name mismatch in VSMatch VS host to K8s svc name
High latency after installTracing 100% sampling overheadSet sampling to 1% in Telemetry
Circuit breaker trips oftenoutlierDetection too aggressiveIncrease consecutiveGatewayErrors
External APIs failingREGISTRY_ONLY mode activeAdd ServiceEntry for external host
PROXY_STATUS: STALENetwork issue to istiodCheck istiod pod health, port 15012

🪜 FIRST-RESPONSE DIAGNOSTIC LADDER — run these in this order

  1. istioctl analyze -n <ns> → config errors?
  2. istioctl proxy-status → SYNCED or STALE?
  3. kubectl get pods -n <ns> → 2/2 READY?
  4. istioctl x describe pod <pod> → which policies apply?
  5. istioctl proxy-config endpoint <pod> → endpoints exist?
  6. kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy → check Envoy access-log response-flag codes

🚩 ENVOY RESPONSE-FLAG DECODER — the code after the status in the access log

FlagMeaningCheck This First
UHNo healthy upstream hosts (0 Ready endpoints)readinessProbe; proxy-config endpoint <pod>
UCUpstream connection terminated (reset) — not UH!mTLS mode mismatch / app crash
UFUpstream connection failed to establish (refused, not just reset)Is the upstream even listening on that port? App crash-looped or never started
UOUpstream overflow — circuit breaker trippedoutlierDetection / connectionPool settings
NRNo route configured for the requestVirtualService host + route match
DCDownstream connection terminated by the clientclient / LB idle timeout

📎 Appendix E: Istio Terminology Glossary

Every chapter defines its terms the first time they appear; this appendix is the single landing page for all of them, alphabetized, for the moment a term resurfaces three chapters later and you want the definition without hunting for where it first appeared.

TermDefinition
ADSAggregated Discovery Service — one ordered xDS stream
Ambient MeshSidecar-free Istio mode using ztunnel (L4) + waypoint proxies (L7)
AuthorizationPolicyIstio CRD for access control — defines WHO can call WHAT
Canary UpgradeRun old + new istiod side by side; move namespaces via revision
Circuit BreakerPattern: stop sending requests to a failing service automatically, to prevent cascading failures
Citadelistiod's built-in CA — signs and rotates workload certificates
Control Planeistiod — manages configuration, certificates, and policies for all proxies
CRDCustom Resource Definition — extends the Kubernetes API with Istio resources
Data PlaneEnvoy sidecars, or ztunnel proxies in ambient mode, that handle actual service-to-service traffic
Delta xDSxDS mode sending only changed resources; default since Istio 1.22
DestinationRuleDefines policies for traffic going TO a service: LB, subsets, circuit breaker, mTLS
Dry-runAnnotation istio.io/dry-run — test a policy without enforcing it
East-West GatewayGateway for cross-cluster traffic in a multi-cluster mesh
Egress GatewayDedicated exit proxy — force outbound traffic through one point
EnvoyHigh-performance L7 proxy; Istio's sidecar proxy handling all mesh traffic
exportToField scoping which namespaces can see a VirtualService/DestinationRule/ServiceEntry
extensionProviderMeshConfig entry naming a tracing/logging/authz backend
Fault InjectionDeliberately inject delays/errors to test system resilience
Gateway (Istio)Entry/exit point to the mesh for external traffic (ingress + egress)
HBONEHTTP-Based Overlay Network Environment — the ambient mesh tunnel protocol
istioctlIstio CLI tool — like kubectl but for Istio operations
istiodIstio control plane daemon — Pilot + Citadel + Galley combined into one pod
IstioOperatorInstall-time API: profiles + component overrides (IOP)
JaegerDistributed tracing backend; visualizes request traces as Gantt-style spans
KialiIstio mesh visualization console — service graph, validation, YAML wizards
Locality Load BalancingPrefer same-zone pods; failover requires outlierDetection
mTLSMutual TLS — both client and server verify each other's certificates
Mutating WebhookK8s admission hook istiod uses to inject the sidecar
Outlier DetectionDestinationRule setting that implements circuit breaking by ejecting failing hosts
PeerAuthenticationIstio CRD that configures mTLS mode (PERMISSIVE/STRICT/DISABLE)
Pilotistiod component: reads CRDs, translates to Envoy config via the xDS API
RED MetricsRate, Errors, Duration — Istio auto-collects these from every Envoy proxy
RequestAuthenticationIstio CRD for JWT token validation at the mesh level
RevisionNamed istiod install (e.g. 1-22) targeted by istio.io/rev
Secure NamingMaps service identity → service name; stops impersonation
Service MeshInfrastructure layer that manages service-to-service communication
ServiceEntryIstio CRD to register external services (Stripe, SendGrid, S3) in the mesh
Sidecar (container)Envoy proxy container injected alongside your application container
Sidecar (resource)Istio CRD to configure sidecar proxy scope
SPIFFESecure Production Identity Framework — certificate standard used by Istio
SVIDSPIFFE Verifiable Identity Document — workload X.509 certificate
TelemetryIstio CRD for configuring metrics, tracing, and logging collection
Trust DomainIdentity root of a mesh (default cluster.local)
VirtualServiceIstio CRD defining routing rules: URI match, weight split, retries, timeouts
WasmPluginCRD (extensions.istio.io) — run Wasm modules in the proxy
Waypoint ProxyAmbient mesh L7 proxy per namespace — optional, replaces sidecar L7 features
xDS APIProtocol used by istiod to dynamically configure all Envoy proxies
ztunnelAmbient mesh L4 proxy per Node; handles mTLS without per-pod sidecars

Reading alone will not pass the ICA — each fortnight pairs the chapters above with hands-on labs against the anihpj cluster, and every checklist item names the proof that it worked. 📎 Appendix G: Local Development Quick Start (Minikube + Istio + anihpj)

Every hands-on drill in this guide assumes a live anihpj mesh already exists somewhere. This appendix is that somewhere — the exact command sequence from an empty minikube VM to a running, sidecar-injected anihpj, so no chapter's drill ever blocks on "but how do I even get a cluster."

bash — From zero to Istio mesh in 11 steps 

# 1. Start minikube with enough resources for Istio + anihpj
minikube start --cpus=4 --memory=16384 --disk-size=40g

# 2a. Install Istio (demo profile = istiod + ingress + egress ONLY, 3 pods)
curl -L https://istio.io/downloadIstio | sh -
cd istio-1.22.*
export PATH=$PWD/bin:$PATH
istioctl install --set profile=demo -y

# 2b. Addons are a SEPARATE apply — no profile bundles them (see 4.3)
kubectl apply -f samples/addons/

# 3. Verify installation (7 pods Running, from 2a + 2b combined)
kubectl get pods -n istio-system
# Expected: istiod, istio-ingressgateway, istio-egressgateway,
#           kiali, grafana, prometheus, jaeger

# 4. Create and label anihpj namespace
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label namespace anihpj istio-injection=enabled

# 5. Build Docker images (see Appendix B.2 for Dockerfiles)
docker build -t anihpj/jobpost-api:v1 ./anihpj/jobpost/
docker build -t anihpj/user-service:v1 ./anihpj/user-service/
# ... repeat for all services

# 6. Load images into minikube (skip if using a remote registry)
minikube image load anihpj/jobpost-api:v1
minikube image load anihpj/user-service:v1

# 7. Deploy anihpj services (see Appendix B.3 for YAML)
kubectl apply -f anihpj/k8s/ -n anihpj

# 8. Verify pods have sidecars (2/2 containers)
kubectl get pods -n anihpj
# Expected: jobpost-api-xxx  2/2  Running

# 9. Verify Istio sync status
istioctl proxy-status
# Expected: ALL pods show SYNCED

# 10. Validate config (0 errors expected)
istioctl analyze -n anihpj

# 11. Open dashboards
istioctl dashboard kiali      # Service topology graph
istioctl dashboard grafana    # RED metrics dashboards
istioctl dashboard jaeger     # Distributed traces

# BONUS: Generate some traffic to see in dashboards
kubectl port-forward svc/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system 8080:80
for i in {1..100}; do curl http://localhost:8080/jobs/; done
# Now refresh Kiali — you'll see live traffic!

🔁 Local Dev Workflow — daily routine for anihpj development with Istio

  1. kubectl get pods -n anihpj — All 2/2?
  2. istioctl proxy-status — All SYNCED?
  3. istioctl dashboard kiali — Open topology
  4. kubectl apply -f canary-vs.yaml — Deploy canary
  5. Watch Kiali as traffic splits — monitor live
  6. istioctl dashboard grafana — Check RED metrics
  7. istioctl analyze -n anihpj — Validate config
  8. kubectl logs deploy/jobpost-api -c istio-proxy — Debug the proxy
📖 Key Term — minikube tunnel

Minikube is the quickest personal Istio lab, but it has sharp edges that cost newcomers hours — the five gotchas below explain almost every "Istio is broken on my laptop" report. minikube tunnel is a helper process that routes real traffic from your host into LoadBalancer Services, so istio-ingressgateway gets an EXTERNAL-IP instead of <pending>.

⚠️ Minikube Gotchas — the five traps that break local Istio labs

⚠️
Gotcha 1 — Memory Too Low → istiod Stuck Pending

Symptom: kubectl get pods -n istio-system → istiod 0/1 Pending
Cause: minikube's default 2GB VM cannot fit istiod + addons
Fix: minikube delete, then restart with more resources:
minikube start --cpus=4 --memory=16384

🐳
Gotcha 2 — ErrImagePull for anihpj/jobpost-api:v1

minikube's Docker daemon is NOT your host's — pick ONE fix:
a) eval $(minikube docker-env) — build INSIDE minikube's Docker: docker build -t anihpj/jobpost-api:v1 .
b) minikube image load anihpj/jobpost-api:v1 — copy from host
Either way set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent (Always forces a pull)

🌐
Gotcha 3 — EXTERNAL-IP Stuck <pending> on istio-ingressgateway

minikube has no cloud LoadBalancer — open a second terminal:
minikube tunnel — keeps running; asks for sudo/admin
kubectl get svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system
→ EXTERNAL-IP now shows a real address you can curl

🔀
Gotcha 4 — Tunnel Process Annoying? Use MetalLB Instead

minikube addons enable metallb
minikube addons configure metallb — then give a small IP range
e.g. 192.168.49.100-192.168.49.110 (inside the minikube IP subnet)
→ LoadBalancer Services get stable IPs, no tunnel process needed

🔐
Gotcha 5 — Pods Stuck Pending Under Restricted PSA/PSS

Symptom: istio-init container denied — NET_ADMIN/NET_RAW
Cause: namespace has restricted Pod Security Admission (PSA)
Fix: use the Istio CNI plugin instead of init-container injection (no NET_ADMIN needed in the app namespace):
istioctl install --set profile=demo --set components.cni.enabled=true -y
→ CNI plugin runs iptables setup at node level — no per-pod NET_ADMIN/NET_RAW required, so PSA restricted mode is fine

istioctl authn tls-check <pod> -n <ns> was removed from istioctl years ago — ignore old guides that still use it. Modern replacement: istioctl x describe pod <pod> -n <ns> (effective mTLS) or istioctl proxy-config secret <pod> -n <ns> (live certs), plus Kiali's graph lock icons or openssl s_client against the pod's port. 🧭 Istio CRD Selection Guide — which resource solves which problem

I want to...Use this Istio resource

Add retry logicVirtualService (retries)
Add a timeoutVirtualService (timeout)
Inject faults for testing / test resilienceVirtualService (fault)
Load balance requestsDestinationRule (loadBalancer)
Add a circuit breaker / stop cascade failuresDestinationRule (outlierDetection)
Encrypt service-to-service trafficPeerAuthentication (STRICT)
Block a service from calling anotherAuthorizationPolicy (DENY)
Validate JWT tokensRequestAuthentication
Call an external APIServiceEntry
Audit all egress trafficServiceEntry + EgressGateway
Add non-K8s workloads to the meshWorkloadEntry
See service topologyKiali dashboard
See request tracesJaeger (istioctl dashboard jaeger)
See latency / error metricsGrafana Istio dashboards
Control resource usageSidecar (resource) + EnvoyFilter
Run the mesh with no sidecars (ztunnel handles L4 + mTLS)Ambient mode: label namespace istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient
Add L7 policy in ambient modeWaypoint proxy per namespace (istioctl waypoint apply -n anihpj)
Extend Envoy with custom codeWasmPlugin (extensions.istio.io/v1alpha1)

sidecar.istio.io/proxyCPUOverride sidecar CPU request (also proxyMemory)
traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeOutboundPortsComma list of outbound ports to skip capture
traffic.sidecar.istio.io/includeInboundPortsOnly these inbound ports get intercepted
istio.io/rev (ns/pod label)Pin injection to one control-plane revision
